I'm very pleased with this game.  I bought it on sale for $4 and was a little skeptical about it specifically because it looked like the kind of game I would probably enjoy a lot (I was afraid I would be pumping it up just to be let down).  I'm very glad I was wrong and I can easily say that this game is worth full price.
A few bits of personal preference to start off with; I personally prefer to have the color saturation turned up in the game.  There's two modes that you play in, one is in the light and the other is in the dark.  The dark provides plenty of the gray color palette to satisfy any inclination for having it feel gloomy.  The game itself does a good job of setting that mood even without having the colors being washed out.  I also made the darks less dark and the lights less light, just so I could feel comfortable being able to see everything there was to see.  The second personal preference is to NOT turn up the difficulty in the game.  The default difficulty is satisfying enough for me.  For players who might get frustrated enough to put the game down, I would suggest setting the difficulty to 'less deadly' right from the start.  The weapons are 17th century weapons and as such are slow and feel a bit cumbersome (although not at all as inaccurate as I was expecting).  You're going up against supernatural beings who are every bit as deadly as you are and if you die, they all respawn (in new spots -except inside strongholds) and you'll just have to find them and kill them again.  Avoiding them is very difficult and once they spot you, they'll chase you all the way back to camp if you're not able to take them down.
The visual style of the game is excellent.  The sense of walking around in the woods is truly convincing and immersive. When the wind picks up to make all the vegetation move, it's nothing less than breathtaking.  I go hiking on a regular basis and this game comes as close as any game has ever come to replicating that experience.
Navigating through the game and the story can seem a little confusing at first but it's actually very simple.  You basically use two things to tell you what to do.  Early in the game, you'll get a map and you'll get special senses.  Basically, all you have to do is turn on all of your map markers and go to the site of each one.  In addition to that, just keep using your special hearing skill (x-key by default) and follow the sounds to lead you where to go.  That's it.
The game is pretty scary to me in a fun ghost story kind of way and it would make a great game to buy and play around Halloween, although there's certainly no need to wait for the next Halloween to come around.  If you have a system that lets you set all the eye candy to maximum, it's worthwhile to do so but the game is well designed, with a sense of peril and accomplishment that really satisfies.  I haven't finished the story yet so I'll update the review once I make my way through the whole game.
Edit:
Ok [I think] I've finished the game although it seems a little strange that it doesn't have any credits available, but I guess that's because it was a small team.  Anyway, here are some pros and cons.
Pros:
-Great overall story which is worth sticking around to see where it leads.
-Great presentation.  Sort a combination of light versions of Skyrim, Far Cry 3, and Blair Witch Project.
-Just about the right length considering how repetitive it starts to feel at the end.
Cons:
-Lots of structures but not a single one is open to you to take a look inside.  It's all bunch of external shells and doors that won't open -basically just scenery.  Considering it's a period piece, it would have been nice to get a closer glimpse into what the daily lives of these people might have been like.  Maybe the sequel (?) will include this.
-No voice acting.  I know this is unfair considering that it's an independent game with a low budget and also that it's available in multiple languages.  Nevertheless, maybe this game will be so successful that they'll be able to have a few more bells and whistles next time around.  Having said that, I'd very much prefer to have it be all text than to have any bad acting so there's that.

From my past experience with Bioshock from the ps3 i didnt much care for the game. Since i saw it was on sale with all the dlc thanks to the HD collection i thought of giving it another try. To see if my opinons of the game has changed. I will be looking at the game in a pro/ con style and ending the review with my final conculsion.
Pro:
The game looks amazing. The graphics certainly look better than what i experienced back on the ps3. As for how does it compare to the Bioshock original game on steam...i dont know. I probably wont ever touch it since it is the same game and i have no need to play the original copy.
The story is great. I was getting really into the narrative of the story.

When you get sucked into the game then you get a little fright at some moments that were just odd and creepy....The flickering lights didnt help ease that tension.
Gameplay or better gun play was good. The guns felt like they did work. Though at times i do wish a headshot ment a headshot on enemies even if they had one of those plastic masks. A bullet should still be able to fly through plastic and in the the head. There was a nice variety of guns to use like a handgun, tompson, shotgun, .ect. Not to mention a few plasmids to spice up combat by setting your enemies on fire or shocking them in water.
Equipable items adds more depth to the gameplay. Besides combat the player can equip tonics to boost their defence, wrench damage, research bonus exp, or damage done to machines. One can mix and match tonics to fit their play style.
Music was ok. Cant say much about it since the game does not have much music...its a horror game, the lack of calming music or music at all helps build tension and fear.
The game has additional content which is very cool to look at. The first that i will be mentioning is that there is a museum of content that was scraped during development. So you can go and look at the enemy models that could have been in the game or the concept art of what the big daddy could of been. The big daddy art is really sick looking and definantly worth looking at. The other additional content was a video documentary of behind the scenes of the making of bioshock or commentaries by the developers of the game. I didnt really look at it but for those who do or just interested in these things you find these video documentaries scattered in the game. Just collect them and watch them now or later in the main menu. Finally there is dlc...i will talk about it real soon.
Con:
The dlc was short and just challenges. 3 challenges. They are not very fun to do and quite short. One mission is to fight all enemies in an arena style mission, another is using witts to turn the farris wheel to free the litter sister but you must use electricity to power up the switch and there are limited electrical equipment. I dont mind the using your witts to complete a challenge but its just boring and doesnt capture the strenght of the game.
Frame rate issues. Initially i had some really bad frame rate issues. My frames were at like 10fps. Then  i set the game to run a different GPU and it work well. I know many people have frame rate issues and that does really suck. Even when my frame rate is at like 60fps i did on rare moments where the game froze for like a second then continued. It was odd and kind of ruined the emersion sometimes but for the most part i overlooked it since the game was running at 60fps than 10fps.
Conclusion:
Bioshock HD or Bioshock Remasted is a great game for new commers to experience the bioshock world and gameplay but for a fan that played the game before you may not want to buy another copy of bioshock that is said to have better graphics. It would be a nice walk down memory lane though. For me it was an experience since after my first playthrough of bioshock on the ps3 i hated that game and pretty much the entires series other than infinite. I will review that game another time. I've had great fun playing this game, despite not being a fan of stealth games or open-world games with item-hunting being a major aspect of gameplay. The game has a great atmosphere, especially with its nice touches, such as realistic wind effects, and the ability to change the colour saturation when playing.
At first it appears as though the game has no story. You arrive in a wooded area with scattered forts and military outposts. Everyone aside from one NPC are dead and it's your job to find out what happened to this place. As you travel from one open area to another, you find clues and remains of the conflict. In each area you are able to traverse between the normal world and the dark world. In the dark world you are able to communicate with the spirits of the dead, hearing out their side of the story, and eventually putting together the clues that tell you how they died and why.
In each area, there is a variety of enemies you encounter, each of which poses a threat, especially when they come in groups. This means you often have to approach them with strategy and stealth, because most weapons are either not that powerful or take a while to reload. It kind of felt like Dark Souls but in 1st person - dangerous enemies, dying takes you back to a safe place with all enemies in the area revived, and most of the story told through clues in the environment.
I generally enjoyed the game and found myself very immersed, but there were a few minor drawbacks. For example, it started to feel like it was dragging on a bit in the latter stages since the gameplay did not change much between each area. I also found exploring the dark world to be a bit tedious because the environments were being bland. I think it could've been made a bit prettier with some more detail in the environments. Just because it's meant to be grey and dark does not mean it has to feel empty. There were also very minor gripes, like some wearable charms having useless bonuses, like having a 4% chance of being harder to spot (why equip that when I can equip charms that increase my melee damage by 50 or even 100%).
In general, this is a solid game. If you're into games with an open-world feel and lots of things to collect, and story being subtle, you should enjoy it. If you're not into those things, you might, just like me, enjoy it still.

I had just finished playing through Skyrim, a one-and-done game, and was looking for something completely different. Small scope, not fantasy, but a better role-playing experience. Because face it: trying to role play in Skyrim is just silly. What I found in Rebel Galaxy was a refreshing change of pace with no commitments.
Starting out it really reminded me of Privateer crossed with Earth & Beyond. Loved the former and wanted to love the latter. I tried to role play (I wanted to be a bloodthirsty pirate) but the pirates weren't welcoming and money was tight so I went with Merchant and Mercenary after my first save game corrupted. For a little while I tried to get into the "events" and trading but the simple math of the game finally proved itself out. Upgrade, upgrade, upgrade. Kill, kill, kill. Mission, mission, mission. Click through the conversation trees because nothing they're saying matters a bit. Oh, final mission done.
The music is really good at first - setting your mind in the "Firefly" wild west mentality. Then it gets a little repetitive. Rather like the same 6-8 talking heads. I never got bored enough to switch to custom music and I did find myself humming some of the tunes at work.
For a few hours the non-combat mechanics are worth exploring. Mine some asteroids. Jump from station to station moving commodities. Shop the mercenaries. Experience the array of 6-8 mission types. It didn't take long to get a handle on deciding what's worth it in risk vs. reward - factoring in time, of course. These mechanics quickly lose relevance.
Combat mechanics are pretty simple. Load your ship with the best turrets you can (in a variety that suits you), a broadside that you can maneuver well enough to bring to bear, and over-level your shields and hull first. Roll into the fight and sweep them if you can. Run away if you can't.
One small gripe is the extremely shallow pool that is the ship customization. The hull I was in never really seemed special (it's just ports, turrets, and cargo space). And I felt just as effective in my tier-6 armed Destroyer as I was in my tier-6 armed Dreadnaught. But, with the system as simple as it was, I enjoyed not needing a spreadsheet or helper tool to deck out my ride.
And my big gripe that kills this game for replayability: no choices. I ran a straight line from beginning to end with some grinding (a lot, really, in the early game). No impact. No changes. The galaxy just rolls along without the events making any real impact or change. The story is alright but predictable. I was relieved when I saw the end of it.

Unfortunately, the missions become extremely repetative, and the alternatives (such as mining) do not help you accomplish your end-game goals. Speaking of combat: While it neglects the third axis of movement and newtonian physics, it does 'borrow' broadside firing from some of the more well known naval combat games.

This is not the Outlaw Star game I've always wanted, but its the closest I've played so far. Considering how almost synonymous the names are, I wonder if that's what they were going for.
Rebel Galaxy is an addictive and light space sim. It has all the usual trappings of a space sim (bounty hunting, mercenary work, trading and exploration) but everything is simplified enough so you won't need to find a guide on how to pilot your ship or complete a job. If that sounds like a bad thing, go play Elite: Dangerous. I like how the system map keeps track of what space stations buy/sell. It doesn't feel cheap since it only updates when you visit the station and its way more useful than getting some dumb colored lines painted all over the universe. If you like dumb colored lines all over the universe, go play Elite: Dangerous (I like Elite: Dangerous but I use third party websites whenever I go space trucking, the in-game trading info sucks).
Three things Rebel Galaxy has over most space sims are big ships, a customizable soundtrack, and a story. The game is all about piloting big tanky frigates and dreadnoughts. There's no option to pilot small fighter craft, but you can hire one to escort you. Piloting the ships is more like piloting a boat. You move on a flat plane and will be focused on firing your broadside cannons during combat. If you liked the ship combat in Assassin's Creed: Black Flag or Sid Meier's Pirates!, this is very much the same. I think its a missed oppurtunity that your ships are fully automated. You are the only crew member. A crew management metagame could have been cool and opened the game up for more unique characters. Being able to have a hanger that can deploy fighters would've been cool too. I'll give the devs the benefit of a doubt that they had these ideas, but scrapped them for budget or time reasons.
The soundtrack is a cool mix of Blues and Rock music. Quite a few of the tracks even have vocals. The best part about it is you can replace or add to the soundtrack with your own music. It also lets you designate which songs should be played during combat, station visits, idling, etc. You are playing a lesser version of Rebel Galaxy if you don't include the soundtrack from your favorite space adventure anime in the set list (The Blue Submarine No. 6 OST is also encouraged). If you don't have a favorite space adventure anime, go play Elite: Dangerous
.
Rebel Galaxy has a story. It's just OK and it's there. That's more than I can say for a lot of space sims. In Rebel Galaxy, your Aunt gives you a strange device which turns out to be a sentient AI which guides you across the universe to search for things that will let it do a cool thing that everyone else wants. There are also ugly badger people who want to kill you. In Outlaw Star, the dad gives the protagonist PTSD and he inherits a sentient android who guides him across the galaxy to find a planet that will let her do a cool thing that everyone else wants. There are also sexy cat people who want to kill them.
See? They're different. Now that I think about it, Rebel Galaxy has a severe lack of sexy aliens. I probably shouldn't recommend it but whatever, it's fun.

If there's one complaint, it's that the beginning and ending are a bit poor, for different reasons. It takes too long to get started, it takes too little to end. But everything in the middle, the 85% of the experience? Just an absolute joy.

I found this game really beautiful and gripping. It shows us the true horrors of war and what people have to go through during these times. The game is also quite hard and requires a lot of planning and patience.
The Good Things:
-Non-Linear Storyline. There are many different stories to pick (After you finish the first one) and many different scenarios to witness in the many different places you can visit. If you are angered by a soldier who is going to♥♥♥♥♥♥a woman you can change it's outcome!, If you are worried about some kids with a sick mother who is about to die you can change her fate! The survivors reveal their story over time and comment on actions of other survivors.
-Realistic Combat. Except for the bullets and stealth, the combat is very realistic. Players don't have more health over enemies (Unless you're playing as Boris or Roman), and killing is not always the option because some enemies will surrender.
-Realistic Simulation.
There is no Easy, Normal, or Hard, there is only Realism. When the tempertures drop, people can get sick. When crime is on the rise, the group will suffer a lot of raids. When survivors are depressed, the group falls apart.
-Different ways to play.
Players don't always have to steal food. They could trade for it or even grow their own. Players don't always have to use stealth kill enemies, with enough bullets and body armor they could rush in and shoot everyone.
-Beautiful Graphics.
The graphics perfectly captures a war zone and contributes alot to the atmosphere. By the looks of it
the game seems to take place around eastern europe during the 1990s.
-Shows us what war really is.
This game is a big ♥♥♥♥ you to people who support wars or even play the so called "Game of the Year" Call of Duty or similar. It shows us that the Military will do anything for "Glory" and will abuse
their power for their own desires.
The Bad Things:
-You are only able to have one save. It autosaves after every night and it prevents you from making backups saves or restarting a day incase you make a mistake.
-Food is extremely scarce and limited. There are only 4 types of food: Vegetables, Raw Meat, Canned Food, and Cooked Meals. There is no existance of Rice, Fish, Bread, or other foods which are commonly found in many places. Some places, like the Military Outpost, Have a lot of food but not enough to keep a group of 4 well fed for a week.
--Water is kind of useless. Nobody drinks water, only Coffee and Alcohol. Water is only used for in making Moonshine, and Cooking Food.
My Score for this game is: 9/10. Many of the bad things were not that bad but some tweaks should be implemented. Overall the game is really great for an Indie game and it's worth your money!

That being said there are a few things that I find frustrating about this game and should be improved upon. Another thing is a lot of the time a connection to your opponent cannot seem to be made and you will get kicked back to the main menu. This is expecially frustrating as you will need to navigate through multiple menus and then select your deck once again which can get frustrating if you experience this connection issue more than 2 or 3 times in a row. The collection manager is also hard to navigate and look thru as you almost are required to have a mouse wheel to zoom in and look at your cards text in better detail. There are also a few glitches here are there in game that cause you to lose which can be a pain as you lose your ranks because of this.
All complaints aside, the game has some really awesome single player campains and amazing music and sound. Reccomended for first timers who havent ever played magic before as this game is a great teaching tool. I am LOVING this game.  Looks like I've about a hundred hours in, and I've barely begin to scratch the surface - but I've been having a heckuva lot of fun playing.  This is a deep, rich, immersive game.  I start it up and the hours happily fly by.
I'm gonna keep this short because given the choice I'd prefer to be actually playing the game.  I've only ever bothered to write one Steam review before, but I wanted to toss in my two cents on this game.  I don't know if you'll like it (evidently a good proportion of folks are still determined not to like it) - but I do know this game has given me what I've been searching for a long time.
I've been trying a bunch of space / sci-fi games - many of them great games - but to greater or lesser degrees I always felt something missing.  I finally figured out what it was.  It was what I loved most about good sci-fi: the sense of Wonder.  Well I've found it here in this game.
This is a richly imagined space game, with a bit of a high fantasy edge - places feel different and alive and beautiful.  I've apparently spent a hundred hours just flying around, exploring, admiring.  I've done some missions, I've done some fighting, I've made some credits, I've made some friends and some enemies - but mostly I've just been smiling a whole lot.
I've only seen the tip of the iceberg.  I haven't yet assembled a fleet, or even bought my first Capital ship; I haven't yet built an empire, any stations, or even my first trader; I haven't yet captured my first ship, or even fully pimped out my own.  I have yet to dip into the Teladi DLC, and have already pre-purchased the upcoming HoL DLC.  I see many many many more happy hours ahead.  I think I've finally found my Space Skyrim.
It must be disheartening for the Devs to see so much obstinate negativity; they had a vision and they've been working hard to keep polishing it (I'm on the 4.0 beta).  For my own part a big thank you to them, and their next X game will be an instant buy for me.
Anyhoo.  If the first hundred or so hours are anything to go by, this game is right among my few all time faves - don't know if you'd like it, but then I don't know if you like ice cream either.  Back to SPAAACE!

Despite all the negativity surrounding this game, I gave it a shot.. firstly because it looks very nice and modern, and secondly because Elite: Dangerous is a complete disapointment. I'm really glad I did because I enjoy it quite a bit. In fact, so many times I've said to myself "I wish Elite: Dangerous was THIS, but multiplayer." The game is so detailed, so rich and living. Ignore the X fanboys who are upset because X Rebirth is not a clone of X3, and ignore the reviews of the technical issues that apparetly were horrible on release. As of now at v3.6 it plays great. Good fps (45-60 on Ultra with GTX 770), loads of mods installed, no crashes. In fact, there is an OS X Alpha (alpha mind you) out right now and I was shocked to see it run perfectly smooth on medium settings on my 2015 Macbook Pro with integrated graphics only. Clearly there has been a LOT of work (and love) put into this game since it was released. You really should give it a shot if you like arcade-style flight controls and a *massive* world with so many things to be done within it.
All that said, please stay away from the story mode. Yeah, I know, that sounds stupid, but listen... it's not very good. You'll get missions with little to no info as to how to complete them. You're going to fly around at a loss thinking "wtf am I supposed to be doing?" and very quickly "man this game blows, uninstall". Please don't do that. Ignore that bit. From what I've read the story isn't all that compelling anyway. Instead, choose Free Play. You get a ship, a few credits, and off you go. Now you're just like Elite: Dangerous - you make your own way in the universe doing whatever you want. You'll be sort of overwhelmed at first, but Google some things. See what's out there in the X:R universe and decide what you want to do. Then go do it. It's a wonderful experience and like I said above, this is what I wish Elite: Dangerous would have been.
Still, there may be some people who will complain, rightfully so, that this is what the game should have been 2 years ago when it was released. And others who wanted another X3 game will never be happy with this one. But for new players on the fence over whether to try it or not, or those coming from E:D with disappointment deep in their hearts.. give it a shot. Trust me, when you fly over to the shipyard and build your first capital ship and then sit there watching the drones assemble it in the dock, it'll feel amazing. The first time you stumble across an abandoned ship in deep space and you send your crew on to it, fix it up, and then fricking drive it away, it'll feel amazing too.

Betrayer has proven to be a game worth picking up.
It's biggest selling point is it's beautiful graphical style, which really set the tone of the game.
It's story started out very strong, told through a series of non-voiced text boxes which really was a positive aspect as it stayed in line with the overall theme of the game and didn't ruin the immersion.  Without ruining the plot, the theme is that you arrive on land after a ship wreck.  You meet a girl, and shortly thereafter you are unraveling the secrets of what happened to the inhabitants of the island.  The story is overall told very well, however one of the big downsides is the last reveal.  It's meant to be vague, but also was thrown together almost as if it were an afterthought.  Despite this, the rest of the game and plot is worth getting through.
In terms of gameplay, one of my biggest gripes was in this department.  Some things were done fantastically, such as using environment to plan attacks, planning type of weapons for different enemies, and the fluidity between melee and ranged weapon use.   There was so much lost potential for what could have increased the immersion.  For example, all of the items can be found by using the map that you already have at the beginning of the game.  Most of the "quests" as you progress through the game require no thought - just simply find an item, bring it to a person, choose the only option to make you progress.  It reminded me a lot of Far Cry 3, which also for me lost it's appeal due to this idea of "run here, kill this, make waypoint, hand in item".  My suggestion to make this better?  If a sequel to Betrayer is made, I'd like to see something implemented such as in Condemned: Criminal Origins.  When you have to solve a mystery, you need to really engage the environment, piece together the clues, and figure out what happened.  Give the player choices with consequences, and allow it to have an effect on the plot.  Adding this aspect not only will help the player feel more like part of the story, but we can use our brains to take a break from the repetition.  It may also change the fate of certain characters and the overall ending if done right.
With all that said, I really hope the developers plan a sequel.  This game has a lot of potential, and the next plot can really be fleshed out on the next go with good script writing.  Cheers to Blackpowder for a very successful game.

I didn't know what to expect when I began Betrayer, but it was pretty good. While it's definitely focused on first person combat using bows and 17th century firearms, there's a large focus on exploration and figuring out what happened. It's straight forward and linear, as horror stories tend to be, but good, nontheless. One of the major draws is the desaturated graphics, which are adjustable from fully desaturated aside from red, and full saturation. You can adjust these as you please, which is pretty cool, although I will admit it's easier to pick out items and enemies when it's played in its default state (and it actually brings a horror aspect to bright daylight areas).
You go from map to map piecing together what happened, along with collecting weapons, charms, ammo and cash. There's a sneak mechanic to the game which works well, and isn't finicky. There's a melee attack, but aside from charms there's no variation there. Bows and tomahawks are reusable but not as strong as firearms initially, so a lot of the first half of the game you'll be balancing what weapons to use, etc. The maps are of a medium size aside from the tutorial map, and there's even fast travel and "return to last location" so you can hop back to town to pick up some stuff and go right back to where you were, which is nice and leads to more engaging gameplay over endless walking.
The game is about 8 or so hours long if you do everything, probably 10-12 if you go for all the achievements. The story is interesting though it'll require a lot of reading. It's definitely a more subtle kind of horror, which I think works a little better in the long run for a game like this. I'd say at $20, this is a decent buy, but I got it for $4 which is a huge steal for this.

This game... I LOVE and HATE this game!!! Its survival in a way most don't think about it: sure, fight the elements, fight the enemies-but wait, fight your own conscience? Yes. In this game, your biggest enemy is YOU: not in game you, REAL you.
This game, after the first time i played through ONE of the stories, had my nerves frayed SO badly, I NEVER wanted to touch it again... but at the same time, it captivated me so thoroughly that i REALLY wanted to play through the next story, and COULD NOT put it down! (although I did force myself to take breaks when I was obviously too nerve-fried to make objective decisions).
Its terrible in a way that it makes you FEEL! And OH how you'll feel the first time a Character dies, because it WILL happen at least once, but at the same time, its WONDERFUL because is captures you, it binds you to your characters as if you were there, you WANT to survive the war with a passion. But the Strongest feels of all, are the ones you'll have to face from other people.
Guys with guns and prisoners? Bad. Obviously that's not a hard moral choice. But... lets say you visit the little old cottage where an elderly couple lives... but just barely... they don't attack, as a matter of fact, they directly ASK if you're with the bandits, and BEG you not to take what little they have... but wait... they have bandages and medicine, and your favorite character is at home, severely wounded/sick and dieing? Sure, the couple don't need the building supplies or maybe gears you may come across... but... the old man begs you not to take his wives medication, she's not well... and they might not have enough food to last the winter, even if you DON'T take any of it... now what? Who's good? Bad? In a bad spot that you can choose wither or not to take advantage of? Or leave them alone? Or help in some cases?
Are the people who hoard their food and water bad? Or protecting their families safety? Are the people raiding your base doing so out of malice? Or desperation like you might have done the night before? or the one soon to come?
All in all, if you don't mind frayed nerves, and long nights, at the payout of GREAT satisfaction and peace of mind, then I BEG you, give this game a high priority: you wont regret it.

A beautiful game, but lacking a sense of purpose or motive. Sadly this makes it a rather disposable experience.
This is the game equivalent of someone saying "but why?" repeatedly. It demands the player determine the significance, purpose, and meaning of all of its components, and contributes nothing of its own. The author abjectly refuses to provide their own interpretation of any of the issues raised. While I appreciate that the point of free will as a topic is to allow the player to choose, I may just as well explore the concept by washing the dishes anti-clockwise rather than clockwise. If the author didn't wish to say anything specific and unique about free will then why does this game exist? The saddening conclusion I reached is that there is little reason for it to do so.
The humour falls flat when the game counter-productively demonstrates why the mechanics it is mocking are actually extremely useful and sensible. Without a suitable target to ridicule, it just becomes whining. The game is also overly reliant on the main character and narrator "arguing" with one another, which is mildly amusing at first, but tires out almost immediately. The narrator really tries his best, but without a conversation partner he eventually devolves into something reminiscent of chiding a pet - just frustrated and tired.
The philosophy is vapid, the humour is half-baked and meandering. Having a great voice and beautiful appearance cannot make up for lacking an opinion on anything and frankly being dull.

This is a very strange and dark game. A seemingly demented, all knowing artificial intelligence has 5 people trapped and is constantly torturing them for over 100 years. Each person has a different story as for why they are being tortured. These stories are where your gameplay is at.
First and foremost, this is an old school game. Which means it has old school difficulty such as trial and error and illogical steps. You
get yourself stuck where there is no way to complete the episode correctly, forcing you to start over. Luckily, the episodes are not too long.
I struggled to enjoy the game. It has a good story and great concept, but is frustrating. You must complete a lot of tasks in order or else you’ll appear to be stuck or not have a certain option available when talking or interacting with objects. Some of the things you must do, especially in the final ending episode are illogical. It really drags the story down and I had to unfortunately resort to using a walkthrough several times throughout the episodes and totally rely on it during the final episode.
The graphics and sound are good and get the creepy, depressed feel across well. Voice overs are ok and the amateur-ish voices add more to this game than another due to the subject matter.
The gameplay and interface are also pretty straightforward. Be aware, there is no “main menu”. When resuming a game you must load your game after AM talks.
+Great & unique story
+Dark atmosphere & themes
+Art style
+Unique environments
+Frustrating
+Dead ends
+Illogical steps
+Pixel hunting at times
I’m torn on whether to recommend this game, but I have to regretfully give it a thumbs down. The trial and error really kills the pace of the game. With such a great story and concept, I’m giving this a rather high score for something I wouldn’t recommend.

I was skeptical of Beyond Earth at first.  The hype was that it would be the long-awaited revival of the brilliant cult classic, Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri.  After what I'd heard about Beyond Earth mechanics, it sounded like the defining characteristics of the game had been passed over.  Social Engineering and Prototyping are nowhere to be found, shaping the very continents through terraforming and sea bases are missing.
But now, with a few additional playthroughs behind me, my perspective has changed.  Do NOT look at Beyond Earth as an Alpha Centauri remake.  Treat it as a stand-alone project.
I have heard this title described as 'Civ 5 in space' and I feel like it's a mildly misguided assessment.  The elements that tie Beyond Earth to Civilization V are simply the baseline elements that make a Civilization game.  As a veteran of Civilization games since 1991, I can confidently say that Beyond Earth stands as much apart from other releases as any other and you'll enjoy learning the new technology trees, units, buildings, and virtues (similar to the previous game's Social Policies) and bending them to your advantage.
For new players to Sid Meier games, this is a fun 4X title that may overwhelm you with choices at first, but in time you'll come to appreciate them and use them to your benefit.  The visual and audio aesthetics of the game are pleasant and smooth, lending a great deal to the atmosphere, though I would say the faction leaders could use more development and variety.
For loyal Civilization fanatics, you may find the new mechanics (especially the technology) fractured and far more open than previous games, but it will become a benefit as you learn your way around the trees.  Variety and freedom of optimisation are the name of the game.
To summarise, it's a fantastic game and money well spent.  Where Civilization V crash-landed with severe multiplayer issues and coarse gameplay, Beyond Earth arrives with a relatively smooth landing.  There are no gamebreaking bugs.  Across some fifty hours of gameplay, I have had one crash and it did not repeat.  I look forward to the release of expansions sometime in the next year, with any luck, and what they will add to an already well-rounded title.
That said, please remake Alpha Centuari for us, changing as few elements as possible.  We beg you.

I have mixed feelings about this game. I played it on free weekend and have to say I enjoyed it a lot. Though I can forgive a lot from the game, if it has a scifi setting.
First I must tell, that I never played Alpha Centauri, so I can't tell you how bad this urinates on AC's grave. Even though I've been a huge fan of strategy games since childhood, I never really touched the Civilization games until Civ V few years ago. And then it was too late to revert back to outdated mechanics of AC.
However it is painfully obvious Firaxis intentionally left major gameplay elements (only 8 factions, none of which have alternative leaders!!) out of the game they intend to release later as an "expansion pack", like they did with XCOM: Enemy Unknown and Civ V and IV. The difference is that those games have enough content in them so that they can function perfectly on their own without the DLC.
The starting opinions is a nice new feature. You are no longer tied to just the faction specific perks.
The victories, aside from domination, are way too similar. Build a teleporter platform, march your troops through it and you win. And the affinities are way too tightly tied to the tech tree.

Five years and two platforms later, still a fantastic, unique title.
+ Story is interesting, albeit a tad contrived. Servicable voice acting, decent plot and a good protagonist make uncovering the next story event something to look forward to.
+ Lively, well developed characters.
+ Myriad of fun and effective weapons. Combine two weapons into one of extreme power. Combo weapons are creative and worth the hassle.
+ Leveling up your character gives rewarding incentive to do some sandbox and replays.
+ Fantastically recorded and generated sound assets.
+ Fortune City is a colorful, enjoyable map with plenty of fun and surprises.
+ Zombies are dismembered in satisfying, dynamic ways.
+ Visuals are obviously dated but serviceable.
+ Decent amount of PC options. Controls are relatively problem free. Not a Mad Max quality port, but certainly a giant leap from something Arkham Knight quality.
+ Co-op can ease up more difficult missions and add substantial enjoyment to the slaughter.
+ Vehicles are a great transportation/murder tool, even if the controls can be a bit over/under compensating.
- The timer is the biggest controversy of this game. I personally hate being paced, stressed, and rushed. The only reason I reccomend this game is because you can disable/slow the timer with mods and trainers. The timer adds a decent challenge to the game but leaves little time for fun screwing around or side missions.
- Competetive online is dead, but it was never really "all that" in the first place. Fairly generic "American Gladiator"-esque challenges that involve zombie death.
- Side missions; particularly the survivor escorts, are repetetive and pretty boring. Survivors can slow you down and become a time wasting liability.
- Although the "psychopath" boss fights are memorable and contain great characters, they are rather annoying and dependant on your level rather than your skill and adaptability. They often boil down to the same "dodge this then hit me" formula.
- Some combat mechanics wear thin quick and become a chore. Shaking your mouse in a QTE to shed a grappling zombie (which happens OFTEN), getting knocked flat on your♥♥♥♥♥and stunned by almost all human attacks, stopping to cough sporatically when the later introduced enemy attacks you.
- Normal, non-combo weapons feel a bit underpowered for the most part. Firearms have their damage heavily reduced against human enemies for no explained reason. Uncombined melee and throwable weapons break very quickly and yield very little experience.
Overall, Chuck Greene's a pretty cool guy who makes pretty cool weapons and kills zombies in pretty cool ways in a pretty cool set-piece. The only overbearing cons are the timer which can be circumvented via mods and the lousy side-missions which are totally optional. Picked up for about $7 which justifies almost thirty hours of play.

Well, I'm a fan of the X3 games. I like the whole empire building, trading, exploring etc concept. I also tend to like more complex, steep learning curve games; this qualifies as that.
Is this an X4 for those who have played X3, NO. Is it based in the same universe that and X3 gamer would recognize, YES. Can you change from a trading ship to a scout to a heavy fighter then to a capital ship, NO. Can you build huge complexes that are self sufficient and make you tons of money , NO. Can you set up universal traders to make money, NO.
Something else that is different from X3 is the use of highways to move around. Previously in X3 to speed up movement one would engage SETA (basically a fast forward button). The issue with SETA is that it hogs up ram and on a 32 bit program you have a limited amount of ram to work with. The use of highways can get you from place to place without SETA and FPS going into the single digits. Rebirth is 64 bit (now) and this is not so much of an issue, but the highways are still there.
Space stations can still be built, but they are now built in stages and cannot be connected to one another to create a complex. The price of building a station has gone up quite a bit as well.
Trading is changed as well, since you cannot fly a freighter yourself, you must delegate trading to individual freighters.   Say you want to trade energy cells, you need a freighter capable of hauling energy cells and you then bring up the trade menu to see who is selling energy cells the cheapest, and likewise who is buying them for the best profit. You tell the freighter where to go, but this is all unseen it's kind of boring.
Capturing ships is still possible as well. Fighters can be captured should you make the original pilot bail, but you need to have your own pilot onboard your ship to be able to do so. Capturing larger is easier then in X3. Now you can cripple a ship's engines and weapons prior to launching your 50 marines (how do they fit in a corvette sized ship?).
So, bottom line, if you like complex trade empire building games and can get over the differences from X3 then you will have fun with this game.

A good story with some great characters and humour, but gameplay is a bit mixed - rigid stealth mechanics with an arcade/consolitis feel. Sometimes you get detected for something that you would get away with in real life and vice-versa. Confusingly, enemy eyesight is matched to their torso instead of the direction their face is looking towards. The challenge is annoyingly increased artificially by over-populating levels with guards. To get past them you take things slowly and memorise their pre-defined patrol routes - which can get a bit tedious. The mechanics have a “puzzle game” feel to them. There is little room for improvisation. At least you can always go the guns blazing route if stealth gets too annoying. The gameplay does offer good replayability though, if you want to improve your score for each level and beat the scores of your friends.
Levels are on the small side and too linear, but many have nice detail and feel very alive with huge crowds of AI. Some also have funny things and some great easter-eggs. On a technical level though, the graphics are just average (aimed at xbox360 limitations). levels also take unreasonably long to load.
The control scheme feels a bit cumbersome. Shooting mechanics are acceptable, but melee combat is poor - clumsy and harsh quick time events that break the flow of the action. The screen FOV is low by desktop standards. The lack of frequent checkpoints or a manual save system can be annoying if you slip up and have to start from the beginning of a level. Also, your gear and outfit are not saved between levels. Even worse, if you reload a checkpoint, some enemies are alive that you killed before reaching that checkpoint.
So, gameplay is arguably not quite as good as in Blood Money, but I did find the story in Absolution much more entertaining. Other than some minor issues like very slow loading levels, a few bugs and glitches (once an AI spotting me through a floor), the game runs stable.
Overall it is a decent game to get when on sale.

I’m going to start off by saying that I thought this was a great, high-quality game.  I really enjoyed the high-production-value inherent in all of the facets of the game.  The graphics were crisp, the controls were smooth, the writing was interesting, the acting was excellent, etc.  This is a high-quality game, period.
Moving on from there, I also personally felt that the game was extremely fun and that it does a great job of appealing to a wide audience (which, whether you personally like it or not, is the goal of any developers/publishers).  Now I understand that some people felt let down by this game after they had greatly enjoyed previous installments in the franchise.  They didn’t like some of the directions the developers chose to go with
and thus formed a very vocal group of disappointed customers.  If you are among these people, then I’m sure nothing I can say will sway your opinion, and that is fine.  It is impossible to please everyone, and the developers did their best to appeal to as many people as possible when they made this game.
In my opinion, disregarding how it stacks up against its predecessors and strictly looking at the game as its own entity, I can whole-heartedly say: I think this game is extremely fun.  Most gamers should be able to find a way to enjoy playing this game.  If you only want to play through on easy and enjoy the AAA quality story and cinematics, you can do that.  If you want to be frustrated with extreme difficulty and be challenged to your maximum breaking point, you can do that.  If you want to replay levels to explore different paths and collect hundreds of in-game achievements, you can do that.  And of course, if you want to fall somewhere in between those extremes, you can most certainly do that.
One thing I will admit I was not a fan of was the checkpoint system, or lack thereof.  Trying to experiment with various ways to complete levels can quickly go from fun to frustrating when you realize you have to start the level from the beginning every time you mess up.  I personally feel having a quick-save option would have been nice and would have allowed an even more widely varied audience to be able to enjoy the game.  Those who don’t want to play with quick-saves could just simply not use it, or they could have made it unavailable in the top difficulties, but still allowed it in the “normal” difficulty.  But, having said all that, most levels can be beaten in less than 5 minutes, so having to start from the top isn’t that awful… and it does prevent the game from becoming, maybe, too easy.  I still will always prefer having the choice to decide for myself if I want to use quick-saves in a game, or challenge myself not to.
To put it shortly:
is an extremely fun game with a noticeably high-production-value quality about it.  It is certainly different from previous games in the franchise, and in some people’s opinions it is not as good as previous games in the franchise; but regardless of whether or not you agree with those people, the game itself is still a good game.  Most gamers will able to find this game enjoyable by customizing the experience to their preferences.

I found this game really beautiful and gripping. It shows us the true horrors of war and what people have to go through during these times. The game is also quite hard and requires a lot of planning and patience.
The Good Things:
-Non-Linear Storyline. There are many different stories to pick (After you finish the first one) and many different scenarios to witness in the many different places you can visit. If you are angered by a soldier who is going to♥♥♥♥♥♥a woman you can change it's outcome!, If you are worried about some kids with a sick mother who is about to die you can change her fate! The survivors reveal their story over time and comment on actions of other survivors.
-Realistic Combat. Except for the bullets and stealth, the combat is very realistic. Players don't have more health over enemies (Unless you're playing as Boris or Roman), and killing is not always the option because some enemies will surrender.
-Realistic Simulation.
There is no Easy, Normal, or Hard, there is only Realism. When the tempertures drop, people can get sick. When crime is on the rise, the group will suffer a lot of raids. When survivors are depressed, the group falls apart.
-Different ways to play.
Players don't always have to steal food. They could trade for it or even grow their own. Players don't always have to use stealth kill enemies, with enough bullets and body armor they could rush in and shoot everyone.
-Beautiful Graphics.
The graphics perfectly captures a war zone and contributes alot to the atmosphere. By the looks of it
the game seems to take place around eastern europe during the 1990s.
-Shows us what war really is.
This game is a big ♥♥♥♥ you to people who support wars or even play the so called "Game of the Year" Call of Duty or similar. It shows us that the Military will do anything for "Glory" and will abuse
their power for their own desires.
The Bad Things:
-You are only able to have one save. It autosaves after every night and it prevents you from making backups saves or restarting a day incase you make a mistake.
-Food is extremely scarce and limited. There are only 4 types of food: Vegetables, Raw Meat, Canned Food, and Cooked Meals. There is no existance of Rice, Fish, Bread, or other foods which are commonly found in many places. Some places, like the Military Outpost, Have a lot of food but not enough to keep a group of 4 well fed for a week.
--Water is kind of useless. Nobody drinks water, only Coffee and Alcohol. Water is only used for in making Moonshine, and Cooking Food.
My Score for this game is: 9/10. Many of the bad things were not that bad but some tweaks should be implemented. Overall the game is really great for an Indie game and it's worth your money!

This is a fun little single player trials type driving game where you try to race through levels while carrying a load of stuffed animals in the back of your truck.  You go over bumps and jumps and dynamite obstacles and such as you try to keep the stuffed animals from spilling out onto the ground.   Each level has 5 goals, one being to get through the map with all the animals with any time, one to get through with at least one animal with a fast time, and three others with intermediate combinations of going fast and getting to the end with more animals.    You earn stars for these goals and you have to earn enough stars if you want to unlock the higher difficulty levels.
The graphics are very charming and the game is kid friendly. but it is a mobile port in Unity with no in game settings (video or sound or controls) at all as far as I know.  You can change the control mapping or video mode before you launch the game in a separate configuration mode.  Like all Unity games it will try to resize the game to fit the graphics mode you have chosen in the best way it can.  This will leave black bars on the sides during gameplay if you have a wide screen since I believe the game was designed with 4:3 aspect ratio.
You control it with keyboard using W to go faster, S to go slower, A to tilt your car back, and D to tilt your car forward.   The game has partial gamepad support that allows you to use the game pad to drive during the levels, but not in the menus between levels. The game does not support Steam cloud saving so if you use it on more than one devices I don't think it is easy to transfer your progress.
The game used to have a place to create your own levels and share them online and play other people's levels, but that appears to have been discontinued so you only get approximately 40 levels to play I think now. Magic Duel is WOTC's foray into free-to-play Magic:The Gathering for those whom want to play Magic without having to dig far into the Magic library in the form of this game via Steam. Having poured as to now 80+ hours into the game I have a lot of good and bad to point out as in to whether you should pick this game up or not even though the game is free.
The gameplay consists mainly of one on one matches between you and an A.I. controlled opponent (or human controlled one via Magic Origins matchmaking on Wizard's server) in a best of one match where the better skilled player will come out victorious depending on what kind of deck you are playing. There is also a 2vs2 team mode known as Two Headed Giant where the teams of two share the same life but different card pools to defeat two opponents with the same stipulations and goals as their own. There is a story mode that kinda explains what's going on in the game storyline wise with some of the characters you see in some cards but it's there mainly for padding purposes and story buffs.
There are many decks to play and choose from in the game which seems like a lot in the beginning but as the time I am writing this review there are only two sets and one starter deck set which you can build decks from and having collected all cards from both sets limits me from making newer decks or broadening existing themes but WOTC has announced that more sets are being added later on through the games' life span to keep players interested. As of now it's very limited but not to the point you can't have an enjoyable time.
The main game is fine but the only problem I have is the ability to gain the cards you need to even create a deck to your liking. You win in-game currency (Coins) which can be bought via Steam dollarie doos or gained in-game via winning matches and beating in-game dailuy quests etc. The packs generally go for 150 coins and matches usually generate from 20-30 coins a match and daily quests only generate only one to two quests a day that maybe at a max generate 50-80 coins a day which turns the game into a grind quest. Even when you get the coins you need when you go to buy the packs you often get multiples or even duplicates of the same cards when even in real life you hardly get alot of what you need. I've spent $100+ dollars and fortunately have all of the cards from the two sets but I feel that there should be a better or even higher payouts for players so people who don't have the extra money and want to play comfortably could have a chance to gain the better cards whether it be via trading system or a card exchanging system for extra coins or something of the sort.
With that out the way I do recommend Magic Duels for those that want to try and learn the basic in-and-ous of Magic:The Gathering and hopefully ignite the Planeswalker spark in you as it did for me.
-Young Dank Stank

Snuggle Truck is basically like a Trials game - control your vehicle using accelerate, brake, and tilt forward/backward, attempting to get to the finish line as quickly as possible. At times you get activatable powerups, either a cage that keeps your animals inside for a few seconds while you do maneuvers, or that plus rocket boosters for the same time.
There's not much to say about Snuggle Truck, really. It's like Trials if it was a small-team indie game, but Trials Evolution Gold Edition is right there and easily worth the $20 instead of the $5 this costs. Sadly, both of these games have gotten worse since launch, Trials Evolution by going through uPlay, Snuggle Truck having shut down its level-distribution server so that only the 41 levels included with the game are available.

So in short, this is one of the best single player space sims out there. Highly reccommended if you love the genre. What I think most people that wrote a negative review did is that they reviewed the early game (which was in fact buggy, slow as hell and generally undeveloped) and most important - they compared it to their predecessor X3: Terran Conflict (X3TC). More explanation below if you care to read.
X3TC is simply the best single player space sim out there, period. Rebirth is a different game that borrows some things from its predecessor but is essentially completely new. Most people (including myself) expected just a better X3TC which, thinking back, would in fact be almost impossible to achive (in my opinion).
So what made me play X:Rebirth so much? Because is without doubt one of the best space sims out there. Most of similar games have a much shorter life span, meaning that you reach a point when there's simply nothing to do. X:R is a sandbox. You decide your own rules, you shape the universe (literally), you can play it almost infinitely.
Want to ruin the economy in AI controlled sectors? You do it. Wanna be a hoarder and own every acquirable ship and every buildable station in the game? You do it. Wanna play the pirate that plunders one or more factions? You do it. Wanna have a fleet of 500 capital ships and lay waste to the entire universe? Well you can do it but it's not permanent since the AI will eventually rebuild space stations.
After almost 400 hours of gameplay I still find many things to do, many things that would get me occupied for at least 100 more hours. And then I'd set myself a new goal and play 100 hours more.
Like I said, the game is a sandbox. Play the story mode once, and then start a new game and set yourself some personal goals and rules to stick to - i.e. play a merchant that cannot own any combat ship and can only defend itself if attacked. or play a pirate that plunders all but one or two factions.
Compared to some other space sims I've played (and I've played many) X:R is not the best but it's in the top 5 for sure.
Pros:
- you can acquire almost everything you see in the universe
- it's a sandbox so basically infinite lifespan
- combat is dynamic and fun
- combat can be HARD if not approached without a plan - you can't just go in alone and fight a destroyer with escorts. They will rip you apart in seconds regardless of your ship mods.
- build, fight, trade and THINK - sometimes you face an ingame problem that might seem as a bug, but it can be resolved ingame (i.e. resource shortage and the economy won't produce the affected resource - once you're familiar with the game mechanics, you can solve this by yourself))
- the interface has been GREATLY improved since the game came out and is now really user-friendly
Cons:
- only one flyable ship - but in the long run it doesn't matter that much because you always end up flying one most of the time
- can't really customize the fleet (i.e. different weapons for your ships)

I have played this game on the xbox and the PC.  If you ever played the original Dead Rising on xbox, then you know just how hard and unforgiving the original game was.  Well this is an easier game.  The first game gave you 1 save, this one gives you 3.  The survivors you rescued were dumb as nails in the original and needed constant babysitting, but here they are not really smarter, but more capable in avoiding zombies, which makes the game less frustrating, but maybe a little too easy.
The basics of the game and the series is that zombies have attacked, in this case, a Casino/mall.  You have cases to complete, people to rescue.  But the best part of this game is the weapons you can create to kill zombies in the most interesting way.  Did you know that a group of gems and a flashlight combined together make a light saber?  Well here that is one of the many weapons you can craft.  There is also an electric rake, an electric wheelchair, an amplified guitar, and other crazy ways to kill zombies.
So in short:  This game is a tongue in cheek, but really fun zombie apocalypse game.  Not as challenging as the original, but more challenging then Dead Rising 3.

Perhaps you've played the first Bioshock and perhaps you're wondering if to indulge yourself into Bioshock 2? This review should help you make your decision. Firstly, Bioshock 2 is set 10 years after the original Bioshock; with a little teaser cut scene at the beginning for those who have either forgot the Bioshock ending or simply just wanted to mordernise to Bioshock 2 (4 years ago isn't exactly modern huh). After that you're left with brand spanking new game (for those who are new) that 2k Games have placed into your lap. Let's breaking down this eerie game and see if Daddy wants a bite.
Bioshock 2 is set in the fictional underwater dystopia of Rapture. The game opens with a cutscene set in 1958 then jumps 10 years to when Delta (the protagonist) wakes up in 1968, ten years after the events of the first BioShock. You are searching for your little sister AKA your daughter who's mother has taken and plans to do evil, motherish thing to them to better the world. The whole story spans about 12 hours (maybe less as I did try get the a particular acheivement) which is decent for a Bioshock game. Unlike the other Bioshock, the storyline is
easy to follow as there is an arrow above the first person camera view but more importantly the story is well crafted and much thought it put into its structure. Without giving away spoilers, there is decision making regarding the outcome of the story. You will find this out as you play but let's just say that what you do dratically changes the outcome of the ending. The storyline seems to be split up into zones or 'sections'. When you arrive at one place you will have an objective and, to progress further, will need to complete the objective in the set area. This proves to be very effetive in setting the storyline as it builds tension and envelops the player in a gripping sensation. However, there is a lack of side missions which can be a downfall as Bioshock 2's lifespan decreases. Luckily 2k Games have made the story so ecentric that there is no need for side mission or diversions.
No I'm not crying because they are good or even that they're bad but I mean literally! As Rapture is set underwater there will be sections of the game where you will be in water and let me tell you now it is fantasic. The water graphics for this game are very good especially on high detail and the helmet edges on the first person screen just adds to the realism (I thought actual water droplets were on my screen and tried to dry them). I may be nitpicking here but the water graphics have surely been outdone and if you play this game you will understand what I mean. The overall scenery and attention to detail is truely flawless something which was missing from the original Bioshock. The plant life and marine life really brings out a uncogested feeling in the game along with a surprisingly stunning environment. The colours and textures work in conjunction to allow you to get as close as you can to realism of living underwater (without having to take a pipe to the beach and test it). However the graphics within the combat scenario have withered slightly as killing an enemy may render its death animation(s) to appear rather blocky and ridgid. This is something is isn't vastly noticed (especially when you're
but it is there an it is a minor kink. There are also some graphical glitches which can make the game seem unreal but these are generally quite rare and seemingly irrelevant in the grand scheme of things.
To begin, the gameplay is very similar to the original Bioshock but also quite different. You still play as a Big Daddy and you still use ADAM which is a plasmid that grants superhuman abilities. However, plasmids have recieve a massive overhaul including many different types of plasmids as well as upgrades for most of them. Plasmids are the most useful power in the game and allows you to take on any foe (BEES). You can also apply traits to your character which grants additional abilities that naturally come around useful in combat or exploration. There are varieties of weapons to choose from which allow customisation in which plasmid to use in conjunction with which weapon. Character control is generally quite impeccable with the occassional traps (thought you could jump that pile of scrap, think again). Enemy AI's are quite well done and 2k Game have done an exceptional job adding little dark, heinous moments to your Bioshock experience by adding
Overall the gameplay is beautiful and is very smooth in terms of consitency. The gameplay allows you to navigate around the maps effectively and engaging in combat is kept pure and simple with no added complications. Sometimes the gameplay is cut short by some crashing and closing but that is through no fault of 2K Games but rather Steam.
With a almost flawless gameplay style and an absolutely gripping storyline its all you really need to get the maximum out of your Bioshock 2 experience. I highly recommend this game to anyone that enjoys a well crafted, well structured storyline. This is a game that's had every aspect thought about it to ensure that you're experience is phenomenal and to ensure that you stay on the Bioshock bus for the entire ride. Thanks for reading my review and if you thought this was helpful please let me know. :)

Hitman: Absolution is an amazing game, it looks great. It plays great. Overall it IS great. However, like every game, it has its flaws (which may just be my own personal opinion) but here we go!
Pros:
The ability to enter the area and slaughter everyone in interesting ways. With plenty of ways to start a mission, it makes the game very replayable. Killing guards and other enemies is also optional, leaving the game open to plenty of playstyles.
A large arangement of weapons to take out anyone in your path. From a simple switch blade to a high powered sniper rifle and everything in between, there are plenty of ways to clear out the mission area.
Vast amount of ways to complete the same objective. It adds to the replay value, since not only are there differnet ways to enter certain areas, theres also plenty of ways to do the same objective. Sure you could just shoot your target outright infront of everyone, but would you rather poision his cocaine and watch him snort up his own death?
Cons:
THE SCORING SYSTEM. Honestly, this thing gets my panties in a bunch. When I think of Hitman, I think of someone who is supposed to literally clean house discretly and professionally. Instead we have to march around constantly changing disguises and either NOT killing anyone who isnt our target, or just passifying them and then hiding their body. Sure this is where the opinion thing comes in, but there arent many games like Hitman where you can just kill everyone without consequesnces. Dishonored may seem that way, but it has one of those "hidden endings until you beat the game" endings. Thief can be a little like hitman, with the stealth element. However killing is 100% optional and so is knocking out the guards. Assassins Creed could fufil my lust for an endless slaughter, however I like the professionalism of Hitman. I suppose Im just a hard to please person, but either way. The scoring system is just an annoyance in the long run as I feel like Im being watched. Judged for my playstyle, if I ended the level with a negative score I feel like I didnt do the game justice. If I end with the highest positive score I feel like ive played the game I shouldve played it.
Conclusion: I personally love this game, Ive played it roughly 4 times over from start to finish. However the scoring system seems to hustle me to do everything to the games liking, not to how I really truly want to play the game. With it being a review from a simple minded gamer I dont expect many to see this review as 'helpful' but to just see me rant a little.
All in all, Id give this game an 8/10.

Let's be honest. this "Remaster" doesn't look a sh*t ounce better than the original. Is it still a great game after all these years? Yes. Does this remaster live up to expectations? Hardly. Aside from the obvious lack of graphics options, the crashes were more than plenty.
But my most annoying grip with this version is the message you receive upon relaunching the game. In order for the difficulty achievements to properly work, you must ALWAYS select NO. IF at any time, you hit YES, the difficulty settings (including vita-chambers) are reset. The easiest way to resolve this, is just to load a previous save and reselect the difficulty you were on. you don't even have to save after you quit, just reload the save you are currently using and everything will be normal.
I got severely paranoid when i did this and i hoped that my difficulty achievement would still be earned by end game - which thankfully, it did. I've never experienced this issue on PS3, 360, nor the original on Steam or even the DRM-FREE version from Humble Bundle.
The inclusion of SURVIVOR difficulty is nice, but doesn't really feel any different than HARD. Plus, the inclusion of the CHALLENGE ROOMS will add extra hours of play time - as well as NEW GAME PLUS for repeated playthroughs with all your equipment. These features were previously exclusive to the PS3 version.
The MUSEUM itself is not that great. its cool seeing things in model form with concept art attatched but overall - it should have been an unlocked progress from the main game itself instead of just giving it to you all at once - like with the GOLDEN REELS.
So do i recommend this? It's hard to say. BioShock is as every bit a great game as its always been - but this could have been severely better, especially when its given the "remastered" treatment. The extra content might give it justice, but overall - i'd probably just stick with the original. At least it was stable.

Edited and update review here. I wanted to re-review this after seeing how good/bad the game was after you finish the story. I had a very strong positive reaction to my first 15 hours playing, but after you finish the majority of the main story mode, the game is basically over. It wasn't built for a "sandbox" experience or anything, as the systems get less and less fun as you move along the main story path. I'll explain that more below, but if you want a one sentence recap: good game, worth twenty bucks for sure, but it has a few glaring problems.
First off, I really like this game. Almost every aspect is fun and it isn't often you get good space games on Steam. The price is good, and I do recommend it overall.
With that said, there are some major flaws. The first one being the trade and economy system. It's so poorly handled that it's hard to justify it being in the game at all. The only time you will find the market scheme useful in any way is very early in the game, in the first or second systems when you are stuggling to earn credits. The work it takes to get goods and then find the station that is buying high is just way too hard to justify when you start earning $100,000 per mission - let alone when you are getting $1mil per mission later on. The 90k you might make off trading is insignificant. Your time spent grows significantly and the gains never justify it. The whole thing could have been alleviated by having actual up-to-date pricing information available both on the main map and while in a dock, but the developers failed miserably on that. It's true they did implement a (very minimal) scheme that shows you current pricing in each station from the main map, but it only works if you've already visited the station or happen find a message transponder that gives you the information. Even then, the information is only good for a matter of minutes. The game will randomly change the goods and prices in each station, so usually by the time you get enough of the goods to matter, you will never find the right place to sell it unless you get really lucky and accidentally stop at the right station. Couple that with random events like famine, celebration, tech boom, etc., it's like a lottery except the profit is meaningless. There is no logic or reason to the system, no attempt to mimic actual markets in any logical way. The one and only way to make real credits is by doing missions, which are fine and fun, but I think they should have either cut the entire trading system or made it universal and simplified. Instead it's like they started out with a good idea, but lost it halfway through.
The other huge issue is the "proximity stop" system. Basically, if you come within a certain distance of any other object in the game, you will be instantly halted out of warp. This would be fine and make sense if they tried to limit the amount of debris and roaming hostile fleets, but as the game progresses and you meet more factions, the maps stay the same size. So what you end up with are huge fields of debris from battles needing to share a shrinking amount of space with asteroid fields and huge fleets of enemies wandering around. By the fifth system or so, there are a half dozen factions on each map. Then you have merchants and traders randomly criss-crossing the place on top of it, and they have their own bodyguards with fighter ships. It all adds up to way, way too much crap on the map and fewer and fewer routes you can take just to do simple tasks, like going to turn in a mission or finish a trade.  After the 100th time you get stopped mid-warp just because a piece of debris or friendly merchant came within 400 sm (in-game unit of measurement) of your path, it gets incredibly frustrating.
It's also worth noting that the "escort" missions are mostly broken at present. They might patch them again, but right now only about 75% of them work as intended. The pathing is poorly coded and there are too many random objects that only confuse the AI even more. Occasionally you will get a big piece of ship debris and it will cause the AI's ship you are escorting to start moving forwards and backwards, over and over, in a loop. You can abandon missions at any time, so when it does break, it's easy enough to just forget it and move on.
So, those are my main frustrations. Otherwise this is a great game and is easily the best space game on Steam right now. It's definitely better than Elite Dangerous, plus it's only twenty bucks. I got this on sale for $13, and for that price, it's a major bargain. If you are looking for trade simulation or a long-term sandbox mode you can play in after the (approximately) 25 hour storymode is over, this might not be the best game for that. I got over 30 hours out of it and that was definitely worth $20 to me, but your mileage may vary.
The simplicity and monotony have ruined this game. Not recommended.

Rebel Galaxy goes for the western in space vibe, and it succeeds at it. The soundtrack and characters definitely feel reminescent of Firefly.
One thing I particularly enjoy is that the game puts you in control of massive capital ships instead of tiny fighters like most games. You start off with a smallish cruiser, but can work your way up to massive dreadnaught vessels that feel great to pilot.
The story is nothing special, but I enjoyed it. The side quests can get repetitive, but if you don't mind a bit of grinding then you probably won't get bored of it. I enjoyed the combat, so the side quests remained engaging to me.
The combat is quite simplistic for a combat game, but enjoyable never-the-less. It's inspired by naval combat, and takes place on a 2d plane. Every capital ship has an assortment of broadside cannons and turrets. You're turrets are enough to take out most smaller vessels, but for other capital ships you'll want to get along side of them and use your broadsides.
There are a ton of different ships, items and upgrades to unlock. There is also a good variety of side grades, allowing you to pick a unique playstyle.
As for actual in game activities, there are story missions, delivery runs, dead drops, trading, mining, bounty hunting, and various other mission types.
Highly recommend if you're a fan of scifi/space combat games. It's more of an arcade game then a sim, and you can only fly on a 2d plane though.
