I awoke on a beach; my ship had been caught in some crags. I watch another ship skirt the edge and sail away.
I loot the beach and find a note, warning me to turn back, lest I be trapped on the island too.
Another note from a merchant; I am both sentimentally and financially significant to him, thus, he gives me a bow and arrows - allows me to take of his goods, trusting that I'll leave the correct compensation (no doubt strictly a plot device to reinforce isolation (absence of merchant); there is no option to steal).
Come across what seems to be a conquistador. My first arrow ricochets off his helmet. My second finds purchase in a chink in the trunk (torso). Grab his pistol and move on to a Fort.
Explore the area with the color saturation at 0.1.
Come across another conquistador; he takes a third of my health 'fore I dispatch him.
Continue, crouching all the while, only sprinting when the wind blows, so as to muffle my steps to any other adversaries.
Neglect the Fort for the countryside; I find a note presumably from one of the men stationed in the fort: He expresses concern at his superior's wanting to confiscate and hide treasure amongst the hills and fields.
Another foe put down with one arrow to the neck.
Jump atop a rock, to witness a panorama; flashing indicates loot to either side, red indicates enemy before me off in the distance. Unsure of how to consider gravity and whatnot, I move closer... though not enough; arrow seems to have nearly grazed his head. Second arrow either connects or does graze; his rage makes the distance 'tween him and myself seem a few meters.
We exchange; I take cover behind my rock to reload. I try out the different weapons (bow, pistol and a rifle I had picked up). Connect with the pistol (on the second shot); rifle seems to have a spread. I peek over, with an arrow notched. I get a face-full of pellets.
This game... is awesome.
The visuals, the environment(al features), the ambience.
The combat: No medium; painstaking stealth, oddly hectic firefights with flintlock and powder based firearms.
The story: From what little I know, you can shift between two realms. Your mission is to glean what's going on, to put wandering souls to rest.
I recommend this game.

I went in expecting an increibly fun, sadistic, and over the top isometric shooter. Hatred delivers exactly that. The game is somewhat difficult even on easy, but once you get the hang of gunpay it becomes second nature. The destruction is beautiful, my jaw dropped the fist time I kicked in the door of a house and subsequently threw a high explosive grenade in the living room. Walls can be shot through, most cover can be destroyed, and Michael Bay seems to have left all of his extra set pieces lying around the levels which adds a lot to the destruction. I beat the game in 3-4 hours on easy, but even though I had most of the "sidequests" I still wanted to see more. How many limbs can I take off with one shotgun shell? It was a decent game with great visuals, but it was VERY short, and instead of acting like a collect-fest style of game, it instead forces you to recollect any plain old stones that you may have picked up before. It's almost more like a high-score scenario. The difficulty curve of the game is weird. It goes from really easy to quite challenging very quickly (due to the short number of levels), and then back down to fairly easy.
Additionally (and I think that this is the biggest flaw) is that there is no progression in the game. You get all of the items you need at the very beginning of the game, and after that it's just a matter of personal technique. If you can master mechanics like this very quickly, then this game will seem almost laughably easy, aside from level four, but if you aren't great at mastering mechanics like this, then you might get a decent number of hours out of the game.
It's not a bad game--it's actually quite good--but it is almost criminally short with little replayability, and that is why I cannot recommend it unless you pick it up in a sale.

I have been looking for a modern 3D platformer for some time now, and those that I have played have been good but have left me less satisfied than I would like.
Tiny and Big: Grandpa’s Leftovers didn’t do that at all. The only element where it had me wanting more was its length, but I would gladly take this shorter (but still long enough to keep you busy), but much higher quality experience.
I played with a controller, I can’t say much about the gameplay with mouse/keyboard. Just a 3D platforming experience, the gameplay was pretty much flawless. But on top of that are the physics mechanics and the tools you are given (no spoilers!) and that makes for a really refreshing experience. The tools at your disposal don’t feel at all like gimmicks, which is a risk many developers face when trying to incorporate interesting mechanics into a game. The levels are also designed really well to make use of these mechanics.
The story isn’t ground breaking but there is one and I find that really important, it is present enough to have me keep playing and it doesn’t feel like an afterthought. The fact that there is another character that really does engage with you helps in this regard. The scripts are also written well and leads to a pretty funny experience. It helps build the sense of charm around the game.
And boy is there charm! You can see it firstly from the graphical style of the game, it just looks really good. The comic book style sound effect labels are awesome and were always accurate. I love the level intros and the game has pretty good graphical diversity for being based entirely in a desert - especially towards the end.
While it is short, it has all of the bells and whistles - collectables, secrets, plenty of achievements and goals to complete each level in ridiculous ways.
If I had to come up with some complaints, I thought that the death sequence was a bit long. It also seemed kind of arbitrary how far you had to fall in order to die - it seems to prevent you from going to parts of the level in the wrong order.
If you’re looking for a good 3D platformer, I don’t think you could look past this.

TL,DR: I haven't read the book on which this game is based, but I'm left with the distinct impression that my time would have been better spent reading the book than playing through the game.
At first, I puttered around a bit, trying to play it "the right way", by which I mean reading/listening to the dialogue, exploring the scenarios, and puzzling things out myself. The dialogue sets up the story, but *in no way* sets up the actual mechanical challenges that each character will face, so I quickly resorted to "wiggle the mouse around in every area of every room, hoping to stumble onto some object with which I can interact, and try most every obvious combination of actions and objects until something seems to work."
After some frustration with this method, I resorted to looking for walkthroughs on the Internet. Very quickly it became obvious that specific items that were neither visually obvious (i.e. they looked like background, or often were so small that they were difficult to even mouse over) nor particularly interesting or distinct were absolutely crucial to solving puzzles vastly further down the line, and failure to grab them at the start would (best case) necessitate backtracking from the very end of the scenario back to the first few rooms or (worst case) starting the scenario over, because some mechanic prevented said backtracking.
So, because I'm an adult with a day job who doesn't enjoy using trial-and-error to puzzle out menial, arbitrary, and meaningless "puzzles", I pushed through the game using a walkthrough. The story is interesting, sort of, although I don't really know why I'm supposed to care about any of the characters, and therefore my only driving motivation to finish the game is to be able to say I finished the game, and to check it off my completion list for Steam games in my Humble Bundle backlog.
If the premise sounds interesting, go read the book, because you'll get (I assume) more or less the same story, but without the annoyance and frustration of puzzling through nonintuitive, uninspiring, arbitrary brick walls between interesting dialogue. This is exactly the sort of game that illustrates why point-and-click "adventure games" deserved to die out, because they're basically low-res movies hidden behind the facade of puzzle solving, packed with filler to give you the (false) impression that you're doing more than following a linear storyline (or, alternatively, you've made some arbitrarily "wrong" choice and therefore you will "lose" the movie and have to start over, whee! Gameplay!), and "playing" them is a misleading term.

Hatred is a beautiful but incredibly bland title with shallow and repetitive gameplay, lacklustre combat and exteremely dull levels. I found the experience completely mundane and had no choice but to claim a refund under the circumstances. This game is not even worth a third of the asking price.
This controversial title is essentially a twin stick isometric shooter that looks very impressive with a dark and gritty atmosphere. Sadly this is the only postitive aspect of Hatred as everything else is lacking on a significant level. The controls are wonky and the concept of killing everything and everyone becomes tiresome very quickly indeed. The game doesn't really have a shock factor either to warrant the controversy that it's generated - I feel this was more of a publicity stunt to draw attention to the game as opposed to people having legitimate concerns about the premise.
It is also a very challenging title which isn't really a negative but the difficulty can often frustrate due to cumbersome controls and incredibly accurate AI. If you fail a level at any time; you have to go back to the start. You can however regenerate health but this involves performing executions which result in a repetitive cinematic cut scene over and over - sometimes you'd rather go without health just to avoid having to watch yet another same cut scene. You also have the opportunity per level to earn a respawn token by completing a secondary objective but as this often surrounds executions which like the above; you may want to avoid as this aspect just kills the flow of what is already exceptionally mundane gameplay.
Overall; Hatred is a very impressive looking title that lacks any substance whatsoever. The gameplay mechanics are irritating and the lack of depth along with the bland structure leave the product significantly lacking. It'll only take a few hours to finish but you'll be bored long before then. If you are still interested in taking a punt on the game; just don't exceed the two hour criteria for a refund - this game is essentially the same throughout. Everyone else should simply avoid - it's not worth the refund hassle even if you're mildly curious.

The powers and weapons are pretty fun to use but aren't quite too effective until upgraded a decent amount. The weapon challenge values are a little high and take a bit longer to achieve if you've already completed a lot of activities so your best bet is to actively go after them while you do ones like survival or extraction facility takeover. There are a lot of great jokes and references to both previous games and pop culture just as you'd expect and the story is pretty quick, simple and enjoyable with a nice selection of endings. Seeing as this is just an expansion and pretty short (and the fact it takes place in Hell and you play as Johnny Gat or Kinzie), the limited selection of cars and lack of additional outfits are both forgiveable. However, there are absolutely no radio stations or music to listen to while you conduct your mayhem which is quite disappointing and a missed opportunity for some good heavy metal. If you compare Civ V and Civ Beyond Earth on the same level (Not counting the dlc's), Civ Beyond Earth is a somewhat better game. It takes a long game or two to understand the new features the game adds but if you played CIv V, then you will be able to still have fun and win the game while still trying to learn beyond earth.
Unlike in Civ V, you get units based on the tech you researched and your level in Harmony, purity, or supremacy(which are called affinities) which you level up by choosing certain tech that levels those categories. Though because of this, each of these profided only a few units so if your expecting to have a very diverse army and play competivly, it ain't happening. Besides units, certain buildings are only available when you reached a certain affinity level.
Though unlike CIv V, which affinity you should go for and your victory type (which there are five of and are challenging to get to) all depends on your sort of starting area on turn one. There are three main rescources, each important one affinity. To use really good buildings or strong units that belong to one affinity, you need to have a good supply of the rescource belong to that affinity. So if you wanted to win having purity as your main affinity but only have a good supply of the rescource beloning to Harmony, then you better switch to wanting Harmony or good luck trying to trade with players and/or A.I. Note: Don't think you can level all the affinitiys equally because the game will make it harder to level up the affinities that arn't your main and you won't be able to get the best units from any of the affinities.
For now that is all I can say about the game without nickpicking it. When not compared to Civ V (WHICH IS ONLY BETTER BECAUSE OF IT'S DLC"S), Civ Beyond earth a fun enjoyable game with the same strategy as the previous titles.
Though they need to work on the alians/barbarians difficulty curve as the game progresses since there is none.

With the addition of Rising Tides, I decided that a full update to this review is in order.
With the addition of Rising Tide and several major patches released in the months following it, Civilization Beyond Earth - Rising Tides (BE-RT) is finally deserving of a full, unconditional endorsement. As it stands now, this is unquestionably a superior game to previous Civ's, and more importantly, it is a *different* game.
Comparing to Civ V: While the initial critique of "Civ V with a sci-fi skin" may have been a justified comment (although a tad harsh) in the early days, it is now completely unjustified. The basic mechanics are essentially the same (map, movement, resources, cities), but that's about it. Everything else is different, and there are some major changes in those differences. With Rising Tides and subsequent patches, BERT is worthy of being called a completely new game, and a completely superior game to the old Civ V. Still lacks some of the things that made Alpha Centauri so awesome, but it has its own strengths, so I won't knock it too badly for that.
My first big warning for new players is regarding unit diversity. If you are used to Civ V where you had hundreds of different units, it will seem like a shock. Instead you'll see a hundred different variations of about a dozen units. And these variations aren't nailed down by faction, either. As you progress through the tech tree, you'll be offered choices as to how to upgrade your units. For the generic set, you will probably have 4-5 upgrade choices over the course of the game, and which options you get to choose from differ depending on your tech choices. Effectively, there's probably at least a hundred different versions of each of the basic units, although probably only about 20 or so that are massivelydifferent. Beyond the basic units, there is a whole slew of specialty units of various kinds, each with their own 3-5 upgrade steps, but as they have specific tech and affinity requirements to unlock, it is quite likely that you won't see even a quarter of the unit types in any one game. Long story short, you may be building the most basic "soldier" unit right up until the end of the game, but whereas it is a basic militia sort at the beginning, by the end of the game it's a futuristic combat squad with a host of abilities.
Espionage: Forget the old Civ V style spy game, spies are back, they are different, and they are worth paying attention to. Like a lot of things, the basic spy game is similar to Civ V: You put spies in your cities to defend them, or in enemy cities to spy on them. End of similarities. First off, you pick what you want your spies to do. Initially, they can't do much, but as they build up their contacts in the city, they gain access to bigger and better things. You can also keep spies back at HQ to provide some civilization-wide bonuses for you, or send them to the black market to buy or sell strategic resources. Lots of options to fit a wide variety of different strategies.
Pro:
- The tech web is awesome. So much more variety and options to diversify gameplay.
- Espionage is much improved. Actually interesting now.
- The Seeding (Starting setup) is much more varied, and a lot more interesting.
- More interesting unit abilities
- Oceans are very interesting now.
- Every faction has a solid chance at winning every victory type.
Con:
- Affinity is everything. If you're going for any victory type other than Contact or time, techs that give affinity progress trump all other considerations. Trumps EVERYTHING.
- Less variety in unit types, hard to tell the difference between different versions of the same unit. And a lot of the units are affinity specific, meaning you need high levels of a particular affinity to get them. So they tend to be rather rare.
- The stupid black copyright box that pops up at the start of the game is really annoying. (same as Civ V's)
- You can't peg factions anymore. Each civ only has a single bonus that is constant, all the rest of the civ-wide bonuses and traits vary from game to game.
My recommendation? Buy this game! If you like Civ games, and you like sci-fi and the thought of colonizing another world, you will almost certainly enjoy this game. My caveat, however, is to get Rising Tides with it. BE without RT is good, but not awesome. With RT, it is an excellent game. (This whole review is written based on BE with RT. See review below for my old review of it before the expansion). This game isn't Alpha Centauri, and will likely  never replace it, but it is the next best thing, and has its own strengths.
Old review (written well before Rising Tides had ever been mentioned, so applies to Vanilla game only) beyond this point:
Overall, a good game. It is a very nice change to go forward into the future instead of trying to rewrite the past. After a first play through it seemed kind of weak and lacking in variety, but there's actually got a reasonable amount of variation in there, especially in starting conditions. If you liked Civ V, chances are you'll like Civ BE, but be forwarned, there's going to be some culture shock, as you won't be faced with hundreds of different units. Instead you'll be dealing with hundreds of different varieties of about a dozen units.  If you play this game, give it three or four play throughs. And remember, it is highly likely there is going to be DLC for this. I expect it will get the Civ V treatment. If they respond to community concerns, there's a solid chance this will end up being an excellent game. Not as good as Alpha Centauri, but still a great game.

Con:

While the game was absolutely terrible and broken when it got released a long time ago, Egosoft did a really good job of improving the game in many aspects, improving the interface and adding completely new features to the game. I also enjoy the DLCs quite alot (only one is shown in the shop so far, but another one is coming, which is even more worth purchasing).
To be frank, the campaign story is kind of meh, especially the last mission, but the story was (except for the very first X-title X-Beyond the frontier) never a focus point of the games.
As a fan since the beginning of the series, i hated the new highway system in the beginning because i thought making the warp gates more rare and instead focussing on highways was a betrayal to the series, especially since i did not care about the Albion sectors in the X3-series. But after a while i must say that i love the new highway system, its a great way to enjoy the scenery and to take a short break while flying from sector to sector.
It also has great mod support, a really nice mod community and a really great community overall.
And i must emphasize, unlike many developers who have a bad/broken launch and just abandon the game, Egosoft is known for supporting and improving the game even years after it's initizal release, and while almost every title in the X-series was incredibly broken at launch (hence the many bad reviews) Egosoft always did their best to improve the game to make their games great, even if it takes many years of (usually) free updates and patches.
The only huge gripe i have with this game is it's over-complicated and over-complex menu/sub-menu system to do simple things. But after a while you get used to it.
Unpatched on release it was garbage, over time it became acceptable, now i think it's a nice addition to the X-series and i'm always eagerly waiting for Egosoft to put in new updates.
Is it perfect? By all means no.
Is it enjoyable? In my opinion yes (why else would i play it over 500 hours?), as long as you don't have problems with fiddling around with menus.

I don't mean to rehash other reviews, so I'll try to be short:
I'm running it on max settings with a good, large monitor, btw and still:
* Hard to distinguish what's on each tile.
* Unlike Civ V, many resources and technologies have unfamiliar names. There's very little intuitive about what you're getting by researching or building certain things. Especially since sometimes the bonuses aren't fully explained or apply to other new or renamed concepts.
* Tech tree pretends to be less linear, but it's not. The exponential tech required for each subsequent trie means that you still end up going in a more n-level preferential pattern. I tried digging deep initially and paid for it.
* Maybe my game was bugged or I did something wrong, but I was constantly surrounded with 2+ Krakens and 2+ siege worms at all times. For reference, since that doesn't mean anything if you haven't played, these are alien monsters that one-hit the majority of units in the game. They take about 5 turns to kill from a distance with mid-game units. I was unable to expand due to the siege worms and being surrounded by "miasma," which damages and hinders units on tiles with miasma. While I'm aware there are techs to get rid of it, the rest of the AI didn't seem to have the same problem.
* I kept wishing I was playing Civ V, or something that more closely resembled it, actually--even the base game without the DLC's. They should have used more familiar concepts with regard to resources, technologies, and buildings.
* While they could be an interesting game mechanic, the constant quest popups get old quickly.
On a positive note, I really liked how intra-civilization trade was a viable option in this game, with included techs and culture (or whatever) options to boost that option; most especially because I was surrounded by aliens that would blockade my trade routes otherwise.
Maybe with updates and DLC this game will be better but honestly I think there's a fundamental problem with the art design and the general naming conventions etc. that would stop me from playing--again for context, this is coming from someone who loves scifi novels and has an engineering BS and is a year away from an MD, it's not like I'm unfamiliar with the pseudo-scientific terms they were trying to use.
Last, sorry I know I didn't keep this short, I found the interface overall more difficult to use than Civ V. They repositioned many of the old menus, and there's no longer the top-left drop down menu with the most important views (units, tech, etc.)--I made significant use of that panel in Civ V and its exclusion was frustrating. WRT menus, the art design used a very monochromatic theme with poor visual differentiation. Hard to read.

Note: I write this as someone who loves story-driven games, and couldn't care less about an FPS. I played through Bioshock on easy difficulty, not caring a whit about the combat or combat mechanics. If you want those reviewed; look elsewhere.
Overview:  If you haven't played the first Bioshock, then go play that instead.  If you have, then Bioshock 2 makes for a fine, if not terribly ground-breaking, addition to the franchise.
The setting and atmosphere are the same here as they were in the fist Bioshock.  If you loved that, then you'll find this more of the same.  There are certainly some new touches here and there to flesh out the history and culture of the City of Rapture--enough so that it never felt repetitive.  Still, there really wasn't anytime when I thought to myself "Oh, that's different!".  And the music is still gorgeous.
The characters here are superb: Sofia Lamb is the best villian in the Bioshock series (hands down), and Eleanor makes for a much better guide and moral conscious than Atlas.
Themewise , however, I think Bioshock 2 takes a small step backwards.  But the first Bioshock had the advantage of hitting a single thematic note: the dangers of making the worship of free markets into a quasi-religious belief.  Bioshock 2 muddies the waters, still periodically reminding us of the themes of the first game (it does take place in Rapture, after all), but also now warning us about the dangers of hyper-communistic ideology.  (Not Marxism--communistic as in communal living.)
The story is also not as good as the first one.  The minor compaint is that the ending is a bit more bittersweet than the first game, lacking the first Bioshock story's finality.  The more serious complaint, however, is that the fates of several major chacters remain completely unexplained at the end of the game.  The ending just felt unnecessarily truncated, and not nearly as satisfying.
Still, for anyone who played and enjoyed Bioshock, Bioshock 2 is easily worth your time.

If popular opinion is to be believed, Bioshock 2 is a game that suffers under the shadow of the remarkable first game in the series, which is mostly regarded as being the better of the two journeys into the depths of Rapture (that is, if one can actually classify separate journeys into the depths of madness and depravity as being somehow being “better” than one another).  Some of this opinion is warranted, but in other crucial ways this game actually manages to outshine its older sibling.
Let’s talk a bit about story and setting, as I feel that these two elements define the heart of the Bioshock experience.  Much like its antagonist, the first game was responsible for creating Rapture, the ugly, decrepit, and rusted out undersea dystopia.  In Bioshock 2 well you’ll sure see more … of the same.  The trouble with a setting like Rapture really is that it’s a bit self-contained, both literally and figuratively.  It’s wonderfully detailed, and there are hundreds of stories to be told (as evidenced by the many audio diaries that reappear in this game), but it’s still a microcosm.  So Bioshock 2 returns you to the same old Rapture you've seen before, to visit the same old menagerie of drug addled psychos you've set on fire before.  In a lesser setting this might prove to be an issue, but that’s just it; the world of Rapture has enough texture and atmosphere that it can
stand strong even if you do have some sense of déjà vu upon your return.  The weight of dread, hopelessness, and despair bears down on you every bit as much as the weight of the ocean around you, which in turn allows you to once again soak in the experience of Rapture.
In terms of story, your reaction may depend on how you feel about canon and its role in a larger story arc.  Indeed there are some potential issues here in terms of overall canon.  It takes some firm suspension of disbelief to swallow the premise that the Rapture we saw in the first game survived another 10 minutes after our first departure, much less another
.  The character of Sofia Lamb is bolted on to the canon in such a way that it begs the question, if Lamb was such a prominent figure in Rapture, why did we not hear of her in the first game?  How are there still splicers down here, being that they seem to be a pretty nonfunctional self-destructive lot, and I can’t imagine that they’d be capable of reproduction (nor would I want to …
).  So yes, there may be some issues with Bioshock 2 in terms of the overall canon of the series, but here’s the clincher, and a statement which may net me some detractors.  If you can look past the minor issues above, the story in Bioshock 2 is actually better than the first game.  Sorry Ken Levine, but the boys at 2K Marin may have managed to top the amazing story set forth in the original Bioshock.  In the first Bioshock, one of the major premises of the game revolves around the question of, “Why am I doing this?”  (And I’m hoping at least
answered, “A man chooses, a slave obeys”).  The original Bioshock is brilliant science fiction populated by a colorful rotating sideshow of psychotic freaks.  But it missed a bit of the human element.  In Bioshock2 you know immediately who you are (in a basic sense), what you must do, and crucially
you must do it.  This opens up the opportunity for a more humanist approach to Rapture, being that the resolution of this tension allows for huge opportunities in characterization.  And Bioshock 2 seizes upon that opportunity in spades.  In the first game I was purely vested in the mystery itself which was great, but in this game I was actually attached to the characters as well.  This manages to add some emotional heft to the story which I felt was missing a bit in the first game.  (In truth this is probably helped by the fact that I myself am a parent, and the central themes of Bioshock 2 revolve heavily around what it means to be a parent … err … Daddy)
So how’s the gameplay?  Well a lot like the first game, the difficulty curve here is a bit frontloaded.  As you gain plasmids, tonics, and weapons upgrades the game becomes significantly easier.  In some ways this is a bit unfortunate at least insofar as it would have been nice to feel that rush of badassery immediately upon stepping into the brass boots of a Big Daddy.  As it is you start off a bit weak and underpowered, slowly growing into your role as a walking fortress.  And that’s fine really.  It wouldn’t be super-fun or challenging if you
as the biggest badass in Rapture.  Just as in the first game, Bioshock 2 really finds its groove when you start gaining power-ups to assist you in your endeavor, and it’s at this point that the gameplay absolutely shines.  It’s still an absolute blast to figure out interesting and advantageous combinations of plasmids, tonics, and weapon upgrades in order to rain death upon the doomed denizens of Rapture.
There was one element of the first game that I did miss in Bioshock 2 which was the open world component.  In the original Bioshock  you felt the massiveness of Rapture in that you could travel from one end of the city to the other if you were so inclined.  In Bioshock 2 your experience is firmly divided into a level-based structure.  There are plot devices in place to help make some sense out of this particular element, but it warrants a mention.  To say that the game plays on rails is an understatement, being that your conveyance between levels for half the game is in fact a train.  It’s a minor thing, but I certainly would have loved to have the ability to return to previous levels for more in-depth exploration.  Oddly I also found some issue with repetitive tasks in the game, which I feel is also partly related to its strictly structured levels.  The way in which you’re tasked with the repetitive task(s) of rescuing a Little Sister, gathering Adam, dealing with the Little Sister, fighting Big Sister, wash, rinse, repeat … starts to feel a bit grind-y by the end of it.  It also impacts the pacing of the story a bit.  I think an open world setting might have relieved this issue somewhat in that it would have been nice to set my own agenda for handling the Little/Big sisters rather than being forced to handle everything in a level before moving onto the next without hope for return.  Once again this is a small issue in the grand scheme of things, but one that definitely became noticeable to me.  Luckily the combat allows for so much creativity and improvisation that this cycle rarely becomes a dreaded chore (despite my comments on grinding).
So there you have it.  I must say that after two games of being trapped at the bottom of the ocean with the worst sort of abominations imaginable, I’m looking forward to taking my Bioshock experience to the sky in Bioshock Infinite, drifting through the clouds … with the worst sort of abominations imaginable.
At any rate I found Bioshock 2 to be an excellent game particularly suited for fans of dark science fiction and horror, as well as anyone that enjoys story driven first person shooters.

This review comes from the perspective of a long-time player. I've played the cards since childhood, and enjoyed games like Shandalar (if that sounds unfamiliar to you, look it up!). I truly want this game to succeed. However, I am left disappointed and I would like to point out why.
I can only be so lenient when a game like Magic Duels is virtually free. I applaud the new cards and balance. The artwork is always good. Did I mention the game is free? This is great! It's free to play and you may purchase packs by earning gold within matches. You may also purchase packs with real money. The folks behind Magic need to survive of course, so this is expected. This review is focused on the free play (I have purchased a pack, and it's not that rewarding - they should add a foil in there to provide extra incentive).
Let's get straight to it. You find obtain new cards by collecting gold, and you use this gold to purchase "packs," which contain 6 cards. The fastest way to collect gold is against other players online and win matches. You do not get rewarded any gold for losing a match. The game matches can take up to and over 30 minutes! If you win a match you are rewarded 20 gold. To purchase one pack, it costs 150 gold. Aside from small bonus quests, it would take at least 8 wins to afford a pack. They need to provice some incentive to hang around and lose. Players tend to quit on you the moment they realize they may lose so they don't waste time playing if they are not rewarded in any way. Losers should get rewarded 10 gold so that they have a reason to hang around and still play.
The matchmaking - if we can call it that at all - is as follows: The game awards you "ranks" in the most simplist manner possible. If you win 1 match, you gain 1 rank. If you lose a match, you lose one rank. The first thing you'll notice is that ranks don't matter at all. You're still matched with people who have grossly different ranks then you.
Even worse, if you join a match and leave, you lose a rank but are otherwise not penalized. Playres abuse this by leaving matches to lower their rank and play quicker matches against weaker players. Why? Because the only incentive to play is to WIN. Bummer to the new players :\
TL;DR: Because of poor matchmaking and no incentive for the loser of the match, players who have powerful cards may force matches with weaker players to finish games asap.

I feel like this game had two lead developers, we'll call them Tom and Lumpy. Now Tom is a reasonable guy, good head on his shoulders, and has a knack for coming up with good ideas. Lumpy was placed there because he was someone's cousin and someone owed someone else a favor. Lumpy is not a good designer. Lumpy's only talent is to uncerimoniously shart on any new idea presented such that it immediately becomes terrible.
But because he's someone's cousin and someone owed someone else a favor, Lumpy gets veto power over Tom.
So the two sit down at the first development meeting and I imagine the conversation going thusly:
Tom: I think a more open world-style game that allows the player to explore and roam at will through a large area would work best. We can make it a casino, that way there's plenty to do and look at.
Lumpy: Perfect! We can break everything up into chunks that take forever to get through unless you run and miss most everything interesting!
Tom: Erm...ok, so as far as story, let's have the plot revolve around the main character's daughter. They've developed a cure but she has to keep taking it.
Lumpy: Great! We can attach it to a timed mechanic that means you have to sprint through the complex and sprawling levels to get back to her to give her medicine or else she dies and the game instantly ends.
Tom: Ummm...I guess. I was also thinking we could do the custom weapons thing again. See what kind of crazy things players will come up with.
Lumpy: I love it! Then we'll make these weapons super fragile so they break near immediately and the components are hard to get so you don't get to use them hardly ever and the rest of the time you just have to wail on zombies with whatever is handy!
Tom: *sigh* Ok, ok, ok. The main character is a reporter, so let's include a kind of photography system. Adds a new dimmension to game play and opens up a lot of avenues for sharable content and humor.
Lumpy: Brilliant! We can force that to be a core part of gameplay and jerk the player out of the action and tension with unnecessarily long animations and grading screens!
Tom (who by now is close to tears): I...I guess we can do that...but we need something to add some tension to the game. The daughter thing is good but some overarching tension in terms of the surroundings would be great.
Lumpy: I know! Let's have the whole game run on a timer so that you have to race through and miss most of the cool stuff before the time runs out or you automatically die! And it'll mean people have to replay the game over and over again!
Tom: ...I hate you so much right now.
That's about the formula for the game; take one good idea and smash it to death with bad ones until you find yourself sobbing at your desk asking the game gods why and wishing dearly to be able to get this game out of your library.

I'll start off by saying that this game is very similar to bioshock 1. It improves in some aspects and degrades in others.
STORY
The story is pretty straightforward, save Eleanor Lamb (aka your little sister). The whole story and background is explained through the audio logs found throughout the game, so exploration is recomended. The story overall is good, but it never came close to the story of the first one, so you'll probably feel dissapointed by the linearity of this one. Despite this fact it's a compelling and heart-breaking story.
GAMEPLAY
Gameplay-wise, they didn't change much from Bioshock 1, the plasmids and the weapons are basically the same, with slight variations of effects and names of the weapons. The only notable difference is the drill, which can help you cut through a huge mob of splicers, or just become obsolete after you got your first weapon.
GRAPHICS
I didn't notice anything different from the first game, they upgraded some textures and some shaders, but it's basicaly the same. One thing i noticed is the lack of atmosphere in this game, in Bioshock 1 there were many moments where i would feel genuinly scared of what is coming next (especially when the lights went out), in this game it's almost always rooms with more then enough illumination to see where everything is.
In conclusion, this game didn't live up to my expectations of a sequel, the gameplay and graphics didn't see much improvment, the story isn't as good as the first one, but it's stil good, and the atmosphere just isn't there. But after all that said, I would still recomend you play the game, since it's dirt cheap these days, and despite it's flaws compared to its predecessor, it's a damn good first person shooter!

Ah Bioshock, my first introduction to the joy that is the first person shooter. The original Bioshock has become a classic, even a legend, and became a hugely amazing argument for video games as art. Bioshock 2 brought mixed reviews from the fans, though, with some complaining that it wasn't nearly as good as the first and not liking the change of focus from storyline/gameplay to character development/gameplay. This was balanced somewhat by the cool factor of getting to play as a big daddy.
As for me, I think Bioshock 2 is a solid and enjoyable sequel. Yes it has it's issues with a somewhat weak storyline but as I love character development I was still super pleased with the game. Bioshock 2 brings in new plasmids, new enemies, and new strategies for combat with your ability to now set up ambush/kill zones. 2 also works at fixing the lack of handicap from choosing to save the little sisters instead of harvesting them from the first game. The choices you make during the game all have more of an impact on the ending than in the first one which really only had two endings. Bioshock 2 has 3 main endings but, according to your choices, those 3 endings have several variations.
Come back to Rapture and enjoy exploring the further devolution into madness and decay after the end of the first game. Explore further the evolution and creation of the Big Daddies and little sisters and see what future awaited the little sisters left behind when Jack escaped the city. Explore the DLC Minerva's Den where you play an entirely new character and learn even more about the city and how it works. You can also join in on multiplayer to experience the Rapture War first hand. The game definitely has it's flaws but like I said, I still find it a solid additon to the series and a very enjoyable game. Bioshocks 1 and 2 both hold spots on my Top 5 favorite games list.

KNOW THIS, the game is great, I enjoyed it alot.
The reason it is not recommended, is strictly due
to technical issues.
Gameplay:
You go through 9 areas in Rapture City in just
the same fashion as in the first game; Taking on
Big Daddies to get to Little Sisters, looting dead
enemies and every kind of containers you come
across, obtain and upgrade your weapons, plasmids
and gene-tonics. It's all in there.
The main differences being first off how this
installment is not as free roaming as the first
game was, where you could move between the areas.
In this sequel, you have to make sure you've done
all you want to do in a level before you move on,
because there is no chance going back once you do.
Then you have the so called Big Sisters, a new
enemy that will make Big Daddies seem like a 90
year old, compared to Bruce Lee.
Not only are you merely playing as a Big Daddy,
you can also do his main-duty of adopting Little
Sisters and protecting them, while they collect
ADAM from corpses to give you more.
Controls:
Not much to say, the controls are fluent.
I can't see anything amiss in them, there are
slightly more features than in the first game.
Music:
It's music includes old real life classics, a new
collection of course, mostly in the Jazz genre.
You can tell from the background music when a
tough enemy is on the way, it gets dramatic.
Graphics:
The graphics are done exactly in the same delicate
way like in the first game, having great water and
fire effects.
Story:
Takes place 10 years after the first game, which
should then be 1969. You are a Delta model of a
Big Daddy, having been shot dead, but resurrected
and stored within a Vita Chamber by your own
Little Sister, this back in 1959.
The 10 years pass, and you awake with your goal
of reunite with your, now grown up, Little Sister.
Bug and Drawback Listing:
*Random crashing, which is the most common issue
you may experience when playing. It may differ
on exactly how it happens, depending on who you
ask. For me, the game just shut down without any
information at all, close to 20 times in total
during my whole playthrough.
*Hits on enemies just refuse to register alot
of times while in battle. This occurs often if
the enemy is doing some kind of animation while
you hit it, and is therefor seen mainly on Houdini
Splicers and Alpha Series, as they are using alot
of graphical effects. But sometimes even a slow
walking Ledhead Splicer at distance, can somehow
be invulnerable, the shots will just go through
whilst leaving its impact on the wall behind.
This leaves little to no use for the improved
zoom upgrade to the speargun for example.
It feels like the game design was primarly aimed
for the player going for the drill and plasmids.
While the gun selection is showing a great mix,
the hit registration sometimes drags it down.
*Enemies can suddenly spawn out of thin air.
This causes a problem if you have cleared a room
and are setting up traps for a planned battle.
Suddenly random enemies can spawn behind your
back and trigger your traps that you have put time
and effort on for a upcoming fight.
Conclusion:
I'm afraid I can't recommend this specific port
version of the game.
By purchasing this, you are putting it all up to
chance. Its a lottery how the game will run on
your PC, depending on a combination of your
hardware, drivers and other OS softwares.
Such application behaviour is by me, unacceptable.
Get a console version instead.

Summary
Hitman Absolution is a 3rd person stealth game. You play the game as agent 47, a rogue assassin. The game is a series of stealth puzzle sand boxes linked by a very simple story. There is no save system which makes the game more and more frustrating as you progress. But if you get too frustrated you can forget stealth and just kill everybody rampage style. The game has great production values. The cut scenes, level variety, level graphics, voice acting etc. are all very good. The game has a huge amount of replay value. And it is great that you can just play any section in any level. This is the most flexible game in the series and the least frustrating game in the series and the best looking, so I would recommend this game over any of the others. Runs acceptably on windows 10.
Detail
Hitman Absolution is a 3rd person stealth game. This game is a series of stealth puzzle sand boxes. You play the game as agent 47, a rogue assassin, the game is story driven linking all the puzzle sand boxes together. Unlike the previous hitman games that can be impossibly frustrating, this one tries to be a bit more fun. But it is still missing a decent save system. So you are given a sand box you have to explore, yet you are often punished for exploring and experimenting by having to replay the same part again and again and again. For example you may have 2 or 3 targets to kill and then escape. But you will have to repeat the kills again and again and again while you learn how to escape.
The game is better designed and more flexible than previous games making it more accessible to people new to the franchise. It has a half finished checkpoint system on easier difficulties making it a tiny bit less frustrating early on in the game.
As the game progresses the need to explore, the difficulty of exploring and the complexity of the areas all increase. So with the punishing resets the game gets more and more frustrating. Although you "level up" skills, these have no benefit what so ever. In many of the later levels, the punishing resets were so frustrating I gave up with stealth totally and just shot everybody in the head. But I had to give up on the 360 controller and use the mouse and keyboard to get the head shots fast enough.
I would recommend this game, as it is the least frustrating game in the series. But I was disappointed that it doesn't deliver the level of fun that the designers wanted, or that I was expecting from all the interviews and hype. The game wants you to explore and experiment and yet punishes you for doing it. I want to play a hitman, I want to love the hitman games, but without a save system the games are all too frustrating.
There are lots of challenges per area/sand box. These are quite addictive, but can be very frustrating. As the challenges are often the extremes of the designed gameplay, you notice that the controls start to hinder you rather than help you. I was using a 360 controller.
With all the challenges, the game has a huge amount of replay value. The characters have slightly different Reponses based on who you are disguised as, or how you are acting. On the early levels it makes each run through feel a little fresh. On later levels there are just a million guards. So the levels have much less personality about them. All the levels feel unique which is great. And you can play any section is any level at any time which is great.
The designers talked about a great main story and if you over heard the characters dialogues during play you would discover stories within stories. It is a very, very simple story, but the main characters are interesting and their dialogue is well written and the voice acting is good. So I enjoyed the cut scenes. On the early levels it was fun watching the characters interact but on later levels it just feels like the levels are all guards. I was trying to listen out for interesting dialogue, but didn't pick up on any stories within stories.
I had a few technical issues on windows 10. The game crashed every couple of hours with directx errors. When restarting from a checkpoint again and again and again. The loading times would tend to get very long. I would need to exit the game and restart.

This game is so much fun,but it have a few problems Hitman Absolution is the fifth in hitman series. A super ,clone ,assassin. The story is more cinematic and personal as before.
. It's a good story,but not a great one. The characters are portraied like morons, dumb, sex addicts and plain ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Exept for 47 and one,two other characters of course (a drug kingpin and a wrestler) . Every hardcore series fan will have a problem with the level presentation. It's not a huge sandbox anymore (except for a town) ,the levels are broken in smaller sections. For a casual gamer this is a good thing, if you screw up you can restart the section and not the whole level. But I prefer the sandbox feel. It's not all as bad as it sounds, the design is gorgeous, crowds are huge with a lot of conversations between NPCs. So the story is avarage but the design is marvelous, Let's talk about gameplay. The gameplat is beautiful.Mechanics well done and very smooth. A new and good addition is the cover system.It makes thngs better. A bad addition is the new disguise system.. Yes,it makes the game harder,a good thing for perfectionists but also it's too damn sensitive. If you stay close to the same type of enemy your disguise is from, you are revealed. It makes sense in a small town,where everyone knows each other but when I'm wearing adisguise witch contains a sky mask,it's too much.(I'm wearing a ♥♥♥♥ing mask,how could you know I'm not one of the crew?) . The checkpoints are broken. If you die and respawn at a checkpoint, all your previous enemies respawn as well, no matter if you let them in plain sight or stashed them in bins. The assassination methods are multiple and creative. As 47 you take control on your enemies fate. There are many objects you can pick (busts, bottles, knifes and others) you can use as weapons or distractions. You can find in levels some collectables as well( evidences) .from this point of view the game is a ++. Many accidents and assassinations are avalible.(around 11-12 for a target in any level) and many other creative kills.On gameplay, sound, voice, this game excels. I have a lot of fun with 47. But this game is not all about singleplayer, it has multiplayer. The contract mode, where you enter a level,mark a target from the NPCs and perform an assassination, based on your play, game unlocks chaalanges and you can share the contract online to be played by others and race in points. It's a fun, but limited mode because of small level design. So yeah, I'm not a professional reviewer and not very good with words, I'm just someone ho likes stealth games. Bottom line: Pros: Great ganeplay, great replayability,multiplayer mode( still can be improved) voice and sound in general and most of all, a hell lot of fun. Cons: avarage story, chracters (exept 47 and the kingpin) annoying checkpoint system. I had and still have a great time..I ♥♥♥♥ing love 47 . This game is a solid 8 in my book of stealth. I recommend this game even full price, if you got it on sale even better. Special thanks for Cezar ,a friend of mine, who gave me this gem as a gift.

This is a great and unique game. It does an excellent job of using sound both as a gaming device and for atmosphere/intensity.
At its core it's a game of Marco Polo where you hit the "Listen" key and listen to the responses; taking note of both the direction and the intensity of the sound to find out direction+distance; this is far more satisfying than the typical RPG that just shows an exact location on the map or a magical compass point. Throw in creative use of color contrast for the "ghost" and "regular" worlds, with harrowing investigations and you have a winner.
My only compaint is it can be a bit repetitive at times. Having to cover both worlds on every map gets a bit much, especially later in the game when you have to do back tracking. All-in-all though the mystery keeps you hooked until the very end.

Betrayer tries to work more with audio then most games and to it's credit pulls it off nicely. I would seriously recommend using a decent headset while playing this game. Most of the times when a game tries black and white(and red I guess) gameplay it can become difficult to differentiate objects, especially when off in the distance though I never had an instance where I had any issues. The game also has some decently implemented mechanics, like the wind rusteling through tall grass and tree's to drown the sound of your footsteps out makes for a great effect.
Sadly enough I feel asif Betrayer has far too few mechanics to keep it intresting. There's not a big variety in enemies or weapons to use. But my biggest complaint of the game is the dark world.
Basicly, the game has 2 'worlds' ; the light and the dark world. The light world would be considered the 'normal' world,  You feel asif you are in a real forest as the light world is richly detailed with plantlife, small settlements, filled with audio effects,.. Basicly you feel asif you are walking through a real forest. The dark world, is basicly the exact same as the light world, without the many audio effects, a much smaller view distance, a darker light filter and different enemies; though in theory, those 'different enemies ' are just reskins. the standard light world enemies use bows/muskets while the standard dark world enemy shoots bones. You'll deal with them in the same manner so they are pretty much the same.
I also feel that the many mysteries involving the deaths of the people on the island could be a bit better worked out, you can never seem to speculate what happened untill the puzzle is solved through the various NPC's you'll encounter, you pretty much run from one place to another gathering evidence, showing it to NPC's and they'll tell you the story.
All in all, I liked Betrayer; asmuch as I disliked having to go to the dark world because it felt like padding out the game just to reach a justifyable play time, the light world does carry it as it's simply a beautiful environment

With 46 levels and 149 recipes to craft, Brushwood Buddies can start to seem like an exercise in futility. Certain levels will take only a few steps of crafting to achieve the end goal, while others may take upwards of 20 steps. These include attracting animals, killing them, harvesting their hide or meat, using these new items to aid in the creation of more recipes in order to attract and kill craftier animals... you can see the pattern emerging. Later levels can become very difficult but the best hints come from the recipe log, where it's easy to see what leads to the creation of a certain item by following each step.
One mechanic I do not like, however, is the randomness of each level's layout. Sometimes it would be in my favour with what elements are spawned across the board, but on the rare occasion I'd find that the item I desperately needed would refuse to drop due to poor luck, forcing me to reload the board. Despite this I'm having fun trying to solve each level while trying to keep each of my little friends happy. It's nice to see that such a small game like this even has official mod support.
The art style is cute and very simple. There are only two music tracks but they are played at infrequent intervals as to not become an annoyance. The only problem I faced was that the game would not enter full-screen mode despite enabling it in settings and, while I do appreciate the extensiveness, I feel the settings menu has been poorly laid out.

Prior to the praise, let me say this.  I eagerly await SOME form of update or additional content to bring us...well...additional content.
That being said, after spending a few days with this gem, I'm blown away!  This is exactly what I've been craving in a space/flight game.  I have tried and tried to gain proficiency piloting in Elite Dangerous via keyboard and just can't get it down.  With this game, you navigate on a single open plane.  This is a nice simple navigation and "broadside" battle setup that you will not find overly complicated.  If you played Assassin's Creed: Black Flag and got relative enjoyment from the broadside battles at sea, then you should already be downloading this game.
Although the battle is not overly complicated, it is by no means simplistic.  There is plenty of strategy to the battle and the biggest payoff is in how you outfit your ship (Black Flag again).  The main story keeps you going, no dullness yet. Also, extra big kudos to the soundtrack.  I could fly around the various systems picking fights and hauling cargo all day long with this music jamming!
I truly hope the developers push this a little further with maybe some deeper missions or stories to pursue.  It is, after all, a REALLY big sandbox.  Also, if it's not to much to ask maybe a tad more complexity be invested in the space stations.  It's not a game breaker like some whiners say, but I can see where a little more polishing could help.  Frankly, I'm in and out of stations in the blink of an eye so I don't mind copied and pasted stations.  I'm more eager to get back out there and destroy something!

Everyone is a critic. I think that anyone looking too deeply into this game should be playing something else. If you got the idea that there would be story from watching the games trailer, your perception skills are SEVERELY lacking. Although the game has had issues with AMD hardware, in game bugs, and some lackluster AI... I still find the game enjoyable as something mindless to do. I bought it knowing exactly what I was getting, and I was given exactly what I was expecting.My only negatives are the healing system, getting shot from offscreen, using grayscale on top of the already present grayscale to show enemy outlines behind walls, and the cars that are made out of gasoline soaked paper and illegal chinese fireworks.
To elaborate... To heal, you need to execute wounded victims, which can be hard since it's a random chance to actually wound someone. I think either regening health or first aid kits would have absolved this issue. Maybe even have Med Kits that you pick up and use, while keeping executions in the game. Getting shot from offscreen is more of an annoyance than a problem, mostly because 9/10 times I can just right click and see who's shooting at me. I think a better way to show people behind walls, instead of the gray and gray look, is to use the objective finder red outline instead. It's much more noticable, and a simple way of doing things.The cars are a neat idea, but dear god, trying to drive one at all, even without getting shot at, is a horrific experience in and of itself. A shotgun blast sends your car into flames, and then a bird ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ on the hood is the final kicker for it to explode on you. Those are really all my complaints, but everyone else seems to like to find everything wrong with a game and make a big deal out of nothing.

In "This War of Mine", you find yourself in the middle of an ongoing civil war. Which is fine until you realize that you don't get a gun, or a knife, food, or water. As it turns out, you don't get to play as a soldier!
Oh no, you are not a soldier. You are a civilian, stuck in the middle of No Man's Land. And depending on the choices you made in the beginning, you may or may not be alone.
"This War of Mine" presents itself as a hybrid 2D/3D side-scroller. You give commands to your civvies and hopefully your commands make them survive. A good hand-eye reaction is needed in combat scenes, as one moment of delay can determine whether or not you get to take shotgun or depression home.
There are variations on the civilians available, some being good - like having 5 extra inventory slots or culinary experience, and some being bad - like being an old man.
There are also variations on the available civilians' reactions, but generally helping your neighbors = good = morale up. On the other side of the token you get hurting your neighbors = bad = boo-hoo. Which pisses me off a little because it's a goddamned war and you still worry about stealing stuff from bandits? They're probably the same people who raid the shelter at night.
Also, the AI aren't autonomous. If I may, I'd say that there is no actual AI. You do the mapping, the movement, et cetera. Sure, it's all done by a few clicks, but is it really hard for them to cook hot meals by themselves? All they do as far as I can see is take a book/make coffee/light a cigarette and then make a beeline for the nearest chair.
And then there's the combat. I've made it work by ditching melee, but I have once died and I couldn't quite figure out why. So imagine this: me = with gun, axe and ammo, enemy = with gun and ammo but facing away from you. I click on the attack button and do 50% damage (it's a shotgun at close range) but as I clicked on the attack button again, the idiot
towards the guy to hit him with an axe. Needless to say, I got bashed by his shotgun's butt
RIP Pavle.
But despite all of this, I found myself sticking around for... 70 hours. You might ask, "Why?"
For one, it is strangely refreshing to survive a playthrough. Like, when it says "The war is over", I stare at the message and wonder to myself, "Did I survive? Oh yes I did."
Two, if you actually read the bios of your civilians (which update at intervals - I can't say if the intervals are fixed), story time! I haven't taken the time to read them all, partly because I'm trying to survive, partly because you only get to control a maximum of 4 survivors at a time (please don't increase that cap).
Three, it's a war simulator! It's like Call of 12-Year-Olds! Except that there are no twelve year-olds in-game, and that you don't get guns until you murder someone who has them (or repair broken guns you find, play the game to learn more).
So there you have it, a review of mine for the game called "This War of Mine".

Magic is like chess. You and your arch enemy (everyone is arch enemy online) sit yourselves down and get an imaginary board between you, where he got his side and you got yours. Then you each got a collection (that you build yourself) of 60 chess pieces, and draw seven random ones. Then you get to beat with them on your opponent, while he beats back. The fun part is, put into chess terms, that you should always try to kill as many opposing pieces with as few of yours as you can. Here comes mind games, trickery, epic turns of events, and conceptually this game goes so much farther than chess. Would you like to play a piece that wipes the whole board, leaving nothing? What about stealing one your opponent's pieces and beating him with it till he succumbs in a pool of tears? Or how about combining a strategy where you got huge crowds of tiny nasty critter pieces that don't really care for whatever strategy your opponent is running, and just overrun him or her, in a true zerg-swarm style?
These are just a few examples of things you can do. You know what I am thinking about right now? Building a strategy entirely based around tentacles. Giant crabs. Weird fish. Entangling. That's right.
Magic Duels is one of many Magic games, and this one serves best as an introduction. It's free, and it's got a nice short tutorial that teaches you all the basics. In fact this game is where it is easier to start if you are interested in trying to see whether this is a game you would like to play in real life.
But it goes beyond that, although the depths of it aren't that exciting. It gives you a pool of cards (the pieces) to play with at the beginning, but if you want more, you have to purchase packs of random cards (which means that sometimes you will open something epic, like a big tentacle creature, and other times you will open something really boring, like a non-tentacle creature). You can pay real cash for them, but you also can do various daily game-play oriented quests to earn them shiny coins. But it is a slow progress: you will end up buying a booster pack maximum every third or fourth day, giving you like 12 new random cards each week. It's not so exciting, really.
If you are familiar with magic, this game only includes the newest sets: 2015 Magic set, and Battle for Zendikar. Oath of the Gatewatch set is set to come sometime during March or April.
So yeah, I recommend this game because it gives a nice intro to Magic the Gathering. It's very basic, there is no trading, no other game modes but simple duels against other people or A.I.

So, my review is going to be a little bit different to everybody else's that I have read so far. It seems people tend to commonly go on about storyline and the colour scheme, and how spooky the game is. I'm going to give you a couple of brief sentences about what I find enjoyable about the game, rather than what the game is about.
1st of all a couple of notes on colour. Yes, it's a stark monochrome black and white world, but in a later patch, they've enabled the ability to turn the contrast and brightness all the way up or down, and also to turn the colour saturation all the way up or down. the screenshots that you see in black and white, are the default colours for the game, and the ones in colour are with the colour scale at about a quarter. There are not sections in colour, and sections in greyscale, as I got the impression when I saw the screenshots.
I personally played with everything turned all the way down, and the gain off at night. It can be nice to have a bit of colour during the day though, to turn the situation up a little actually makes it and more enjoyable world to stomp  around in, and turning the saturation all the way up gives you a "Far Cry 3" feeling to the game.
on the subject of Far Cry 3, this game has many elements in common with it. You can go in stealthy and killed as many as you can, before you get detected and it all turns into the shooting fest. Saving and reloading is only the checkpoints. Billy game you feel like a stiff breeze would knock you over, and late game you feel like a complete wrecking ball able to charge in if you want to. the only thing really missing from Betrayer, is a really cool kill animation if you manage to sneak up behind enemy. That would have made the sneak attack approach much more worth it - in fact, that is the whole reason why I love our client. I played the entire game with a knife. Literally the only time I used weapons was on animals, or in sections that forced me to.
Some of the default key bindings are not particularly intuitive, especially the one about throwing a Tomahawk. I did change a couple of key bindings in regards to some of those things, but what you do with that is up to you.
I am not a fan of having background music killing in game, and sound as a very important mechanic in this game, precludes the use of music in the background. I enjoyed this particular aspect quite a lot.
I liked the size of the maps, they were just big enough, but not too big. There were enough of them, and not too many. The only thing is they were all very much the same, they were too similar format to map the scenery did not change very much at all, if at all.
There are a lot of "secondary missions" in the form of running around investigating lost souls and murders, and the like. It's not really mentioned by most people in the reviews, but this is the best method I've ever seen of doing investigations in any game, ever. It does use the sound of clues to lead you towards the next person, or the next item that you need to find, and that does help quite a bit at times. But what it did differently, as the investigations although a key part of the story never really felt frustrating like most games, where the puzzle orientated. This one had a flow and it never really stopped. It was more of a matter of being part of the journey, rather than bashing your head against someone else's idea of a brick wall. If you've ever played♥♥♥♥♥♥games we've got to do investigations, such as the Sherlock Holmes series, or  murdered: Soul suspect you'll find this a welcome relief to their horrible investigation mechanisms.
I've seen a couple of complaints about the lack of the number of types of enemies, but I find that there was enough variety in the enemies, and your approach to taking down, to keep it interesting. Mostly, because once I figured out how to find those little flaming guys before they left at, a kind of became like hunting the Hunter, except that the hunters were more like rabbits with big sharp teeth - oh, and flames. And short bows.
I really got dropped a little bit in and have to try and figure out what's going on, especially early in the game. I really recommend that at least for the 1st couple of levels, maybe the 1st 3 maps really try and stay away from looking for a walk-through of what's going on. That's really where the discovery of the game happens, and that's really part of what makes the game enjoyable.
One thing I didn't like a lot was there was a lot of to-ing and fro-ing from the 1st met at the last minute to the 1st met the last map again by the end of the game. Maybe that could and have bothered me quite so much, if it didn't have quite long load times between maps. I didn't mind too much, because every time you load it, all the enemies respawn, and I get to kill the more all over again. That's probably why have every achievement in the game.
Considering the direction of the game took, and how you got there, I personally found the ending a little bit incomplete? At least, I found an underwhelming. It felt rushed or unfinished or to sudden, or not thought out well enough, but the journey there was enjoyable enough to make it worth, so don't let the knowledge of the fact that it has an ending victory from from wanting to play the game. Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion is a unique space RTS games that centers around moving from planet to planet conquering and establishing your empire. The closest thing you can compare this game to is like playing CiV 5 in space, but its in real time.
Other than the homeworld franchise and a little nastalgic empire at war, this is one of the only space RTS games in existence that not only does not suck more than a tai hooker, but it actually pretty well done. Featuring massive and i mean massive battles between fleets of ships by the end game your ships will probably ram into eachother from a siezure because of all the laser beams flying everywhere.
As previously stated you start on 1 planet that revolves around 1 star, you then migrate to neighboring planets exterminating anything you come across around the planet, then you invade and conquer the ♥♥♥♥ out of it like a space age christopher columbus. Maps however can be extremely large, featuring multiple stars, each with their own set of planets revolving around them to conquer and add to the might of your empire.
Oh did i mention when you attack a planet already controlled by another main faction of the game you literally nuke it from orbit (because its the only way to be sure) until everyone dies and you can recolonize it, if that isnt enough for you then i dont know what is.
The reason i also say this game is a real time space version of civ 5 is because the game moves at a slow enough pace that you are playing an RTS, but at the same time you can manage your empire and economy etc with ease. The game also has one of the most well done camera systems ive seen in an RTS game, allowing you can look and go anywhere despite the map being gigantic, all with the simplicity of a scroll wheel.
But seriously, one of the best space rts games in existence, So if you are into either i would absolutely recommend buying it. Ever since i bought the original game its given me YEARS of entertainment.

Simply charming puzzle-crafting game.  It starts out innocently enough, with woodland creatures forging basics for survival, but eventually it turns dark and you're wandering through a post-apocalyptic wasteland with a ghost trying to craft something to banish the evil wizard who turned all the humans into zombies or ghosts (aka dead).
Story playtime took me about 7 hours.  The crafting starts very simple and gets progressively harder and more complex.  There are some shortcuts, but quite a bit of repetition (you'll need a cauldron for most of the puzzles, although the way to make it will change).  The final battle is more than a bit nerve-wracking and frustrating, but it's certainly not insurmountable and gives a real sense of accomplishment at the end.
There's also a 'challenge' mode where you have to do things like complete recipes within a time limit, but I'm not a fan of such modes.
8/10
Highs:
+ Oozes charm
+ Good tunes (although few of them)
+ Challenging puzzles
+ Satisfying crafting
Lows:
- Happiness system can be a source of headaches and it's not explained know how to make people happy
(turnip - apples, bugs; ghost - dismantling/making various human items; witch - leafs, magic; chicken - I have no clue)
You can't completely screw yourself, but it can be annoying trying to get everyone happy again.
- About 1/3 of the recipes are one-offs for story purposes and never used again; another 10ish are 'hidden' and entirely optional
- Recipe book only shows one possible solution for a recipe, even if there are multiple ways to do it
- A bit RNG heavy for a puzzle/crafting game
TL;DR: if you're a fan of crafting and/or puzzles, this is a hidden gem.  Well worth it at full price.
If you get stuck, check out Blara's youtube walkthroughs for the game (on the video page).  Incredibly helpful (and charming).

That's right! You know those ugly undies that your grandpa wears -- and that you probably wore when you were a kid? You should value them more, because they hold a power beyond imagination! On
you take control over Tiny, a young inventor on a quest to recover the pants passed down by his grandfather, which were stolen by Big. The plot seems extremely silly and childish, but T&B is truly a work of art with an eloquent sense of humor perfectly captured on the cartoonish art style and the indie-folk soundtrack.
The gameplay is based on a sandbox variation that lets you modify the world around you, but don't think that sounds promising if you're a construction sandbox fan!. At first it might seem like you'll be able to have lots of fun cutting things and changing the scenery, but the false sense of freedom soon falls flat and if you were expecting a true sandbox, you'll be disappointed. If you can cope with the fact that you'll only get things out of the way and eventually modify the world only to walk around, then the core mechanic becomes enjoyable, seemingly fresh and different. Aligned to how linear the levels are, this is the game's biggest weakness as well as its strength, considering how the puzzle difficulty escalates (not challenging, yet enjoyable).
Story-wise the title delivers an enjoyable and unforgettable experience, but there was probably more room for development. The characters and the world around them are interesting, but the journey is just too short and linear, leaving us thirsty. With all my failures, it took me only three hours to beat the story.  Be it a sequel, a DLC or a comic book, T&B's world and characters are sure worth more content!
Considering how linear and relatively easy the game is, would've been beneficial if the developers had come up with a more simple modding tool (the existing one available at ModDB) and made use of Steam Workshop. If that had happened, T&B's could've been one of the best indie games of its generation with a large fanbase -- considering players could contribute lore-wise, expanding this amazing experience.
Worth the full price, worth on discounts and the soundtrack edition is a must have for indie-folk fans! Despite its short length and no replay value, the experience doesn't disappoint if you can understand its quirky art style and humor!

Betrayer is one of the most unique FPSs I have played in the last couple of years. It is an unsettling adventure with lots of tragic stories to uncover and I thoroughly enjoyed playing through it.
By just looking at the gameplay videos, you can tell that the game is very heavy on atmosphere. The world has an eerie feeling to it and from the very beginning you know that something went very wrong here. The first time you are transported to the shadow realm, I guarantee some nerve-racking moments. Betrayer's setting is great because while you might not find many enemies, the tension is always kept very high. It is horror done right, not with cheap jumpscares but an atmosphere that is undoubtely chilling.
It also doesn't help that your weapons are true to the game's 17th century setting. If you thought that evading screaming skeletons and floating skulls wasn't enough, then imagine frantically reloading your muskets and pistols that use gunpowder.
The game does not hold your hand along the way and this is a very positive aspect in the age of dumbed-down game design. There is no objective marker, just a "listen" button that vagely gives you an audio cue about where to go next. This greatly helps immersion and you truly feel like a helpless chap among mysteries and monsters.
Overall, I can easily recommend Betrayer to people who enjoy a refreshing, immersive experience in a unique setting. I really hope that the developers will continue this story with an expansion at least and this is a very rare thing for me to say!
