To start: I used to add a much longer header to these reviews, but since it often made the reviews too long to submit, I've opted to leave it on my Backloggery.
Gameplay: There are a couple of comparisons that are hard to not make when talking about this game; the first comparison is Metal Gear Rising. This game's main gimmick is a laser that lets you carve up a good deal of the levels, and things can be carved freeform just as you could slice up certain objects in Metal Gear Rising (it also makes me wonder why the hell MGR is a 23GB download considering this game has pretty similar technology but comes up at just under 1GB). Most of the puzzles in the game are environmental in nature, giving you at least a couple of objects you can manipulate as well as the tools needed to manipulate them in order to get to where you need to go. It's never that hard to figure out where you need to go, but there are some times where the physics can make things slightly trial and error-y. Speaking of other tools, you've also got access to a rocket for forward pushing and a grapple hook for backwards pushing. Sadly, you don't have the ability to swing places using your grapple hook.
The levels themselves are very big and certainly do give a great sense of exploration. There's also various collectables strewn throughout the levels, which do require you to go out of your way and solve some sometimes kinda tricky puzzles. While I never did collect all 100% of the items ingame, I did get pretty close on most of the levels. That's where the replay value of this game lies, as this game is short. Very short. In fact, my first playthrough was just about two hours. That's because there's really only five levels in the game as well as a boss fight at the end which... just isn't very good. The final boss fight only has you using one mechanic, and even that mechanic has a tendency to just kinda not work at times. Yeah, the final boss is definitely the worst part of the game, which is a shame because the rest of the game was a pretty enjoyable romp.
Honestly, there's not much else to talk about for this game. It'll take the average player 2-4 hours to beat their first time, and maybe a bit longer to 100%. I've found a few secrets so far, and they were pretty well hidden. Overall though, this game is definitely short, but it is at least a very good couple of hours. I just really wish they made this game Steam Workshop compatible so that we could make our own levels for it. 8/10.
Story: The other thing that it's very hard not to compare this game to when talking about it is Adventure Time. While this game has a lot more profanity than Adventure Time (read as: has any profanity), the humor is definitely very similar. This is a game about recovering magical underwear from some big jerk named Big who stole them. Who is Grandpa? I dunno. The game never really goes into detail, but then again it doesn't really need to. Again, there's really not much to talk about on this front, but it's still a good bit of fun. 7/10.
Graphics: This game has downsampled resolution available out of the box. Lemme just run that by you again. This game, an Indie game, has DSR available by default. In fact, I didn't even need to do anything special; the game just launched at 2X 1080p. All it took was turning on V-Sync to run at a perfect 60FPS throughout the entirety of the game. As for average temperatures, downscaling from 2X 1080p ran my GPU at about 55degC, so nothing too harsh. Not that the game needed downscaling anyways; the art style and hugeness of the world is impressive enough as is. Again, the comparison to Adventure Time is hard to not make; hell, Tiny even looks like Finn. There weren't any graphical glitches, the game has DSR by default, and the world itself just plain looks fantastic. Great stuff. 5/5.
Sound: This game uses a lot of obscure Indie music, usually either jazzy or more rock oriented, and it all works very well. You can collect more songs by finding collectibles in-game, so you never get tired of any one song (although to be fair, there isn't enough game time to get tired of the songs anyways). If you're into pretty good, obscure bands, then this game has some material to offer you. Voice acting is Sim-ese, but it works well enough for comedic effect. Pretty solid effort on the audio front. 4/5.
Overall scores are: 8/7/5/4; cumulative score of 8.0/10. The length is gonna be a kicker for some, but if you think the price is right, odds are you'll come out of this game feeling pretty glad with your purchase. Again, it is just a 2-4 hour long game.

I recommend this game for anyone who like post apocalyptic adventure games because that's what it is. Ihose who like Sci Fi especially by Harlan Ellison would like this too as it's based on a short story of the same name by the same guy. Don't worry, if you read the short story it won't spoil the game for you. :) It's a looser interpretation.
Throughout the whole game, one points and clicks through several simulations for each of several characters which are essentially non linear levels. To beat the game you have to play them all successfully but in any order you like.
The GUI and art are nice especially for the time. They are very detailed so it feels more like watching an ascii painting unfold before you than an 8 bit retro adventure. You have several options for interacting with your world. (Talk, Walk, Look, Use, Eat)
Each simulation delves deeply into the characters past. The object of the game, the way to escape, is basically to confront the characters demons and conclude the narrative. There is a small morality system in place where the games ending is affected by how well your character did dealing with their past and flaws. Or if you simply make a mistake in surviving the simulation itself you are transported back to your torture box. Sometimes these narratives approach disturbing topics like♥♥♥♥♥♥ genocide, human sacrifice. However I wouldn't say the game itself is particularly disturbing or scary, it has more of a sense of dread and whatever atmosphere the setting you are placed in creates atmosphere.
The music and sound are okay. The voice acting is pretty good actually, but it does have it's hammy moments.
The puzzles aren't really normal puzzles. They're more like symbolic puzzles. There's this sequence where you kill some animals, and have to wipe your hands clean before you can progress in Gorrister's simulation. One wouldn't immediately think of that, but from a narrative standpoint it totally makes sense. It definitely shows that Harlan Ellison wrote this game.
This is a unique, moving experience with beautiful ascii graphics. Get it :)

Unlike the rest of society I refuse to take the moral high ground here. Hatred’s presence in the collective gaming press has been rife with petty sensationalism,  one could say the reactionaries turn my stomach and have permanently affected how I perceive many more established figures within said community.
On Hatred, one essentially takes on the role of a brooding dread-lord who sadistically murders people as a part of his genocide crusade. Framed in a gorgeous black and white cinematic scheme with tasteful chromatic effects entirely suited for the grisly journey one will undertake.
We have all had bad days, however if one dwells upon committing such acts for a considerable fraction of your existence, Hatred is the perfect game for you,  treat it as a culling holiday.
For this reason I am glad this game exists,  albeit cold,  stark and sociopathic,  ugly true enough. In it’s purest form effectively cathartic.
~Visceral execution sequences~ Endlessly enjoyable destruction of the game environment,  much like a sword this cuts both ways,  both for and against the player.
Presentation aside the game runs reasonably well save texture oddities and physics bugs, persistent clipping is a tad annoying as well however not something I feel detracts from the game-play on a whole.
**Note how the game runs is relative to specs,  only very recently did DC add an advanced graphics options for tweaking on lower end systems,  as of my initial review I was running Hatred with an Nvidia GTX 780ti my second machine couldn't even play Hatred till the very recent optimization patch,  even so there is a drastic difference in performance.(The Marina Sewers and Powerplant levels really take an excessive toll on my AMD Radeon 7570 HD)**
I do feel some decals(blood splatters on npcs) could have been executed better in terms of both visual fidelity and frequency,  particles however are to die for,  great job!
Some feel that the control scheme is atrocious,  I do not have any issue with the default mouse and keyboard controls,  this is probably due to being conditioned to worse control schemes over a decade i.e. the first two Gothic games and Secondlife. While there can be some line of sight issues at given moment nothing stands out as a red flag.
**if one experiences any excessive clunkiness it is probably hardware related - tweak your settings or upgrade your rig.**
As of this review I am at the Military Base, the second to last mission. Based upon my overall experience playing on Hard Difficulty I give Hatred a solid 4 out of Five stars.
**I have progressed further since that point however decided to replay prior maps to unlock certain Steam achievements,  up until mobo failure on my main rig at least. Only very recently have I been able to play Hatred again as the DC team has released a patch which optimizes performance for ATI/AMD hardware to an extent.**
**Don't say Destructive Creations never did anything for their consumers!**
A brief reprieve worth remembering,  kudos to Destructive Creations.
**Lastly,  do not let my review be a standard to how one should feel on this game,  if you hate this game so be it,  however if one feels I am supposed to apologize for enjoying Hatred - ♥♥♥♥ you. Gotta love double standards.**

The game's name is self-explanatory. Essentially you run around shooting wave after wave of aliens. It's not an arena style game, although a few levels give you that feeling..., but mostly you progress stage to stage clearing aliens. Sometimes you're helped by friendly characters. Sometimes you have to protect the character and sometimes you can let them die if you want.
The production value of conscription is somewhat lower than alien shooter two reloaded. The dialogue is very poorly translated English and the story, which is mostly nonexistent, is told only in a series of pop-up bubbles. I out about 2 hours into the thing and I'm still not quite sure what's going on. I also got stuck on the terrain far more often.
If you've played alien shooter revisited will be familiar with a lot of the gameplay. They've gone back to some of the, in my opinion, cheap gameplay mechanics where you have a lot of enemies you have to fight through to get to the device that is spawning more to destroy it. The early levels of alien shooter revisited and many levels in alien shooter two reloaded were better designed. A lot of times aliens got stuck on things like stairs and I just stood back and picked them off.
I enjoyed blasting things, but it just never was as much fun as I'd had in alien shooter 2 reload. I didn't enjoy the timed parts where you have to hurry to reach another area or the babysitting ones where I had to guard a character who had atrocious AI (they made up for it with insane number of hit points) who ran directly into the enemies and forced me to take hits blocking for her purely because she behaved so stupidly. This led up to possibly the most boring and stupid boss fight I've ever had, where I kept ducking into a side room, coming out, shooting the boss for a 30 seconds or so, then ducking back in, repeat. The boss barely seemed to notice/care I was blasting it.
The weapons are also curious. When I played I never had enough money for decent guns, until the very end when it handed me the superpowered weapons to fight the end boss. I mean there was an $80,000 difference in the price of guns. Where alien shooter two reloaded let you work your way up a little more evenly. As with their other games, there is a level where you get to control a turret near the end, but it feels completely tacked on only lasts maybe 30 seconds.
The game also has some now standard modes like survival and gunstand mode. That's a pretty fun level where you can use a turret to try to stop wave after wave of enemies until you eventually die. It's quite fun, but if you have any of the other recent Sigma team games then you already have these modes.
; My honest opinion, it's a fun game but ultimately, if you have both Alien Shooter and Alien Shooter 2 I'd avoid it as there's not a lot of point of buying this game. If you can get it on sale for a buck or two, it might be worth it, otherwise... nah...
Its also worth noting that getting this game to work on anything higher than Windows Vista is a pain...

Personal Rating: 4 of 10
Before you begin judging this review do take time to read why I gave it a 4. This is a pretty decent game with tonnes of potential. To top it all, it comes with a great plot which is the only thing to keeps me playing.
As you can already see, Dead Rising 2 is a zombie massacre game with seemingly illogical/nonsensical gameplay with a dash of humour. You can do cosplay, dress-up, mix and match almost anything you can find in the game to create new weapons and discover new ways to slaughter the zombies. But with all this, the plot actually comes up as rather serious and touching. Personally, I think the ridiculous dress-up (unless you buy the DLC) that comes with no purpose, spoils the mood. Imagine you are comforting your daughter dressed in a womens under garment.
The gameplay, as you can already see is exactly what and as it is. Each mission, you are to butcher your way out with whatever weapon you can find laying around. The weapons degrade rather quickly so you will need to get use to what is available to you. Combining weapons can be a chore as your inventory is extremely limited and finding the right weapons to combine requires you to do a little hunting while holding on to them. Not to mention you will need to stock up on food and bonus pamphlet (seems like it) that takes up even more inventory slot. Larger weapons/props does not allow you to store them so you will need to hold on to it as your primary weapon until you find a maintenance room.
Side missions will require you to fetch items, escort survivors, fight mini bosses and etc. Survivors are annoying as they can come up with ridiculous requests and they also die rather easily. Handing them weapons is a great strategy but hanging to a good weapon for them will again take up your slot. I have no issue with the AI as the path finding and combat intelligent is alright. However, boss fights, again is another chore. You simply need to find the right timed action to perform and repeat until they dies.
This game solely focuses on killing zombies to the extend that they actually respawn right in front of you if you manage to clear them off in a large scale in an open area. Just like that, poof! and there appear right there. You cannot store weapons in your base when there are plenty of boxes/cupboard lying around. It is also really sad that you cannot expand or relocate your base when you can actually clear out the mall bit by bit.
After a while, you will get bored and simply pushes off and avoid the zombies by travelling within the shop in the mall. I have no idea why the zombies will not spawn in the store. Maybe its because random looters will spawn in them time to time; which again makes no sense as they are yelling and breaking stuff but the zombies simply ignores them.
Maybe on co-op it will give you more dynamics and options. I only manage to play the campaign and it really is annoying and frustrating rather then fun.

I've played and enjoyed Sid Meier's Civ games for years now. Hours and hours of solid, enjoyable gameplay later I thought people had to be wrong about their criticism of Beyond Earth.
Lots of complaints were that it was a Civ V reskin, but after playing it for some hours, over a couple days on the free weekend, I have to say it is worse than a rehash of V. All of the things that were polished in the progression of the previous games were thrown out the window.  The UI just isn't as good and that is the skeleton of a game. There are so many tiny things that add up to a huge bungle in my eyes.
The cursor is hard to see while moving with its no/low contrast color scheme and "slick" minimalist design. Note: I found no way to slow down the mouse within the application and I won't slow my fast mouse for one clunky game.
Camera panning is more touchy. I think you start to initiate panning mode while slightly farther from the edge of the screen.
UI elements are all smaller and/or closer to the screen edge OR ommitted in terms of being visible during normal gameplay. Sure, it leaves a bit more space for viewing the screen and your map, but did it ever feel cluttered before? Not to me. This kind of game just doesn't need the reduction of UI. It's not an MMO or an FPS where me not seeing enough the screen can get me killed. I want to be able to see all pertinent stats at a glance across my screen. AND, most importantly, I do not want want to go to click on a button to see info (that used to be on the screen all the time but is now tucked away), or even worse, to go to click the Next Turn button (which you do all the damn time!) and have the camera pan. Quickly. Even on the slowest pan setting it moves fast. Annoyingly so. Why? I don't need to swiftly pan the camera with lightning reflexes to shoot my foe. It's an RTS for crying out loud! Or, if you want the option for fast as $%#@ panning, fine! But, give me slower panning, too.
Combine all the above and I find the game annoying before I even get to the actual "content" of Beyond Earth, because I keep accidentally speed panning the camera when I am pressing a button or checking out a menu or clicking a pop-up. Thinking I was being a crabby old person, I launched Civ V to compare and all of my instinctual frustrations of "I don't remember this being so..." are valid. With the UI confirmed as clunky, it makes it that much harder for me to be unbiased about the game itself.
Content-wise, it just feels like there was so much potential, yet the ball got dropped somehow. Like they wasted time and money (badly) tweaking the UI (that didn't need it!) and had no time or budget for designing content. The preview trailer made the move from Earth to colonizing planets in space sound exciting. Important event of a lifetime, of a species' existence happening! But then you get out there, wherever it is you are, and the alien environments feel underwhelming.
Aliens are all animals (i.e. Civ Beyond Earth's Barbarians). You don't diplomatically interact with aliens (a la Star Trek or Wars). You interact with Earth culture mashups like "IndoFrance" or the like. Because the aliens are just brute animals, there are no alien monuments to discover. Your explorers instead find shipwrecks and sattelites which have fallen to the planet. The angry brute aliens run rampant, especially at nests, and unlike Civ V and prior, your explorers may likely get ganged up on - and killed - much more frequently. Especially at the beginning. This is a definite brake-slammer sort of thing. You either have to produce a lot of scouts, wasting production cycles on what is essentially  an expendable unit. Or you micro-manage their every move, which I don't appreciate given how useful it is to have some automated units, like scouts and workers. Or you sorta go without while you build a big military force to route out any (HUGE! I mean they aren't like Barbarian sites. I am left wishing that the innovation of this new game could have led to something like units that could link up. Maybe an explorer could be linked to a marine, whose mission was to protect the explorer as he uncovered new territory and resources.
There are probably more good things about this game that could be said, but I *know* there are more bad things that I just can't bring myself to carry on ranting over in this review. It could have been so good, but Beyond Earth is clunky where it didn't need to be and underwhelming where it could have been a groundbreaking title in the series.
I recommend you go play your other Civ games, another RTS game or your fav space game and wait for Sid Meier to put out a better Civ product next time. I wouldn't even pay the reduced $20-30 bucks for this one, let alone $50. Makes me sad to say, but it is true. If you really wanna see Sid in space, and have $50 to literally burn instead of buying other games, feeding an Ethiopean kid, curing ebola or buying porn, well... who buys porn, but you know what I mean... Hitman is a simple concept: someone gives you a target, or targets, and you take them out. The genius of it is the way the designers let you do that. It's not just about deciding whether to sneak past people or get into a gun-fight - it's about slowly tracking the movements of people through large environments and observing the ways you can manipulate them and their surroundings to bring about their downfall. Perhaps you place explosives where you know they'll wander, or maybe you arrive just in time to nudge them over a railing into a deserted alleyway, and often you do all this dressed in borrowed clothes that conceal your identity from all but the most detailed investigation.
Hitman: Absolution includes all of that stuff, and on the higher difficulty levels it leaves you to figure a lot of it out on your own. You sneak or roam in disguise through police stations, courthouses, dilapidated mob-run hotels, maize-covered farmland, factories and science labs, teasing out details about your target from overheard conversations and useful objects left on shelves or in poorly guarded rooms. Then you formulate a plan and try to pull it off.

I just started playing, and have finished 9 out of 50 campaign puzzles, most of which are basically tutorial levels to teach you the mechanics.  This is a very unique and very enjoyable puzzle game.  Basically it's crafting made into a puzzle, with area management to effectively craft the right items at the right place, so you can continue crafting everything else you need to make the finished product.
The puzzles are multi-stage crafting, e.g. you first need to craft some flint, then you craft a pointed stick sharpened flint and a stick.  Then you use the stick to craft something else, or craft an animal separately in another location, and use the pointed stick to skin the animal, which in turn you use the animal pelt to craft the final item.  And so on, and so on . . .
There are lots of levels, and I can see them getting really complex and thought provoking.
There are also a bunch of challenge scenarios, that are deemed expert level only.  I haven't tried those yet, but it's just more goodness in this very fun and relaxing game.
For $3 it's an excellent deal.  Thumbs up.  Get it.

Let's start from the top, shall we? First off, there's only one thing I can say regarding the environment: absolutely beautiful. From the details of a single leaf (straight down to the dew), to the rocks on the ground (actually ROUND when you look straight down, not like flattened choco-chips of even the latest generation of games), to the flowing water, bustling trees, and dimming landscape, there's little to say but phenomenal. Caught myself more than once trying just standing admiring the landscape..... inspite of the oncoming errors finding their way to my knee in hopes of ending my journey as an adventurer (shut it, Skyrim fanboys). Best part is, regardless where you are and the color saturation, the landscape still remainds creepy as hell in areas.
Speaking of the color-sat settings, Betrayer works a great-but-simple slider system in order to turn your landscape from shiny-green trees with monsters waiting to kill you, to some "Sin City" black-and-white-with-red-highlights setting to solidify the creep factor. But, wait, there's more for you traditional suspense-horror folk. Want to go back to that creepy, B-rated 80's horror film feel? No problem. Adjusting light, dark, and color saturation gives you that all-star black-and-white feel for when you're about to be eviscerated.
Aaaand speaking of eviscerated (and moving on), there are a number of enemies to preoccupy your time between smelling the roses. Unfortunately, every time a new one pops up (literally, I mean exploding out of the ground to eat your entrails), it's a whole new world of "oh S%!^!! as you've now got to learn the attack pattern on the fly, which still won't help you much, while all the other enemies are swarming after you..... And that's if your lucking to land 'em all in the same spot. Even as much as the newer, harder enemies introduce themselves, the older get stronger, faster, smarter, and, in the zombie-Spaniards cases, better equipped. One prime drawback to the enemies, though, is one shared on the aestetic side. Whereas the flora and overall landscape of the game looks down-right gorgeous, the fog, wraith's miasma, totems' and world's corruption (don't worry, you'll find out), look blocky and pixelated. Don't be discouraged though, as you'll inevitably see from the up-close and personal view of their heads and whatever solid extremities they may have, they're still creepy as hell and will still kill ya.
Combat is simple, but having to manually work the pistols, muskets, bows and crossbows feels natural. By natural, I mean loading a pistol will take a lot longer then a shortbow, but it'll also do a hell of a lot more damage with less chance of deflecting off surfaces. Headshots, as expected, will deal more damage, and as with the old adage, "Nobody wins in a knife fight," if you're going in for a close kill, don't expect to come out unscathed as you're human. They're not. They're faster. You'll find out who "they" are.
Story-wise, Betrayer definitely takes its cues from older horror and suspense movies, only there's no chance of a happy ending with any of 'em, and they're generally more depressing and brutal then you were expected. It's more of a mystery novel with a horrorific veins than an adventure/FPS. The closer you think to completing a puzzle, the more you find out how many pieces are missing. Those pieces are generally worse then you were thinking, as well. Betrayer does not earn its name for no reason, folks. Oh, and once again, there's no way any of the "arks" end well, which holds especially true for the first few missions.
In summary, even with  a few quirks you'd expect in an "indy" game, Betrayer holds up in all grounds, combat, scenery, and storytelling. Without further ado, you'll F^!(ING HATE THE ENDING.

Do you like Firefly? Do you like flying around in a ship and blowing stuff up? Then buy this game.
Play as a pirate, smuggler, merchant, miner, mercenary, soldier or any combination you like!
The story is nothing to write home about, but this is mostly a space sandbox anyway. The game itself is absolutely gorgeous and an incredible pleasure to play. There are many different ship types to play around with and different weapon combinations to keep you interested for a good while. The little dinky tugboat you start out with isn't much, but it won't take you too long to throw some bigger guns on it and start slugging it out with the bigger ships.
Ship flight is arcade-style and takes place in faux-3D space: that is to say smaller ships like fighters and bombers (which you don't pilot) fly around in 3D, but the bigger ships, from corvettes to dreadnaughts, stay on a 2D plane. Ships have turrets and you can pick up a hireable strike-craft to help you out, but most of the firepower is concentrated in naval-style broadside weaponry.
Difficulty is mostly linear and is determined by the tier of your equipment, not the size of your ship, so you're not forced to play a huge, sluggish battleship if you don't want to (or don't want to save up for it.) Some people have complained about the "risk estimate" for certain missions being a little inaccurate, but I haven't really had any issues with it provided I upgrade my equipment properly and am not afraid to bug out when the going gets tough.
Default soundtrack is great - a pleasureable selection of hard rock music that fits the tone of the game. You can add your own music, or replace the whole soundtrack altogether if you want. Controls are smooth, with the occasional futzing required with overlapping cargo containers (protip: use your targetting scanner to lock onto the container you want.) Graphics are absolutely stunning and the sound effects are top notch.
Definitely worth picking up this gem!

I'm not gonna bother too much talking about the controversial♥♥♥♥♥♥ I'll say that mowing down civilians in it makes me feel kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ and uneasy but really going any more in to that is just beating a dead horse that most media outlets can't seem to get enough of. That said, at its core it's a pretty fun twin stick shooter. When it's time to deal with some actual threats the game's actually pretty challenging and rewarding. Ducking, dodging, and generally evading gunfire is pretty intense and the guns themselves feel like they have a proper oomph behind them.
The destructable environments lend a lot to that effect as well when desks, glass, thin walls, and just about anything in the level really is destroyed and blown up by gunfire and  explosions. The destructable environments themselves also allow for some creative approaches to combat as well. SWAT team swarming the house you're holed up in and you need a quick way out? Shoot the conveniently placed oxygen canister in the garage to blow a hole in the side of the building to flee through. Need to clear out a heavily fortified building but can't get through the front door without getting mowed down? Steal a SWAT van and drive it through the side of the building.
That said, it's not without its faults. The driving mechanics feel extremely clunky and sometimes it's easy to glitch the vehicles out on the geometry in really weird ways. I mentioned before that just about anything in the level can be destroyed. Well the game can be pretty stupid at times about what qualifies as just about anything. It's pretty silly when you can ram an armored van straight through the side of a solid concrete building but at the same time it just stops dead in its tracks when it hits a chest high brick wall. The monochrome color scheme can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥at times as well. A good example would be the sewer level where it makes it extremely difficult to tell whats blocking your path and what isn't, which makes it fairly easy to get caught on the terrain during a firefight or duck behind what you might think is a pipe running along the floor only to realize after taking two shells in the chest is actually an overhanging pipe.
Overall though, while the premise behind the game might be understandably off putting to people the core mechanics themselves are pretty great. If nothing else, it'd be pretty cool to see what the developers could do with it outside of a mass murder simulator.

Hands down one of the best Space RTS games to date. This is what Master Of Orion 3 should have been. no you cant mess with ship loadouts, but it has the same simplified macro-scale management without falling on the NEED for intesne micromanagement of EVERYTHING.
This allows you to focus on the more fun elements on the game, tactical manouvering of fleets though hostile terratory, or in combat. Reaserch - still insanely powerful but not always 100% required - you must balance your need to advance your tech, vs you need to expand, vs your need to field a fleet, vs your need to build defences (if any), vs what you can support.
because of this, and the varried nature of the factions, AND the simplistic interface, this game is incredibly fun and deep, and you will rarely play it exactly the same way twice, even vs. the AI as the various Maps force youre play style to shift from heavily offenceive and fast expanding, to defencive and slow build up, to a balance with a focus on diplomacy - collecting bounties and issuing your own in hopes of keeping the universe unstable enough to eek out a win.
I could talk for too long about the factions, but the quick and dirty is:

70 hours and I still do not know why I can't do two runs when I finish one with 5 hours to spare.
In "This War of Mine", you find yourself in the middle of an ongoing civil war. Which is fine until you realize that you don't get a gun, or a knife, food, or water. As it turns out, you don't get to play as a soldier!
Oh no, you are not a soldier. You are a civilian, stuck in the middle of No Man's Land. And depending on the choices you made in the beginning, you may or may not be alone.
"This War of Mine" presents itself as a hybrid 2D/3D side-scroller. You give commands to your civvies and hopefully your commands make them survive. A good hand-eye reaction is needed in combat scenes, as one moment of delay can determine whether or not you get to take shotgun or depression home.
There are variations on the civilians available, some being good - like having 5 extra inventory slots or culinary experience, and some being bad - like being an old man.
There are also variations on the available civilians' reactions, but generally helping your neighbors = good = morale up. On the other side of the token you get hurting your neighbors = bad = boo-hoo. Which pisses me off a little because it's a goddamned war and you still worry about stealing stuff from bandits? They're probably the same people who raid the shelter at night.
Also, the AI aren't autonomous. If I may, I'd say that there is no actual AI. You do the mapping, the movement, et cetera. Sure, it's all done by a few clicks, but is it really hard for them to cook hot meals by themselves? All they do as far as I can see is take a book/make coffee/light a cigarette and then make a beeline for the nearest chair.
And then there's the combat. I've made it work by ditching melee, but I have once died and I couldn't quite figure out why. So imagine this: me = with gun, axe and ammo, enemy = with gun and ammo but facing away from you. I click on the attack button and do 50% damage (it's a shotgun at close range) but as I clicked on the attack button again, the idiot
towards the guy to hit him with an axe. Needless to say, I got bashed by his shotgun's butt
RIP Pavle.
But despite all of this, I found myself sticking around for... 70 hours. You might ask, "Why?"
For one, it is strangely refreshing to survive a playthrough. Like, when it says "The war is over", I stare at the message and wonder to myself, "Did I survive? Oh yes I did."
Two, if you actually read the bios of your civilians (which update at intervals - I can't say if the intervals are fixed), story time! I haven't taken the time to read them all, partly because I'm trying to survive, partly because you only get to control a maximum of 4 survivors at a time (please don't increase that cap).
Three, it's a war simulator! It's like Call of 12-Year-Olds! Except that there are no twelve year-olds in-game, and that you don't get guns until you murder someone who has them (or repair broken guns you find, play the game to learn more).
So there you have it, a review of mine for the game called "This War of Mine".
Game is enjoyable once you've mastered the basics.  However once you've played a few times it's very repetative even with random maps and changing the level of difficulty.  Poor value for money
Solid story, you might need a walkthrough after your first playthrough to go and experiance all the endings.
Really fun if you want to kill a quick 8 hours.

I only played this during the free weekend, and was only able to get through one game.
I only have vanilla Civ V and do not have any of the expansions. So my comparison is on a vanilla Civ V to vanilla Beyond Earth, which is more fair as most other reviewers had the Civ V expansions.
However, based on the poor reviews I was expecting the game to be pretty bad. However, it was actually quite fun. I like new and different and this certainly is that.
Pros:
- Civ V but feels newer and different (in a good way)
- I liked how the other civs land some number of turns after you have got started. It's an interesting approach and adds immersion to the game.
- The Affinities are pretty cool and I could see how that could lend itself to unique strategies. On my playthrough I just did everything. I'm glad they don't shoehorn you into just a single affinity.
- Graphics are beautiful and really feels like an improvement over Civ V.
- I really like the trade system (most of it anyway - see cons for the bad parts)
- Diplomacy: Feels a bit better than Civ V. The animations are great. I really love the whole "favors" concept - where you give them stuff in return for a "favor" that you can trade back to them later for stuff. Also at least on an easier difficulty setting, the AI didn't make insane decisions (like ally with you and then backstab you a few turns later. I've had that happen in Civ V). Also some cons.
- Virtues seemed better done than the culture rewards of Civ V. I personally like them better anyway. It made more sense to me and plus you weren't forced into making tradeoffs like Civ V does.
- Quests are new, cool and fun. At least the first time through. I didn't do enough repetitive play to tell you if they would be annoying over time.
Neutral:
- Units feel the same as Civ V. You have your melee, cavalry (faster melee but no terrain bonuses and can't fortify),  archers, artillery, and air units. Different names. But they behave identically to Civ V. Good in some ways, but nothing pushing the envelope.
Cons:
- Tech tree. While it's less linear which is cool, I also found it confusing. They need a new view of the tech tree. I felt lost trying to decide what to go for next. I think the zoomed out view didn't show details on the sub techs which made the zoomed out view worthless. So then you had to go zoom and and spend a bunch of time figuring everything out. I strongly felt like this could be organized in a linear fashion which made more sense (industry down this path, science down this path, health down this path, military down this path, trade down this path, culture down this path). Also they could have a different view which reorganized the tech tree by affinity. That also would have helped. As it stood I probably wasted an hour or more in the tech tree which is pretty ridiculous and frustrating.
- Wonders don't seem all that great or really powerful. They provide a very minor advantage. I built a LOT of them and it never really felt like I gained much from them. They need to make wonders more powerful. I am almost tempted to say that you could skip them and put the production towards military units and go stomp someone instead and you would probably be better off.
- Diplomacy: While I love the "favor" concept, all the AI treated the "favors" as practically worthless which made me quite angry. In several cases I had given away quite a few strategic resources for around 300 turns and had accumulated around 10 favors in return. When I tried to bargain with the AI with my favors, I think they valued my favors at around 1/10th what I had given them. Basically I could trade all 10 favors for 30 turns of a very small amount of strategic resources. Seriously?!?! What a friggin joke. So while favors is a cool concept, the execution make them effectively totally worthless and very frustrating. I give them a giant F in execution here. How can a diplomacy system ever be effective or fun for the player when the AI constantly devalues you and the favors you do for them? So once again, I feel like the diplomacy system had a chance at finally being decent - but the execution made it terrible.
- Comparison / statistics view. Needs more detail on being able to evaluate your civilization to others. I thought having embedded spys would improve this, but it did not.
- Spying is a cool concept, but one thing that was frustrating was the UI did not provide a simple way to evaluate cities you had spys embedded in and to see the extra info that provides. You physically need to go scroll around the map and find the cities (if you can even remember which cities you have spys embedded in). It's a long and tedious process. Very annoying.
- They BADLY need a strategic resource view. I swear Civ V had this. This would help tremendously when trying to plan out where to settle new settlements.
- They BADLY need a resource view. Right now the only way you can view resources is when you FINALLY have a colony unit, and even then it only shows resources nearby. Having a resource view (I swear Civ V let you toggle it on/off 24/7) again would help planning significantly - as I could figure out where I want to settle ahead of time and send military units to clear a path.
- Trade: Whenever a trade unit finishes a full cycle of its route, it seems like it wants you to give it new orders. This doesn't seem too bad until you have like 30-40 trade units. Then suddenly each turn you are having to give 2-5 of them orders. It's very annoying. I wish you could just say: keep doing this forever. Or an alternative option would be: keep doing this until a potential better route opens up - then notify me so I can chose at that point. As it is, this makes trade very annoying.
Overall:
It was new and fun. Different enough from Civ V to keep my attention despite the host of annoyances. I wanted to keep playing it after the free weekend was over. That's enough to give it my recommendation. Though I cannot strongly recommend it.

Oh darn it, should have started from Alien Shooter 1 but whatever -shrug-
So Alien Shooter series... if you had a computer back in the year 2000-20005 you probably heard of and played this game which was made by a russian team. Against all odds [and mostly because we dont have that many good action games back then] the game became quite famous and is probably one of those game that holds the most amount of sequel with barely any differences in between the series.
With that said if you know what Alien Shooter is and probably want to validate your opinion on this game before buying it and killing hordes of aliens feel free to skip this section, I will talking about what the series mainly is.
Now let me get this out of the way first, the game is old, ancient, archaic, obsolete, and fun. Which means you will encounter graphics from the early 2000s because this game is made in the early 2000s. Now shut up about the terrible graphics on the store page and listen.
Basically Alien Shooter series has you controlling a mute guy or gal who usually is either a mercenary or some other form of that. In the early game of Alien Shooter the guy has more health while the gal runs faster, easy. The newer ones might give you some preset personality and background and you can now upgrade your charcater stats. Still the same. Now the game is basically you taking this person and using the whole lotta weapons to kill aliens. Lots and lots and lots of aliens. Back  when it was release the amount of gib was pretty f***ing impressive because once you kill an alien the corpse will not despawn so you will see the map covered in literal amount of gore and gib. The game is so old [and the engine basically retooled over and over again from Alien Shooter 1] that you cannot even turn the camera, yes the background is static 2D with only the character and alien being 3D and every single alien has a canned animation in the way they die. Hahahah.
And that is pretty there is to the game. Some version added objective then the next one improved on it by adding a story and finally you have a full blown campaign while still shooting aliens endlessly. There is something so heartwarming shooting and killing aliens across so many games. Its like a pair of well worn mitten that you slip on before drinking tea and engaging alien genocide. That is not to say the game isn't without its fair share of issues no. The camera angle is bad, sometimes the geometry decides to eat you, and progression in some of the game are f***ed because of how rushed the developement is. But hey it is still fun to shoot and kill aliens.
Release after reloaded yet features a far more shooter story, less weapon, and less time to level up and get more weapons so by the time you reach the final boss [who is pretty frickin dissapointing if I may add] you are probably quite underleveled and underarmed unless you pick the hidden area perk because in every single Alien Shooter hidden areas mean = money, guns, free armor.
I honestly feel after finishing this in just over 2.30 hour that this is one of the weaker game in the second series. Reloaded gave us a full campaign, a narrative that ends properly, more level to grind and weapon to buy, plus a ,pre varied setting.
In contrast Conscription narrative is a bit bland, disjointed, and just ends like that. It actually feels like you should play Conscription first before Reloaded because of the quality jump. Plus it's also shorter. So lets jump to the verdict.
New Buyers: Familiarize yourself with the AlienShooter series before deciding to pull the trigger [heh] and buy the game. I suggest Alien Shooter 1, Conscription then Reloaded because of the quality and because those are the only ones on steam.
Veteran Player: Better than some worse than some. Harder than most because of the short money collection and exp farming but otherwised the same donut filling with a different layer of doughnut.
Pretty much that will be all. Hope to see you on Reloaded! [and maybe 1 but dear lord that is so archaic and ancient.]
EDIT: I forgot to mention, no controller, 60 fps most of the time but due to the way the engine was made too much explosion will still reduce it to 15 for a few sec and it runs on a toaster. Literally Intel 4000 can play it. The keyboard control is good to. Sounds are pretty basic and I am pretty sure they just recycle it over and over again.

Laugh maniacally as you gun down the weak and feeble, wading through crunchy bone fragments. Crush your enemies, see them driven before you, hear the lamentations of their women, and then stomp on their womanly skulls!

Snuggle Truck is a straightforward but fun physics puzzler. You've got a truck, there are things to snuggle in it, and you've got to keep it that way. Unfortunately, the rest of the world seems out to prevent that, as harmless as it sounds. The bulk of the gameplay is managing the bounce of your plush toy cargo since you couldn't be bothered to invest in a net or a closed truck bed, which is surprisingly more fun than it initially seems.
The risk/reward balance of Snuggle Truck is such that the game becomes a great deal more engaging than you'd expect. The first few levels, you'll screw up a few times, but learn what bounces where and how to recover when it does. As things ramp up, however, you start actually caring a bit about how many snugglies you deliver, until the game sucks you in for more levels than you expected. It's not super deep, but it's enough to keep you going for a session. You can also try your hand at making levels if design is more your jam; there are already tons of them out there, so you'll never be at a shortage for things to complete.
I'd say Snuggle Truck is worth it as a pick up and play title to keep tucked in your game library for downtime or when you need a good distraction. It's unlikely to rock your world, but it's hard to hate.

I can't actually recommend Bioshock 2 by itself. It's a superb Unreal shooter wrapped in mediocre level design and story. The gunplay is worthy of a sequel to Bioshock, but the story itself fails in one key point: making you care about the characters that occupy the world. Bioshock 1 had great pacing for introducing characters that seemed reasonable and slowly descended into the realm of madness as the game progressed - 2 just throws you into the madhouse and asks that you kindly shoot it up.
There are tons of brilliant and unique ideas in Bioshock 2, but they're missing that master touch - it's like a poor imitiation without really understanding the reasoning behind the design decisions of the first game. I have no doubt that with another 8 months and a rewrite the game could've been stellar. If you really like the shooting, then by all means play the main campaign, but that's about all you're going to get from it.
The multiplayer is dead nowadays, but it was one of the better Unreal experiences online when it launched since it relied on the excellent gunplay and plasmid mechanics of the campaign.
The reason I am recommending this game (on sale) is because of the DLC. Minerva's Den is an excellent piece of design, in both level and story. It's a phenomenal experience and is convincingly alive in the world of Bioshock. Buy the game and DLC (again on sale) and play Minerva's Den. The pacing, writing, dialogue, and thought that went into it is worth of some real Bioshock material. Game: 5/10, DLC: 10/10

Hitman: Absolution is a stealth video game developed by IO Interactive and published by Square Enix.
Its the Fifth game in Hitman series.
The game was released on 20 November 2012.
Story:-
In the aftermath of Hitman: Blood Money, Diana Burnwood, Agent 47's handler with the International Contract Agency, suddenly goes rogue, carrying out a catastrophic sabotage that includes publicly exposing the Agency.The Agency reforms under Agent Benjamin Travis; Travis assigns 47 to kill Diana and bring Victoria, a teenage girl in her care, to the Agency.rather than executing her, comforts the dying Diana, who gives him a letter and asks him to keep Victoria safe from the Agency.47 hides Victoria at a Catholic orphanage somewhere in Chicago and contacts an International Contracts Agency (ICA) informant named Birdie, who asks him to kill a wealthy gangster nicknamed The King of Chinatown before he'll play ball. After eliminating him, 47 meets with Birdie, who briefs him about Blake Dexter, the CEO of Dexter Industries, who may have more information on Victoria. As payment, 47 is forced to give his signature Silverballers to Birdie.
Plot twist:-
in other words I'll simply say that 47 was Betrayed by the agency.
it was the agency who was using us.
you will find your answers when you play the game.
I recommend the game.
Game-play:-
the game is played from a third-person perspective and takes place primarily in the United States, mainly around the city of Chicago, Illinois, and the fictional town of Hope in South Dakota. The player controls Agent 47, a master hitman.
Players may use pistols, bottles or bricks, assault rifles, shotguns, fiber-wire, or steel pipes, against enemies if opting for the action oriented approach, or avoid enemies all together, not being seen, using disguises, blending in the environment, and only attacking the set target, if using the stealth oriented approach. Agent 47 also has the 'Instinct' ability that lets the player monitor enemies more easily.There are also environmental ways to kill or distract individuals; players can use poison to spike coffee, pull switches to make a disco ball fall and break, cause a massive explosion at a gas station, pull a switch to cause scaffolding to fall down, cause fires, or set off fireworks. Players complete chapters in order to progress through the story. The player journeys to a mansion, library, strip club, gun store, wrestling arena, courthouse, and hotel, during the story
The game introduces an on-line option to the series, 'Contracts', where players can create their own missions for other players to complete.Players choose one of the areas in the game and modify it to create a different level. Players change the location of items, remove items, or add items, choose an objective or add a target, add a time limit, or choose which areas of the location are inaccessible and vice versa.
Challenge your Friends by Creating master mind missions.
If you are a stealth lover, you must try this game out if you haven't yet.

It's not really a successor to X3, even though it continues the story about 50 years after where X3 Albion Prelude left off.
Gameplay wise it's a definitive reboot, so if you're looking into more of the same from the X3 games you're probably wrong here.
However, this doesn't mean old X fans can't enjoy the game. And don't worry about the older bad reviews, In the current state (3.61 + Teladi Outpost) it isn't bad at all - just different.
And just like with the old X games, mods fix the things that Egosoft won't or didn't (yet).
The Steam Workshop integration means the mods are easily installed.
Want to get rid of nebulas? Mod. Want to win the conversation and hacking minigame every time? Mod. Automated traders and miners? Mod. Jumpdrive in your ship and not just NPC ships? Mod. Want to see the stats of hireable NPCs without playing the minigame? Mod. And definitely get the "Capital Ships Bridge" mod, it's makes piggy-backing on one of your capital ships much more awesome!
Really, it's fun, in a different way than X3, but still familiar. It's more of a cross-over between Darkstar One (1 upgradable player ship, cockpit view dogfight combat, randomly generated side missions) and X2/3 (build stations, build/capture ships, assign them to tasks, make money the 'economy spreadsheet' style) with some new features thrown in for good measure (giant stations you can land in, NPC hiring, hack/scan/mine-laying drones you can remote control) and some very, very pretty graphics.
If you can get it cheap and like space games, definitely give it a try.
Get it: If you like the X games in spirit (trade build fight think); if you like Freelancer; if you like pretty space graphics; if you want something arcady to feed your flightstick with; if you can get it cheaper (not more than 30€ I'd say, including the Teladi Outpost DLC; I think I paid like 20 € for the bundle and will get about 100 hours out of it, and Egosoft is still working on more updates and DLC)
Don't get it: If you want Borons or Paranids - there're none in the game (yet?); if you want to build a massive, galaxy wide, automated trade empire with dozens of station complexes and hundreds of automated ships (theoretically possible in Rebirth, but takes much more time and effort to build and maintain); if you can't accept that you personally can only fly one (upgradable) ship; if you don't want to try out mods (fun and convenience at least -50% without mods)

I picked this game up during one of the weekly bundles and had zero knowledge of it beforehand. While the game is far from perfect, it has plenty to offer and is a refreshing change from the style and pace of other modern FPS titles.
The game's visuals are a clean and stark monochrome. The world is immersive due in large part to ambient wildlife sounds and the wind that gently blows the plants back and forth. There is a lot to explore and a lot of optional content that does not advance the main story but fleshes out its characters. Betrayer is also quite light on its 'game' mechanics. There is not much combat, and the enemies you run into are often no trouble to take care of. The true meat of the experience is exploring the world and piecing together the stories of its inhabitants.
Total play time was around 6 hours for the main story, but there is still more to do if you're so inclined. I found the length to be fine, considering that the story and action mechanics are not deep and got repetitive, especially toward the end. There is little variety in enemies and locations but the game feels well executed for what it is.
In short, I recommend this game because it was refreshingly different from other games in its genre. Its world is moody and atmospheric and the lack of depth in game mechanics detracts little from the experience. The stories are well-written and enjoyable to see unfold as you find more clues. I would play it not as a game to be beaten but as a story to be explored. Definitely worth picking up on sale but maybe not at full price.

Author's Notes: Just last year, I discovered the greatness that is BioShock. In fact, I played the first game twice last year. This year, I got the chance to play the game once more due to this. If you wish to see my review on BioShock, feel free to visit my profile. This review is strictly on the Remastered edition.
Back in 2007, the legendary series kicked off with its first game, "BioShock". Now, a couple of sequels and years later, we've been given BioShock: Remastered. If you've never played BioShock before, definitely get this! If you've heard some negative things about the remastered version, you can at least still play the original. For those of you that got the free upgrade and are not sure what to do, I'll share my experience with the Remastered version.
Like I said before, I'm a recent fan of BioShock and I've become a big fan of the series so, I jumped on the opportunity to play the game again and gave this a shot. I heard that it had its ups and downs, but I wanted to experience it myself. Others have been saying that they've experienced frame drops and low fps, but I never had that problem. My computer's not the best computer out there by no means, but it ran very smoothly on it. I also never encountered any bugs in the game. So, the game may or may not run smoothly for you, maybe I was just lucky. Now, is this a good remastered edition?
First, what are examples of good remasters in a world of newly filled remasters? From what I've seen, The Uncharted Remasters and The Halo Remasters are probably the best so far. Does this remaster compare to those? Well, the short answer is no. The game definitely does look better, I'll give it that, but some of the changes actually make it seem a little worse. If you take a look at some of the comparisons out there, you'll see what I mean. The remastered kind of takes away a little bit from some of the atmosphere in certain places. Does the game still look good though? Yes, definitely.
Now, here's the thing, the remastered edition isn't just a remaster of BioShock, it comes with some extra fun. They've added mini-games that you can play at any time (They're found in the main menu) and I've gotta say, they're pretty fun. One of them is that you have to rescue a little sister and fight your way to her! If you also wanted to see some behind the scenes stuff and some concepts, this is your chance. There's a visual museum that you can walk through in the game. The museum is pretty cool and unique. There are some pretty cool early concepts that have never really been shown before.
Here's probably one of the greatest things about this remastered edition....golden reels that contain directors' commentary. There are 10 of these spread out in the world of Rapture and they are definitely worth finding. Each one has about a 10 to 13 minute interview with Ken Levine (basically the father of BioShock) and Shawn Robertson (Animation Lead/Director of BioShock & BioShock Infinite) and I found these to be extremely entertaining! Each commentary talks about different subjects like art inspirations, some of the animation process, and a lot more. If you're a returning fan, these are a great break from gameplay. If you've never played the game though, definitely save them till the end, they do contain spoilers (As soon as you find them, you can view them in the main menu). They're definitely great post-game videos to watch.
In all, this isn't the greatest remastered edition ever, but it's pretty good. The commentary reels definitely make it worth it ;) If you got this as a free upgrade, what's there to lose? If you're a first time player, remember that if this one doesn't work on your computer, the original probably will.

I did enjoy this game for some time, and reached a score of 2700 with a unique deck-attempt, but the more i play, the  more it is getting clear, that the balance is out of control, and that, in order to compete on the higher ranks, you are forced to play a couple of decks, that are built aroung overpowered combos and insane cards, or simply dont stand a chance.
It demotivated me immensely, to play against combo-decks which's value is far higher than my standard deck, or to outplay my opponent for the most part of the game, just to have my whole army destroyed by a single card.
Which is a shame, as, in its core, the game is great, and i had a blast against players with "normal" decks. But, as much as it hurts me: as a whole, i cannot stand the extreme design any longer...
From a personal perspective, there are more reasons to not recommend this game:
There are no animated cards, i find the card-prices too high, and the rewards too low, some keywords are really annoying, in the sense of tough to play around (stealth, chain, explode, AOE cards that cover 60% of the board...), and i really, really dislike the turn-timer, and the following sudden-death-mechanic, with both the damage per turn and the extra card-draw.
On a technical side, it happens that the server goes offline without warning, that multiplayer games freeze, and that turns end before the timer burned down.
I will still continue to observe top players, but wouldnt recommend this game to players who are looking for a free, serious and/or deep game, and wont support it any further...

I loved this game as a kid, and I love this game now. It's brilliantly written, and gorgeously messed up in it's own way. It's a point-and-click puzzle adventure, published in 1995, that explores the storylines of five people, all very different from the last. Everyone's storyline is fantastic, and I recommend them all. It doesn't take long to play through, but it's worth it the whole way.
I will warn though, that this psychological thriller has very sensitive topics, such as insanity, paranoia,♥♥♥♥♥♥ and genocide. If it starts causing incredible discomfort, I would recommend stopping, and seeking emotional guidance, as it will likely only become worse.
To anyone who does enjoy this game, I would also recommend reading Harlan Ellison's short story of the same title, first published in March of 1967. It's very well written, and very enjoyable to those interested in this sort of dark psychological literature.

Sid Meiers Civilization is a game that has been in my heart since Civ III. Through the years, we have had many bumps and curves in the francise and now, I am ready to judge the side game Civ: Beyond Earth.
From the get go, I feel you need to know this game is mean't be to different than a normal civ game but has enough similarities that if you have played Civ V, it doesn't take a genius to figure everything out. Figuring everything out is easy and if you listen to the tutorial, you possibly couldn't get lost. The one thing the tutorial doesn't go over is the menues but once you check out all the buttons on screen, it shouldn't be a problem. Anyways, now I am going to go over big parts of the game that many have had issues with but I am going to say why I feel this game is allot better then others say.
Aliens, they are the barbarians on this game. But don't expect amazing rewards for killing them off. In this game, killing them is a way to have civs get mad at you. They are a threat that makes expanding a bit of a pain. Though if you mind your own business and don't tempt them with workers or colonists, you should be fine. Especially once you get a fence to push back the aliens away from your city. But know, you are still gonna have to be careful with them.
I feel aliens make the game very interesting and I like this sytem allot more than barbarians.
Another thing I like about the game is miasma. Imagine playing Civ with death traps scattered around the map. You take damage if you end your turn in it. I like it because one, you can get rid of it later. Two, it makes planning pretty fun and exploring is a bit more dififculty then before. :D
One thing I can say about previous Civ games is that I generally only play Domination mode where I kill everyone. But this game... I feel doing so is a crime. You see, there are 3 ways you can play this game. You can try and make unity on the planet, you can try and return to earth, or you can start a new earth and abandon the old earth. I can't explain this well but I can say that if you only have domination on, going back to earth is pointless.
There is tons of things I could go over in this but I would be writting a novel. I could go into the replacement for social policies, how the unit upgrade system in this is more interesting, and ect. But I will end it off with this, I think this is the best civilization thus far! Civilization V is now going on the shelf because this game is definitely more interesting and I think it will improve even more when DLC comes out.
This is a game you have to play yourself to judge but I will say one thing, if you are juding this game. Don't try and compare it to Civ V, you can but in the end, this game is meant to be different.

As much fun as slicing up the environment and attaching rockets to objects is, that's the one part of this game that frequently shot holes in my sails of amusement. Running along, fall off the side of something to my death, or much less inconveniently, to having to reclimb the environment. Nevertheless, the game's music, distinct visual style and gameplay make up for that, for the most part.
The slicing and dicing of the environment is plenty fun, and adding rockets to stuff to make it fly off or up or wherever is pretty great. Pulling stuff down with your grapple hook is also pretty satisfying, but it does leave you wondering why you couldn't also use it to zip up to stuff from time to time. The reason I emphasize all of this is that, aside from environmental navigation, that's most of what you'll be doing to solve fairly straightforward puzzles of slicing up the right parts of the environment (or sometimes the wrong parts, to make your own path) to make paths to get to the end of the level. As the game moves forward, there did appear to be some reduction in the variety of ways you could create paths, sometimes in frustratingly finicky ways.
However, that could have been just me missing something to it, so I wouldn't put it against the game. I might say that some instances of slicing objects thrown at you are a little more flaky than they should be too, but again, I might have spent too much time before those moments undermining the enemy tossing stuff at me instead of practicing slicing objects up in midair, so that too may have been me at fault.
Whatever the case, it's a silly, lighthearted game that tosses up some interesting new ideas that, if you can catch it on a sale, I'd definitely recommend. Also, keep an eye on your pants.

I'd heard about this game for a long time and now I've finally had the chance to play it. Put simply: it's awesome! The atmosphere, the story, the puzzles, all of them combine to give you the feeling that something's off about everything. It's horror in the sense of Frankenstein in that it's more psychological. If you're into story and puzzles, this is a must. If you're into engaging, intense gameplay, try it anyways. It's gotta be one of  the best point-and-click games out there, so here are some pros and cons.
Pros
-Great storytelling with intriguing characters that are made more so by their flaws.
-The music and art style, though maybe outdated, ages well and contributes well to the atmosphere.
-Good replayability, you can play the individual segments in any order you like and choice plays a fairly large role.
-There is more than one ending you can get depending on what you decide.
-You can generally interact with most things in any given scene, even if your character just examines.
Cons
-The music and graphics may be a bit out-of-date for some, though I personally feel they age well.
-Most choices don't affect the game overall even if they impact a particular character on a major level and bring them closer to redemption, but this is a minor complaint.
So not really anything I can complain about. The characters can be deep or shallow depending on how you play them. The main antagonist is great - you don't often get sentient AI that are so humanlike in their insanity and pain. Overall, if you haven't played this game, you should. No exceptions.

I've played every iteration of CIV. Including the early imitators. I was excited, expecting something more like Alpha Centauri. That was CIV with a twist and more. Yes, it had mindworms and fungus. But you could adapt. It was humanity reaching for the stars and trying something new. Action at sea was just as important as anything on land. The build your own modular unit aspect was a definite plus. Drop squads and hovertanks, how cool was that? But What I got with BE was just a stingy version of CIV with childish bad art. It was CIV minus all the things that made CIV fun. One aircraft on a carrier? Really? Only two types of warship? You're kidding!
It seems to be a trend with CIV to subtract all the things that made play fun. Dumb it down, boys and girls. I think CIV III was the zenith of the series. It has been a long, slow, decline ever since. The basic problem with BE? The premise is that people left Earth to make a fresh start. But all they did was bring the same, tired, old approach and same mistakes. And the quotes from the leaders? The worst sort of drivel. If you like what Abrams did to Star Trek, you'll probably like Beyond Earth. But  Abrams really just ripped out the heart of that universe. It was all about hope and a better future once. He madecynical frat boy cheese product out of it. Whoever made BE did the same for CIV. It is dull, boring, and limits your imagination. Is that really all people want? Maybe I'm too old school and miss the point. But it seems to me that we are losing something very important. People used to be more thoughtful. We used to be able to look at the stars and dream up gods and monsters. Now we just hit the escape key.

Snuggle Truck is a relatively fun casual deliver x stuffed animals in x time game. It has a nice amount of content, levels and an awesome editor meaning the community can make levels giving an unlimited amount of playable content. However, the game itself has too many minor errors making it not worth the hassle and here is why:
Pros:
♦ Decent Graphics and Sounds (These are alright for what it is, they are not amazing but fit the game)
♦ Medal Concept is Great (Unlocking medals for completing x goal in a level is nice as it gives you something to do in the level and adds a nice amount of content to the level)
♦ Gameplay is fun and works with minimal glitches (Driving through the level and delivering x stuffed animals in x time just works. It is pretty fun if you are the type that likes to be number one on the leaderboards and must complete all level challenges. If you don’t like playing a game for leaderboards or completing challenges, then you probably won’t find this as fun as I did)
♦ Easy to 100% with Achievements (Has a nice number of easy Achievements which are mainly unlocked by just using features of the game and completing the game)
♦ Steam Trading Cards (This is always a bonus)
♦ Each level design is unique (This is nice as every level feels different and no two levels feel as though it is a repetitive copy of the last level)
♦ Decent level editor (Amazing level editor that allows anyone to create a level and upload for anyone to play. This is an awesome feature as it adds an potentially unlimited amount of levels and content to the game)
♦ Truck and Stuffed Animal skins are very detailed (Custom Skins are designed very well for what they are and add a nice little bonus to the game)
♦ Price is reasonable ($5 for a game is decent as if you look past all the cons you’ll get your $5 worth)
Cons:
♦ No Steam Cloud Storage (I’ve had to restart this game 3 or 4 times for the sole fact of no Steam Cloud Storage and me always losing my save file. You could say I should’ve backed up the savefile, but there is no easy way to tell which games you own have SCS. Therefore, as the game progresses by completing one level to unlock the next, SCS would be relatively beneficial. Plus, If a game is on Steam and doesn’t make use of this free feature, then in my opinion it shouldn’t be on Steam)
♦ Method to activate custom skins is annoying (Firstly to be able to even use them you have to go and enable them in a “+more” menu. The “+more+ menu doesn’t lead on to what it is until you click it which is annoying as I had no idea what It was until I clicked it. Though, once you’ve enabled all the custom skins, you have to then get into a level and click the truck until your truck has the skin you want. This concept would be fine if it didn’t mean you had to waste a play through just to enable a skin. The skin should be able to be enabled and selected from within the “+more” menu)
♦ Lacks Steam Workshop (This is bad as the game makes you upload to their servers and for some reason created levels don’t always stay. I say this as I created a level a while ago and started playing Snuggle Truck again only to find my level deleted. Plus, custom levels not moderated properly as the only way is by a star rating which doesn’t explain much. With Steam Workshop levels would be moderated by the community via ratings and comments etc and would be more likely to stay in the game)
♦ Has DLC activated automatically (This is a weird concept as the game calls certain features DLC but you can’t actually buy any DLC for the game. This confuses me as to why it’s even called DLC)
♦ Custom level highscores don't load and you have to quit the game to continue playing (When you click the highscores in Custom levels made by users, it just shows a spinning loading circle and does nothing else. You can’t close out of the spinning loading circle, meaning you have to close the game and re-open it if you want to continue playing)
♦ No way to delete a Downloaded Custom Level (This is annoying as I stated not all levels are moderated. Therefore, if you download a bad level there is no way to easily delete it within the game. This is annoying as it fills your list of custom levels with a lot of potentially unwanted ones making it hard to find the ones that you actually enjoyed and work)

It's safe to say that Gat out of Hell is easily the weakest of the Saints Row franchise. Now, to be completely fair: the game isn't a total waste of money. Some of the weapons are pretty creative, such as the seven deadly sins' weapons, a stake-launching shotgun, or a submachine gun that shoots locusts. The ability to fly around using wings is pretty fun, and the super powers mechanic from Saints Row IV returns, only with a "dark magic" twist. The city of New Hades is pretty cool, and you can finally live out the dream of playing as Gat or Kinzie. Sadly, there's no way to really customize them, which takes away from what makes this series so great. Aside from that, the game is very short, and can easily be beaten within a few hours. There are some extra collectibles and challenges to do, and they can provide some extra replayability, but only a few hours worth.
In conclusion, Gat out of Hell isn't terrible. There are some merits to be had; the typical Saints Row humor is there, and I personally enjoyed the few hours of gameplay it provided. On the other hand, the game is hard to recommend since it's so short. Due to this, I'd suggest only getting Gat out of Hell when it goes on sale, or buying it in the Ultimate Franchise Pack so you'll get more for your money.

After being more or less forced to provide an answer to Hearthstone, Wizards of the Coast decided to put forth a PC version of their insanely fun and popular TCG that's free to play. Unfortunately, Wizards has once more skimped on something that wouldn't give them a lot of profit out of the gate, and there's no signs of them putting effort into supporting this.
Sadly, once you're done with the story and want to test your decks against another person, you're SOL. Games will disconnect, freeze, or downright exit entirely for seemingly no reason. The sad part, this isn't because of some recent patch, it's been like this since release when they assured us it would "get better" To add salt to the wound, should your get disconnected then buy a pack or complete a quest, the server won't register you as having done it, so you'll have to redo it and hope the servers hold steady. The first few times are inconvenient, the 20th and 30th times are downright rage enducing.
Pros:
-A free version of the most popular TCG around
-New player friendly with plenty of hand holding
-2-Headed-Giant game mode makes for fun co-op
-Plenty of in game toggle options to help with card ability triggers
-Deeper card pool and interactions than other PC card games
-Cards are very well balanced, a deck of just commons can compete with a deck of rares
Cons:
-Experienced or returning players will feel a little too coddled
-Getting coins for a pack takes a little longer than other card games
-Very inconsistent connectivity puts a damper on the experience
-A seemingly nonexistant developer/community relationship
-Missed opportunities on which game modes and cards appear in the game
-Packs are purchasable with real world cash, but nowhere near worth it
-Worse than a Call of Duty in terms of "rehash the same engine"
End of the day: While a newbie friendly version of a mechanicaly fun game, it's  marred by poor build quality and a lack of interest from the creators to improve upon it's infastructure to deliver a quality product. If you want a quality product, just pay the $10 for MTG:Online.
