*Listens quietly for the sound of nails being hammered into wood* I so wanted to love this game even after having come to the X-universe late but X-Rebirth isn't so much a Rebirth as it is a nail in the coffin. Yes, the Teladi outpost DLC fixed a few things but it doesn't change the fact that Egosoft threw out almost everything good about the X3's and gave us... This.
Pros
The graphics are simply stunning. I cannot deny the vista's are utterly jaw dropping
The music is sweeping and epic
New sector system-In the previous game each 'map' was one sector which had so many stations, ships and jump gates leading to other sectors. The downside to this is that they had a rather definitive edge to them and expanding beyond the default size of a given sector was difficult. In Rebirth they have highways linking regions withing sectors so that they are now exponentially bigger
Cons
The highway system to enable FTL travel between regions means they decided to do away with the SETA drives. Singularity Engine Time Accelerator. In a nutshell, it would speed the game up to a maximum factor of %1000 to allow you to cross even massive sectors rapidly however here your only options to move swiftly are to take the highways, which are fixed and only link between regions one way or to boost your way across at speeds not all that much greater than your normal. However that introduces annother problem:
Boosting drains your shield. Fair enough, in the last game boosting would eat away at your shield but only if you didn't have enough energy cells to power it. In Rebirth your only options are to arrive at a fight late, or with your shield depleated.
Steering is either by joystick (and it doesn't have pre-built profiles so you have to bind everything manualy) or by cursor flight. Either pointing at a spot on the screen and clicking the mouse until you're poiting where you want to go or by moving the mouse around on the screen and it will keep turning that way. Now, for those of us without a joystick this can act as a virtual stick, meaning we don't have to move our mice up and reset them mid-manouver however it also feels difficult and can serve to dull reaction times. This was an option in the previous games but that's where the problem lies. It was an OPTION. Here you have no choice in it.
The Ship. Now, as I recal in the first X games you only had on ship you could be in, fair enough it was a while ago in computing terms and resources were limited however they soon corrected this to the point where you could fly around in just your space suit, a small one man scout ship, bombers, corvettes, frigates, destroyers, carriers or even, if you had balls that clanked as you walked, The Valhalla. A ship so large it can't actually fit through a gate. In Rebirth, you're stuck in one ship. This wouldn't be an issue if the ship were any good but it isn't. From the top:
It's name is the Albion Skunk. I don't know who thought of this but in the previous games it was named the Albion Pride. And no, you can't even change it's text. I might be able to live with it if your co-pilot (more on her in a sec) didn't say it every time you came into dock
The ship computer from previous games makes a comback, I'd gotten used to her and quite liked the announcements she made but here, the only thing more irritating than 'Betty' the computer is Yisha the co-pilot telling Betty to shut up
The speed is not great, made all the worse by the lack of aformentioned SETA drive and the only boost feature eating up your shield
Drones, missiles and weapons are all limited. And you only get one gun... One. You can have a few on your ship at a time but you can only shoot one. Even the samallest, least combat capable scout ships in X3 Albion Prelude have two.
And of course, you are stuck in this one ship. Sure, you can get out and walk on stations but you have to come back to it sooner or later. Or spend the rest of your life running the vents like a rat, trying to make a living out of oddly placed credits and random junk you can sell. Either or. Frankly, I'd choose vent rat

Essentially Pirates! Gold but in space. Almost literally, so don't expect too much depth with this one.
There are a great many annoyances with the game, so I'll start with those.
-No depth: The story is extremely simple and relatively cartooney. Likewise, everything you can interact with in the game comes as is.
-Ships aren't nearly as customizable as I'd like. You can't pick paint jobs or any other cosmetic differences.
-No real differences between sectors.
-No real differences between factions aside from token good/evil.
-Ship variety is merely cosmetic difference and stat upgrade.
Negatives aside there are a ton of things this game does right.
-Extremely simple gameplay and cartooney atmosphere with space cowboy aesthetic adds up to an extremely pleasing feel. You're basically playing a saturday morning cartoon featuring space cowboys.
-Astoundingly pleasing aesthetic on all levels, but specifically the ship combat. Firing weapons is pleasing as hell, and so is just cruising the space lanes looking for work.
-Soundtrack seems to be a hit or miss for some people but I throughly enjoyed it, even though it repeats a lot. Very twangy, high quality considering the indie origins.
-You get to pilot a totally rockin spaceship. In space.
-Lots of things going on at any time.
-Game is extremely pretty to look at.
-Aliens are fairly various and fun to interact with. Bonus points for the team putting lots of effort into making each race distinct and also voicing all their dialogue, each with a unique language that sounds alien and cool.
Overall, a very fun albeit simplistic game. Have you ever wanted to fly around in space, looking for work? This is the game for you. Just don't go in with pie in the sky expectations.

tl;dr: If you loved Freelancer, Starpoint Gemini 2, or any of the 2D/top-down "open world" space combat/mining/trading games, buy this immediately.
I never write reviews, but man, this game. This game hits way out of its weight class. Watch the trailers, listen to the music - the whole soundtrack is that awesome, and they match tracks to gameplay so darn well. The characters, the music, the ships - the whole vibe fits right alongside Firefly or Cowboy Bebop.
But how about gameplay?
This game is darn near everything that I loved about Freelancer - open choices about alignment, how you wish to accumulate wealth (with net worth being the best equivalent to RPG "level"), and so many over-the-top, very expensive upgrades available beyond what's needed to "finish" the game that's any space grinder's paradise.
It only deviates from that mold on three critical points, by order of significance:
1) Combat is dramatically different.  This is not, and does not pretend to be, a dogfighting/piloting simulation. There is nothing that approaches "real" inertia. You have two axes of freedom (yaw and velocity front-to-back), not six. In that respect, think of it like SPAZ or other 2D space games, but with phenomenal graphics. This game is 2.5D, not 3D.
But it works. Combat is less adrenaline-fueled flips and rolls, and more stately dance of large ships, where positioning far outstrips reflexes - half way between something twitchy like Elite: Dangerous and point-and-click orders of EVE Online. Everything you fly is a "capital ship" and mostly behaves like one. (That's not to say there aren't plenty of size class upgrades - you could double-park your starting ship in the exhaust ports of some of the larger ones.) This plays more like AC: Black Flag's naval battles, in that your biggest (and manually controlled) weapons are mounted broadside, so this is big ships barrelling up side-by-side to blast the hell out of each other.  In an interesting conceit, fighters are given 3D flight capabilities and can fly over and under you, while capital ships (you and AI) are stuck on a 2D field - 3D flight is there, just for the annoying gnats that you don't fly.
So combat can take a while, and it'll feel dull to the adrenaline junkies, but it's just the right mellow level of exciting for the person who finds RPG combat exciting and laments their survival skills in FPS deathmatches against all the coked-up squirrels who make your reflexes look like dial-up latency. (So... me.)
2) The world is just plain smaller. Systems are bigger, but there's only about a dozen of them. There aren't a whole lot of factions or terribly interesting power dynamics between factions. But you know what? This wasn't a $50 or $60 game. I felt like there was a totally reasonable, if not Freelancer-scale, level of world available to be for the price tag. Should they ever decide to DLC in more content, I'll be first in line: it would be a better game for it, and completely reasonable to come with an additional price tag, given what the base game sells for.
3) No multiplayer (or the accompanying dedicated server). This one's a bummer, as the only thing I like more than this genre is this genre with friends, but that's a big jump in development complexity for a budget title. So it doesn't feel like a glaring omission or a developer shortcoming (and indeed, leaving it out of scope is better than a broken implementation), but I would love to see a Rebel Galaxy 2 with full multiplayer support Freelancer style.
Otherwise, this thing is dreamy. Every time I find an annoyance in this game, it's because the level of graphical polish, voice acting, and audio design fool me into thinking I'm playing a big-budget AAA title. Then I remember the price tag, and I'm again floored how hard this game hits for its budget.

This game, while addictive and very much worth the purchase for someone who is a huge fan of Freelancer and have been looking for a proper game similar to it (this is definitely the closest it's ever gotten). But, there is a lot of aspects of the game that felt very cheap as though the devs were very restrained with budget and time. For instance, why is there no real cut-scenes of anything? Why is there no directional 5.1 true surround? Why is the AI so basic and limited in capabilities (they never use boosters and very rarely use deflectors). AI has no strategy at all and no fear either. And combat dialogues are all the same and very repetitive and annoying. Story dialogue options are pointless as none of your choices make any difference (worse than Fallout 4). The story was ok, but very cheap and extremely short if you think about it, and it doesn't help the fact that there was no cut-scenes to improve it or extend it. Also, the game's difficulty relies very heavily on the equipment you have and barely on your skills. You go from too easy to way too hard really quickly simply because... as an example... you have MK4 shield and hull and deflectors when you now need MK5 stuff, and there's no warning or indications that you'd need something like that. Sure, they have mission difficulty ratings which raise or lower as you upgrade your ship, but as you soon realize, even the lowest difficulty and the highest difficulty rated missions could be the same.
As far as bugs and major flaws go... there are a few. Escort missions are improbable no matter how skilled or well equipped you are as the AI friendly is extremely delicate and somewhat defenseless, so don't even bother trying to do those side quests (and that 1 main quest where you need to escort someone safely through the mess of enemies... good luck cuz my guy died almost instantly, good thing it didn't fail the quest though). Hired mercenaries are useless for the most part. There's only 5 to choose from and they come back to the bar after death as though nothing happened and I'm a stranger. They cost a lot in the early game and constantly die in battle, even easy battles and since they only fly small gunships, they hardly do any damage either. All they are is bait to keep a tiny percentage of the projectiles and lasers away from you for a minute or two until they die. Merchant missions are so easy even though they very predictably throw enemies at you constantly while you're trying to get to your destination. The reasons it's so easy is simply because it's really easy to out run them all... they don't use boosters. There are also weird sound issues. Every time I was in a heavy battle, voices would change in speed to the point of not knowing what they're saying or fade in and out. Undocked from a station to see a dumb AI ship pushing against the station, refusing to simply back up, ended up killing himself. In the alien world in which there are no stable jump gates to, the map looks just like any other solar system as though it was populated with bases, friendly mercenaries, merchants, millitia, civs, pirates, etc... probably just an oversight though as I didn't actually see any friendly bases while I was there. Also, it's very easy to fail a mission simply by flying too far away from objective area during battle or during quick retreat which is really annoying. It was one of the reasons why I didn't explore at all in the alien solar system... it was a long mission and I didn't want to have to do it all over again simply because I veered too far off from the objective.
I definitely love this game way more than I should, but I can't help it simply because it feels so much like a Freelancer game. This game filled that desperate need. But now that I finished the story, the replayability is pretty much non-existant since the story was rather basic with no cut-scenes or anything. Also, there's no reason at all to continue playing after the story ends since continued upgrades just make the side missions even more easy than they already are, and it's not like there's hidden gems to discover in the game aside from over powered alien weapons that very rarely drop from an alien Lords which very rarely appear in the solar system.
Comparisons to Freelancer:
-  I think Freelancer has 480p textures but it also has mods for 720p or maybe even 1080p HD textures. Rebel Galaxy either has 480p or 720p textures by default with no mods for HD textures (at least not yet). I'm not entirely sure on any of this though. But you can clearly tell when doing a closeup on anything that the textures are not full HD, which is why the game runs so smoothly on any decent gaming hardware.
-  Freelancer has basic lighting features with mods to greatly improve it and I don't think it has shadows at all, if it does, I'd imagine it's very basic. Rebel Galaxy has great lighting features as well as smooth detail in shadows.
-  Freelancer has mod support with an insane amount of mods out there and continued semi active but small modding community even to this day. Rebel Galaxy does not... at least not yet.
-  Freelancer is very well balanced in difficulty. Rebel Galaxy suffers a little in that regard.
-  I've never once seen any glitches in Freelancer aside from dumb AI flying into planets on occasion. I've seen quite a few in Rebel Galaxy, including dumb AI destroying itself into a base.
-  With mods, Freelancer allows you to fly both small nimble ships all the way to massive carriers. Rebel Galaxy only allows you to fly massive carriers.
-  Freelancer has a massive variety of ships and weapons to choose from with hundreds of mods out there to extend it even further. Rebel Galaxy has maybe 15 ships and 15 weapons?
-  With Freelancer, you're constantly upgrading to completely new styles of weaponry, keeping it interesting. Rebel galaxy, not so much. You find what works and stick with it till the end upgrading damage output of that weapon as you progress.
-  Freelancer is 3D in that you can fly vertically and horizontally. Rebel Galaxy is 2D... but the AI can fly a little bit vertically.
-  Freelancer has great cut-scenes for pretty much everything. Rebel Galaxy has basic animated dialogue cut-scene and extremely short jump gate cut-scene, that's it.
-  Freelancer space looks extremely well made with all kinds of variety in background imagery and large dense foggy nebulae. Rebel Galaxy feels like it's the same image for every solar system, no variety, and always too bright. It doesn't even feel like space, and the nebulae are so pathetically tiny, it makes me wonder if the devs know what a nebula is.
-  Both Freelancer and Rebel Galaxy have the same constant sized stationary planets with similar ozone features.
- Freelancer has trade lanes which realistically make no sense if the planets and stations revolve around the sun. Rebel Galaxy eliminated that issue with warp drive.
-  Flying in formation worked really well in Freelancer because most of the time, you lead the AI which solved possible AI issues. Rebel Galaxy made flying in formation a complete nightmare.
-  Freelancer has a massive spider web full of solar systems in which you can go to... each one feeling different and unique from the other. Rebel Galaxy has what felt like 5 or 6 solar systems, and they all look identical to each other, including the alien world.
-  Freelancer has multiplayer which worked well. Rebel Galaxy does not.
-  I could go on forever but you get the idea. The 2 are very different in many ways but also similar in many ways. Rebel Galaxy is simply just a newer but much lower budget version of Freelancer.
I definitely recommend this game to any Freelancer fans, just don't expect it to be as good. I really wish the devs would continue working on the game. We've waited way too long for this, and for it to just end like that... makes me sad.  :(

Does Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion come highly recommended? Yes. Alright, I guess we're about done here.
Really, though, Rebellion is simply a good strategy game. As the player, you'll be in command of one of three great star-spanning empires, managing resource income, the colonization and exploitation of distant worlds, technological advancement, diplomatic relations with other factions; and once diplomacy breaks down, the fleets of warships that you'll be employing to conquer your enemies, or to defend the last ragged survivors of your meagre civilization, depending on which way the solar wind is blowing.
Maybe it all sounds a little overwhelming, but in actuality, Sins of a Solar Empire isn't a difficult game to learn. Experienced fans of the Strategy genre will probably have their feet wet in just 15 minutes, but even for new players that haven't touched anything like it in their life won't be ripping their hair out. Sins is a game with a simple ruleset and a very clear-cut, easily navigable user-interface. We can zoom in to invidivual planets, click on them, and find the button that improves the citizen's living quarters from "space yurt" to "apartment complex" with a few clicks. We can see that the higher level of development costs ___ credits, ___ metal, and ___ crystal, and we can see that it increases population all in the same tooltip. More population means more tax income (credits), which is good. Building mines on resource asteroids improves metal and crystal income, which is good. Researching technology improves metal, crystal, and credit income, and this is good. There's nothing much tricky about the finer details, as you'll find, and the ingame tutorials are about all you really need to get started.
So what's new in Rebellion compared to the older Sins? The Rebellion, that's what. After decades of pointless fighting, the three in-game civilizations have each split into two separate factions over disagreements in ideology. We have the Loyalists, and the Rebels, each with different unique bonuses tailored to different playstyles. The TEC Loyalists, for example, true to the original cause, are defensively minded, with the ability to deploy two starbases in a single gravity well and equipped with stronger shielding and thicker armor plating on their vessels. TEC Rebels aim to take the fight to the aliens with more combat oriented bonuses. You get the picture. This gives a lot of fresh gameplay flavor to the original three factions, but most importantly, it also gives the opportunity to play with the new "Titan" class vessels unique to these factions. They're the biggest, baddest, (most expensive) ships around, bristling with heavy weapons arrays and supremely powerful abilities; the tide-turners of of long wars. Beware locking horns with one from behind anything that isn't a fully-upgraded starbase, or a Titan of your own.
Diplomacy's not really spectacular, but there's definitely an incentive to do it because getting friendly with the other factions can secure you some powerful bonuses. What it all boils down to is either you building 10 Envoy Cruisers (which you will then park in another faction's territory, and wait for the relations to magically improve) or that periodically the other factions might offer you a mission, something like, "kill 5 of [faction]'s ships". If you do it, then relations will improve, and if you decline or ignore it, then relations will sink. Now the A.I players don't care what kind of relationship you have with other people, they're eager to offer you a job to go attack your long-time ally and then seem surprised when the offer obviously goes ignored. They're only motivated by whatever faction seems to be the most direct threat to them, whether it's just purely based on the empire rankings or if they share a border somewhere. This isn't the game for any kind of in-depth political simulation so don't expect to find it here.
How about combat? Well, you won't have to worry about to getting your ships into Delta Epsilon Formation 12 to defend against the enemy's Thuban Thrust, or whatever. It's easier than that. So there are several different types of ships: Light cruisers/corvettes, anti-fighter frigates, siege frigates for bombing enemy planets, missile/beam frigates that engage the enemy at long range, heavy cruisers, anti-structure ships, and support ships like carriers, command, and repair cruisers, and the capital ships. You don't have to be Napoleon to understand that the heavy cruiser is good at fighting and hard to kill, that anti-fighter frigates shoot down aircraft, that siege frigates siege enemy planets, or that the capital ships are the strongest vessels with the heaviest weapons and various abilities that support the fleet. These different classes of ships are specifically designed to fill one role, and being successful at beating the enemy will mean making a good composition of different types of ships that cover each other's weaknesses. Micro-management of your units beyond ordering everyone to focus on the enemy capital ship isn't strictly necessary. Your capital ship's combat abilities can even be set to 'Auto-Cast' so that the AI can worry about the railgun for you. As you become more skilled, though, it's generally a better idea to manage the abilities yourself.
What else? Oh, how about presentation? Well, it's a damn good looking game, for one thing. Gorgeous skyboxes, beautiful weapon effects, detailed ships, damn it's pretty. Watching a a fight between fleets, or a Starbase holding down the line, or a Titan RIPPING AND TEARING THE ENEMY'S GUTS, it's all wonderful to watch. The soundtrack is some A+ work, with faction specific music tracks and ambience for both peace and wartime that changes dynamically when you zoom in on the action. Besides the music, the sounds themselves are also some nice work. Beam weapons, plasma pulses, missiles, autocannons, explosions, great sound work all around. Nice voice-acting, too, professional stuff, even if you do hear their lines repeat too often.
The game comes with two DLC packages, "Stellar Phenomena" and "Forbidden Worlds". The former adds various new star types and anomalies, as well as a set of random events. The latter adds several new planet types, a new gameplay mechanic where you can specialize the development of your worlds, and a host of new planetary artifacts to discover. If you were made to pick between one of these two, you should pick "Forbidden Worlds." Neither are necessary to own, gameplay wise. I do think that the DLC was handled well.
Last important note: The game's got mod-support, and the mod-making community is really fantastic. There's a whole host of excellent mods for Rebellion both in development and already released, if you're looking for something to shake the experience up a little.
Too long, didn't read version:
-Command a unique faction of one of three different civilizations, each with different playstyles
-Manage resources, research technology, expand, colonize, form alliances, crush your enemies
-Large scale, with maps that can expand across multiple star systems and hundreds of planets
-Massive space battles comprising dozens of ships of every type, including the war-ending "Titan" class superships
-Not too difficult to pick up and understand, good user interface
-Solid gameplay, clear-cut ruleset
-Good atmosphere; beautiful visuals, great effects, great soundtrack
-Active modding community that's produced some excellent quality stuff, the shelf-life of this game is a long one*
-Slow pace (Games on large maps may take hours to complete)
Heartily recommended to strategy fans, or anyone who seems interested by the short list of points up there.
*Some mods might require that you own the game's DLC. The DLC is well done, I think. The game's not incomplete without it, and it's not dramatically changed with it.

I love This War of Mine, even though it bums me the hell out.
Its premise revolves around civilians surviving in a fictional war-torn country. You start out with three characters all residing in a shelled out house, which you can switch between with the "Tab" key. Each member has their own peculiarities (some smoke, drink coffee, etc) and skills (better at sneaking, scavenging, better at cooking). You give orders to them based on context bubbles that hover over interactive objects in the world (open doors, eat, cook, sleep, take meds, dig through rubble, attack, etc). When you first start out, you need to scavenge what is in the building to survive. Food, water, and parts. Parts can be used for a variety of purposes, from making beds so your guys can get a better sleep, to chairs, to workshops so you can craft crowbars to force yourself past locked doors, to shovels to help move debri faster, to cooking stoves, water purifiers, the ability to board up windows to lessen the chance of looters, etc etc. That's a VERY small list of what's possible, but to give you an idea.
This is basically what the game revolves around: resource gathering and crafting. There are two phases to the game: daytime and nighttime. Day's are about 10-15 minutes long, nights about 5. During the day you're at your house, building stuff to help in dealing with hunger (building a stove, a trap to catch rats, a water purifier, etc), shelter (boarding up windows, setting up traps to stop intruders, making beds, chairs, etc), comfort to make your guys content (making guitars, radio, a moonshine distillery, etc), and tools that will help outside during the night segments (knives, lockpicks, crowbars, guns). You let your guys sleep, eat, and do things to keep their spirits in check. You require a diversity of resources to accomplish all of this, and once your place has been ransacked in the first few days it's necessary to venture out at dark to scavenge for supplies to be able to live another day.
To get an idea of the gameplay at night, think Mark of the Ninja, though it's much slower paced. You make sound in whatever you do which is indicated as a visible ring that pulsates outwards, which also allows you to hear what's nearby, indicated by a red ring. Venturing out in a warzone is all kinds of unpredictable, and you'll never be sure of what you'll find. You're limited in inventory (some members can carry more). You can take stuff from your place out into the field, such as meds for those in need, crowbars and guns for weapons, lockpicking to reduce the noise of getting through a locked door, but doing so risks using up one of your slots that could bring back much needed loot for the next day. You'll meet people who are in need, who are suffering the hell of war at the mercy of the unmerciful, those who mind their own business, and those who are not all that friendly to say the least. Your job is to get as much resources as you can be any means necessary to sustain your crew.
Straight up, overall I have to say this game's pretty depressing.....it's a demonstration of misery. Not to say it's not a great game, I'm very much enjoying it, but it can be a downer. Your guys are always hungry and tired. They have the ability to get sick and wounded, and require antibiotics/bandages to survive if this befalls them. Most importantly, This War of Mine is mostly a psychological battle. Everything your survivors do (killing, stealing, being unable to help someone) holds ramifications on their mental health. It's very easy for your group to fall into utter despair, and this threat becomes just as big as bullets or hunger (they can commit suicide or become "broken" and won't follow orders). When you think things are finally starting to get better, you're hit by a raid. It just always seems to get worse and worse. So far I've only survived 15 days, my last guy hanging himself. RIP Bruno.
No game really has made me feel grateful for the things I have; this one does. It's a decent survival experience that delves into the psychological torment and endurance ambivilant of morality necessitated by being in a war. Tough moral choices have to be made, and that's what makes this game so fun and impactful.
Prepare to die, and die a lot. Highly recommended.

For those that still don't know: This game is based on a short story by Harlan Ellison first published in the late 60s. This point&click adventure in turn was first published in 1995 and is now available again (unaltered) running on ScummVM.
For those that have read the short story: This game is not a 1:1 retelling of the short story. Rather it is a collection of gameplay episodes featuring the characters from the short story, set in the same cruel world of AM's creation.
Positives:
- great, dark sci-fi story that reminded me alot of the vibe of Dark Seed and its sequel
- awesome atmosphere with grimy, depressing background artwork and character design (poor Benny!)
- no glitches playing from start to finish
- lots of experimenting and trial and error to get a good ending (I know some people take this as a negative)
- voicework is very fitting, especially AM (the antagonist) which is voiced by Harlan Ellison himself
Potentially negative points:
- as with any point&click adventure: if you don't dig the genre you won't dig this game (obviously)
- the trial and error nature of some puzzles might frustrate people who want an easy game
- few settings for graphics and no remastered visuals (basically you get the 1995 version, keep that in mind!)
So who do I think should give this game a go?
Basically anyone even remotely interested in storytelling who digs dark sci-fi/horror themes and can deal with the point&click adventure genre. If you factor in the normal price of EUR 5,99 and the regularly offered discount price of EUR 1,49 you can't really go wrong either way.

This is one of those games where a "mixed" recommendation would come in handy, because it's certainly a Saint's Row game, but it's really not a great one. There are so many staples of the SR series present: The over-the-top scenarios, the humor, the characters, the open world, the activities. So why then, does this feel like a bite-sized SR experience?
Well, for all the good this game does, it also gets a lot wrong, and it's missing some critical features which would bring this on-par with SR IV. Let's start with the most obvious ones.
-Weapons. Where are the weapons? You're telling me that we're literally IN HELL, and you don't have some ridiculous weapons? SRIV had a dubstep gun, and giant purple♥♥♥♥♥♥♥called "the penetrator", but what does GOH have? A frat paddle and a gold-plated SMG?
-Customization. I can let this one slide because you've got a pre-fabbed character, the iconic Johnny Gat, and Kinzie Kensington.I never really customized cars since the super-powered antics of SR IV (since you could run/jump faster than any vehicle could travel). But it would be nice to have homies to customize, a crib to customize, all of the fun customization options that made the other games great. Of course, none of this really matters since:
-You don't have time. Seriously, with each side mission you complete, a small meter fills up, and when that meter reaches certain incriments you have to play an unavoidable story mission. Now, don't get me wrong I enjoy the story missions, but the thing that made them all great (SR 3, especially) was being able to play through them at my pace. When it's all said and done, what reason do I have to continue doing the rest of the game's activities when I'm no longer working towards anything? Am I going to gain more experience to gain abilities, or more money to help me buy the scarce, cheap weapons offered? What are any of those things going to help me do? I think this was a major shortcoming by the devs.
While it has some major glaring problems which may stop is just short of being a genuinely enjoyable Saints Row game, I did still have fun in the 4-ish hours it took me to play it through start to finish, but it may have been more because I was laughing at all of the well-written jokes, rather than the actual gameplay.
At the end of the day, I may only be reluctantly recommending this because I'm a die-hard Saints Row fan, and for very few other reasons than that.

Make no mistake about
....it is NOT a horror game, at least not in the typical sense. It's not trying to make you jump in your seat and scream in shocked terror. It has no interest in what many would call "cheap thrills". Instead, what this game wants to do is provoke your thought-process. It is a very cerebral game, with dark undertones that force you to think about the dark side of humanity, and whether or not there is redemption for our fatal flaws. It isn't afraid to present you with disturbing topics such as suicide,♥♥♥♥♥♥ even genocide, and make you deal with them. Although there is a tint of light-heartedness, 99% percent of the game is drenched in an atmosphere of hopelessness as you scramble to make amends for the characters' pasts in an attempt to thwart the diabolical supercomputer, AM.
This game is loosely based off of the short story of the same name, and the writer of the story (Harlan Ellison) provided support in its development, even lending his voice for the character of AM. The voice acting is a bit hammy, but more in an entertaining other than distracting way (Harlan Ellison sounds wonderfully maniacal; he IS the voice of AM, truly). This game is not a re-telling of the original short story, and even some of the mannerisms and traits of the characters seem to have been changed a bit. However, the game still stays true to the overall atmosphere that the story created.
As far as gameplay is concerned, this is a point-and-click adventure game from the mid-90's, but you probably wouldn't figure as much if you didn't already know. I fired up
after completing this game, and was surprised at just how janky and akward that game is as opposed to this one. The game controls very nicely for it being 20 years old. It takes a bit of getting used to, but they're still intuitive enough that you should have gotten the hang of them after a short amount of time. Controlling the game feels pretty good, and the only complaint I have is that sometimes the screen freezes, so that when you scroll over crucial items, they are not highlighted and you end up skipping over them because you don't know they're there (it's really the only major source of frustration I came across). The game uses a sketch art style that has allowed it to age much more gracefully than its FMV counterparts.
But what about the puzzles? Are they exceptionally hard? Well, they
be, and it's mainly because of the little problem I mentioned at the end of the previous paragraph. I got stumped hard more than a few times because something wasn't being highlighted when I scrolled over it and I thought it couldn't be used. There are also instances where you pick up items that have no real use or are not really all that important in the progression of the story (Gorrister's scenario comes to mind), but these are very few and far between. It's an old point-and-click adventure game, so not everything will seem 100% logical, but with a little critical thought and trial-and-error, you should be able to solve most, if not all, the puzzles on your own.
Other than that, the game gives you subtle hints in something called the "Psyche Profile" (it's the blue book in the character's inventory). You can look at it when you first enter the character's world for a hint, and a new hint will appear whenever you make progress. As you make (good) progress, the background of the character's profile picture will gradually turn a brighter green until it is completely white (meaning you've completed the character's scenario perfectly). This is somewhat of a morality score: the more good actions the character performs, the more you've completed their scenario. Be careful, though; any bad deeds or otherwise traumatizing events will lower this score. I've read that even looking at the Psyche Profile will lower this score, but it must be to a negligible degree, because I never observed much of a difference. But to be perfectly honest, I'm not even really sure what the point of this score is, other than to give you a sense of completion. Harlan Ellison had said that they designed the game so that you can't really win it, and I have an idea of what that may mean, but I don't want to spoil anything here (there ARE multiple endings, by the way, and the bad ending is obtained in a way that you might not expect; and as a quick note, nothing is dependent upon the order that you complete the characters' scenarios, so do them in any order you want).
That end scenario, though...man, that end scenario, haha! It's probably one of the most confusing levels I ever played in a video game. If you decide to embark upon the journey that is this game, then I'll be a nice lady and give you a little hint: when it comes time for the final part, use the good doktor first.
Don't let any of my minor complaints deter you from playing this wonderful game, though. It's still a classic for anybody who enjoys obscure games. Just be wary that it does touch upon some serious topics, and so it might not be for everyone. For everybody else...what are you waiting for? Buy this game and enjoy!

Underdeveloped, unbalanced, overpriced half-hearted would be civ V mod.  Even on easy the AI refuse even the resemblence of a fair deal (they kept offering me trades, then when I would accept they would refuse), and the combat is garbage.  There is virtually no variety and while the advancement system is cool to start, the fact that there are so few upgrades means you're almost always on the same level as your advisaries.  The air combat is just pathetic, and my fully upgraded ships couldn't win a fight against tanks on water.  That isn't a joke or a metaphor or anything, that actually happened.  Worse still is that in some weird handicap, the AI takes pitiful amounts of attritional damage.  The whole part of the game feels like some bad afterthought.
Some new aspects were good.  Choosing what some buildings bonuses would be was pretty cool, and I liked the idea of the tech web which I think was well executed. The affinity was done in an interesting way, but feels unpolished.  It seems inevitable that you can just get all three anyway.  Antoher nice touch was how many upgrades you can get/make for tile improvements, with more than half a dozen to choose from.  Another new and interseting touch was the orbital units, which brings a new element to the gameplay.  And as a final nice touch, they allow you to choose from several benefits and starting resources, allowing some customization of your colony each time you play.
While these new features are great, the would have been awesome... if they were in Civ V.  Beyond earth cuts out so much from the original gameplay (mainly combat which was my favorite part) and waters down the rest, that It makes the whole thing feel somewhat unrewarding.  Who cares if you got a super-cool advanced unit, so did everyone else.  Built a wonder?  Enjoy those very moderate benefits and a picture of some boring blueprint. Tiny & Big is a kind of first-person puzzle platformer set in an almost completely destructible environment. Armed with laser, grappling hook, and rocket, you take the role of Tiny and set about carving up landscapes, obstacles, and objects to create a path forward in pursuit of Big, who has stolen your rightful inheritance from your Grandpa. (Hint:
.)
With 7 total levels, including the very basic tutorial, the game is not very long, but if you're an achievement hunter/speed-runner/perfectionist, it holds a lot of replay value. Graphics have a unique and quirky visual aesthetic, including comic-book-style sound effects spelled out in giant letters as you chop up giant rocks like so much celery. The story (and your goal) is enjoyably strange, and the dialogues between Tiny, his intelligent radio, and Big are sufficiently campy and funny enough that the occasionally rough English translation won't bother you. The radio is also your source for the game's excellent soundtrack, which is picked up piece by piece in the form of tapes as you explore each level.
Biggest downsides are the lack of length of the story (relative to the length of time you'll end up replaying in search of every achievement), and controls/camera that are occasionally awkward or oversensitive in tight spaces (a bit of a bother when you accidentally walk yourself off a ledge while trying to complete a level without dying). These weren't major problems for me, though, and I recommend checking this out if you're looking for something simple and just a bit different.

*Original Review:
I'll start by saying that Hitman Absolution isn't a bad game, it's just not one that I'd particularly recommend- especially with so many awesome other games around these days.
My main gripes are the restrictive options and odd workings of the game. Firstly, while the game may give a few good options for taking down a target each mission, there are a whole range of ways that you can just never do that (to me) seem obvious. Whether it's knocking someone out and wanting to take their costume, but the game won't allow me, so I have to traipse around looking for another costume to KO, when the first one would have been fine.
Other examples are like when you are suddenly targetted by hostiles who are shooting at you and 47 doesn't have the instinct to drop the body that he's dragging to return fire or run!  For some reason I constantly get caught out dragging a body when a random 'randomly' enters the room and I somehow fumble for the 'B' so I can fight back. Usually I just die. :(
Like I said, it's not a bad game per se, it's just not one that I really derive great pleasure from while playing. I guess waiting around for some guys to finish a random (often stupid) conversation so that I can sneak in and take someone down isn't my idea of fun.
I last played Hitman 1 or 2 many years ago and found it better to just go in, guns blazing to complete the missions. This time I really wanted to do them better, but just can't seem to find the game's flow. Hopefully, when I give the game another go next time, it will click and I'll love it. Until then... :/

I managed to get this game for £6 from a Chinese website. I've read loads of the reviews warning me about this installment, but I absolutely adore Egosoft and I've been revelling in the glory of X since X2: The Threat. (I have over 400 hours in total clocked on all X games) £6 seemed like a fair price compared to the ridiculous price Steam is charging on here, so I thought I'd give it a go.
I wish I hadn't. I feel like I've been robbed.
Egosoft state they wanted to make the game accessabile to new players, but what they've done is remove everything that the X veterans loved about the game, but also made the game so poor that new players are not going to want to pic it up. They've failed both markets.
The game was released completely unfinished, as we all know, but they've release 3 revisions and numerous 'patches' over two years and they still haven't addressed any of the underlying problems with the game. I have no idea why they re-wrote the engine, the original one was fine. They could have just expanded on the original one. The storyline is  basically the same, the lore and story follows on loosely from the previous games, but it feels completely disjointed, it doesn't make any sense. The graphics are terrible. The textures are terrible. The voice acting is terrible. Hell Roguey even 'quit' the X community because he was so mortified with what Egosoft had done to the game.
Empire building is gone. Real trading is gone. Flying a million different types of ships has gone. There's no jumping in an M5 and racing around, bouncing off asteroids, then jumping in to an M2 and annihilating an entire system single handed.
But my biggest problem with this game? The controls. In X3:TC they introduced the horrible control system for mice... the 'follow the cursor system'. It vaguely worked okay, but they gave you an option to use 'Classic flight mode' (shift + n) which was how X was meant to be played and works fine with a mouse. In Rebirth they have implemented another follow the mouse mode as the ONLY and compulsory method of flight, and it SUCKS. It's horrible and basically makes dogfighting impossible. I know many people like this kind of control and that's fine, but there's many of us who hate it. Egosoft has refused to implement this for the veterans. Egosoft spent so long trying to make this game feel like a console game with the controller inputs (the radial menus?) that they've forgotten that its a PC game. I wouldn't even mind that much if any of my PC controllers worked with the damn game?!
All in all, don't make the same mistake I did. No matter how much you love space sims and/or the X universe, don't be tempted by this travesty. You'll regret it.

WARNING: SPOILERS AHEAD
Well, this was certainly an interesting and different jaunt for me. The game puts you in the shoes of a happless explorer, waking up stranded on a beach. And right away, the game disquiets you with the fact that everything around you is in black and white. It is almost as if you're wandering about in somebody's dream, though you find soon enough that the one color you're not blind to is red - it permutates nearly everything you run into, in this story.  You see it in the eyes of strange monsters disguised as Spanish soldiers. You see it on the tattered flags of derelect settlements. You see it splattering the ground with fragments of violent events from a distant past. You are the only person left to piece together the clues of what happened, save for a maiden wearing a red cloak. As far as style goes, this game kept it simple but vibrant. It truly felt like I was wandering lost through the forest trails of ancient New England, trying to figure out what happened to the Roanoke Colony (this game isn't directly about that particular incident in history, but it's not hard to imagine how much the event inspired this creation).
As far as style and visuals go, this game is an easy 9. It was slightly flustering having to take so much time reloading your weapons after each shot, but hey, it's the hazard of being a 1-man platoon in the 17th century. Thankfully as the game progresses you manage to secure higher quality weapons and charms that increase your health or allow you to reload faster. Some enemy encounters can get overwelming, but as long as you can keep a good tempo in combat, things get pretty easy after a while.
As for any criticisms I have, I say them only out of love for this game. But Betrayer does feel like it was a bit rushed in some aspects, particularly with the ending. Not that the ending was terrible, but it was a bit of a hasty punch-out. The free-roam mode after you win provides some context as to what happened, but I would have preferred just closing the case once and for all. If your main character gets the girl and they say their final farewells to Tabitha over her grave hand-in-hand, great. If Allison ultimately regresses and decides to push you into an open grave and betrays you as the title suggests, that's fine too. If the programmers wanted a free roam mode so badly, they should have had a hot tub you can climb into with Allison, Tabitha and that native princess. In short, the ending just felt kind of phoned in, and the free roam mode just felt like padding.
Please don't take that to mean I hated the game, though. I recommend the hell out of it to anyone that wants a different kind of challenge to a 1st-person wilderness-survival-paranormal sim. The weapons test your abilities (and the threshold of your patience) as a marksman in frantic combat situations, and the mysteries of each neighboring fort settlement adds so much intrigue to exploring the countryside. I eagerly look forward to any news of a sequel or new content that might spring up for this game, and I hope more people try this out until then. This is a very unsettling, twisted look at the depths of human cruelty to his own people, and I hope this game becomes more widely known as time goes on.

6.5/10
Overview: FPS Action/Adventure
The Good:
+Artistically and technically the game looks very good. The game also gives you the option of adjusting dark/light/color saturation levels to find the desired graphical effect to your liking.
+Interesting setting taking place mid century. The entire game takes place mainly in forested areas
+Interesting story that slowly unravels as you progress
+Easy achievements
The Average:
The combat leaves a lot to be desired. You have a handful of weapons: bows, crossbows, pistols and none of them felt truly satisfying to use.
The game doesn't do much in terms of changing up the gameplay or scenery. The game is split between a number of areas and all of them look, feel and play the same. Enter an area collect all treasures, clues, clear corruption, rinse and repeat.
A lack of enemy variety
The Bad:
-The game gives you the option of using stealth rather than charging head first into battle. The problem however is that stealth is awful. Sometimes enemies will spot you a mile away and other times they won't. It lacks consistency, although there are items that make stealth slightly easier however most of these items are obtained late in the game.  This doesn't really matter though because most of the time enemies will just surprise attack you  as you make your way through the forest.
-The only AI the enemies have is to charge you. Thus, combat revolves around enemies spotting you and then charging you relentlessly.
Conclusion
Despite the low score I do feel there is enough in this game to justify a purchase, albeit at a low price. The developers seem to truly care about the game providing constant updates and responding regularly on the forums.
You are playing this game more for the setting and story and less for the gameplay.

Betrayer is an interesting experience. It has a bold look to it, being only black and white with dashes of red seemed (to me) like a gimmick until I played the game. The developers give you the choice of playing it black and white, or with a variety of levels of colour, varying from off-white all the way to realistic. Despite the choice I still played in almost black and white, it was design move that works heavily in favour of the story. Throughout the game you will encounter peoples tormented souls, and you will figure out what happened to make them all ghostly. The stories are usually mundane and it feels almost pointless to do it except for curiosities sake. However, once you approach the end of the game all these peoples stories will come together to affect what will happen. You will have choices to make, and I found it surprising how invested I was in what I was doing.
The gameplay is very crisp, a solid stealth system that does not hold your hand. If you are not behind cover or in the shadows, and you see an enemy, chances are he will see you as well. You have bows and guns, bows have a higher chance of deflecting off armor but are silent, guns hit hard but are noisy and draw huge aggro. There is also melee and some other weapons but you get the idea.
There is no music, but you will want headphones. You're only indication for what you have to do next is to listen. If you press X you will hear some noises, and you will need to know where they are coming from to find them. Also the game sounds beautiful. Exactly like the outdoors. It's got crows and everything.

A game that is brilliant in its scope, quite well executed for an indie, fantastically stylised and laden with atmosphere. Unfortunately the manner in how well it plays out is rather hamstrung due to lack of feedback, repetitive environments and said stylisation hampering orientation.
Betrayer is a first person, semi-open world adventure game based in  the late 1600s in the new world of America. In this you progress through a colony to find out what the heck has gone on, plus trying to figure out who the mysterious maiden in red who follows you about is. The setting helps set the game out from the crowd, mixing small English outposts, strange ghostly Spanish conquistadors, odd natives and numerous ghosts thorough out. It should also be noted that the game is almost entirely supernatural with few people met who are still of the flesh, where most NPCs are ghosts the player goes to sort fetch quests for, unravelling the situations surrounding their deaths.
To further the ghostly, otherworldly nature of the setting the game has a unique aesthetic, where 90% of the environment is in high contrast black and white with items and enemies highlighted in bright reds. While a little uncanny at first, it does give the game a very interesting atmosphere, especially when it comes to the shifting between night and day mechanics. If players want however, the stylising can be switched off, though it does ruin the mood a slight.
With its HUD displaying a compass and locations of note on it, the game is possibly going to be associated with a Bethesda title such as an Elder Scrolls title or one of the modern Fallout games, however in execution the game is split into a number of small areas that reward exploration and small scale investigation more akin to the stalker games. Also, like Stalker, this is not an RPG so to speak. While your character does improve as the game goes on, it is done mostly through improved items as opposed to gaining levels or experience etc... You gain better guns and charms which kill your enemies faster, from longer ranges and you can sneak and move quicker with charms. Due to the era the game is set in you mostly deal with bows,  crossbows and very crude, slow loading guns. While this may sound cumbersome, and I admit it is, it gives shots a degree of weight. Fire a gun for maximum power with the risk of a slow reload and a mass of noise, or let loose with a number of silent arrows from a bow? The choice feels a little more pointiest than an endless supply of assault rifles.
The combat in the game is generally tilted toward the stealthy approach. Enemies can be taken down in single hits (provided the weapon is good enough) when ambushed, and due to the supernatural plot it even justifies that to a degree. While you can go all out and fight the enemies toe-to-toe, the slow loading of the weaponry usually favours killing things off as fast as possible. To help with this the stealth is reasonably fleshed out, using wind and sneaking to cover you, though I'm not sure if light effects this at all. Unfortunately the AI is a little dopey and you can quite easily hide behind a tree while reloading and strafe around so as to cover yourself while reloading. As such the combat can get a little cheesy at times and fights veer from occasionally overwhelming to simple AI exploiting to get around problems.
While the game does very well for an indie title in its initial hour or so of play, it falls flat on its face once the player starts moving on to the later areas. While adventure and intrigue may drive some people, the utterly random nature of where to find things on the maps is frustrating. Mix the game's unique stylised graphics and a very repetitive landscape with few minor landmarks and its a bit of a crapshoot as to whether you find all the ghosts in an area or not. Sure, Stalker's environments were not too handholdy, but here there just are not enough unique landmarks per map to be able to find things. Also, in stalker items or NPCs would be in logical locations. Where you find the ghosts is just a case of combing each map to see if you missed anything. Mixed with the fact the map only updates the locations of fast travel locations and not the unique clues you need to help solve the mysteries means you need to memorise each location for each item. As someone with a poor short term memory, this is an absolute chore to do. Kudos to the designers for making items of note give off a audio que, plus they tend to stand out in red, but it is still messy trying to progress when its not clear where you are supposed to go or what to do.
All in all Betrayer is a laudable game and certainly worth a look if on offer (I got it in an indie bundle, so nice and cheap). However only don't be too worried if you drop the game if you don't have the patience to seek out all the little odd secrets the designers randomly scattered across the game. Just recommended, but not for people with limited time.

It's actually a demotivating game - it most likely wants to be that way. Your items in the shelter constantly get stolen from bandits after almost every night. But of course you can set your people on watch. Guess what happens then? Your stuff doesn't get stolen but your people will get hurt 90% of the time. The gameplay actually is extremely repetitive, there's only some variation in places. But in the end you always do the same. You fight against your own group that is going to die or flee.
If you wish to play a badass group that just wants to kill anybody too loot and survive - you can't. They get depressed about just everything, they can't even hurt a fly. So it's not YOU making the decisions. It's a lie.
The game tells you exactly what you have to do!
Once you get depressed people, the game ends extremely quickly and you barely can do anything about it. I just had a member leave the shelter and he pretty much took everything with him. After this point, you could simply bash the button "Next Day", skip the missions and wait until the end of game. Or you just rage quit and end it yourself.
Most of the time you will not even win the game. It will just stop somewhere and leave you with a bad feeling, a feeling of having your time wasted because the game with all of it's randomized events has been unfair to you.
You just have to be extremely lucky to have a friendly generated world with good loot opportunities and only the best "help missions" which are all randomized and you need to know exactly how to trick the game and use flaws in the game mechanics.

Cards and Castles is a particularly enjoyable genre-mashing game that doesn’t drown you in too many stats and variables to keep track of. It’s just complicated enough to make you feel like you’re playing a heftier strategy game that is hiding underneath the cutesy, cartoon exterior. Matches tend to balance delicately on each player’s choices and all it takes is one wrong move to completely swing the balance of power in a match.
The game is clearly not supposed to be a somber, intense struggle of number crunching; with a lighter tone in presentation and execution, it definitely lies at the more accessible end of the spectrum. Nevertheless, it still remains to be quite a deep and strategic experience overall.
With the recent update including the Tournament of Champions card set and some modifications made to the drafting system that have improved it a lot, now is a great time to be getting into the game. If you’re at all interested in turn-based strategy games or collectible card games, this is an enjoyable blend of the two genres that you shouldn’t miss. It has the potential to be an enduring success if they continue to “play their cards right” (see what I did there?).

The Mood:
Once I started playing, I could not put this game down.  Its a heavy game.  It sets the mood perfectly and there's never a moment that you're waiting for something.  You are always in need, on edge, and nervous about how bad its going to get trying to obtain that next thing.  Your characters may have a very difficult time with a lot of situations, so its not really about how you feel about what you're doing, its about how the people in the story feel about whats happening.  Killing or stealing from the innocent will have long lasting effects on the person committing the actions, as well as the rest of the group once they hear what happened.  Some characters will need to smoke to keep their sanity, others will drink coffee.  Sometimes when something terrible happens you may need to use some survivors to comfort the others.  Perhaps you want to build a guitar for a group member that can play and lift everyone's spirits.  Maybe build a radio that has some contact to the outside world.  The crafting system is very deep and intuitive and all survivors have some special trait about them.  Everything has an emotional impact and it grows an attachment to the characters more so than I wouldhave imagined.
The Combat:
The combat in this game mechanically is nothing special.  You select what you want your survivor to wield when they're out scavenging.  Based on what you're wielding, you will get different options.  For example, if you have a gun out your guy will take aim at anyone in range and it will display you a icon to fire.  If you're hiding or behind someone you'll get an icon to attempt a backstab attack.  None of this is particularly innovative or interesting, however there's one BIG difference compared to a lot of games.
If you engage in a fight with someone else and they take a hit or you take a hit, often times, both parties sort of freak out and try to leave because nobody wants to die needlesly.  You're rarely just going to areas to kill bad guys and then take their loot, it plays out a lot more humanly (is that a word?) than that.  I was in a situation where i was looting and some people didn't like where I was doing that.  One came at me with a knife and he made me bleed, I hit him with a hatchet and he seemed to immediately just want to run away.  Neither of us wanted to fight any more really, just take as little loss as possible because medicine and bandages are hard to come by for everyone.
TLDR: Combat isn't about killing the other guy, its about surprising and damaging them to the point that they run away, unless the situation really calls for some cold blooded murder.
Replayability:
I'm pretty sure I marathoned a 15 hour single playthrough.  Now thats only one playthrough with 1 group of survivors, of the 6 total starting groups.  You have different endings for each character based on how bad things got and how close you were to not making it at the end.  The war ends at some random time based on your group, you have to listen to the radio to know when its coming.  The locations that you're able to travel through progressively widen as you play the game, and even though the locations on the map are the same, the layouts and the scenarios that happen at these locations vary each playthrough.  There is a lot of randomization to keep things fresh.  Loot, trader visit frequency, some variation in scenarios at all locations, if other survivors come to visit your shelter, you get the idea.  I'm definitely looking forward to my next playthrough with a different group of survivors.

Tiny & Big is a kind of first-person puzzle platformer set in an almost completely destructible environment. Armed with laser, grappling hook, and rocket, you take the role of Tiny and set about carving up landscapes, obstacles, and objects to create a path forward in pursuit of Big, who has stolen your rightful inheritance from your Grandpa. (Hint:
.)
With 7 total levels, including the very basic tutorial, the game is not very long, but if you're an achievement hunter/speed-runner/perfectionist, it holds a lot of replay value. Graphics have a unique and quirky visual aesthetic, including comic-book-style sound effects spelled out in giant letters as you chop up giant rocks like so much celery. The story (and your goal) is enjoyably strange, and the dialogues between Tiny, his intelligent radio, and Big are sufficiently campy and funny enough that the occasionally rough English translation won't bother you. The radio is also your source for the game's excellent soundtrack, which is picked up piece by piece in the form of tapes as you explore each level.
Biggest downsides are the lack of length of the story (relative to the length of time you'll end up replaying in search of every achievement), and controls/camera that are occasionally awkward or oversensitive in tight spaces (a bit of a bother when you accidentally walk yourself off a ledge while trying to complete a level without dying). These weren't major problems for me, though, and I recommend checking this out if you're looking for something simple and just a bit different.

Magic: Duels is an electronic collectible card game (CCG) based on the Magic: The Gathering physical card game.
What is Great about this game:
- This game is a pretty faithful recreation of the Magic: The Gathering card game, likely the best collectible card game around for a few decades
- Unless you are deep into Magic already, this is by far the best entry point into the game as a whole and generally the best way to play some quick Magic duels
- Over the decades, Magic has become a deep and sometimes complicated game (which means lots of rules to track), and playing it electronically allows you to focus on just playing such a deep and strategic game - rather than focusing on rules adjudication
- The free-to-play mechanics of buying boosters is generally fair (if a bit grindy), but one huge improvement over the physical version of the game is that you cannot get more than the allotted cards, so the more boosters you get, the more likely they are to have few commons and more and more rare (i.e. better) cards
What is Good about this game:
- There is decent variety in the types of games you can play, but they could certainly stand to have more - perhaps have the campaign available to go through with your own deck
- The campaigns and tutorials are generally good at onboarding new players
- Good use of Steam features such as achievements, trading cards, etc
What is Bad about this game:
- The game is quite stingy in the way that it hands out coins to buy boosters.  It doesn't award coins for playing against friends or playing two-headed giant.  I think they are fixing the 2HG issue, but it still seems dumb that I can't earn even 5 coins for playing against a friend
- The amount of cards and card sets available to play with is fairly small right now.  It has plenty of gameplay possibilities just with what it has right now, but it's hard not to want some more of the vast number of card sets available in the physical game
- For such a relatively simple game graphically, the performance is generally a little slow both in connecting to the network and in gameplay
Conclusion:
Unless you are already a Magic afficianado, this is simply the best way to get into and play Magic which is the best collectible card game around.

This is the voice of someone completely new to Magic (apart from some minor knowledge picked up from the Friday Nights sketch series, and playing through the XBox 360 tutorial/demo of Magic 2015), so make of that what you will.
This game seems to me to be full of questionable design choices, which is incredibly unfortunate:
- I'm not the pickiest about graphics usually, but a bit of antialiasing to make the mostly-static cards look a little nicer wouldn't have hurt. The end-of-campaign cutscenes looked like they belonged in the early 2000s, such was the animation quality.
- The tutorial campaign teaches some things in the wrong order, meaning you encounter mechanics only after they became relevant.
- The story campaign itself, though short, is somewhat enjoyable - but many encounters involve decks balanced completely against you, causing the entire match to be based on luck of the draw/poor luck on the AI's draw to win.
- Certain important mechanics are broken in strange ways. Tap lands manually before playing a spell to try and ensure you have the right colours left over for the next one? Game decides by default to tap extra lands rather than using the floating mana first. Prompts asking whether you want to activate a certain ability cover the entire screen, so you have no idea what it will do and have no way to plan how to play it out. Turning off the option to automatically order blockers won't necessarily do so. The list goes on...
- There is very little way to try and learn using control decks against real people. When against an AI, with the "Zoom Card" option on, the card stays in a place where you can read what it's going to do, then continue and "pause timer" to act. Against a real person, it plays an overly long animation of the card swinging past the screen, a split second to look at the portrait, and then a second before it's too late to do anything about it. Less than ideal when you're trying to decide whether it's worthwhile to counter something.
- Deck customisation is surprisingly limited. The "Deck Wizard" is useful in theory, giving a bunch of possible 'archetype' templates to base a deck off of... but at the start it's very unlikely that you'll be able to cobble together anything half-decent with the cards you begin with in any of those styles. You're forced into choosing a certain number from each "category", many of which don't actually fit together properly. Even worse, once you've created a deck with this wizard, there is no way to edit it without going back into the wizard again, meaning if you crack a pack and want to try a specific card out, chances are you'll have to rebuild manually from scratch. This is a step backwards from Magic 2015, where you were given a full-fledged starter deck in whatever colour combo at the end of the tutorial, and could freely customise it with whatever cards you had thereafter. I don't understand why this would have changed back like this.
In short... I wanted to enjoy this, but it just ended up a frustrating experience for me. How much of that is down to me being utterly new to Magic I can't say for sure, of course, but with the UI quirks and the like I feel it's on the whole not a well implemented experience.

Civ BE would be a great add-on to Civ 5. Unfortunately it is not an add-on, but in fact a stand-alone game. The mechanics and in general gameplay are EXACTLY like Civ 5, which while being nice for the first couple playthroughs, was ultimately disappointing as I was hoping for something new. There are some cheesy swaps, like putting a wig on Happiness and calling it "Health", but otherwise it feels and plays like a moderately cool mod.
The one thing that really sets it apart are the quests, which give an almost story-like feel to the game, and lets you both personalize your civ as well as make dull parts more interesting. Unfortunately the thrill of this lasts only a few games, at which point you've exhausted all different options.  Affinities are also "new", but really just a downgraded (yes downgraded) version of ideologies.  The civilization options are exciting for exactly 3 playthroughs, as they don't really stand apart that much.  It's not like you're comparing England to the Zulus, with exciting pro's and con's to each civ.
There are multiple ways to win of course, and that can be somewhat interesting, one time each. The maps are not as diverse and the tech tree, while more robust, gives you a oddly small variety of units, making your unit creation very boring.
This was good for a mod, but HORRIBLE for the price. I LOVED my first playthrough, liked my second, and tolerated my third. By the time I exhausted all of the endings (just for kicks), I could not believe I had wasted so much money on this. Wait for Civ 6 to come out or for this to go on sale.

Excellent game. As of current version (3.61 IIRC) it runs like a charm for me, is graphically amazing, interesting, very immersive, and the few bugs I encountered (i.e., ships not spawning when they were supposed to during the plot once, this kind of things) didn't bother me and were really rare.
Most of the critics I've read/heard were either obsolete (game at launch was a mess, okay), or were due to wrong expectations: XRebirth is not X3-enhanced, and wasn't supposed to be; you can only pilot one single ship yourself, but that was perfectly advertised and is technically understandable. It's actually a good decision they made, even gameplay-wise, from my point of view. Landing on stations... well many players did ask for that a lot in the past years, so they finally went for it. Not the greatest part of the game, but it does add to the immersion and diversity, it works okay, so whatever.
Of course there are "buts", and rather significative ones. Some design decisions still don't make much sense, or were poorly implemented.
- Smalltalk game. A rather interesting idea after all... BUT it's quite random, time-consuming, and very repetitive. You HAVE TO go through it a lot, to get trade updates (which you'll want, systematically), or hireling's profiles (which you'll want, regularly). Can be lightened by mods.
- Fleet management is... almost non-existent. Because you're not supposed to bother too much with it: here you don't manage fleets of bots, but captains, defense-officers and pilots, and they're supposed to do their jobs and organize their own squadrons themselves. Problem is, they're not very effective.
- AI is fine... mostly. For basic routines. It definitely needs more "I", though...
- Annoyance that persists from the previous games: all the other factions in the universe are more-or-less static and scripted: you can help or hinder economies, but you'll never make any major difference in the end; you can destroy PMC fleets, they'll just spawn new ships out of thin air; you can help Canterra restart their economy, but they'll never really grow and adapt...
- ...
I'll put X-Rebirth aside for the time being due to these issues and a few others (first of all, my lack of free time). But at around 100hours, this is definitely worth much more than what I paid for it. At some point, it gave me the nostalgia of the previous installments; but when I replayed X3:AP for some time, I realized Rebirth was a huge leap forward. Beautifull, more immersive, more lively, more "believable", more fun.
In the end, despite these annoyances, I can still totally recommend Rebirth. Plus, the fact that Egosoft planned for it to be the basis of future games: with this engine and these designs as a new start, they'll definitely make something amazing through expansions and sequels. But this is not just a "proof of concept" for the future, it definitely is a great game by itself.

The red-headed stepchild of the Bioshock series, Bioshock 2 was kind of unceremonious at release and mostly forgotten about after a few months. Where does it stand, years later?
Bioshock 2 doesn't have a cool twist, or even a cohesive story, really. It's a criticism of Collectivism, but it doesn't really get anywhere and kind of gets lost in the noise. You're a Big Daddy, Subject Delta, and you are bonded to a certain Little Sister, who is apparently a savior of some kind. The story is told through radio transmissions and audio logs, but it gets very muddy very quickly. You are given some more choices than Bioshock 1, but it basically boils down to "kill this character, or let them survive," three times, along with either saving or harvesting Little Sisters. Six endings stem off of that... but they don't change much. The story does give some interesting insights into characters met in Bioshock 1, as well.
Despite the somewhat-confusing story, the gameplay is what shines here. The gunplay is vastly improved over the first Bioshock, and more options being available for you to deal with enemies. You can hold a ton of passive tonics, which can alter your playstyle in various ways, including giving you the ability to repair and name security bots, or stand in water to heal, or giving you an advantage while hacking. Hacking has changed from a repetitive game of Pipe Dream to a time-based minigame, which is completed in real time. You can even hack from a distance or equip auto-hack darts. The game feels tighter around the edges, and it shines. You're also able to use both plasmids and guns at the same time, which is a huge improvement over switching back and forth.
Although the story isn't quite up-to-par, and the recently released Bioshock Infinite DLC pretty much pretends that Bioshock 2 never happened, the game gives you a good exploration of some more themes in Rapture and allows you to visit one of the best settings in a video game one more time. It's definitely worth checking out.
