A game that is brilliant in its scope, quite well executed for an indie, fantastically stylised and laden with atmosphere. Unfortunately the manner in how well it plays out is rather hamstrung due to lack of feedback, repetitive environments and said stylisation hampering orientation.
Betrayer is a first person, semi-open world adventure game based in  the late 1600s in the new world of America. In this you progress through a colony to find out what the heck has gone on, plus trying to figure out who the mysterious maiden in red who follows you about is. The setting helps set the game out from the crowd, mixing small English outposts, strange ghostly Spanish conquistadors, odd natives and numerous ghosts thorough out. It should also be noted that the game is almost entirely supernatural with few people met who are still of the flesh, where most NPCs are ghosts the player goes to sort fetch quests for, unravelling the situations surrounding their deaths.
To further the ghostly, otherworldly nature of the setting the game has a unique aesthetic, where 90% of the environment is in high contrast black and white with items and enemies highlighted in bright reds. While a little uncanny at first, it does give the game a very interesting atmosphere, especially when it comes to the shifting between night and day mechanics. If players want however, the stylising can be switched off, though it does ruin the mood a slight.
With its HUD displaying a compass and locations of note on it, the game is possibly going to be associated with a Bethesda title such as an Elder Scrolls title or one of the modern Fallout games, however in execution the game is split into a number of small areas that reward exploration and small scale investigation more akin to the stalker games. Also, like Stalker, this is not an RPG so to speak. While your character does improve as the game goes on, it is done mostly through improved items as opposed to gaining levels or experience etc... You gain better guns and charms which kill your enemies faster, from longer ranges and you can sneak and move quicker with charms. Due to the era the game is set in you mostly deal with bows,  crossbows and very crude, slow loading guns. While this may sound cumbersome, and I admit it is, it gives shots a degree of weight. Fire a gun for maximum power with the risk of a slow reload and a mass of noise, or let loose with a number of silent arrows from a bow? The choice feels a little more pointiest than an endless supply of assault rifles.
The combat in the game is generally tilted toward the stealthy approach. Enemies can be taken down in single hits (provided the weapon is good enough) when ambushed, and due to the supernatural plot it even justifies that to a degree. While you can go all out and fight the enemies toe-to-toe, the slow loading of the weaponry usually favours killing things off as fast as possible. To help with this the stealth is reasonably fleshed out, using wind and sneaking to cover you, though I'm not sure if light effects this at all. Unfortunately the AI is a little dopey and you can quite easily hide behind a tree while reloading and strafe around so as to cover yourself while reloading. As such the combat can get a little cheesy at times and fights veer from occasionally overwhelming to simple AI exploiting to get around problems.
While the game does very well for an indie title in its initial hour or so of play, it falls flat on its face once the player starts moving on to the later areas. While adventure and intrigue may drive some people, the utterly random nature of where to find things on the maps is frustrating. Mix the game's unique stylised graphics and a very repetitive landscape with few minor landmarks and its a bit of a crapshoot as to whether you find all the ghosts in an area or not. Sure, Stalker's environments were not too handholdy, but here there just are not enough unique landmarks per map to be able to find things. Also, in stalker items or NPCs would be in logical locations. Where you find the ghosts is just a case of combing each map to see if you missed anything. Mixed with the fact the map only updates the locations of fast travel locations and not the unique clues you need to help solve the mysteries means you need to memorise each location for each item. As someone with a poor short term memory, this is an absolute chore to do. Kudos to the designers for making items of note give off a audio que, plus they tend to stand out in red, but it is still messy trying to progress when its not clear where you are supposed to go or what to do.
All in all Betrayer is a laudable game and certainly worth a look if on offer (I got it in an indie bundle, so nice and cheap). However only don't be too worried if you drop the game if you don't have the patience to seek out all the little odd secrets the designers randomly scattered across the game. Just recommended, but not for people with limited time.

Betrayer is fantastic! It really saddens me that this game really didn’t get a lot of publicity or praise. So many lesser games are receiving more appreciation than they deserve.
Betrayer is a bit of a mixed bag as far as genres go. The story and atmosphere is very much rooted in horror and paranormal. Mechanically the game is a first person shooter/melee adventure. There are mild RPG mechanics granting some basic equipment upgrades and a few nice skills here and there. Gameplay consists almost entirely of stealth survival with a very strong focus on limited resources and few but deadly enemies. To wrap all that up, the world is staged in a re-imagined colonial America fighting against skeletal Spaniards.
With just an eclectic mix of attributes it would be unsurprising to find that the game plays like an incohesive mess, but instead it brings this incredible breath of fresh air. Captivating and enthralling just begin to scratch the surface of what it’s like to boot up Betrayer for the first time. The button mappings are a bit strange but easy enough to rebind, and while you’re in the menu, make sure to fiddle with the mouse sensitivity. Once the controls are sorted out, you’ll find yourself constantly pulled forward into this dark, death filled world. It was incredibly hard to pull myself away; I wanted to just find that next scrap of information, or find out what happened to this one more lost soul. Riddled along the way I got a few good jump scares but none of the horror was contrived or staged, it was all very natural and unsettling. The weapons have serious weight to them, but at the same time leave you very vulnerable. I found myself tiptoeing through the underbrush, only covering distance quickly when the breeze picked up, rather than confronting any enemy outright.
If you've read my other reviews you know I don’t do the whole numerical rating because they are meaningless; however, out of my entire game collection Betrayer sits very comfortably amongst the top ten and won’t be going anywhere anytime soon.

*WARNING* Possible gameplay spoilers, read ahead at own risk.
Betrayer is not a bad game, but not as good as it could have been.
A visible effort into making a stand-out first person shooter-stealth horror game. Personally, I liked this game quite a bit. I'm fond of the design and setting and the gameplay wasn't bad, but there is plenty of room for improvement.
The first thing a player will notice is the color scheme, black and white with red filters to create a unique visual setting which perfectly complements the lonely and abandoned theme of the game. It creates an unsettling environment and is capable of leaving a memorable impact on a player. But I found that while it does look neat, the style lacks substance and eventually becomes a chore to look at for prolonged periods. Thankfully you have the option to adjust color and saturation on the main menu, so therefore only half of the game gets tiresome to look at.
Betrayer's gameplay can be considered as a FPS with stealth and horror implements. The player has an open world dotted with enemies to be looking out for, and three weapon slots to fill with your choice of weapons. While the gameplay wasn't atrociously bad, there are some loose screws that break a chunk of the experience off. The game takes place in the 1700's in the new world (AKA modern day America if you don't know history) and takes advantage of the technology of the time period: Bows and powder loaded single shot firearms comprise your selectable armory. One of the problems I have with Betrayer is the weapons itself, being a first person shooter weapons are a very important part of the gameplay, and the weapons available are of short variety and are slow and meticulous to use. To fill your three weapon slots is a selection of 5 weapons, 3 kinds of bows and 2 firearms. The bows are unreliable in combat because a heavy chunk of enemy distribution are covered in a kind of armor that has a chance to harmlessly deflect your arrows, and the guns, realistically but kind of frustratingly, take a long time to reload. This makes the combat either frustrating or uninteresting depending on the player's approach.
Stealth mechanics are also implemented, enemies start off unaware of you but can detect you if they see or hear you coming. To counteract this, you can stay crouched and in shaded, obsure areas and move when the wind blows to block out the sounds of your footsteps. Stealth is even encouraged in the prologue level as it explains that enemies become enraged when in combat making them stronger, and that attacks while undetected deal more damage. A problem with this is that the stealth mechanics aren't as polished as they should be in order to suggest such an approach for the whole game. Enemies will always know exactly where you are if you mess up, and you cannot escape and try again, making a stealthy capture of a fort or outpost a "do it right the first time or not at all" deal. Also, I find that using arrows is more difficult with the black and white color scheme since its harder to determine where your arrows are flying, so it takes longer to determine the arc and most often giving yourself away.
For the horror aspect of Betrayer's design: I think it's subjective. I didn't find anything scary but that doesn't mean others will too. I liked some of the enemy designs, the maddened beasts wearing spanish inquisitor armor and the burned men (who are IMPOSSIBLE to see with black and white settings) are some of the most unique and creative designs I've ever seen. But at the same time the enemies are also so uncreative and boring. Other types of enemies include giant spiders and skeletons, might as well go all the way and throw in Frankenstein's monster and dracula to get the real Disney's Haunted Mansion effect. I was really disappointed at this turn, since the other types of enemies are creative and fit perfectly with the game's setting only to erase them out entirely halfway through the game and rely on cliche monsters you'd find in a kids halloween drawing. On a side note here, one of the most memorable and fun parts of the game is where you come across a large fort that you'd expect to be infested with enemies, only to find it empty. You feel slight relief at the unexpected respite when you hear battle horns in the distance and then find yourself under seige from the spanish inquisitors. This part was so unexpected and fun, I really wished that more of Betrayer had moments like this. Nobody suspects the Spanish Inquisition!
Now to the final point: Betrayer is a semi-open world game with a sort of mystery setting for the story, setting out a bunch of clues in the map and letting the player explore to find them, no handholding. This leaves the entire experience of Betrayer to the player's whim, do you scour the map finding each and every bit or do you rush through to the end? While this is a good idea, the game's design is flawed and incapable of supporting it. Resulting in a lot of backtracking, boredom and searching. Being "alone and abandoned with no handholding" requires that the game fully captivates its player, getting them excited and invested in the experience making them want to discover everything and providing positive reinforcement with a sense of accomplishment. Betrayer has none of these, you find a clue, make a note of it and maybe a ghost will say something about it.  This results in the exploration of Betrayer being uneventful and disappointing. Not to mention that in order to uncover a large majority of items hidden you need a shovel, which can be found roughly half way through the game, resulting in a LOT of backtracking.
While Betrayer missed the mark, the ideas are there. It could have been so much better, creating a unique open world mystery game in the 1700's with supernatural twists and heart pounding stealth combat. Instead Betrayer is flat, repetitive and lacking in a lot of substance. Despite my enjoyment with the basic idea of the game and all of it's potential, I can't help but feel disappointed with the direction the game took instead. The appeal is there but doesn't build up to anything worthwhile.

Disturbing story, leaves you thinking... Violent stuff has happened and you must find out who did it (find artefacts and present them to related 'persons', no puzzle other than finding the stuff in the first place), and ultimately you must judge whether or not those people should be set free or left to torment on their deeds. Boils down to a binary choice, yes, but it made me think about stuff I probably wouldn't otherwise.
Game-play is quite fun, actually, with you exploring several right sized locations for items and 'people' to talk about those items. The maps are populated with some enemies, that re spawn when die, and a nice mechanic is implemented to let you approach those enemies with some stealth. You also have perfect indication if you have been spotted or not, as well as noises that you learn to recognize that point to nearby enemies - which can be pretty hard to spot when not enraged and charging you. New enemies (with accompanying attack mechanics, mostly hit and run but with different flavours) are introduced at a right pace. At least one of them made me jump when they first showed up, which for me is quite hard to achieve in games where the character has some means to defend itself... You must also use a nice mechanic to switch to 'dark mode', which changes the enemies, the colour scheme turns dark, and severely limits your view range. The idea is to explore in light mode, mark up the spots (by hand or by cellphone photos, as the map has no marker functions) and then revisit some places when you have the equipment or on the right mode to progress in story. You also can ask for audio and visual cues to where you should go next, which will help you find the elements relevant to the story.
Overall the game was a dark and tense experience but also a quite enjoyable exploration. You are not powerless or forced to do stealth, and although you are encouraged and should use it to at least dispatch the stronger enemies first in a surprise attack, charging up in the right zig-zag pattern might left you alive at the end. Still I recommend do not panic and remember an axe to the face is quite effective in discouraging those pesky charging foes.

The game is a very slow paced RTS based in space (big surprise).

Dead Rising 2 is an open world survival horror beat 'em up game which was released in mid 2010 on both console and PC. You play as Chuck Green, who is a motocross rider, as you try to survive a zombie outbreak. The game is set in a shopping and casino complex which is filled with zombies. You encounter up human survivors throughout the game, as well as finding and crafting weapons.
Game play wise; Dead Rising 2 is a very typical hack and slash style. You find weapons around the levels such as crowbars, sledge hammers, pistols, right the way up to silly items such as garden rakes and party hats.  As you progress through the story you get more experience  points from completing missions and saving survivors. The game is also heavily based around time constraints too; you have to do missions at certain times; if you miss the time you either loose the game or the mission is gone and you can never finish it. This to me made me have to make a lot of sacrifices to what content I actually got to see; I personally didn't see a huge need to have the time constraints in place as you just end up missing out on content that the developers have worked hard to make.
That being said; all of the missions and side quests are virtually all the same. Side missions consist of finding the survivor, and escorting them back to your safe house. Whilst main story missions are "walk here" and "kill that" goals. To me the lack of creativity really felt like it let the game down here.
Graphics wise; Dead Rising 2 is a game which has been out for close to five years now. Whilst at a glance the graphics look OK, but if you get a closer look you can really tell the age of this title. Poor quality textures are the main culprit here. I can sort of forgive it as it is an open-world game though.
The main story right up to the ending had me intrigued the whole way through. Although some of the plot twists are kind of predictable if you pay attention; it was still enough to keep me interested. Sadly though the ending of the game really annoyed me. I don't want to spoil it for people but it kind of had an anticlimax feel to it which didn't leave a nice taste in my mouth afterwards.
Dead Rising 2 isn't exactly a difficult game, there are a couple QTE type actions you have to carry out when you are grabbed by a zombie, but personally I found the most difficult aspect of the game was to be finding weapons which don't completely break from durability loss after a couple of hits. Ammo for guns is few and far between so the majority of the time you are in melee - so ideally you need a couple of melee weapons each mission due to them breaking all the time. Towards the end of the game, if you managed to rescue a couple of survivors, you really do become quite overpowered; once my speed skill was maxed out I was able to dodge most  zombies when running between objectives. Boss fights are pretty "meh" too; none of them have any real difference, they all tend to be just a regular enemy but with more health. I did find the fight with the helicopter to be quite interesting but that was the only real original boss fight concept in the game.
Each zone/level is pretty hectic, like I said, you can have up to 7000 zombies on your screen at any time, there are an abundance of items to pick up and craft into different weapons, not to mention lots of little Easter eggs to find, such as playing a golf simulator. The atmosphere in each of the levels actually really reminded me of Las Vegas; and if you have been there it will really feel like you are there in the game (even though you aren't there location wise in the story).
A full playthrough of Dead Rising 2 with the majority of side quests being completed, took me just over ten hours. I personally cannot see any reason why I would play through the single player story again as it's very linear and you cannot change the events that take place. The multiplayer is also pretty derelict too - at the time of writing this, there are only 40 people in the game.
Technically I didn't have major game breaking issues; just a small gripe with the crazy amount of loading screens this game has. Literally every couple of minutes you get a loading screen, whether it be for a cut scene, ending of a cut scene, changing zone, I counted 7 loading screens in the space of 10 minutes at one point. For me, that is unacceptable and I am surprised not many people actually picked up on it.
In conclusion; do I recommend Dead Rising 2? Personally I wouldn't recommend it at full price. For starters there are much better zombie games like this out there in the form of Dead Island. The game's length is too short for me - and all this being compounded by lack of multiplayer activity just makes this a single player game. So I cannot recommend Dead Rising 2 at full price; if you can get it for at least 50% off, you may as well pick it up as it's an OK open world title, but nothing more.

I really liked Kung Fury the video game. Although, after the 2 hours I did play it, it started to get a little old.
But, to be fair, I didn't hate the movie that the game was based off of it.
I just didn't like it that much.
Kung Fury has bathed deep in the cliches and dumb cheeziness of old 80's movies, combined with nerdy fantasies that you could see popping up during a really crazy D&D session. It not only pokes fun at those cliches, it also glorifies them and the over-the-top action that follows them.
However, that's where my problems come with Kung Fury.
Those very cliches that Kung Fury makes fun of by including in the script make the film very predictable. Black Dynamite was a similarly made film, but it managed to bounce off those cliches that it poked fun of and would manage to keep the film's story and action rolling steadily.
Kung Fury tends to stop a few times and its humor in those scenes where nothing happens is really... cringe-worthy. Dumb slap-stick and over-the-top 80's jokes fill these otherwise pointless scenes, like where Kung Fury meets vikings and is sent to the right time he wants to travel to by Thor. Some people might enjoy that idea, but I found it kinda stupid.
Along with that, the budget does show specifically with the CGI included in the film. The backgrounds and fight choreography look nice and are stylized well but the dinosaurs and robots look so blatantly fake, that it just got distracting.
Kung Fury isn't perfect, but it is enjoyable. If it looks like your kind of 30-minute action flick, then check it out. I mean, it's free! But I'm gonna give Kung Gury a 6/10. It's enjoyable, but it wasn't my cup of tea exactly.

I suppose a decent place to start would be to address the games supposed shock value. After all the main character is a genocidal maniac bent on murdering hundreds of innocent people, however despite this grisly and sinister concept, Hatred does nothing to make you guilty of the atrocities you find yourself committing. The supposed shock value is simply not present here, while playing Hatred I felt no remorse and no guilt for killing all these innocent people, and that is not because I’m a horrible person, there are many games which managed to produce an emotional response from myself and many other players, however Hatred is not one of those games. You will care about as much about the civilians in Hatred as those roaming the streets of GTA 5s Los Santos or Saints Rows Steel port. These people have no names, no backstory, no personality. They are nothing but pixels on a computer monitor, and no matter if you kill, 10, 100, 1000 of them, the emotional response will be about the same as if you were instead shooting zombies.
You will not care at all, and more to the point from the moment you start playing, you will find it simply impossible to take Hatred seriously. The games main character is perhaps the most obnoxious and ludicrous antagonist I have ever played in a video game. He doesn’t feel like an introverted and mentally disturbed spree killer, instead he is much more akin to a James Bond villain. That is if a James Bond villain was written by a twelve year old. Indeed his dialogue is so utterly absurd and his constant one-liners so cheesy and ridiculous, that instead of feeling shocked by this guys psyche I found myself bursting into laughter on multiple occasions.
But I digress. Hatred was never intended to be a deep look at the physiology and mental condition of spree killers, and none of what I previously mentioned would at all matter if only Hatred was a fun video game, which it saddens me to say, it is not. At its core, Hatred is a fairly mediocre top down twin stick shooter. It’s gunplay is unexceptional at best and utterly frustrating at worst. Far too often the clumsy movement combined with the lack of a cover system means that often you will have no idea where you’re being shot from or indeed if you can hit a certain enemy that might or might not be behind a piece of cover. This issue is made even worse by the fact that Hatreds levels have no checkpoints, and should you die you will be forced to restart the entire level. The only way to get around that is to earn so called “respawn tokens” which do exactly what it says on the tin and can be obtained by completing certain side objectives, of which there are about two or three in each level. But perhaps the worst crime committed by Hatred, is being a boring video game.
Some games are short but sweet, others are long and monotonous, however Hatred manages to combine the worst of both worlds, and even if you can pull yourself through the often frustrating combat, even then Hatred will become boring and repetitive long before the credits roll. Most of the levels here work in exactly the same way, the main character arrives in a certain area, after which you have to kill a certain number of people and then proceed to the next level. Rinse and repeat. There is practically zero gameplay variation on offer here and therefore the game gets repetitive extremely quickly. The same goes for the executions, which you will be doing a lot considering they are literally the only way to regenerate your health. Fortunately there is an option to skip the cutscenes which these executions trigger, because just like almost everything else it this game, they get old extremely fast. Any novelty that Hatred might have expires very quickly, which frankly is utterly unforgivable considering that the game itself is not very long at all. It personally took me a mere three hours to complete Hatred, and that is including doing just about all the side objectives in each level, so if you really wanted to rush this thing I could see someone completing the game in around 2 hours, but chances are you will probably get bored before you get there. Destructive Creations wants $20 or £15 for this game, and even if it was any good, which it clearly is not, I still highly doubt that many people would want to pay that amount for 2-3 hours of gameplay.
The only redeeming factor here are the games visuals. The almost exclusively black and white colour palette, combined with some nice film grain effects make for an aesthetically pleasing experience. Hatred also utilises Unreal Engine 4 and Nvidia’s Physics technology to bring a great deal of destructible terrain. Grenades destroy walls and send out flying particles, cars can drive through buildings and bullets tear up walls and architecture. Its truly impressive stuff, unfortunately it’s stuck in the middle of an otherwise un-exiting and outright boring game. But Hatreds problems don’t end there. For one things it’s terribly optimised, and at 1080p I saw the game constantly dropping below 60 frames per second on a very powerful dual GPU setup. The game crashed on me twice, I experienced an array of audio bugs throughout my play trough and the enemy AI is just simply awful. They either blindly rush your position, usually one by one, or simply stand around doing absolutely nothing.
On almost every single level, Hatred is frankly an underwhelming failure of a game. It, rather understandably fails to live up to all the hype that people have built up around it before it’s lunch, it fails to present itself as a piece of meaningful satire and most of all it fails to be an enjoyable  video game. It’s short, repetitive and looses any sense of novelty within the first hour of playtime. It will not inspire any spree killers and it won’t turn gamers into sadistic lunatics with a thirst for innocent blood. But you probably already knew that. Instead Hatred commits the greatest crime a video game can commit, at the end of the day, it is simply boring.

Disclaimer: this is going to turn into a slighly long and waffly review about what I think of the Saints Row games in general (since I've got most of them on XBox rather than Steam so I can't review them here).
Saints Row 1&2 were basically decent Grand Theft Auto clones. I felt they were probably trying a little too hard to be gritty and it didn't entirely seem to ring true. 2 was better than 1, largely because they'd ironed out the minor issues, and the gameplay was fine although nothing original.
Saints Row 3 was the definite high point of the series for me. It had dropped the attempts to be gritty in favour of silliness (and the silliness was a sort that appealed to me) but still felt grounded in a sort of reality. With all the various leveling up it ends up pretty easy at the end, but there's a challenge at the start, so it kind of feels earned.
Saints Row 4 went a bit far for me. Nothing feels remotely related to reality and the superpowers remove the driving element and make it all rather too easy. It's silly enough to be fun though, so still worthwhile.
Gat out of Hell has most of the same issues as Saints Row 4 (no real link to reality, overpowered superpowers). I kind of prefered the Hell setting to the SR4 virtual reality setting, so it has that in it's favour. It's obviously a shorter game (but is cheaper) and is missing some of the fun free-form aspects of the previous games, like character customization. It's still fun though, and provides a good run of mindless OTT violence. I'm just not convinced it's the place to start with the series.
On a side note, the Linux port wasn't phenomenally good - it was a little unstable, the process needed to be killed manually after quitting, and it occassionally ran into sound issues where it would start stuttering and never stop. This was in early 2016, but I don't think it's been updated since. I appreciate the fact that it exists and it was playable, but it could have been better,

After replaying this after the 3.0 patch, and with a fresher mindset, i feel I can give this game a fairer review.
In a word, X rebirth, is alright. I really wish steam reviews had a better system than a thumbs up or down, because I do not believe this game to be praiseworthy, but neither should it be within the mostly negative on the steam page.
It is not by any means a bad game, but it is not a great one either. I still feel if you are wanting to get into the X series, to start you should play X2: the threat or X3: Terran conflict (or Albion prelude, AP is essentially an expansion for TC anyway) however on its own, X Rebirth stands a good space 4X first person space simulator. It has some nice looking paint, a tutorial that is excellent for teaching new players to the X series (whereas before, the game plonked you into a grand universe, without even controls to do anything, with the exclusion of X3, where there is a flight school, that simply tells you how to move your ship. To start this mission, you must open communications with it, which the game neglets to give you the command to do so)
Many people were also afraid of the bugs when it first came out. Most of the serious bugs have now been squashed, and the game playable, there are still errors that can be easily seen, but thankfully none that impact the gameplay massivly (the worst ive seen is a group of NPC ships getting stuck together). Although I feel that Ego was going for a major shift in gameplay, alienating many fans of the X series. I do not think that this was made to be a Space management game. Trading takes too long, and profits made during runs are often not worth the time. However, I feel that Ego was going for a more, action RPG type game, and tried to blend the X formula into it.
For example, combat is a lot more profitable now, than in previous games. Repairs for your vessel could cost upwards to a few million credits in any previous X game. Here, it should cost less than 100 grand, no matter your hull. This isnt even accounting for the seemingly Hyperinflation that occured during the time of Rebirth, money is no longer measured in the hundreds of thousands, but in up to 4 digits. For example, say I had 5,264,194 credits in my account. Any previous game would show that as 5,264,194, here it is shown as 5.264M. It does not go into detail about exactly how much money you have, which would be necessary in a detailed management game.
The speed of combat, and the changes in the combat system have also been changed to be a lot more faced paced. Another change to make it into a more robust Action game. There have only been a few instances in which the player was actually given a character, however those were really only referenced in the main plot missions, and then it was simply by name most of the time. Here Ren Otani (thats you) is not only given a name, but a voice and a very slight personality. He can walk around on ships, engage in talks with other people, and the player now actually thinks about who it is driving their ship, rather than the mystical being who manifestes as a space suit.
I shall be continuing this review as i get further into the game, but for now, a TLDR section.
X Rebirth, is not worth $40, it is an okay Space sim, with some light space managerial options and a heavy emphases on combat. It is a good game for new players into the X series to try out to get used to the ideas of how a X game operates, before moving onto a previous title if they are intrested in the management and stratergy of those games. But for now, pick up the game on sale (for $15-20 bucks or less), itll be worth your time if you havent tried out the X series and wanted to learn about it, although this game is not an accurate representation of how a X game operates. Although, space exploration is an absolute pain in this game, and areas quickly become generic.

I've played every single Hitman game and loved every single one of them.
Is Hitman: Absolution a bad game? Most definitely not!
Is it a true, classic Hitman game? No!
How come it isn't a bad game? Well
There is no such a thing as a bug free video game or software so i'm 100% sure that there are some bugs and/or glitches. However i did not experience any.
It's not broken. It's not boring...The story is kind of bogus but more on that later.
Even if the story would be boring then the amazingly fun stealth gameplay makes it up for it. The game is not boring nor broken - It must be a good game.
So why so much hate?  It's just not a true Hitman game.
It added couple of new features that really improve the franchise. Couple of features that I myself personally have been waiting for...But they also "downgraded" some of the old features. Features that were already there and didn't require changing - If it's not broke, don't fix it.
Aight, time to talk about some pros and cons aka "Not Hitmans"
- In previous Hitman titles when you picked up a disguise the enemies didn't recognize you...Unless of course they found the dead persons body whose outfit you're wearing or when you just started shooting everyone or walked into a restricted area without wearing a proper disguise. Not all disguises required you to kill someone tho.
In Absolution every single person who wears the same outfit as you will know that you're not one of them and your disguise is blown in seconds. This makes disguises somewhat useless. Lets say i need to get backstage of a strip club. Naturally you seek out a security guard outfit. Now what happens is that every single security guard will know that you're not one of them and will alert everyone (EVERYONE WILL INSTANTLY KNOW) that you're nothing but a bloodthirsty phony. No warning, nothing. Shoot first and ask questions later appears to be the theme of this game.
Next point might seem like pointless whining but it's actually quite important in the entire stealth genre: You cannot switch off lights. Removing such a simple feature...Is just a very stupid thing to do.
- Previous Hitman games never had checkpoints nor did they let you save your game during a mission.
In Absolution, however, you get rolled back to your last checkpoint every time you die. You can even reload your last checkpoint if things weren't going exactly how you planned. This, this little thing right here makes the game TOO easy.
To make matters worse, the enemies now RESPAWN. Yup! Respawning enemies in a singleplayer game! If you move from check point one to checkpoint two and then for some reason want to go back to checkpoint one area then you better not do so.
Oh and the levels are smaller and more linear than in the previous titles.
- You can finally take cover in a Hitman game! All previous Hitman games needed this! Every now and then you either screwed up or things just didn't go your way aaaand...A shootout happened. A good cover mechanic would have really helped.
The only problem in here is that you can always reload your last checkpoint when you screw up so you can actually avoid shootouts and sneak your way through the game.
I'm not 100% sure but to me it seems that there are actually more creative ways of disposing each of your targets. Previous titles gave you like maybe 1-2 sneaky options or you could go in guns blazing as the 3rd option. It seems to me that this game gives you like 3-5 choices with almost every target.
What i also loved is that Absolution has this Splinter Cell kind of targeting system where you can pause time, set your targets and then 47 just kills 'em all in matter of seconds.
+Fun and brutal ways of "assassinating"
+Great gunplay
+Good cover mechanics
+One of the coolest easter eggs i've seen in games
These all make this gameplay a masterpiece.
The game is well optimised, everything can be used as a weapon...It's just a joy to play.
- Just don't quote me on this one in front of the little ones.
Agent 47 is supposed to be the deadliest and most skilled assassin ever. He was genetically enhanced...He is a perfect human being.
He is as physically fit as humanly possible, has inhuman reflexes and is as intelligent as you can get. Oh and he doesn't do anything based on emotions.
He's been in the game for many years and he got out alive...
...But now the Absolutions story...47 actually gets captured TWICE. The perfect assassin. A veteran assassin. The most intelligent and strongest man in the entire storyline...Gets captured by some rednecks. Sure.
How does this happen? Well the first time around, for an example, he makes a complete rookie mistake. A bad judgement call. This should have never happened.
The story is full of plot holes actually. The story makes no sense at all. I don't want to fill my reviews with spoilers so if you want to ask me about the spoilers then visit my profile and we'll have a chat.
Let it just be clear that the story in this game is pretty much garbage to anyone who has been a long time Hitman fan or who just enjoys logical storylines.
The story, however, gives you the reason to visit plenty of different places and oh god the settings and places in this game are just amazing!
The game got that much hate because it's a Hitman game.

I've only put a few hours into this game so far, and I'm enjoying it immensely. Broadly, Rebel Galaxy reminds me of a mashup of the Assassin's Creed series, World of Warships, and good old Freelancer. The former because the way that the map and locations work (markers and missions within the system map), the second because of the similar broadside naval combat mechanic (which, given the lack of a traversable Z axis [for simplicity's sake] in the game, works surprisingly well), and the latter because...well, you fly around in space and do whatever you want for a career.
Rebel Galaxy is very smooth. Everything looks wonderful, the theme music and some of the game's feel are obvious homages to Firefly and Serenity, but the overall experience is pretty fresh. While the exploration and side mission elements of gameplay can get redundant (see Assassin's Creed), the constantly evolving state of your own ship keep things fairly interesting.
The difficulty curve can be a little intense. Like AC, this is forgiven somewhat because the game autosaves every time you leave dock, but there are a number of bloody lessons to be learned early on while you learn how to poke around the galaxy without dying with some frequency.
Combat mechanics are very nifty. In addition to hired help and the already highlighted broadside combat system, turrets, auxiliary weapons, and various modules help keep combat pretty fresh and interesting. Plus it all looks very pretty, and blowing up pirate capital ships is viscerally satisfying in a way that Eve never accomplished.
Very, very recommendable to fans of any of the above listed titles (disparate though they may seem), as long as you dig things in space. A great, sandboxy capital ship combat game that really WORKS, unlike so many halfhearted efforts.

Oh Cards and Castles, When i ran into this game over 2-3 years ago, I have to be honest I didn't expect much. Now looking where I am and the game is today I felt like this game may have been one of the greatest games I've ever run into. The game itself is a great combonation of Collectible cards and strategy with very intersting mechanics and a meta that keeps gameplay interesting.
The evolution of the game has been a positive one in terms of graphics and gamplay. The graphics back in the day of course looked pretty floppy but it eventually evolved to fit the faster pace of the game in which it is currently in. The several Mechanics of the game provide for startegical thought as well as positioning which throws aspects of chess like thinking into the game. Not to mention deckbuilding which throws even more thinking in the game due to thoughts like determing how you wish to play or how you would want to win matches. The state the game is in currently certainly shows its progression and for people just discovering the game you may find it to be pertty well made
However there is the argument of P2W, a central issue for all card games. The shop found within the game gives off a mood of "Please use your money to do well", while that is not the case. The store merely provides for players who want try out startegies with the pre made decks or boost their collection with booster packs, this IS NOT a P2W model. the model found here is very genrous imo, If you are a new player, you start out with a great amount of starter cards for deck options. If you are a consistently returning player, the free packs allow you to boost your card collection, or shard count depending on your collection. Speaking of shards, another aspect of the game that allows you to create (or craft) a certain card without having to buy packs searching for it, a good way to get what you need without spending cash.
The community is also great, people who are always willing to help test out strategies and give advice to anyone who needs its. The devs are also better here and more responsive than in other games you might come across.
To me, these negative reviews may have come from people not giving the game enough time to show what it can do. I really enjoy the game, I know many other people enjoy the game, and I hope to stay through all of what happen in the game itself. Keep up the great work Red Team Games.

Cards and Castles, the game that I have been playing for around 2-3 years when it's still in mobile. Probably the game I've played the longest. It's a good game.
Gameplay: Most people will say that it's a combination of chess and card games, and that's pretty accurate. It combines the strategic depth of the two genres, because in addition to playing your cards correctly, you also have to position your units around properly. There is also the element of deckbuilding, which adds another layer of strategy as it determines how you want to win and how you will play.
It is also rather fast-paced due to the Sudden Death mechanic, which you may either love or hate.
Graphics: The game uses a bright cartoony artstyle (take note: cartoony, not anime) and it's rather pleasant to look at imo, and fits with the fast-paced nature of the game.
And then, there's the sacred topic in all card games. Pay to Win.
Imo, this game is decently generous with it's payment model. The game gives you a decent amount of the basic cards through a free timed pack system, which may be a bit annoying for some. You are also rewarded for progressing through the ranks. Some of the higher rarity cards may seem like it's necessary for winning, and it might actually be. And it may seem like it's P2W. But imo this is way more generous than Hearthstone or other alternatives in the market.
The devs are also more responsive than Hearthstone devs, and the community is way better than HS.
Basically, ditch HS. Get this game. Jumping to the conclusion of not trying this game because the negative reviews which are claiming P2W in a CCG is a bit close-minded.

It's not a horrible game, but ultimately it's just boring and frustrating, so I can't recommend it.
I've had my eye on the game for some time, as it has a very interesting look and a unique setting.  I wasn't willing to risk much money on it, though, since it didn't look like there was much to the gameplay.  I'm glad I waited until I could pick it up cheap from Indiegala.  The graphics and overall feel of the game are certainly good, but playing the game itself just isn't very fun.  In fact, for an FPS, it's one of the more boring games I've played in a while.  You're given very little instruction or direction, just that you're supposed to "do" stuff and "find" stuff that's scattered around the map in an effort to "solve" investigations.  I don't really know what the point was to collecting this stuff and solving these investigations, as everything seemed pretty random and didn't do much to advance a plot, at least as far as I could tell.  Mostly what I ended up doing was wandering around aimlessly, looking for something with a bit of color or following audio clues until I stumbled across something to interact with, at which point I would press F to collect or read something.  Occasionally there would be some enemies to fight, and those encounters ranged from either being easy one-shot kills, to practically impossible battles with sizable groups that come from all directions.  Mostly there was just a lot of walking around, though, wondering if the game was actually going to go anywhere.  It's not that I mind this kind of gameplay - I spent dozens of hours wandering around the wastelands of Fallout 3, for example.  But in games like Fallout, there's a sense of accomplishment and progress when you discover things that I simply never felt with Betrayer, making everything seem more a chore than an adventure.
There was a kind of stealth system, but it was pretty laughable.  Bascially you could either crouch, which rendered you practically invisible but meant it took an excruciatingly long time to get anywhere, or you could walk, which gave the enemies supernatural awareness of you at all times, or you could stand around until the wind kicked up, then use the noise to scurry forward for a couple seconds until the wind died down again.  Maybe it sounded good in theory, but it was pretty pointless in practice.
It's not nearly the worst game I've ever played, I can't even say it's particularly bad, but overall the game was just too boring to put up with the frustrations, the ambiguities, and seeming lack of any progression.  I have plenty of other games in my library that are just more deserving of my time.

Want a real review?  Keep scrolling, because this is a port rant.  No, it's not just GFWL, calm down.
Even with GFWL gone, this port is dreadful.  While the game itself is definitely worth the asking price, I can't recommend it unless you love super-cinematic 15 FPS at random times, along with several pathetic issues that ruin it for you.
First off, one of my smaller annoyances.  The textures are horrendous.  I don't mean "old-looking" horrendous, I mean that they look like crippled and downscaled versions of textures, like they're rendering in 1/4 res or something.  I sincerely doubt that these are the textures they made-- it's probably just the downscaled versions of the textures that they used for Xb360/PS3.  I wouldn't complain, had performance actually been somewhat decent.
Regardless of your framecap (which is nicely placed at 120FPS... we're making progress, Capcom) Cinematics also seem to be at-- you guessed it-- "cinematic" 30 FPS.  Want to hear something even worse?  In both cutscenes AND gameplay, your mouse cursor will just appear at random times!  I've even tried alt-tabbing out and restarting the game, but no, it's just the port!  It's got THAT little effort behind it!
The controls are a bit all over the place.  C for the Transponder, T for your watch, and a million other stupid binds that anyone could have placed better.  It's another small complaint, but definitely worth mentioning.
I find with MSi Afterburner's overlay enabled that RAM usage will never go over 2GB, only 300MB max will be used of my 3GB R9 280 (usually hovering around 30% usage with max settings), and the CPU will just tank performance at random times-- yes, even during cutscenes and in the shelter, where NOTHING should be that taxing, I'm getting 100%/99% usage for my cores.
The port woes make this game unenjoyable.  Avoid it, unless you've got enough processing power to brute-force it.  Even then, you're not missing out on much.  Capcom is a joke, and I highly suggest avoiding their products as nothing they release has been even half decent on PC.

Like the first game, weapons and health are generally all around you only this time around you can combine two specific items to make another weapon that's possibly cooler, sillier, practical, or a combination of a number of those. You can find out what item goes with what via Combo Cards which are unlocked through general progression of the game such as examining certain posters, leveling, defeating psychopaths, etc. You can combine items without the specific card however the item produced won't be as effective and rewarding. It's highly encouraging to produce the Combo Weapons because using them generally nets you PP for leveling and curiosity in how they'll work will become pretty high.
You're free to run around the world as you please (aside from some areas that can only unlocked from doing certain missions) though its criticized time limit makes a return so you only have so much time to get to doing the missions. If you stick to doing missions, not be as distracted, and perhaps if you're at a decent level it won't feel like it's rushing you to go do something so much. Even if you fail a task no matter how important and until the timer runs out or you choose to restart the story you're free to run around freely doing whatever. Restarting the specific save file's story allows you to keep your level, money, and Combo Cards for that next playthrough.
The plot & dialogue is full of cheese, especially with the psychopaths. I think it's for the better that that's the case.
There isn't much depth to the actual zombie killing aside from just having good weapons for the situation and the psychopath fights. The psychopaths can be extremely cheap in their own special way but at least for most of the fights you're free to leave and return to the area in case you don't feel ready for the boss fight.
The co-op's overall doable. A bit easier (if no lag is present) but adds enjoyment to the game. The money and level you've earned anywhere in a save file can be used in both single player and co-op where the only thing that doesn't carry over for either is the story if you're not hosting the game. The entire thing could have probably used an implemented in-game chat and give-item-to-partner feature as opposed to dropping or chucking the item for them to pick it up.
Fetch quests, escorts, and just messing around. Probably better with a controller since keys are unrebindable.

An ambitious RTS that tried to do a lot of things and actually pulled it off rather well.  Essentially it takes some 4X game elements, simplifies them a bit, and puts them into a sci-fi RTS environment.
+Lots of exploration, technologies to research, and planets to be built up while you amass a fleet and defences
+AI puts up a decent fight on hardest non-cheating setting
+Decent variety of units and defences to keep games interesting, with each race broken into 2 sub-factions for more variety
+Starbases and titans are really neat
+Save function in multiplayer so you and a friend(s) can takes as long as you like to finish a large map.
+Smaller maps for those who want a quicker, more aggressive game
+TCP/IP and LAN multiplayer options; possibly one of the last games to have such options.
-Competitive multiplayer, which was never really alive even at the game's peak, is dead at this point
-Even with saves, not really an RTS that's suitable for short sessions beyond small 1v1 matches.
-Pretty barebones diplomacy system
-Pirates were a cool idea, but the 'ebay bidding system' for them is horribly done and you'll probably end up turning them off.
-There is no campaign or story mode whatsoever.  Who are the Visari, who are they running from, and why do Advent hate the TEC?  Damned if anyone knows.
Overall, if you want a good single player FFA or co-op vs AI multiplayer RTS with a bit more depth to it than your usual RTS fare this is a great game.  The lack of story for what seems to be an interesting sci-fi setting is sorely lacking for a game like this though.

Well... Hatred is here, and it sucks.
Okay, first of all, I don't have a particular problem with the game's theme itself. Unfortunately, our society isn't perfect and yes, there are tragic occurrences when some bolk goes mad and kills a lot of people out of God knows what. It happens. And as such, a game in fact has every right to touch such a sad subject. It's not even a new thing, just check on Postal for instance!

But man, Destructive Creations screwed up everything they could do right in this case. The engine itself was a bad idea, UE4 is poorly optimized and unnecessary for a top-down-view shooter, Unity would have been a far better choice. The game is sluggish, runs horribly on the same PC that makes GTA V fly, and ugly as hell too. So there's that.

In the terms of gameplay, it shows nothing new, and gets boring after a few minutes. Is it cool to kill people without a reason? Well maybe it could be, but isn't, thanks for the horrible AI that makes them feel like mindless idiots wandering like zombies. It's just bad.

Just like the shooting mechanic: aiming is difficult, there is no cover system, the enemy is always overpowered, and it's just simply not fun to shoot. Which is sad because in such a game, using guns might be a selling point.

And the game ends in 4 hours, giving us absolutely no reason to play it again. Sorry DC, this isn't the crusade we wish to see.

Tiny and Big: Grandpa's Leftovers is one of those games that you wish was just a tad bit longer, if only to see what more they could have done with the game's interesting world slicing engine. See, the game is a 3D platformer, decent controls and all that, but what sets it apart from other platformers is the power to cut up objects in the world, which in turn can allow you to progress further in the game and deal with some of the tricky platforming it throws at you. In a way, it is almost a minor puzzle game, in that sometimes you have to take your time to look the problem over and figure out how to progress.
I quite enjoy the mental stimulation, but it isn't all slow paced platforming. Sometimes the game suddenly starts testing your reflexes by having objects tossed at you, requiring you to cut it in half before it crushes every bone in your body. It keeps you on your toes, and I like that.
It also helps that the game has secrets hidden around for players to seek out, rewarding clever explorers with an interesting discovery (and for Achivement hunters, an achivement for each one).
As I said earlier, the controls are decent, although sometimes I did have a little trouble moving in the direction I wanted.. But other than that, it works just fine.
The music track is interesting, but nothing I could care a whole lot about. Still, it gets the job done.
But, alas, what holds this game back from being great is it's short length and the fact that it ends on a rather... Let's just say it isn't really that satisfying. But while it is sadly short, it certainly is a nice journey while it lasts, cutting your path all the way to the end while trying not to break your bones every step of the way. I suggest you wait for it to come on sale before you think about buying it, though

Interesting 90s point & click that passed me by until now.
Good:
-It's based on a novel and the story/concept is pretty cool. The novel's author also wrote most of the game's dialogue and voiced the antagonist. Story is fairly 'deep' for this kind of thing, heavy on metaphor - reminds me of Silent Hill 2 in that way.
-Surreal nightmare environments are pretty cool
-Controlling multiple characters in their own 'episodes' which are united at the end - different format from most p&cs
-Multiple possible endings
Bad:
-Obscure fail states. If you fail an episode, you have to start it again (or reload save). Trouble is, it's not always obvious that you HAVE failed, let alone why you've failed. You can be running around for hours looking for a solution that doesn't exist because you've already broken it. Terrible design.
-Usual point & click issue of certain puzzles making no sense & having ridiculous/obscure solutions that defy any logic. Problem is the old 'use everything on everything' trick can break the game (as mentioned above) so you have to resort to using guides :\
Picked it up for a fiver, worth a punt at that price if you like point & click games.

I played a bit the Civ3 game on my friend's computer who introduced me to the Civ series many years ago, but soon after that Firaxis released Civ4 and i never bought my own Civ3 copy.
My Civ4 gameplay is 500-1000 hours (it's not Steam) and my Civ5 is 500+ Steam hours (it's on my brother's account, i did a wrong install a few years ago).
I bought Civ4, Civ5 and all expansions at full price the first days after their release dates. I also bought the complete Civ4 and Civ5 packages (the same games again) when their price dropped to 10 euro and now the whole Civ5 game is on my account too.
I bought CivBE on 40% discount Steam sale. I really can't understand all these negative reviews. It's obvious that a lot of people were expecting some other game, not a new Civ. I guess the hype has huge and people started to imagine various versions of a game that the developers never showed to the public and never promised to their customers. Many wanted something like a new Alpha Centauri, that was some other game with different gameplay that Firaxis created and not a Civ game. Looks like a huge misunderstanding.
My opinion is that CivBE is a good game, true to the Civ formula. Firaxis developers said that every Civ game must have a limited complexity and number of features, so that many people can play them and not only a few very hardcore strategy gamers. So for every new feature they add to a new game, another feature must be removed. They said they want every new Civ game to have 33% new, 33% modified, 33% same features. Also the Civ series was never sim strategy, always had cartoon (unrealistic, like clowns, childish) leaders (no matter the quality of graphics) and many unrealistic features, people play many strategy games and looks like they started to confuse the various games and genres.
I think CivBE has a decent amount of new (good) features that make it a worthy succesor to the Civ series. Good graphics and very good music. Absolutely no performance issue for me, very polished game, i think maybe it runs a bit better than Civ5 (i have AMD graphics card, so i picked the AMD Mantle option, i had an issue the first time when i tried another way). I like CivBE now better than the original Civ5 with no expansions. I played the Civ5 for 30-40 hours only, i didn't like it much, then 60-70 hours after the first expansion and the rest 400+ hours Civ5 gameplay was for the full game with the BNW expansion.
I expect to play CivBE for many more hours, i think it's much less boring than the vanilla Civ5 and offers much good strategy and tactics. I like the leaders, the tech web and the overall mood. I think that patches and expansions will make it a more balanced and more rich game. My opinion is that it's worth the full price.
To all people with negative reviews, Civ4 was the peak of complexity, no new Civ game will be more complex and have tons of features. Maybe you are bored and fed up with the Civ style and don't want to play such games anymore, but it's not the developers fault that they sell a game named Civ that plays like a Civ.

A very unusual title, Betrayer has its fair share of pros and cons that separate it from the majority.  I'll try and cover some of those points.
First of all, the game is very visually striking...  Sometimes too much so.  The eerie, black and white contrast certainly gives a rather cinematic sense at some points, and since most important things have some red to them it can be easy to pick out the things you should be paying attention to.  However, I eventually found it tiring and went on to spend some time tooling around with the graphics settings...
As it turns out, the game's graphics actually have quite a bit of color to them, and are very pretty even when not going for the marketed look.  I would recommend any player to try mixing and matching a bit, finding a mix that you find most pleasing.  I wound up going through most of the game with a "normal, slightly washed-out" look that I felt showed off the color palette while still contributing to the game's haunted atmosphere.  All in all, the environments are very pleasing, respectably varied (considering you can't exactly go hog wild with biomes in New England) and something I got comfortable with rather than got bored of.
Now, at this point we have to actually look at the gameplay part of the game, and there are a few things that break down here...  There's no voice acting, but personally I think it's better not to have any than to have too much of the bargain variety.  Combat is probably going to throw a lot of people off, because it's not what you might expect from the previews (I certainly didn't expect it).
If you're looking for a realistic combat simulation of discovery-age fighting, you're barking up the wrong tree.  This is a back-to-basics shooter where enemies can see you from a mile away unless you're prescribing to the somewhat arbitrary "stealth" mechanics, and who will then beeline directly towards your position while firing or slashing mercilessly and without form.
It's not Mount and Blade, it's Quake.  It's a bit of a jarring system, what with how advanced and complex a number of fighting systems have become over the past era in the gaming industry, but once you get used to it and wrap your head around it it's not that bad.  You'll have to kind of compartmentalize it away from the rest of the game, because between the very game-y combat "feel" and the at times hilarious ragdolling, it doesn't *exactly* fit in with the rest of the game's atmosphere.
The game has got some absolutely fantastic sound direction, and I just realized I meant that half-literally...  Instead of an "objective compass" or other big arrow on the screen telling you where to go, there's a command to "listen", which will cause the nearest quest item or person to send out what effectively amounts to a ping.  By listening for the ghostly whoosh of wind, you can tell what direction it's in and roughly how far away it is.  It's also worth noting that it will point you in the direction of quests you haven't even started yet, so it makes "clearing out" each zone reasonably simple.
The game's enemies, despite being almost entirely humanoid, use animal noises to communicate.  This starts off being more just of a curious footnote when you're fighting off the growly-snarly spaniards early on and their wolf/bear noises, but later in the game you come across natives who communicate to each other using whooping, warbling bird calls.
I make special note of this because it is amazingly creepy and suspenseful.  The little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s are damn hard to pick out from the foliage at times, and in groups they can be quite dangerous...  Hearing that bird call when you're out searching the woods will make you instantly drop into a crouch and double-check your weapons and health to make sure you can survive a potential conflict...  Which there almost certainly will be, because even trying to escape may result in you blundering into them by accident, as evidenced by the predatory screech they'll let out once they've spotted you.
I've mentioned the quests a couple times here, and...  Well, there's really not that much more to say.  They're quests.  You talk to someone, they say something vague, and then you have to kill someone or find something and talk to some other people before talking to them again.  The quests are all very "fetch this" or "kill that", but the writing behind them is actually very much worth a read, and some of the stories lead down twistier roads than others.  After a while, I was honestly just puttering through the required steps so that I could read the next scrap of story and find out more about all the myriad little stories kicking about, because I was geniunely interested.
The big wallop ending of the main storyline is...  Really a phone-in.  It is.  The Big Ending is not that great, and it really just smacks of early development that never got out of being "early".  There are also some minor bits and pieces of interaction with the main countercharacter in the game, the mysterious Lady in Red, which are a bit arcane...  Through completing quests you will wind up with certain trinkets or mementos that you can then offer to give to her, at which point you need to explain *WHY* you're giving it to her...  If she likes your answer, she'll like you more, and if she doesn't, she'll be pissy...  This has no real effect other than getting or not getting some items at the end of the game, but it's a bit irritating that you have no idea how she'll respond to any one tone or statement and basically just have to guess what the "right" answer would be.  Oh, yeah, and it might also screw with your being able to complete the final quest the "good" way, minor detail that...
All in all, Betrayer is definitely worth a play.  The fighting is jarring at first but becomes greatly satisfying once you develop your deep-seated hatred for the various enemies in the game.  The sound direction is a bit empty at times, but otherwise is deeply refreshing and immersive.  The graphics are at best stunningly gorgeous, and at worst rather janky and headache-inducing...  Player meddling is encouraged.  Despite its numerous flaws, I went from being at first disappointed to being pleasantly surprised by the experience of playing it, and I do not regret buying it in the slightest.
I wish the developers all the best in their future endeavours, and hope to see a more fleshed-out example of what they were going for here...  Because I think that if they'd had the time and money they needed to see Betrayer become what they set out to make, then it would have been spectacular, rather than just good.

An updated Freelancer with a great soundtrack.
Alot like how Starpoint Gemini reminds me of the old Freelancer, this game follows much of the game basics but with a definite twist.
If there is any gripe in this game is that it is pretty much exclusively a capital-ship "style" game on a mainly 2-D plane of combat. You personally will never have any 3-D motion off that hovering base plane - but despite that it does not really detract from the feel of the game. Instead it almost helps lean towards its intended goal of a combat-oriented feel that helps lean heavily into making it feel great.
That soundtrack sure helps - but even I have to admit it can feel repetitive after a long session of playing. Despite that, they have turned out a remarkably well-polished game that shines well. They did however sacrifice some in the way of overal variety but instead have ended up granting one heck of a great-looking game that incorporates simple cutscenes to help add to the immersion into the galaxy.
Combat-wise, as I said it is a capital-ship "style" game. I emphasize "style" as the scope leaves a bit to be desired, but the feel of it is still great. Your ships are equipped with turrets that can freely fire at will, backed up with mainstay broadside cannons and a secondary sytem - all of which can be adjusted to suit your style. However I must admit that the game is a bit broken in the balancing acts to which you'll find a good deal of its options may fall short compared to others that far outstepp the effects. It can over time lead to quite a rinse-and-repeat style of gameplay. Despite that, the feel of the rush in a battle, seeing turrets fire at random and swing your ship around for the broadside on the bigger targets can sure make the fight feel impressive.
Defensively, the game isn't a slouch - you get shields, armor and a deflector that can help absorb damage. And you'll need it. Shields recharge fast, but sustained fire can strip them down - and once your armor is gone you'll fall quick. The shields and armor is segmented to fore, aft and port/starboard angles, however the deflector is an all-in-one effect that can negate a sizeable ammount of damage. Kinda works like a boost button for movement - press to activate, and time or damage will drain it before its need for a recharge. That recharge gets longer if its is drained to empty.
The mix in addtion to special abilities and effects sure helps add even a bit of variety, but the gameplay will still fall into reppitition. But again, despite that - the way the game makes the atmosphere feel, and its simplicity helps it lean towards a fun experience.
The story helps too. Its not spectacular by any means - but it does help add a bit more into it.
All and all - very much like the old Freelancer. With a few updated tricks and gimmiks (and a few more things I have not mentioned) to where it can be quite an enjoyable game to play. One I would reccomend getting into, even if only for a little bit just to enjoy its polished presentation.
Tho, if you want something bigger and with more variety I might suggest Starpoint Gemeni or Elite: Dangerous instead. But for the price, and what it gives - this is well worth it as well.

Betrayer is an FPS with emphasis on stealth that is both very atmospheric and has some very interesting supernatural elements that adds to the gameplay. However, there just isn't much... "game" there. It's almost all a "sandbox" to play with, and there really isn't much to do except run around until you encounter something you can kill. And unless you want to challenge yourself to stealth kill everybody, it would almost seem there is very little activity in the game, when this game just needs a bit more... shall we say... handholding to be a really good game.
You were supposed to arrive at this British colony in the New World back in the late 1700's, in a convoy, and two of your fellow ships have turned back due to heavy damage and storm... and your ship finally sank in a storm almost in sight of land. You woke up on a beach, with nothing except your cloths, and nothing salvageable except a weapon. You walk inland and somebody wearing red, apparently a woman, shot an arrow into a post near you... it is a note to be careful. You continue slowly found some weapons, and found that Spanish Conquistadors have apparently taken over, and is attacking all strangers. You kill some with your new found bow and captured some weapons and whatnot. You arrived at Fort Henry, and found it empty of life. There were some ash figures, human sized, as well as grave markers all around the area, some dead of disease, some from attacks... you also found various pages of writing scattered about. Notices, diaries, etc. There were signs of Indian attack on the fort. What happened to the colony? What could have cause the ash people?
The problem there is you don't really have anything else after this. The scattered bits of text do add some back story, but your objective screen will tell you if you've found all of them, as well as all the graves, and whatnot. The conquistadors respawn when you load a savegame or when you die and respawn. And they can be better armed than you at first. You will have to kill a lot of them to gather loot, including old weapons, and trade those in at the few merchant spots for better conditioned weapons (which will do more damage). And being historically accurate, the pistol and mustket are VERY slow loading, but packs a real punch.
The game has heavy emphasis on stealth and ambush. You are encouraged to use the wind to cover your approach. As the wind russels the tree branches, you can rush in and whack the enemy in the back. Surprise attacks score extra damage. You can also throw your tomahawk, which does quite a bit of damage at a distance. On the other hand, ammo is very limted. You're limited to 8 musket shots and 12 pistol shots, and 16-20 longbow arrows, your starting weapon. Don't waste them. In fact, you can reclaim them from corpses (but you'll lose a few here and there)
And a bit of spoiler from here...
Most games that have free roam have a "find next mission" or "find next objective" button or such. This one does not. It basically left you to figure out everything, and that can lead to "WTF do I do now?" questions, which often leads to "why the **** am I playing this?" and rage quit.
I've been told the ending was  a real letdown and the game almost without warning turns into a free-roam game where your sole purpose is to go for completion achievements (i.e. find all the notes, all the graves, etc. etc.)
All in all, this is an experimental game that managed to achieve that certain mood, but in the end, failed to create a real GAME out of it. I can't recommend it it at full price. It may be worth picking up when it's very very cheap for the experience, or you like games that don't tell you what to do.
NOTE: default game graphics was set to black and white palette, which can be very jarring to some people. You can adjust the graphics to add a little color, which IMHO contrasts better with the pure gray "dark world".

One of the most well-paced, compelling and atmospheric first person "action" games I have played in a long time. I will summarize my thoughts categorically in the following bullet points.
* The combat is slow-paced and challenging but ultimately rewarding. Multiple weapons are unlocked and can be upgraded throughout the game, and the variety is adequate. Enemy variety is not exceptional either, but the deliberate methodology required to dispatch hostiles reliably makes the combat more tactics focused yet somehow nothing about the it feels forced or obtrusive. In other words, you might be surprised with how enjoyable it is to exploit simple mechanics like line of sight and the terrain in order to deal with encounters creatively and effectively.
* The game world is one that adequately balances the threat of the unknown with the reward of exploration. Enemies often lie in ambush when you are off the beaten paths, but collectibles and monies are scattered across the maps serve as adequate encouragement to explore. Nonetheless, it still combines well with the other aspects of the game to accomplish it's ultimate goal; you will feel as if this is truly a land of the forsaken.
* The story is purposely vague at first but is willing to offer answers to those willing to go deep inside the dark and twisted rabbit hole that it is. It consists of an unexpectedly dark collection of tales about betrayal, suicide and human savagery. I thought it would simply be a matter of "we are all dead because of the spooky skeletons", but I was (un)pleasantly surprised by it, and it is this aspect of the game that is perhaps the one I find to be most memorable.
* The visual aesthetics of the game are, oddly enough, the thing that I was least impressed by (and by "impressed" I mean it quite literally as "that which left the least impression on me") despite the obvious hard work that had gone into it. The enemies appeared intimidating, the items looked realistic, and the use of red to highlight objects is more than just a gimmick once you've been engrossed by the atmosphere of the game. The look of the terrain and objects in the game is all tied together very well, stylistically speaking. Besides that though, graphics are not something that I pay that much attention in a game to unless something about it is very unique. And to be frank about the black-and-white filter(s), it just felt off to me and after no more than an hour or two I had lowered the contrast and increased the saturation to slightly more natural levels. I like that the option is there for those that find it just a bit too harsh on the eyes, and I feel as if the changes I made kept the original feeling well enough to not impact my overall experience negatively.
* The audio design is minimalistic, but entirely functional. Perhaps there could be more work done to add music and improve the sound effects and maybe-just-maybe add some voice acting, but I think works well enough without those things. In fact, the lack of music actually helps further impress the game's lonely and bleak atmosphere, at least for me.
