One of the best games I've played in a while. Probably the most original game, conceptually and mechanically to come out in the last several years.
The fact that it takes place from the perspective of the victims of war opposed to every other war game which is from the perspective of soldiers or the military, makes it a very real and unforgettable experience. I actually wrote a paper in college on the excess of shooter games, specifically military based themed ones. So its very refreshing to see a negative, horrifying, unglorified take on war video games. Very admirable.
The game its self is very morbidly beautiful looking, with a story and pacing to match. Its very unique in context of a side scrolling video game, which I havent seen very many of untill recently. Its more about stragety and stealth opposed to reflex and speed, like most games from its genre. Its not quite turn based but is time based, so there no rushing through this one.
I really want to go into specific detail and event in the game that make it one of a kind, but I'll actually leave it up to you to decide. The only thing Ill say is that the game forces you to make incredibly hard and uneasy decisions. The game really tests and questions you morally on what you would do to survive. Playing this game is not about good or bad people, but to what extent you'd got to to save you and your group of survivors. Whether to save, feed or shelter other survivors, or loot, steal or kill, to maximise your supplies with out betraying your consciousness. Unlike games like Infamous: Second Son, or Fallout where they make you decide between one side or another and once you've picked that certain path you intensively and frantically try to reach that pirticular goal, This War of Mine, only allows you to make decision on pure circumstance. You only do what you must when you have no other options, balancing your survival with real guilt and remorse, at the same time subjecting you to the same circumstance and vulnerability you put other in.
Highly, highly recommend it.

In This War of Mine, players control a small group of civilians as they try to survive during a civil war, in the fictional city of Pogoren. Its a really unique experience, emotional and brutal.
Gameplay is split into two sections: day and night. During the day, your survivors are at home. You need to keep an eye on any negative status effects - when they're hungry, give them some food, if they're sick, give them medicine, bandage their wounds and make sure they sleep when tired. You can build equipment such as a stove to cook food, a workshop to craft tools and weapons, rain collectors and filters to get clean water, traps to catch small animals to eat, beds to sleep in, a furnace for heat. And you can craft valuable trade items like cigarettes and booze.
During the night, you can select one survivor to scavenge local buildings for supplies, while the others either sleep, or guard your home from bandits. There are lots of areas to visit around the city, and you'll encounter some tricky situations. There are only a couple of completely abandoned areas where you're free to take everything without consequence. Sometimes friendly people will trade with you, but if you don't have anything valuable, would you steal from them instead? Would you murder innocents and take their stuff so your own people can survive? Some areas are occupied by dangerous bandits, who will attack you on sight - but if you're desperate, you might have to risk it.
The combat system, like the rest of the gameplay, is managed through a point and click interface. Left click to walk to a location, right click to run, left click icons to interact with an object or person. I found the combat to be very hard, but I think that is probably by design. Our survivors aren't trained soldiers, and powerful guns are rare and expensive. So far I've tried to avoid combat as much as possible. There's no reloading or respawning, so death is permanent.
There are several scenarios to play through, where you'll start with between one and four survivors, and sometimes another will ask to join your group. Even that can be a tough choice - an extra pair of hands can be useful but its another mouth to feed. Each survivor has their own story and some of them have a special skill. For example Katja can get better value in trades, Bruno spends less resources when cooking and Arica can sneak quietly.
Its the kind of game where you'll generate your own stories. I thought my second attempt was looking good, until we got several days of snow. I couldn't keep the house warm enough, so Bruno froze to death overnight. Realising that every meal would cost me more resources, I started to take risks in the dangerous areas. Arica stealth killed two bandits but a third one shot her dead. Katja went to the same place the next night, figuring one more bandit would be easy enough. Turns out there was more than one and they shot her dead as well. Now alone, and very desperate, I had Pavle murder an old couple and steal all their food, but the next day he was depressed, wouldn't eat anything, and overnight he committed suicide. Game over. But its failures like that which made my next, successful run feel so good.
TWOM is a fantastic game and I thoroughly recommend it as a full price purchase.

To my utmost shame, I wasn't even aware of this game when it came out originally, I was probably off playing System Shock.  So my review isn't coloured by any nostalgia for it, specifically, but some nostalgia for Point-and-Click games from the mid-90s in general.  Also, although I'm a big Sci-Fi reader, I'm not a huge Harlan Ellison fan (only because I'm yet to read any of his work).   I picked this up because I was fed up of battling with DOSBox and Wine to get old games working, and thanks to NightDive Studios, it's been made compatible with modern PCs, and even given an OpenGL version in case the older software rendering is glitchy.
The history of how this game came to being is long and complex.  I recommend going and having a read of it on Wikipedia.  Some said that it was the 'unmakeable game' (much the same as Tristram Shandy could never be transformed into theatre):  It defied all the usual structures that would normally make a book convertible to interactive media (so I've read).   Therefore, apparently, with the original writer's help, they wrote in a load of structure around the story, and made this game (along with Harlan Ellison voicing the antagonist!), using elements of the short story.
You've probably gleaned that the game is 'unconventional'.  It's not a polished AAA game for starters with amazing CGI FMV or big orchstra scores like some of the Lucasarts games.      For starters, it moves away from the PaC games of the time by providing not one main protagonist, but five.  Each has their own voice actor and ministory, which can be played in any order.  While you're playing as one of the five, you can't "lose" per se (initially), which is a nice twist on the adventure games of the time, but you can be knocked back a bit to a 'hub' where you're just mocked and asked if you want to try again, so save scumming is a good tactic here.
Secondly, the game is set in a cyberspace / enhanced reality, so things don't work the way you expect.   Hitting a button may do nothing, but hitting it four times may work...  Talking to something may yield nothing, but do something unrelated, and then return, and hey presto, your target is garrulous and full of information.  You may not have an option in your speech tree for NPC "C", until you've spoken to NPCs "A" then "B", chosing a certain set of options, but there's no hint from "C" like there would be in modern games.
Lastly, the game isn't laid out before you like most games.  You play as five people, you gather they're being tortured, but you don't know why, and as you join them, they're being goaded into playing 'games'...  Each time you win (or lose) the game,  you inch closer to the true plot that's underlying everything.  As you play through, the underlying strata of plot pokes through as an anachronistic item, weird talking animal, and so on.  Sometimes it answers a question, sometimes is poses one.   The idea is to keep reminding you that it's not all real, or rather, it's as real as it needs to be.
The graphics are typical of the age, with low-res sprite scaling, MIDI background music, and some nice (but low-res) hand-drawn FMV videos.     It certainly tugs at the nostalgia strings, especially when some of the midi arpeggios and harp instruments make it sound similar to the Ultima Underworld soundtrack on occasion.      The voice acting is excellent, and the accompanying sounds and music do good jobs of setting the background.
The game play is Point-and-Click, but as I alluded to earlier this game breaks a few of the cardinal rules.  Some it does so in innocent ways e.g. there was one artifact which I couldn't actually figure out what it was due to the low res, until I "Used Everything On Everything" (UEoE), and it finally worked.     Some can be a bit irritating, e.g. when something only works when you've done something else, but the two are unrelated.  Day of The Tentacle did this to soame extent, and in this case, the setting allows me to be more forgiving.   The non-repeatability 'breakage' is what caused me the most strife... So it always pays to click things a few times, and if you're stuck, go back and do things you've already done but ruled out as useful.
The five 'stories' are very varied, each one playing out differently.  I won't ruin it by saying what they are, but each one has its own challenges, and you must perform a task which is tailored to the personality of the protagonist.
I've  uncovered three of the endings, but I suspect there's more.  The problem is that UEoE becomes rather fatal in the last level, and I got fed up of dying to find the alternate endings :)  I think I'm happy with the ones I have, since they cover the two most likely results, given the plot.
I think that kids in this modern day and age might balk at the fact that the game doesn't hold your hand much.. It's proper old school in many ways.  I suppose people had more time, because there were fewer games, so spending an hour trying to open a door was 'fun'.  Nowadays, pacing is all important, so I can see a few people being irritated by it.  Also, the graphics are as old-school as the gameplay, so kiddies these days will be wondering where the 1080p vector graphics cartoons are.  Also.. This game is bleak.  There's no wacky zany honk-honk humour.  It's hard post-apocalyptic sci-fi.
All-in-all, I had a really enjoyable satisfying time playing this.  Although I'd never played it before, it was really nostalgic, and didn't feel 'mainstream'.  The story was offbeat, the setting nice and post-apocalyptic, and the presentation quite good for its age.     Well recommended for anyone of an age (or gameplay leaning) who likes good old solid Point-and-Click adventures with a Sci-Fi theme.

There is a question that is posed to every man in his life.  One question that he must endeavor to answer to his own satisfaction and to hell with the naysayers.  One choice between confining support or uncertain freedom that will ever after determine the fate of his junk:  boxers or briefs?  Tiny and Big: Grandpa's Leftovers would emphatically tell you that tighty whiteys are worth fighting for, yet everything about it feels loose, free, and spacious.
Why on Earth are you talking about underwear to describe a 3D platformer/physics puzzler, reviewer?  Because in T+B, you play as the titular Tiny, a young man on a quest to recover his grandfather's hand-me-down underpants that have been stolen by an unscrupulous bandito.  That's one of those ideas I can't possibly make more ridiculous than the game presents it.  And as a framing device, it works.  I've played more than a few puzzle games that have forgotten that you need to give your game a definitive character to make it stand out from the piles and piles of mental exercises that boil down to merely an expensive Sudoku.
The visual style looks like something Pendleton Ward might come up with if you limited his palette to muted blues and oranges and does a good job of communicating the game's overall character in a sort of graphic novel way.  The soundtrack to the game is also special enough to note.  It takes the form of cassette tapes that you collect and listen to on your radio and, in addition to providing more reason to explore, covers a wide range of engaging jams from latin beats to funk to rock n' roll.
That's all well and good, but if I'm going to put myself into Grandpa's Leftovers, I'd better get some play and the experience had better feel good!  Relax, reader.  Thanks to Tiny and Big you'll feel great grabbing your stones and watching them swing free and easy and that's nothing to say about whipping out your rocket and blasting away a huge load.  Yes, in Tiny and Big you will use your mining laser to cut up your environment and a winch and rocket to move the pieces you cut into place.  What did you think I was talking about?
Anyway, the game strikes a nice balance between levels that are more freeform and open, like a sumptuous pair of boxers, and more puzzle-focused linear affairs that are tight and clean, like the familiar TWs.  This lets you get the most out of these unique mechanics as you move between trying to literally carve your own path to your objectives and examining your environment to find just the right object to cut or pull so everything falls into place.
If there's one fault with Tiny and Big, it's that it feels a bit short: five levels and a boss fight.  This might be a bit of a dividing point for some players.  If you just want to cruise to the end of the game in the most efficient way possible, you'll probably be done in a couple hours.  But if you enjoy hunting down tricky secrets and trying to make alternate routes, T + B will occupy you for quite some time.
If there are two faults, it's that Grandpa's Leftovers contain a few bugs, which, as you can imagine, can make your experience a bit uncomfortable.  None of them are explosively bad, but when you combine them with inevitable physics screw-ups, you'll find yourself losing a little hard-earned progress hunting for the tough secrets or flailing angrily because you've just lost your no-death run of a level.  As I've implied, you won't have a lot of issue with them unless you're going for the optional challenges that add a lot of meat to the game.
You can get Grandpa's Leftovers for less than the cost of a fresh bag of undies when it goes on sale and I definitely recommend you do.  It's a stand-out game that delivers on all those promises of "fully destructible environments" that almost always prove to be a disappointment.  Most importantly, it's a fun game; fun in the vain of things like Psychonauts.  And that's why you should definitely slip into Grandpa's Leftovers.

I didn't want to like this game or play it at first due you not being able to load your character from SR4 for some reason. I decided to play it for a bit anyway just to see how it was. However, "a bit" soon turned into a lot, and I ended up finishing the game pretty much on 100%. Besides not being able to load your character, here's what this game got right that the previous two games [and a lot of other open world games] didn't: 1) A "small" number of side missions. 2) The game in its entirety is just the right amount of gameplay. It isn't too short and it isn't too long. It's enough gameplay where I can finish it and just move on to another game. 3) Upgrading was far cheaper to afford which made for great progression. and 4) Obtaining the "special weapons" (the 7 deadly sins) was an absolute joy. It would be nice to see special weapons obtained in this way in the future.
The content cut from this game compaired to the previous titles are as follows: 1) Can't load your chraracter (the devs know about it and have yet to care to address it). 2) Limited number of vehicles (you fly everywhere so this is understandable). 2) No stores (except weapon vending machines). 3) No radio stations (as far as I could tell). and 4) Limited side quests (which is a good thing in this case).
Gat out of hell is a departure from the previous two games, but that doesn't mean that it's bad...it's just diffrent...and how much you enjoy this game initially all depends on how well you can deal with change. However, it is a good game in my opinion, and it deserves an opportunity to be played.

Of course, rather than being completely different, Bioshock 2 is just better than the first game in just about every way.

-  The levels are more varied and less filler-y.
-  The characters are better explored.

-  You will be made to feel for the villain and her family.

I'm not sold on this game (literally, because I played it during a free weekend and didn't buy) because even though there are a few differences in mechanics, it still seems too much like a sci-fi reskin of Civilization. Really, I'm not all that excited about any of the Civilization titles anymore because they're too "gamey" while the trend in strategy games for me has been to move to things that are more like simulations that strive for better realism. (For example, Europa Universalis vs Civilization.)
Arguably the main problem with C:BE is not the overly "gamey" approach, but that it sticks too closely to the Civilization formula. For example, anyone arriving from orbit should see all terrain on the map, but instead the mechanics assume that you're just some slightly higher tech cave men who arrive in a magical UFO. While some things might be invisible from orbit, the whole map shouldn't be Terra Incognita that requires units walking around just to reveal terrain. This is especialy true once you start launching satellies. If this were less of a reskin of Civilization then you wouldn't have complete Terra Incognita and game mechanics would be updated to compensate for that, but unfortunately we're still stuck with almost prehistoric assumptions about what the player should be able to know.
I give the developers some credt for attempting to implement some sort of "religion" that pits Terraforming against Transhumanism, but it isn't really done in a very good or convincing manner and the diplomatic system isn't well designed. The Virtues system is too much like a parallel science system with "culture points" that just gives you bonuses to different things instead of access to new units and structures. The opportunity cost tradeoffs you're presented wih aren't very apparent in the science or vitrue trees so instead you're presented with these dialogue boxes asking which thing you'd rather have a bonus in. A better designed game wouldn't need to present you with tradeoffs in such an artificial manner.
Overall I'd say the game just isn't very compelling. The mechanics just haven't changed enough from Civilization to handle the planet colonization scenario.

The consensus about this game has always been "It's not good as the first one". Do I agree with it? Yes. But what some people fail to mention is that there are some things that the sequel improves upon the original. The most notable one is the gameplay. While the first game already has one of the best gameplay experiences I've ever had, I thought the sequel had the better gameplay.
I think the two main reasons this game isn't as popular as the original and Infinite are the weaker storyline and it taking place back in Rapture. Still, while the storyline lacks the depth of the first game and Infinite's, it's still pretty good and definitely better than the average FPS storylines, especially if you listen to the audio diaries. And I don't think the game being back in Rapture is a rehash. There are some significant changes and improvements that will totally differentiate this game with the original.
If you like the first game, I'd totally recommend it. If you like Infinite, I'd strongly suggest you to start playing the first game because it's such an amazing game. And if you like it, then chances are you'll at least enjoy this game too.

X Rebirth is a reboot of the previous X Series games. I first got into the X Series back in X2: The Threat. Being able to command big capital ships was something that was a very memorable experience. Trying to get into big fleet battles was interesting. You had the whole universe of hundreds of systems to play in and play with which is the best part of any X Series game.

X Rebirth was something of a disaster, especially at launch. Many of the bugs were fixed with upcoming updates for X Rebirth but the gameplay and the Freedom that was once there is no more. You no longer have the freedom to fly other small ships or “Captain” Capital Ships in any way or form. You can “Own” many ships but cannot “Fly” any ship. You are locked to a ship named “Albion Skunk”,♥♥♥♥♥♥poor name in my opinion, and are limited in not only a dozen weapons.
There are only, currently I believe 4 or 5 systems vs the Hundreds of systems previously accessible in the other X Series games. Would rather have hundreds of systems to explore rather than 4 or 5 with smaller sub areas you can visit.
X Rebirth, has certainly improved somewhat in combat and most certainly graphically from its predecessors. There are many new gameplay mechanics, such as the Space Highway System, Bigger Space Stations with multiple dock locations and areas to explore. However, many interiors are identical to one another, faces on all characters are all nearly the same and various other small things just almost don’t make it worth your time to dock and talk to people.
There have been many improvements since Launch, and some great content has been added. But the freedom to do what you want, that made the other X Games so successful, is no longer there.
To summarize this all up without going into a 5 page essay as to why this game is a disaster, I would NOT recommend buying the game unless you got money to blow.

Area desgin: despite great visuals, areas are just vast rectangular fields of nothing but same reused meshes and textures. There is very little variety although despite the lack of assets every area feels unique and remarkable in some way. A testament to the area designers who had to work with few materials.
Quest design: the investigation is neat in concept and if you forget about gameplay conveniences (such as quest compass), requires you to pay attention to the dialogue but quest progression is extremely linear and all of the backtracking involved make, what could have been, a compelling and engrossing investigative experience, into a nuisance.
The bad:
Enemies: There is no variety. AI is terrible and very easily exploitable.
Backtracking. There is simply way too much of it even with fast travel and quest compass it becomes tedious amd pointless as hell.
As for the story:
You are a nameless guy that ended up in a 17 century Silent Hill where everyone is an ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and you have to find out their grimdark stories to make things right. In short, everyone is a horrible human being and it is in your power to cast final judgement and doom them for eternal torment or release them into nothingness.
Your choices bear no consequence whatsoever though.
All in all, the game appears to have been rushed. A few promising concepts that went nowhere and decent story that is buried under tedious gameplay.
P.S.: The game would have benefitted greatly if you could leave markings on the map for navigation, imho.

ID LIKE TO START BY SAYING THAT IVE PLAYED THIS GAME FOR A COUPLE OF YEARS NOW, BEGINNING MY EXPERIENCE WITH 'CARDS AND CASTLES' ON THE MOBILE DEVICE (BEFORE STEAM), HAVING POURED HUNDREDS OF HOURS INTO THIS GAME AND ADAPTED TO THE EVER CHANGING MECHANICS THE GAME HAS UNDERTAKEN.
I REALLY ENJOYED THE STRATEGY/CHESS LIKE CONCEPT OF THE GAME WHILST EARNING NEW CARDS TO BUILD A DECK THAT SUITS MY PLAY STYLE, BUT UNFORTUNATELY THE GAME HAS SUFFERED SOME DRASTIC CHANGES THAT HAS LOST ITS APPEAL TO ME.
MATCHES THEMSELVES USED TO BE A BIT MORE THOUGHT OUT, A BIT MORE TIME CONSUMING, YOU WERE GIVEN LONGER TURN TIMERS, CASTLE BURN ONLY OCCURRED WHEN YOUR DECK REACHED ZERO, CARDS WERE FOCUSED ON SPECIFIC ROLES IN YOUR DECK INSTEAD OF THE ALL ROUNDED FEEL THAT ALOT OF THE OLD CARDS HAVE BEEN TURNED INTO AND THE NEW CARDS MADE AS. MATCHES FEEL RUSHED WITH MINIMAL EMPHESIS ON STRATEGY.
THE RECENT CARD NERFING THOUGH HAS ASSISTED IN THE PAST ANNOYANCE OF VERSING OTHER 'EARLY STAGE  GAME RELEASE PLAYERS' THAT HAD RECIEVED MOST OF THE LEGENDARY CARDS AND HAD BECOME UNBEATABLE. TO AN EXTENT THE GAME COULD HAVE BEEN CONSIDERED PAY TO WIN FOR A LONG PART OF ITS EXISTANCE. FOR WHICH PLAYERS WHO DID ACTUALLY PAY/CONTRIBUTE TO THE DEVELOPMENT OF THE GAME AND RECIEVE CARDS ARE NOW VERY FRUSTRATED THAT THEIR MONEY WENT DOWN THE DRAIN WHEN THESE CARDS WERE CHANGED.
ONE MAJOR ISSUE THAT HASENT CHANGED AND EFFECTS ALL PLAYERS REGARDLESS OF SKILL OR LUCK OF THE CARDS IS THE CONSTANT CONNECTION ERROR THAT OCCURS, TIME AND TIME AGAIN THIS HAS COST ME A MATCH LOSS.
I WILL ALWAYS HAVE MY FOND MEMORIES OF THE PAST VERSIONS OF 'CARDS AND CASTLES' AND I WILL STILL EAGERLY WATCH THE FUTURE DEVELOPMENT OF THIS GAME, RECOMMENDING IT TO OTHERS, BUT THE GAME HAS SEEN BETTER DAYS.

Post RTMI Review:
After the recent changes introduced with the Return To Monster Island expansion, I have decided to write a new review.
I'd like to preface this review by stating I have played Cards and Castles on and off over the course of about two years, that I'm a former top player, and that I've had a hand in beta testing the game.
With the release of Return To Monster Island, Cards and Castles has seen quite a bit of a shake-up, with old sets being rotated into the Legacy format and Warlock Academy being rolled into Age of Dragons, as well as a host of new changes to core game mechanics (such as not being able to pass through enemies and not being able to directly target the Castle with burn spells) and some key classic cards (which now make up the foundation for every new players' collection.)
But wait, there's more! The deck limit has been increased to 40, and you may now have up to 3 copies of a card in your deck, regardless of rarity, which means more consistency, and going hand-in-hand with that is the update to card distribution, which now allows multiple Rare/Epic/Legendaries in a single pack, plus increased frequency of Epic and Legendary pulls.
Overall, I can say from experience that this expansion has really brought Cards and Castles up to speed and made it a much better game than it already was. Do please note that this game is still freemium, you can earn cards and packs for free, however, packs can still be acquired via cash currency (although you also earn a little bit of that with quests and playing games as well!)

Connection loss is common and will ruin more than a few games.
Single-Player is utterly pointless, and costs ludicrous amounts of Card Points (Did I mention you can buy card points?) to even begin to play, let alone finish.
The game is massively pay to win, as the free card packs and ones received from quests provide consistantly common cards.
Overall a potentially good game spoiled by pay to win, hostile devs and poor connection.

Cory in the House is a television show, which aired on the Disney Channel from January 12, 2007 to September 12, 2008 and was a spin-off from the Disney show That's So Raven. The show focuses on Cory Baxter, who moves from San Francisco, California to Washington, D.C. with his father, after Victor Baxter gets a new job in the White House as the official head chef. The series marks a Disney Channel first, as it is the channel's first spin-off. This is also the only Disney Channel spin-off series to be broadcast in standard definition for the entire length of the show. Reruns of the series have not been produced on Disney Channel, or on Disney XD; however they continue to air on the Family channel in Canada. Raven-Symoné guest-starred, reprising her role as Raven Baxter in one episode. In 2014 Disney Channel started airing a weekly block called Disney Replay on Wednesdays nights, during which episodes of Cory in the House air alongside That's So Raven and Kim Possible, among others.

The Game Runs like Absolute Trash.
This might not be extremelly noticeable at the begining or when you play on small maps against  1 to 2 opponents, however on bigger maps with many foes, the game starts to run like a slideshow after 4 hours. Concurrently in a game in a large galaxy with 5 other opponents about 6 hours in, the average fps which I am getting is around 8. Not exactly acceptable.
So why is this? Does my computer just suck? No. Its because the game is not at all optimized well for 64-bit systems. The game can only access 2 gigabytes of your ram and for me uses only about 15% of my processing power on average. With mods such as the Large Adress Aware you can make the game use  3 gigs instead of 2, which will give you a couple of frames, but maybe for like an hour after that it will drop to hell again as the sizes of fleets of the AI increase.
Conclusion:
- Later in Games it runs like a slideshow, if you dont mind the mindblowingly low fps, its a fantastic game in every other respect, in fact possibly my favorite RTS of all time. Save yourself the pain of having to abandon this masterpiece due to the broken performance and buy some other game.

There are still the three primary factions: Vasari, TEC, Advent. This game, however, splits those factions into Loyalist and Rebel factions that the player can choose. These factions diversify the choices and play styles of the factions. The Vasari are still, in general, very war and destruction focused (you get cool gravely voices and get to strip planets). The TEC are still pretty trade and defense focused. The Advent are still rather culture focused. The factions do add a little difference to the play style.
The primary reason to play this game is the feeling of power as you conquer planets and then galaxies. The game is very long with even a one galaxy game taking hours. It is loads of fun in multiplayer, but you might find that you have to dedicate an entire weekend to a good multi-galaxy 3-5 player game. Purchased this after the 1.2 update. Great little game. Despite using the traditional 2D platform configuration as its base (I've really haven't enjoyed these types of games since I was a kid; when that was the only thing on offer). What attacted me to this game was the genre, base building, character management and art style-ALL FANTASTIC. But what I didn't expect was depth and its addictiveness.
I would suggest trying a couple of runs before turning to the internet for tips. There are some really cool surprises and mechanics that are fun to learn without doing this. BUT, even if you've looked for tips and hints, there seems to be some behind the scenes mechanics at play to keep the game balanced even if you get off to a strong start (but not in unfair ways). This game will constantly throw curve balls at you; forcing you to take risks and make tough choices. Just when I thought I figured out how to get ahead via collecting resources, managing my survivors, and prioritizing what to build in my shelter...areas on the game map all of a sudden became unavailable because of rebel conflicts...slowing my progress to a halt and causing me to shift strategies. While in transition, I was forced to take some risks...and paid for it by losing a survivor. So, here I am on run 13...hoping to make it through this thing with no casualties (note: you don't have to restart because you lost one survivor. I may have even had another one show up at my shelter, but I like the challenge of trying to get out with everyone alive).
The more you play, the more you'll see how the game adapts to your strategy...always making it just difficult enough to stay challenging but not impossible to beat. In the end, you'll get a great gaming experience. Also, for you much better at this type of game than I am...the more you play, the more characters and scenarios open up for you to choose at the start of a new game. Each character has their strengths and weaknesses and the starting group dynamics are all different...along with number of characters in your starting group (from 1 to 4) and time of season (from summer to the dead of winter).  You can certainly get this when the price comes down, but for me, this was $20.00 well spent for such a supremely designed game.

If you want a textbook example of cashing in on a brand, then this is it.
I played over the free weekend, and reaffirmed why I'm waiting for this title to go on sale. It is just an expansion of of Civ5, just like everyone else has been saying.
Except in this expansion, it makes sure to introduce some incredibly annoying micromanagement aspects like trade route management. Where the hell is the check box for 'renew last route'? The build ques seem intended for small maps where oyu only have a few cities, because there are no build order lists and unless I'm missing something, there doesn't seem to be any city governer AI for the build que either. After all this time developing a 4X game, it seems the designers are retroverting to make it only suitable for small maps, and incredibly tedious for large ones. I really miss stacking. Moving  large groups is still just annoying as it is in Civ5 with units unable to end their turn on the same tile.
And really, a civ game with no nukes?
The visuals are only mildly interesting and it doesn't take long before wanting to turn unit move and combat animations off because it just slows the gameplay down to a crawl. The AI as usual loves to contantly beg favors and make demmands, but any done by the player is scoffed off. Just lik e before you can crush an AI and they will happily surrender their cities, but if you ask for open borders or some gold per turn it is 'unfair' and unacceptable.
Forget about setting some units on autoexplore because they won't get far past your borders before making a beeline for some dangerous monster to be wiped out the next turn. The game has a satellite layer, but you still have to use units to map out the landscape? Really????
At least the different 'paradigms' are interesting, giving you a choice between different philosophies that affect the appearance of your cities and units. Seems like anything other than harmony would be at a disadvantage, given that it allows you to use certain kind of tiles to your advantage. Still, having at least some variation in your units is welcome.
That said, I still look forward to getting this game. I'm just not going to bend over and pay the same as a AAA title for what amounts to an expansion pack, thank you very much.

I feel like this game is getting a bad rap due to the expectations that it would be a revolutionary game like Alpha Centauri.  This game is not as engrossing as Alpha Centauri and does not really scratch that Alpha Centauri itch for those who have been waiting for a sequel, but it is a plenty fun game in its own right.
The aliens provide an interesting mechanic; they are not just a hostile force to be wiped out.  You can certainly kill all of the aliens for fun and profit (and science by choosing the right virtue), but it is also possible to remain neutral and even befriend the aliens.  The unfortunate thing is that aliens become largely irrelevant after about 100 turns into the game.  They do not get any stronger, so they become easy to destroy.  This makes it useless to have the aliens as either friends or enemies.
The tech web is a great new take on the classic tech tree that has been in 4X-type games for decades.  Each main technology can unlock a couple of other main technologies, but also unlocks a couple of leaf technologies.  This opens up a wide variety of strategies, where at each tech juncture you can choose to go broad or go deep.  I have had successful games with both approaches, so there is not just one viable path through the tech web -- though the first few technology choices tend to be no-brainers.
The virtue system will be pretty familar to those who are used to the Civ 5 culture system, but it also has a new take.  Like the tech web, you can choose to go broad or go deep with the four different virtues (military, prosperity, knowledge, and industry).  Unfortunately, the difficulty of raising health means that going deep into the prosperity tree is pretty key to winning on higher difficulty levels; I am not convinced that going broad or even focusing on another tree is even viable right now.  Once you have gotten some key prosperity virtues, there are a bunch of different approaches each with their own value.  With some tweaks to the game, this could be as interesting as the tech web.
The military system has caught a lot of flak from what I have read, but I actually really like it.  Gone are the dozens of similar, slightly different units of which you will only build a few -- there is one unit type for each role, and as you gain "affinity points" through technology or quests you can upgrade your units to a stronger version of that type.  When you upgrade a unit, you choose from one of two benefits and all of your existing units get immediately upgraded.  The one thing I did miss from Alpha Centauri was the opportunity to create custom troops by combining together various, weapons, armors, and special abilities; the upgrade choices tend to be modest boosts that do not necessarily specialize the unit in any particular way.
The victory conditions are great and another thing I got tons of enjoyment out of in this title.  Each affinity has its own victory condition, as well as a generic victory condition open to any affinity and of course the ever-present domination victory.  The most interesting victory condition is the purity victory condition; you build a warp gate to bring in settlers from earth and have to find space for them to settle on your new planet.  This may involve going to war, since at this point in the game much of the world tends to be already settled.  It realy spices up the end game when you cannot just click a button to win.  The supremacy victory condition has you send troops back to earth to establish 'peace' there, which makes you choose between weakining your military and winning the game faster.  The harmony victory is unfortunately boring in comparison to the other two; just build the winning wonder structure, build some of the supporting buildings, and then wait.  The only thing I did not like about the victory conditions is that they come much earlier than I would like.  I am often only halfway done with the tech tree when I achieve victory.  There are some techs I have never researched because I can always win before I have a chance to grab them.
Many have said that Beyond Earth lacks 'personality,' and that is too true.  The leaders of the different factions have no real personality of their own, and the faction bonuses are small and rather bland.  This contrasts with the very well defined characters of Alpha Centauri, and the powerful and varied faction bonuses.  Wonders in Beyond Earth are almost all similarly bland, with one late game wonder seriously giving 4 culture per turn.  That's it -- 4 culture.  There is a regular building that gives 4 culture.  The game remains fun nonetheless.  I am hopeful that balance patches and expansions will make the factions and wonders more interesting, but unfortunately I do not think leader personalities will ever be patched in.
All in all, Beyond Earth is well worth playing.  It just is not a replacement for Alpha Centauri.

I found Betrayer to be both unsettling and fun to play. Everything you encounter is shrouded in mystery, be it your marooned situation, the person that shoots an arrow in your path to pass along a message, or the "darkness" you enter upon ringing the settlements' bells. At first I found it to be a rather unforgiving game. There's not a whole lot of handholding that happens with this: Here is your bow. Be careful with your ammo. Try not to die to ravening conquistadors on your way in. Pick up some clues and try to piece together what the hell happened if you make it that far.
Visually, I really enjoyed the black and white color scheme with the splashes of red to indicate things of importance (like piles of dirt, pools of blood, and things that want to kill you). But if black and white isn't your thing, and you don't enjoy that creepy Blair Witch vibe, you can adjust the color to the saturation you're comfortable with.
There is no voice acting, which I find only contributes to the atmosphere of the game, lending itself to a rather solitary and unnerving experience. There is no musical score to speak of, but rather the things you would normally hear in my neck of the woods (the birds, the breeze, and your own footsteps). A lot of this game works on audio cues. You can hear the enemies if you care to listen for them. Stealth is the name of the game (not literally... but achievements! And... health!). So I highly reccommend it.
Overall I enjoyed learning the story of these colonists. Some things, like the explosives you pick up, I have never found a use for, other than getting myself mercilessly slaughtered by every conquistador in the surrounding area. The ending, if not completely satisfying, is nevertheless what I would expect from this sort of eerie game. Definitely worth a look.
Very relaxing game with some humour and some sad bits. Very very good for the price and highly recommend if your looking to cool down and relax

The Simple Review:
So, a review, This game is a new Space adventure game, using Egosofts newest gaming engine. This new engine i should warn you likes to use the newest computer hardware possible, so if you think ur PC is as strong as a PS4, you may wanna upgrade (at least if you are obsessed with playing on ultra at 60FPS) <- dont kid yourself, you wont be able to without somethign beyond anyones budget. The reason is because this game is meant to evolve over years, you play it, and come back years later and the visuals look even more amazing because Computer Hardware has become more amazing (I'm a Computer Enthusiast).
Graphics:
As i said above its really a 10/10 if you can even play on medium, but if you just wanna see the future, find a not to clouded area and set it to Ultra, it becomes 30/10,
The only issue with the graphics is the NPCs, they are not as pretty and refined as they COULD be, but seeing as its the first attempt at this, ever i think, and on a newly designed engine, i let it slide.
Sound:
Space game with a good sound track, (I think i still prefered X3's but thats a matter of opinion, and if you play one game for years, you tend to put that music on a pedestel)
Gameplay:
you literally do WHAT YOU WANT....
Sandbox means, you can be a pirate, and just kill and steal, you can be a Trader, making your money to fund your empire via cargo, Adventurer, doing missions to make your Billions, or start your own factory (late game, or specific start) to become rich. hell you can mix all four if you'd like.
Community:
Developers and Beta Testers work hard to find and fix many bugs glitches and gaps in the game, patches come out often because of the hard work.
10/10 would suport Egosoft again, even with the rough start back in 1.0-3.00

Return to Castle Wolfenstein was the 4th installment (technically 5th if you count Spear of Destiny) of the Wolfenstein series. It was released 9 years after the events of Wolfenstein 3D.
The plot in this story basically puts you in the role of our favorite hard-headed anti-nazi american, William B.J Blazkowicz. Who is out to kill Nazis in WWII and needs to escape from Castle Wolfenstein to put an end to Hitler's regime. While you may be confused as to why he's, again, escaping from Castle Wolfenstein. Simple answer - this was more of a reboot/remake to get Wolfenstein modernized for the 6th generation of gaming back then in the early 2000s.
So, there's nothing to really delve into here other than you're out to kill Nazis, in all of Wolfenstein fashion.
Age has not been very kind to this entry. The engine it uses is the ID Tech 3, which was first used in Quake III Arena. While that engine was great in an Arena FPS setting. It didn't seem to work that well in Wolfenstein's case here. Enemy hitboxes seemed to be off center than the models they're based around. Shooting, even using snipers, seemed strayed off a little either to the left or right than dead center.
It was also pretty funny watching soliders die and just slide down the stairways. Watching guns pop out of them too and land on top of thin air. Soldiers make obscure pathfinding and even run away from you. When you play this game, you'll realize how out of date it plays. Which could either be good for you, if you've got the nostalgic shades on. But pretty bad if you expect anything spectacular and for this game to have aged like fine wine. It's not to be found here.
To be honest, there were better Wolfenstein games made before and after this installment. This game was made for it's time and done it's job. It's pretty easy to forget.

As a gigantic fan of first-person shooters, it's nice to go back and play the classics.  Today's games in the same genre tend to be quite cookie-cutter, hold your hand, and remove a lot of the challenge from what made these games great.  Return to Castle Wolfenstein is a great example of what games used to be, and it's still worth a playthrough nowadays.
If anyone wants to experience this game again, though, it is a good idea to do some quick modding of the game; some of the Steam guides do a fantastic job of helping out.  Personally, I used 3 mods.  The main one that is basically needed is the unofficial 1.42d patch -- this not only adds fully native widescreen support, it also fixes a multitude of crashing problems if a modern PC is used.  I also tacked on QeffectsGL for this game, for additional graphical support.  The other (optional) mod I used is the Venom Mod, which retextures much of the game to look great.  However, should you choose to go that route, it's recommended to remove the AI files from it (Steam guides also help with this) to avoid the unfair difficulty programmed in the mod.  These three mods combine to treat this game like an HD remaster, and it runs very smoothly.
That being said, the actual difficulty in the game is fair, even on I am Death Incarnate (hardest).  It's tough enough to give an actual challenge, but not too tough to the point where it becomes trial-and-error with brute force.  As long as the player does the tried-and-true tactics of strafing and shooting, using corners as cover and shooting around them, and using the right weapons for the right enemies, they'll be just fine.  There's no health regen, unlike most shooters today, but there's way more than enough health around.  Return to Castle Wolfenstein is easily beatable, but the game isn't going to hold your hand to do so.  It's fine.
RTCW does a fantastic job of giving the player a slew of weapons to use.  There's everything from SMGs, to silenced weapons, to explosives and super weapons.  All these are needed to perform different types of missions in the game, and RTCW throws you in a large variety of them.  There's stealth missions, run-and-gun missions, long range sniping missions, and other missions with boss fights.  All of them are pretty well done and very fun.  The types of enemies are varied, from Nazis to the undead and mecha robots, and require different strategies to dispose of them easily.  The variety in gameplay is what makes this game fun even today.
Given this game's price on Steam, it's worth picking up -- especially on a ridiculously cheap sale.  Just remember that if the buyer has a modern machine (and don't we all), it's highly recommeded to mod it at least with the unofficial 1.42d patch.  This should help avoid optimization issues and help with rekindling that nostalgia, and Return to Castle Wolfenstein has FPS nostalgia in spades.

I've only gotten a few hours into this game, but I'm already loving it. It appears to have the full range of activities in the Freelancer tradition: exploration, trading, mining, and loads of combat. You have faction relations that can go up or down depending on who you do missions for, and there seem to be space ports all over the place to dock at for missions and equipment. I've only barely scratched the surface of the main story, but it's intriguing so far.
Combat seems to be the focal point of the game, and it's really well done. I'm not sure how much more layered it can get, but it's nicely varied so far. You control a capital ship rather than just a fighter, and you seem to have two primary classes of weapons: broadsides and turrets. Broadsides do massive damage, but are slow and can't track fast moving ships. They're great against other capital ships though. Turrets can lock onto targets and tear up small fighters, but they can overheat if you don't give them a break from firing. And the cool thing is, they will automatically fire while you're controlling the broadsides. In addition, you have a thruster boost mechanism that can increase you speed, but which can also be depleted from over use, such that it needs a rest to recharge. On top of that, you can get a deflector add-on which is something like an extra shield that absorbs essentially all incoming damage. When it's up, you can't fire your weapons, and it has limited energy which drains over time or rapidly when it's taking hits.
What all this means in practice is that you've got a lot of systems and energy bars to keep track of, which keeps combat really engaging. It was a tiny bit overwhelming or frustrating initially, but I felt like I got the hang of the essentials within maybe half an hour. At that point, combat was a blast.
I can't say much about the main story, since I've only gotten a couple missions into it, but it seems to revolve around some form of advanced technology and finding a lost relative. Interesting enough that I want to see where it goes. The world feels large and full of activity. Visually, the game is gorgeous, with great effects for all the weaponry, and the music is awesome, a dustry, countrified rock soundtrack that really adds a lot of character to the experience. I love me some electronic music, but this is a nice change of pace that gives the game a distinct personality.
In summary, if you ever played the old Wing Commander games, or Freelancer, or anything similar, you will love this game. It even more closely resembles another game call Nexus: The Jupiter Incident that came out about a decade ago, which had an equally interesting story. I'd say the primary difference with that game is that combat is much more refined and well done here. If you're like me and aren't sure, but crave space adventures, get this game.

First impressions are good! Great soundtrack, the early space battles have a nice intuitive rock-scissor-paper-feel (probably got them in the wrong order).
Mid-game, I'm kind of grinding for credits. I need so and so many million to reach tier 6-weapons and to maybe fight the big battles and come out on top. I don't know if I made it too easy, but I went for the fast "Barracuda" so I could out-maneuver and out-run my enemies and then pick the fighters of off in bite-size chunks and move in to the "blind spots" of the capital ships and just wear them down with ma lazers..  Where was I.. yes the grind! It came to a point where my strategy was sound, but I still didn't feel ready to further the main quest.
Lots of grinding later I had my weapons and went in to the much to short late-game and now I'm the hero. And still don't feel like I care about my aunt! I mean, for a game that has the plot-hook, that I want to find my aunt and help her, then they should have focused more on the story-line and flesh out the characters of the game.
Most of the missions where fun the first 25 times I did them, except for the escort missions, they NEVER became any fun. While you're in the middle of fighting capital ships and fighters, your escort-buddy up and killed himself. Poor form!
The funniest side mission was when a discreet gentleman needed my assistance to reacquire lost items. When I get to the pick up, the cargo is pin-up monthly magazines! The gentleman was shipping dirty magazines and suddenly I understand why I was under oath not to tell his wife. Those kind of quirky side-missions makes me smile. I don't know who that man is, but I instantly like both him and his wife and I'm curious about their relationship and his business enterprise.
It's like the developers have good story-writers but they are put on writing up side-missions instead of making sure the follow-through for the main story is solid.
If you want 10+ hours of fun, go get it! If you another 10 hours of grind look no further!

One of the best games I've played in a while. Probably the most original game, conceptually and mechanically to come out in the last several years.
The fact that it takes place from the perspective of the victims of war opposed to every other war game which is from the perspective of soldiers or the military, makes it a very real and unforgettable experience. I actually wrote a paper in college on the excess of shooter games, specifically military based themed ones. So its very refreshing to see a negative, horrifying, unglorified take on war video games. Very admirable.
The game its self is very morbidly beautiful looking, with a story and pacing to match. Its very unique in context of a side scrolling video game, which I havent seen very many of untill recently. Its more about stragety and stealth opposed to reflex and speed, like most games from its genre. Its not quite turn based but is time based, so there no rushing through this one.
I really want to go into specific detail and event in the game that make it one of a kind, but I'll actually leave it up to you to decide. The only thing Ill say is that the game forces you to make incredibly hard and uneasy decisions. The game really tests and questions you morally on what you would do to survive. Playing this game is not about good or bad people, but to what extent you'd got to to save you and your group of survivors. Whether to save, feed or shelter other survivors, or loot, steal or kill, to maximise your supplies with out betraying your consciousness. Unlike games like Infamous: Second Son, or Fallout where they make you decide between one side or another and once you've picked that certain path you intensively and frantically try to reach that pirticular goal, This War of Mine, only allows you to make decision on pure circumstance. You only do what you must when you have no other options, balancing your survival with real guilt and remorse, at the same time subjecting you to the same circumstance and vulnerability you put other in.
Highly, highly recommend it.

In This War of Mine, players control a small group of civilians as they try to survive during a civil war, in the fictional city of Pogoren. Its a really unique experience, emotional and brutal.
Gameplay is split into two sections: day and night. During the day, your survivors are at home. You need to keep an eye on any negative status effects - when they're hungry, give them some food, if they're sick, give them medicine, bandage their wounds and make sure they sleep when tired. You can build equipment such as a stove to cook food, a workshop to craft tools and weapons, rain collectors and filters to get clean water, traps to catch small animals to eat, beds to sleep in, a furnace for heat. And you can craft valuable trade items like cigarettes and booze.
During the night, you can select one survivor to scavenge local buildings for supplies, while the others either sleep, or guard your home from bandits. There are lots of areas to visit around the city, and you'll encounter some tricky situations. There are only a couple of completely abandoned areas where you're free to take everything without consequence. Sometimes friendly people will trade with you, but if you don't have anything valuable, would you steal from them instead? Would you murder innocents and take their stuff so your own people can survive? Some areas are occupied by dangerous bandits, who will attack you on sight - but if you're desperate, you might have to risk it.
The combat system, like the rest of the gameplay, is managed through a point and click interface. Left click to walk to a location, right click to run, left click icons to interact with an object or person. I found the combat to be very hard, but I think that is probably by design. Our survivors aren't trained soldiers, and powerful guns are rare and expensive. So far I've tried to avoid combat as much as possible. There's no reloading or respawning, so death is permanent.
There are several scenarios to play through, where you'll start with between one and four survivors, and sometimes another will ask to join your group. Even that can be a tough choice - an extra pair of hands can be useful but its another mouth to feed. Each survivor has their own story and some of them have a special skill. For example Katja can get better value in trades, Bruno spends less resources when cooking and Arica can sneak quietly.
Its the kind of game where you'll generate your own stories. I thought my second attempt was looking good, until we got several days of snow. I couldn't keep the house warm enough, so Bruno froze to death overnight. Realising that every meal would cost me more resources, I started to take risks in the dangerous areas. Arica stealth killed two bandits but a third one shot her dead. Katja went to the same place the next night, figuring one more bandit would be easy enough. Turns out there was more than one and they shot her dead as well. Now alone, and very desperate, I had Pavle murder an old couple and steal all their food, but the next day he was depressed, wouldn't eat anything, and overnight he committed suicide. Game over. But its failures like that which made my next, successful run feel so good.
TWOM is a fantastic game and I thoroughly recommend it as a full price purchase.

This is an old point-and-click adventure inspired by the homonymous sci-fi story by Harlan Ellison. Long before the introduction of Skynet etc, AM was the computer that lead to the destruction of civilization and to all humans except five remaining survivors which are tortured for 109 years.

Cons:

I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream has quickly become one of my favorite games. The story is one of the best I've experienced in some time. The game does have some glaring flaws, however.
The game begins with a monologue by the game's antagonist, AM (voiced by Harlan Ellison, author of the novella), describing his hate for humanity and the five humans he's enslaved for 109 years. After this, you're given a choice of the five available characters.
Each of these five stories are relatively short, but the problem comes in the way the game was designed. This is a game of trial and error, moreso than that of other point-and-click games. There are times where you're allowed to go to the end of a chapter, only to find out that you haven't done something correct, or even worse, misclicked something, leading to you having to restart that chapter if you haven't a multitude of saves. If you're not going to save in a separate slot every few moments, I'd reccomend a guide. I've never been very good at these sort of games, and so that's what I did.
Despite these flaws, this game is still quite good. The voice acting, for the most part (I never did like Ellen's voice work), is quite good. Harlan Ellison does an amazing job voicing AM, with every word dripping with sarcasm or hate. The sound design is also quite good for the time. Character sprites are beautifully grotesque (as if they've been tortured for 109 years, perhaps?) and the backgrounds are full of detail.
Despite the inherent flaws in the gameplay, I would still reccomend this game, though again with a guide. If you're a purist or want to play without one, just be prepared to reload saves or restart chapters quite often.

Well, a lot is said about the remake of the original BioShock and I can confirm that:
- There are occasionally some nasty crashes during map/gene display screens and save menus, that can ruin your most current save game.
- There are some audio issues that make 5.1 settings problematic (not to mention that the overall audio setup sounds like more compressed and inferior to the original).
- Some wet surface/tile effects are missing.
- Old Unreal engine v2.5 (heavily modified) is in use.
+ The gameplay is almost identical (with an xbox controller) and faithful to the original.
+ 60fps are easily achieved (though this can lead to different gameplay experience compared to the original 30fps target)
+ The overall graphics and textures are superior.
+ It is obvious that the developing team gave some “love and affection” on the remaster (perhaps not enough for the public demand, but certainly not lazy run).
Opinion: When I try to play back the original version of the game (especially after finishing the remake), I feel like travelling back to 10+ years old xbox360 graphics & limitations. The original wet surfaces can’t really justify the fact that it feels like dumping down the resolution of textures to 720p standards (even at 1080p PC settings). Frankly, I sometimes pause the original game to verify that it is set (in PC graphics options) at full HD, because it doesn’t feel like. On the other hand, the original version still looks relatively OK on xbox360 (but mainly because of the upscaling blur).
Verdict: The new version looks graphically superior, though it sometimes feels a little bit different. It’s just that if more attention to debug crashes & audio were made and a feature patch (to bring back wet surfaces and tiles) was issued, we should consider Bioshock Remastered, a quite decent remake by all means. As it is right now, seems more of a modified HD+ version to slightly approach modern console gamers rather than modern PC gamers. Still, the aforementioned issues, won’t prevent the hardcore fans of the franchise (like me) from finishing this version (although it takes some .ini editing or use of surround only audio and saving at least twice per 20 mins!). Therefore, I should encourage old and new players to pay a re-visit back to “The Rapture”, given they are patient enough to overcome some “technical difficulties” and can’t wait for a future version (mostly unlike) based on Unreal engine v4.0+ .

Cards and Castles is a free to play PVP only CCG with a 9 by 5 grid based battle map with castle on each end.

At level 4 and below you have to use Starter decks, and level 5 and above can use 2 faction (pre-made or created) decks.  I guess level 5 players are losing battle points to play in the battle queue against lower level players to farm battle points or quests.  Or only higher level players are playing this game.  Higher level players should be restricted to Starter decks when playing against lower level players, Which is NOT THE CASE in this game.

You receive a level appropriate card pack (2 to 5 cards = Commons or maybe Rare) for free every 4ish hours (2 pack limit in storage) and pack or card rewarded for daily quest of winning pvp battles.  Units have a various attack, movement, special abilities and health.  There is spell cards also. There is 5 faction themed card sets and a common card set.
The game take a tactical mind to play, but you still have random luck to deal will.
Has a Single player vs AI mode for practice, but the AI is sort of horrible player and you don't get rewards out of it.  Has an asynchronus PVP battle mode, that notifies you by Steam, when you have your turn.  You earn Tournament playing at level 3, making a one game deck from random cards, you can earn card pack based on score, eliminated after 2 losses, have to pay something to play again.
There is a timer on your turn.  If you run out of your deck cards, you lose health on your castle.  There is no global chat or chat between opponnents, but if you friend someone you can chat with them.  You can only complete Quests by playing Battles or Tournaments. You lose some battle points, if you lose a battle or surrender.  There is no annoying emotes that can be used as a endgame teabag, so you don't have painfull losses.

Now battles have 19 turns, then goes into Sudden Death which causes 2 points of damage to castles each turn. Devs took out the beginning campaign.  Devs nerfed the Wizard ( It had an across board teleport when played ) There is NO complete explanation of the current rules and gameplay, there is no manual.   All the players playing now are more bloodthirsty.  You can use 3 of the same card in your deck, and that counts for the Rare, Legendary and Epic cards too.

The game is Pay to Win, since you can buy the Epic, Legendary and Rare cards Quicker with real money. Also having many less expensive units in your deck lets you attack the castle quicker by zergging them.  Just have to collect card packs for a long time.
Your best starter deck to play is the Ninja deck, use the stealth units to sneak attack the castle only and the fast units like cruise missiles.

Betrayer is an excellent game with some very clever ideas. You start on a beach with no knowledge of what you need to do. As you travel through the land you discover things that start to fill in the larger picture. The story line is good and it keeps you going, looking to find out just a bit more.
You can play this game in greyscale or if you change the default setting you can choose to play in colour. Some parts can only be played in greyscale but however you choose to play it's good. The combat is nicely done. You won't need reflexes of a God or knowledge of any fancy blocking or offensive moves to survive. Having said that it isn't a walk in the park either. You'll need to get weapons and choose your tactics.
You will die but death isn't a major factor unless you choose the option to leave your belongings at the scene of your death. This means you have to go and recover them before you die again or lose them permanently. Death normally just means you're resurrected and the enemy has respawned, possibly at different locations and you have to try again.
There were bits I thought could be done differently but overall a very enjoyable experience. It's nice to see someone trying something different in game development. Well done. Recommended.

The graphics are generally gorgeous, the sound design is inspired if not perfectly executed.  The environments are pretty if somewhat repetitive.  The enemies don't show much diversity, but serve the purpose of giving you something to shoot at, and can be quite challenging if you're not careful.

Try out the demo first. I know I should have.  The game looks nice. The trailers pretty realistic about what you can expect visually, but not gameplay wise.
The stealth mechanics are really lacking, or almost non existing. Enemies see you through grass, so if you're coming up over a hill then they will have seen you before you knew they were there. The wind-blowing mechanic is cool, but you wont use it nearly as much as the game will have you think. Encounters with enemies are mostly just "what order do i have to kill things to save on HP. They don't see you if you go behind them, but wether you are able to chance upon them from behind is seemingly random, as the blurry camera makes enemies even capable of seeing you before you see them in a straight line.
The AI is dumb as bread. Enemies either A) run straight at you. B) shoot at you. C) in the case of the natives, just move around a bit to "seem" like they're doing dodging things. The only time i was impressed by the AI was when a monster walked up to another monster he had seen get killed. Other than that, you'd almost wonder if there was any thought into the AI at all.
The quests are OK if you like storie telling. Everything is text. Everything consists of fetch/delivery quests and dialog with NPCs. you press the "listen" button to get a noise indication of where you have to go next. You would think that with all the stories and footnotes the game stores in your journal, it would expect you to take on the challenge of thinking about where to go next, but no. You can beat the game by just spamming through dialog all meanwhile doing dull-as-water fetch-quests where you have to battle the♥♥♥♥♥♥poor AI that pops up every now and then along the way.. though once you've unlocked all the quick-travel locations in an "area" then you're just going to try to do as little walking as possible.
I got to the third and last area, and realized they want me to backtrack through the game for the rest of the story. That's when I quit playing.

This is one of the ABSOLUTE BEST point and click games from this era. I have heard complaints about how it's too difficult, requiring random clicking, and, yeah... I understand that. But the thing is, I don't know of a single PAC from before 2000 that WASN'T like that. It's just a blessing that the internet exists, making it a lot easier to enjoy these games. I realize that this does feel shameful, but what I do with old fashioned PAC games like this, along with the original Kings Quest games and Gabriel Knight: Sins of the Fathers, is I have a walkthorugh on standby. I understand that a game shouldn't be so stupidly difficult that this is nessicary to enjoy the game, but this game was made 20 years ago, before a lot of developers truely understood game design. But, I do agree that this game is unbelievably, unreasonably, difficult.
But, the reason this game is worth buying, even though you'd need to constantly read a walkthrough, is because it's hauntingly creative. It's based off the short story by Harlan Ellison, and even has him voice acting as the main villian, this goes through punishments of the 5 people left on Earth, at the utter submission of an evil, all-knowing, computer. Some of these characters are deeply flawed, while some others didn't really do anything wrong, but it's still interesting to witness every characters living hell.
This game is also very dark, bringing up issues like domestic violence,♥♥♥♥♥♥ murder, the Holocaust, and, although this was cut out from the game, you can watch cutscenes on Youtube that were taken out; like one of the main characters becoming so overwhelmed with hunger, he eats live baby.
Absolutely not for the faint of heart, but an absolute must for anyone who is a devout horror fan.

A pretty fun game all-in-all, though a bit short and has a few performance issues at times. Looking forward to seeing what the modding community can do with it. As a side note, Tim appears to be partially colorblind. Kudos to the devs for adding some diversity to video games.

By no means is this game perfect. It can be hard to find the solution to a puzzle,  or even realize what the puzzle is. When a track of music (which is great, by the way, making this even worse) ends, it takes what feels like forever to start again.
Even with the flaws it has, that makes me think one thing: This game needs a remastering. However, because of it's age, this game has become even better. The game has essentially aged like wine instead of milk, which is an interesting contrast to other games made around the same time.
Part of it's beauty is the time it was made in. The music almost sounds as if it were taken from a 90s edutainment game (4th grade typing deluxe), then made melancholy, bringing on feelings of regret and acceptance of horrible sins. Seriously, it's a strange feeling when you mix those together. The graphics aid this kind of feel too. This is all so fitting for supercomputer that has gone insane; It cannot move, yet it can think and torture the last humans alive in the digital simulations it creates. That 90s kind of feel helps this.
As far as the story and game itself goes, you have choices. Except these choices aren't just presented to you directly. It's your small individual decisions, as little as attempts to try burying something. These build up change the outcome of events.
There are no real good endings or resolutions in this game. AM (the computer) will physically not let you die. You have options here: Cowardly commit suicide, only for the cycle that you are trapped in to repeat and repeat, or die with honor, atoning for and confronting your horrible sins, showing mercy and compassion as you die knowing that this is the closest you'll ever get to morally fix your past. It doesn't matter though. You're one of the last humans "alive", if you count this as living.
You don't win. You can die as a coward, or change yourself in the process of death. There is no way to win.
When I first played this, I wasn't really in the right mood for it. If you are buying this, I have some suggestions on how to enjoy this game the best you can:
Make sure that you're in the right mood. If you ever feel depressed, play this game. It won't make you feel better, but you'll get more out of the game.
Don't use guides. It breaks the atmosphere and immersion. If you get stuck, consider your options and logically think for a bit. If this doesn't work, then just come back to the game later. Your mind will have refreshed then.
Play the scenarios in this order: Gorrister, Ellen, Benny, Ted, Nimdok. It makes sense judging by the feel and content of each one.
I feel like this is obvious by now, but play it in a dark room with headphones on.
Really, the problem isn't that the game looks bad or anything. However, the real problems are invisible at first (especially to the buyer). The problems are mostly technical stuff too. If you can look past this, the game is amazing.

Completely uninspiring, unfinished, and unworthy.
My first game I choose the most alien-sounding biome: fungal (there is also a lush forrest biome and a desert biome) and for a grand total of about 50 turns it's very exciting. But then I realise: everything is blue. While Earth has a vast variety of terrain and biomes, each of Beyond Earth's biomes are monochromatic, and for fungal, that color was blue. Many resources blended in with the blue fungus trees on blue fungus grass with blue hills and blue mountains and blue snow and blue-green water. Even the unit-damaging miasma is a sort of blue that makes it blend in as well. It didn't help that my sponsor (one of only 8 leaders in the game) also had muted blue borders and city names. The UI was all blue and, at the time that I played this, all of the tech web was blue so you couldn't tell anything apart (I believe that has since changed).
I endured the fatigue my eyes weathered from trying to pick every shade of muted blue out from each other only to find that diplomacy with the other factions is garbage and, again, uninspired. There's no real reason for diplomacy in the game, since there are so few options, so I stayed away from it all together. At times it became real annoying attempting to tell my units apart from others, since they all look the same until you reach an affinity level. Then anyone sharing one of three affinities has the exact same looking units (and there are very few units overall). The only way to tell them apart is the marker floating above their heads.
There apparently will not be varied military units in the future, as there is only one airborne unit, two seaborne units, and a handful of land units with which to wage war. The affinity system allows you to upgrade your units, but in the end it's usually just a skin and a perk for all those units. Instead of a bomber and a fighter unit, you have to choose for your air unit to be either a bomber OR a fighter for the rest of the game. There are no nuclear or equivalent weapons anymore either.
The affinity system is supposed to make the sponsors change drastically as they follow their chosen belief system, but in reality, they mostly choose different color palettes for their wardrobes and makeup, with the occasional cybernetic hand. Your cities change into one of three different styles based on your affinities too...so if Brasil, India, and America all went Purity they'd all have the same brown buildings. Exciting the first time, not really as gripping as culture-representative cities in Civ V.
The trade routes get out of hand by mid to late game and Beyond Earth shifts from an uninspired, lacking Civ Mod to a trade-route-manager-simulator. You have to hand pick where each of your 20 or so trade routes go every few turns, taking up a good 5 minutes each turn to scroll through the long list of possible cities to trade with trying to find the best one.
The AI as a whole is just atrocious, the workers always build terrascapes, forcing you to either manually assign every worker you have (another five minutes per turn) or accept that your economy is going to tank from improvements that hurt you more than they help. Espionage is so incredibly overpowered you could win the game with spies alone.
Victory (or failure) nets you a game over screen with a couple of empty words that mean nothing, and no statistics for the game. This left me absolutely clueless as to how I kept losing my first game. All victory conditions were shown at 75% or less for each civilization, so how was I suddenly losing? Even if you win, it's still extremely underwhelming, especially for a game that supposedly has some underlying story or something.
In all, the game is uninspired visually, mechanically, fundamentally, and over hyped as something it is not. Some feelings of underwhelmedness throughout the game you just can not put into words. Had this game been made by an individual as a mod or small DLC for Civ V, it would be amazing, but the fact that a large company with years and years of experience made this as a stand alone game makes it feel rushed with the least amount of work put into it to make the most amount of money.
