I would argue if given more guidance, effort, and common sense, "I Have No Mouth" could have been one of the best. It's less-so a game of wasted potential and more a sad product of people who failed to take it as seriously as it deserved to be.
The plot is fascinating here. It incorporates genuine themes of humanity, morality, and mortality, and explores the struggle of each individual character searching hopelessly for some kind of redemption. Each path is extremely unique in some way or another, and really tries to make interactivity key to the experience. Only problem is a lot of the choices are cookie-cutter dry and painfully transparent, but, hey, it’s the thought that counts, right?
The original "No Mouth" short story by Harlan Ellison is an incredible cautionary vision about the relationship between us and technology, as well as a bleak tale of human suffering. The game does only a half-decent job reflecting on those concepts and a half-decent job expanding on them. It gets some things right, other things horribly wrong. Voice acting is extremely hit-or-miss, the gameplay overall is unpolished and the puzzles, in typical point-and-click fashion, are often nonsensical. The dialogue is sadly forgettable, and while the characters are fleshed-out slightly more, some of the changes/additions are worse-off, rather than improvements (example: changing Benny’s backstory and sexuality).
Harlan Ellison’s short story being adapted into a video game is a huge leap for the medium because for once it attempts to elevate games to the level of real literature. The general public often fails to take games seriously because more often than not they serve as purely entertainment. No Mouth isn’t so concerned with entertaining you as it is to try and make you think. It’s an endeavor not often seen in video games, and it’s something definitely to be applauded here, even if it doesn’t fully succeed. Recently there's been a shift to change that, but it’s always been mostly unheard of. In fact, I would say a lot try and fail, but No Mouth gets marks for being one of the real firsts of its kind and not misfiring completely.
So what am I saying here? I'm saying it's an incredible experience if you get past what it could have been. None of the somewhat obvious flaws are even remotely dealbreakers. It remains essential gaming for anyone with an interest in interactive storytelling, and especially for speculative fiction fans.

Let me start with this - Apsyr, who did the Linux port, did a brilliant job and the port runs flawlessly on my machine (Ubuntu 14.04 32 bit, Phenom II X6 1090T, Radeon HD 7880, Catalyst). Some linux games can be hit or miss, but Aspyr have brought the full AAA experience to Linux. Bravo Zulo Aspyr!
The game itself... It's Civ V, in space.
That's damming with faint praise, as Civ V is very, very, very good (and the Aspyr Linux port of that is equally flawless). If you don't already own Civ V and its myriad of expansions, this is a great way into the franchise and very engaging. If you already own Civ V though, while a lot of new stuff has been added and there are new things to do and new ways to play (all good stuff, for the most part) it just doesn't capture the magic that Civ V has. Part of it is that the various factions (which in Civ V are recognisable cultures fronted by famous real historical leaders) are, in BE, much more generic. When you fight Gengis Khan in Civ V, it feels like you are locking horns with *someone*, whereas in BE, the various leaders have no... souls.
So it winds up being a game that is simultaniously immensley rewarding and teeth-gnashingly frustrating - and the frustration is simply "it isn't Civ V"
In a universe where Civ V didn't exist, I would never stop raving about this game. But Civ V exists, I have it, and despite an entirely enjoyable experience on a "free to play weekend" I find myself reluctant to shell out the $50 the game costs. And to be honest, the only reason why I haven't just cleared the cache and moved on is that I want to see Aspyr rewarded for the very good work they did on the port, and I'm debating throwing them a bone and taking this one for the team.

BioShock 2 is the sequel to the highly successful BioShock game, and I must say 2K Games have really improved the graphics on the game! It is absolutely beautiful and very rich and diverse, there are new splicers to kill, the new and scary Big Sisters and the return of the famous Big Daddy!
What I love about this sequel is that now you can play as a Big Daddy and rip the enemies apart which is really satisfying and makes me cringe my teeth whenever I do such a task, its awesome! (Used to do the same with the new Shadow Warrior with the Katana mechanic)
Although the game looks beautiful and has done some improvements that BioShock suffered with, sadly, the game is not as good as the first one. Don't get me wrong, the game is awesome and really cool to return to Rapture, but sadly, it does fall flat
Some of the missing sound effects that was a constant problem and the downgrade in audio quality in the first game have been resolved to a certain extent, however once or twice I have noticed a missing sound effect or two but till now I haven't noticed a downgrade in audio quality
The textures on the signs and billboards are just horrible, and my gaming PC can play this on high, let alone if the game had an Ultra High option, but, the textures just look horrible
The difficulty has been slightly tweaked from the last one, thankfully Splicers are no longer as stupid as the first game, however they are really cruel and I have died multiple times on Medium difficulty, I understand you have to die once or twice but not most of the time, it makes me just want to stop playing the game
The first BioShock was creepy and a bit scary, however this sequel is not as scary. The only bit that made me a bit scared was the first encounter of the Big Sister, its loud screech did make me jump out of my seat and the few jumpscares of splicers popping out here and there is in this sequel, but it is not as scary as the first game
The story (till where I have reached), is pretty poor,
Although it is good, it doesn't have a OMG plot twist like in the first BioShock, its just mentioned to you and that's it! Nothing more, nothing less! However, I haven't finished the game and this is just a first impressions review, so, who knows?
And... the fetch quests are back! BUT there is not as much as the first game, but I still hate fetch quests, developers just put them in the game in my opinion just to lengthen the story!
I have heard from many people who have played the sequel saying that the game is not as long as the first one, if you check my playtime, I finished BioShock in 6 hours,
and I am already (probably) half way through the game and according to Steam I have just played 2 hours of it! So if the length of the game is short, then it is a pretty short game!
Even though all the above stuff I mentioned may be a bit negative, don't feel discouraged to buy this sequel, its not bad nor is it unplayable, its just not as good as the first game but if they ever have another 2K Weekend or sale and are selling the BioShock Triple Pack for 15.00EUR or less, GET IT, it is worth the money

Cons:
-Awful Name
-Boring, mandatory tutorial
-Tutorials dispersed throughout the first hour of gameplay (sometimes in the middle of a match)
-Atrocious 3D cutscenes
-Automatic land tapping broken
-First stage of Campaign is played with boring prebuilt decks
-The interesting scenarios in the campaigns of the previous entries are gone, replaced with boring poorly themed fightsm disappointing given they got to make your deck as well. Seriously, there is only one interesting fight per campaign, and they're quite a bit less interesting than basically any of the encounters from Magic 2014
Pros:
-Great soundtrack
-2D artwork is impressive (what do you expect, it's magic card art)
-Good visual design with playing area
-Slighty better menu navigation then M14 and FAR better menu navigation than M15
-Deck Wizard is interesting and gives new players the right perspective for building decks
-Getting new boosters can be a slog but for a free game ultimately it could've been quite worse.
-It's Magic: The Gathering, one of the best trading card games ever made.
Ultimately I'd recommend giving it a look, especially if you're new to Magic and want to learn the mechanics. While I find the tutorials incredibly annoying (especially since they're mandatory if you want to build up a decent sum of ingame currency early on), the scenarios they present give a far deeper understanding of certain mechanics and their tricks than I could explain to someone.
If you try the game and it's not to your liking, I'd reccommend MTGO (far worse interface but access to almost every magic card ever printed), Tabletop Simulator (People have recreated many of the card sets of MtG and besides buying the game itself, they're all free), Magic 2014 (more fun in general but decks are somewhat prebuilt, which can be a good thing for learning and balance, and the game is pracitcally dead), or simply trying out the physical card game - intro decks are cheap, and if you do your research online you can buy very competitive decks for a low cost.

Snuggle Truck attempts to do something very simple in what it offers, and for the most part it succeeds. The main problem comes with the frustration of acquiring all medals available.
The basic premise of the game is to go through groups of increasingly difficult levels and achieve specific goals in order to earn medals. There are easy, medium, hard, and extreme groups of levels. In easy and medium, it's actually fun to hone in your skills and fight for all the medals. In the hard levels, the fun begins to diminish into something comparable to an annoying task or a dreadful job. The extreme levels are so much worse than the hard levels, that the experience ceases completely from being a game and fully becomes a terrible chore, or a punishment.
If getting the basic medal for all levels is enough to please you, then you'll be able to easily beat the game in less than an hour. On the other hand, if you're a perfectionist, and getting all possible medals is your goal, I'm sure that there may be at least ten hours of entertainment here for you. There are also some bonus developer created levels, as well as thousands of user created levels for you to download from within the game, but actually wanting to experience this much content will depend on how patient you are and how much fun you are able to get out of Snuggle Truck.
Snuggle Truck is okay.

TL;DR: Cute aesthetic, awesome soundtrack, but the controls really let it down.
I really wanted to like this game, the idea of being able to freely slice up a level to progress, or impede your progress is really fun and the fact that almost everything in a level can be sliced and diced any way you choose is pretty damn cool.
But the problem is this game wants to be a precision platformer at the same time as letting you cut your own platforms willy-nilly. Movement is jerky and inconsistent, which doesnt gel with having to pull off well-timed jumps or navigate along, very often, very narrow bridges and ledges.
Then we come to the cutting mechanic which, while fun, is not intuative to control, at all. This makes it often frustrating when a misplaced cut can mean having to reload to the last checkpoint.
It also means that when the game puts you under preasure, forcing you to line up and perform cuts very quickly, you will die. A lot. Having a very cumbersome, slow and counter-intuative aiming mechanic does not partner well with having only a couple of precious seconds to aim, line up and cut a giant rock that's flying at your head.
And then there's the problem with using physics to place your platforms. When you cut down a pillar to make a bridge, because of the physics, it often won't make a bridge. It'll tumble down that gaping crevasse you were trying to cross. Also, if you're the type of gamer who wants to get every last collectable, you will watch them tumbling down that crevasse, even if the bridge lands properly, because they too, have physics, and will bounce and roll straight into the abyss.
The soundtrack, though, is truly awesome, but I wouldn't reccomend this game unless you are very patient, or a masochist.

It can be a little boring in the beginning learning how magic works ( as a irl magic player I knew it already, but you got coins for the tutorials so...) but it is explained really well for a beginner and Gideons storyline gives a more interesting approach than just basic tutorials. I do wish there were an choice i the beginning where you could choose if you where an already experienced player or a beginner though, but you can't have it all.
The gold earning in the game is fair for a F2P game with the possibility to buy coins if you WANT to.
5 coins for an easy opponent, 10 for a medium, 15 for a hard and 20 for a player vs player win (with the bonus of an extra 20 for your first win of the day against a player) on top of the quests and the gold you get from the storylines. I have never felt that I needed to buy coins, some diligent playing and deck building experience will make it easier to earn after a while. (It goes ALOT faster than heartstone in my opinion!!)
Some people say that the AI is sometimes too good even at easy, but as always in magic a good hand is a good hand no matter if you are an AI or not. It is a game of luck in some sense, as these games usually are.
So my final conclusion is: Magic Duels is better than no magic at all. And as a F2P I think it is an OK one! :)

BioShock 2 is a First Person Shooter sequel to BioShock, the second game was released  3 years after the original (Release date: Feb 9,  2010). The game feels very much like you've returned to the city "Rapture" for more game play, however events are taking place about 10 years after those that transpired in BioShock 1.

Welcome back to Rapture, please keep your arms, legs, and morality inside your big daddy suit the whole time and enjoy the ride! Jesting aside, this game is dark and twisted... which is what most people seem to love about it.
In this game you play as a "Big Daddy" (Basically the guy you see on the cover art, big armored behemoths) named Delta who is searching for his "little sister" (those little girls with the red demon eyes) named Eleanor.
Just like in the last game as you play you unlock new abilities, weapons, upgrades for your weapons, and ("force skills that require that blue stuff" Sorry, I can't help myself) Plasmids that require EVE to use. The game is very linear with no going backwards through levels, the game is rather challenging (unless you relish huge challenges, in that case this game is probably too passive for you. Basically the difference in difficulty is just how hard your enemies hit, not AI difficulty etc.)
Controls for this game are standard, the big difference between 1 and 2 is that you can keep more passive abilities called "Gene Tonics" active. There are a couple new weapons and a handful of new Gene Tonics.
The starting weapons are the same ones you had in BioShock1, I don't want to spoil any of the next weapons just know they're fun, but I tend to find myself sticking with the bread and butter weapons. There are new secondary ammo types, for several of the weapons. I won't lie, I really like setting traps.
It should be noted that I felt like I was playing in the exact same city, graphic-wise the whole city feels exactly the same with small changes. I don't like to talk about graphics in video games but for me this actually did feel like a continuation of the first BioShock Game.

There are three types of achievement categories in this game: single player main story, Multiplayer competitive, and DLC. At this time I'm still working on many of the achievements (12/17/14) I have a majority of the single player achievements, nothing unusual to report on these achievements. The multiplayer ones require playing until max online level, so that will be a bit of a grind, it is also oftentimes difficult to find people to play with (depends on the time of day). Lastly DLC achievements, which I have always felt is a cheap way to get more life out of a game. (Blame the sims3 and EA, okay? That's why I'm so cynical about paying for DLC. haha)

BioShock 2 is priced at $19.99, I acquired my copy from a Humble Bundle, so as usual I recommend getting the game on a steam sale or in a humble bundle. Since this is an old game, if you don't already own it I recommend waiting for a 75% off or better sale.
As far as quality is concerned, I have 14 hours in this game and about half of the achievements, I think it's close to a good buy if you're just playing through the game once, if you're going to play on a higher difficulty, or through the game multiple times this game is a very good quality.

Story = Awesome. Game Play = Effortless, natural and fluid to play. Achievements = Meh...could be better. Price = Fair. This game tends to appeal to people who like First person shooters and story games, with the addition of multiplayer it could appeal to the competitive crowd but there aren't nearly as many people actively playing.
I recommend this game for people who like darker stories, and tend to enjoy first person shooters, regardless of their difficulty. Rapture will warp your perceptions of "right and wrong"; as always, I've been impressed by the story.

Despite to rather rocky start, X Rebirth 2.0 and greater have fixed many of the issues that made the game unplayable. It is still not as diverse and vast as its predecessors in the X series but I have found the game enjoyable enough to play almost 500 hours in little over a year.
Starting with the graphics, they are satisfactory. Much of the gameplay will take place in the Albion Skunk's cockpit which allows you to look out at the beautiful galaxies and stunning spaceships which the X Series have never seemed to fail in impressing us. Then there is the staion/ship deck veiw... Although walking around in the many ships and station is really cool and the interiors are as great as the galaxies you get to admire, the people are somewhat unimpressive statues that come with one of three different faces. Although getting to walk amongst a station/ship's crew and interact face to face with a trader, the whole experience is lessened by the fact that the people look like they were taken straight from a 2004 pc game and just pasted into a 2013 one. Overall the exteriors/interiors, shadows and lighting are enough to make you overlook the fact that the NPC's are just so awful looking, however I still have a lot of fate that Egosoft will pull through and revamp the npc's appearance.
The campaign storyline is awesome! Fighting alongside the renements of  rebel forces against a massive power hungry corporation always scores big points in my book. Without giving too much away, I would like to just say that storyline introduces you to some fascinating characters (That still look terrible!) that only thicken the plot and further immerse you into the storyline. My favourite part is that you are no longer alone in  the vastness of space, you now have a copilot/partner?/Friend to enjoy space with. Though she is very similar to the other female npcs in terms of appearance (can be fixed using certain mods), she is actually quite comical in the campaign and actually a real good addition to the normally lonely universe we've grown use to in previous X games.
The ships and Stations you encounter and can buy/build will not disappoint you but I know one thing that will! You can't fly them...Any of them, you can dock and tell the captain to take you somewhere but thats as close to flying a capital ship as you will get. I do not mind such, personally I believe it is more realistic in not being able to pilot a capital ship. especially now that you get to hire members of your crew yourself. But I too have spent many hours flying my Thor in X Prelude and blasting Xenon to bits, its just so fun.
The music is okay, it isn't quite up to par with that which we listened to in X3 series but its still not bad, except for the bar music though. I hate the bar music (Did I forget you can visit a Bar while docked in a station?) The voice acting is okay as well though there is a lot of repeatitive dialogue amost NPCs but the small talk mini-game is fun to play when you really want something at a station.
The game as a whole has come a long way since its release, many features have been added (I've left out a lot, I might add them to my reveiw at a later date) and many of the bugs that resulted in crashing have been fixed. I have only had my game crash once since 2.0 and it may have been my fault as I was running a lot of other programs in the background. Despite the poor game rating and hundreds of negative reveiws this game has recieved during its intial release, it has become a VERY enjoyable game to play. There are still many things left to fix but given the amount of work that has been put into fixing and patching the game, my hopes are high.
To anyone looking to buy this game, it is well worth it at this point. There are many mods out there right now that fix many of the issues many people have ingame and some added new features or galaxies which helps keep the gameinteresting while the developers continue to patch and add features themselves. I recommend buy the Teladi Outpost DLC with the gam though, it adds several more ships and fractions that only add to the game as a whole.

A wonderfully cryptic story with a Madworld visual style that is unfortunately let down by less than stellar gameplay. The premise is simple but effective: piece together what has happened through notes and talking to mysterious figures (dead? alive? are you?!) while relying heavily on stealth. As with anything like this at first it all seems fun and simple enough to either sneak into position or wait for an enemy to move out of place but with the wide-open map and the imprecise routes this becomes incredibly tedious.
Furthermore you have factor in that the map does not reveal what areas you have visited, what items have been retrieved, place of note discovered and does not give you the option to place your own map notes in lieu of an automated system. This can be quite frustrating when you switch between the "light" and "dark" worlds (spoiler I guess?) and trying to keep track of where you've been becomes tiresome, especially if you find yourself returning to camp to heal and restock where needed.
Despite all that I would recommend at least giving this game a shot because it's strangely enchanting and I'm sure there's a diehard, old-school fanatic out there who has the patience to really enjoy the game for what it is. However there's just a few features missing that would make this game possible for someone like me.

A game about exploring, investigating, uncovering mysteries, with combat more or less as a side activity.
This review basically complements or simply adds to the hundreds of other reviews already posted.
The highlight of the game is the stories you uncover. Each wraith you meet can't remember what has happened or what is keeping them from resting in peace, and will at first only remember one thing that happened. For example one will only remember staring into the barrel of a gun, which will make you assume the wraith was murdered, until you uncover more clues and belongings which will help the wraith remember what happened and you will eventually realise that your assumptions of the events that took place are completely different from what actually happened. Your first impressions will never be correct. In fact, they will be far off. And this is what, to me, makes the game really shine.
There is no true horror in the game. The game will feel creepy for the first hour or so but after that you will realise this is not a horror game.
There is virtually no hand-holding or tutorial. There is a mysterious woman, also with amnesia, who has her own past she is trying to discover who will a few times direct your next move, which include assisting her in figuring out her own. The majority of the side stories also tie together to the main story line involving the said mysterious woman.
The combat is challenging at times but revolves around switching between weapon types for either faster firing or more damage for different enemies, while dodging their attacks.
Virtually no replay value however (unless you want to witness the ending again) as all investigations are recorded in a book so you can always read back at what the stories are, and there are no cinematics.
For $20, you may be wishing there to be more content, otherwise when the game goes on sale it is definitely worth a buy. Lots to do for 100% completionists out there too!

Full Review:
A first-person open-world-survival horror game set in the 17th Century New World presented in a bold monochromatic visual style. Is this refreshing recipe bound to succeed?
No intro, cutscene or voiceover explains what happened. I wake up on a beach. Everything is black or white (not even gray). On the horizon I see a wrecked ship, there is only one direction I can take: A small path leading into the island.
Soon I notice something red stand out in the monochromatic but serene looking dense forest of the island. Before I know it a Spanish conquistador with glowing red demonic eyes is out for my blood - his growl lets me know that he’s not really human anymore. Thankfully I have a bow and a knife to defend yourself.
After these first intense moments as well as an mysterious encounter with a woman in red, Betrayer got me hooked. Venturing out into the wilderness where I discover graves, handwritten notes or other clues and hints that tell me more about what happened on the island give me the feeling that I love the most when playing a new game. Exploring and getting to know a new and strange world.
Yet soon after I discover that Betrayer greatest strength lies somewhere else: After some events that I don’t want to spoil you encounter ghosts of deceased that speak in riddles.
These lost souls and their story unfold like little detective cases. You need to find evidence, murder weapons or remains of the ghosts to solve what lead to their demise. Their mostly terrible fates are not only well written and interesting, they also create an atmosphere of desperation and really makes you feel that the island is not a place you wanna stay for a longer time.
As interesting as these ghost mysteries are, as problematic is their integration in the gameplay. After figuring out how the game and the environment is set up, you are basically just running from clue to clue and fight every enemy that pops up in between. The game keeps the battle interesting by offering a good weapon roster like Tomahawks, Rifles and Crossbows - all with different attributes in the RPG side of the game. The combat encourages you to plan ahead a bit as stealth gives you an advantage and realistically long reload  times force you to rather switch weapons, but after a while it gets repetitive and there aren’t really a lot of different enemy types. The AI is not really challenging as most foes just chase you straight down once they see you.
All in all, Betrayer is a very interesting game that definitely tries new things in a refreshing scenario. The visual style, the writing as well as the gameplay mechanics are good and interesting, but combat and exploration gets repetitive after the first two areas and the horror subsides after you become familiar with the few enemy types. I still enjoyed my stay on the island and would like to revisit the place in a possible sequel with more refined mechanics.

The graphics are simply amazing, the greyscale style looks great, and if you don't want it in greyscale the saturation can be changed in options. The story is mostly told through the stories of ghosts, what the maiden in red tells you, and notes that you find. The game is open world, and while the world is split into maps, they're large maps with varied terrain, and there are treasure chests and buried treasure that gives a reason to explore, if the great scenery isn't enough. There are armored soldiers and stealthy natives patrolling the area, and stealth is a viable option if you don't want to run in guns blazing. The weapons are well designed and animated, with 2 flintlock guns, 2 bows, a crossbow, a tomahawk, and grenades, a nice break from the usual "pistol, SMG, rifle, etc.". The guns, bows, and crossbows can be bought in different qualities, and there are unique weapons with even better stats hidden around the maps too.
On each map there is a bell that moves you to a very atmospheric alternate dimension where you can talk to ghosts and try to solve some of the area's mysteries while fighting skeletons. There is a unique "listen" feature that helps you find clues, ghosts, and statues by making a sound near their location, which prevents the frustration of not being able to find the next clue.
Overall, definately worth buying.

Betrayer is full of betrayals (as one might expect), most of which are discovered in the course of playing through this intriguingly visual mystery first person adventure stealth shooter all the way to the end.
You awaken, shipwrecked on the shore of pre-colonial North America, the world around you rendered in vivid black and white with bare highlights of red. This art design decision works well to frame the story, but also describes the almost exclusively binary decisions you'll have to make in the game. You can change the visual settings if you wish, but I recommend playing at least once with the original settings.
Walking to the British colony to which you were traveling, you'll encounter hostile Spanish troops, and maybe catch a fleeting glimpse of the local natives who reportedly still populate this quiet land. There are also, other... things. Guttural sounds, glimpses through the underbrush. Something here is displeased at your presence. Best to keep moving.
Overall, the story is fairly muted within the gameplay. You can have frequent conversations with game characters, who offer cryptic clues to the story. Combat with the limited period weaponry is the same throughout the game, although you can find/buy better versions. A few useful items you discover allow you to sense things others cannot, almost mystically.
A HUD compass at the top middle of the screen shows your heading and any discovered locations in the current region. You can use a map to fast travel among them as well. This is very helpful as the game regions are all open and explorable. Many additional details can be found if you explore outside the beaten paths.
The sound design is excellent, as it must be since a crucial game mechanic relies on listening. To find clues, stop and use the “listen” key (once you've acquired the item that let's you hear things that others cannot).
When you “listen”, if there is anything to be heard, you'll hear a low sound from the direction of undiscovered items. On the compass' right and left edges will appear guides indicating if the sound is stronger from your right or from your left. It will make sense when you use it.
It can be easy to lose track of your purpose, but these are three things you should remember:
1 - Your journal is pretty thorough. Check it frequently.
2 - You can “listen” for locations of characters and hidden objects. This is crucial to resolving the story.
3 - You can ring the village bell to move from the daylight world to a world of twilight, each world having its own clues and mysteries, most of which all tie well together in the end.
The game's pace is deliberately slow and combat is infrequent unless you're careless. When you hear the howl of an enemy who has just discovered you, there are a few frantic moments as you look around trying to see from which direction the threat is approaching.
But that's about the height of “excitement” in this wonderfully atmospheric game. I took a chance on this game because it offered a fresh look, and it makes for an enjoyable few hours to pull the story bits together until the final betrayal. I'm glad I did as it's well worth trying.

When you get down to it, "Dead Rising 2" is nothing more than some dev studio's gameplay concept testing that had AAA graphics wrapped around it.
Really.
Maybe it's my fault for not doing my homework more thoroughly, but what I thought I was going to get and what I actually got were very different things. I was primed for a roaring trek through a zombie-filled city, where dispatching the undead was hilarious fun and the key to success. The actual game (when I finally got it to work) is a boring loop of backtracking through the same, small piece of real estate, where killing zombies borders on being an afterthought.
Maybe "Dead Rising 2" is supposed to be a parody of itself? I don't know. If there's a joke, I'm not getting it.
Anyway.
The idea of having a very tight time limit on the various goings-on is actually a great idea. It forces you to prioritize and creates a killer sense of tension. The realization that I'd have to find Zombrex for my kiddo, by myself, and on an actual deadline definitely got my attention.
The problem is that the thing you would think would be fun and central - taking out zombies - turns out to be boring, clumsy, and peripheral. Combat and associated movement is ponderous and awkward, with a high likelihood that you'll be grappled. There are HUGE delays between an attack animation and the next action, making fights feel walking through quicksand. Kills net you a miniscule amount of experience, and experience is only good for making you incrementally better at...getting kills. Weapons break very quickly, which makes the slog of weapon crafting (pick this up, set it down, pick up another thing, several-second cutscene, off you go) seem monumental after only a few go-arounds.
...and, as I said, it's peripheral. You don't get anything useful from zombie killing. You don't find anything to trade, which means that combat doesn't provide an alternate path to getting Zombrex for Katy. The zombies apparently respawn, which means that putting a large dent in the population fails to make getting around any easier.
Speaking of getting around: The real key to the game (other than the main missions) seems to be going out into the world and bringing folks back. Fair enough, I suppose, but the repetition is boggling. There's exactly one way in and out of the shelter, which means you're going to be seeing the same thing over, and over, and over, and over again while getting bogged down by zombies over, and over, and over, and over again. Once you find somebody, there follows an infuriatingly awkward sequence of trying to talk to them, such that they'll "join" you. The gaps in time between character thoughts being voiced (and anything happening) are so large that you could comfortably taxi a large aircraft through them...and sometimes, the "follow me" script won't trigger on the first attempt.
After only a couple of hours, I thought to myself: "If this is going to be the whole game, I think I'll do something else." As I said, the feel of the experience is that a few ideas for some open-world game elements were implemented without regard for how they fit together - and then somehow shipped as a complete product.
No, thank you.

Rebel Galaxy.
If anyone can look at pretty pictures like I can you would see that this is indeed a space game, somthing that a lot of Developers do wrong, very wrong. This however makes a very nice change of pace, you start in a old tech spaceship that has been fighting with engineers to keep going and with that being said you arrive in some questionable system thats located in the middle of nothing and make do.
The great thing about this game is making do is great fun, you can do the main story missons or go full pirate and talk trash down the communication system to the trader making him drop his load (no pun intended) and then sell it for some glorious credits and make your way up in the world, its such a simple system but as I said so many do it wrong, I could sit here all day and blow air into this games intake but I doubt I'll do myself any justice, so let's go over the pro and cons, please note I may be baised due to liking the game a lot!
~ PROS ~
~ Sandbox
~ Easy controls
~ Missions don't feel bland or boring
~ Ship design is very well done
~ The game looks glorious and the soundtrack doesn't make my ears bleed
~ Storyline keeps you interested and wanting to know more
~ There is a nice amount of weapons and upgrades
~ Recruit a wingman to help you ingame
~ CONS ~
~ No fleet management
~ Trading seems rather pointless
~ Reputation takes forever to build up
~ Simple shield and armor damage notifications - (Sometimes you will not notice you are taking hull damage)
If I'm being honest here I really can't think of any great cons, I mean this is a very good game for the price, there is easily 40 hours of content in this game and frankly theres not enough good single player spaceship games on Steam, this is a hidden treasure and if you don't buy it you are missing out.

This game is laughably amateur. It rides 100% on the controversial nature of its content, and even thats a let down.
Lets start with the gameplay. Its boring. Quite possibly the worst twin-stick shooter I think ive ever played. Aiming in both normal and precise mode are floaty and inaccurate. Instead of a line pointing where your aiming you have a cross hair. Guess the devs dont realize its not a FPS and come to think of it this game would be a lot better if it where. Sure you can get an aiming line (In precise mode as I call it) but thats even worse, so much so that I never used it. In this mode you hold down the trigger that moves the camera away from your character to the area ahead. However the aiming in this mode is very twitchy. Combine this with the fact that this almost always leaves you unable to see your character leaving him open for attack.
The environments are ok I guess and I do like the destructible buildings, but you only get a few grenades and those are even more inaccurate and jerky then the guns. They try to go for this Sin city look with the black and white graphics but thats boring and sometimes a hindrance to gameplay as in dark areas you get stuck on things that are hard to see. For example in the second level you have to escape a sewer being swarmed by cops and SWAT teams. But more often then not its hard to see your enemies and if you fall in the watter your dead. You have to run to vault over things and you cant run in the water. So that leaves you moving slow till you can find a spot that you can walk out of the water. All the while your getting shot up by extremely dumb and unrealistic AI.
And the AI is some of the most basic and dumb AI I think ive ever seen. Cops just rush you, with no thought of cover or tactics. A cop will run up alone and just start shooting you despite the fact youve got a shotgun and mowing down everything. The SWAT teams arnt any better as they take an unrealistic amount of damage and zerg rush you like the flatfoots do. And the civilian AI is even dumber than the cops, acting like mice locked in a box with a cat.
So in closing let me say this, the game has potential but its not worth the 20 bucks.  Full Disclosure I diddnt finish the game and am taking advantage of Steams new refund policy. Its an OK game but should be 5 bucks not 20.

Though a good first step for those looking to learn how to play, I will never recommend this to anyone. Not because I'm a butthurt loser, I am a noob after all, but because of a few LEGIT reasons.
1) The cards available are terrible. Yes, I get it you start off with the weakest or crappiest of the crap and normally work your way up (or if you understand how this game is supposed to be played you learn that a simple Child of Night can decimate with the proper setup) and that's not what I'm here to pick at. I'm here to point out how bullshet the AI is. Even on an Easy (yes, EASY) match up in a Solo Battle the AI is pulling bullshet card after bullshet card out of its asz. I was just on Easy testing out a new deck I built and this mofo plays 2 Ruin somethings that require 7 mana and have 7/5. ON FOKING EASY MODE! HOW IS THIS SUPPOSED TO BE EASY?! THIS IS THE MODE I CHOSE TO TEST SOMETHING OUT AND LEARN A FEW EXTRA THINGS. Playing cards like THAT should be reserved for a tougher difficulty, especially when the highest card I have is a 5/4 (including its ability mind you) and I only have 1 of them. I just shut off the game after it played those two cards because with what I have available to me right now, there was no hope in winning and I wasn't about to sit there and lose to a bullshet azpull like that.
2) Playing off of the above reason, online TCG are easily rigged. The system can easily give you a hard time while your opponent is getting everything he/she needs. AIs are even worse with the ability to draw whatever whenever, essentially rigging the game against (or for) the player in order to promote sales. This is all too common in online TCG which is why I personally prefer actual decks while reserving crap like this 'game' for learning new strategies or combos.
That first reason may sound like whining or complaining but it is a legit issue, yes we all know RNG is a ♥♥♥♥♥ but in a TCG where shuffling and drawing are supposed to be 100% luck rather than probability-generated, online will never work out. It's just too easy for the system to cheat or 'favor' one person over the other without ever being able to challenge it, since you don't ever get to pick up your deck and see what order it's currently in. I'm a noob as I said, but I'm not clueless nor do I have no skill or not know how to play. My friend is pretty dam good and a force to be reckoned with here on campus and if I can beat him on this 'simulator' due to random bs while he kicks my az irl with actual cards, there's something wrong here.

X rebirth in its updated state is by far one of the most interactive and approachable X game to date, no its not as complex nor does it have the same sense of customisation as previous titles but it is able to be picked up from the start without the need for large amounts of cash grinding or endless travelling back and forth through sectors as seen in previous titles.
Combat to is much more approachable as the controls feel much more responsive and streamlined to a point where you actually want to participate in fights rather than just rely on the autopilot.
Trading and empire management are the defining elements of any X game and whilst rebirth had a rocky start and still has a few problems rebirth by far has the best trading system to date. once trades have been unlocked all available trades can be accessed through the one screen and available ships can quickly be swapped to as needed, additionally trade requests can be qeued up to be conducted automatically (autonomous trading mods are available to bring back stuff like galactic traders)
The most important thing to note is that rebirth has a live economy which is generated on your pc (not some silly cloud computing) meaning that blowing up trading vessels or stations can have a big impact on the economy (without SETA however this can take real human hours to notice), additionally trades are conducted automatically between stations within each zone through the use of mass traffic (no its not just FPS eye candy).
Stations too have improved apon the old complex system getting rid of the spidersweb of stations seemingly linked together through a bunch of string with individual parts of the station being assigned to raw materials (e.g steel plates) final products (e.g drones) or effeciency improvements with the option for station defences to be constructed (so you no longer need a fleet to protect your stations.
All of this can understandably cause a few problems (my game for example loves to chew almost 8gb of RAM) or result in some tradeoffs (First person mode is not all that exciting after awhile) but for a game that tries to achieve the best of both worlds (space shoot em up and economics management) Egosoft did (and is still doing through regular updates) a pretty good job and where it feels lacking you can often find a solid mod to help you out.
In conclusion Rebirth is really a game that depends on your tastes, if you just want to shoot stuff with lite trading elements try Elite dangerous or if you want a full on space trading sim try picking up x3 Terran conflict. But if you want something a little more involved that isn't too steep a learning curve then give rebirth a shot

Rebel Galaxy... Bought it because of the soundtrack in the trailers... Took a gamble and hoped it would give me some entertainment... Man was I surprised...
Sooo.... Breaking it down:
1. You will feel like a frikking space cowboy.
2. Music so damn good that you want the soundtrack in every possible format.
3. The sheer size of this game is just shocking! Did NOT expect that when I started it.
4. Broadside battles between two large spaceships might be the coolest thing ever.
5. BROADSIDES!!!! (It´s so damn cool I had to mention it twice!).
6. Voice actors are actually kind of good for a game thats not a AAA.
7. Did I mention broadsides?
8. Simple, but complex.
9. One bug, ONE(1!), found during my entire playthrough. EA, Bethesda, Bohemian and just about everyone else, LOOK AT THESE GUYS AND LEARN!!! It was not even a gamebreaking bug! All it did was made me crash into a station after warp and my ship autodocked, which I had planned to do anyway so the bug actually made me save some time since I didn´t have to "slowboat" all the way after warp.
Downsides then? Yeah a few actually, but many of them is just me being picky.
1. Game gets repetetive after a while and considering how many ships there is you may just finish the story halfway through the ship line.
2. Main story line is waaay to easy.
3. Considering it´s a space game, you may actually believe there would be free flight in all directions... like up and down... but nope! ship stays leveled and all you need to think about is right, left, back and forward... However this is forgiven thanks to the awesomeness of broadside battles.
4. Soundtrack makes this game, without it (sometimes the music stops) it just feels empty.
5. Characters kind of lacked depth and you probably won´t get too attached to them.
Despite the downsides I still give this game a solid 7/10. It has the right "feel" to it and It´s absolutely one of those "If this gets a sequel, the devs will get it all right" kind of game.

It's Hearthstone and Final Fantasy Tactics rolled into one. Gameplay is fun and balance updates occur frequently which is a blessing and a curse. On one hand, overpowered strategies are made fair in a timely manner, but on the other, cards that take a long time to earn (or were bought using real money) are nerfed or changed. I can see why someone would get mad at that, but I don't personally mind. I started playing, on and off, very early in the game's development and as such, I developed a good collection of cards. It takes a while to earn really powerful cards and losing to rare cards in ladder can be frustrating. Pulling a legendary in a pack or earning the shards to craft one is extremely rewarding, however.
This game, in my opinion, is a little bit niche and won't appeal to everyone. If you're into card games like MtG and Hearthstone and like strategy games like Poxnora or Final Fantasy Tactics, I'd recommend giving this a try. Just don't expect to win all your games if you don't spend a lot of time grinding or using money.

Summary: Explore colonial America and uncover mysteries behind strange going-ons.
Type of game: Think Skyrim crossed with a murder mystery.
Pros:
- Great atmosphere.  Great use of sound as well. You really feel like you are in the place the game puts you in.

Cons:
-- There is a map in the game but it in no way updates when you find things. It also doesnt let you make notes on it. This is my single biggest complaint. Overall the game is really good. It has just a few issues that could be easy enough to make it better. But it is a good game worth your time.
I would give it a 7.5 or so as it stands.

Well, I bought this on a whim, but it turns out, money was never better spent.
All in all, I would defintely recommend it to anyone who's wanted to fly their own starship in a mostly lawless zone. If you've ever played Tachyon: The Fringe, you're going to love this game.
I know that quite a few might be turned away due to the thing's lack of vertical flight. Put simply, the lack of a vertical axis isn't a drawback - it's a feature. The kind of ships you'll be in charge of, you won't need a vertical axis.
I'll list out the good stuff and the bad. Hopefully that'll help.
The Good:-
1) Low-cost title that plays like a AAA game.
2) Fast-paced and simple to learn.
3) Quirky in many aspects.
4) Great soundtrack, with an obvious inspiration from Firefly.
5) Very nice ship design, and a used-up feel that's surprisingly cozy.
The Neutral:-
1) Star-systems aren't particularly unique, but the graphical detail and insanity offsets that to quite some extent.
2) Trading and Mining are viable alternatives to a kill-em-all blitz, but it can be boring or tedious after a point.
3) Fairly interesting characters, but their full potential was never realised.
4) Cash is something weird - either so much that you don't know what to do, or too little, resulting in you getting outgunned.
5) Mercenaries are a nice touch, but again - like the main characters - not realised to their full potential.
The Bad:-
1) Some missions can be hilariously broken, and tougher than they look, which can cause hair-pulling at times.
2) Rather short single-player campaign.
3) Can be slightly boring after a certain point, though not too bad.
4) No further development on this title, it would seem. Hopefully there'll be more on this after some time.
Definitely give it a try. You won't regret it!

I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream is a point and click that was released on Halloween in 1996. The game is based off of the post-apocalyptic short story of the same name by Harlan Ellison, which was first published in 1967. It is classified as one of the top ten most reprinted stories in the English language, and it is highly acclaimed. It's also noteworthy that Harlan himself voices the antagonist in the game, a computer called AM.
The plot of the story takes place 109 years after the destruction of human civilization, which was caused by the escalation of the Cold War into a full blown world war. The three warring nations, Russia, China, and the United States, had all built super computers which were put in charge of running the war; as they were deemed more efficient at the task. The computers were referred to as AM, which originally stood for Allied Mastercomputer, then later Adaptive Manipulator, and finally Aggressive Menace. One of the computers eventually became self aware and absorbed the other two, and then carried out the mass genocide of humanity; save four men and one woman.
The final survivors of the human race, Gorrister, Benny, Nimdok, Ted and Ellen, are housed in a seemingly endless underground personal hell. The master computer, AM, harbors an immense hatred for all human kind, and has spent every available moment for the last 109 years torturing the poor souls that he 'spared' from the mass genocide. He not only has kept them from committing suicide, but he has made them nearly immortal over the years, thus allowing them to survive for such a long period of time.
Throughout I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream, it is your duty to get each of the five survivors to the end of their scenario without letting them die, commit suicide, or otherwise make a wrong decision that could end up ending their scenario early. If the character dies or commits suicide, the scenario ends and you must begin again; if they end up making a wrong decision, it will have an effect on the ending that you will receive. There are multitudes of endings available, although some of them are very similar; you have a chance for the best, worst, and bad endings.
The game has a disturbing, morose atmosphere that is carried by an overall darkened setting throughout each scenario. From the inside of a grungy airship, to a remote forest inhabited by a tribe that sacrifices its people to AM, to a Nazi war camp in 1945, each character has their own distinct setting, with many gruesome discoveries to be made. However, what makes the game truly disturbing is the thought of actually being kept alive and tortured for over 100 years, and the effect that it would have to have on the human psyche. It would be a living hell, wherein you ultimately forget that there ever was anything else, questioning reality and if you had perhaps actually died and gone to hell. Coupled with the haunting knowledge that we are, as a society, getting closer every year to creating such advanced technology, the idea behind I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream should be more spine-tingling now than it was 40 some years ago.
While many people in the forums have stated that they've ran into bugs and glitches that have prevented them from finishing the game, I had no such issues during my four hours with the title. The most that happened for me was the background music stopping entirely, which was a shame since the musical score is incredible for its time period. I also somehow managed to unlock the debug screen during Nimdok's scenario... which was weird, but not game destroying.
Overall, I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream is a solid horror point and click, which was ahead of its time in 1996. The atmosphere is dark, lonely, and grim. It does a great job of conveying the sense of dread and loneliness that each of the characters experience, and the idea of the main plot will really linger in the recesses of your mind for a while. Harlan Ellison even wrote most of the in-game dialogue, and coauthored this expanded storyline. However, I do not find this title better than other horror point and clicks of the same era, namely Sanitarium. If you have a choice of only one or the other, I would go with the latter. For the true horror fan though, I still recommend this title for its capability to truly haunt the human mind.

I enjoy this a bit more than Civ 5.  While on the surface, it is mostly a re-skinning of Civ 5, if you look deeper, there is more.
--  There is now a reason to NOT research a given tech, aside from it not being immediately useful.  The path you take in the tech tree influences how the neighbors see you, as the affinity points are representative of how you live on the new world.  The story line, as it were.  The affinity and story line also limit which win scenarios are available.
--  The change in how espionage is handled affords players some protection from what before was just walking up and stealing tech.
--  The military unit system is more streamlined, no more finding that when you get gunpowder in Civ 5, you lose the advantage of those nice ranged archers and forces other things to be obsolete.  You keep you unit class, and all of them get upgraded, no need for that one Wonder which upgrades units in the previous Civ games.  Additionally you get to CHOOSE the boons.
--  The quest / storyline events also allow for customization of buildings.
In all, I say this is a Reskin of Civ 5 mixed with a bit of Endless Space, and this other online non-steam game I can't remember the name of where once a day you make a decision about an issue and that decides the majority of how your nation develops.

Hatred has caused quite a few waves within the mainstream media. People have called it everything from a political statement to absolute proof of the degeneration of society. While there were a few cinematic executions that I found pretty cringe-worthy, most of the game is spent too far in the sky to discern much of the destruction happening down in the isometric hellscape that “The Antagonist” is intent on creating. Hatred certainly has its strong points, such as destructible environments. However, it also falls short on basic things like dialogue. Some lines are so cheese-covered that I’m going to need some nachos before finishing this review. The variety of objectives is lackluster, but if you go into Hatred with the idea that it really is just a brainless isometric shooter, it can easily work its charm on you. Is it worth the massive amount of hype? Let’s take a deeper look at Hatred.
The first thing you will notice as you burst into the streets will probably be the smooth gunplay, followed closely by the fact that AI civilians are extremely stupid. As you fire your assault rifle many will flee, some will cower, and a few will run directly towards the barrel of your weapon. This is a bit of a positive note, since the only way to recover health is to execute the injured, and the police are extremely determined to end your killing spree. As you advance through the game you will take down local cops, SWAT teams, and the army. There are only five weapons and three grenades to pick from unfortunately, and this along with lack of enemy variety hurts the replayability. I’d love to face down a tank with an RPG, but it never happened. Antagonist, I am disappoint. Hatred does have its fair share of clipping and optimization problems. The plot and execution are far from being innovative. The Antagonist is the antithesis of likeable or believable, but somehow even with its blemishes, underneath is a wonderfully built game.
The monochrome aesthetic is extremely effective here. Red and blue are the only real colors, which keeps Hatred from feeling too real. This might be a negative for some, for me it’s a definite positive. Sounds are extremely realistic, from firing a gun to pleas for mercy. The lines for The Antagonist are cheesy, but delivered well. There’s not a lot a voice actor can do with a script like this one. The game is extremely difficult even on normal mode, you get a respawn for completing side-objectives. While these do help a ton, if you die during the level’s main objective, you will be forced to start the entire level over. I enjoy the level design a whole lot, and if you don’t like something in the level, you can simply blow most of it up! Grenading your way through the side of a building and opening fire on anyone inside is extremely gratifying.
I won’t attempt to take the supposed moral high-ground, as I play games with a similar amount of violence almost daily. Hotline Miami, Grand Theft Auto, Postal… Hell, even the fatalities in Mortal Kombat are far more gory than anything this game offers. If you feel bad about shooting civilians, let the police shoot you without reason (and they will) so you can feel justified. The only reason this game was awarded an AO rating and effectually ostracized from console gamers is simply due to lack of corporate ties, and maybe some marketing that was a bit too good. I don’t hesitate to say that Hatred doesn’t live up to the hype, but that doesn’t make it a bad game by any means. Firefights are a lot of fun, especially when you keep shooting the door jamb and expanding the hole. Overall Hatred is worth a look for anyone who enjoys isometric shooters and a touch of gore. Big thanks to Destructive Creations for the review copy, I hope you guys will continue to get under the skin of the mainstream gaming industry for a long time to come.

There is nothing on the market that delivers the kind of experience you get from this game. Tiny & Big screams “Indie” but in a good way, from the memorable soundtrack, the visuals that are stylised that of a graphic novel, innovative and unique gameplay, and somewhat shallow, yet still enjoyable story.
The graphic novel style was flawlessly executed, the open and bright areas to enclose dark ones, the art style never fails to deliver. The striking Central American/Eastern European Jazzy soundtrack fits in seamlessly with the story, setting the mood, while the addictive gameplay grabs you.
The slicing, pulling and rocketing is an interesting mechanic, which gives you unrivalled flexibility to alter the world around you. Since almost every part can be manipulated, it gives new meaning to “the world is your playground”, as you can choose the linear path outlined by the developers created for you and drag a block here and cut a block there or have steer off track entirely and explore and be creative. This is where this game shines, but unfortunately, the clunky controls will prove somewhat frustrating at the best of times.
If you take this game in pieces, you’ll enjoy every aspect of it. The incredibly simple story gains a surprising amount of depth, especially towards the end where you will find a surprisingly pleasant discovery. Overall, the Tiny & Big delivers an entertaining and refreshing experience that certainly overpowers the control issues and the occasional feeling of tedium.

Luckily I didn't have to go far until I figured "huh, why not this one?"
The start of the game, or the "training" intro, almost threw me from continuing any further.  The gameplay was fine, it was the color scheme that I didn't care for.  It pits you inside of Tiny's gameboy so the levels are all lime green a la the games of yester on the 80's/early 90's hardware.  I wasn't impressed.  But I pushed through and boy was I glad I did.  Only in the training mode does it look drab.  When you get out of it and into the actual game, there is a wonderful palette of desert colors as you are in such an environment.  The exteriors are wind-blown sandstone and other various browns and the insides of temples are darker much as you'd expect given the lighting differences.
Above all this is a physics game.  Aside from moving and jumping, you have three actions available to you--the rocket, the cutter and the grappling hook.  The cutter will cut through anything much like the lasers in movies.  This enables you to chop down even the mightiest towers into pieces.  Some pieces are huge and others small and in order to move them you either throw a rocket on them to propel them or grapple them to pull them.  In this effect, you can create your own stairs or literally cut your own ramp system out of mountain sides in order to progress through the game.
The music is awesome and catchy and each time you find a cassette tape it will start a new track and then create a longer list loop.  Given the concentration with some of the puzzles, even skipping tapes is fine because your mind is focusing more on what you are doing than what music is playing.  Still, when I saw a tape I went out of the way to collect it because they did a good job for music selection.
My only complaint is that the game is rather short.  Do they make up for it with gameplay and variety?  Absolutely.
I've played four-ish hours at the time of this review and I've only gotten a handful of achievements.  If you are a completionist I can easily see this game giving you a lot more play time for your buck, especially if you refuse to watch youtube solutions.
TL;DR
Great game to keep your brain sharp and to have some fun making pieces of levels fly all over.  Well worth the price; a must buy on sale.

After playing the first two games in the BioShock series and starting the third, I can honestly say I like 2 more.
BioShock 2 managed to fix the clunkiness of its predecessor when it comes to shooting. It allows iron sights, which is awesome, and quick plasmid usage. The way this works it you have a weapon on your main hand and plasmid on your off hand at the same time. The variety of plasmids is also cool. The customization of BioShock games never cease to amaze me. Whether you want to be big badass Delta with a drill and offensive plasmids, or take a more subtle approach with the spear gun and stealthy plasmids, Bioshock 2 can provide such an experience.
This game decided to simplify hacking. Instead of having to play a puzzle minigame like in BioShock, you now need to land the hack needle on green or blue zones, green successfuly completeing hack while blue doing the same plus giving a free item. The Research system was overhauled. Instead of taking pictures of the target to gain research, now you have to video tape them. To get the best possible research, one must kill the target using a mixture of weapons, plasmids, npcs or security bots.
I don't understand why people don't like the story of BioShock 2. Though it doesnt follow Jacks life, which was clearly ended at the end of BioShock, its still pretty interesting.
BioShock 2 does a great job in keeping the experience atmospheric, just like in the first game.
This game is better than the first one. If you like any of the above features, its a must have.

Notes: I am reviewing the vanilla X-Rebirth, without any modifications at all. I must do this in order to baseline the review, at the time of the writing the release is 3.5 - and rumors are another bugfix patch inbound soonish. Which the game frankly needs.
After playing close to 22 hours in X-Rebirth, I can honestly say I do not recommend buying it if you are an adult, unless you have PLENTY of time to kill; This could be great for a younger teenager with plenty of time to spare, I'd have loved it back in the 90's.
Like many other people who have played prior X games, I heard the negative comments. I ended up buying it anyway. I don't really regret the purchase, but I realize now one of the biggest obstacles for me is the feeling like I am going to get anywhere with this game.  Everything takes too long, and with no way to speed it up, I just don't see myself finishing anything in this game.
90% of my 22 hours invested has been flying around, not really fighting, not trading, not even really having fun playing. You could I suppose call it "exploring", but that really isn't what it is. You have wormhole like paths you can take that do speed up your travel, but that is riding on rails like many racing games. It definately feels like artificially slow flying, and the empty space between objects makes this "exploring task" just boring, even using the highway system (wormhole like paths) barely improves upon this problem.
You do have the option of using something called boost. With boost, it allows you to spend your shielding for a very short burst of speed. The trouble with that of course is that without shield, you take hull damage from enemies. So you can't always justify using the only real protection your bubble encased ship has, just to go faster, especially since enemies are almost always right around the corner, even if we forget the fact that the boost does not last very long at all.
I can't fathom the design decisions behind the amount of time this takes, its almost like the developers didn't play the game at the speed we are.  I'm unhappy with my purchase, but enough positives exist that I will likely continue playing it. The gameplay at its core is not flawed beyond repair, for example, the combat missions can be pretty enjoyable, if you can find them. And that is really why I can't recommend this game. It requires SO much exploring that you don't get to really think, trade, build, or fight.

long story short: being able to play magic for free is great.
Positives: MTG can be a very expensive hobby, i know from experience. This game gives you the ability to collect cards and play them completely for free. unlocking cards by simply playing magic is great value. Especially so for players who are new to the game, players without the financial capability to play magic on paper or on MTGO, or players who don't live near a FNM gamestore. Other positives are the casual gameplay, and the sleek design compared to MTGO.
Now the negatives however: The game has bugges. It's out for quite some time, and a number of bugs simply haven't been fixed. There are connectivity errors, causing you to lose coins or sometimes even boosters you buy. The coins are deducted from your account, but the boosters are simply not awarded. I'd say this has happened to me around 3-5 times in the 50+ hours i've played. Another problem I have with the game is the lack of communication between players. There is no chat. This is bothersome in 1v1, but simply mages 2 headed giant unplayable. You can't ask your teammate what they're planning to do, who is going to attack and block, etc.
However what made me recommend this game is the fact that I've contacted customer service about the boosters i didn't get awarded, and within 3 hours they contacted me back and refunded me the coins I lost. I found this to be decisive in giving the game a positive review. Also, the ability to play MTG for free is great. If the bugs are fixed in upcoming patches, it could be a truly great game.

If any video game deserves to be remastered Bioshock certainly does.
So how does the remastered version fare?
Initial impressions were mixed. Graphical and frame rate/animation improvements are very good.Couldn't get surround sound working unitl I changed settings in Bioshock to 7.1 and switched my soundcard (HT Omega Claro) to 8 channels which now gives surround - (not quite correct surround but it is giving enemy locations in a 360 degree arc) Some audio does repeat,specifically the audio logs on some occasions which it never did in original Bioshock.The sound is still good and it's not a game breaker but if it worked before,why is it broken now in the remaster?
The visual and gameplay overhaul I like.The enviroments IMO look the best they ever have and the increase in frame rate actually improves the gameplay ALOT.
However,speaking of the gameplay experience for Remastered Bioshock the first game crash causing me to restart the PC was when I opened the map via my controller.Their is also a delay now when you click to open the map where their wasn't in OB so another introduced flaw into the remastered version.
The other troubles with crashing so far seem to be related to the save game feature.Manual saving can on occasion cause Bioshock to crash which also results in that save game being wiped.Relying on the auto save is also a bad idea as it seems to only save at the beginning of each new level and this has caused a crash also on random occasion.
If 2K games can resolve this instability with the save game causing crashes and fix the audio bugs and Bioshock Remastered is an essential recommend however the gameplay experience is unfortunately lessened by the remaster in it's current state.Having to stop and save every couple of minutes breaks the immersion and flow that the game now offers with the smoother gameplay.That being said it is still enjoyable so if you are going to buy it be prepared to save every 3-5 minutes and use at least 3 different save files and don't overwrite the autosave.
2K games,Bioshock is one of the best video games ever created but these crashes and bugs are not doing your product,your name or your potential sales much good , especially when you are calling the product a 'Remaster'..Hope to see this improved.
As a side not : the inclusion of the Bioshock museum I think is cool and the and the interviews with the game dev's have been interesting also so good job on value adding their 2K.
Final verdict : Even with some audio bugs and the save every 2 minutes scenario this is the best Bioshock has ever been and comes recommended.

A bit simplistic, yet a very fine game, inside the limits of features, declared in its description.
The in-game list of occupations consists of wondering the forests in the real plane and somewhat like a beyond-the-grave one, looking for items and clues you need to reveal what had happened here before you showed up, talking to the ghosts and shooting the undead and hostile spectres. A nice blend, i'd say. And completely corresponding to what was promised - an FPS action, an adventure and a horror game in one piece.
The set of monsters is poor, and the story-telling is a bit too schematic, besides you could think in the beginning that the game's world is too empty for a nice one. Skip the latter, as you will get enough mobs and skirmishing soon. As for the first too faults - it's an indi game, besides, all the little it does have has been made perfectly. Nice picture, fine controls, exhilarating fast-pased fighting, scary undead guys(ones in the beyond-the grave plane at least).  I don't remember myself paying so much emotional reaction to the undead from games or movies since distant times when i first visited the Crypt of Inubis and other places, inhabited by walking skeletons and zombies in Gothic 2 (for those who remember that feeling). So images, sounds and a bad habit to show up suddenly of the undead are quite all right here, scary enough to feel good :).
Maybe the way the undead look and sound here are the main dignities of the game, disguising all it's lacks, they're definitely more than worth seeing and hearing for those who seek that kind of show.
Not sure about the game's high replayability though, yet i've had a lot of what i wanted from a horror game during my first play through, and gonna try it another time later.

Внутриигровой набор занятий состоит из блуждания по лесам в реальном и потустороннем плане, поиска предметов и улик, необходимых для расследования предшествовавших появлению в этом мире игрока событий, разговоров с привидениями и стрельбы по нежити и злым духам. Короче, неплохая смесь.
В целом наблюдается полное соответствие списку: экшен от первого лица, адвенчер и хоррор.
Бестиарий несколько скудноват, и подача истории немного схематична, к тому же в начале игровой мир может показаться несколько излишне для хорошей игры пустоватым. Но последнее больше кажется, основное время игры будет достаточно плотно забито стычками с противником, а в рамках заявленных составляющих, с учетом того, что это инди проект, все сделано на отлично. Картинка красивая, управление удобное, стрелять весело, нежить жуткая(та которая в потустороннем плане). Насчет эмоционального восприятия последней - не помню, чтобы что-то из игровой или кинематографической нежити производило на меня такое же сильное впечатление со времен первого посещения мной склепа Инубиса и прочих пещер и углов с серьезной нежитью Готике2, если кто в курсе о чем речь. С качеством образов, озвучкой и внезапными появлениями у нежити тут все в полном порядке, положенную жуть наводит :).
Пожалуй изображение и озвучка нежити в потустороннем плане и есть главное достоинство игры, перекрывающее все ее недостатки, там реально есть на что посмотреть и что послушать по этой части.
Не уверен насчет реиграбельности, но на первый раз точно не жалуюсь, и наверно потяну второй.

I did all this after some trial and error, and noticing occasional lag or dropped frames despite no other games having issues.  As soon as I disabled in-game Vsync most of my performance issues went away, I turned the rest off since they were all set in NV Control Panel.
Only gripe is not being able to transfer or use save games from the original BioShock.  Would be nice to not have to start over and have just a save point where I can pick up.  Oh well, didn't hurt enough to not recommend, so far it's been a fun playthrough :)
