Well, just finished my first game of this, so I figured it was time for a review. So, where to start?
Well, I'll start basic. This game is basically what it looks like: a space trucker sim with combat that is similar to the ship-to-ship combat in Assassins Creed: Black Flag, with the primary weapons being broadside cannons and turrets. If you've heard that this game starts out kinda crappy, you heard right. The starting ship (a Hammerhead called the "Rasputin") is exactly what the intro cinematic says it is: a near-derelict ship with lousy hull & shielding, and the cannons are more akin to pop guns than actual weapons.
But that's the whole point, isn't it? You build yourself up by killing baddies, taking quests, maybe mining some, although I personally avoided mining as much as I could in this game. (Too boring.) The idea is to earn enough cash so you can spend it on upgrading your ship's weapons, shields and armor to the point that enemies that once gave you a mountain of trouble will now regret ever♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥you off... right before their ships explode and you suck up whatever cargo they dropped.
[As an extra note, some games may think it's cool to have increased prices for purchases, lowered prices for sales. Not this one! Here, if you purchase a turret for 5,000 credits and then decide to sell it later (possibly because you'd just picked up a better version), you'll still receive 5,000 credits back. Same goes for hull, shield, and engine upgrades.]
And of course you'll want to swap out your starting ship for a better one as quickly as possible. One with more turret slots, more broadside cannons, more cargo space, and a better hull. You'll also want to purchase some special components for your ship, like Heat Management which reduces the amount of heat your turrets generate when firing, allowing them to fire more often.
Which brings me to weapon setups. When it comes to setting up your strategy, your first perrogative will be to find a setup which works for you. Personally, I ran with Tachyon broadsides for their fast rate of fire, Heatseekers for secondary weapons, and my turret of choice was the Pulse variant for their range & damage per shot, although I do recommend equipping a Korian Viridian laser cannon if you happen to find one. (I managed to find two, one a Mrk 2, the other a Mrk 5 late in the game.)
Your second concern will be learning how best to maneuver in a high-tension battle. This is a 2D arena, so you won't have to worry about capital ships hitting you from above or below. But fighters will swarm around you, attempting to knock out your shields so their bigger cousins can finish you off. And by the way, your shields deplete based on which side gets hit, meaning that if you take too many hits to starboard, your starboard hull will be exposed and vulnerable; take too many hits to starboard after that, you're a goner. Oh yeah, I've had a couple of deaths where the shields were still strong on everywhere except where the enemy was currently hitting me en masse.
Here's my pro strategy though: when engaged in a pitched battle, move out to the sidelines to draw the fighters away and have your turrets take those out first. After which, you'll want to position yourself so the capital ships will be on only one side at a time. Then throttle down so that you can turn faster as needed. Just keep fire broadsides at them while your turrets provide backup, and when your shields on that side start to lose their charge, turn around so the other side will be facing them and then repeat the procedure.
However, there is something I should mention: up until the third star system, your main obstacle is pirates who fire nothing but regular rounds and missiles at you. Once you get to the third system, however, you'll meet the Greel. These guys (both their fighters and their capital ships) feature Leech weapons which fire EMP missiles at you. And these things  not only do a good amount of damage to your shields, but they do a number on your engines as well. So your best bet is to get the EMP Ablation component (what the hell kind of word is that?) so that EMP weapons won't cause quite as much trouble.
Nevertheless, a well-upgraded ship can handle just about anything. Just find the style and setup that works best for you and get out there. Just remember if things start to go♥♥♥♥♥♥up, there ain't no shame in making a run for it. All the money in the galaxy won't comfort you if you're dead.
As the game itself, it's single player only and can be played offline if you please. Although you won't be able to make progress on achievements without being online, I found out. Also, the musical tracks they used in this game, while good, can get really repetitive; I ended up muting it. And if there's one gameplay feature I'm iffy about, it's that the best lasers in the game (the Korian Viridians) are random drops, no way to purchase them in a spaceport.
There's also the issue with communications with the npcs in the game: they're pretty limited. Not to mention that the pirates seem to have trouble realizing when they're outmatched and that surrender would be in their best interest. Like I'll be flying an Arcturus-class Destroyer (which is strongly reminiscent of the Imperial Star Destroyer from Star Wars) armed to the teeth with top-notch weapons and they'll still be talking♥♥♥♥♥♥.. right up until I blow them to smithereens.
And speaking of the AI, there's the escort missions. Now, the way it works is that you fly to a location, approach the client, and hold down E to Pair Warp. What that does is that the AI takes full control of your ship, keeping it alongside the ship even as you two go into warp. Noble in itself but it can lead to some annoying results. For one, when two ships are alongside each other, a human would say that the best course of action is to throttle down and turn right to line up with the client; the AI meanwhile turns your ship left, causing your back section to collide with the client's. And why is it that every escort mission has to start in an asteroid field or a ice field? Because just now I had a mission start in an ice field, I was flying a dreadnaught and it took 5-10 minutes just to get started! The AI kept maneuvering us around the ice field, taking me one direction him another. And just when I thought we were getting out of this mess, it had the client move back into the field, prolonging this mess. I had to break warp pairing, and move my ship out of the ice field myself just to get us going.
Was I annoyed by all of this? Yeah, I'd say it goes without saying that I was.
Then there are the missions where you fly in and save someone from enroaching hostiles. There's a good chance they'll get themselves blown up because they decided to fly into the middle of a pack of hostiles. And as Harrison Ford said in The Last Crusade "Are you crazy?!? Don't go between 'em!!"
All in all though, it's a good game, well-worth the asking price. Combat can get a little challenging at times (especially with the Greel I mentioned above) but it's easy to learn & of moderate difficulty to master, just the way I like it. And if all that wasn't enough, the developers also made sure to include a risk analysis for each mission that adjusts based upon anticipated enemy strength against that of your own. And while not all the ship designs are prize-winners, there are some really good ones.
So yes, I definitely recommend this game. It's cheap, it's challenging, and it'll last a long time. Hell, there're some triple-A titles that won't last as long as this game will! [cough, cough... Star Wars Battlefront: EA... cough, cough]

Betrayer is a game you might want to play. If you see it on sale and you want a very aestheticly pleasing game to look at while you wander it's game world, this might be a good pickup for you. Otherwise ...
I'll give you the bad, then the good.
Story. I've played games without a narrative, and that's fine. I've played games with a narrative so tight you can see the stitching between characters. That's fine as well. And then there's Betrayer. If you've ever wanted to ask "Just how many people in a small community would wake up and straight up murder each other over super petty things, when their survival really depends on them working together as a community to build a better life..." Oi. Just ... don't expect the stories or Story in Betrayer to stick with you in a good way. There's ONE. ONE, that I felt a little feels for during the reading, and that's only because it was an actual Tradgedy involving parents losing a child. Every single other story, including the main one which is meant to explain the weird shazz going on, is just a damned soap opera set in the 17th Century.
****Spoliers****
Do you want to hear about how a young woman was hunted, tied to a stake, stripped naked and had her throat slashed by her father? Because you will. Do you want to learn about how it was necessary to lure someone you considered a friend and companion out to the woods and cave their skull in with a rock? You will. Do you want to come to understand that pretty much everyone's husband or wife cheated on them with everyone else's husband and wife? Sure thing!
Now, do you want all this presented in bland, voiceless text which emphasizes not the emotional gravity of each ghost's story, but only serves to distance you from the terrible, soulful tale of how they killed a man... over an insult... but they're not sorry... except they are.... when it turns out the worman they burned at the stake wasn't a witch but the man who burned her at the stake did so to keep his adultery a secret from his wife whom I believe was killed by the woman who was accused of being a witch or something honestly the whole thing blurs together.
That's the kind of thing the individual Ghost Stories you find during the game are based on. It's like the ships of settlers were just chock full of rapists, adulterers, and psychopaths. Seriously, one of the stories is just flatly stated to be "We saw a native girl one day. Thought she was pretty. So we♥♥♥♥♥♥♥her then killed her. Now I'm all confused, and a ghost, because her brother found out, came and found us, then shanked us until we stopped moving."
What the sweet grassy knoll?
The ending is no better. I actually made it a point not to check any guides or sites which would spoil the ending. I did everything properly. Found all the notes. Uncovered all the stories, found all the graves, gave every Ghost their name back, freed EVERY spirit. Gave the Maiden in Red a decent, hopeful response every time I needed to make a dialogue choice.
The game ends the same way. No matter what you do. Free the sister. Talk to the Maiden. Oops. it was her all along. Bam, back to the ♥♥♥♥ing shadow world with you.
BuuuuullllllllShit.
There is no reason what so ever to give interactive dialogue choices if they don't affect the story in any way. Doing so is a giant finger to anyone who's ever played a story based RPG or non-linear branching path game. Betrayer bills itself as neither, that's true, but to insert a mechanic which adds both the illusion of choice and increases the players stress due to having to think about it and make the "right" choice? .
♥♥♥♥ off. It's your story. Don't ask me how I want it to turn out and then at the end tell me there's no way to get a happy ending. If you do, expect the players to expect a change.
Ok. Story aside for a moment. Aesthetically Betrayer is BEAUTIFUL. Flat out, hands down. The lighting, the monochrome high contrast black and white, every little tuft of long grass and tree branch swaying in the breeze. Fantastic. I could literally make a game called Walking Simulator and just have it be this game with everything removed except for the environment. And it would sell. Turning on the color is even more impressive. Every color is super vivid, bright and distinct.
Walking or running around these environments with the color turned on and the effects all the way up made my machine chug a little, but overall the game is well optimized for the number of moving objects on screen at any given time. When the wind picks up, you can see each leaf and bush ripple. It's very, very pleasing.
The combat is pretty straight forwards. Hope to see the enemies before they see you. You can sneak around if you like, but the environments are so large that sneaking from one end of an area to the other is just insane. You can restore your health simply by drinking out of water barrels, and can carry up to three weapons, plus your melee attack, Walk down the road, see enemies. Equip Musket. Blam. One down, switch to pistol. Blam, second down. Switch to bow, quickly loose  an arrow at the one still coming, then slash him once when he gets too close and bam. Reload rifle and pistol, keep walking. Getting caught in the middle of a group of shadow world skeletons, or suddenly hearing the alert noise from a moss of conquistadors, as you're sneaking through and having to line up rifle shots while trying serpentine to avoid ranged and melee attacks is just not worth the risk.
I would still recommend this game, but not for the story. Don't invest in any of the characters. It doesn't matter. Play the game as a game. Take what enjoyment you can from it that way, and let the rest go.
Cheers.

I rate this game between 8.0 and 8.5/10 because the difficulty is, in part, fabricated by unbalancing the characters' emotions.  If civilians really reacted this way in a siege (i.e. degenerating from sad to depressed to broken so easily), they'd die by the millions weekly rather than pulling through, even after many months, as they so often bravely do.
It's difficult to suspend disbelief this far because real conditions in war zones are so gravely distressing; e.g. having game characters deteriorate for lack of cigarettes was contrived to create more tasks, but it doesn't say much for humanity's priorities in a crisis.
So, even though This War of Mine is an intensely stirring social commentary on the horrors of war, and well worth buying if you enjoy survival games, there's room for improvement should the developers decide to upgrade it.

This game confronts the player with the harsh realities of war. The player plays from the perspective of a group of civilians in a fictional war-torn city, trying all that they can to survive in the difficult circumstances, holding on until 'the end'.
There is a mixture of assertive and reactive elements (due to RNG) to this game, there is also a sufficient number of avenues for players to explore within. The 2D layout and the arcade-styled movement within makes it quite engaging. This game does however, suffer from the lack of significant replayability after two or three successful playthroughs.
Nevertheless, it provides a poignant reminder of the effects of war, done very well within the confines of a game. It is highly recommended.

What´s to say about Battlerite - It´s PvP stripped down to it´s core, which one has to like. I really enjoyed already the predecessor from Stunlock Studios (Bloodline Champions), which was exactly in the same vein as Battelrite. Because Battlerite is really coming down to skill based toe-to-toe matches it really develops the competitive drive I wish from a pure multiplayer game, following the principle easy to learn, very hard to master. And with the champion diversity (if you really want to master one) there is more than enough change in the game, because every chanmp plays differently and unique.
Neverhteless, the balancing is very good in my opinion. If I lose a match, I usually can easily track the reason down (wrong positioning, mismanaged cooldowns, burned wrong EXes, etc.) and so you constantly strive to get better and climb the latter. If you are interested in such sort of PVP, I can fully recommend Battlerite, also because the matches are usually rather short, the game is perfect for people who don´t have the time for a 1hour LoL match in the evening as it is for me.
Making the game F2P (I bought the EA) is a good move, as all the buyable things are purely cosmetic and do not change the game in any way, which I would call very fair. So if you like Battlerite, support the devs and see you in the arena!

"I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream"  is one of the earliest point-and-click adventures. Although time flew from this game, it still maintains its place as one of the most noteable games of the past.
Graphics:
Back then, seeing how graphics are formed really kept us coming back for more on PC games. The graphics are mostly 2.5d, an appearance of 3d but acts as if it is 2d. Overall, the settings of the game on various scenarios were pretty good and well thought out.
Voice Acting:
Wait, this game that is this old has voice acting?! Believe it or not, it does. I feel the actors really put theirselves in place of the character. However, I have to say that the voice acting of Nimdok was very terrible. It was annoying, slow, and monotonous. I know it was just an old guy, but come on learn to put some character in it (if only this review was done in the past).
Gameplay:
The gameplay is more complicated than the traditional point-and-click adventures we normally see on Steam...well...judging from the games such as Anna, Enola, and Kairo. Certain things need to be "Push"ed, "Use"d, "Talk To"ed, "Look At"ed, to "Give" stuff to, and rare cases "Swallow"ed. Yes, those commands plus "Walk To" to move and "Take" to take certain items. Regardless of that, you can easily learn from trial and error.
The goal of the game, although not specified, is not to lose spirit, aka the background surrounding the character portrait in the playthrough. You cannot lose any spirit at all. You'll notice that you've maxed out when your portrait turns from green to white at the end of the scenario (excluding one). Thankfully, if you made a mistake, you can save at any time and any scenario during the game.
The only problem is that during Nimdok's scenario, just simply using "Talk To" can instantly kill you. Also, some things are not reversible and certain scenarios are "needle in a haystack" type, in this case, trying to get the best ending for the game.
Story:
I have to say the stories were creative during the 90s era. While I have seen more disturbing things in other games and the internet, I do say they still captured the feel of chaos and fear in a demonic sense. Each story is unique to each character, going from someone who abuses to another person being abused, and others who look for forgiveness or those who commonly lose their way by fulfilling desires.
Overall: Regardless of some annoyances in gameplay, "I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream" is a memorable classic that is part of the history of PC gaming. The stories of the characters can leave you feeling a bit heartbroken, sad, angry, remorseful, and even turning the other cheek. While most old video games get lost in the junk pile like AM's hellhole, this one stands out like a gem and rises up to continue to be noticeable in the history of gaming.

I still can't tell how exactly I've felt at that very moment when the protagonist became my alter ego, all those years ago. A Big Daddy, one of my old enemies; About three years ago, I was just fighting against these huge guys over those Little Sisters. I've never imagined these "people" as people, but monsters - living among us, as mindless machines, grinding for the same exact object as... like... forever.
But about five years ago, Jordan Thomas, the Creative Director of this piece of art, introduced an Alpha Series Big Daddy with the former name of Johnny Topside, a poor man with an unfortunate life. Became an experiment in the hands of psychos, established a bond with a Little Sister, Eleanor Lamb, daughter of Sofia Lamb. - And how I've felt... Well, it was tough. Just started this game and yet I am already Johnny Topside, feeling this sorry man. Feeling his death.
Then my journey begun. MY journey, not someone else's. There was only me and my little daughter, seeking my aid.
BioShock 2 changed my perspective forever, from that point. How I've seen the world; How I've handled my own truths. - Was a freshman, back then and it was an amazing experience with so much to learn from a "monster" - an experiment, an animal in pain; A man with a daughter, far away from him, kept shackled in shadows.
This game has been criticized because of its overall concept of being in Rapture again with same old city, with same old people - but not of the Storytelling aspect, the connection it establishes between the protagonist and the player who's witnessing these events and have the ultimate control over them. Feeling sorry for the actions, suffering the consequences.
And these are the things that this game, BioShock 2, is all about. It is worth playing for its very endings of your choice. - It's worth playing to become Subject Delta, and not just another blank character shooting things.

So I played Bioshock and I thought it was *okay* but not the best. Despite the twist ending that I didn't have spoiled for me (Yay!) I still felt that the game was a bit of a slog and honestly quite difficult to get through. The fact that I never could feel at ease with the weapon/plasmid switches plagued me throughout the game, but I did enjoy the throwback to the 20s-40s era with the art, decor, and music.
Okay, now my review for Bioshock 2. I think since I'm not a uber fan of the original this will be easy for me to be objective, yes?
So I loved this game for what it was, overall. There were so many more voice logs for me to snap up and listen to the backstory of many different characters, most of them that didn't even make an appearance but whose actions prior to the game's present you could still feel. I loved the fleshing out of the background and the politics of Rapture. I don't think I really understood what Andrew Ryan's deal was in Bioshock: It felt like the game was alluding to something, something deeper, but I either wasn't catching on or the narrators made it too vague. With Bioshock 2 I finally got it: Andrew Ryan is an ultra-capitalist on par with Ayn Rand, to the point that it's almost like Stalin-era communism in reverse. It explains how easily Fontaine was able to secure his own market in Rapture in the first game. Hurray for me connecting the dots of the original in the freaking sequel >_>
Sophia Lamb was Andrew Ryan's foil but still just as twisted and demented. In some way I understood what she was saying, but her collectivist "for the good of us all" mantra still didn't sit right with me. Also, maybe if you took better care of your daughter this♥♥♥♥♥♥wouldn't have happened in the first place!
My complaints of this game are as follows:
-The game crashed at least three times. It gave me a warning that my video card wouldn't be able to handle it, and after the first time it shut down I feared that I would never be able to play it. But I went back in, lowered the graphics to their lowest settings, and barring some confusing crashes, I managed to play it seemlessly with stellar graphics regardless the whole way through (So, a complaint turned into a positive?)
-At times, Eleanor felt a little..I don't know, heavy-handed with her dialogue, and with all of the fleshing out of the characters through audio logs and radio communication, I would have thought that Eleanor and you the player as Delta would have had much more personal background featured, but oh well.
-I never got the hang of switching plasmids and weapons fluently. The fact that I couldn't order them the way I wanted was very frustrating once I got more than 4 of each. Urrrrrgh.
-Loading screens were a bit long
Positives:
-Beautiful scenery and environment
-The quick save feature ran about 10x faster than in the first game. Oh my God thank you so much.
-I found it a little bit scarier than the original. There were actual scares in this, whether they be the occasional jump scare or I scared myself by not noticing an enemy behind me.
-The multitude of collectable audio logs were fun
-Lots of unnecessary but just as fun hidey holes and abandoned rooms with goodies, ammo, extra gene plasmids abound
-Much like Dead Space, you could infer exactly what occurred in a blood splattered room by listening to an audio log or looking at the details (hm, bloody foot prints and hand prints, a knife, some pills...wonder what happened here?). A nice touch, to me.
So I think that yes, this sequel WAS necessary, at least for players like me that aren't great at mental world-building or who hate ambiguity when it comes to background and actual story. This game honestly plays better, offers more, and was much more enjoyable than the original Bioshock despite the flaws I listed.

What a game. I don't understand why so mant people disliked it.

Things I do like:
Cards per deck are limited by their rarity along with their name. This, along with the specific card pool makes Duels in essence a new format.
When opening packs, you can't get more copies of a card if you already have the limit of that card. This means as you get more cards you don't want, the chance of getting cards you do want increases.
A reasonably nice interface. While it's quite clunky in a few places, at least it looks better than Magic: Online and Cockatrice.
Avatars. While some people ignore this, you can give each of your decks a face. I can't help myself from coming up with some personality to go with the avatars I choose, but that may be just me. I've also found the majority of players who settle for the default avatar play RDW. An impatient colour for impatient people, I guess.
Things I don't like:
Very short timer. When anything is put onto the stack, you have about 3 seconds to press the spacebar (which works about 9 times out of 10) or click the pause button (which works about 6 times out of 10). If you miss the timer, or your method of pausing fails for whatever reason, tough luck.
Very sensitive casting. When you click a card, you'll play it immediately. If you miss-click, or you've played too much Hearthstone, tough luck.
Grinding speed. One pack of six cards costs 150 gold. Every game you win nets you 20 gold. This along with the daily quests means you can get a pack every 5 - 7 games. While this is a little slow, it's not that bad and I believe the micro-transactions are justified seeing as this is a free game and all.
No chat. This could be there too stop harassment, so there's no chance people new to magic would be driven away by ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s or salty people on a loosing streak. I haven't played 2HG myself yet, but if theirs no chat there as well, then it would be nigh impossible to strategize with your partner unless you know each other personally can  communicate in some other way.
Who I would recommend this game to:
If you are new to magic, then I would recommend Duels. It's free, it's pretty good at teaching you the rules and getting you into the game. Clear descriptions, the "Deck Wizard" that lets you pick the type of deck you want to play and guides you through building it, and no-one calling you names, due to the lack of chat.
If you already play the magic, but mostly casual "Kitchen Table Magic", then I would not recommend Duels. You would probably not enjoy the grinding you have to do in order to get access to cards, nor the lack of a chat system.
If your already quite experience with Magic, then I would recommend Duels. Rather than see it as another duels game, the ranked 1v1 matches should lead you to see it as another format. Try it and see if you enjoy it, it is free after all.

As of this writing, I have spent 70 hours playing this game.  Pretty much just been playing Solo Battles once I completed the pretty short Story Quests.
The Story Quests were pretty fun and I did really enjoy those.  I wish there were a lot more of those to complete or that they added more on a regular basis.
The problems I have with this game:
The AI is simply "amazing" at it's ability to draw the exact cards it needs, when it needs it.  I guess they program this ability in order to make it a challenge vs a human, but come on, there has to be a better way to make an AI challenging than giving it the ungodly ability to draw any card in it's deck to overcome what is going on at the time.  I mean, just put a few Enchant Aura's on a creature to make it more powerful than what the AI has out?  Well, this AI with no cards in its hand, amazingly enough is able to draw a card that returns your creature to the top of your deck.  That is just one example of the seemingly endless ability of this AI to get the card it needs.
The Deck Shuffler is just bad.  You either get a Flood of lands or a Dearth of lands.  Can't tell you how many times I have to restart a duel just to get a decent, initial draw.  And heaven forbid if you get a draw with a few lands, some enchant aura's and no creatures.  All you will draw from that point are more lands and more enchant cards until the AI has its big guns out and you have no way to recover.
The way to obtain cards is just annoying.  You either grind coins to purchase boosters or you spend cash to buy coins to purchase boosters.  I have no problem with that with it being a F2P game per se, but I have an issue with just being able to purchase boosters.  I wish you had more purchase options.  The AI seems to have access to all manner of cards and to have to fill your decks out with 6-card boosters is just boring to the extreme.  Getting tired of going up against Planeswalkers with no way to seem to be able to obtain any myself.
There seems to be no way to back up a phase ...and the Stop Timer is annoying in that there seems to be some delay when you click it and if you are a tad bit slow, you may end up in the next Phase before you meant to get there.  There also seems to be something off during the Block and Damage dealing phase but that just may be me.
Wish there were an easier way to see a stack of lands than currently.  For example, if the AI has tapped several lands and I want to cast something that can target a Land, the only way to "see" what is in that stack is to hover my mouse over it and wait for it to pop-up with text.  Cumbersome.
I have fun playing it most of the time, but the AI is beyond frustrating!

There is an attempt of an explaination near the end but it's so weak and vague that it makes things worse. I just feel there was so much potential for "Oh wow!" moments that blow your mind (see Bioshock), but you just get a few forgettable "oh, ok"s which is a real waste.
Overall though, if you see Betrayer in a bundle or on sale, I'd recommend you pick it up as it's different enough to be worth checking out, plus a lot of people seemed to have enjoyed it more than I. However if you get bored, my advice is don't feel pressured to finish as the game really doesn't have anything new to offer after the first hour or so.

Well, its a Wednesday today which may be news to you but if it isn't and by some miracle you've actually returned to this site, you'll know that this isn't my usual release date. Something went awry with my schedule however. I was all set to review some game that some right old knob has been asking me to review for a while when I saw that there was a Steam sale. 'Blimey', I thought,' I wonder if any recomended games would be worth buying'. You see, I take punts on games like these. More obscure games that have some sort of gimmick bolted onto the end of it. So I bought the Betrayer.
Now I love atmospheric games and having recently weaned myself off Alien Isolation with a bit of Outlast and Betrayer, I have to say I've been craving more. The Betrayer IS an atmospheric game for damn sure. Made by Blackpowder games, this black and white tale takes place in New England and if you're from New England then allow me to tell you that New England actually means America. You arrive stranded on a beach, waking in a anamnesia state with your vision blurred and no other backstory about how you actually got there, so basically just my average Sunday. You can see a few ships off the coast, however you never seem to try to make contact with them. Odd enough when you consider that you are supposed to be trapped there. From there you take a linear path up to your first location serving as the only form of communication between player and game, which is pretty much how the game starts to go on. You are not lead through the game thats for sure. Once you find the first location, Fort Henry, you're pretty much on a free reign to discover at your own pace all the while being blue-balled by a literal red riding hood.
The game's gothic influence is a strong aspect I have to say. There's no disputing the fact that the eerie sound design, black and white (with a hint of red) visuals and the spooky monsters you fight all fit the bill of old gothic literature. Having said that though, it reminded me more of those old horror films set in time periods similar to this one (17th century) like Witchfinder General and other masterpieces that have been cut from the same cloth. It's definitely not Five Night's at Freddies where things jump out at you for a few minutes before passing out face-first into the dirt, but Betrayer is asking for more than three pound fifty, so it knows it needs to grip the viewer preferably by the gonads as you're lead through dark forests and solve elaborate and chilling mysteries of the land's previous inhabitants. The lack of direction may be a middle finger to some players who are used to the half arsed games like Skyrim where you can click a location to immediately and inexplicably warp there. In Betrayer you can only use this trick if you're in the specific location and only to travel to the predetermined 'safe points'. I gotta admit, I quite like this system. There will no doubt be a literal horde of angry GTA fans, still wounded from last week, that will claim that the game doesn't direct you enough, but that's just it. The beautiful thing about this system is that you are lost, destined to wander the world in search of the next enlightening piece of the story pie. It feels atmospheric and gothic with only a slight whiff of the pretentious artsy-ness about it which only becomes obvious when the black and white mode is on (which you have the option to switch off).
If I were a gambling man, I'd be ready to say that you may be worried for my health at this point viewer. After all, I am the kind of guy who's idea of a wild night is to sit in his room with an oil burner silently getting drunk and slinking into the arms of the weeping abyss of self loathing. But even I like things, and the Betrayer is one of the things I like. It oozes atmosphere all over the place which is pretty difficult to explain when people come to visit. Guest scaring aside however, I like the Betrayer because it's something a bit new. I could play through the thousands of modern warfare games in a week and walk away like I've just been given a frontal wedgie by Hulk Hogan, or I could sit down to play some original games. Sure, modern warfare games are good for spectacle if nothing else but that's not what a game is there for. If someone said you were going to watch a good film and hands you a book that's just a lie and it's the same principle when a game developer gives you what amounts to a film with a few button prompts. Luckily the Betrayer doesn't betray the gaming audience and instead gives us an atmospheric and mysterious little gem that's got a few cracks in it, but ultimately would make Indiana Jones a very happy man.
Having said that, there is a point in this game where the atmosphere receives a little hairline fracture. If you've played the game you'll know what I'm talking about because I don't want to spoil it for anyone, but I want you to let me know if you had the same experience. It's a moment in the game where straight-up combat takes sway and you're forced to fight wave after wave of evil dudes, kind of like World War 2 without the fast pace of a heavy machine gun. For the combat here is effective yet slow. As to be expected with a company that names itself after a slow-firing weapon, the combat has some pacing issues in that fighting large numbers of lads can result rather quickly in your brutal demise, which is fine... For a while. However when you're only way to stop the armoured target running towards you is to shoot him with a horribly inaccurate blackpowder weapon that has a 10% chance of deflecting off of the target and there's five of the buggers now so hurry you ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, I can't help but wonder if there's a bit of a design flaw. I would say that it's intended though. As I mentioned, when you're fighting a reasonable amount of guys with rusty, inaccurate and slow-firing weapons, the encounters with the fast brutal enemies can become all that more intense. After all, man hath no fear of hell, if handed a high-grade assault rifle.
8/10- Yes! I've done it! A good review! Well, as good as I can get before downing the rest of the bottle and passing out in a road side ditch.

Battlerite is probably one of the only MOBA-style games I can tolerate nowadays. This is due to the fact of time-constraints and extremely long learning curves of traditional MOBAs, and other games that are not like the traditional MOBAs but not getting steam and launching off properly. Battlerite is an intense team-based brawler arena skillshot-heaven game with WASD controls. That's quite a chunk to take in, but now that it is Free-To-Play, there is no sense in NOT trying the game! The controls and mechanics are straightforward and accessible, but they can go very deep and especially when in the thick of things! This game rewards your time nicely and respects it as well. If you do terrible in a match, there is no fret, you can just pop right back into the next round or match within minutes. The game is very fast-paced in that sense, but I deeply love the fact that I can move on from a bad match and straight into another one without being frustrated by load times, queue times, or having to build up to the team fights. Which is another point to bring up. If you love the team fight aspect of MOBAs like League of Legends and DotA, then you will feel right at home as this is basically team fights the game. Which again, is probably my favourite part about it. You get right into the action and get out. It is highly adrenaline-based and intense fast-paced action distilled into 10-15 minutes of some of your favourite moments in LoL and DotA. Those games have a certain art to them because of their complexity and options available, but it is great to not worry about every single thing like feeding and staying on top of your farming game. Overall, if you want to take a hack at this game, you are no longer held back by possibly regretting a purchase. It's Free-To-Play for a reason! So get in there and join the fun! I'll see you guys in the arena!
TL;DR: If you love the team fights of traditional MOBAs and want to get all of that within 10-15 minutes combined with no RNG and completely skillshot-based aiming, then you are looking at this game. Since it is now Free-To-Play, you have nothing to lose, except the experience of delving into some of the most intense and fast-paced teamfights you've ever had in a MOBA. With the added benefit of being able to experience that again and again due to the fast queue times, load times, and general pace of the game!

For me, this is a difficult game to rate as it is a combination of genres the main being  adventure horror and FPS unfortunately, as another person stated in a previous review I found it almost impossible to relate to the characters in the adventure element of the story but, really enjoyed the FPS part.
Perhaps that was the problem, the FPS element was, for me, more fun than the adventure and therefore I didn't really play it or want to play it like an adventure, I usually enjoy adventures but, found that here I was only playing the adventure out of necessity to progress the FPS.
IMHO the story was complex to the point where I felt the it was holding me back from progressing and became just incidental rather than in integral part of the game.
The cross referencing between people places clues and events involves flipping between menus to understand the multiple links which to me seemed to impede the progress of the game. Whilst the story behind the events was actually quite interesting and complex it quickly became a chore that got in the way of killing enemies, finding clues and treasure, upgrading weapons and removing the evil on each map. There is not a lot of reading involved but, it does frustratingly slow down the game if you are playing it as an FPS.
To get the full benefit from the game it needs to be played first and foremost as an adventure and not an FPS.
The graphics are good, if your eyes are comfortable with the black and white default it heightens the atmosphere also, the night brought on by ringing the bells is particularly atmospheric, I preferred 50% colour during the day which for me, made the day night transition more dramatic.
Sound also plays an important part in the game as locating an item, enemy or event can be done just by following a sound to its source, headphones are probably an advantage.
Although there is a compass it is not possible mark any locations on the in game maps this can be a problem as some items can only be accessed with a shovel and relocating them once you have found a shovel can be very time consuming. The ability to be able to print out maps for the player to mark locations currently inaccessible of items for later return would have been useful.
The game has little if any replay value except for playing on more difficult settings however, I shall play it again when I get time as an adventure and concentrate on following the story, although I completed it only a few hours ago apart from the main character I recall very little of the interrelationships of the other dozen or so characters in the story.
I bought this in a sale and believe that I got value for what I paid however, I also believe there was a lot of potential missed because the two main game play genres failed to complement each other effectively, despite that, it was still an enjoyable game.
I shall definitely consider any future offerings from Black Powder Games.

When done right, this is where quality shines rather than stretching it out for quantity. For example with Bulletstorm you only need 8 mins to understand a game play segment, then this is repeated for 11 hours. This is not the case with Saints Row: Gat out of Hell where everything is paced well.
Of course the humour never stops. What's a prison like in Hell? Singing "the wheels on the bus go round and round ..." XD
I was also very surprised at the
. Top notch for a video game. Excellent programming, well done once again Volition.
EDIT:
The only let down for me was the multiple endings. I'm sure I've mentioned this heaps of times in some of my other reviews, but I'll reiterate it here again since nobody seems to be learning from this common mistake. It just doesn't work in games and is down-right frustrating. The only exception is IF the game is an instant-classic AND IF the ending is tied heavily to the choices you make in the game play right from the very start AND IF you're not forced to make a choice. Now these are pretty big IF's. The only game that has gotten this right imho is Vampire: The Masquerade - Bloodlines.
Lots of potential, but too rough around the edges to be enjoyable. I'd look into a game with similar gameplay, refined and improved, from these developers.

I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream is a truly horrific and well made game based on Harlan Ellison's short story of the same name. It isn't fun, it isn't truly "winnable" as sometimes in life, there are only losing situations. It does some things wrong just as most point and click adventures did, like pixel hunting, but for everything it did wrong, it did so much right with the presentation. It is truly dark, depressing, disturbing, and sometimes downright offensive. And I love it so much.
Story: Cogito ergo sum; I think, therefore I AM
Without getting into spoilers, a Cold War era computer, the Allied Mastercomputer, or AM for short, is created. AM is a sentient, self-aware computer who is filled with hatred for humanity and essentially ends up causing the absolute death and destruction of the entire human race, except for 5 people. He refrains from killing these 5 to take them to the center of the earth, extend their life span, and torture them. After being tortured for 109 years, they are given a message on a monolift from AM stating just how much he truly hates them and has a new game for them to play, and he created a mission for each of them. Their quests each have something to do with a fatal flaw of theirs which AM plans to use to his advantage to further break the  final humans. In other words... He's a huge ***hole in power. After blatently explaining to you via exposition why he feels hatred for each one of them, the "games" begin. You can choose your own order in which character to play as. The characters have been changed slightly from the original story (Which in fact IS included in the Bonus Content folder) but none are too annoyingly different. Most changes were made for gameplay purposes and probably because in the gaming industry, certain things are taboo.
Presentation:
The game's S.A.G.A. engine hasn't aged as well as the SCUMM engine it was based on, but it is still easy to navigate and a simple engine for the type of game IHNMAIMS is. Graphically, the game is both beautiful, and sometimes frightening depending on the story you are doing. The character art of each person on the bottom left of your GUI is well drawn and very detailed. Nimdok, one of the characters you play as for instance, is so detailed and well made that it is scary. He is... SO OLD! The only actual problems when it comes to visuals is a little bit of pixel hunting for specific items, but almost every 90's adventure game had that issue, and the character animations could have been better. Other than those two issues though, the game as well as the soundtrack is amazing and truly disturbing. Fits the story perfectly.
I would definately recommend the game, but you shouldn't play if you are faint of heart or sensitive to some certain topics. Some of the 'triggers' in the game include mentions of the Holocaust, insanity, murder, suicide,♥♥♥♥♥♥ and paranoia, so if those things truly bug you, maybe you should avoid the game and the book as it may offend you.
Extra Content:
Original manual from 1996 release in PDF format
Full soundtrack by John Ottman consisting of 33 ingame songs with 21 bonus tracks in both MP3 and OGG format
The original short story the game is based on in PDF format
The Making of I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream in PDF format

This game, as several reviews state, is unlike any other.
It's a dark, horrible environment that you play in, with tough decisions to be made.  Some will save your group but make them depressed, others will use precious resources but cheer your group up, and some may get you killed.
I will state now that I haven't made it past day 14, I usually get to that stage (with various group lineups) and decide to take a chance at a 'dangerous' scavenge and always find myself dead fairly quick.  I know I should delay the 'dangerouss until I have better gear and resources but I always start to panic at 2 weeks heh.
What it does show me is that this isn't a game you can rush.  Everything is slow and careful, some nights (later in the game) with no scavenging but scouting instead (if you have the right group set up).  You need to plan in advance your resources, both food and workshop.
The graphics are very atmospheric, adding to the darkness and grittiness of the game.  It's black, white and grey,  No other colours, so don't expect a pretty game.
You start off with a few set group choices, and often in the game other characters will appear asking to join you.  There are plenty of guides on Steam that explain each characters pros and cons, and I really recommend reading them.  Some you will want to be cruel and turn away.
And that leads to, in my mind, the one bad thing about the game.  The characters and their skills.  Some skills are still unknown, others aren't obvious, some are just generally useless.  All of which leads to a set 4-5 chars you want in your group.  Every guide states the same.  I've tried it my own way and found that yup, the longest I've lasted is with at least 2 of those 4-5.  It's the same chars over and over again, which gets dull and boring.  It would be nice to mix it up, perhaps chars with 2 main skills each, allowing cross-over and use of the other 'useless' chars in the game.
Please note, by useless I mean long-term use.  Each has a skill which could be useful if the game was easier and you could support 6-8 chars easily.  You can't.  The most you can generally support AND survive the 40 days is 4 chars.  So you have to be brutal and choose only the most useful out of all 12 chars.  It just so happens it's the same 4-5 chars every time :-(
However, if you ignore that one con, the rest of the game is amazing and addictive.  Hours pass by without you realising it, as you concentrate on your group so much, and what you need next, then it's just one more scavenge so I can make item xxx then I'll log out, but you make xxx then realise you need to make item yyy so it's just another quick scavenge...
When you get to approx day 10-11, it opens up new group set-ups on the main menu.
This War of Mine is one of the few games that I actually read the 'bunff', in this case the character's and their stories.  I read each and look forward to learning more about them.  Each story seems dark (as with everything in the game) and sad, and gives a terrible perspective about what it is really like to survive in such a situation.  I have yet to finish them, but there are guides on Steam that tell every character's story.  Personally, I want to wait until I've earnt it.
However, I do recommend reading some of the guides on how to survive.  Don't just read one, but several, as each gives different advice, some work for some people and some for others.  After trying and testing, I've found I do bits from all of them.  I did try doing it without reading the guides to start with and never made it past day 5.  After reading the guides, I found out where I was going wrong and it made a huge difference.
So to end.  This game is definately worth the money.  It seems to be well supported by its developer.  It's a dark, gritty and brutal game, and that works.

Bioshock 2 brings back Rapture to our hearts in a big way....a Big Daddy sort of way. In this installment, you play Delta, a big daddy who was murdered by main antagonist, Dr. Sofia Lamb. All of that pretty much happened during the first game. Through audio files you find that Sofia Lamb was essentially removed from the public eye sometime before the events of Bioshock 1. Now after the ten year span she has taken over all of Rapture. The story is interesting, but the main character, i.e. Delta, is too one dimensional for my taste. However the two big driving forces of the story is: one Dr. Sofia Lamb, as she is constantly on your case about why you try to get in her way and is almost automatically hated after your first encounter. Two is your little sister who even while taken away from you is helping you from the shadows with gifts aplenty and who's cries of help urge to go faster and harder to save her. Also not that big a twist this time, but your choices are as heavy as ever.
Gameplay wise the game is much the same as it was before. You acquire weapons and upgrade them one power station at a time. Your plasmids still work the same way where you acquire them either in the world or thru the gatherers garden. Three big differences though that make the game flow a bit more are: weapons now have a third upgrade unlocked once you buy the first two, which make them incredibly strong, dual wielding your guns on the right and plasmids on the left, and the quick reload of both guns and plasmids. Again as before you have objectives to do and are told what they are over the radio from your associate, Sinclair, who is helping you find Sofia Lamb.
Specs wise it is much the same as with Bioshock 1, so if your rig is pretty recent there should be no problems. Main concern is that VSync after every exit of the the game comes on by itself, so just make sure to check once in awhile to make sure it's off. I don't think it looks as good as the first one, but that may just be me. Also note: at one point, mostly during the third section the game crashed multiple times on many different days. It might have been an isolated incident, but just be wary of saving.
Overall this game is a great game especially for those who loved the first one because it brings you back to Rapture, which is so awesome and as cruel and heartless as ever. While the stroy isn't so interesting conceptually speaking, the character design and the relationship between you, your little sister and Sofia Lamb really makes the play through worthwhile. And hey you get to be a Big Daddy; at long last to be so powerful.
Simply put, this game is something all fans of interactive literature should experience. The music and voice work add to one of the most harrowing, spine-tingling stories in the industry.

I had never even seen a shooting star before. 25 years of rotations, passes through comets' paths, and travel, and to my memory I had never witnessed burning debris scratch across the night sky. I stared entranced, soaking in owlchemy Labs' new material, chiseling each gameplay moment into the best functioning parts of my brain which would be the only platform for the material for months.
This is an emotional, psychological experience. Snuggle Truck plays like a clouded brain trying to recall an alien abduction. It's the sound of a development studio, and its leader, losing faith in themselves, destroying themselves, and subsequently rebuilding a perfect entity. In other words, Owlchemy Labs hated being Owlchemy Labs, but ended up with the most ideal, natural game yet.
The experience and emotions tied to playing Snuggle Truck are like witnessing the stillborn birth of a child while simultaneously having the opportunity to see her play in the afterlife on Imax. It's a game of sparking paradox. It's cacophonous yet tranquil, experimental yet familiar, foreign yet womb-like, spacious yet visceral, textured yet vaporous, awakening yet dreamlike, infinite yet two hours long. It will cleanse your brain of those little crustaceans of worries and inferior games clinging inside the fold of your gray matter. The harrowing sounds hit from unseen angles and emanate with inhuman genesis. When the headphones peel off, and it occurs that six men created this, it's clear that Owlchemy Labs must be the greatest developer alive, if not the best since you know who. Breathing people made this game! And you can't wait to dive back in and try to prove that wrong over and over.

This is literly the worst Magic game I have ever experienced (and I have experienced most of them). I was excited about the game when it was announced but that quickly fell apart once I tried it.
I have really tried to like it but there is just no way that I could recommend this over Duels of the Planeswalkers 2013/2014. They are far superior games in almost every single way. Even the 2015 version, (which was the worst one yet), is much, much better than this one. The fact that this game is Free-to-Play is honestly not exactly much of a redeeming factor with a game this flawed.
----------
----------
- The decks you can build are very boring. The cards have very little synergy and in general it feels like any exciting card combinations are just not there. You never feel like you have a truly powerful deck.
- Connection issues - This game will crash a lot and often you can not get progress, which also means you do not recieve coins, (currency for buying booster packs).
- The entire gameplay feels extremely slow for someone having played the earlier versions like 2014 or 2013. The gameplay needs to be swift and responsive. This is NOT the case!
- No lobbies - Why would you remove the most convinient way of getting together to play and select which deck you want to use? This is madness!
- No chat or online interaction of ANY kind. This means that it is impossible to coordinate strategy with you team mate. This is beyond stupid. It makes the online gaming feel like playing against an AI. There is no way of telling the difference. If a player gets replaced with an AI, you have no way of knowing it apart from the message, (which you can miss entirely if you turn your head for a moment).
- 3 & 4 player Free For All is not implemented. Why would you remove this mode from the game? It is just lazy.
- Bugs prevent certain cards from not working as the should. And by certain I mean several.
- Story of the game is boring and more importantly really short. Recently a new campaign was added. It is 5 games long. It feels extremely lazy and rushed. Even for a free game this is completely insulting.
- You can only recieve currency for completing the campaign ONCE. When you have completed a match, you will recieve ZERO coins for completing it again.
- The coin system looks good at first glance but feels more like a massive cash grab once you experience how slow progression is in this game. Makes you want to buy coins for real money (I would strongly advice you not to do this). In earlier games you could pay 1 euro to unlock a whole deck. There is a massive difference to this than unlocking 6 random cards.
- No Plane Chase mode. This is a minor complain because it was last seen in Duels of the Planeswalkers 2013. Makes the game a little more exciting and different. It's a refreshing change of pace. Would like to see this mode return to future releases.
----------
----------
- Deck building is easier than ever before. There is more support on how to get your deck started and also an auto complete option. This is honestly pretty solid.
- Nice to see good in depth tutorials. Makes it easier for new players to pick up. But why on earth would you force players to get through the tutorial? It is very long and tedious for experienced players who knows all about Magic. Forcing a player like me to get through it is a bit insulting.
- 2 Headed Giant mode is back, (removed in DotP 2015), but how do you invite friends to play? This does not seem to work as intended.
- Nice customization of Avatars for your decks. This is a pretty cool minor feature.
----------
----------
I would NOT recommend this game at all. Maybe, just maybe if you are completely new to Magic the Gathering and don't feel like paying for the real experience just yet. Although I think chances are that this experience may hurt your overall opinion on Magic.
I would much rather recommend Duels of the Planeswalkers 2013/2014 even 2015 (better chances for online matchmaking). I recommend putting these titles on your wishlist and grab them on the next sale. They rarely get on sale but it happens.
Good luck!

This game fails as a stealth game, even when not compared to other Hitman games. I've played all previous Hitman games on a high difficulty and enjoyed them but this game gets extremely frustrating on high difficulties. This is by far the worst stealth game I've ever played.
The major problem is the A.I. They can spot you from very far away. They have a 180 degree field of view, meaning they'll spot you in less then a second from the corner of their eyes. They have a hive mind, so when one person becomes hostile every guard on the map becomes hostile. Disguises are somewhat broken in that every single person who wears that disguise will instantly recognize you (again from vey far away) but you get used to it. They see through walls/objects at times if you're not using the 'cover' button to glue to it.
The second major problem is the amount of enemies they place on the maps. Which is somewhat decent on easy and normal difficulty, but becomes insane on the highest difficulties. They also have the tendency to put additional guards at choke points on higher difficulties.
The nail in the coffin is the checkpoint system, which again works pretty decent in easy and normal difficulty. On higher difficulty it forces you to replay a level over, and over, and over again untill you find the optimal way you want to play the level. Previous Hitman games had limited saves which was better because you could focus on getting good at one part and then saving and getting better at another part. No so in this game, you have to constantly replay from the start and do the parts you have already mastered to get a chance to do another part.
The levels themselves aren't that bad, they are more linear than previous Hitman games but they're pretty well designed. The story starts really interesting (though it's not consistent with the previous games) but doesn't get delved in deeper and very quickly becomes a carrot on a stick to move the game along.
In conclusion: There is some fun to be had if you play the game as an action game on lower difficulties (the challenges can be fun). But the game utterly fails as a stealth or Hitman game and that's why I've given it a negative review. I have more memories of being utmost frustrated then I do of having fun.

I wish that Steam had a button somewhere between "Recommended" and "Not Recommended" for these reviews, because there's a lot to be said for
Since we don't live in such a world, however, I'll have to tilt toward the red side of things, because the game's many good qualities are ultimately overshadowed by its infuriating design and failure to live up to its own aspirations of profundity.

First the good, and that right off the bat:
has one of the best opening monologues I've ever seen in a game -- a joyously hateful screed delivered in blistering fashion by the game's antagonist, an insane supercomputer called AM. It's the year future-future-something-or-other, and AM, being a supercomputer in a video game, has (surprise!) taken over the world, killed off most of humanity, and spent the last 109 years keeping our five "heroes" hostage and subjecting them to all sorts of tortures in an underground lair. AM narrates this backstory with a chilling mix of glee over his own sadism, and bone-deep bitterness over the fact of his own miserable existence. Here's a
of this cheerful setup -- dig it, you won't regret it.
Unfortunately, the pace immediately drops from headlong to plodding, as the five flawed protagonists are split up and sent off on banal individual quests. (The player can freely choose the order in which to tackle them). AM tantalizes each of his victims with a promise of freedom, if only they can navigate their way through a personalized test of AM's making. The point of AM's game is, apparently, to explore the individual vices and psychology of his five playthings.  The protagonists are therefore forced to make choices that test their strength of character and, ultimately, determine whether the player achieves the "good," "middle," or "bad" ending of the game.
This is a terrific setup for an adventure game, but the execution here is botched for two main reasons. First, the choices facing the characters are so black-and-white that you almost have to
to fail the subquests. At one point, for example, you're offered the choice to rescue a small boy on a sacrificial altar, or... eat him. Decisions, decisions!
Second -- and this is more of a design flaw than a narrative one -- if you don't perform your tasks within a subquest in the exact (often arbitrary) order that the developers intended, certain necessary branches of the story won't open up even when you
what to do next. After pulling your hair out for a while, you'll look up an online guide and see that the reason your character won't perform an obvious solution to the challenge at hand is because you failed to talk to an unrelated character four screens away and three saved games ago. The upshot is that you're forced to replay the entire subquest in a slightly different manner in order to get the plot moving again. This is every bit as tedious as it sounds.
Broadly speaking,
seems like it's aspiring to Say Something About Society, but I'm not quite sure what that could be, other than (perhaps) "human vice + technology = tragedy," or maybe "our ability to make moral choices is what makes us human." Both of which are undoubtedly true, but hardly original or even all that deep. So without interesting ideas or a smoothly-flowing narrative, we're left with a slow-paced and sometimes tedious game that fails to live up to the promise of its wonderful opening moments.
has a lot of good qualities (e.g. its disturbing central premise, Harlan Ellison's scenery-chewing voiceover work for AM, or the occasional inspired horror sequence), but for the reasons described above I didn't have a particularly good time playing it, nor was I left with much to think about in terms of interesting themes. Not recommended, with regret.

Snuggle Truck is quite possibly the greatest game ever made. From an objective standpoint, nothing else comes quite close to delivering the kind of experience that this game is capable of. If I were to choose one game in existence to prove to somebody that video games are art, it would definitely have to be this masterpiece.
Firstly, I would like to begin this review by asking the question: what is a video game? Some people would simply answer this by saying that video games are an interactive medium with the sole purpose of delivering entertainment to the players. Others prefer to give long philosophical answers which tackle every facet of this age-long riddle. After playing Snuggle Truck I can honestly say that any answer to this question is meaningless, and one only needs to play this game to fully appreciate the marvellous wonder of this pastime known as "video games."
With that said I would like to break the game down as much as possible within the limitations of purely text-based reviews; after all Snuggle Truck is a deep, complex experience which would transcend standard, traditional review formats. One of the most notable things I would like to bring to the forefront is Snuggle Truck's graphics and visual style. When I first loaded this game and began playing, I thought the game had crashed. Let me explain: I'm an avid fan of trucking in general, and as a result my desktop background is a constantly-changing slideshow of truck imagery. The visuals in this game are so incredible that I mistook graphical images for photography. The animation is also so incredibly smooth and lifelike that I actually started to feel brief motion sickness after only a few seconds of play.
This soon passed however as I quickly became immersed in the truly innovative and revolutionary gameplay found in this work of art. Snuggle Truck takes similar games such as Euro Truck Simulator 2 and completely slaps them in the face with its own brand of hyperrealistic physics and gameplay scenarios which leaves a completely before-unseen impression on the player. Because of how intuitive, responsive and predictable the controls felt, I was very quickly able to adapt to how the game must be played; and it even left me thinking "hot damn, this is so lifelike, I could probably do this in a real life truck."
That's not to say the game is easily played, however. While the game presents itself as being extremely accessible through its  controls and simplstic gameplay objectives, this game has a very steep difficulty curve which constantly demands the player to step up their game. The difficulty is fair and never feels artificial, and if you mess up, it's 100% your fault.
The audio in this game is beyond noteworthy. No lie, when I finished playing this game because I had important things to do - such as sleep so that I would have enough energy the next day to play more Snuggle Truck - I basically had to leave the game idling on the title screen because the music is so incredible. It's insanely catchy and would make great classical composers of past ages such as Bach and Mozart weep with envy.
With everything said, I believe it stands to reason that Snuggle Truck should be considered one of if not the greatest game ever made. If, after reading this review, you still have any doubts as to whether or not you should buy this game, you are probably literally Satan; though I doubt even the dark lord himself wouldn't get a kick out of this truly magnificent magnum opus.

You're explained little at the start, which allows the player to piece together the mechanics so by the time you're late game you should have most of it figured out.
For those who enjoy a slower paced game, focusing on sneaking up on enemies and taking time to aim, this could be for you.  It is not a *bad* game -- but it's not one with high replay value, repetitive levels, and three achievements based on grinding over being actual achievements.  The simplicity of the game would almost be a strength had the pacing been different and more thought put into not making things feel like a game (chests and the typical game-style merchant) would have helped it a lot. Betrayer is a weird beast. It's another game that holds its narrative higher than its gameplay, but it still tries to fit more combat into its story and atmosphere than other games like Gone Home, Master Reboot, etc.
It also features a very striking artstyle at first, although I'm not quite sure the developers knew exactly where they wanted to go with it.
You arrive in 17th century America, and go from camp to camp, trying to figure out the world around you. To do this, there are some pages spread around the maps, and also ghosts. You can see and speak to them, and little by little, by finding clues around the maps, you'll be able to understand who they are, how they died, and thus investigate the strange happening of each camp.
I really like the concept, and it's certainly
, but I don't think the execution is perfect, for the game's length. It feels like it would be a great element in a game, but not the sole focus, as is.
There are various enemies spread around, with different tells. You'll have to be methodical in dealing with them, and use sound to your advantage, moving stealthily to avoid certain death.
Let's go more in-depth with its
. You've probably seen from the screenshots that it's a very important aspect of this game.
The game is essentially in greyscale, with heavy contrast and lighting, and then features some live red for you to spot enemies and other important clues. There is the option to set normal colors though, and it looks pretty good as well, as long as you adjust the contrast and the lighting as well.
There are two worlds, a living world, and the ghost world, which you switch from and to, depending on your objective. The ghost world is far grimmer and darker. However, since both are black and white, I think it loses its punch, in general. I played the whole game as it was by default (always greyscale). After that, I went back to find missing collectibles, and used normal colors. Even in the living world, the game is far more tense with colors off, but the shock in switching worlds is significantly lessened.
Playing without colors can also be quite confusing at first, and I honestly don't know how I feel about it. It's just weird. And in the context of this game, it works! The whole time, I was just trying to understand what exactly the game was trying to do.
Another crucial aspect on this game is its
. There's no music, it's only ambient sounds.
Now, the greyscale serves a purpose in the game. It makes you realize that you see the world differently than others in that world. You can clearly see enemies and interactable objects, while they can not. This also plays a role in sound design, as enemies have a much harder time seeing how. They can however, hear you if you're not careful. So you'll constantly be trying to walk crouched if you hear enemies around (or see them) not to get spotted. There are also occasional gusts of wind that mask your sprinting sound.
Some enemies are very clear with their red tells. Others, however, are also hidden, until they spot you. The only way for you to tell they're around, is through the sounds they make. There's a lot of nuance to it regarding its sound and visual design and the combat, actually, it's pretty cool.
There are also audio tells for when you are near an objective, or a collectible. You can also press X to be guided towards a close ghost/main objective, with a distant sound effect. There is a visual aid to it in the options menu, but I recommend playing only based on the audio cues.
It's hard to review this game, as it has so many details that shape the experience. I'll have to say the it's very heavy on atmosphere. It's not an horror game, but it can make you uncomfortable at times, and unexpected enemies can make you jump every once in a while. But I loved how tense it made me. The visual and audio design was spot on to make you feel that something was wrong at all times. Great job on that.
Well, there goes half of the review and I haven't began talking about gameplay.
Each map if self contained, and you can only progress to one after you've done every important objective for the previous. If you guide yourself with the sound cues, you'll have no problem with it. Most of the maps are very empty and barren woods, with 2-3 camps or important landmarks in each one. There are Pages, Chests, Clues, Ghosts, Graves, and Totems spread around. You have a notebook that checks most of what you find, regarding clues, locations visitted, graves found, etc. You also have a map to guide you (and fast travel between landmarks), but you can not make annotation in the map.
If you're after the chests, pages and clues, it's a nightmare to go look for them again without map markers. There are also some clues that you can't uncover until you get a Shovel late into the game. Without marking these when you find them, going back after you get it is a pain... You'll forget most of them, and overall, it's very inconvenient to simply walk around hoping you'll stumble into something. This is only a problem with the optional stuff, but it's annoying nonetheless.
Regardless, let's go back to the game. There's also a vendor, from whom you can buy weapons, ammo, and the like. Enemies also drop weapons, although much weaker than the ones you get from the vendor. There are also 16 unique weapons that you can find from Chests, or with the Shovel. These are even better from the ones in the vendor, and it's worth scavenging for them.

In the normal world, you'll have to clear the camps of Spaniards (to set your checkpoint there) and find a Bell, to mount in it. By ringing the bell you change worlds. This is where it gets more interesting.
In the ghost world, you'll go around trying to find lost souls and wraiths. There can be both colonizers and natives. If they're lost, you'll point them to the camp, you can speak to them there. As you find more ghost and clues for each map, you'll be able to ask them questions about each other, and the items you find. This reveals how they died, little by little. It's usually episodes of people betraying one another (hence the name). While they're not groundbreaking, I thought they were cool, and also set the tone for the game's world. It's not historical or anything. It's mostly a way of integrating the narrative with the gameplay, and that's very good.
There's also a main plot (that's related with these side-stories as well), about the normal human being you find. She can't quite remember what happened, and so you go around trying to find her family.
The problem with this, is that I can't understand the point of this story. There doesn't seem to be a message in it, for the most part. It's just... there. And while the world itself, and the side-stories make the game interesting, it doesn't seem as directed as I would have liked. Don't get me wrong, I really enjoyed playing the game, but there's something missing, and the potential is there!
I hope you get a good enough idea from this to know if this is for you. I just find it really hard to fit this game into a review.
Another aspect that I want to touch, is the moral of your actions. With the enemies, they completely dehumanized the enemies, weirdly enough. The Spaniards are just armored humanoids that sound like bears. Seriously, if you hear a freakin' bear, it's a Spaniard. They also have a full helmet, so you never see their face. The natives are fire-y ashen being and whistle to communicate with each other. None of them feel actually human, so you have no problem with killing them, as they're just hostile beasts.
Overall, it's a very interesting game. Execution is half stellar, half lacking. It feels a bit incomplete, pacing-wise. But I'd say give it a go! You'll probably have an odd feeling of enjoyment while playing it!

Very good. If you like top-down shooters and good soundtracks, you'll love it.
You will feel like you're cheesing its system most of the time. The AI is not smart; things either make a beeline for you or forget that they've seen you, and they'll completely ignore the wall you're breaking down until the hole gives you both line-of-sight.
However, it's got a few addictive loops to it. There's the whole "peeling the onion" thing, the enjoyable process of wearing down a heavy security force until you're easily picking off the last guys. There's the level checkpointing: five office floors followed by a boss (and unless you make it past the boss, you'll go back to the first office floor in this segment when you die). There's the constant hunts for incremental increases in your stats or the cash to buy them, and this means that death never feels like a waste; you go back to the hub, and get a chance to spend the cash you've found on upgrades so that you'll fare better next time.
