I have thoroughly enjoy I Have No Mouth, and I must Scream as it has handles some very mature subject matter that makes many a modern game look like a Disney adventure, it works well on Linux, the graphics are still passable for this day and age and it doesn't suffer from pixel-hunting as much as games of the same generation
Unfortunately, there are a few things wrong with it: the game is extremely buggy. I can easily make it crash or perform actions that are seemingly not intended to be performed (yet). You can also rather easily break your save game, forcing you to replay some or all adventures over again. Whatever you do, always make sure you have more than one save-game going and save often.
You can also -die- in this game which forces you to restart the current adventure. Luckily, the game will let you know when this happens. It's a minor nuisance in comparison to breaking your save game and trying to figure out what to do for hours on end.
The game also has a tendency to 'spawn' items that weren't there before and 'locks' certain actions so you can only do them when the time is right. This is confusing because sometimes it doesn't and lets you perform actions prematurely, causing the aforementioned problem of breaking your game. And you might not think of performing an action again because you have already done so five times and it didn't work the first 5 times and the feedback given to you seems to indicate that it is simply not possible. Until it suddenly is.
I was forced to use a walkthrough on a number of occasions: one involved pixel-hunting and the two other occasions involved me saving the game after I had made irreversible choices without the game telling me I had lost the game. Then there was the part about selecting the right character for the end-phase first otherwise you might ... You guessed it! Break your savegame.
If you can live with all of the above, IHNMaIMS is for you. If you are easily frustrated and think point 'n' click games shouldn't break your savegame; look elsewhere.

This game is amazing. there's so many good things to be said about this game, but since others have covered most of the stuff I wanted to talk about, I'll just talk about the point that I loved the most; new perspective on wartime situations. It's horrifying how realistic they'd managed to potray this game.
I don't think I have ever seen a war/survival game in the perspective of the civilians before, which is quite bizzare, considering that in modern warfares approx. 90% of the people affected by wars are civilians. The characters are not too different from ourselves, and whilst it may not be all shooting and excitements throughout the game, it makes it that much more relatable and realistic, and you will quickly find yourself emotionally attatched to the characters. When you don't think twice about stealing from the old couple, your character feels devastated by the acts of their wrongdoings - and when you see them so broken, it makes you think twice about the acts you'll commit in the future.
Anywho, all I wanted to say after this long rant is that this game is amazing. It's slow-paced. It does get repetative after a while. BUT it makes you think and feel about the issues that you've never given too much of a thought. For that reason alone, I think this game is worth playing. Everyone who comes across this game should play it.

I Have No Mouth And I Must Scream is something of a stealth classic of horror point-and-clicks, or at least, it's rare I hear people talking about it. A few screenshots and the title itself whispered at me for years after seeing it in a PC gaming magazine as a kid, but it wasn't until recently I got a chance to play it.
The game's certainly aged well, for starters. Scene after scene looks beautiful and colorful despite the morbid themes permeating things, with the environments toward the end (once you've played through every scenario) being some of my favorite from any game, ever. The story is essentially split into chapters, each one following the psychological torment of one of the game's five protagonists by a world-encompassing and really, REALLY angry supercomputer. Each mental torture chamber is tailored to play specifically to each subject, whose fears aren't as simple as gore or spookiness. In fact, only one or two scenarios deal with anything particularly supernatural, though I should mention a trigger warning for an implied sexual assault in one of the character's histories that she briefly relives.
Since these are computer-generated projections of each character's imagination, the peculiar logic of point-and-click adventures does tend to apply more often than not. Gorrister's situation in particular is kind of all over the place, so keep that in mind when you play as him. Also, try to get a feel for each character's personality as they react to and interact with things, as it may help with choosing proper responses for them later on. Just sayin'.
Despite having come out ages ago, I Have No Mouth And I Must Scream is still absolutely worth a playthrough. Maybe more than one, as the demands for the "perfect" ending are a bit exacting. Everything's even voice-acted quite well, with Harlan Ellison deliciously filling the role of the morally questionable supercomputer running everything. Appropriate, since he penned the short story it's (kind of loosely) based upon. If you like your horror more subtle and less in your face, pick this one up.

This War Of Mine takes a new approach to the "post apoclipse" genre by, insted, making a game that feels real and impactful. You start out with three survivors, in my case I started with Pavel; a football player looking for his purpose in the tragity of war, Bruno; an overweight smoker but a damn good cook, and Katia; a young reporter with bargening skills. Katia was by far my favorite.
Pavel was killed pretty early on by a group of militants, "shot like a dog" to quote Bruno.  But Bruno was't exactly the most likeable person himself. I distinctly remember him stealing from an old married couple, the wife was sick and the husband was too weak to fight back so Bruno just took from them. And he seemed to be the only person not bothered by this.
Soon after the death of Pavel a new man arrived at the doorstep of my home looking for shelter, his name was Nicola, and of course we welcomed him into out home, and they lived happily in there own little house. It seemed somber and seprate from the war. And with nightly scavenging runs, food seemed to be in abundance.
But like all good things, this soon ended. On a supply run Katia was gathering supplies from an abandoned house, but as it happens it wasn't as vacent as she had originally thought. A young man burst though the door yelling:
"Get out of my F*****g house! I'll F*****g kill you!!!" as he shot Katia once. Katia ran for her life as the man continued to take shots, and she was hit once again before eventually escaping. This left her on the brink of death, and barely able to function, she was bandiged up and put to bed. But the house had supplies they need.
So the next night Nicola went out to gather the rest of the supplies, and this time he did it with a knife. He not only found supplies though, he also found out that the yound man was surviving with his parents; an old couple no younger than 70. But he was inexperenced and was soon cought and meeting a similar fate as Katia, exept Nicola didn't get away. He was on the ground, at the feet and mercy of the young man with the shotgun. And the young man let him go.
"Just this once," he said "but if you ever come back, I will kill you."
Nicola's injeries were far worse than Katia's. And they were out of bandiges. Nicola died soon after.
Enraged by his death, Katia decieded that she would deal with the pain of her wounds, and she would take everything from the bastrds that killed Nicola. But insted she ran into the young man's old father. He screamed for help and by instinct; Katia stabbed him twice. The young man and his mother didn't even fight back this time. They just sat at the old man's courpse and cried silently.
Katia died the next day, from what no one was sure. Maybe it was from blood loss, maybe from the overdose of pills she took to end her own life. Either way, Katia was dead and nothing in hell was gonna bring her back.
Then Naomi came. She was a happy, upbeat musican that seemed to carry a good energy where she went. But it wasm't enough help Bruno. He became severly depressed, and insted of taking the easy way out like Katia, he took all the food they had and ran while Naomi was sleeping.
Now Naomi lives alone, unable to find food, unable to stay warm, unable to heal from a wound she god defending from looters. She counts the days until eventually hunger, the cold, or even her own depression overtakes her.
This War Of Mine is not a game, it is an experence, and one that must be played. I have never felt so attached to anything other than my cat, then I was to these imaginary people that seemed to real, and personal and amazing. I wish you the best of luck.
But serously, PLAY THIS GAME!!!

Sid Meier's Civilization: Beyond Earth is a really fun and addicting game like Civ 5 was.  This gives me a sort of feeling for a lot of space colonization that I am a huge fan of.  It's one thing to watch people settle on a planet and fight the threatening alien natives, but it's a whole other thing when you actually get to experience it yourself.
Now I am not going to just praise this game, I do have one or two problems with it.  So if you're expecting me to just tell you all the good stuff about the game, go find another reviewer. So lets get started...
Problem 1: Civ 5 = Civ Beyond Earth...
One of the major problems I have with this game is that it's almost way to similar to Civ 5.  The combat system, unit movement, environment layout, and animation all seem to similar to Civ 5.  There were, however, a few changes here and there but not a lot.  I was expecting sort of a better high def animation in the environment or little more advance combat animation.  It seems to me that if you were to merge the two games together, you would more than likely see BE as a DLC or expansion of the game.
I can probably best tell you that Sid Meier could've been better off calling this game, "Civilization 5: Galaxy Quest" or "Civ 5: Interstellar Journey."
Problem 2: What's the story again...
Now I can probably bet that most of you are probably going to say, "You create your own story in Civ," and you are right but in this game you are given a story to sort of follow.
You goal is to create this new coloney on a far away planet with one of eight governements sponsoring you to do so.  You also have to choose to be apart of a certain political party or Affinity: the Harmonists, the Purists, and the Supermacists.
The only thing wrong with this is that it doesn't do much for you.  The only thing the Affinites do is give you certain unit and, possibly, building modifications.  The Affinties don't have a lot of purpose than just that, and pretty much sets you victory style if you so choose.
It would've been nice if the Affinites were incorporated as plot points for a story.  I kind of expected this to have a more solid story than a minecraft like story.
Problem 3: Talk to me...
One of the main things that annoys me is that the deligates don't talk a lot, or at all.  The only time you mostly get to hear their voice is when they first arrive on the planet...and thats it.  I do hope that Sid Meier will release a patch or something that will fix that voice problem.
Now that I am done talking bad, let's look at the good stuff...
Praise 1: Alien > Barbarians...
Aliens in this game are far more agreesive than what I expect them to be.  These things don't mess around when you attack one of their units.  Once you attack them, it's pretty much all out assault on you.  They will destroy your units if your men are singled out.
Also, the seige worms are freaking beasts.  The will wipe out your units in one hit while taking little to no damage.  They will tear you apart.
Praise 2: I'm caught in the web...
Once the new things to Civ BE is the technology web.  It is so much better than the tech tree from Civ 5.  You get to hope around from research to research and you no longer have to research in order of advancement in tech.  This web is  huge improvement.
Praise 3: I'm going on a quest...
Quests are, to my knowledge, new to the civ franchise.  You finally minor goals to complete that can occupy your time other than trying to build your empire.  There are quests of science, production, military, culture, and Affinities.  I'm so glad to finally have something else to do in this game, other than expand and kick America's butt.
Praise 4: Let's be BFFs...
I'm so glad that they finally fixed the delegates in this game.  In Civ 5, whenever I tried to make a friendship with another nation, the friendship will last like ten turns before they either denounce me or declare war on me. Now my friendships are finally lasting longer and no one is constantly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at each other.
Now my final verdict for this game is a 8/10.  This game has many elements that make it similar to Civ 5 but it also has many elements that seperate itself from Civ 5.  Overall i really love this game and I can't wait to see if Sid Meier plans on expanding upon this space theme or will he return to the original civ and improve that universe?  Personally i want to see both.  I want to see like a Civilization 6 that has better detailed graphics, better combat animation, and an aging landscape.  I also want too see an Alien Civilzation where you either found you civilization on an alien planet or you invade earth and start building a coloney there.  Either way, I can't wait to see what Sid holds in the future.

The mechanics are solid, there is depth in terms of content, and the execution is superb. I wouldn’t call this one a “thrill ride,” but Snuggle Truck can be your burst game, that title you play when you’ve got three minutes to spare.
It’s hard to just peg Snuggle Truck in a genre. I call it a side-scrolling racing game and then toss in the caveat that it’s highly physics-based. In the game, you control a dirty truck that can be highly reactive to the terrain its meets -- the smallest dips and jumps cause the truck to lean back and forth. You can correct its arc with the arrow keys, but you don’t do it for the safety of the vehicle -- you get lined up to protect the cargo, those cartoon animals riding in the back. Each animal is just as reactive to the truck’s trajectory, and the point is to hit the end point as quickly as possible with as many animals as possible. Easier said than done, I've learned.
There’s a lot of stuff that can get in your way in the process of getting to the end goal, the "zoo": there’s an assortment of bumps, massive hills, dips, and even a few surprise environmental objects like explosive crates that get thrown into the mix in later levels. For the most part, Owlchemy Labs does a fantastic job providing change of pace opportunities: there’s a ton of different layouts and jumps experimented with, which give you plenty to do and think about.
Hitting and landing a jump without losing your animal dudes is all in the wrist and in the finger. You can use your keys to correct the trajectory and also use the basic movement mechanic -- pressing your fingers on either the up or the down key -- to slow or speed up your truck.
Snuggle Truck introduces one new mechanic at a time, giving you the ability to slowly learn and react to obstacles as you progress through the levels. But there’s a big trial-and-error element as well since you never know what’s around the bend. One small jump, for example, can take you straight into a wall while another of the same exact kind might not present any mission critical navigational issues.
To its credit, Snuggle Truck remains fun despite its clumps of middling level design. I chock this up to its relative snappiness -- levels take, generally, under a minute to finish, so it’s not a great loss to start over again. Nor do you really need to ace a level since there’s so many in each tier.
Of course, there are carrots on sticks to chase -- Snuggle Truck goes heavy on the rewards after completion of each level. You can earn your traditional star medals, as well as completion medals based on completion and number of animals you save.
While Snuggle Truck actually feels like a game that went one direction and then the other, I recommend it. The truck controls well, the physics respond well, and the level design has that right mix of snappiness and intrigue. Check it out if you’re in the market for another racing side-scroller, and keep your eyes peeled for updates. Owlchemy Labs has crazy plans for Smuggle Truck which include implementing community-generated levels which could lead to some awesome replay value.

Snuggle Truck is a physics-based driving game where you must deliver your cargo full of "Snuggies" as fast as possible to the zoo.  On your travels you will encounter various obstacles and will have to overcome them with the various power-ups that you are provided with.
Snuggle Truck's gameplay is decent, and can be challenging if the player wants to unlock all the medals the game has to offer. However the game has definitely lost character since its late production change from "Smuggle Truck" to "Snuggle Truck".  Rather than using a rundown pick-up truck to smuggle immigrants over the border you have to transport stuffed animals to a zoo in a similar fashion. In other words, they are both the same game.
Overall, Snuggle Truck is an average game which has sadly had its unique concept ripped out from underneath it via censorship of Apple. Like many games of this nature it is great for those that are looking to lose a few minutes. I would recommend "Smuggle Truck" instead as I believe this is the game that Owlchemy Labs wanted their audience to experience. You can only access the original from their website.

Overview:
Agent 47 returns in the fourth install of the series as a much older role but is still as deadly as ever.  The format is the same but with better graphics, mechanics, and variety.  A multiplayer element has been added along with leader boards and user content integration.
Pro(s):
Multiplayer: There is a simple and intuitive system implemented that allows players to create there own challenges and share them with the community.  One just plays the map of choice and assassinates a player chosen set of NPCs with a specific weapon and in a specific way.  You must first beat the challenge before you can share it with the community.
Con(s):
The Hitman Feel: To me this Hitman felt the least like a Hitman game.  The emphasis isn't so much on assassinating a high profile target as it is about sneaking to the next destination.  There are still plenty of high profile target assassinations but it is just not the same as the previous Hitmans.
The Stealth System: The developers this time round decided to give the player not only a mini-map with all the enemy units on it, but also a threat meter system that shows what direction and how threatening the threat is.  I felt this was a little overkill and made the stealthing much too easy.  Even on one of the harder difficulties these two systems make it very easy to play and towards the end of the game I had figured out how to basically sprint through the levels exploiting the system to my advantage.
Conclusion:
Another good installment in the Hitman series but not as good as Blood Money.  What this Hitman has over the older ones is more modern graphics and mechanics.  If your looking to try out the Hitman series this one isn't bad but I'd suggest Blood Money first.

First let me mention this game is much better with a few mods which you can get from the workshop or nexusmods. I do like this game but my review focuses more on what I don't like about it. You play as Ren Otani, pilot of the Albion Skunk (You can change the ship name!), a small space craft seemingly about the size of the Millennium Falcon. The engines, weapons, shield, ect can be upgraded. While you can't pilot any other vessel, you can acquire and issue commands to pretty much any class ship in the game. Your ships will also watch you get destroyed unless you tell them to attack each target one at a time or agro on every enemy they get in range of which will just cause unnecessary engagement. There really needs to be a "destroy anyone attacking your squad" option.
I can see a lot of work went into this game and the scripting is impressive but it was obviously rushed out of production and nearly committed suicide by releasing in what was basically an unmarked beta stage. The bugs were so bad people started thinking if they couldn't find something it was a bug so they would just edit their save file as a fix. Currently most alleged "bugs" are due to "user error" and you should probably visit youtube before doing anything drastic like saved file editing but there are still a few minor bugs/issues.
The biggest issue remaining in this game is the lack of in game information. Not only on how to do anything or where to start looking for a particular item but also info such as how a crew skill stats affect anything and the fact that you can't buy cargolifter drones from drone dealers but rather ship dealers at a shipyard.
The economy is very much like elite dangerous but not quite as bad. NPC ships spawn in with cargo and deliver it to stations if you don't intervene. That cargo is then used to build parts to be sold to the quickest buyer, to build ships you order or NPC ships that do nothing but despawn shortly after construction. If a shipyard is constructing a (NPC) ship you can't use it for repairs, buying drones or anything. To make things worse if the shipyard doesn't have the resources for the ship it's building you can wait for a delivery if it ever happens or find and sell them the parts your self. Stations can't be obliterated or taken over, only badly damaged but they will get repaired after a time.The only station players can't build is a shipyard but fortunately there is a mod for that.
I must mention once you acquire a missile on your ship, there is no way to remove it from the weapon list even after getting rid of it. Nothing like flipping through 10 types of missiles during the midst of combat looking for one you DO have. Also the same button for missile launching is used for scanning which is the equivalent of modifying a hand gun to function as a lighter when the safety is on. Additionally you will encounter a similar issue with your main guns, only two of which are deemed useful in combat but you may not want to toss your mining laser (oddly enough Elite Dangerous did the same thing).
AI in this game must stand for "Artificial Idiots" because it has caused me several saved game reloads. Once my ship auto piloted it's way into the center of a station trapping me inside and another time my fleet of rihannas tried to jump through a warp gate all at the same time causing what looked like an Autobahn pile up.
Graphics aren't bad for the most part but they do look years behind and nothing close to Elite Dangerous. The face textures for station crew however are kind of horrendous and everyone has a face only a mother could love.
It's unfortunate there aren't more people playing this game because a broader audience would mean more modders and the modding community is what made this game enjoyable (rather than a tedious head ach) to me. But the bottom line is, if you can put up with a bit of a learning curve, enjoy long relaxing space flights and dogfight style combat intertwined with the strategy aspect of fleet commanding then this game is worth buying but best wait for a sale because $40 is a bit much unless they release a 4k graphical pack and more updates (last one being released Mar 13) to fix the things so many people are complaining about.

By far one of the most original concepts in gaming that I have seen in a long time. After watching vids, reading a few short reviews and "first impressions", I was sure that I had a full understanding of what this game was like, what it was trying to achieve, and, most importantly, what type of titles it leaned on to give it its general feel. Very soon into the game I realized that everything I thought I knew about the game was wrong. There is really nothing like it. It doesnt appear to have "leaned" on or borrowed any ideas from other games. Game play is simple and solid. Nothing weird. Nothing that takes a special touch or extra time to master. So many games try to go crazy with making unique gameplay that they screw-up the basics. This doesnt do that at all. They dont need to. The originality is in the way the world unfolds in front of you and not in the form and function of core gameplay. So everything works just fine and anyone can start this game and start playing immediately.
This is one of those small publisher games that everyone should play. Its also a small publisher game that large publishers will likely borrow ideas from.
The color scheme is really pretty genius. I thought I would bring it up to full, regular color early on. But I didnt. I put just a touch of color saturation into the world and it seems that that graphics engine really looks cool that way. But again, its all preference and I cant believe that no other games had this option before.
Betrayer also fills a market gap on time period of the game setting. We have futuristic, modern(early 20th-21st century), medieval, and even ancient FPS games. But the 17th century is a relatively underutlized time period. I think the reason is that the time period itself is just not as popular as the latter I listed. But it does make for an interesting environment. Many games have a bow. But few games take place in the time period where the bow is a relatively strong option when compared to other weapons available to you.
It just seems that the devs and the publisher ticks all the right boxes when it comers to making a truly unique game. I have been watching this title for some time and I am glad that I finally pulled the trigger today and purchased it. But there is nothing to compare it to. So I cant say "If you like [insert game title here] then you will love this!", but I do highly recommend this game.
The only downside so far is that the enemies dont seem very challenging. With that being said, the stealth mechanics work just fine but because the enemies are easy, there is no real reason to be stealthy. That may change as I am only an hour or so in the game and I have now seen a new type of enemy. Will update if it becomes more challenging.

The short version – Paranormal investigator extraordinaire meets Far Cry.
You appear on a shore, behind you a ship. Likely the vessel that brought you here. A land devoid of color stay for an unpretentious amount of red.
This game is not just visually strking, its stunning. You are given the option to play in shades of grey or blast the color saturation up to see lush forests and gated strongholds.
The actual gameplay mechanics more or less revolve around two things. Exploration and killing things. Through your exploration you are likely to discover chests with goodies, pages with exposition that give insight into the goings on, gravestones among other things. Bascially, it's a completionists absolute dream or worst nightmare. The main draw though is to gain insight into the investigations about the ghosts.. I didn't mention the ghosts?!
There are two worlds/dimensions to explore, though the same clues and collectables can be found in either. The dark world, the world in perpetual night where hostile undead things will spring forth from underground to ward you off the investigation. Where items must be "cleasned of corruption" before preceeding. And the light or daytime world. Hostile baddies still are here but their purpose seems less warding and more left over neural pathways of repeated and ingrained behavior from their time in life. Very real since of LIMBO here.
Character progression is not necessarily "gated" but there is a very real MetroidVania -esk feel to upgrading your characters weapons from damage, speed of reloading, noise levels, amount of ammo held, amount of water (health packs) and charms that aid in movement speed, reload speed, and enemy detection.
The sound design is absolutely phenominal. Listening to the wind to find your direction. The wind insisting its innocent. Audio cues to detect the natives who are virtually undetectable otherwise. I should mention the wind I speak about is more a button to listen to the wind as the actual wind is used as a stealth mechanic to hinder your noise and detection level. The beasties make crazy scary noises, very distinct ones. To the point of knowing what enemy is behind the bush. The screams are unnerving, you don't really get used to to ambiance, comfortable perhaps, its always slightly disqueiting. Even at the end when I was fully confident in my ability to survive I was still nervous to face enemies to some degree. My only caveat remains that enemies don't react to your shots until their health is completely depleted and become victims to the physics. I just wish you could interupt their attack to some degree.
Overall, one of the more memorable and unique games I've played in awhile.

Calling this a horror game would be a bit misleading as it is less like Amnesia: The Dark Descent where death looms at every step you take and more akin to Bioshock where you are exploring the aftermath of some possibly terrible event. Even the basic bow feels nice to shoot with.   The only complaint I would have about combat is the lack of variety of enemies when in the dark side.  One other complaint would be the bug where stepping into certain rock formations can leave you perpetually stuck in them as you can never jump out, forcing you to save and quit and reload the game. The game can feel repetitive after a while, but for those looking to do a bit of exploring while shooting enemies with a one shot pistol or crossbow, this game is fun to play.  I hope the developers make another game in the same vein as this one as it shows good potential to become something even greater and more complex.

Magic Duels is quite similar to all the Magic 20XX titles that came before it, but with a more open deck builder (yay!) and a very limited card set (boo!)
The campaign missions are enjoyable, but fairly short, and the solo play experience is much more limited than was available in the other titles.  However, the actual style and quality of this experience is pretty much every bit as good as the other titles, with the benefit of being free.
You will quickly discover that it takes a long time to build up a decent collection of cards to work with, as the play-to-unlock approach is very slow.  This mostly doesn't matter, but there comes a point where the game decides you've played enough, and starts equipping the AI with high end chase rares in all its decks.  At that point you will need to either just make your decks more optimized (the AI is ok, but not smart), or switch over to playing more against humans for a while (who likely have decks like yours, except for the occasional paid guy with a ton of chase rares).
The card set is quite limited, but does offer a decent range of potential strategies.  Once you do unlock some cards, you'll have fun making a few decks.  I am guessing this is meant to be some sort of MtG starter experience.
If you enjoy MtG, then give Duels a play for some free quick enjoyment.  If you enjoy CCGs but haven't played MtG, then if you haven't already disappeared in a puff of broken logic, play it for a nice tiny taste of what MtG can be like.  And, if you don't enjoy CCGs, then don't bother, you won't like this either.

I could just describe it as cyberpunk rogue-lite twin-stic shooter.
But I have to say more because this is one of THE BEST GAMES I have played. Ever.
Visual side of the game is just gorgeous. Eye candy.
Especially if you are from VHS era. Or you like cyberpunk from 80'. Or neons (There is NEON in game's name for a reason :)
Music is well suited and I can't say bad word about other sounds.
And gameplay is the part where this game shines the most.
You play as one of five classes: hacker, cyber psycho, soldier, assassin or techie. They differ and prety much everybody states that one of them is overpowered. Although it would be different class each time. They are well balanced - have strong sides and flaws - all you have to do is find the one that suits you and your playstyle the most.
Levels are generated ramdomly (with exeptions) and each playthrough would differ. They are themmed acoridngly to floor you are currently in (like living quarters, hospital, warehouse). And there is boss after each floor.
Enemies have different abilities, strong sides and weaknesses.
Colectibles are changing rules drastically - you can collect new weapons, energy consuming secondaries and cybernetic implants. You are also collecting money.
Only way to spend all cash is to... die. You can buy upgrades of health, damage, energy and luck. But in first place buy all slots for cyber-implants (max 10). Then choose new "asset" and try again.
After few tries (and upgrades) game will become easy enough to kill last boss and finish story.. or not?
It took me about 6-7 hours to do that. Although you can start over - to fight against stronger enemies, to find new items and special rooms and see how far you can go. Theoretically dificulty can grow infinitively.
It's really worth buying.

This game is more like an introduction to Magic: The Gathering and its upcoming sets. Do not treat this as a substitute to Magic Online or paper Magic.
With that said this game does suffer a number of issues (right now). I'm pretty sure you can find them on other reviews but I guess I'll point out some of them quickly.
1. No chat. Period. If you're playing Two-Headed Giant, too bad, you'll just have to telepathically tell your opponent you're playing this or that.
2. Computer opponent cheats. Ok, most of the time when you lose you'll probably just blame it on the cpu having better cards than you... at the right time... with the right mana. Uh... on second thought maybe they are cheating. More often than not if you play a bunch of creatures, just the turn before you finish them off they'll probably play some game changing card such as destroy all creatures or all their creatures get lifelink. Deal with it, probably intended too, but we'll never know.
3. No upkeep phase. It's the game's terrible way to speed up the game by skipping this phase entirely unless it's mandatory by some effect. Again this is not a real MTG game just a reminder.
4. Game shuffles your deck horribly. Now this is what I hate most. The standard amount of lands for a deck is usually 24. If you play a deck with at most 4 or 5 mana cost cards, 24 lands should be good... right? Let's look at our starting hands:
2 lands 5 spells. Keep. 5 turns of no land draws.
5 lands, 2 spells, uh why not, Keep. 5 turns of all land draws.
6 lands, 1 spell. Keep. 3 turns of all land draws.
3 lands, 4 spells. Ideal hand but... sorry this doesn't exist. LOL
Mulligan any hand stated above: 3 lands, 3 spells: Indeal hand but again, sorry this doesn't exist. LOL AGAIN.
All 5 situations above appear very frequently. The game's shuffling coding is so bad that you tend to see these hands A LOT, except for the last two, they just don't seem to exist. And you know what's worse? When you are on the upper hand and then the opponent destroys/disrupts your field, you'll start drawing lands, not spells. The opponent will start drawing spells endlessly and you'll never have a chance to come back.
5. Computer plays the same "annoying" deck. This game likes to p1ss you off even further by playing the same lame deck every time. When i say lame i mean a deck that constantly destroys your field and/or disrupts your field just at the right time to draw out the game to a 20 minute battle. Before the Battle for Zendikar expansion, all the computer played was a black deck and they seem to get out languish at the right moment. When it wasn't languish it was a splash red deck with chandra's ignition. If not that then splash blue with displacement wave. Now with the expansion I have never seen a deck other than Blue/white splash whatever. The computer just constantly destroys your creatures with 2 mana spells or puts them back on top of your deck. So instead of a 20 minute battle it's a 30 minute battle. GREAT!
6. Gold and the method of obtaining them are pretty stupid. Daily quests are one way to get quick gold but seeing as how you only get 1 daily a day you'll be begging to pay Wizards some money for quick gold. A hard difficulty computer gives you 15 gold but only if you win and a pack costs you 150 gold. So that means it takes 10 games to get 1 pack and each game can last up to 20 minutes with the current t-bagging deck the computer only plays. What happens when you lose? You get a consolation prize: 15 minutes of your life wasted (meaning not even 1 gold is rewarded).
The community quest is one giant stupid quest that other players work together to complete to get... um... 40 gold. Yeah, the time limit is 7 days and even if you don't participate, if it is completed you still get the gold. Problem? If it is completed ahead of time, let's say with 3 days left we still have to wait it out. Hey look at the bright side, in one month we essentially get 1 free pack!!!.... yeah... wizards really cheapened out on community dailies.
UPDATE as of 3/5/2016: Apparently they had a "ghost" update. Certain dailies give up to 100 gold! They seem to appear frequently so that's a plus. Also community dailies now give 60 gold Whippie! Except we still have to wait til it ends even after it's finished. It's better than nothing.
So that's pretty much it. I would complain about limited card quantities but again this isn't actual Magic so it's understandable. This is just an introduction to Magic and it's upcoming sets so if you're looking for the real thing then  you're better off with that.
Rating: 3/5 Playable, just that it becomes quite bland with limited card pool with almost endless grinding. Improvement to obtainable gold makes this game a little more playable for a longer period of time. This is probably to compensate for the upcoming 2 sets, requiring even more gold to buy packs from both sets. Nevertheless, it shortens our "grinding" efforts by a bit.

Wow, just wow. This is an absolutely beautiful game. No game has ever impacted me as much as this one has, despite how minimalistic it may seem at first. But it is this minimalism that makes it so much more powerful and therefore have a greater impact. Most war games nowadays just show the "glory" of war - whether it be shooters or strategy games where you must crush all opposition. The games in which the civilian toll of war is explored are few and far between. Even strategy games where you besiege a city or planet to force the population to surrender gloss over the civilian toll. Probably the most notable instance of civilians being involved in a conflict game would be *that* level in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2. But even then, This War of Mine is completely unique in that you are controlling the civilians. While you may encounter combatants from either side, you don't participate in the conflict at all, you just try your best to survive on the peripheries of the unmentioned Civil War tearing the city and its population apart.
This is a very meaningful game in ways unlike most others. War is Hell, and no game demonstrates this as well as this one does. There are many conflicts in the world right now, and civilian casualties are a very real, and very sad part of this reality. Having a keen interest in military history, and knowing just how destructive city sieges are/were, let alone the bombing raids on cities, this game really does strike home just how terrible war is. The hard choices that civilians must make in order to survive in such situations is a really important part of this game, and truly one of the standouts. Just like in the real world, there is no black and white, just a whole lot of greys. You are unlikely to make it out of this game feeling like a champion; there are terrible decisions to make one after the other. The decisions you must make, and the consequences of these decisions, are incredible, and I needed to take a break after some of these decisions. No spoilers here, but you may feel like a disgusting monster, or a hero, and well... will either decision even affect the survival of your own group?
The playable characters, though with Eastern European names due to the geographical setting, all have excellent back stories and personalities which actually influence how they may react. Some characters may be more or less willing to do certain things, and certain actions will either positively or negatively your group's morale. Being caught on combatants aren't the only hazards, however, starvation, dehydration, and depression can be, and are real killers in This War of Mine. Depression is particularly well handled in this game, given the tough choices you must make, and the effect that these choices will have on your group. Special mention owing to the difficult nature of depression and other mental illnesses.
The graphics and sound may not be complex, but they convey the themes of the game excellently. For the game's theme, the simple 2d side view of the game works better than something which would be provided by either a first-person or third-person perspective. The 2d nature of the game allows you to better encapsulate what it is all about, from building your shelter to scavenging for supplies. The audio is also brilliant, with a haunting soundtrack punctuated by the sounds of combat in the distance.
Meaningful and excellent in a way that few games are, I cannot recommend this game enough.

I Have no Mouth and I Must Scream is based on the short story by Harlan Ellison (who also voices the evil AI, AM). It's a terrifying tale of 5 people that AM tortures for 109 years, until it decided to let them either confirm its reasons for hating them or redeem themselves.
As far as gameplay goes, there are a lot of that can go wrong (pixel hunting, easily missable clues, annoying mechanics - for example, some doors will work with "use" and others with "walk to") and there isn't much to see here.
The big strength this game has is its storytelling. The story deals with some mature themes such as torture,♥♥♥♥♥♥ murder. The journey to redeem each character isn't very long, it is though emotionally stressing. In case you want to get a specific ending, I'd highly recommend following a walkthrough, as you can easily miss some stuff and there is no going back once you do.
Overall, this was an interesting experience. It isn't relaxing, but rather thought provoking. Just wait until the end to see how it got its name.

Please read the review before deciding on if this was helpful because although there was a LOT i liked about this game I cannot reccomend it.
MAIN POINTS
+new type of gameplay
+emotion-evoking scenery, soundtrack, overall tone
-lacked any kind of emotional character attatchment in what should be an emotional game
-no replay value whatsoever
This is a game that was widely reviewed as a 'must play' and a 'gamechanger' because it puts you on the other side of war. Despite enjoying my playthrough (s, I lost quite a few times before surviving to the end) I didn't at all see how this was a moral or introspective game at all. What i will say is that the game makes you regret a choice to steal from a kind family or kill others to keep your own group alive, but the only consequence is a sad character which can be salvaged by having another character talk to them for a little while. I won't go as far as to say you don't care about killing people, but it is largely as inconsequential as killing in other games. You end up strategizing to keep your characters from being bothered by your orders rather than feeling guilty about them yourself.
That being said, I liked the game. It looked good, it had a really sad feel to it in the artwork and the music, and even in success you are pointed back to what you had to do to get there. The gameplay itself was unlike anything I had played before, but wasn't revolutionary to the point that this is a selling-point.
The game is not worth the money. If it is on sale, by all means try it on, it is a new type of experience. I had two huge problems with it that keep it from being worth the price.
-first, as I mentioned above, the game is really sold as a moral dilemma type game, where you sacrifice ease for doing the right thing, etc. It isn't that. If you want to challenge yourself by all means walk the high road, but there is not connection with any of the characters, especially the ones you are in control of. There is a little bit of background for each reavealed as the game progresses, but they all have repeated, generic lines, without voice acting, that occasionally play and do little to make them endearing, or even disliked which can be a connecting point.
-Lastly, and the main reason i can't reccomend is that the second I actually finished the game, I was done with it. There was absolutley no replay value at all. I don't want to sound hypocritical, because as you can see I put some serious time into this. I have often heard said about games that they can be addicting without being fun, and I never really bought it. This game is that. I had to survive, I had to win, but once I won I really wondered why the hell i bothered to do all that, I didn't even enjoy the ride.

OK, the questionable reviews and the fact I didn't have a lot of free time anyway when this game came out made me decide to just wait.  I've played every version of Civ since the two-floppy masterpiece that was the original Civ (and that includes Alpha Centauri) and I figured I would get this eventually, but wait until it was cheaper and I had more time.
Well, a "free to play" weekend is about as cheap as it gets and I happened to have a little time this weekend so I sat down with the game.  And I have to say, I was pleasantly surprised.  I was not initially all that impressed with the mechanics since it runs on the same engine... but what I began to realize is that I really felt like I was exploring something new again.  I knew I wouldn't have a LOT of time so I played on normal difficulty but I wasn't completely leaving the other factions in the dust... in fact, they were getting most of the wonders.  I found myself struggling with low health for my faction.  I found myself unsure what "the best" techs were to chase after with the new tech web design.  And I found myself feeling like I was playing a new game.  Even Alpha Centauri, as awesome as it was, still felt more like a redressed Civ than this does.  I did NOT have enough time to play to an endgame, but I enjoyed what I did play.
Just the same... the mechanics ARE much the same and I suspect that once I play it a few times and get a feel for the tech web that it will feel much more like an update to Civ 5.  I didn't snag it at the $30 it was this weekend, but I intend to once it falls more in line with higher end DLC, somewhere in the $10-$20 range.  Well, unless I find myself with a lot more time on my hands or start dwelling more on it in the meantime.   I recommend the game overall, but it's definitely what you'd expect by the version of Civilization after Civilization V; it's a sequel, but this time instead of updating the mechanics they changed the story line. I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream is a point and click adventure psychological horror game where a mad god-like supercomputer named AM (short for Allied Master Computer) has destroyed humanity in a way that is not explained in the game (though I personally think AM turned the world's supply of nukes against...well, the world) and left only a few survivors. How many, you may ask? 1,000? 3,000? Over 9,000? (Overused meme, sorry) Nope.
Gorrister, Benny, Ellen, Nimdok and Ted. AM has trapped these unfortunate five in a chamber in the hollowed out core of the destroyed Earth and is torturing these people. Not only that, that AM has altered to them to not age and be impervious to harm, meaning they can be tortured forever. When I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream starts out, Gorrister, Benny, Ellen, Nimdok and Ted, after 109 years of torture and humiliation, find themselves at a pillar with a burning message about how AM hates them etched into. AM tells them about a new "game" to play and asks "Which of you five would like to play my little game?" It's there that you can pick which of them should go first. When you make your pick, that survivor is whisked away to a strange place somewhere in time, where AM is watching them. There, you must make choices as what to do next and must help that unfortunate human solve the mystery of what is going on. After you beat a character's story, you must complete another character's story. In order to beat I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream, you must make the right choices and prove that humans are better than machines. If you can beat all the stories making the right choices, Gorrister, Benny, Ellen, Nimdok and Ted may have a chance at escaping AM and finally being free of their torments.
The game is unique in it's gameplay and story, and is one of the scariest games I've ever played. There are no cheap jumpscares like in Five Night's at Freddy's, nor massive amounts of gore like Harvester. The game has a general feeling of hopelessness and a very dark atmosphere, and what's more is that aside from brief moments of attacking something, Gorrister, Benny, Ellen, Nimdok and Ted have no real way of defending themselves aside from outwitting their adversaries. Even worse is the fact that you're always being watched, and unless you can outwit your stalker, you're just going to suffer more and more toment. All of the survivors are also pretty saddening too. They've all suffered what no-one should ever have to suffer in AM's complex, and they're all pretty messed up. Gorrister seeked death before he was captured by AM, Benny has been mutated into a sentient chimpanzee by AM, Ellen suffered something terrible in the past, Nimdok was old before AM captured him and has guilt for something horrible he can't remember doing, and Ted is even more paranoid than me (Until I played this game, I wasn't sure if that was possible) because he did something in the past. And yes, there is a good bit of disturbing imagery along the way.
I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream is truely a terrifying game which I'd recommend if you're a horror fan or want to play something original rather than all the first-person shooters that are everywhere nowerdays. However, if you are sensitive to ethical subjects like suicide, Nazism,♥♥♥♥♥♥ paranoia, insanity and guilt, I wouldn't recommend getting the game, as it has all those themes in it. Oh, and if you don't have a walkthrough of the game in another window or a friend to help you through, you won't get very far. Yeah, it's that hard.

I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream was a '67 post-apocalyptic short story by Harlan Ellison that released to immense critical acclaim, garnering it a Hugo Award. Its dark dealings with the subjects of pure human sin and the struggle for redemption gave it an enduring legacy that lasts to this day; however, the same cannot be said of the piece of garbage that came out of it. Turns out Ellison eventually helped write and direct this game of the same name, released in '95. Unfortunately, the game renders Ellison's most basic themes unrecognizable and instead offers a laughable imitation of the actual story.
While its overall atmosphere remains artfully crafted and deliciously gloomy, the game's graphics, point-and-click gameplay mechanics, and overall presentation have aged hideously - the game's "spooky" parts and cringe-worthy voice acting become just bad enough to be laughable at worst and just plain weird at best. It doesn't help that I Have No Mouth moves at a snail's pace; illogical "puzzles" hinder your progress in the game, and without a walkthrough to occasionally consult, it'll take you anywhere from 10 to 20 hours to complete the game.
As an added insult, the plot of Harlan Ellison's original short story is made very difficult to comprehend due to some puzzling plot changes and multiple endings/storylines to worry about. Several bugs, glitches, and clunky/antiquated mechanics will make your playthrough even more miserable. It's a true shame that I Have No Mouth fails to capitalize on Ellison's cerebrally intense work in the successful way that it deserves to.
Don't buy this unless you're just dying to see Ellison's writing represented in a different medium.

Overview:
Agent 47 returns in the fourth install of the series as a much older role but is still as deadly as ever.  The format is the same but with better graphics, mechanics, and variety.  A multiplayer element has been added along with leader boards and user content integration.
Pro(s):
Multiplayer: There is a simple and intuitive system implemented that allows players to create there own challenges and share them with the community.  One just plays the map of choice and assassinates a player chosen set of NPCs with a specific weapon and in a specific way.  You must first beat the challenge before you can share it with the community.
Con(s):
The Hitman Feel: To me this Hitman felt the least like a Hitman game.  The emphasis isn't so much on assassinating a high profile target as it is about sneaking to the next destination.  There are still plenty of high profile target assassinations but it is just not the same as the previous Hitmans.
The Stealth System: The developers this time round decided to give the player not only a mini-map with all the enemy units on it, but also a threat meter system that shows what direction and how threatening the threat is.  I felt this was a little overkill and made the stealthing much too easy.  Even on one of the harder difficulties these two systems make it very easy to play and towards the end of the game I had figured out how to basically sprint through the levels exploiting the system to my advantage.
Conclusion:
Another good installment in the Hitman series but not as good as Blood Money.  What this Hitman has over the older ones is more modern graphics and mechanics.  If your looking to try out the Hitman series this one isn't bad but I'd suggest Blood Money first.

Hitman: Absolution is an action/adventure stealth game that gives you multiple ways to eliminate your targets. The game is powered by the Glacier Engine 2, which is a graphical powerful house that covers the flaws in the game. Is Absolution worth your price?
Absolution is a double-edged sword where, at time, the game has good element while in the other hand, the game fell short. It is hard to describe the game. You do have multiple ways to assassinate your targets, but most missions have "one" unique way to kill your target to maximize the score to "Silent Assassin". The score system is an interesting mechanic, but the score system seems to treat players as a form of encouragement and punishment. For an example, if you accidentally messed up, points will be deducted from the score. If you have to improvise when you are caught, prepare your score to drop by a few thousands. In a way, the scoring system encourage players to play in a careful or stealthy manner. Unfortunately, the scoring system seems to "force" players to get the highest score as possible and psychologically restrict the player to play as freely he or she wants to play. In addiction, disguises mechanic is a failure. Putting on a disguise will make every enemy NPCs in the game to immediately recognize you when you get too close even for two seconds. While it is "understandable" that (some) people would recognize most of their buddies, it is also realistic that other people can't recognized 20+ people, by heart.
The story is pretty decent with solid voice acting and cheesy dialogue. Arguably, the best dialogue system comes from random NPCs with unique stories about them or giving hints about your objective. Absolution did very well with dialogue varieties for the NPCs and it is actually worth listening to. The mission levels feel very linear, but have environmental elements (like gasoline tanks, kitchen stoves, etc) to use for your advantage. There are 20 missions (or levels) in the game, but the game feels more of a drag as you progress.
Absolution tried to distinct itself from the other Hitman franchise and it failed. The developers acknowledge their errors and will compensate with the Hitman sequel. It is not a terrible game per se, but the number of flaws caused me to dislike the game as I finish through the ending. It is best to get it on sale for -75% or 80% off. In short, Absolution is a decent stealth game that should have been a lot better.

Have you ever wanted to sit in the captain’s chair of an all-powerful dreadnought with enough firepower to evaporate a fleet of foes? Then this might just be the game for you.
In Rebel Galaxy you take reigns of a huge ship and carve your own path through a randomly generated quadrant of space. You can choose the path of a hero and save those you meet from a vast array of pirates and rogues. Or you can fall prey to greed and debauchery, siding with the Red Devil Cartel and carve your way through every enemy that stands before you.
But that being said you could choose to do neither. There is always the option to be a humble miner and strike it rich in one of the vast amounts of asteroid belts and nebulae that litter the universe. Or perhaps the life of a trader is more up your alley, with a huge amount of commodities and a living breathing market place that varies from station to station and can be influenced by every day events the choice is yours.
The game looks great, it may not be the most stunning graphics available today but I loved how it looked. The ships have super details models, the stars and planets were a joy to look at. The battle effects were bombastic and colourful. Every shot from my huge broad side barrage lit up the night sky as it ripped through the hull of my enemies.
The audio is fantastic too. The music chosen for the sound track really adds to the title; each song filled with a defiance that really gets the heart racing and only adds to the reminiscence of Firefly or so many spaghetti westerns that said screw you to the man. The sounds were great as well, the whirring up to using your warp drive or the blasting sounds of laser-fire as it rips through shields and hull alike. The only let down is some of the voice acting was not stellar, but what’s there is good enough to convey the story.
Speaking of which the story serves only one purpose, to convey your ship from one star system to the next. Most of the adventure in this title is not from the main plot but from the tales you form yourself. Taking on a trade mission and getting ambushed in a system that is far beyond your ships abilities, warping in to help a trader being pirated by xeno scum or the joy of stumbling upon a fleet of pirates and having them throw your offer of surrender back in your face and blasting them to dust as punishment. The main plot is not bad by any means but the game is so much more.
Now gameplay, there are so many facets that it would be impossible to go through them all. The main game is either menu-based, exploration or combat. The menus are as expected. But the meat of the game is its exploration, so much to see and do and the ship controls fantastically. The one drawback is turning speed; the manoeuvrability of the larger ships is very slow and can make tight turns laborious. Combat on the other hand is snappy and fast and only hindered by turning speed. But since a lot of your turrets autofire you feel like a god when your ship can decimate everything in its path on its own and when finally you bring the broadsides to bear its goodnight to whomever you are aiming at.
The ships themselves are fully customizable. From engines to weapons, turrets to warp drives, even the size of your cargo hold, everything can be modified, changed and improved. Starting with the most basic of equipment you soon build a ship Mal Reynolds would be proud to call his own. From the tiniest corvette all the way to the mightiest of destroyers each has its own quirks and I enjoyed playing all of them.
This game is phenomenal and will have you enraptured for hours. Some people may feel it’s a little slow to begin with or the combat is a little tricky with slow aiming, but if you can get past all that it’s a real gem and I had a whale of a time with it. Plus at full price it is still cheap I would recommend buying this all day any day sale or no.

Good: The visual style is a smart way for players to seek small details in a seemingly endless forest. There are plenty of notable audio cues to guide the player to important quest objects as well as to detect enemies hidden in the forests. The combat mechanics are mostly well built and well polished, the encouters are mostly well balanced with just the right amount of complexity to make them challenging. The writing is creative even to the very end of the game and will still draw enough interest to carry on the story. The visual tones and audio cues allow this game to have a daunting feeling, even when you're 6 hours into the game, you'll steel feel some chill when you go into darkness.
Bad: The stealth mechanic is gimmicky, once you shoot an enemy your position is immediately known by all enemies within range of that enemy. 100% stealth kills is not possible in this game. The listening mechanic is also a gimmick that forces that game into a completely linear experience. While it may be possible to complete investigations in different orders, relying on listening will ensure that you complete the game in the same sequence every single time. They should have just used quest markers like in skyrim, it serves the exact same purpose while saving the player some extra time that is spent honing in on ghosts/objectives. Exploring and finding chests simply is not that rewarding, aside from the slight chance that you'll find a very good weapon, most of the time you'll just get some gold or a charm that you might not even want to use. Perhaps if they didn't have anything interesting to put in such a big forest, then maybe they shouldn't have spent the time on making it so big in the first place.
Ugly: This game simply turns into a linear chore after a while. You gather all the evidence while in light, then go into darkness and follow a string of dialogue and other bits to finish that zone. In essence this game is comparable to "Dear Esther" with some combat thrown into the mix. The primary content of the game revolves around going from place to place and reading dialogue. The combat itself might have some polished mechanics, its simply ruined by the unnecessary gear level system. There are like 4-5 different qualities of each weapon, and each one does slightly more damage than the last. the improvements are absolutely marginal, and in the final sequences of the game it seems frustrating that the items you just spent several thousand gold on don't seem to be making a real difference in how well you can kill things. Combine this with an annoying AI pathing system that ensures that the enemy you're about to hit with an arrow will zig zag around some terrain right as you shoot towards it, leaves the player longing for something slightly more polished and more fun.
I would give this game a 7/10. It's not perfect, but its unique in its own way and offers some decent fun factor, its worth playing, but get it on sale.

Starts strong but doesn't really manage to deliver.
In the beginning you will ooh at the environment, get lost in the soundscape and explore the stark and spooky environment collecting clues, piecing together what's going on and getting attacked by evil ...things. It really is quite brilliant. However once you've wandered through the tutorial and first area and you reach the second area you'll pick up the pattern - i.e. how the levels work - and there really is no variety from there on in. You do the same things you did in the first area in a slightly differently landscaped environment. It's not until (I think) the 6th environment that you get the shovel necessary to dig up rocky blobs that have been scattered across all the previous levels (and these are not helpfully marked on your map, nor do you have any way to make any marks on your map yourself) meaning you are left to painstakingly search your way through areas you've already been encouraged to ...painstakingly search your way through... again.
It starts out with a huge amount of promise - a really awesome environment, some great mechanics and the prospect of a pieced together story. However the gameplay really isn't expanded on past the first area and the story, rather sadly, ends very weakly. Your character's presence is never explained - you don't fit into any of the narratives really and the seemingly organic discovery of other characters stories is quickly rendered into a "go here, click this, go back, click that" as they are actually surpisingly linear and you simply can't discover the details out of order.
Oh and one of the achievements completed for me in game but not on steam.
It's totally worth a look at, especially if you can pick it up in a sale or a bundle because the first couple of hours you spend exploring will be truly spooky and quite awesome. Definitely will be keeping my eye on further offerings from this company and I may well return to this just to amble around in such a nicely crafted world.

This is a game, that somehow got into my steam library through some bundle i purchased.  I decided I might as well give it a go, and I am glad I made that decision.
In this simple to play, yet hard to master game you are in the role of a truck driver, who is driving a truck filled with stuffed animals.
Your goal is to get from one side of the map to the other in the shortest amount of time, losing as little animals as possible.
Each level takes about 30 seconds to complete, but you get addicted to completing them one after another and before you realize it, a whole day has passed by.
The levels are split into 4 groups or easy, medium, hard and extreme.
There are 5 medals you can collect in every level, and you need these medals to unlock more difficult levels.
The game soon turns into a very fun grind experience, as you replay the same level over and over again attempting to beat the time record or safely deliver the animals to the end. But that doesn't mean the game becomes boring, in fact it even becomes more interesting, and due to the cute nature of the stuffed animals you don't really get too frustrated with your failure.
Overall, I think this game is a real hidden gem and is worth the original price (but it still might be wiser to get it at a discounted price if you are unsure if you like this kind of game)
I give it a 7.3/10

This War Of Mine takes a new approach to the "post apoclipse" genre by, insted, making a game that feels real and impactful. You start out with three survivors, in my case I started with Pavel; a football player looking for his purpose in the tragity of war, Bruno; an overweight smoker but a damn good cook, and Katia; a young reporter with bargening skills. Katia was by far my favorite.
Pavel was killed pretty early on by a group of militants, "shot like a dog" to quote Bruno.  But Bruno was't exactly the most likeable person himself. I distinctly remember him stealing from an old married couple, the wife was sick and the husband was too weak to fight back so Bruno just took from them. And he seemed to be the only person not bothered by this.
Soon after the death of Pavel a new man arrived at the doorstep of my home looking for shelter, his name was Nicola, and of course we welcomed him into out home, and they lived happily in there own little house. It seemed somber and seprate from the war. And with nightly scavenging runs, food seemed to be in abundance.
But like all good things, this soon ended. On a supply run Katia was gathering supplies from an abandoned house, but as it happens it wasn't as vacent as she had originally thought. A young man burst though the door yelling:
"Get out of my F*****g house! I'll F*****g kill you!!!" as he shot Katia once. Katia ran for her life as the man continued to take shots, and she was hit once again before eventually escaping. This left her on the brink of death, and barely able to function, she was bandiged up and put to bed. But the house had supplies they need.
So the next night Nicola went out to gather the rest of the supplies, and this time he did it with a knife. He not only found supplies though, he also found out that the yound man was surviving with his parents; an old couple no younger than 70. But he was inexperenced and was soon cought and meeting a similar fate as Katia, exept Nicola didn't get away. He was on the ground, at the feet and mercy of the young man with the shotgun. And the young man let him go.
"Just this once," he said "but if you ever come back, I will kill you."
Nicola's injeries were far worse than Katia's. And they were out of bandiges. Nicola died soon after.
Enraged by his death, Katia decieded that she would deal with the pain of her wounds, and she would take everything from the bastrds that killed Nicola. But insted she ran into the young man's old father. He screamed for help and by instinct; Katia stabbed him twice. The young man and his mother didn't even fight back this time. They just sat at the old man's courpse and cried silently.
Katia died the next day, from what no one was sure. Maybe it was from blood loss, maybe from the overdose of pills she took to end her own life. Either way, Katia was dead and nothing in hell was gonna bring her back.
Then Naomi came. She was a happy, upbeat musican that seemed to carry a good energy where she went. But it wasm't enough help Bruno. He became severly depressed, and insted of taking the easy way out like Katia, he took all the food they had and ran while Naomi was sleeping.
Now Naomi lives alone, unable to find food, unable to stay warm, unable to heal from a wound she god defending from looters. She counts the days until eventually hunger, the cold, or even her own depression overtakes her.
This War Of Mine is not a game, it is an experence, and one that must be played. I have never felt so attached to anything other than my cat, then I was to these imaginary people that seemed to real, and personal and amazing. I wish you the best of luck.
But serously, PLAY THIS GAME!!!

I am a really big fan of Sid Meier's Civilization series, but not that big of a fan to have a total negative viewpoint of this version of Civ: Beyond Earth. I'm a Age of Empires fan, but I perfer RTS games like Blizzard's StarCraft, and Westwood's C&C.
So here is my take on Beyond Earth.   I wasn't able to complete a victory single-player game, although I was into a 500+ turn game taking my sweet time building up and sacrificing a Friendly.  I enjoyed burning my time.  I knew the free weekend wasn't long enough.  But long enough to get my attention.
My first few matches, I played the game like I didn't know how, (who reads the turtorials these days?)  That doesn't mean the game is hard to pickup, because B.E. is a revamp of the same gameplay style of Civ, it wasn't hard to adapt to the new build and command structure.   Pleasently it was a quick learn.
The graphics on a Dell Studio 1737's ATi HD 3650, was good enough to enterain me zoom in to watch the battle actions the game held up pretty well.  I had a couple moments where my laptop was warming up due to all the expansions I was churning out in game. (I was taking over colonies)  The screen would go blank.  blackout for a moment, and right back into playing.  Only once did the game crash and close, which wasn't a big deal, I was testing settings.
Overall, the game was very repetative conversation with other colonies. I wanted more discussable deal makings, and possibly a better way of letting friendly colonies know to STOP ATTACKING OUTPOSTS I trade with.   I mean twice my closest colony friendlies attacked outposts, I went in to defend.  I'd "condem" their actions, but that wouldn't stop them from destroying the first outpost.   I went to war, even with a friendly I gave cities to, whom quickly condemed my actions of defeating their attackers.    Stupid AI, is what I saw.
I really couldn't make every colony happy, no matter how I kept to not interacting with other colonies.  It wasn't until I did trades with all of them did the shaming would stop.  But as soon as one colony went to war with another, I was always in the middle of it.   ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ Humans! can't take the hint, we are on a new planet to get along with one another.   (Russians brought Vodka, what would you expect!)
I only had one colony friendly that didn't do♥♥♥♥♥♥with me.  I surrounded it, gave it cities to expand, protected it from other colonies that would attack it.  It was the only one that kept to my side... my inner side.  I quickly took over each hostile colony.  You don't realize how quickly your army and 15+ cities providing new units every 2-3 turns makes you overwhelmng.
You build those Networks, Roads to connect your cities, and you can transfer assets across the globe in one turn.  Quite awesome.  The one thing that I couldn't figure out was building Carriers.   I just didn't figure out building a Navy.  Although I kept upgrading things I nearly completed the whole Technology tree, and my Virtue's were to the third Teir.
Didn't matter, you want to have at least 6 explorers running at all times. When one dies turn out another one.  Colonies will complain you are "exploring" near them, but it doesn't matter, just humor them.  Keep the explorers going.  Quickly get trade convoys going to any and all outposts.
Is this game worth buying at $49.99?   Nope.  If this three day weekend is an example of a complete game, then I was sorely let down by the repetativeness of the dialog.  After all the previous Civ's this one lacks a whole lot.  Is this game worth $29.99? (-40%), Not unless I want to finish my current game.   Nope, still not worth it.  I can literally not give a damn about my 2 day long game if finishing it for $29.99.   However, is it worth buying in the Bundle $34.99 for 4 games.  YES.   But I already have all the previous ones, so...  damn...  I'll wait a bit longer for this to be on Summer Sale.

An idea.
Here's what this game is.
A brilliant, amazingly interesting, scandalous idea.
Let me explain;
In Hatred, you play a rather demonic looking character who keep reminding me of Dracula from Castlevania: Lord of shadows. Huge, monstrous, long hair... The only difference is... Well, Dracula was a kick♥♥♥♥♥vampire of amazingness who was a violent killer with remorse and a suave, smooth voice. The Hatred guy, on the other hand, is a blank canvas of a man with a voice like he was chewing on pebbles or marbles or god knows what and who's fed up with the world. In a blind rage, he decides to go on a killing spree to take down as many people as possible and then die "A violent death".
The lack of a personnality sure doesn't help with the character being an horrible psycopath... In fact, he feels more like a guy who took a bit too much of (Insert the name of any drug you want) and went batshit crazy seeing the world through Team Fortress 2's psycho's eyes. You go around a black and white (For reasons unknown) level, looking at seemingly different maps but with certain points definetly the same (Looking for something to blow up a house? Look in the garage. Everybody seems to keep some propane in there right next to a jerry can of gas and a container full of hydrogen.) and with blank enemies who have repetitive dialogue and, god forbid, repetitive DEATH. Wow, just wow. This is an absolutely beautiful game. No game has ever impacted me as much as this one has, despite how minimalistic it may seem at first. But it is this minimalism that makes it so much more powerful and therefore have a greater impact. Most war games nowadays just show the "glory" of war - whether it be shooters or strategy games where you must crush all opposition. The games in which the civilian toll of war is explored are few and far between. Even strategy games where you besiege a city or planet to force the population to surrender gloss over the civilian toll. Probably the most notable instance of civilians being involved in a conflict game would be *that* level in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2. But even then, This War of Mine is completely unique in that you are controlling the civilians. While you may encounter combatants from either side, you don't participate in the conflict at all, you just try your best to survive on the peripheries of the unmentioned Civil War tearing the city and its population apart.
This is a very meaningful game in ways unlike most others. War is Hell, and no game demonstrates this as well as this one does. There are many conflicts in the world right now, and civilian casualties are a very real, and very sad part of this reality. Having a keen interest in military history, and knowing just how destructive city sieges are/were, let alone the bombing raids on cities, this game really does strike home just how terrible war is. The hard choices that civilians must make in order to survive in such situations is a really important part of this game, and truly one of the standouts. Just like in the real world, there is no black and white, just a whole lot of greys. You are unlikely to make it out of this game feeling like a champion; there are terrible decisions to make one after the other. The decisions you must make, and the consequences of these decisions, are incredible, and I needed to take a break after some of these decisions. No spoilers here, but you may feel like a disgusting monster, or a hero, and well... will either decision even affect the survival of your own group?
The playable characters, though with Eastern European names due to the geographical setting, all have excellent back stories and personalities which actually influence how they may react. Some characters may be more or less willing to do certain things, and certain actions will either positively or negatively your group's morale. Being caught on combatants aren't the only hazards, however, starvation, dehydration, and depression can be, and are real killers in This War of Mine. Depression is particularly well handled in this game, given the tough choices you must make, and the effect that these choices will have on your group. Special mention owing to the difficult nature of depression and other mental illnesses.
The graphics and sound may not be complex, but they convey the themes of the game excellently. For the game's theme, the simple 2d side view of the game works better than something which would be provided by either a first-person or third-person perspective. The 2d nature of the game allows you to better encapsulate what it is all about, from building your shelter to scavenging for supplies. The audio is also brilliant, with a haunting soundtrack punctuated by the sounds of combat in the distance.
Meaningful and excellent in a way that few games are, I cannot recommend this game enough.
