Please read the review before deciding on if this was helpful because although there was a LOT i liked about this game I cannot reccomend it.
MAIN POINTS
+new type of gameplay
+emotion-evoking scenery, soundtrack, overall tone
-lacked any kind of emotional character attatchment in what should be an emotional game
-no replay value whatsoever
This is a game that was widely reviewed as a 'must play' and a 'gamechanger' because it puts you on the other side of war. Despite enjoying my playthrough (s, I lost quite a few times before surviving to the end) I didn't at all see how this was a moral or introspective game at all. What i will say is that the game makes you regret a choice to steal from a kind family or kill others to keep your own group alive, but the only consequence is a sad character which can be salvaged by having another character talk to them for a little while. I won't go as far as to say you don't care about killing people, but it is largely as inconsequential as killing in other games. You end up strategizing to keep your characters from being bothered by your orders rather than feeling guilty about them yourself.
That being said, I liked the game. It looked good, it had a really sad feel to it in the artwork and the music, and even in success you are pointed back to what you had to do to get there. The gameplay itself was unlike anything I had played before, but wasn't revolutionary to the point that this is a selling-point.
The game is not worth the money. If it is on sale, by all means try it on, it is a new type of experience. I had two huge problems with it that keep it from being worth the price.
-first, as I mentioned above, the game is really sold as a moral dilemma type game, where you sacrifice ease for doing the right thing, etc. It isn't that. If you want to challenge yourself by all means walk the high road, but there is not connection with any of the characters, especially the ones you are in control of. There is a little bit of background for each reavealed as the game progresses, but they all have repeated, generic lines, without voice acting, that occasionally play and do little to make them endearing, or even disliked which can be a connecting point.
-Lastly, and the main reason i can't reccomend is that the second I actually finished the game, I was done with it. There was absolutley no replay value at all. I don't want to sound hypocritical, because as you can see I put some serious time into this. I have often heard said about games that they can be addicting without being fun, and I never really bought it. This game is that. I had to survive, I had to win, but once I won I really wondered why the hell i bothered to do all that, I didn't even enjoy the ride.

Rebel Galaxy is a fun space combat/trading/mining/exploration game, giving you a lot of ways to earn money and kick♥♥♥♥♥ The ship piloting controls are on a 2d plane, which may seem frustrating to some, but it's honestly a great decision. This allows you to go back to stages and have increasingly awesome characters. This game was my life until I beat it. Then I pushed away from the table. Starts strong but doesn't really manage to deliver.
In the beginning you will ooh at the environment, get lost in the soundscape and explore the stark and spooky environment collecting clues, piecing together what's going on and getting attacked by evil ...things. It really is quite brilliant. However once you've wandered through the tutorial and first area and you reach the second area you'll pick up the pattern - i.e. how the levels work - and there really is no variety from there on in. You do the same things you did in the first area in a slightly differently landscaped environment. It's not until (I think) the 6th environment that you get the shovel necessary to dig up rocky blobs that have been scattered across all the previous levels (and these are not helpfully marked on your map, nor do you have any way to make any marks on your map yourself) meaning you are left to painstakingly search your way through areas you've already been encouraged to ...painstakingly search your way through... again.
It starts out with a huge amount of promise - a really awesome environment, some great mechanics and the prospect of a pieced together story. However the gameplay really isn't expanded on past the first area and the story, rather sadly, ends very weakly. Your character's presence is never explained - you don't fit into any of the narratives really and the seemingly organic discovery of other characters stories is quickly rendered into a "go here, click this, go back, click that" as they are actually surpisingly linear and you simply can't discover the details out of order.
Oh and one of the achievements completed for me in game but not on steam.
It's totally worth a look at, especially if you can pick it up in a sale or a bundle because the first couple of hours you spend exploring will be truly spooky and quite awesome. Definitely will be keeping my eye on further offerings from this company and I may well return to this just to amble around in such a nicely crafted world.

Highly recommended. This is an interesting, immersive space/science fiction game. I like games that have "grand strategy" as an element, and this certainly does. I didn't want to stop playing, and the first time I began I played for six hours with just a few breaks. I restarted some games to explore different aspects (races, empires, etc.), so I'd have a feel for the overall experience. This game has broad tech-trees that may (and... may not) be interconnected, which means a player isn't locked into that old system of "Research Pottery --> Research Ritual Burial ---> Research Ironworking", etc., that is common in a very popular game of civilization-building games most people are familiar with. Although I'm not a "techie" and could never develop a mod myself, the game studio must've been designed this in such a way as to foster creativity in players/modders. There is a fascinating, comprehensive, detailed, and expertly mastered mod for a Space Opera Saga whose Seventh Episode will reach cinemas in Winter 2015. Having been born in 1977, I really enjoy not only that particular mod, but also both the capabilities inherent in this game... and the very game itself. I don't just play this game for a galactic Empire or a rebel alliance, I play this game because this game is so much fun even if those weren't available.

Betrayer is an interesting take on survival horror genre. The developers trust the players enough not to lead them by the hand. The gamer is given quite a huge map to explore, filled to the brim with hidden fragments of a spooky story (or, rather, stories) to piece together. This leads to an amount of freedom not usually found in similar titles. Artsy graphics, ambient sounds and some good writing create a truly eerie atmosphere and add much to the experience.
On the other hand, one of Betrayer's core mechanics — the stealth — is deeply flawed, and the overall gameplay starts to get repetitive towards the end.
Nevertheless, a decent effort by a talented team.

I can't believe I'm playing a game older than myself yet still feel intrigued.
Supervised by the original story writer himself, this is more of an interactive story than a point-and-click game. Every actions you take, every decisions you make, will affect the outcome (and ultimately the fate of each characters). With multiple ending you can try to get the ideal happy ending, book's canon ending, or even new endings not implied in the book.
Story and narration wise, it's like someone is reading a book for you. You can just take it easy and enjoy the narration, but considering it is interactive, you must think before choosing your actions. Also do take note it's a horror story, but instead of cheap jumpscares common in today's horror genre, this game gives you the tension to always keep you on edge. "Did I do it right?" "Am I doing something wrong?" "What am I supposed to do to not mess everything up?"
Overall, a great game if you're into reading. Will definitely play again to get all endings.

I have no mouth, and I must scream is a classic adventure game first released back in 1996. Since its release, it's acquired a large cult following, hailing it for its dark and very mature storyline. It's based on a short story by Harlan Ellison, released in 1967.
The game takes place 109 after the destruction of mankind. A computer calling itself AM, which was originally created to wage war with the other super powers. Wars had become so complex that humans could not oversee them, which resulted the three super powers (USA, Russia & China) creating their own super computers, which ended up wiping out humanity.
AM hates humans. It hates humans for what they've done. Hate drives it to torture 5 specific humans, the last living humans on earth, making them immortal, so that it can torture them forever. These 5 characters are the characters that you play as.
Each character gets its own short (<1h) storyline, where you have to guide them through their own personal hell, based on what AM view as the most just punishment for their past deeds.

The game plays like a typical mid 90's point & click adventure game. You have an inventory, and most of the puzzles are about figuring out which item goes where. Many sections have multiple solutions, and depending on which solution you find, you'll get a different final ending ("kinder" solutions generally result in better endings). Actually solving the puzzles needed to progress the story is quite easy, far easier than the puzzles of most contemporary adventure games, but figuring out how to get the good ending often feels like you're trying to read the puzzle designers mind. It feels like this was made with replay value in mind, as the game is quite short, but it ends up being rather frustrating, as you can end up getting a bad ending simply because you walked through a door at the wrong time, without the game properly warning you about it.
The graphics is quite good for the era. While the animation quality might not be up to par with the greatest games of its genre, the scenes are very atmospheric and all feel like they're made to convey a certain mood.
The voice acting is also good, but not outstanding. Compared to its contemporary counterparts, it would be considered really good, but voice acting tends to be a bit better these days. Still, all the voices fit, and the voice actors do a good job at conveying how their characters feel when they speak.
I have no mouth, and I must scream is a game that I feel has a well deserved good reputation. While it might be a bit too short, and trying to figure out what the developers were thinking when you try to solve the puzzles if you want a good ending is not always fun, but the story is very well told. When I say that the story is "Mature", I don't mean mature as in there being a lot of gore & nudity in the game, but rather it's a story dealing with some very dark subjects in a mature way, and this helps lift the game above the masses. It might not be a perfect game, but for anyone who enjoy point & click adventure games aimed at a more adult audience, it's a must play.

I really should just write these reviews on a movie site instead.

This is an interesting game... that said, I thought I'd like it more than I did, but it wasn't terrible by any means. Just, not quite what I hoped.
My general feeling on this title is it just sort of throws you into a scenario with a vague sense of what to do from beginning til end. This would not be a bad thing, but the game is remarkably... well, empty. You cross large tracts of wilderness looking somewhat blindly for clues to an investigation as well as treasure. The former you can locate easily by using a special listening function whereas the latter is just a matter of being in the right place to hear the chime. There's a great deal of backtracking and exploration, which I usually like to some degree, but the landscape has very few landmarks, let alone features to it. Everything winds up looking pretty much alike and the setting (not the scenario) lacks character.
As for the plot, it mainly ties together in the end, although I didn't find the overall investigation to be particularly interesting. There's a lot of wandering from one empty town to another, reading small notes and talking to conveniently amnesiac wraiths in a poorly utilized 'otherworld', but you never really feel for anyone or care as the NPCS are a mix of boring and a--holish. It's mainly just a series of exercises that feels more like padding out the game than really telling a story, at least until the end.
There's a lot of potential in Betrayer, but it just doesn't go far enough with the premise or the writing to really sell it. I enjoy exploration titles a lot, but like many things in Betrayer, the experience is sort of empty. Mind you, I don't mean to sell this as a very negative review, but this is already a very niche title that doesn't really work for me in execution.
Be advised, there is a suspicious amount of downvotes for any negative review of this title. Keep that in mind when you read the positive ones.

I had never played Dead Rising 1 as it was not on PC. I was very into L4D2 logging over 200 hours into it. I had expected Dead Rising 2 to be in the vain of L4D but in third person and whole lot more zombies. Instead I got an open world zombie game with slow pacing, long grind, clunky combat and unbalanced boss fights.
Pros:
Runs well on a AMD Phenom II X4 940, 2GB DDR2 and GTX 670. Sometimes under 60fps.
Cons:
-Huge grind. As described below about boss fights, you need to level up in order for boss fights to be fair. I am at level 20 and boss fights are still not balanced at all. Avoiding boss fights can be futile at times as described below.
-No running. You walk faster by levelling up. Levelling up auto assigns attributes (attack, speed, life etc..) so their is no customization. I am currently at level 20 and still walk very slow.
-Time based gameplay, all missions are based on a certain time, the absence of running really adds frustration to this as you cannot get to some missions in time, especially story missions that forces you to load from a user savepoint which could be 30 mins back.
-Save points are limited to "restrooms", if you can find them and remember to do so. Current game design is that after every mission the game should auto-save. Not with Dead Rising 2, if you had beaten a hard fought boss, you must remember to find a restroom ASAP. Even then, you could be low on health after this boss fight and die on the way to a restroom.
-Numerous boss fights that are unbalanced. You need to be leveled up and on a 2nd playthrough in order for the boss fights to be fair. These boss fights show up in your missions list and you have to assume from the mission description that you will fighting someone, it doesn't tell you outright. I essentially have to read, thnk and pick rescue type missions in order for me to level up so when I do encounter bosses, it will be more fair but so far still unbalanced. Even if you intend to avoid boss fights, some missions force you to go into a certain area which will trigger a boss fight, and because you walk so slowly, it is difficult to evade the boss fight after

I had my eyes on this game since its very release, back in March. Watching its updates, reading further reviews about its content and gameplay, I saw quite a fair amount of both appraisals and negative criticism. I was sceptical for a while, but the months reinvigorated my interest as I witnessed some clever updates addressing a few issues that were hindering its potential. Then I recently bought it and, about only one week and a half afterwards, I've finished it.
Betrayer is a fantastic indie enterprise, like few I've seen. It combines visual astonishment (directly affecting the atmosphere of ethereal mysteries) with no-nonsense combat, enhanced by the evolution of enemy hordes and also of the player's arsenal and fighting techniques. Running about with musket and bow has never been so much about timing each one's shot and adapting them for the precise circumstances. Missing *your* shot might very easily mean taking the enemy's back at you, since their aiming is relentless, and your health bar, friable.
The theme is reasonably innovative, and the game's approach is downright unique. The year is 1606, and you land on Virginian soil, only to find a very primitive colonial process that has crumbled under inner conflicts and treason. On the other side, Native Americans are hunted, violated and burnt, as the names of their ancestors slowly fade away throughout the narrative process. The several notes found in the game tell (in fairly neat writing) of leaders from both sides being conspired against, sons and daughters being slain or assimilated. The player is then left with a visual that matches the storyline: ghosts float about the dense woods without remembrance of their actual lives, and beg for closure for their sins and/or misfortunes. The player may or may not remind them of who they were and what they did, bringing them either peace or torment. Amidst all this otherworldly saga, the true game's nemeses are embodied by steel-armoured bears (the colonisers) or burnt owls (the natives), which can be interpreted by their roaring or hooting beyond their human silhouettes.
Play this game bearing in mind that it is a heavy experience. Being able to adjust colour saturation and contrast is also a nice feature for atmosphere adaption. If I were to point out a mistake, it may have been the walking and searching necessary to locate clues, letters, chests, and weapons. These are vast forested lands that are excellent for territorial combat, but a bit tedious for repetitive treasure hunt. Apart from that issue, a game that is well worth the cash and is beautiful to explore.

An old game from 1995, but keeps its ground even to this day.
Five people with their own interlocked stories, you pick in which order they are played out. Its a point and click linear adventure game with a very dark story and atmosphere. Each character has a good deal of depth to them, giving you reason to succeed.
Each character leans toward a particular topic, such as sexual assault, genocide and murder, betrayal, and abuse. It is very mature and contains a lot of content that some might find sensitive.
The graphics are for an old game so I can't comment on that, but it seems like were relatively good for its time. The game itself is simple enough, only on several times did I need a guide to progress.
Easy to solve puzzles with some that make you think for a second. I'm not a really big puzzle player but I found no problems throughout the entire game.
Its short, each story only being 1-2 hours long, depending on how much you want to explore for a total of 5-10 hours of gameplay.
Give it a go, its a fun journey and the game is pretty cheap and a steal on sales.
Personal Rating: 3.5/5

Betrayer is a first person stealth-survival game with a slight twist of horror that is all about getting lost in the forest. The storyline is as follows, you wake up in a strange place with amnesia as you do in all horror games and then decide to make your way into the woods. You soon come across basic weapons as well as easy to kill enemies, You also find out that you are being followed my a mysterious maiden in a red cloak who most likely became lost on her way to granny's and stumbled into betrayer. After you exit the starting path you find yourself in a more open area with an abandoned English settlement where you can perform a large variety of interactions including having the ability to access a completely unmaned store that you still have to pay for for some reason, you can talk to the maiden in red who will ask you to find her lost sister, you can find clues as to what happened to the town, you can use one of the games almighty waterbarrels which restore all your health, and lastly, you can ring the bell that takes you into dark world. Dark world is a (predictably) much darker version of the regular world except you can talk to the shades in the settlements, the regular conquistador enemies will be replaced with skeletons that shoot magic missiles at you, and lastly you can cleanse the totems which involves fighting off a few waves of skeletons. If you cleanse all three totems in an area, you'll be allowed to travel to the next area.
Stealth combat consists of either sneaking up to the conquistadors and putting an arrow through their skull, however if you're spotted then the game really urges you to have pinpoint acuracy because only a headshot will take down an enemy in one hit and when ammo is rare and your firearms have fifteen second reload times you really don't want to miss. However I cannot stress how satisfying it is to kill enemies in this game. The sound of a helmet being forced in followed by the crack of a skull breaking of an enemy that kills you in three hits feels amazing. My only complaints with this game are that a lot of the time you have no idea what you're doing and there aren't many guides online to help, the NPC's all have the personality of a baked potato, and that there isn't really much of a penalty for dying.
So just to clarify
PROS;
-capturing story
-beautiful, fresh art style
-simple barter system
-Dark/light world theme works very well
-simple, yet immensely satisfying combat
CONS
-combat can be a little too easy if you have easy access to a water barrel
-Charecters can be dull at times
-you get lost, A LOT
Overall I would give this game an 8 out of 10 and would recomend it to anyone even remotely interested in this game.

Negatives:
- Lack of innovation. This is a copy of the (working) Wing Commander Privateer formula, albeit in two dimensions.
- Balance issues when it comes to weapon choice.
- Minor progression spiking issues. For example, there are times when you find one salvage item that is worth more than your next 10 entire missions.
- Lack of end game. Basically once you have Mark 6 shields and pulse turrets the game is over.
- The decision to make this a 2D game makes little sense to me. It takes away from the astrobatics experience and simplifies gameplay.
- Some tedious game mechanics with warp travel. Finding an asteroid belt with some salvage seems meant to be a nice surprise, but in reality it's just annoying because it drops you out of warp and the only salvages (as far as I know) which give high-credit equipment rather than commodities are the ones you take off of ships. The number of times I had to veer just to the right or left of an asteroid and use thrusters to get back into a safe state to use warp drive was far too many.
Positives:
- Provides good value for $20, especially if you are a huge fan of the series' that it takes from (Privateer, Dark Star One).
- Stable. No real performance issues.
I know the negatives list is longer than the positives, but I would still recommend the game if you are a space exploration fan just looking for a remake of Privateer without the daunting depth of X3.

I don't remember purchasing this game but if I did, it was for a very low price.
I read the excellent short story that this game was based upon years ago, and that made me want to try this.
I wasn't disappointed.  The game uses a post-apocalyptic universe involving a malevolent A.I. to explore the various psychological and moral shortcomings that human beings have in general, and many of the choices you make will draw upon your personal ethics.  Sometimes, the right choice is very clear, but there are other moments when you're in a "damned if you do, damned if you don't" kind of situation.
For this reason, the game can be quite challenging since the very best ending can only be obtained if you fill up the characters' Spiritual Barometers, and there are several ways to complete a scenario or die trying. Generally, you can increase your Spiritual Barometer by engaging in noble acts while avoiding ignoble ones, but I still had trouble figuring out which choices were the best for some characters (Ellen, in particular).
This is one of the main flaws in this game, as some of the puzzles are counterintuitive and require you to save and reload your game several times in order to achieve the best result.   Moreover, I encountered a couple game-breaking bugs during the end scenario and also when I played Benny.   You should definitely keep multiple saves before making a story-altering choice.
Despite the game's technical and logical flaws, this is one of the most interesting and disturbing adventure games that I have ever played, and I highly recommend trying it out if you want to experience a great sci-fi/horror story.

This great sci-fi horror story lost some of its edge when it was adapted into a point ‘n’ click game, and it does suffer from many gameplay ailments that were widespread at that time, but ‘I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream’ is still one of the essential titles for any adventure game fan.
Harlan Ellison is one of the most-acclaimed and productive American science-fiction writers, author of hundreds of stories, including ‘I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream’. It is a dystopian tale set 109 years after a sentient supercomputer, AM, eradicated the entire human race… save for five, who are kept virtually immortal for AM’s sadistic pleasure.
While the setup is the same, the novella and the game have different plots. The former was about the group trying to find canned food and eventually killing each other; the latter is split into five scenarios, all written by Ellison, exploring these people and their psyches by confronting them with their own (rewritten) past… a past some of them forgot during their long suffering. These stories are narrated by AM (voiced by Ellison), and the passive-aggressive tone does a great job filling them– and the player– with dread.
AM’s twisted mind is reflected in the game mechanics and puzzles. As usual for a point ‘n’ click of that era, you mostly spend your time with hopeless pixel hunting, but there is an added mechanic: every scenario has several outcomes based on how thorough the player is finding and solving optional puzzles and tasks. If you can get the best outcome for everyone, you may have enough mental health to reach the end of the final puzzle and see the hidden optimistic ending; otherwise, you’ll see the canonical one.
Strange enough, the “bad” ending somehow fits the story better; it is a pessimistic tale, a rare sight in adventure games. Rare enough to earn this one a place in the collection of all point ‘n’ click fans, even today.

That was a nice 20 hours experience. :-)   Not less, and no more.
+ Simple gameplay, nice combat mechanics. You're flying in 2D on a med to large ship. So fight mechanics is like a sea battle. You have broadside weapons you have to aim with, you have turrets / torpedos / mines. You can also ram opponents with a special deflector (buy fast thrusters and a fast ship for that!). It is up to you to change the ship and fight dynamic and distance.
+ Nice music (you can set it to your own music if you wish).
+ Bright and colorful space. I know that this is unrealistic. But this is just the thing I wanted in X3 and the thing I've enjoyed in Freelancer. You can freely travel among a few systems with a warp  jump drive. Driving during a warp jump within a solar system is cool!
+ The space exploration is a nice part of gameplay. Although, it's not very rewarding. You'll find some bounties, stations to be hacked, save a lot of miners from pirates (or the other way). But you won't be able to find any true gems / hidden space stations (the thing I've enjoed in Freelancer).
+ Trading looks nice. However, never tryed that. Just like the feeling that I could. Newsboards, station switching states. Lively (not very lively, still nice).
+ Pirating ability and "change the side" possibility is also a nice part of the game.
+ Something original world setting. Looks a bit like Warhammer (edge of it) - you're trading with religious tracts! It's shame that they didn't say more about it.
- Few (only one) side quests. Quests from mission board sometimes challenging (take "hard" and "very hard" only!) but, you'd get dull after 20-30 of them.
- You do not really influence the solar system state with your action. So.. No stategy here. I think it would be nice to take stations from one side to another and do some other sort of global things (like in Pirates or in Space Rangers / Seadogs).
- Bad keyboard mapping and froms GUI. At least for PC users. At least during first 2 hours of gameplay. You'll get used to it and it would be OK after an hour of gameplay. In general, the fight controls are nice. But....  First, there were no presets for some important buttons, so I had to manually select some buttons. Then I changed the whole mapping since some of the presets were awful. Then I figured out that I am not able to use my Thrustmaster gamepad here (so what is "full controller support"?). it took me 3 minutes to figure out how to close the tutorial message. It took me 2 hours to find the right spot where to click "sell this good" in the commodities market. After 10 hours I've figured out that I can use arrow keys instead (which I set to do nothing in game settings), not with WASD keys (wich I used). After 3 hours of gameplay I've figured out how to use map (press 1 and use the mouse wheel). After 17 hours of gameplay I've figured out that there is a menu when you're in space where you can switch between missions / cargo (here's how one drops the cargo!) / AI turret preset (wow! but still this wheel widjet works strange). And it turned out that I can change pages only right to left. Not the other way (there is "Esc" button assigned to it wich should change the page, but closes the window).
- One button to rule them all: collect cargo with tractor beam, warp jump, receive incoming hail, close windows. Everything is done with holding the same button. Most of the time it's ok. But I hate the moment when I want to collect that damn cargo and talk to the pirate instead (for 10 times in a row, having him in a long range). Or want to jump and hear only "the ordinance is full".
- Buy the I still do not understand how to sell ordinance. Took something in the beginning of the game and now I cannot collect any more and sell it. I do not use rockets / mines, though.
So, this is a nice arcade game. If you like arcade games that took place in space, you'll gonna enjoy it. If you prefer solid-like games (like X3 or Elite) - than you'll probably get bored at one point.
Kinda boring, but it's pretty entertaining, if you have a tiny pea-brain like mine. Bottom line: Don't get it if you don't like waiting...

Update: I have now beat this turd. The last few levels are really easy if you crouch and fire at the extreme range of your rifle or mounted turret. Charging in will get you killed.
There are, in fact, two brutal metal songs, one briefly heard from some headphones as diegetic sound and the other plays during the end credits.
Reactors don't work that way.
Protip: Hitting spacebar while sprinting makes you do a diving roll. Tutorial did not mention this.
Expectations:
The original Postal but better, with slick graphics, cover destruction, blistering death metal and Nathan Explosion saying stupid♥♥♥♥♥♥over it all. As an added note, I knew nothing about this game (or its controversy) until yesterday and was planning on picking it up and enjoying a guilty "b-movie" experience. I was also curious as to what could possibly rate as AO, assumedly without graphic sexual content, and still be sold on Steam.
Reality:
I'm not sure if this game wants to be serious or farcical, but it fails at both. There is no humor to be found here, except for the few half-hearted smirks I had, which stemmed from the protagonist's terrible lines of dialog. Sadly, the dialog is not grimdark enough to actually be silly and  too overblown to be impactful . Hatred can't be taken seriously because there is nothing to take seriously; Nothing of substance, neither in its gameplay nor its presentation.
Gameplay:
Good:
The "kill to heal" mechanic can occasionally lead to some tough tactical choices in a firefight. If you retreat, the fact that your "health pickups" run away from you or scoop up weapons to shoot you still provides constant pressure and adds an element of chaos to the proceedings.
The explosions look pretty cool and blowing buildings apart is pretty satisfying.
The levels are much larger and more detailed than I expected.
Bad:
No brutal metal songs.
It has a sewer level.
The keyboard & mouse controls for Hatred are sluggish and imprecise. Navigating through doorways or rubble is particularly frustrating at times. You are supposed to be able to climb through large windows and vault over low obstacles, such as benches or counters, but I only managed to accomplish that a handful of times. The rest of the time I spent running in place and being frustrated.
The black&white graphics look reasonably good, but they obscure the actual gameplay. Losing track of your targets or your player's position in a run n' gun shooter because it is too dark to see or  too bright to see the muzzle flashes of who is firing at you is not a good thing. Even with the aid of the minimap, targets are often difficult to place.
Pressing the highllight key (left alt) will outline enemies in red, and show you where items are located, but it ruins the aesthetic by being too garish. A more subtle effect would look better. Briefly highlighting the enemies as they fire on you might help alleviate some of the general gameplay problems.
Weapons are not picked up unless you step directly on them. Given the fact that you can't see anything half the time and combined with the control issues, you will be hitting the highlight key a lot.
Story/Theme:
There is no controversy to be found in this game over the violence, as there is no greater context for it. I have mowed down helpless civilians begging for their lives in COD's "No Russian" mission and felt kinda bad about it. The COD character was ostensibly trying to be a "good Guy" by doing his duty for his country and gaining the trust of terrorist organization he had infiltrated. By taking part in the massacre, you get to see what lengths people go to in order to fufill a sense of duty(It's right there in the title, "Call of Duty). That's something you can hang your hat on, be appalled by, empathize with and argue about, etc.
In Hatred, Not Important's (yes, that is apparently the main character's actual name) only stated reason for going on a rampage is that he hates humanity. Through his dialog he conveys that what he is doing is reprehensible, but gives nothing beyond that. No PTSD, overprescribed pharmaseuticals, racism, nationalism, bigotry, misguided sense of duty, moral convictions or anything else drive the player's avatar. Mr. Important might as well be represented by a robot or an alien sport hunter, as he is simply a monster wearing human skin and a trench coat. His motivation comes off as a saturday morning cartoon villain's desire to do evil for evil's sake, but with none of the hammy charm.
Conclusion:
If the devs wanted to shock and disgust with violence and gore against the innocent, they were far too mild.  Maybe if they patch in some teens, children and babies, or a torture mechanic, they can generate some more sales from controversy. If this is what passes for an AO rating based on violence, half of my games catalog should be rated AO.

Based on the Harlan Ellison short story, I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream is a video game like no other; for a start, there's no real way to win the game. You'll find yourself making some unsettling choices along the way, which may enhance or corrupt your story, depending on how you want to play through it of course. I recommend this game with some issue. It isn't anything that is seriously wrong that makes me feel this way but 1 thing: THE FACT THAT THE GAME TELLS ME I AM SAD (or more so my refugees). This works against the game way too much. A game like this would've really benefitted by leaving this out for the main reason that it should be up to the player to choose how they feel. When the game makes it a debuff that we can't control and can lead to some horrible concequences when we may not feel that way just isn't a smart design choice. I mean, what would've been a stronger option would be forcing us to face who we've killed either when losing other ways or at the end. I say this because people deal with the things they do in different ways. I certainly felt bad at the things I had to do when playing (WHICH IS AWESOME), but I rationalize my action personally. When I had to steal or murder, it was because it was that or dying.
Take a game like Papers please, which had a similar tone to it. That game perfected this by leaving emotions to the player. When we did good, we felt good. And when we did bad, we felt bad. There was no debuffs and that gave the players a more immersive experience.
Other than that, this game is awesome. Everything is amazing, and awesome, and amazing. Gameplay is really fun. Scavenging and surviving is great. Your refugees have interesting skills and a lot of personality. So if you can look past the "Press F to Feel" styled sad debuff, you will find an extremely immersive and excellent adventure of depressing survival.
Final Rating: 8/10 High Pressure Rice Cookers

BioShock 2 is good.  Not exactly a surprise given the content of other available reviews on Steam, but why is it good seems the more important thing, something I'll try to address here.  I'm going to tell you why I think BioShock 2 is a worthy successor in the series.
First things first, to get right down to brass tacks BioShock 2 is a sequel, it is mostly more of the same gameplay (with a few twists) and the few innovations don't exactly break the bank in the inventiveness department.  A few new weapons and interesting plasmid variations and a small smattering of new enemy types don't do much to dispel the notion that the combat is totally more BiShock.  But that's not what makes a BioShock game, not really.  Sure, the combat has to be engaging enough to drive the narrative forward, but in this game it does that just enough.  No, much like the first, the true draw is the dark and twisted story, the narrative tapestry that shows the dark and twisted nature of those living in Rapture.
This game has you playing as a Big Daddy, the stalwart if myopic defenders of the Little Sisters.  In particular, you play a “prototype”, a nameless everyman changed into a monster but also a kind of father, and it is the theme of fatherhood that, like the first game, shares the roost with a political ideology to form the basis of the disastrous tale of the fall of Rapture.  Where the first game gazed on what genetics truly determine, on the pure unbridled force of Libertarianism and Capitalism, this game focuses on what it means to be a parent, and the equal sociopolitical dangers of a Communistic ideal that crosses the line into religious fervor.  It is the other side of the coin to Andrew Ryan's Rapture ideal of the individual's power in Rapture, the ideal of not just the social as one entity in a metaphorical manner, but what might happen if science could allow us all to actually become one.  And just as in the first game, the dangers of extremist politics show how such ideas can rip a society, and in particular a family apart.
This is the crux of the story: as the first game contained two father figures for the original protagonist, the Big Daddy is one of two parent figures presented in the game. Unlike before where you were being acted upon as a child with two parental figures, now you are one of the agents of change, and your actions effect the story in a more noticeable (if still superficial) manner.
It also drips the kind of scary, jarring atmosphere that is at once engaging to behold and terrifying to think about, the constructive and destructive nature of humankind.  Water drips, walls crack, but unlike before the underwater world outside Rapture is at least nominally explored, and it is beautiful, but sadly littered with the detritus of the once grand city.  The decay of the amazing city of Rapture is at once enthralling and disturbing, an emotional range that was demonstrated in BioShock, and is absolutely in full effect here.
To add to the positives Minerva's Den, a small DLC adventure contained within this game, is a wonderful look at how every last person in Rapture was hurt, changed, damaged by the vision of Andrew Ryan.  Rapture is a crucible and all it seems to produce is tragedy, and each game with it as it's setting allows us to see something of ourselves in it's tragedy.
With arresting visuals, a story just as dark as it's sibling, and the upgraded combat engine, this game is well worth the time.  It is the other side of the coin, the “2” in this case being a quite literal extension of the first, and that is a very good thing indeed.

Tiny and Big is a game which, just from looking at it, doesn't seem too great. But once you start to play it, it reveals its greatness.
The game follows a weird-looking "Tiny" and his attempt to retrieve his grandpa's underpants that a similarly weird-looking "Big" has stolen.
The basic premise in this game is that Tiny is an inventor, and you use his odd little gadgets to help you through the game. Included inventions are A Radio that talks, A laser that can cut rocks, a grappling gun to pull said rocks, and a rocket gun that can push those rocks.
The simulation behind the destructible environment is very good. The game can handle just about any cut you throw at the destructible rocks, and disintegrates any cut rock that is irrelevant to simulate.
This game can be controlled with a controller, or a keyboard and mouse. Both work, but I find that the mouse offers more precision.
The way the levels are designed is very good, offering pretty large areas to explore, and subsequently cut apart and destroy. It really does a good job of making the place look like an old civilization.
The cartooney cell-type shaded graphics in this game are very nice, and the textures applied to the environment are likewise good at portraying an abandoned desert. I do find that the textures applied to character models are a bit odd though.
The sounds in this game are great, both from the environment itself and the weird sounds the characters make instead of speaking. That goes well with the speech bubbles.
The great thing about this game is that the physics, sounds and look of the rocks make it so incredibly satisfying to just cut up the massive rock structures and enjoy them falling apart.
My only major complaint is that it is far too easy to die in this game by running into a rock that is moving. The devs should really have raised the limit of how much force is needed to kill the player, in my mind.
Overall, this is a gem of a game that I don't think has enough attention. Styled like a playable comic book, with a great gameplay experience, it is definitely worth a play.

X Rebirth is the marriage of an economic simulator with an arcade flight sim. The basic gameplay centers around completing various missions for pay and reputation with different factions. Inbetween these, you manage your other assets, including myriad capital ships, freighters, mining vessels, and space stations.
Combat sends you against marauding fighter bands and massive carriers, hostile space stations and shoals of drones. Shield energy powers your boosters, meaning the player must choose when to fight and when to run, and guessing wrong with leave them naked and stranded under fire. Enemy fighters dogfight with the player and each other. Huge capital ships can wreak havoc, but their engines, turrets, and shield projectors are vulnerable to damage. The weak AI is an issue, and larger targets can seem rather bullet-spongey for a player with few resources. Still, disabling and capturing that troublesome destroyer near your new factory is very satisfying.
On the economic side of things, the Great Material Continuum flows like a river from station to staion in the form mass traffic, cargo vessels, and large frieghters. And it is constantly under attack from pirates and other hostile forces. This means there are plenty of opportunities for would-be tycoons. Materials must be mined. Food must be grown. Parts must be manufactured. Freight must be transported. Ships but be built and supplied. Stations must be constructed and defended. And everything needs staffing. It's a lot of fun to plan out your installation and manage its construction and operation. Oddly moreso when you've screwed up something and have to rework everything on the fly.
While I recommend the X Rebirth, it's certainly not for everyone. It's a trainset of a game, crossing into simulation territory just enough to be intellectually stimulating, while still providing the visceral thrill of arcade space combat. It's a casual-friendly game that lets you dip your toes into the deep end of the pool.

Honestly, Return to Castle Wolfenstein (hereafter referred to as “RtCW”) is one of the best games ever, even by today's standards, and not just in the FPS genre, but in general among every other game out there. It is truly the classic that I would recommend to anyone, thanks to its superb gameplay and presentation.
Upon starting a new game, the player is presented with three different difficulty settings (listed from easiest to hardest): “Don’t hurt me.”, “Bring ‘em on!” and “I am Death incarnate!”. The damage dealt by the enemies is the same on each option, but their reaction times and accuracy ratios increase proportionally to the higher difficulty settings, heavily impacting the gameplay itself. Regardless of the difficulty, it surely becomes evident early on that calculated approach and substantial caution are crucial steps towards victory in virtually every level of the game. Considering that this is a game from 2001, merely staying behind cover and waiting for health to regenerate automatically is out of the question. The player has to scavenge not only for ammunition, but also for health and armor (with a maximum capacity, that is, 100), by looking for supplementary items situated within the game world. Such items, however, may appear in various forms throughout the game; for instance, health can be regained back by picking up med packs or even food. Even on a Normal difficulty setting (in this game known as “Bring ‘em on!”), it is important to pay attention to your own health, because even with armor, enemies can deal great amounts of damage in a matter of seconds and they can sometimes react faster than the actual player. It is also difficult to predict in which rooms the enemies are going to be, so simply storming into a room without making sure whether it is safe or not is certainly not a good idea.
What is also worth mentioning about the early experience of the game is that there is great variety of enemy types. Except for standard Nazi soldiers wielding firearms that can be later picked up by the main character himself, new enemies are swiftly introduced during early chapters of the game, including Ghost Zombies, Undead Shield Creatures, Elite Guards, etc. Each individual encounter with these enemies will require a completely different strategy, because even a face-to-face incursion with some of them may instantly lead towards death. That is why the game requires critical thinking and thorough analysis of the environment; it is possible for the player to turn the tables on the tough foes in the upcoming battle, merely with effective exploration and sufficient utilization of available resources.
Speaking of exploration, RtCW maintains ample collectibles left for the player to find, mainly represented as treasure items; they have actually no major influence on the gameplay itself and its only purpose is to perfect the score on each level. The game also conceals an enormous amount of secret areas that contain very valuable items, such as ammunition, health and armor, along with treasure items mentioned previously. Spontaneously running across a secret area can prove to be very salutary, yet it can be extremely elaborate to purposefully look for them without a guide, since reaching these secret areas requires a lot of platforming, puzzle solving and pure luck. Often does improvisation play a role here, because secret areas can be even hidden behind certain destructible objects and walls that usually look indistinguishable compared to the other ones that do not hide anything, and there is plentiful of them within the game. At the end of each part of a mission, the game shows the record of how many treasures and secret areas have been uncovered, along with time of completion and amount of attempts. Additionally, the player may find notes within the game that give further insight into the story, but they mainly appear in plain sight and do not count towards actual collectibles.
It is also worth mentioning that there are no checkpoints nor autosaves in RtCW; each time the player will want to save, it must be done manually, but fortunately the game can be saved at any point of any mission (it is possible to save even during a fight). There is lots of space for multiple saving, too, so in case the player will make a mistake, it is very easy to load any previous save, assuming that it has not been overwritten before. The loading times are also very short, and they only appear when moving onto the next part of a mission or loading a save from the menu.
In order to avoid revealing any spoilers, I will only mention that the story is best experienced while playing through the game on your own for the first time. The visuals and sound effects truly complement the tone of the game’s atmosphere, and the plot is very well executed.
In conclusion, I consider RtCW to be one of the best games of all time, simply because it is one of the last few that upheld the gameplay mechanics that demanded the player to act strategically. Unfortunately, such mechanics were later abandoned by the game developers, and it is hard to find a similar game like this one nowadays. Nonetheless, I would indubitably recommend this game to anyone out there, because it is simply a great experience.

I had never played Dead Rising 1 as it was not on PC. I was very into L4D2 logging over 200 hours into it. I had expected Dead Rising 2 to be in the vain of L4D but in third person and whole lot more zombies. Pros:
Runs well on a AMD Phenom II X4 940, 2GB DDR2 and GTX 670. Sometimes under 60fps.
Cons:
-Huge grind. As described below about boss fights, you need to level up in order for boss fights to be fair. I am at level 20 and boss fights are still not balanced at all. Avoiding boss fights can be futile at times as described below.
-No running. You walk faster by levelling up. Levelling up auto assigns attributes (attack, speed, life etc..) so their is no customization. I am currently at level 20 and still walk very slow.
-Time based gameplay, all missions are based on a certain time, the absence of running really adds frustration to this as you cannot get to some missions in time, especially story missions that forces you to load from a user savepoint which could be 30 mins back.
-Save points are limited to "restrooms", if you can find them and remember to do so. Current game design is that after every mission the game should auto-save. Not with Dead Rising 2, if you had beaten a hard fought boss, you must remember to find a restroom ASAP. Even then, you could be low on health after this boss fight and die on the way to a restroom.
-Numerous boss fights that are unbalanced. You need to be leveled up and on a 2nd playthrough in order for the boss fights to be fair. These boss fights show up in your missions list and you have to assume from the mission description that you will fighting someone, it doesn't tell you outright. I essentially have to read, thnk and pick rescue type missions in order for me to level up so when I do encounter bosses, it will be more fair but so far still unbalanced. Even if you intend to avoid boss fights, some missions force you to go into a certain area which will trigger a boss fight, and because you walk so slowly, it is difficult to evade the boss fight after

Neon Chrome is a fantastically enjoyable twin-stick shooter and I heartily recommend it if you are in the mood for some old-school arcade action.
The setting is a very Judge Dredd-esque mega block where you control a series of cyberpunk agents and blast your way up the semi-randomly generated block until you reach the evil Overseer, unlocking new weapons, abilities and cyberenhancements as you go and earning credits to upgrade your agent's base stats. When your agent dies, you can pick from a new set of agents, each from one of several different classes and with a set of gear & abilities randomly selected from what you've unlocked before. Do well enough and you can have that new agent start from a higher floor, and each time you beat the Overseer it is like a "new game +" mode, where you and the enemies all get bonuses.
I have been having a stupid amount of fun with this game. The graphics are crisp and colorful, the controls are easy and responsive with a PC compatible X-Box controller, and it is just very satisfying overall. The difficulty curve, once you get used to it, is also just the right side of hard, where you feel like you have a handle on each enemy type but each encounter is still threatening and tense, and resources are always scarce.
There are some (very!) minor issues. The story is fairly basic and minimal. Sometimes the level RNG will generate rooms where your upgrade and loot containers are surrounded by explosive barrels, so it's almost certain every thing will blow up before you can get to it. On levels with walkways, the money and energy drops from the enemies will frequently fall off the side into the abyss. The game has some issues with certain graphics cards (like mine!) so if you play in full-screen it will often do a quick switch back to the Steam program and then back to the game, so you have to play in a window. And last, but not least, the sound effect for the normal doors sounds just like a melee "whiff" from a ton of other games, so I keep thinking there is a dude I've missed who is taking wild swings at me.
But regardless of minor problems, the rest of the game is just silly fun. And lots and lots of explosions.

Betrayer is a bag of mixed emotions. Appealingly presented in beautful monochrome and undeniably atmospheric, it's a falling star that will mesmerize you for a moment before its light disippates into night sky.
What do i mean by this ? Well, give me a moment to explain.
Year is 1604 and you just woke up on the beach of the New World among the debris of a marooned ship carrying nothing but your knife. World around you is presented in stylish monochrome with pleasant sounds of splashing waves and schreeching seagulls. It could almost be idyllic if it weren't for the fact that you barely escaped watery grave. With only the vaguest idea of where you are and what to do next, you scrounge up what you can from boxes that are strewn around the shore and head up inland. It doesn' take too long until you stumble on a first sign of life in a form of a warning arrow, shot by a person clad in red. A friendly advice on a piece of paper will introduce you with a opportunistic merchant who provides you with your first weapon and hope of future, mutually beneficial relationship. Wepon in hand, but caution in mind, you'll proceed to face whatever dangers stalk the tall grass of this newly colonized country.
Incidentaly, stalking is the best approach to combat. Your crude longbow won't do you much good in a straight on fight and breasplate worn by your enemies will deflect most arrows. Stealthy approach is very much encouraged - hiding in tall grass and utilizing shadows and gusts of wind to mask your footsteps before you can close in for one deadly strike. However, if you cross their direct line of sight they will spot you and charge to your location which creates a lot of intense encounters, at least in the beginning until you size them up and get better equipment. Like in Dark Souls, you lose all your loot when you die; (an option which can be turned off in gameplay menu), so you want to choose your fights carefully. There is a modest variety of weapons, appropriate for that era. Powerful, but slow-loading muskets and flintlock pistols for your short range, fire-and-forget needs with weaker short/longbows and crossbows doing a nice job at long range sniping. There are also quick-throw explosives and tomahawks when enemies get too close.
Exploration will reveal small bits and pieces of information - page scraps provide lore and insight into past events, puzzling clues an evidence into violent misdeeds, graves engraved with names and causes of death - these are constant reminders that something  has gone terribly wrong. Immersion is an overused buzzword, but it's really appropriate here. All this culminates when you reach your first settlement; a small fort mysteriously deserted, showing signs of struggle. Here you'll be introduced to another gameplay mechanic, where you need to collect a bell, hang it from a beam and ring it, whereupon you'll be transported to a darker version of normal world. Dark world is populated by skeletons and floating shades; your vision is limited, and you have to orientate yourself by "listening" and/or following small appearing pointers on the screen. These will lead you to lost souls, remaining echoes of colonists who will explain the significance of certain clues and slowly unravel their mysterious fate and events that led to their untimely, violent deaths.
In these first few hours it looks like Betrayer will settle into a nice rythm, providing a good balance between atmospheric, nearly horror experience, exploration and combat, but it never quite comes to that. New areas you discover feel and look pretty much the same - they're mostly empty and while collectibles offer a decent incentive to explore, it will inevitably become tedious. Enemies that seemed dangerous and sinister before will show all limitations of their AI when you realize there's nothing more to their tactics than relentlessly charging to your location. Most of the combat challenge will come from limited 17- century weapons, and finding more powerful ones is crucial to your survival. These are mostly found on dead enemies or in chests, but really powerful unique, weapons are buried beneath piles of rock that can only be accessed once you find a spade much later in the game. Unfortunately they use exactly the same models as regular ones so it lacks that feeling of finding something really special. Backtracking isn't a problem since there's a fast travel system, but your character is shown as area circle on the map, instead of the usual arrow, which creates  confusion when you're trying to find your way, so I'd recommend turning on compass. Ghostly investigations you have to do will reveal very interesting albeit mostly tragic stories, but ultimately amount to nothing more than running from one location to the next, picking up mementos and presenting them to appropriate shade. It's gets very formulaic and repetitive very soon - get to the new area, retake the settlment from enemies, find the bell, go to the dark world, play the courier for ghosts, rinse and repeat.  It approaches greatness but never reaches it and that's what's most frustrating of all.

Rating: 8/10
Overview: Top Down Twin Stick Shooter Rogue
The Good:
+ Always love cyberpunk aesthetic
+ Like any good rogue lite game there are plenty of weapons, abilities and passive abilities to unlock.  Collecting money is also important because it allows you to upgrade stats permanently for future playthroughs.
+ With all the passive abilities and weapons you can create some creative builds every playthrough, you can focus on offense, health, defense or explosive abilities
+ A lot of the levels feature destructible walls, after a heavy firefight its cool to see almost everything destroyed.
+ This game is a lot more forgiving than most other rogue games on Steam. Its very easy to pick up and play
+ Can be played for short bursts or for long periods of time
+ Every time you beat the final boss the game gets harder, harder enemies, more health, more damage, however you are also rewarded with more money and thus buy more permanent upgrades.
+ level editor and mods
+ Great soundtrack
The Average:
+/- There are only a few bosses and they are not that exciting. Bosses are supposed to be a bit more challenging than the regular gameplay, yet I found these bosses to actually be easier.
The Bad:
- There is a lack of variety with the levels themselves. Although they are procedurally generated, they all feel the same.
Conclusion:
A great rogue twin stick shooter that is sure to please fans of both genres. I would love to see a sequel where more ideas are expanded upon to provide more variety within the gameplay.

I had been anticipating this game since I first heard of it and I was not disappointed.
Betrayer is a perfect example of how less can be more sometimes, who minimalism can really work in favor of a game. The spooky and somber atmosphere with its natural desaturated visuals (which can be changed in the options, but you really should at least play SOME of the game like this) ends up being very engaging. The game lacks any kind of voice acting, favoring solely text, and even music is absent from the game. Instead your soundtrack is the noises of the wildlife around you (birds and insects), the rustling of wind through grass and trees, and your own footsteps. The crisp clearness of sound makes even the sound effects stand out, the sound of an arrow shaft being drawn across the bow limb or filling the musket chamber with gunpowder... every sound is painstakingly focused as sound is the primary focus of this game. You'll have to use sound to locate your enemies, as well as extra items like treasure chests and journal pages.
Hunting down final collectibles in the end can get a bit tedious (namely the chests when they become far less useful to you) and most areas look very similar, if not identical, but can be easily overlooked. Even the terms of story take a more subdued approach, filled in with the journal pages you find (amongst other things that I won't spoil for you).
Betrayer is not a run-and-gun sort of action game and typically requires more stealth approaches and a more reserved style of play, so if you like to take things slowly, the game will suit you perfectly.
Overall, I rate Betrayer an 8.5/10. The beautiful sound effects and impressive visuas far outweigh any negatives.

I can't properly describe the happy dance I did when IHNMAIMS got re-released on Steam a few months ago. As a young lad the demo of this bleak, creepy adventure game had haunted me, but never did I save enough allowance to buy the full game before it disappeared into the ether. Now, at last, I can revisit it and experience the horror for myself... and discover it's not all that horrifying, but it's still a fine adventure game.
Well, the premise is horrifying at least. The mad supercomputer AM has obliterated humanity, preserving only five individuals to torture for more than a hundred years. Now AM wants to play a special game with them, one that could result in their freedom, if they can overcome their fears and regrets. Each of the characters has some dark secret that AM has used to torture them; one was a Nazi doctor, another had his wife committed, and so on. You chose which scenario to play through, and if you die (yes, you can die in this adventure game, but it's only a temporary setback) you get to choose again. The gameplay is what you'd expect of an adventure game, though my impression is that this one is lighter on the item collecting and combining and more on interacting with the scenery and other characters. It can be a bit of a pixel hunt at times, and some of the puzzles are a little obtuse owing to the nightmarish nature of the scenarios AM concocts.
What really got me was the voice acting. I didn't even recall the game being voice acted when I was a child, and honestly the game is probably better served without it. The godlike supercomputer taunts his victims like a stuffy DOTA player ridiculing his team. The one woman of the group talks in some seriously dated 90s forced ebonics that gets pretty cringeworthy at times. The writing itself generally holds up, but there are occasional tonal shifts where a character tries to make a funny in the midst of confronting their horrors. Sadly, this one isn't quite as atmospheric and creepy as I had remembered, but it's a solid enough adventure game from what I've seen. And the world always needs more unique adventure games.

15 hours in and I've done everything, built everything and suffered through whiney survivors, chain smokers and caffine addicts who can't seem to realise it's not a time to want those luxuries and just get on with your damn job. If I was stuck with Bruno or Katia in such a situation I would have left them days ago.
I managed to finish the game in around about 10 hours, not very lenghly for 15 pounds imo and the replay value that I was told was there, simply isn't.
Nothing new comes into play the 2nd time around, that burning building you loot for the basic supplies on your first night is in the same place and isn't any different to how it was the 1st time and even if you get a different location or two from the first time you played towards the end you'll realise you've done pretty much the same thing all over again.
Those 'dynamic' events i read about in reviews are about as dynamic as a college timetable, they happen in the exact same places with the exact same layouts. Sure you get people knocking on your door when your at home but again these aren't dynamic, I played in the same house in 2 different playthroughs and the events from the 1st time happened in the exact same order in the 2nd.
Sure the supermarket and church have a couple of different scenarios, friendly looters or a woman about to get attacked in the supermarket or a frtiendly priest willing to trade or bandits that are a cowerdly bunch to say the least and only one has a gun but he's clearly there to give you some stealth kill practice as he's so easy to sneak up on it was like attacking a dummy, same with the soldier at the supermarket.
Then you get places like the Warehouse which has no kind of change in their scenario, I always have bandits there that shoot on sight and never want to trade so I'd avoid if your not very good at the whole 'stealth' thing.
Which leads me to the stealth, 8/10 it works but occasionally it will glitch and instead of silently walking to a hiding spot you'll alert the whole damn building by charging full pelt at it so stealth is slightly wonky but bearable. But when your caught and surrounded by people who can see you and have guns then your dead, no other way around it and Dead is Dead with an autosave feature that stops you from reverting to an older save. I also found it annoying that this bandit i was chasing, who had no weapon in his hand, managed to beat down my healthy character who was carrying a frigging hatchet! Also even if you have a gun and plenty of ammo, good luck actually hitting anyone before they charge you and stab you in the gut.
So yeah the combat is very poor and uneven, the only sure way to get a kill is through a stealth kill from cover, anything else takes a few hits.
Sure it was fun the 1st time but for £15 I feel like kinda let down at the poor replay value. Maybe I just got unlucky with my scenarios and the luck of the draw was not in my favour or maybe it really is just repetitive garbage?

Having played this during a free weekend, here are my thoughts.
Civilization: Beyond Earth is quite an enjoyable experience and fun to play, although it does lack signifigant character.  During my time playing, it was interesting learning all the new mechanics, dangers, resources, and the new tech tree.
The tech tree itself could use more detal, as I found myself strugging to figure out what techs lead to what victories, and what I had to do for victories that didn't involve a specific tech to achieve.
The alien life is a great addition and replacement to barbarians with it's variable attitude towards civs.  You can be friendly with the wildlife and get along, even use them to your advantage!  Or, you can slaughter them and they get increasingly hostile towards your civ.  Very interesting dynamic.
Miasma is a very interesting natural hazard that truely restricts movement early-to-mid game.  Keeps things interesting, and if you go Unity, you can use it to your defensive advantage.
I will never enjoy this game as I've enjoyed Civilization V, but it's a solid experience that I'd recommend to a newcomer of the series (Right after I recommend Civ V, of course), or to those who are looking for a fairly interesting turn-based strategy.
All that said, the game does lack signifigant character and appears to have much less unit depth and diversity.  Of course the units are as diverse as Civ V, save unique units, it appears otherwise due to how little they change.  Only four-or-so upgrades for units, rather than watching Swordsman go to Musketeers and Infantry.
It also seems that there's less care put into each faction.  As they were started from scratch, I understand it's difficult to come up with interesting civilizations from scratch compared to real-life historical civilizations, but it feels that each Civ is more-or-less interchangable.  In Civ V, picking a certain nation may result in higher resource count of a particular kind of resource, or better navy with unique perks, or better culture buildings.  In Civ:BE, it's much less diverse.
Tl;dr: Civilization: Beyond Earth is a very enjoyable game and I would give it a 7.5/10 due to it's interesting gameplay, enjoyable experience, but lack of character and diversity.  I would recommend you buy it on sale if you already own Civ V, because you'll be getting less content compared to it.

I recommend this game with some issue. It isn't anything that is seriously wrong that makes me feel this way but 1 thing: THE FACT THAT THE GAME TELLS ME I AM SAD (or more so my refugees). This works against the game way too much. A game like this would've really benefitted by leaving this out for the main reason that it should be up to the player to choose how they feel. When the game makes it a debuff that we can't control and can lead to some horrible concequences when we may not feel that way just isn't a smart design choice. I mean, what would've been a stronger option would be forcing us to face who we've killed either when losing other ways or at the end. I say this because people deal with the things they do in different ways. I certainly felt bad at the things I had to do when playing (WHICH IS AWESOME), but I rationalize my action personally. When I had to steal or murder, it was because it was that or dying.
Take a game like Papers please, which had a similar tone to it. That game perfected this by leaving emotions to the player. When we did good, we felt good. And when we did bad, we felt bad. There was no debuffs and that gave the players a more immersive experience.
Other than that, this game is awesome. Everything is amazing, and awesome, and amazing. Gameplay is really fun. Scavenging and surviving is great. Your refugees have interesting skills and a lot of personality. So if you can look past the "Press F to Feel" styled sad debuff, you will find an extremely immersive and excellent adventure of depressing survival.

Managed 24hrs in the free weekend, some of my thoughts on the limited time I had with vanilla Beyond Earth:
The AI is pretty awful . I performed a coup d'etat mission with one of my spies (after another AI spent about 15 turns bombing the capital but not bothering to take over it), the AI leader wasn't even mad I took the capital, no denouncing or declaring war, in fact further on in the game the leader was friendly towards me. They didn't even attempt taking back their own capital.
The content is fairly lacking and the leaders are incredibly generic. I understand the reasoning for not wanting 'Gandhi in space', but at least have
backstory. I really couldn't tell you the difference between any of the leaders aside from their physical appearance. This is a large problem for me because one of the things I loved about Civ V was the personality of the leaders. In Beyond Earth, they are all the same, and they are dull.
The orbital layer is a welcome new addition to the franchise, unfortunately I found most of the units either boring or useless to me. The only one I really used was the ability to create new strategic resources on unworked tiles.
The Affinities is an interesting idea with Purity, Harmony and Supremacy. I'm not sure however that I liked they were tied to the Tech Web. I maybe would have liked to pre-select an Affinity or use them like Virtues and amass and spend Affinity points during the game.  I probably need to spend more time in the game to have a solid impression on that.
Some of the units, especially Harmony's, are really good. Unfortunately the upgrade system is very uninspired and boring with only 2 options available.
I think a certain youtuber said it best when he said that the game was, "Bound by it's theme", I think that perfectly sums up vanilla Beyond Earth. I love the theme, but their is just a stark lack of content. I think the inevitable future expansions will fix a large amount of these problems, but vanilla Beyond Earth isn't worth buying, and therefore I cannot recommend it for now.

tl;dr This game is one of the best I played in a long time. It's very organic and well balanced in almost every aspect: story, music, visuals and gameplay.
Take role of one of the two protagonists striving for survival and/or better life (which is quite difficult, as you will find out). The tragedy of this city lies not only in the recent terrorist attacks, but also in the appearance of an unknown murderer wandering the streets. The game has 5 chapters (with more to come in updates) and multiple endings, depending on choices made by the player.
The developers used music from freesound, masterfully picked and corresponding perfectly. It may be repetitive sometimes but never bothered me, especially radio tracks.
Dialogues are completely silent and show up in the form of text, which some players will most probably consider a flaw, even though it doesn't affect the overall feel of the game.
The game has a minimalistic black & white (and sometimes red) graphic style, very atmospheric and pleasant to my taste. The city buildings and streets look very solid and appealing to the eye. If you don't expect graphics like in major studios titles and can get used to overall game style you won't be disappointed.
In each chapter you are free to go wherever you want, you can chat with people, visit different places and explore the city itself. The game has many little secrets which do not change the track of the main story, but can still amaze when you find them. Some choices you make are really important to the story and will lead to the different endings.
Navigation system is a bit confusing at the very beginning of the game, and you will sometimes find yourself lost in the city and not knowing where to go. The map and birds in the sky can help you orient though. After you play through the game to your very first ending and get familiar with the city, it ceases to be a problem. Your first playthrough can take up to 3 hours, the next ones will be shorter if you know exactly what to do, or may be even longer if you enjoy exploring as much as I do. Some chapters of the game are just literally jaw-dropping and had a high impact on me.
this game is very good, and is going to be even better, because the devs still improve it and add new content. If you like exploring adventures and walking simulators, you should grab this title without a doubt, or at least try the demo.

I can't remember the last time I had so much fun inadvertently killing my character in a game.  This is a fairly short game with a very unique look and a fairly unique concept.  You have a laser you can use to cut through stone, a grappling hook to drag stone around, and a rocket that you can use to launch anything it attaches to.  And then you have physics.  And that's pretty much it; get to the end of each section using your tools and physics.  It's hilarious how easy it is to get things wrong and get yourself stuck, or smash yourself under a pillar, or miss a jump and fall to your death.  Way more fun than I ever would have guessed.  The game design and graphic style is very unique, and the music is varied and interesting too. There's only 5 real levels and a final boss level (that was kind of annoying), for a game I played for 2-3 hours total, but I could easily go back and try the levels again to go faster, or make fewer cuts, or get all the collectibles. This is the epitome of indie games, unique concept, unique look, and a world that you'll never get from a AAA developer. Definitely worth a look if you like quirky experiences.

In Angels That Kill, players have the “privilege” of playing the role of two indistinguishable characters in Noll City, set in a Noir-crime theme. The quietness of the game makes it difficult to be attentive to most of the dialogue since subtitles seem to be overly missed in contrast with the dark, gray scales and obnoxious bright white that populates the game. Most of the time, determining what character is being controlled at the moment is difficult unless players are gifted in multitasking and can diligently watch the sky for birds while reading the subtitles that tend to show without warning. This takes much of the immersiveness away from the game since the story tends to be overlooked in favour of the gameplay.
The basic environmental structure is bland to say the least, which is mostly the case for Noir themed media; and ironically “Bland” is a brightness option in the settings but changes are barely visible. Despite using the old-style theme in Angels That Kill, the tones utilized in the game are intense and harsh. Some players may find the game tends to strain the eye and that headaches ensue.
The gameplay is standard and simple with the options to pick up items, examine surroundings and run slightly faster than the default speed. The game implements a hunger bar but players have the option to switch this mechanic on or negate it from the beginning of the title. When the hunger bar is in effect, players must search for edible food in dumpsters to replenish it or fail to do so, which will result in your death. The hunger bar doesn’t really affect the gameplay much if players are quick to complete each chapter before the player even has to worry about it. Controls are sluggish and can be frustratingly annoying -- especially when one character is suffering through a drunken stupor -- and forces players to navigate the streets with inverted “WASD” controls that seem to interchange when you turn down a street.
Someday I would like to make another playthrough of the game if changes ever occurred.
