Angels That Kill was killing me with it’s ineptitude within five minutes.
The game’s city may have also been killed, because it certainly feels dead. It’s bland, vacant and every area looks the same so navigation is frustrating. The map isn’t very helpful because there’s so few distinctive landmarks. Crows hover over your destination, thankfully, because that’s the only way I could figure out where to go.
The game’s interiors are so dark that what little is there is difficult to see. There’s not much to interact with, and I’m not sure why there’s an inventory at all, as I failed to find a single item I was able to take with me.
Your character’s movement is glacially slow - “running” down the long empty roads is a chore. This is made even more irritating because you need to consume dumpster food to survive. You might spot a dumpster in the distance and traipse down the lane only to find that it's one you’ve already scraped out. It’s also disruptive and unnecessary, I had to leave a crime scene to find a garbage-meal before I collapsed where I stood and was forced through the whole scenario again, and I mean the entire chapter.
Also, it ain’t noire. Noire is more than rain and a monochromatic colour palette, it’s a mood, one that is largely evoked by music, of which this game has almost none. When it does, it isn’t noire.
While the idea of playing as both suspect and pursuer is a good one, and some aspects of its minimalist presentation are appealing initially, very little else here works.

BEREFT : The Game
That's what this game should have been called. It is empty and devoid of any logical story development, game-mechanics implementation and video-audio representation. I understand that this is a work of a small indie team, but clearly this game did not went through proper quality checkup.
The messy and incoherent story, or what's left of it, is about a down-on-his-luck boxer and a detective who are involved in a series of murders. It was intended to be presented as a noir game in style and feel, but it ends up butchering its own ideas with many baffling decisions. It wants to be a classic point and click adventure game with "meaningful" choices where the player can take a look at every nook and cranny, but it also puts a ridiculous survival mechanic where you have to hunt and pillage trash dumpsters throughout the city to stave off hunger meter that keeps draining quickly. It looks like game developers put a fail mechanic in the game just to avoid labels like walking simulator. In the end, you are left with a police officer who has to interrupt investigation of crime scenes and talking to witnesses, just to run down the street and stuff his face in the pile of rotten food like a pig!
Game looks abismal, and while I understand it tried to keep a minimalistic feel to it, there isn't an ounce of texture anywhere, making the game look monotonous and painful to the eyes. Except a quick jazzy tune and a somber song, there is no music whatsoever, and that goes to sound effects as well.
I'm certain that Angels That Kill is not the worst game I've ever played, hell it's not even the worse game that I'll end up playing among many untouched steam games in the library as well, but it also isn't "so bad it's good" material. It's just bereft of anything meaningful; an empty, shriveled husk made out of good intentions.

This game has been in development since 2013. For that couple of years in development, we have around a month of work, well, really lazy, unplanned work anyway. You pay around £10 for an extension to something that had to be rushed in thought and it very much shows.
The problems that existed a couple years ago are still here; not being able to navigate effectively, comedically bad controls, absolutely minimal explenation for what youre even doing or where you should go and a lack of anything that could immerse you. In fact thats my main problem with the game, it tries to be something immersive, an engaging noir experience but what you get for your £10 is barely any sound, awful animations that were in the release a couple years ago and a camera that is constantly tilting down and to the right. The way the camera moves is enraging to say the least.
Earlier I mentioned the problem with navigation, allow me to indulge with you the pure idiocy of the navigation system; the whole you are located within a city complete with skyscrapers and fog, the ONLY way to know ehere you are going is either by memory (more on that in a minute) or by birds in the sky. Those birds do not stick with you and tell you where you are going they just hover over where you are meant to be. Now do you see the purely stupid connection between fog, skyscrapers and small birds? Exactly, you can only see them when you are close. The whole game you have to run around the massive, bland (immersion problem again )city to hopefully find your way. It doesnt help that your character os only outfitted by his, presumably, somewhat crippled legs. In the top right section of the city there is a map, you can find that map by conveniently running around confused and running into it by chance, handy right? That map gives you three landmarks by which you can identify the city. Only three.
Finally, people seem to have an issue with the art style of the game. I have to agree and disagree with them.
Why I disagree with them:
I personally see what the developers were going for, i find the look of the game very charming but not very well done.

The art style is very bland, the city has no sound, only about 7 buildings have any detail at all on them (the rest are just big, grey boxes) and the fog gets in the way more than it gives any aesthetic appeal.

Angels That Kill
Noir Adventure
Rising Sun Interactive
Rising Sun Interactive
is a first-person noir adventure game developed and published by Rising Sun Interactive. As some of you might know, I love the noir genre, but unfortunately this game was a big disappointment.
The story follows two different characters: one is an ex boxer who is down on his luck, and the other is a detective who is trying to discover the murderer that's been terrorising the city lately. In the 5 chapters short chapters of the game you will see different situations from the eyes of the protagonists. While this is a good idea, the overall story is barely interesting (mostly because of the absence of voice acting). You can talk to just a handful of characters, and they are all very bland. However, I do like that you have some choices during the story that will lead you to one of many possible (albeit disappointing) endings.
The game uses the Unity engine, and the performance is pretty solid all around. Unfortunately, this game is graphically very unpleasant. While it isn't the first noir game to use black, white and gray as its main colors, my eyes were feeling tired while looking at the screen.
The huge city doesn't feature that many civilians, the buildings all look the same and there is nothing interesting to see, which is a shame. I do believe that making this a more linear story might have improved the graphical department.
The game is basically a glorified walking simulator: you usually just go from one point to the other, and on the way you might find a couple of NPCs to "chat" with or an item to examine. There are also a couple of instances in which you must avoid police detection, which means you should stay at least 10 feet away from a cop car. Other than that, you don't do much. And the worst aspect that makes this game feel like a chore is the city: it's just too damn huge and confusing to navigate. You do find a map, but it's way too stylized to understand exactly where to go, and especially where you are. There are some birds that fly over your objective, but they are white against a white sky, so good luck finding them.
Other than the stealth sections, the game doesn't feature much challenge at all, and most of the frustration will come from you trying to find where to go.
Easily the worst aspect of the game: the game lacks basically any type of sound effects, with the exception being footsteps and the alarm of cop cars when you are caught. The music is mediocre at best, and it barely plays during gameplay. There is also no voice acting at all, meaning that all of the dialogue is written, and the cutscenes are completely devoid of sound, creating either awkward or boring situations.
There are 5 chapters, and in each one there are subtle choices that will change the outcome. There are also 8 endings to unlock and a some secrets that make replaying the game more rewarding.
Overall, if what you read sounds interesting to you, you will enjoy this game. However the lack of sound and boring city make this a game that will make you tired after a while. It sucks the fun out of most things.

This game is a bit of an odd one for sure, I went in expecting to play it for 2 hours and quit. I actually ended up loving it, the lack of any musical presence and the mystery surrounding the whole island was something I enjoyed, if you can, leave the color settings as they are, as it adds to the immersion quite a bit, I would also recommend using a headset, as finding your way is almost entirely reliant on sound.
The game starts out with you waking up on a beach with a crashed ship out in the sea and broken cargo washed up around you, you have no memory of anything, and you start to explore the island, and you see a hooded figure out on a cliff whom sends you a note by shooting it at a totem near you. After this intro, which you have control of the entire time, I was hooked and a little obsessed with finding out who the hooded figure was, and why was there a destroyed ship out ate sea.
The game play is open world, in the first person perspective with a focus on basic shooting mechanics and very light stealth thrown in there. Your weapons consist of bows, crossbows, and muskets as a primary weapons with thrown explosives that explode on contact and hatchets which are thrown directly in front. Your weaponry is obtained either from fallen enemies, hidden chests scattered around the island, dug up from the ground in predetermined digging spots, or purchased via a weapons rack. The health is more classic, with a predetermined amount of health that runs down with every hit taken, it can be replenished by drinking water from barrels, and you do carry around “waterskins” that can heal you when away from a water barrel, these “waterskins” are replenished when you drink from a barrel.
The dialog is entirely text, and often times blunt, still I enjoyed some of the snarky replies I got from one of the characters. The story is kind of scattered at first, with you finding bits and pieces of events everywhere and you trying to connect the dots between all the different characters, but towards the end everything begins to fall into place and you see the wickedness and cruelty of some of the characters, and stupidity and cowardice of others, with some people getting caught in between and becoming victims. Often times you will be confronted with a choice between replies, some of which can have an impact on the story and maybe difficulty of the game.
If you are someone looking for a game with a lot of backstabbing happening in the plot, and want to shoot human and ghost like beings, than this just might be what you are looking for. I strongly recommend it.

Okay, Seeing as the game only has negative reviews at this moment, I figure I'll bring something positive to the table. The game isn't bad, Its strange, but not bad at all. It has its quirks, and its ups and downs like every game does, but by far it's not a bad game.
The style of the game, is dark, it even mentions it in the description. It following through with saying the games dark grey to black and white style is true to that of noire films, with a low detail style behind it, might not be the best choice for traditional noire but the game hits key points within the genre.
Pro's of the game are,
+Its style is enjoyable, I can see the minimalism in the game, but the fine details of the little things are what count the most.
+Its music is good, very pleasant sounding, even if a tad repetitive.
+The games minimalistic plot and Stark dialog leave a lot up to interpretation but after replaying the game several times, the story comes together bit by bit, adding a fulfilling experience.
+the game does have many small tasks besides the main story line
The cons of the game are,
-There are at times a lack of sound, making it somewhat daunting to keep roaming around.
-sometimes the monochromatic feel of the game is off, but it's also based off of old noire movies which are black and white, along with being dark grey. (the brightness helps though if you turn it up)
-The game is directionless, and it is hard to navigate the city at times but without the map you can also find other things to do and people to talk to.
-It sometimes feels like a glorified walking simulator
Overall, 7/10, It’s a good game, maybe not the best game. You should probably buy it when it's on sale.

Neon Chrome is a top-down shooter with rogue-like elements placed in a dystopian future. Don’t let the cartoony look fool you, this game is harder than it looks.
- First thing’s first, this game plays smoothly. I never had any issues with the gameplay mechanics.
- Looks good and sounds good but it’s nothing spectacular. I did find that the music tied in very well with the cyberpunk theme.
- I liked how the whole story/setting ties in very well with the gameplay. For example, every time you respawn, your character comes out from a new pod, which also happens to be numbered. More details will be revealed as complete the game.
- The main selling point of Neon Chrome is replayability. Levels are randomly generated, and once you
the game you unlock harder difficulties. There are also numerous classes, weapons, upgrades, and abilities you can unlock and pick from.
- I enjoyed the learning curve in Neon Chrome. This game wasn’t designed to be easy. If you don’t play carefully, you will eventually be swarmed by enemies and end up dead. Difficulty progression felt fair and logical;
- The destructible environment can play greatly in your favour or against you. This kind of ties in with the difficulty and learning curve of the game. Breaking walls can help you execute sneak attacks on your enemies, but at the same time, provides passage for other enemies to charge at you. Proceed with caution.
-
- Despite all the different options, it doesn’t feel like there is much variability In Neon Chrome. Within two hours I already figured out which classes, upgrades, and weapons I preferred. Within 4 hours I beat the game and I unlocked a harder difficulty. I feel like I’ve already experienced most of what Neon Chrome has to offer.
- Even weapons with “EXCELLENT” accuracy ratings aren’t that accurate. I sometimes got annoyed that I would miss simply because of RNG.
- There are essentially only 3 bosses, although there are 5 boss fights. It is a shame that you have to refight two bosses.
This is another example of a game that I would maybe recommend. Both gameplay and story are well executed, but I got tired of it quite quickly. In any case, I find the current price of 15 euros quite steep, considering that I completed it in about 4 hours. Considering picking Neon Chrome up when it is on sale.

Homefront had too much of hype. A dated control scheme and needlessly difficult and infinitely respawning enemies hold the game back from it's full potential. Aside from a few other glaring technical issues with an aging engine, the game is somewhat solid in singleplayer but never really takes off. The compelling storyline never really gets off the ground in terms of the big picture and feels more "a day in the life of crappy, unrelatable player character fighting for the resistance movement." The guns are pretty and make a nice bang, but the Korean soldiers are impossibly better shots than you. Any step out of cover, at all, results in bloody-eye syndrome until you die or take cover. There are some tired mechanics Homefront uses that I've come to expect from most recent games, but I was promised a mold-breaking, heartwrenching experience. What I got was a slow paced, buggy, and altogether mediocre game from a studio that knows how to do so much better.

Fun game! I've always liked card games and this one is very well done. It can be COMPLETELY free, or you can spend some money to get better cards quicker. I would strongly recommend buying the starter pack, then figuring out if you like the game or not. Either way, it can be free.
It's NOT pay to win by any means. The balance of the game is really brilliant. There are some basic cards that everyone gets that are actually very good and most people use. Then there are rare, epic, and legendary cards, but they may not be better than some of the common cards that everyone gets (although they usually are). In one of my decks, I am using a few rares, 2-3 epics, and 2 legendaries. More than half the deck is made of common or free cards, and the deck does very very well.
There are 5 factions, each with their unique flavor. Vikings have a lot of strength, movement reduction, and enhance abilities. Warlocks are all about direct damage, ranged units, and squishy units. Ninjas have good movement, stealth, and good damage. Each is balanced very well.
Updates come frequently, with a new expansion coming in January. The dev just reduced shard price so cards are easier to obtain and the game is less grindy. The dev also changed the tournament system a bit, which made the tournaments a lot of fun and much more rewarding.
To summarize:
I would give this a 10/10. It loses some points due to not so great animations and music, but it's free, well balanced and, well....just plain fun!

A very dark and gripping game/depiction of a wartorn city. The survival of a ragged group of people quickly becomes heart-wrenching. Every night of scavenging can be lethal. At one point I lost a scavenger to a group of hardened bandits. The rest of the group fell apart out of sheer grief from the loss.
My first successful(?) playthrough led me to a skirmish against the military outpost. I'd tried to barter with them but the price was too high and when the food-supply finally ran out there was no other option but to fight them.
The game's graphics has a sweet pencil-drawn quality to it and frequently shows a city falling apart. It does look a bit grey but hardly deters you from "gameplay".
The constant toil for food and resources is sometimes fierce (winter, in particular) and does get repetitive.
Thankfully the random visits from strangers in need and merchants help bring some nuance to it.
Combat is intense and requires a strategic approach: risking injury could be disastrous and require additional supplies. The mechanics are a fine but a bit clunky, I wish there was a hotkey for quickly changing stance from "scavenging" to "combat".
One of very few good survival games.

Before getting down to brass tacks, it's impossible to ignore that there was a moderately large controversy surrounding this game; this is because it is violent.
This game is exactly what it says on the tin; you shoot people, the main character spouts out hilariously edgy lines, the game ends.
First, the bad:
1) A relatively large number of people (more than usual for a game) had technical issues with this game. A small chunk of it was due to people not updating their OS, or the installer bugging out, but most of it is because the game is *very* CPU intensive. As in, I have a hex-core AMD chip running at 4.3 GHz and a R9 270, and the game slows down sometimes, especially when there's a lot on the screen. However, people with better (more overclocked) CPUs and worse graphics cards have reported that they're playing it fine.
So, if your computer's outdated by a few years, don't buy this.
2) As of this writing, the game lacks replayability. That is, it's only enjoyable to mow down a crowd of hipsters once or twice before it seems bland. (Thankfully, if that's what you want to do, it does not take very long for this game to deliver.)
This game needs mods, badly; creative challenges centered around knocking off certain types of people in certain ways would be a thing that modders can do, and it would go a long way. Seeing as I'm writing this in the first few days of its release, and given its relative popularity, I hope that I can see modders come in with creative new ideas (on how to mow down crowds of hipsters.)
3) The AI is Bethesda-tier. That is, you'll start shooting, and people will occasionally run towards you.
Now that I'm done digging into it, the good:
1) The difficulty is just right. With only one exception (who in the bloody hell thinks it's a good idea to go on a shooting spree on an army base?), it's not hard unless you're acting like an idiot. That said, you can't act like an idiot.
2) The gameplay is smooth and unbroken. Even though you have to run from objective to objective, you're still trying to kill lots of people. And there's plenty of people on the way to your objectives.
And the neutral:
1) It's unoriginal; this game is basically GTA with all the dull "acquiring weapons and doing silly missions" cut out.
2) The main character is hilariously edgy. "ONE NATION UNDER DEATH. I AM GENOCIDE. BUT ENOUGH FUN..." actually made me fall over laughing.
In summary: It's unoriginal and CPU-heavy, but polished and smooth if you have the processing power to back it up. It has the feel of GTA with the dull bits cut out. If you have to pick between this and a GTA game, you should probably buy this..

A game that relies heavily on consequences. Nay, is composed of said consequences. The moral and ethical decisions one has to make in the game to survive the devastation of a civil war, it can be heart-clenching (or brutally amusing depending on what kind of "person" you are).
Should you steal medicine for a terminally ill survivor from a defenseless elderly couple or conduct an honest trade at the the shelled hospital?
Should you risk your survivor's life to save an unknown girl searching for food for her family from the wrath of a drunk (and armed!) soldier or leave them be and scavenge the area in relative safety?
I often take the time to think through the acts that I make my survivors do, could I bring myself to do if I were stuck in a similar situation like them? This game inspires a deep level of thought from the smallest of actions.
Be warned, there are not many hints throughout or a tutorial, much like in real life.

I made an earlier review bashing this game, probably about a year ago. The game was in terrible shape, and really screwed with my perception of WotC's marketing decisions. Not that it's been that great as of late, but hey at least they're trying to fit into the online medium. It's a shame they aren't shining, and this is a great example of that. But the game went from total dog sh*t to passable. It's very grindy if you want to collect cards, which is the usual MO of a f2p title. That doesn't bug me too much. I play the card game in real life, so my irl collection will always be infinitely better than what they have to offer in a free-to-play format. That being said, keep in mind that this game is excellent for new players, with a tutorial that is very thorough, though it could be a little more engaging. I suppose, though, that my perception is skewed, because I went through the tutorial already knowing how to play. So for an experienced player it was a yawnfest.
The game itself isn't the best medium for a serious player--or one who wants to play casually with friends. Lots of bugs, card rulings that don't always work the way it was intended, and as many have pointed out, THG almost never works properly. While it's broken, the story they tell is intriguing enough to make me come back and grind through it. Might as well, right? If you want to play Magic: the Gathering in a really good online format, I would recommend Magic Online. Costs more, but far more reliable, and it's definitely a great medium compared to this and previous "Duels of the Planeswalkers" editions. The best medium, however, is in real life with friends, family, and random stinky fat dudes at your local hobby shop. Though, irl has its drawbacks. Silver lining about the online medium of MtG: I don't have to be afraid of my opponent eating my cards. So say what you will about the game. It's not that bad if you want to just screw around for an hour, but if you want to really crunch you should look elsewhere. Magic Duels fits my needs, so I give it an indifferent pass this time. You can do better, guys. But it's not as bad as it was.

I'm an X vet. X Rebirth is NOT X3, just leave that thought else where. X Rebirth is a new direction on the X Universe.
There are many differences good and bad and some concepts are implemented a bit more simpler and some are far more complex.
You take the role of a single ship captain and view the universe from one perspective.
I think the latest version is extremely enjoyable, 3.53, far more so with use of Mods. If you loved the role of playing statistical manager from the safety of a itemized data screen then this game is not for you. The ability to directly control mass ships via a remote display map screen in X3 is not as easily, or not at all the same in Rebirth. Think of it as traveling through the universe in a single ship with emphasis on what is in front of you.
As a FPSS (first person shooter ship) this game is a whole hell of a lot of fun. It is easy to organize fighter squads under your wing and with a click order them to attack a target. This aspect of the game is wonderful.
Drones, missiles, and underlings are your path to survival.
Again look at it from a single point character as you fly the Albion Pride influencing the universe as you go. You can personalize the cockpit, or mod your own!, to make your ship more to your own liking.
For Trading I think it is far more satisfying than previous games. No, you can't personally captain the largest freighter in the universe. What you can do is have freighters in your squad and as you fly through the universe quickly assign them trade jobs. This is even made easier with trade software and you can do this all from a menu screen. Give a single freighter 4 or 5 trade jobs and go do something else, or dock on that trade ship and watch the action from the bridge.
You are not the captain, you are the Admiral, and Admirals don't drive, they command.
The campaign I find enjoyable. Much more simplistic than many missions in X3 but it serves as an excellent Tutorial which was greatly missed in prior X games. If you find yourself starting to see the short failings of certain aspects of the game CONGRATULATIONS you've made it further in this game than most do in the previous X3 games :P
With that said, no, Rebirth does not have the same Universe longevity as say X3 TC. You will hit that end game moment a bit sooner and find less to do, at least at the moment. Then again the X series has always been about what you make of it, so try something new, or mod.
In ending, yes I can now recommend X Rebirth as the game is excellent and becoming better and better each official release with amazing mods to make the universe remarkable. Has it overcome X3 TC/AP ? not quite, but it's damn close.

No recommendation, unless you can get it on sale and eventually, not come to the conclusion that you've wasted a lot of money. I had written a rather long review, but apparently there's a limit to how much one can post, so without elaboration, here's a summary.
- It is a sandbox game with a constraining ruleset. You are only allowed to fly one ship (which is upgradable, that's something), and control other ships indirectly. You can build stations, but they can only be built at predetermined locations in the game. You can not actually meaningfully impact the economy as your profits are negligable, you have no meaningful impact on the AI production, the AI can endlessly spawn ships, and stations cannot permanently be destroyed. So, you can only build sandcastles designed by somebody else, the other kids already have sandcastles that you can knock down but they just rebuild it, and you can't kick any other kids out of the sandbox permanently.
- The campaign, like many sandbox games, is a glorified tutorial, which you need (unless you google *everything*) because while the controls and functions are inherently simple, they are not obvious. However, the campaign also arbitrarily sets you up with an enemy faction, no matter how friendly you were with them before, and this event is *entirely* outside of your control. Fly to the mission location, and it will simply happen. Faction relations range from -30 to +30, with the predetermined enemy faction I was at +28 when I decided to continue the main mission, and the game just set it to -20. Because plot. Which has no other function other than to teach you the game and send you on an exploration through the universe. Accept it will happen, or start in Freeplay.
- Nothing you do has any impact. However, since everything in the game moves at a snail's pace, you won't notice this until many hours into the game. You cannot meaningfully impact the economy. Enemy ships just spawn, they do not get built, they will always keep coming. You cannot permanently destroy stations in order to conquer the market. This last one especially has an important player function: you cannot accidentally screw yourself over by permanently ruining the economy and/or production chains. However that also means that once your own productions are set up, the only result is that prices go down due to overproduction and it means jack♥♥♥♥♥♥other than even lower profits than what you'd have expected.
- The only ships that are meaningful (other than your own) are capital ships (L and XL size). Smaller ships are pathetically weak, and even the L size ships are at a huge risk of being randomly destroyed.
- The AI is horrible, in many ways, and has seemingly arbitrary rules that rely on whether or not you are present in the same zone. Pathing is terrible, ships will "ghost" through objects when you are not present and thus follow an efficient path, but if you are present, will become stuck in impossible locations. Your mining ships will fly straight towards hostile stations, inevitable getting destroyed, because the closest resource is in that direction. Ships that get attacked, will never flee, unless they happen to be under your (in)direct control which means you get a message when they are half dead and have to press 5 buttons to tell them to flee, which they may or may not do in time. Fleet groups will not stay together, and will arbitrarily not react when a ship in their fleet gets attacked. The best one I found though: at a jump point in a sector, there was a hostile station close enough for some of its turrets to start firing at my ships if they jumped to that zone. I thought I would solve this problem, by shooting the station's turrets. I did so, and it worked, the turrets stopped firing at my ships, and they moved on without much harm. THE SECOND I LEFT THE ZONE, my ships would get destroyed before they could even make their jump out, because the game arbitrarily decided the turrets were back. This behaviour would stop if I flew back to the zone and the game realized the turrets were in fact destroyed.
- Drone AI is FUBAR. If your ships deploy the drones they have, there's a good chance they will not return to the ship once the fight is over, and the ship jumps out without its drones, causing them to be useless pieces of metal where they were left behind. However, the ship will not recognize these drones as lost, listing them as "in use" forever. Unless you manually find them and shoot them. If you sell the ship's drones, and then buy new drones for the ship, the drones will again be listed as "in use". This problem has been around for a long time, and apparently isn't important enough to be fixed.
- Loading times and mechanisms. You load the game, it gives you a loading screen. Not for the game, but for the intro movie. You skip the intro movie, it gives you a loading screen. Not for the game, but for the menu. You load your save, you finally get a loading screen for the save, which then puts you in the game. Should you get destroyed, you get a game over screen. Once you get that to respond, you get a loading screen. Not for your last save, but for the menu. Once that is loaded, you can again start loading your save. If you are in a tricky situation and get destroyed a few times in a row, this gets aggravating QUICKLY. I'd strongly recommend installing this game on an SSD if you have one, it dramatically increases loading times and performance.
- I-don't-know-WTF-you-are-doing-syndrome, AKA memory leaks. The longer you play this game, the poorer its performance gets. I could launch the game, have fun with fairly well working controls and gameplay. After an hour, I would start to notice input lag on my commands (and there's a lot of button pressing in this game, enough for that to get really irritating). After two hours, I would start to notice sluggish behaviour in nearly all departments. Some googling about this problem revealed that the game uses a lot of memory for behind-the-scenes calculations, and otherwise well working systems with relatively low RAM can suffer. That could be a fine explanation, but when this problem gets progressively worse, it's not a hardware fault, it's the software.
- The game is aesthetically boring. Not initially, the graphics are good, there's a lot of detail on the models, and your first few hours venturing into space (as well as hitting some new areas with distinct styles) will make you ogle your surroundings shamelessly. However, after that, you start noticing that everything actually looks identical. A slightly more red shade of paint doesn't actually make a new ship model. You notice the stations pretty much all look the same, which makes some sense in a space environment, modular designs are effective. But then you notice the planets do too. And the astroids. And the mass traffic, which has no other function than taking up space and making space look more "alive" because mass traffic is a bunch of small ships travelling in a circle around an object, or appearing out of nowhere inside a highway. And after a while, the music, which sounds appropriate enough for a space enviroment, quickly becomes boring.
In conclusion, this game had a lot of potential, and a lot of good ideas, but is overall, fairly poorly executed. You will encounter bugs. The immensely stupid AI will get on your nerves. A sandbox where you cannot meaningfully impact your surroundings, is not a sandbox. A place where every look and sound is repetitive, is not aesthetically interesting. The biggest challenge in the gameplay, is not hitting the wrong button when inputting a needlessly complicated sequence for a command. The plot is a tutorial that doesn't care about the sandbox aspect, since it in no way respects what you've actually been doing. And yet, I have 200 hours in this game, and that is the worst of it all. These problems do not appear until later. My empire of 200 hours, affects nothing.

Bioshock is undoubtably one of the greatest games ever made. It features level design that encourages exploration, a rich story in audio logs, unique gameplay options with plasmids, and an unforgettable setting. The combat feels great with hundreds of strategies to employ. It works well for someone who just wants to shoot things, and works even better for those with creativity and an awareness of their surroundings. It's hard not to be impressed by the philosophical nature of the game. Hours after finishing it I'm still questioning if man is "entitled to the sweat of his own brow" or if humanity is really is as free as it claims to be. You've probably heard all kinds of atrocious things about the remaster, and there are certainly some issues. In my 10 hour playthrough of the game I had 1 crash and 4 freezes, and two of which saw me lose about 20 minutes of progress. The freezes all happened while attempting to access the map/objective screen. To regain control of my computer during a freeze, I'd have to hit CTRL+ALT+DEL, sign out, and log back in. Although frustrating, I don't think the issues should keep you from making a purchase. I have reason to believe 2K is going to roll out more patches, and the crashes weren't as bothersome as you'd think. A few bumps in the road aren't nearly enough to justify a pass on this gem of a game. The immersion, fluidity, and rich story are all something you really don't want to miss out on.

The word "classic" has been uttered many a time ever since hipsters became a thing. I've been guilty of slagging it around myself. But you play through this title and tell me it doesn't deserve that moniker. Go ahead. I dare ya. I burning-undead-knight dare ya. Let's delve right into this (drumroll) classic.
I usually start off with visuals, but let me say a word or two about compatibility first. AFAIK, I only had to edit two cfg files to convince RtCW to run in 1080p. It's not native 1080p support, but it's easy enough to fix. If you're having any other issues, the Steam community has your back.
Now then, visuals: for a game made in 2001, there is some very detailed texturework and the environments are very, very well crafted and varied (castles, villages, forest, winter levels, crypts, labs, the works). The attention to detail is also praiseworthy and there's even a healthy dose of humor thrown in: I'll never forget that memo General "Vorsichtich"(=overly careful) sent to his troops: "don't brew coffee in the Mark II Fuel Purifier". Dead. One of my favorite levels is the village: although short, it just drips with atmosphere - brick houses and narrow streets in the moonlight, popping Nazis in the head with a silenced Sten while Beethoven's Moonlight Sonata plays in the background... priceless. The weapon models are done well. What shows more than a hint of age are the character models, they're blocky and the lip movements are stiff, but this was pretty cutting edge back then, though it's obviously dated now.
I must mention the sound design as well. I think this game has one of the meatiest gunshot sounds known to man, everything, from the little Luger to the Panzerfaust, feels like it just kicks your teeth in when you fire. The music is very minimal, military snare drums and orchestrations, but it fits the mood so well you kind of... forget it's there until you turn it off and something's missing. Voice acting is a bit cringy (and while we're at it, the story - bad Nazis doing bad Nazi stuff - is literally there to give you an excuse to shoot things) but you can easily skip the cutscenes and be done with it.
Production-wise then, this is a fine specimen. Gameplay-wise, also.
While RtCW is, at its core, a simple (fairly) linear shooter, what it does, it does incredibly well. Everything feels balanced and thought-out. Before regenerating health was a thing (here you have oldschool health/armor), level designers had to actually think where to put health and armor so the player would be able to survive, but still not be overpowered. I'd send all those wusses that make CoD to play through this game and study it's tight and compact level structures and weapon/enemy placements. On that note, I'm happy to say goodbye to the endless wandering corridors of Wolfenstein 3D and Spear of Destiny (don't get me started on "Spiral of Doom" or whatever it was from Ultimate Challenge) hello to beautiful European castles, forests, and Nazi secret bases. It's less of a run-and-gun ordeal a la Quake and Doom and more of a strategic placement and weapon choice death-ballet. Speaking of weapons, you have your standard pistols (Luger with optional silencer and Colts), SMGs (the Thompson, sadly with very limited ammo, a silenced Sten and the familiar MP-40) rifles (Mauser and a prototype night-vision scoped sniper), semi-auto rifles (Paratrooper rifle, marry me), throwables (grenades and dynamite), a Panzerfaust... and then you have the "rips everything to gibs" Venom machine gun, a flamethrower (useless against people, great for zombies) and a Tesla gun (which I feel was a bit underwhelming). All the weapons are effective if used correctly, and if you don't do that, well... you die. A lot. Think twice before charging a room in closed quarters with the Paratrooper rifle. Don't try to spray and pray with the MP-40 at medium range. And so on. Enemies are relentless and will punish you for every mistake.
Speaking of enemies, while you've got various iterations of Nazis (officers, guards, paratroopers, leather-clad lady assassins), you also have... SuperNazis, I mean, SuperSoldiers and a few (rather underwhelming) bosses, undead enemies, undead enemies on fire... in short, you have things to kill with, and a lot of things to kill. What more do you need in an FPS game?
One more thing I should mention: this game is challenging, but the right kind of challenging, the one where you go "♥♥♥♥, I shouldn't have done xyz" and not the one where you go "gee thanks for spamming 16 enemies into a 30 square meter room". There are some rudimentary stealth sections, which I can't help but feel were a bit tacked on and underdone, but all in all, the way you move through the levels, popping Krauts with your fine array of death-dealing tools is pure joy. It never loses momentum and if I didn't have other things to do in life, I could easily finish this game from start to end in one sitting over and over again.
So, what's not to like here? Well... to be honest, I'm having a hard time to really fault this game with anything major. Performance/compatibility issues can be fixed, but I imagine some people might have a problem with no native widescreen. As far as pacing goes, this game is pretty much as close to perfect as you can get, but some of the more opened up areas do feel a bit barren and boring by extension, but that's really more of a nitpick. The story, as I said, is a bit bland, but that's hardly the focus here. Stellar title.

Betrayer is a nice game, but you shouldn't get any false expectations.
For starters, it's not a horror game. It's not scary. Well, sometimes you'll be startled, but mostly it's just creepy and unsettling. Something like an Edgar Poe story.
Another thing - there's not much going on. You'll be running around, occasionally fighting skeletons and such, reading notes and trying to find all clues before proceeding to the next area. Yes, it's repetitive. There's almost no gameplay progression throughout the entire game, except for some tougher enemies introduced and some new equipment gathered. Once you learn the mechanincs the game becomes quite easy, too. Especially since you have infinite respawns, as well as infinite sources of loot.
If these characteristics don't look like critical flaws to you, well, then you'll most certainly enjoy what Betrayer has to offer:
- Story. Remember what i said about Edgar Poe? Add some Fenimore Cooper to the mix and wrap it up with Silent Hill, and you'll get a hint of what Betrayer is about. I'm not gonna say it's something AMAZING, but the setting is original, the characters are believable and the main storyline is intriguing enough to hold you tight till the end. Lots of good ol' reading, too.
-Visuals. Doesn't matter if you play in monochrome, as intended originally, or if you use the full palette, Betrayer's visual style is captivating. The haunted forest you're scrambling through looks stunning in its every form, and it really helps to immerse yourself into the game's world. It's actually amazing how indie developers nowadays could achieve this without the need for high budget.
-Sound. The game doesn't have much to offer in terms of different sound effects, but the ones present actually make up an imortant part of the gameplay, as you've got to listen carefully in order to find clues. This feature is implemented perfectly. Atmospheric noises are decent, too.
-Gameplay. As repetitive as it gets, it's still not so bad. You get some RPG elements, like weapons ranging in quality and magic charms that boost your attributes. Exploring for clues and loot is fun, and there's also fast travel in case you'll get tired of running around. Combat gets a lot less challenging over time, rendering stealth elements almost useless, but it still feels rewarding shattering those spectres' skulls or putting down a zombie with a tomahawk.
Overall, Betrayer is an enjoyable experience, with some original gameplay ideas, rather nice story and great visuals. If you like slow-paced games, centered around exploring and collecting stuff, try it out. But if you expect an action-packed heart-pounding thriller - better move along, or else you'll be disappointed.

From the store page of the game: "The year is 1604. You sailed from England expecting to join a struggling colony on the coast of Virginia. Instead, you find only ghosts and mysteries. What catastrophe blighted the land and drained it of color and life? Where are the settlers and tribes who lived here?
Clue by
clue, you must piece together the story of what befell this doomed settlement and find a way to set things right. You will be hunted by corrupted Conquistadors and ravening shadows as you explore an expansive wilderness in order to trace the brief, tragic history of the colony and search for survivors."
***STORY - 7/10
You have to find documents and complete quests/investigations if you want to uncover the truth behind what you "think" happened. This is a good thing and a bad thing at the same time: it is good because it gives your search a purpose, but the drawback is that you might miss something important and will be left with some unanswered questions.
***GRAPHICS - 8/10
The polygons are not the best, but since it is an indie game I'd say they are good enough. The textures on some bushes are really detailed, those on the pine trees not so much, but overall they are better than vanilla Skyrim. What I really liked about the graphics is how the vegetation reacts to the wind, you will see everyting moving, almost every leaves of a bush and every blade of grass.
You can choose to play on two different color patterns, the "supposed" one is black an white... and red. This is what the developers want you to use, it's spooky and it adds something the the game, but I didn't like it very much so I choose the coloured version, which is very good nonetheless. However I still had to play some part black and white for in-game reasons, but in my opinion it was better this way.
***SOUND - 8/10
There is no music in the game, that's because some of the gameplay mechanics are based on environmental sound. For example if you want to sneak upon an enemy undetected and there is no cover, just stay behind them and run when the wind blows, your footsteps noise will be covered and you can stab the enemy in the back.
Another feature of the game that concerns sound is that you have to follow some distant eerie noises that will lead you to your next objective... or enemy.
***GAMEPLAY - 6/10
The gamplay is quite straightforward, you will get no tutorial, but the game is a first person shooter. The only problem is that every quest is a fetch and retrieve. You basically do the same thing over and over again and it gets boring after the 3rd map. However, the game is 7 hours long (more or less) so you will not suffer much for that.
The good thing is that you have a quite nice choice of 17th century weapons and shooting lead balls from your musket is quite rewarding.
Replayable? No, once you have finished it you're probably not going to start it again.
Overall score : 7/10 - Buy it when it's under 10€

Summary:
I have come to a point in my life where I don't find as much enjoyment out of games as I did when I was younger and it has become difficult to play through an entire game and feel excited or compelled to complete it. However, Betrayer is the first game in a long time that has me wanting to play until the end credits. I first became interested in playeing Betrayer when I learned that it was set in older times specifically during the colonization of "the new world"; this combined with the paranormal elements implemeted into the game make up for a very gripping and unique experience.
Experience:
The game delivers a very unsettling and eerie atmosphere through sound, visuals and dark subject matter. It combines history and paranormal elements in a way that works greatly and is actually believable. The game deals with subject matter including murder, betrayal, witchcraft, adultory and other aspects of life during the colonization period. Sounding bells sends you into a ghost demension similar to "the Further" in the Insidious series where you meet the tormented souls of the previous inhabitants of the forts and villages that you explore; through them you learn more about the colony's dark past and the events that led to the dissapearance of its settlers. The plot gets darker and more sinister as the you progresses through the game.
Gameplay:
The compat is a littly clunky, but I feel that this greatly adds to the survival/horror elements in the game. Battles are intense and frantic as a result of the aiming difficulty and long reload times; this forces the player to develop fighting strategies and use stealth effectively in order to stay alive. To me however, exploration and progressing through the story were far more interesting aspects of the game than the combat.
Verdict:
Betrayer is definitely a strange game, but in a good way. Its atmosphere and dark historical subject matter are what make this game so unique and unsettling. I would like to point at that you are not forced to play the game in black and white. There is a slider in the settings and pause menu where you can adjust the brightness, darkness, and saturation to your liking. I recommend playing the game in color because you are forced to play in a desaturated screen setting when you enter the ghost demension; you get the best of both "worlds" this way! See what I did there? Anyway, I would definitely recommend trying the demo if you're not convinced yet; it really gives you a good idea of what the game is like. I also recommend getting this game when it goes on sale for $4.99; You will get more than your money's worth!

Played it on the free weekend.
The game is reminiscent of Civilization 5, but is actually probably a bit better in a lot of ways; the non-linear tech tree means that there is much more potential variation in strategy, and the fact that units are upgraded along a different axis (and are upgraded naturally rather than requiring you to spend large amounts of money or rebuild your units every Xty turns) is a definite improvement - it gets rid of some of the tedium of dealing with your army, and it also means that upgrading your technology makes a very real and immediate difference, rather than having to wait a number of turns to really see much of a change in your force composition. The varied victory conditions are fairly interesting, and overall the game seems to work fairly well. The idea of going through an alien environment, fighting off aliens instead of barbarians, working to tame a wild planet is a good one, but it doesn't really feel quite alien enough in many ways, and I never really felt like as much of an explorer as I would have liked. Still, you do get good rewards for exploring, and I felt like the game more directly rewarded exploration much better than Civilization 5 did.
On the downside, at its heart it is still extremely similar to Civilization 5, and the basic way that the game works feels very similar to Civilization 5, down to starting out with essentially the same units. The addition of quests and the various exploration stuff feels meaningful, and getting access to things like flight and ships vastly earlier gives a little different feel, but honestly I don't feel much like I'm leading a super futuristic civilization here - the flavor is off. That's not necessarily an awful thing, but I think that these mechanics might be better used in a fantasy game than a futuristic one.
I liked a lot of the ideas that this game had, but it isn't vastly different from Civilization 5; it is more like an expansion pack than a whole new fresh game. If you choose to buy it, keep that in mind price-wise.

This is a story of a man named Stanley. Stanley worked for a company in a big building, where he was employee number 4-2-7. Employee number 4-2-7's job was simple: He sat at his desk in room, 427, and he'd press buttons, on a keyboard. Orders came to him through a monitor on his desk, telling him what buttons to push, how long to push them, and in what order. This is what employee 427 did every day, of every month, of every year. And although others might have considered it soul-ripping, he relished every moment the orders came in, as though he had been made exactly for this job. And Stanley...... Was happy.
And then one day, something very peculiar happened. Something that would forever change Stanley; something he would never quite forget. He had been at his desk for nearly an hour when he realized that not one single order had arrived on the monitor for him to follow. No one had shown up to give him instructions, call a meeting, or even say 'hi.' Never in all his years at the company had this happened, this complete isolation. Something was very clearly wrong.
Shocked, frozen solid, Stanley found himself unable to move for the longest time. But as he came to his wits and regained his senses, he got up from his desk and stepped out of his office.
The Stanley Parable.

I tried BE during the free weekend and I have very mixed feelings towards this game. There were things I liked a lot and also some things I really hated. I'm going to tell my experiences shortly so you can make your own decisions if the game is good or bad. Anyway all the base game is very similar with Civ V and the game is more like mod than totally new game.
When you start the game you starting location is fixed so you can't travel through the map to find out better location. Sure you can select the exact location for your first colony between few tiles but still you are stuck in the same tiny shore. Few turns later some stuff are falling from the sky and you can send your explorer to pick those up. The Civ V barbarians are replaced with roaming aliens and those are neutral to you until you reach their nest or start attacking them. The happiness is replaced with health, gold is replaced with energy and etc..  so nothing new here. Still AI doesn't care about those both. It doesn't lose units when energy is smaller than -5 or doesn't seem care about health either. AI can spam multiple colonies around the map and people are in top shape.
Diplomacy is quite passive element in this game. You can totally live without it. The AI doesn't need you and you don't need them either. There is still too little options for good conversations. Though AI can ask for goods and trade those for "favors". I didn't got the idea for those because I never needed those anyway. You can send trade convoys and trade vessels to the colony which owner you hate and it brings back energy and tech. Sure you can't do this during the war but this alone makes the war more pointless than in Civ V. Every game I played I could avoid the war if I liked to do so. Even you have huge military you can't use it because it's maintained by trading. If you attack someone you and lose the trading profit you can't keep up with the costs. And unit upgrade is completely FREE. You just have to research the tech to get needed affinity and click upgrade. There are also launchable satilles and they are giving some bonus to your colonies.
When the game ended I didn't find any kind of graph or numbers to see how well I did during the game play. It left me an empty feeling for all the trouble. The victories are very similar compared to each other. You research the needed tech, build a building and wait 20-30 turns. OR conquer all the other capitals. Once I tried to achieve domination victory but warp gate was ready when there was still 2 capitals left. It was faster to send my troops through the gate than start another war.
After all I can't say the game is bad. It was enjoyable and I had a great weekend with it. Still I won't buy it because it still feels more like a mod than a whole game. If you can get this game cheaper than 15 euros go ahead. In my country you can get 3 beers with that money. It's a money well spend for a weekend game. Still the full price is a grief if you ask me.

I'm a lapsed MtG player who completely skipped over Heartstone and tried
as a freemium game. To its credit, C&C is quite accessible without monetary investments: daily quests have reasonable objectives (so far), completing 2 or 3 of them will allow you to gain a booster pack but the campaigns offer more advantageous rewards while constituting proper gaming content.
Best not to look into the shop page period. I balked at the day-one opening sales pitch as the high-pressure sales tactic that it is. An offer of 99.00$ as "best value" for silver points nearly made me uninstall. No, the proper way to enjoy C&C is by playing practice matches until you're past level 5, doing the daily quests whenever you can and going through the campaigns. I recommend C&C as a side game: something to play between sessions of some other game you bought as a relaxing alternative.
There's ONE change I'd want to make. Presently, in the grid-based arena that is C&C, troops can pass through enemy units like they just aren't there. I'm sure there was plenty of play-testing involved before developers reached a decision but when you make a design choice to have all of your action happen on a grid, then movement matters and therefore obstacles must be an option so that movement has value. Right now movement only has value in the amount of turns it takes to reach the target and this is robbing the game of a primal strategic aspect. Make passing or blocking a keyword but obstacles need to happen if you want people to appreciate the differences between that and Heartstone!
C&C is a free, casual and approachable TCG with a great forum community that offers enough content to be worth the experience. Balance between factions is great and a cursory amount of research was enough to make me aware of the effort that was put into this product. I especially recommend this product to fellow players disabused by the increasingly competitive nature of Heartstone and Mythic-centric MtG. Campaigns, not competition make this experience worth it.

As a fan in general of the larger and more complex space sims such as the old X games I can say I had a lot of fun with this game despite it being "simpler". If you're looking for a game that is very deep and has fully fleshed out trading, reputation, 3d flight you may want to look elsewhere (X3 or Starpoint Gemini 2 come to mind). I don't think that's what the developers were trying to accomplish here. I think they wanted the fun and engaging nature of a naval pirate game with some light-weight trading mechanics, where the focus is kept on the combat with the loot system basically for rewarding the player and enabling progression. In that I think they succeeded and did a great job in bringing that feel to a space setting while adding a distinctive feel with the music and pace. I will say that I did have a minor issue with the game where once I found the right setup it became pretty easy to cheese my way through the fights, but it was still a blast.

At the time of writing this review. I'm a brand new player who just started a couple days ago. I only have about 18 hours in and I sunk 10 dollars in for the hell of it because I'm very much enjoying the game. I bought the Warlock campaign and a beginner only 5 booster pack bundle. I've completed the first two parts of the Warlock campaign and I'm currently stuck on the Open Mind scenario in part three. Wether it's because I'm bad or not I'm unsure, but I feel it's because I lack the deck building ability and cards I need. I've completed both The Ancient Hero and Tournament campaigns with minimal effort just took trial and error to learn the ropes. I also did my first free tournament and got utterly and completely trashed (as expected)
Now that my history is out of the way, I can safely say this is a GOOD game with a couple glaring flaws in my opinion. I believe shop costs are perfectly fine. As long as you do your quests and wind a few matches a day you can build up plenty of points to purchase packs and the non special campaigns. Though at the pace I'm at I highly doubt i will be playing any ranked at all for a long time unless if i were to drop a significant amount of money to get to the point where I can build a solid deck I'm super comfortable with. Though I will say this the game is very well balanced as far as I can tell. It's not like you can't win with economy decks but if the person is plain better than you and has plenty of good cards you don't stand a chance. The game is mostly skill and it should be. The factions are creative and the combinations you can make are plentyful, though I don't know the metagame because I've mostly been experimenting on my own. I've found comfort in a Crusader/Warlock deck the most so far.
As for flaws. The game is, I feel, very beginner unfriendly towards crafting. When required cards cost at least 400 all the way to 8000 shards to craft and you only get 10 to 20 shards per card scrap that's just unsightly and plain bad. It's very demoralizing and I find no way to be able to surmount to those costs anytime in the near future. Really demoralizes me and makes me feel shafted. And another tournament costs. 12000 CP to enter a tournament? really? A card pack costs 2000 CP already, which i believe is a fair price, but 12000 is way steep. That takes DAYS of saving for (this is my immediate impression, correct me if im wrong) ALL players, especially newer ones where they will easily feel their CP is better spent on packs. I have no way to try out new cards and feel out decks and know what i cards i want in teh future if i cant play in tourneys. Not to mention tourney's are the only place in the current game where you can play on fair footing with everyone.
But I digress, I have fallen in love with the game. I really like it. But in the end I feel like it's a great game with a couple BIG flaws. I plan to keep playing, and I want to get into it and try hard and be good at it, but I just feel it's a little impossible at this stage for me. I do recommend it to anyone who will play casually and not care about being competitive. Would advise those looking to be competitive that to be satisfied you'll either need to drop a good bit of cash (because ten dollars won't cut it) or pray and wait for game changes.

Secondly, this game was and is just about the sensless killing of innocent people and law enforcement, if you expected more you didnt watch the trailers or do any kind of research at all before blindly buying the game because of all the media coverage. The game that Simpsons and the like parodied in the nineties after Mortal Kombat and such came out.
This is the game that all the hysterical parents didn't want their kids to play: a murder simulator, full of blood, gore, and mindless ultra violence, made with the intent of corrupting the young. Except it's not.
It's a goofy, over the top look into the minds of angst ridden kids who write misanthropic poems in their bedrooms, walls plastered with posters of extreme metal bands and drawings of satanic symbols, while hate filled music made by grown men wearing clothes either from a military surplus store or the hot topic.
It's a dumb game, but it's also a very fun game (when it isn't keyboard and mouse throwing out the window frustrating). It's fun because it allows you to do what every single one of us have wanted to do when we get bullied at school, fired from work or when a car drives by, hits a puddle and splashes water all over you ruining your brand new clothes. It's a polygons and pixels shooting other polygons and pixels for the sake of your entertainment, nothing more.
Plus you get to light a mob of people attending a political rally on fire with a flamethrower. Who wouldn't want to do that?

This plays like any other twin stick shooter. You carry 3 weapons and 3 grenade types. You pick up the guns/ammo from the dead people, and repeat. You can pick up armor, but there is no health pick ups at all! The only way you can gain health back is to "Execute" people. You can only do this when people are laying on the ground. You will be given a prompt to do an execution, and a little cut scene will play. After awhile though those get super annoying. Luckily in the options there is a "Save Executions Only" which is funny cause there isn't really anything "Safe" about them. It only disables the cut scene executing and just instead you shoot them quickly and move on. There is also a handy kick that helps knocking people down to do an execution quickly.
When you die, you have to restart the entire level, unless you acquire a re-spawn token. You have to complete the "Side Objectives" to obtain these, which are mostly "Kill everyone ____," "Cleanse the people ____," "Blow up ____." Most are easy to do. Completing one of those or completing certain main missions reward you a re-spawn token. And you will chew through those fast if you are not careful. The army will easily take you down. I've went through 4 tokens just on 10 army guys. :/
The AI can be super dumb when it comes to civilians. They will just usually run away, or run in circles, or run straight up to you even! Sometimes the civs will even pick up a gun if there is one lying around and fight back! The cops though, oh man they do not mess around. (See problems.)
OMG this game looks amazing! This game is done all in black and white, while certain things have color, such as blood, fire, explosive objects, police lights, blood, explosions, neon lights, TV's, blood... Just about everything can be destroyed or can be moved around. The destruction level in this game is really amazing. Some of the best I've seen in a long time, like this is on the lines of Battlefield! There is however problems with it. (See problems.)
There are some major problems with this game. Right when I booted it up the game says I can run everything on Ultra settings. That might be true, but I had to lower everything to Low. The reason was this game ran like♥♥♥♥♥ On Ultra I was sitting at 15FPS. I had to go all the way to low settings just to try and keep it at 30FPS. It does drop randomly to about 24-26FPS. I've also had it dip all the way to 1FPS, to where I thought the game froze/crashed (and this was only on level 2!) This game is also extremely dark is a lot of places. Even maxing out the gamma, I still had troubles. I couldn't see doors that I was supposed to go in, or would get stuck on objects that I couldn't see.
I've also had a really hard time with the Aiming/Hit boxes. When I try to line up a shot, I have NO idea if I'm actually going to hit them, or another object that is in my path. I've had lots of times where I end up shooting boxes, or shoot the ledge that I'm standing behind instead of the cop that is in the middle of a room. I've also had cops shoot me through solid walls that can't be destroyed in any way. I've died so many times because of that.
Another thing is VEHICLES ARE YOUR WORST ENEMY! So much as a brush with a vehicle will instantly kill you! This becomes a bigger problem the farther you get, as there is more vehicles later on.
Another issues is any enemy that gets right up close to you. You will have issues trying to hit anyone that is right up in your face. You will just end up shooting past them, and then they kill you.

- The difficulty system, please oh please fix the difficulty system. For those of you that don't know, when you accept a mission the game tells you how difficult it is based on your ship, which is great. Except it's horrifically broken right now, i have absolutely dominated "hard difficulty" missions and been absolutely rekt on easy difficulty missions, the system, to put it plainly, is pointless in it's current state
-Fighter class ships, they are supposed to be these little craft which acompany larger ships to help them in fights. However some missions you get only fighter class ships, and they are hilariously overpowered. In a fight of me vs 7 normal sized ships(roughly my own ships size) i can win if i use tactics, a bit of luck and a lot of guns. But in a me vs 7 fighter class ships? Heck no, i get dominated like a david and goliath fight. Let's not forget that these are supposed to be small, relatively weak ships which fight you AS WELL AS regular ship, it makes some parts of the game completely impossible, such as a mission i went on recently. The mission was simple- destroy a chrono relay and any response squad you encounter. The relay was easy, the response squad? 30 fighter ships surrounding my ships on every single direction. They closed in and there was no way to get through them without ramming through one part of the blockgade they had formed, which i did and i was unsurprised to find my shields and hull drop faster than call of duty's sales. I played MTG for a while in the late '90s, it's been over 15 years since I've played and recently decided to pick it up again.  Magic Duels is great if you've never played MTG before or haven't played in a long time and need a refreasher.  If this is the case for you, Magic Duels is definately the place to start. I don't have that much experience in CCG's and TCG's other than the Pokemon TCG many years ago, but I recently started playing Hearthstone a few months ago. A short while later, I found out about Magic Duels through a friend. Of course, due to the franchise's popularity I had heard of it before, but knew very little about the actual gameplay. The only thing I really knew was the very high barrier to entry, that combined with the fact no one I knew played Magic made me not think of trying it out. Now with the introduction of Magic Duels being free to play, I decided to try it out.
This version of Magic attempts to embrace the F2P model of games like Hearthstone, where you can play for free and slowly grind out the cards, or pay real cash to speed up the process. Unlike Hearthstone however, the process of getting all the cards is more 'fair' so to speak. Unlike Hearthstone, once you get the maximum amount of cards you can put into a deck, you cannot receive extra copies of the card. This contrasts greatly with other CCG's where duplicate commons are the bane of our existence. Hearthstone attempts to solve the problem with the disenchant feature, breaking down cards to craft the ones you want. With Magic Duels, since you cannot receive these extra unnecessary copies, you can obtain a complete card collection with a finite amount of in-game gold or real money. Another bonus is you can obtain gold by just playing with the AI, in contrast to Hearthstone where you are forced to play with real players if you wish to obtain gold. The complexity of Magic could be seen as a pro or a con depending on the types of games you enjoy. I personally enjoy the added depth of Magic compared to simpler games, but some people may not enjoy the steep learning curve as much.
However, there are a few problems with the game. The matchmaking system is very frustrating compared to Hearthstone. You might associate problems like long matchmaking duration to a smaller player base, but the process of even starting to find a match takes several attempts when playing Two Headed Giant mode. I have encountered so many error messages and problems such as one of us disconnecting from the game, but not the other, and even being matched against the friend I started finding the match with, both of us being paired with a random player. Clearly, these issues must be fixed. Another frequent complaint which is brought up by many other people is how watered down this game is compared to Magic Online and other platforms. It is kind of unfair to criticise the game on that since it only has 2 expansions as of date, but the game is in a weird spot where those already playing Magic wouldn't want to play it because it has too little content, but those new to the franchise might still find the game to be too difficult.
Overall, I would still recommend this game as a nice 'first step' into the world of MTG. Having a fairly good F2P model and a quite comprehensive tutorial/story mode makes it a reasonable game for those new to the franchise to try it out. However, I really hope that the problems with matchmaking can be fixed because that alone makes the game much less satisfying to play, especially since what is perceived to be the most 'fun' mode of MTG, Two Headed Giant, is the game mode with the most issues.

This strange, beautiful, pants-obsessed platformer is a surprisingly fun, hidden gem of a game.
Tiny & Big sat in my inventory for a long time, one of those titles I bought because it was on sale.  The screen shots generally don't do it any justice making it an easily overlooked title; the name doesn't help either.
The graphics, although strange, are a suitable stylistic choice that fit well with the theme.  Likewise, the music is unusual but enjoyable.  A couple new tracks are hidden in each level, so finding them is a good idea if you want to expand the game's song list.
The most noteworthy design element in the game is the physics engine with the ability to cut pillars, statues, boulders and most other stone items.  It feels amazing to push, pull, and hack apart such large objects and dynamically alter the game environment.  The simple act of cutting objects at any angle without the use of voxels was something I had never seen before.
I appreciated how the designers encouraged experimentation; most of the trial and error situations encountered aren't that painful.  Despite my low tolerance for gaming frustration and rather poor platforming skills this game won me over and I fought through.  It's a short game at 3-5 hours, but it has a lot of replay value if you enjoy achievement hunting.
Those whom enjoy the exploration of platformers, will surely love hunting down hidden objects and discovering the various Easter eggs that Tiny & Big has to offer.  I enthusiastically recommend this somewhat underrated title to everyone.

Wow. Finished this game in 4 hours. I didn't get too many achievements, but that's ok, because I'm just glad to be finished playing through the story. While I will give the creators an A+ for effort in coming up with a decent physics sandbox and a tool set to play with (rocket launcher, grappling hook and laser beam), the rest of the game is full of fail.
1. The story line is non-existent, save for one meaningful cutscene. Dialogue, which would have been fairly humorous if they had used voice actors, is meh because the characters just squeak at eachother while you read speech bubbles.
2. The controls, physics and surfaces are all tempremental. You can walk back and forth on a plank a handful of times, but then suddenly the next time you walk on it, you fall through it. Not off, *through.* Sometimes the laser freezes the object in mid air so you can cut it, sometimes it doesn't.  Sometimes that beam you just cut falls perfectly and lands right where you want it, sometimes it bounces, spins out of control and kills you for your trouble. So frustrating...
3. The game is criminally short for $10 dollars. Particularly in light of the fact there is no real plot moving you forward.
4. I bought the sound track along with the game for an additional $5 dollars. Sadly, about a third of the music is amusing and catchy, the rest is "meh" at best and elevator music at worst.
5. Achievements are basically grind quests... use this item 1000 times, or collect 1000 of these boring rocks (a quest for boring rocks? I bet that will hold the player's attention...).
6. I get that the art is supposed to be weird and unique. I get that we're in a desert. But the color palette was really bland and the lack of contrast sometimes made it difficult to gauge distances, depth or to distinguish cuttable surfaces from non-cuttable.
Overall, I cannot recommend this game. If at some point it goes on sale for $1, then sure, pick it up. But until then, you're better off buying a better physics sandbox like Garry's Mod.
Again, I will give kudos to the creators for the level of freedom (or total absence of direction?) when it comes to solving the puzzles and navigating the environment in the game. With the tools at your disposal you can theoretically shape the environment to your will. In practice, however, what surfaces are cuttable, the effectiveness of your rocket launcher and grappling hook on moving things in the environment, and your ability to slide and stack stones without getting snagged on something in the environment is somewhat arbitrary.

is a cute 3D puzzle platformer that gives the player more versatility in their actions. The key mechanic in the world is that (almost) everything is destructible, allowing the player to shape his own paths to victory.
The player takes the role of Tiny, who is chasing the antagonist Big to reclaim a pair of legendary undergarments. Armed with only a machine known as "The Tool," Tiny must climb towers and spelunk into ruins on his journey.
Unlike other platformers, the game is neither reflex- nor combat-based. Instead, you use a laser, grappling hook, and rocket to shape the 3D world and create new passages. Nearly everything in the game can be cut and reshaped, giving the player lots of freedom to destroy and rearrange the world to suit his needs. As such, there is seldom ever one way to beat the puzzles in this game.
However, although it is very well executed,
does suffer from a lack of content. Since the game relies so heavily on its game engine, it features only five levels (and the final boss). The overall difficulty is fairly low, so don't expect a challenge. However, there are tons of hidden collectibles and achievements that extend the game time for several hours.
Soundtrack is A+. Visuals are unique and have this adorable comic book style to them, including copious amounts of funny hovering onomatopoeia.
I really liked this game. I think it's definitely worth a buy if you're into puzzle platformers, especially if you are interested in exploration games too..
