Updated for 4.0!
Short version: For the plot, just watch on Youtube. This game cost Egosoft a Roguey (*formerly* a big fan/promoter/guy who runs a nice X-game site) and was a waste of a Cycrow (modder who brought life to a lot of the X-games). This game isn't a sandbox. It's a pretty garbage can.
Long version: Changing the format from my 3.6 review to just be: who did their job right; who sort of did their job right; who did their job wrong; noticed changes for 4.0; conclusion. Misspellings readers notice are prbobabally intentional.
Who did their jobs right?
Well... nobody? Graphics people were here, until I found myself complaining too much.
Who sorta did their jobs?
1) Graphics people! Everything is gaugeous! Big 'ole cap ships with so many guns, to the tiny boarding pods (which open up on contact with a ship! Crazy detail)! Character models are pretty bland, and many are bald; apparently it was much worse in 1.0 though. Travelling on highways is still nice; though they've shortened the 'roller coaster' highways. Stations are huge and feel like realistic-ish space stations. Might not prefer the big empty interiors that have less game impact, but that's minor. Big problem: you still glitch through ship/station surfaces and get stuck on the inside. It seems rarer now; either 4.0 fixed most causes or I got better at avoiding collisions.
2) Combat people! Weapons fire, missiles track, but there's very little balance. Missiles are useless in a firefight against fighters because they'll never connect; missiles are the only real weapon against capital ships because lasers are too low dps. Cap ships regularly have 12+ (think I've seen 17) fighter escorts. When you're trapped in a fighter, 12 to 1 odds means run or die. Or rarely run AND die. Plasma/LR turrets (look like beam lasers) have laser accuracy and can 2 or 3-shot an upgraded player ship (the turrets are mounted in groups of 2 or more, so it can functionally be an instant kill). Boarding operations frequently end with 'How did I die?' I have also never noticed any of my ships or stations launch combat drones, despite the fact I keep stocking up on them.
3) Economy people! Ships fly and trade; stations will build correctly now. People assigned to posts will show up in menus and you no longer have to restart to interact, buuuut... Stations are still functionally indestructible and quickly rebuild if you're not actively shooting at them. Player stations STILL take over 24 hours real-time to construct. Construction Vessels (CVs) still don't get integrated into stations like the description says - they're ugly, inconvenient (extra crew needed, etc.), and a huge vulnerability to a station performing upgrades. I'm going to elaborate on stations later, because it was the biggest non-glitch-related let down for me.
Who didn't do their jobs?
1) Story people! Spoilers!
The game could have been titled "Uncanny Coincidences... in Space!" At least then Ego could have claimed some allusion to
.
Changes I've seen:
Collision glitches happen less rarely than 3.6. Weapon mods - RANDOM modifications to ship weapons that enemies drop. They increase or decrease damage, range, rate of fire, cooling, etc. Not all mods are good. You can craft them with dismantled mods, but the result is random, so you reload a lot. Two new weapons I haven't gotten because the story arbitrarily locks the weapons you can access. Save files are now compressed in .gz format, making them harder to modify. Cargo drones don't seem to get stuck (though we could have used transport devices from previous games and avoided the issue). Home of Light is a thing. I don't regret not getting it, even on sale. There's a tester with a positive review that includes something like "Fix the fog! It's dropping frame rates to single digits!" SETA (time speed-up) is back. There's a jump drive, haven't gotten it (spent time early in the game amassing a big fleet to see if you could kill a station). You can apparently cap certain Xenon ships (stuck early in the plot). There's a mission bulletin board, so you don't have to fly all over to try to find missions. Any mission requiring station defense is a guaranteed win - accept the mission, continue what you were doing before, and get paid. Because stations are unkillable.
The rant:
The state of stations is really irritating. They're the only non-randomly generated things in the game, and therefore their creation and destruction is the only way to truly affect the universe. Well, you can construct your own, over the course of days! Who the f*** thought that was a good idea? DAYS. But you can't destroy NPC stations. You *can* bring their hull to 0, but! AI ships (which you can't directly control without mods) are too stupid to shoot at all the modules on most stations, so those modules can't die. And 0 hull stations will be back before you can "destroy" a second station because they rebuild (repair) so fast. Player stations as defensive installations are pointless - spend days making a station that'll shoot a few randomly-generated NPCs? But even as factories, they fall flat. They make stuff that feeds other factories, which make stuff that feeds shipyards, which make ships. The player cannot have a shipyard, which is limiting in its own right. So you can supply one of the few NPC shipyards. Well you can buy ships from them, when they're not making their own ships that quickly despawn. OH! And you see ship info, there's a section for what command they're executing. 4.0 seemed to make that command "???" more. So you go close and scan the ship to find what it's up to. Well, if it's got the 'explore' command, it's going to despawn soon. So, they hid ship commands with "???" because too many people were aware the ships had that despawn "explore" command. Anyhow, you've got your factories. You've got your ships. But NPC stations aren't sand castles in a sandbox; they're steel bars with sand glued on. So, at some point you'll realize your sandbox is really a prison.

Betrayer is an action-adventure game set in 17th century America. Once ashore you reach your very first settlement but find it completely abandoned apart from some human-sized ash figures. The only friend you have is a girl wearing a red cloak. She is looking for her sister and asks for your aid.
While wandering in the forest you encounter conquistadors who attack you immediately. Stealth is very important - especially at the beginning of the game - as you can quietly dispose of your enemies without having to fire your weapon. Initially, you have a bow but soon you'll be able to obtain a crossbow and also a pistol and a musket. These - as the game takes place centuries ago - require quite some time to be reloaded.
I like the atmosphere of the game. I am not sure why the creators went with the monochrome (black and white) art style but it certainly suits the game's atmosphere. In fact, only some key elements show up in red colour such as the things you can interact with and the enemies. Wind blows heavily from time to time which completely conceals the sound of your footsteps. Both the art style and the sound effects deserve a high five!
While the map shows small settlements and roads you can go elsewhere in the forest to find many secrets as it does not reveal everything. There are hidden chests, graves, clues and even unique weapons scattered throughout the land. Later in the game you obtain a shovel with which you can dig at certain places.
Oh, the clues! Every map has a central settlement where you can install a bell. Once rung the game changes your surroundings completely. Everything becomes dark and creepy and instead of conquistadors you fight skeletons and evil spirits. You find good spirits who will always tell you a story. A story of a murder, betrayal, vengeance or something sinister that resulted in the death of the townsfolk. You can then find other ghosts and clues (items) to reveal the background of these killings.
While not necessarily a long game and repetitive at times, Betrayer offers a refreshing experience in the FPS genre with its unique art style and excellent sound effects.
The game never tells you where to go but you are able to "listen". By pressing X you hear a sound effect that is stronger if you are close to your objective and also if you face the right direction. This is a creative way to make you navigate and the creepy sound effect greatly accompanies the haunting atmosphere of the Otherworld.
Highly recommended and do keep the monochrome colouring style as intended!

Best played in the dark, with the lights off, although you will still be startled by angry Spaniards and wraiths in the daylight.  Some adjustment is needed for your eyes to become accustomed to a monochrome world.  If you find the initial settings invite the onset of a migraine, you can fine tune, color, contrast, and brightness settings live in game to dial in a more pleasing palette.  Given that you are in a monochrome world, colors, when they appear can be startling and attention grabbing, so keeping the color settings close to original helps to deliver the atmosphere intended to work in concert with the directional sound, which really brings the game to life (even though you are surrounded by the dead).
Immersive sound is used for more than just surrounding you with various bird songs, insects, wind, stomping feet, and rustling foliage.  Directing you towards objects of interest, is an friendly shimmering sound while pressing X will fill your head with cacophony of echoing whispers that synchronize in stereo as you point your ears in the direction of the closest objective.  Sound used in this way, is far more satisfying and intuitive for locating objectives than simply being directed by a HUD and map.  Since the sound is directional, it alerts you to the presence of enemies around you and will make you jump out of your chair when they suddenly appear.  Conversely, you can startle your enemies, by sprinting towards them during a strong wind, thwacking them in surprise with your tomahawk, blasting them in the face with a cloud of black powder and shot, or haphazardly toss a black powder bomb their way.
Not burdened by a useless pile of trinkets to sift and sell,  what is found turns intal into coin to use for ammo, weapons, and charms, or is recorded as a clue in your journal.  Weapons and ammo can also be found and turned instantly into coin, if you find them lacking.
Just enough arrows and lead shot are held in your inventory to freely use the period weapons without fear of running out.  Conversely, you do not have an endless supply of ammo to freely send an endless volley of arrows like some games.  Arrows can be retrieved from corpses and the ground, so you can resupply at a fort less often.  Muskets and pistols take a few seconds to load, which adds an old world authenticity and charm that is strangely enjoyable and maddening as you scramble to reload, while a Spaniard does the same, trying to murder you from across a field.
A perfect game to play in the fall of the year on all hallow's eve surrounded by pumpkins, candles, and candy bars.

Review of the game:
The game plays a lot like Civ 5; that's not a bad point. It's only natural that a developer will try to build from a previous game when they put a lot of resources into it and in this case, it's not even a bad match. There are, naturally, a lot of differences.
The game uses a hex-based stategic map, just like Civ 5, and just like Civ 5, you can only have one military unit and one civillian unint per hex. This avoid the doom stacks that previouse verions of the Civ games suffered from, but in fairness, the amount of military units per hex seems low; having three units or so would make more sense to me -- this will allow you to build stacks which build up a diversity of strengths, without making them entirely invincible.
Tech development uses a tech grid or wheel. Each node allows you to branch into new techs as well as open up for sublevel tech -- this is, technically, not at all different from how things have been done since Civ 4. The branching is just less linear, which is.. well, what it is. It makes sense in the context of playing a few decades or even a century of game time, not to have tech which represent major technological breakthroughs in the history of humanity.
The game plays a bit on some of the ideas of Alpha Century, but it's not a clone; barbarians have been replaced by aliens and there's some sort of biomass covering a large portion of the planet; unlike in Alpha Century you have very good reason for exterminating the aliens since they
attack your units, even if you try your best to be on their good side and the biomass hurts your units and can kill them.
Designable units are not in the game, which I think is a shame, but then again, I never really used it in AC, as it was just too damn time consuming with virtually no benefit. Instead your units can be customized through advancement of "affinites".
Affinities are very important in the game, as they unlock certain unit upgrades but also give you permanent bonuses and unlock victory conditions; you can't build an emancepation gate without being high developed in the superiority affinity for example. I think this makes sense and fits the game nicely.
Religion is (more or less) gone. You can found a new religion by researching the right technlogy and then it's more or less just a flavour thing (I believe it unlocks a victory condition as well).
"Complex" espionage has been added and, well, it's not entirely done IMHO. You get spies, which can be relocated to cities to either do counter-espionage (in your own cities) or do something else in foreign cities, like steal money, technology or outright take over the city. The problem with this is that in order to do anything beyond stealing money, you have to advance the "intrigue" level of a city; this is done by perfoming espionage missions in foreign cities, and it's lowered by doing counter espionage. There are also buildings which can
. This is a big problem, since you, virtually, cannot raise the intrigue level of a foreign city beyond 3. I think I've been able to get it to 4 two or three times, having about 10 spies doing espionage in foreign cities. The intrigue level will drop over time as well, which means you don't even have to use your spies to counter foreign spies, simply because doing any espionage takes too long. Great idea, unbalanced implementation.
Overall:
I think the game is great but heavily overpriced. I would recommend it if the price was sliced in half, without discounts.

This is a story of a man named Stanley. Stanley worked for a company in a big building, where he was employee number 4-2-7. Employee number 4-2-7's job was simple: He sat at his desk in room, 427, and he'd press buttons, on a keyboard. Orders came to him through a monitor on his desk, telling him what buttons to push, how long to push them, and in what order. This is what employee 427 did every day, of every month, of every year. And although others might have considered it soul-ripping, he relished every moment the orders came in, as though he had been made exactly for this job. And Stanley...... Was happy.
And then one day, something very peculiar happened. Something that would forever change Stanley; something he would never quite forget. He had been at his desk for nearly an hour when he realized that not one single order had arrived on the monitor for him to follow. No one had shown up to give him instructions, call a meeting, or even say 'hi.' Never in all his years at the company had this happened, this complete isolation. Something was very clearly wrong.
Shocked, frozen solid, Stanley found himself unable to move for the longest time. But as he came to his wits and regained his senses, he got up from his desk and stepped out of his office.
The Stanley Parable.

It's fairly easy to knock about Betrayer if you approach the game like F.E.A.R or another 'ctrl+C, ctrl+V' shooter, but that is totally on you - not the developers. Rather, this should be played like a point and click game in many respects, with an appreciation for the art style Blackpowder has adopted.
Let's start with that. The aesthetic of the game is obviously fairly distinct and this can be a great detractor for some people. Though there is a colour saturation option (that's right, you can play in colour), it is really not recommended as you lose a great deal of the art style that ultimately shapes the atmosphere of the game. However, I found that bumping up colour to 0.1 was beneficial in many cases as it allows for small amounts of extra detail to be resolved, adding a bit more depth otherwise lacking from homogenous blacks that at times were hard to wrap your head around. Overall it's quite gorgeous, and Blackpowder have clearly optimised the look to suit black and white with a little wiggle room for very minimal colouring.
Weapons are by in large period faithful. Crossbows, short bows, long bows, muskets, tomahawks (no, not the exploding kind), flintlocks and rudimentry grenades make up your arsenal. I read elsewhere someone complaining about a lack of automatic weapons - which reflects more upon their own retardation than a fault of the devs. Each weapon feels distinct, and you'll be conciously cycling between certain ones based on the context of the battle at hand, with things like muskets woeful for close combat with multiple enemies but an absolute cannon for longer ranges. Though the mechanics are overall quite simplistic, the hierachy of weapons and their upgrades mean that you'll rarely be dependent on just a single one until quite late in the game.
Other things to note are the actual quests and storyline. All follow a theme (if you can't guess it, log off and finish off your homework of reciting the alphabet) that can at times be a bit "geee I really didn't see that coming," but remain distinct enough so that if you're genuinely interested in playing the game, you'll recall who-is-who and what-is-what. It may not be the strongest storyline, but it is entertaining enough to see the game through to completion with a twist or two.
Finally, the game follows an open world structure most similar to that seen in S.T.A.L.K.E.R games - with open regions to explore that may be left by only a single route in either direction. Though you can teleport anywhere on the discovered map, I find that it actually is inhibitory to your progress as you miss things like chests, buried charms, quest items and unique weapons that you probably overlooked in the early games. These can actually play a pretty big part in how you finish the game, so keep that in mind.
There are plenty of other things I could mention - like the charms, enemies, stealth mechanics, great soundwork or the otherwordly realm; but those are probably best left a bit hush-hush so you can enjoy them yourself. This is a great game that has been well produced but may at times suffer from acute cases of cliche or confusion. If you approach it not like a shooter, but like a point-and-click adventure, you'll enjoy yourself.

This game is pretty much worse than the original in every single way, especially storywise. That said, it's enjoyable for a bit, though it gets tedious after awhile. Fortunately there's the handy dandy super broken hypnotize plasmid that lets you speedrun the game when you've decided you have enough!
So basically the plot goes something like crazy lady steals all the lolis because she wants to change Rapture from Somalia to Sweden by making some superpowered loligod with no sentience  to rule over everyone else with impartiality. Or something incredibly dumb like that. Sounds eerily familiar... It's clear that the game was trying to portray the antagonist turning Rapture into collectivist dystopia, opposite of Andrew Ryan's philosophy. It might have worked, but they didn't really stick with it after the first two hours or so and the result is some incredibly bland chapters. For most of the game it feels like you're just following the arrow to kill the guy who has the key to open the next place and not pursuing the plot. The preacher and the guy in the gardens ("I LOCKED MYSELF IN THIS ROOM UNTIL YOU SAVE/KILL 3 SISTERS, SO THERE!!!"). Some of the bold and lofty lines are there, but not enough. It all melts together quite quickly.
I realize now why Bioshock Infinite had a new setting vs. the other two entries in the franchise: because it sets the theme. It compliments the storytelling. In Bioshock 2 the atmosphere does not compliment the story. It's just there because it's there. Because it was the setting of a universally acclaimed game and the publisher was determined to make more money off of it somehow.
The game also offers little positive in the way of new, meaningful changes to gameplay compared to Bioshock 1. Big Daddy fights were reduced to "equip ice drill, run around big daddy in a circle." Plasmids are pretty much the same save for a few useless new ones, and an altered one that is completely game breaking. To get all the Adam you guard the little sisters. 2x per sister. Up to 3 sisters per level. Six times. Extremely cheap way of lengthening the game and you bet it gets tedious. Honestly the core gameplay was never super amazing in Bioshock, but without another draw in the game it really shows. I don't remember feeling like every gun did zero damage in the original.
Bottom line is that this game is basically Opposing Force. Or Blue Shift. Or one of the original F.E.A.R. expansions. It's a level pack for the original. It's even got the "play as one of the other guys!" thing going on! In other words, if you really really really really liked the gameplay in the original it's worth playing for that. Otherwise it is not worth your time.

Rebel Galaxy....
Probably the most fun I've ever had with a space game like this ever. The soundtrack alone attracted me to this wonderful game, only because it's such a perfect match. Though I must say, at the time of writing this, I have roughly 60 hours set in right now into Rebel Galaxy, but it does not match the potential amount of hours I COULD be spending playing this game. With it's randomly generated "Systems" or whatnot, it provides a relatively fresh experience with every new playthrough. The only downside with this model, is there is a general process that is the same, and it goes with the advancement in tech vs. the contracts price in every system. Right out of the start cutscene, I could spend maaaybe 2-5 hours building up enough money for a new drive that allows for Solar System Gate use, and start working easy contracts in the furthest system. Run into no conflict, and in the matter of hours attempting at getting high tier gear relatively early on in the story breaks the immersion a little bit. Even if you were to stay true to the story aspect, you can get to a specific point and still go do side quests and contracts for money.
There are many directions that you could take with every playthrough, and thats what I'm getting at exactly. No matter how hard or easy you make it for yourself, it's still amazing what one could do in this game.
I will have to say, it does break a little bit of realism/immersion at times, when Juno talks  about "your small ship and how it may be time for an upgrade", and you already maxed everything out. It just seems weird to me. Little prompts like that. Another thing that concerns me is the difficulty overall, it goes from baby steps to smacks in the face pretty quick, and the overall progression seems a little awkward when moving up in tech. I found that the only way I could survive going up in difficulty for the next system was to earn a ridiculous amount of money, go over there, and buy the highest tech because that would be the only way I could even survive there.
The whole concept of Mining or Trading seems a bit awkward to me, because if you want to mine, you have to go at it for a long time to make any real profit. It feels almost useless to me (Mining), unless you find that golden nugget in a desert, the Antimatter Specks, which I have yet to find. The only way you can even make trading profitable is if you attack convoys or traders due to the large amount of items they have that are super profitable OR fighting Pirate lords with high end ship systems, though, they are insanely hard sometimes.
PROS:
1. The whole badass atmosphere (with music) gives the player confidence and has a really good feeling while flying through space in my awesome ship with big weapons
2. Optimization and level of content allow the highest graphics even on lower end machines
3. Ship designs seem really well thought out and allow for a multitude of playing styles
NEUTRAL:
1. Combat feels tasteful and well done, though lack of ways to end your enemies in your travels feels saddening at times. When I'm flying past, I feel the only way to really do damage is broadsides or lots and lots of turrets. If only there were more ways, it would feel just perfect.
CONS:
1. Mining is tacky and has a useless feeling. One could be mining for hours, but unless they are mining the right materials that usually scarce in most astroid fields, so it doesn't feel fulfilling
2. Solar Systems never really feel unique, a few system is a new system. It may have labels that some places are better for trade or mining, but I haven't really noticed a difference anywhere.
3. Factions seem pointless sometimes - because I could be super friends with the militia and citizens, but NOBODY else would like me, and it wouldn't matter because I wouldnt gain anything from them anyways. The only other faction that matters to some degree is the Red Devil Raiders, but they offer mid-game gear from my current understanding. If the other factions had more purpose and personality, I'd be more inclined to try improving relations with them, IF there was a way besides surrendering all of my cargo whenever they see me.
Rebel Galaxy is definitely a fun game and I highly suggest you give it a try!
---NOTE---
The game is not far from its release date, so I expect a lot of changes in the games further history, but for now, this is what I see :)

Words cannot express my distain for this game. It's bad enough for me to write a review for the first time on Steam.
Graphics 4/10: The creators were going for a very obvioys "gritty" look to this game. While the game does maintain a kind of James O'Barr graphic novel look, it's dark, colorless, and grainy look makes it somewhat hard to see items, and weapons. The explosion effects are mediocre at best, as are the character models. The game's backgrounds and sprites resemble an early 2000s or late 1990s PC game.
Sound design: 5/10 Effortless attempts at giving it the "hellish" sounds and music list you'd hear in a modern Doom game, or a F.E.A.R. entry. Mostly you'll just be hearing the same repeated dialogue being screamed by the victims.
Gameplay: 0/10 This is where Hatred fails in every way I could have possibly imagined. Not only is this game painfully glitchy, but the controls are absolutely, and irredeemibly bad. While trying to record a video review for this game, the controls glitched so completely, that I wasn't able to perform the simple task of walking through a door and to another room. Going up went left, going right, went down, going up again went right, then down, and so forth. It not only glitched in one way, it seemed to be going through this bizarre glitch where the controls were on a constant cycle of switching. After a frustrating ammount of time, the controls finally started working properly, and I got to the game proper.
You run around, and shoot. I know that's obvious, but when I say "you run around and shoot"; note that I am not saying "You run around and shoot people."
You aren't aiming, you aren't controlling your weapon. You're spinning around and firing in any given direction, and mindlessly throwing out shots, similar to "SMASH T.V." on the Nintendo. The problem is that in the graphics make it difficult to see where your targets even are, or the perspective of the game makes it difficult to point yourself in the proper direction. It's quite possibly the worst controls I've ever seen in a game.
Overall Score- 1/10: This game is a horrible unofficial remake of the original Postal. When you get right down to it, there's really not much different about the two games, other than the perspective, the graphics...and that's about it. Everything down to the main character design is nearly identical to playing Postal in black and white. I wouldn't even recommend this game if it were sale for a dollar. Terrible, terrible game.

Anyone who has played the original Bioshock knows that doing what's morally right (but less benefiting) is the best way to play. Not only does it affect how you view the game, but it also affects the bonuses you can get along the way for being the good guy. Although, we all know that we sometimes want to choose the evil harvest option for more ADAM. A nice touch to Bioshock 2 is that it gives you more choices than to just rescue or harvest the Little Sisters. You now have Rpature civilian lives in your hands. You get to choose whether to kill them or not.
Gameplay wise, Bioshock 2 is superior to the original. Finally being able to melee an enemy and having the ability to hold a plasmind and a gun in each hand is a nice and quick way to deal with those annoying splicers. The splicers even have more variety than the first game, which is nice but the gameplay does hinder your fun at some points. Since you want to be a good guy, that means you have to put up with all the stupid objectives of having a Little Sister. Other than saying the same 5 lines over and over, the Little Sisters often make half of a level feel like a hard escort mission. Sure, they don't get killed easily but having to defend them while they do their job is going to get you killed easily, especially if you're low on money and ammo. This constant frustration made the game a chore at times.
Story wise, Bioshock 1 is superior but Bioshock 2 still has a nice story in itself. I can really appreciate the fact that the developers of the game tried to detail Rapture from the first game and implement it into the second game in order to build up a good atmosphere. Lamb isn't as threatening as Andrew Ryan, but she is enough of a driving force to make you want to stick a syringe in her eye socket.
Overall, Bioshock 2 improves on a lot of the necessary aspects of the first game. While the story isn't as intriguing or memorable, the gameplay and extended lore makes this game worth playing before you pursue Infinite.

This game has the understanding that many of the more recent space sims do not, namely that a living world creates immersion and that the major component for creating a living world consists of real voices, simulating communication with the player, and a vibrant AI system. Add to it some hearty music and Rebel Galaxy feels warm and alive, unlike its much more expensive predecessors.
The main gameplay feature that sets this space sim apart from all others is that the battle happens with Black Flag type naval combat, where the ship stays on a flat plain and fires cannons from the sides.
Pro's:
Good flow: you complete missions, scavenge ships, buy upgrades, move to more dangerous areas, buy better ships, help out allies, do more missions, etc. It gets addicting.
Dynamic unbalanced world: I once came across an enemy capital ship in a low-difficulty space that annihilated two militia capital ships and was clearly overpowered for the area. Another time, I came across a giant pirate armada next to a planet. Yet another time, the mission was labeled hard but turns out to be super easy if you are fast enough. Maybe these are all bugs, but they make the game feel more dynamic and realistic.
Music: slide guitar rock is great. I bought the songs before the game even came out.
Combat is fun. Lots of ships flying all over in the colourful chaos of battle.
Customizable fighting styles: Buy a fast ship or a slow mammoth; long range torpedo boat or point-blank cannon. You decide.
Good value for your money.
Cons:
Saving behavior. At the time of this review, the game saves whenever you quit the game or at a station and there is only one save. This means: 1. you cannot load a previous game if you mess up and 2. if anything happens to your save, you are screwed. This means you have less freedom to experiment. I have yet to find a game where the checkpoint system did not annoy me.
Flat space: While the naval combat system does work, part of what I love about space sims so much is the freedom to fly anywhere and by restricting the movement to a plain you are cutting at the core of what is interesting about space sims.
Trading system is mediocre: You can buy low by paying attention to the news and then sell high but it is nowhere near as profitable as doing even the easiest of the combat missions and just does not work very well.
In time, a few annoying bugs did reveal themselves, though nothing gamebreaking.

This game lists itself as a casual game and i think that's the most important thing to look at when judging it. Casual can be a broad spectrum of different games, from your multiplayer pick up and plays to the bathroom break games of the mobile market and sadly the game falls into the lower end of the latter.
The game uses a simple mechanic, which is essentially pick up a spawned bomb and throw it to kill the ever spawning enemies, much like the fun and addictive arcade games of the past. However while those drove you forward to increase your score and reach further levels, letting your skill grow this feels uninspired and ultimately plain.
For the most part you are looking at an almost entirely static sprite of the titular clergyman with his 100 yard stare focused directly on you. The other graphics are raw at best and the soundtrack is one bland song on a loop. Which makes it all feel like a mediocre flash game,
Ultimately i don't think it's a completely bad game. It's rudimentary mechanics, visual style and sound might see it enjoy some success as a free to play mobile game or a flash game. But as an actual release it falls far short of even the lowest standards.

Ok, so I originally said that this game was getting better...and it still is.  V4.0 was released (seperate to the Home of Light expansion) and it's far superior to the launch title.  However...all that glitters is not gold.
So, the performance has been improved again - but it STILL suffers from easily replicated performance drops.  This is not a CPU or GPU bound issue, but items in the game that cause it.  Examples include landing on stations and looking left or right - one direction drops the frame rate to 25 the other is a solid 60 (my system caps all games at 60 as my monitor can't display more than that - vsync is always off).
Pathing issues still prevail, in fact the new update has included new ones :(
If in external view zooming out lets you (or the ship you are docked with) fly right through solid objects - this is both a blessing and a curse.  Sometimes you need to use this glitch as you get stuck inside of station modules!
Person selection on stations is still a royal PITA, basically the hit back is too large and often lopsidded.  So if there are 3 people sat next to each other, good luck selecting the one you want (you have to look up/down then look left/right then look up/down again to target the right person).
Often you have no control - litterally.  Currently getting an update from one of your other ships?  Yeah, no more throttle/attitude control for you.  Keep in mind that this is with keyboard/mouse, not sure about joystick/gamepad.
The UI is very inconsistent, as an example talk to a capital ship dealer and ask for the list you will see little icons to the left of each ship - these link to the encyclopedia.  Quite nice, but now do the same for a small ship dealer and you have to select the ship in the list and then hit the "encyclopedia" button at the bottom of the menu!
The above are just a few of the more obvious issues that are still in the game - at this point whilst the game engine clearly has a lot of potential I really am not sure that Egosoft has the ability and/or desire to make good on this potential.  In addition Egosoft has always been very poor at comunicating with customers, and this trend has continued.  The offcial forums have many helpful people - but very few actual Egosoft employees (or offcial affiliates) take the time to talk to their customers.  And if you want any kind of commitment from Egosoft to correcting the issues, you may as well go and read tea leaves or chicken entrails - you will get more information from that then from Egosoft :(
They are a very small company, but the one lesson they have sadly not learnt is to communicate with your customers.

I love the Civilization games. I remember the first one I played, Civ 3, and had such good memories of it, that I've Been trying to play all of them since. I had to adjust through the changes, but ultimately everything added was more than worth anything I liked that was taken away.
Been wanting to play this game since it came out, but didn't have the money, so when they had the free weekend up, I jumped at the chance to play it. Downloaded it, loaded it up, and hopped right to so I could get to dominating the computer like usual.
So it was, obviously, such a huge let down to not like this game. For the first time since I ever started on the Civilization series, the additions are far out-stripped by the things taken away from 5. The resources are less diverse, and less scarce. I even played on Abundant resources, hoping to get more, and still I had issues making them last. The trade convoys stopping every time they've made a circuit to find out if I want to change their travel destination annoyed the heck out of me. When I tell a trader to trade with a certain place, it should keep doing that until I tell it to change. Every time it'd stop and ask me what I wanted, it felt like it was taking me out of everything I've been already planning in my mind to do that turn. Add to it the fact that I couldn't turn off the aliens, this game's version of the Barbarians from Civ 5, if I wanted to... That made it feel like I couldn't play the game my way, instead I had to play it the way the developers wanted, which has never really been the Civ series style.
I can honestly say that I'm glad Steam had the free weekend for this game, because it saved me $50 by showing me this game is not something I want to spend money on. If I want to play Civilization, I'll just go back to Civ 5 and enjoy my time spent.

I don't normally bother posting reviews, would rather spend the time actually gaming. This is the first one I'm posting, as I don't think the game deserves less than a "positive" overall opinion.
My perspective comes from having always enjoyed CCGs and TBS, since earlier days of e.g. Magic: The Gathering and Final Fantasy Tactics/Fire Emblem. Naturally, I was excited to see a game marrying both elements (not that it's the first out there), and I've been playing C&C for months now on mobile. So what's kept me playing, and why should you play, or not play it?
ART:
YMMV. The game goes for a particular cartoonish art style, which you'll like or dislike instantly - just see the screenshots. Clear differences between the 5 factions. If you appreciate the style, the art and animation are excellent. If not, perhaps the game isn't for you. However, there's no reason to diss the graphics as terrible; contemporaneous CCG-type games such as Hearthstone or Card Hunter have totally different art styles which are equally attractive. In comparison, I don't like how March of War looks - it's all personal taste.
MUSIC:
...adequate for the genre - i.e. turn off in favour of your own music after 1 hour.
GAMEPLAY:
5 factions, which you may choose to play solo, or combine with another faction (e.g. crusader/warlock or warlock/pirate) for a total of 15 different combinations. Playing solo factions gains you access to powerful faction-specific "hero" cards, while including a 2nd faction obviously provides versatility. Factions are distinct with their own playstyle, and quite well-balanced (especially after recent changes to pirates). Also, all deck types are viable - aggro, midrange, control, ramp, whatever type your fevered mind can dream up.
P2WIN-NESS:
The obvious bugbear for some. If you're looking to gain a significant collection without putting in any effort, I would suggest against playing any digital CCG-based game.
What some people may be sore about is facing players with many epics/legendaries and getting stomped. Do realise - the game has been out on mobile for > 1 year, and many players have near-complete collections. However, many of them haven't paid significant amounts of real $$, and you're getting stomped as they know the game better than you do, not because their cards are significantly better than yours.
The question is, can you compete as a new player? It's entirely possible with mostly common/uncommon cards, with a smattering of rares. Legendaries are limited to 1 copy each/deck (used to be up to the normal 2 copies/deck until a couple of months ago), which helps to limit their use. Overall, no better or worse than Hearthstone (which seems to be the benchmark, after all) in this aspect.
Finally, no gameplay element is locked behind a real $$ paywall, only cosmetic stuff (e.g. different castle looks) or more deck slots (>9).
ACCESSIBILITY:
Big one for me - the ability to play asynchronous games, which is what I wish Hearthstone had. Not as relevant to the desktop gamer, but hey - you can play on your desktop, and continue to play in short bursts on the go on mobile.
CAVEATS:
I decided against putting in a "Pros" section - I've covered most of the points above. Let the game speak for itself, it's free to try now anyway. However, some caveats are as follows, especially if you're considering putting in real $$.
- As some have pointed out, it's harder to craft epics/legendaries in C&C compared to e.g. Hearthstone. The cost for those was increased a couple of months ago, ostensibly so that crafting them would be harder and actually getting one would be more exciting. ...Whatever the reason, do note that it won't be easy to obtain epics/legendaries without spending at least a little $$.
- Smaller card pool. Currently, the card pool is in no way comparable to e.g. Hearthstone, even vanilla Hearthstone from way back. I don't feel like there's a lack of variety even after 4-5 months or so of playing, but it's just something to keep in mind. There's an expansion (Age of Dragons) coming up Jan 2016, which will help shake things up.
- Grindiness. The gold (non-premium currency) earning rate was nerfed, and coupled with the high cost of crafting epics/legendaries, you may feel pushed to spend just to get the juicy looking epics/legendaries. That said, as mentioned above - you can compete (in a fair fashion) using common/uncommon/rare cards. Some figures for the current state of the game - 1 quest per day (generally 800-1200 gold), average of 15-50 gold/win, 1 booster costs 2000 gold ---> 1 booster every 2 days (or slightly less, depending on how much you play). Whether or not you think it's worth your time, you decide.
- Fluidity. The game has had more significant card/balance changes since its mobile launch days than e.g. Hearthstone, including some changes (e.g. to ranged units, or to many pirates cards) which happened even after the devs posted that they were done with significant changes to gameplay (after the 2.0 update on mobile). While the changes have been beneficial for game balance and shows that the devs are responsive, C&C does not (and may never have) have the stability/polish that the big players (e.g. Hearthstone or MTG) exhibit. To their credit, it's rather hard to match the big boys when you're a small developer with a small team. Anyway, be prepared that what you like/don't like about certain cards/factions can change (sometimes suddenly).
- Fluctuating business model. Let's just say that changes in costs (both upwards/downwards) for many things (crafting, boosters, the recent "wing-based" expansion, draft tournaments) have made some unhappy. While I would not call out the developers for greed/making the game P2W, they're experimenting as they go, so prices may not be as stable as some would like (definitely not as stable as e.g. Hearthstone). Be prepared before you spend any $$ (although, the premium currency prices have not changed at all since I started playing - what's changed is the costs of what you can buy with it).
TL;DR:
- All things considered, C&C has lots of charm, and a good degree of game balance/variation. It scratches my itch for a TBS/CCG mashup and isn't overly complex. Furthermore, there are many potential mechanics yet to be explored, so the game has lots of room to grow.
- The best testament: I stopped playing Hearthstone. I still play C&C.
- Don't want to get stomped by the pros? Join now! Since it's recently out of early access, more new players will be flooding in. This is the best time to fumble around together :)

Beyond earth is the next part in the Civilization series.  Where in V, winning  by science, send your people to the stars beyond earth let you pioneer new worlds.
At the start you can choose between a few conglomerates. Unlike V, where the perks are set to a leader, you get to choose them.

The orders which you could choose in V (after DLC and certain timespan) are replaced by affinities which are there from start. And you have virtues instead of social policies.
The affinities are linked to researching tech and unit upgrades to affinities.
So yeah everything is there and it has a nice ring to it.
Then why the diappointment you might think. Well imo this game has such potential you can only feel sad about the missed opportunities.
The playable factions are just human. Aliens are mere barbarians in this game. The planets you can choose to pioneer are only earthlike planets. You have 3 "choices". One with a few large masses (like earth) One with one big landmass and a big ocean with possibilitie of small isles (pangaea) and an island like planet. But none of them have an alien look.
So all the possibiliteis of strange new planets to explore or some weird alien races to play aren't there.
So yeah at the current state and price I simply cannot recommend the game. It has so much more potential but feels more like a mod than a full game.
Will I keep my eye on the game. Definately. With some nice mods it can become a great addition to the civ series.

Compare this to the points purchased with -actual- currency which will give buyers a head start on anyone that was looking for a free (and fun) time killer. In part due to its recent launch, the game will have you waiting a while when trying to find an opponent for the pvp matches, not that it matters since once you get into a match ranked or non your odds of standing a chance are directly dependent on your cash investment for 4/5ths of those matches. This game should have stayed in testing a good while longer to flesh it out more and make it a fun game instead of a shameful cash grab that has visibly more time invested in how to get you to pay than in how to get you to have fun. It is free to play so you don't risk anything other than time, but for me at least it is time I could have better spent elsewhere.

After playing it over the free weekend, I have to say I am surprised at how good the game was. And yet it is so unpolished that the price even at 40% off is unfustified.
The positive is easily sumarised; it's Civ. It's a fun game.
So what are the problems?
-Tech web: It's a neat idea, but implemented poorly. Just moving the screen again and again to look at what you can currently research to decide where to spend science takes a long time. At the very least there should have been a sidebar with the current options.
-Trade: It's a powerful mechanic. Very powerful. So you can't really afford to ignore it. And yet at one stage of the game I had to set six (or more) trade routes every turn, because the routes completed. No automatisation to help (at least none that I found), no hotkeys to hurry the process along, no option to even turn the confirmation off. Many turns this was the most time consuming task and that should never have happened.
-units: No costumization for units, either design or through level perks, is rather surprising. It's very unusual for this style of game. Then adding upgrades not based on tech but ideology is a rather odd choice and made worse by removing any influence of tech. If you avoid things that strengthen ideologies, you can easily become the most advanced faction with the worst military units.
-Diplomacy: Over the course of the game series diplomacy has improved by leaps and bounds. And now we have a step backwards. With native aliens spawning everywhere and attacking you and several (all?) other factions complaining if you kill them, it's difficult to improve relations.
-Aliens: There's lots of aliens spawning. It's okay on land, even though it's very difficult to deal with worms until very late in the game. But managing the immensly powerful sea creatures? That's just a pain.
-Interface: Cumbersome and slow. Many options are hidden and even buying city tiles can be a pain because it can be hard to click on the one you want.
-Cities: If it's possible to automate cities or set how they should specialize, it's so well hidden that I couldn't find it.
-Intelligence: It's very difficult to manage on such a small screen. It needs to be bigger.
Overall, a decent game, but unpolished as it is, simply not worth the money.

Fantastic game. While I'm usually not very partial the point and click genre as a whole, with its seeming absurdities and illogic in the patterns which the game expects you to find, I found this one to be quite different. The game keeps the environments in a smaller and more concise area, and tends not to be a pixel hunting challenge. Only once or twice did I ever find difficulty in locating an item from poor placement or seeming absurdity. The rest were revealed through exploration or dialogue.
Speaking of dialogue, the game has a fantastic story. Ascribed from a novel bearing the same name, the game loosely follows a similar plot. The characters are all very well created, each with their various psycho-dilemmas and unresolved psychoses accompanied by a suitably ironic punishment from the malevolent AI entity that dominates the world utterly. The landscapes are delightfully surrealist, never totally revealing whether or not the landscapes actually exist in some fashion or are totally inward mental projections of the ruined assortment of protagonists. Each is suitably different from the other, blending a nightmarish mash of hopelessness and machinery with old world landscapes.
The game offers plenty in the way of choice, balancing the typical needs for positive reinforcement with the indomitably crushing environment our cast finds themselves within. Every action and inaction changes slight elements of the stories being told, and each allows the protagonist a chance at redemption or further succumbing the vices or maladies that torment them. It takes either careful savescumming or several playthroughs to fully explore the intricate stories for each character.
A fantastic experience through and through, certainly worth more than the $5.99 being charged for it. I intend to read the story it was based off of at the nearest opportunity as well.

TL;DR: Started playing Betrayer in it's beta release, and loved it. Due to computer problems I had to uninstall, recently reinstalled and still love it. It's unique, in story and atmosphere. Give it a go if you like trying new things.
More detail: Changing the colour scheme from monochrome to full colour is an aspect I really love. It's great to play it the first time round in the default black and white (and red), and then the next time in colour, because seeing the trees and the sky in colour feels like an experience you shouldn't miss. Although I've found I personally like using the half way mark, washed out hues with just a hint of colour gives the game an "old" aesthetic, imo.
I normally steer clear of horror games, but Betrayer seems to only toe the edge of the horror genre. The atmosphere is creepy, and the deranged spaniards are what frightened me the most, but earning a victory makes you feel accomplished, unlike most other horror games where you just feel sick.
I do wish there were more details given when you find out what happened to lost souls, I want more of a reason to go to the trouble of finding out their stories. In fact, more details in general would be nice, but maybe that's because I'm usually more invested in a game's story than the gameplay itself.
All in all, Betrayer is a brilliant idea and I love how it's executed. A sequel, perhaps? ;)

It's absolutely for the adventurous: You start off shipwrecked somewhere on the Virginian colony, with no sign as to why you've arrived. There's a reaspm "horror" is listed as the first tag, for the longer you play the more creepy entities and situations become, thus making you more stealthy and slow. The quests, known as investigations, are mysterious and make you search throughout the map to complete them. Without giving spoilers, the "perspectives" persay are appealing to the mind, making you think a bit, while not being too complex to the point of boredom or frustration.
For those who love to sit back, relax, and enjoy a great first person RPG game with longevity and patience, while maintaining eerie vigilance along the way, this is the perfect game. 10/10.

The Betrayer name and Adventure genre caught my eye and a had quick glance at a short description and without further ado I was plunged into the game. All I really needed to know to play the game was the mention of the Unreal engine and a quick peek at the controls ASWD and the rest was quite intuitive.
The game is quite a mystery too and there were times when I wished I had a better idea about my role in the game, but it was somehow like playing Zork Nemesis or Myst with Guns. Sometimes there were dialogue options that left me wondering if it's also a role-playing game and with a bit of romance, but.. It didn't quite play out the way I thought.
There were a few times that I was getting a bit angry with the game, because of controls and a bit of clunkiness in design, like if you got your finger on fast-forward and open the map window for a quick peek and exit you stop moving even though you still got your finger on fast forward. There are lots of keys for different windows and there were times when I had too much adrenaline going that the keys felt a bit too crowded and since each of them would cancel movement, things were getting a bit to hectic at times.
There is a tremendous amount of moving around in the game and even though there are some nice fast-travel options there is still a bit too much walking, but there are also some really cool, chilly and atmospheric hair-raising sound effects and a lot of sudden encounters. It would have been nice to have an Always Sprint option.
The game use some really old guns, muskets, flintlock pistols, bows and crossbows all with pretty slow loading. Unfortunately you can't dodge bullets or arrows by quick-stepping or jumping, but you can sprint and take cover and it works quite well.
Even though there is a lot of sound, there is no voice acting in the game and I didn't really miss it either. The writing is pretty decent.
I only had to look online for a solution once, because there was a bell I couldn't find in the Deep Woods.
You can play the game in black and white (and red) or increase the Colour saturation from pale to full. I did a bit of both.
It took me 15 hours to finish the game and I was sprinting a lot, but I was also really exploring a lot. I had a good time.

TL;DR: Space travel, big ships, little ships, weapon customization, trading, mining, pirating, enjoyable broadside combat ONLY on one plane (no up or down movement by your ship). Story is so-so, but not what the game is about. Graphics are beautiful, runs smoothly, 8/10 I would recommend for the 20$ asking price, definitely worth it on a good sale.
Rebel Galaxy. Now here's a game I bought on a total whim, thinking if I hated it I could just refund it. Well I put about an hour into it, and honestly, that refund looked more promising that enjoying this game.
HOWEVER. On I played, and I'm glad I did.
Rebel Galaxy story is alright, but I didn't honestly pay it much attention, and it lost my interest quickly, becoming much more interested in ammassing large amounts of money and upgrading my ship. Yuo start out in this dinky little capital ship that seems hopelessly outgunned when compared to some of the other faction ships. But get enough credits and start upgrading, and suddenly you feel like you rule the galaxy. Your ship can be customized not aesthetically, but through a diverse set of broadside turrets and mounted turrets, as well as thing slike cargo hold space, shiels, boosters, engine, armor plating, etc. Buy bigger ships, they're slower and less manueverable but covered in turrets and a hefty broadside arsenal. Smaller ships have less bang, but move and manuever like a charm, boasting high top speeds to simply work around your opponents.
Briging me to the combat. As before mentioned, your weapons consist of mounted turrets and a set of broadside guns, with the number of each depedning on your ship. Different turrets excel at different things, from taking down enemy fighters, disabling shields, or blowing the armor plating clean off a capital ship. Your broadsides are meant to be capital ship destroyers, with you circling your opponent in naval-esque fashion and bombarding them from one side or the other of your ship. Although combat only taking place in one plane, it is very enojyable and rewarding to watch your turrets anihilate enemy craft like mere flies.
Now not being able to move up and down may feel like a real let down, being stuck only moving fowards, backwards, and turning. But really, it isn't, once you open your mind to it. Space is still a very big place, and I can understand how adding upwards and downwards movement may be too much for some people.
As far as space itself, the races have no real lore or background of any sort, and the game is definitely not one to get you any extra information on any of them. However, there is much, much to do, from pirating, to mining, to trading commodities between various stations that can be in various states such as economic boom or famine, driving various prices of various commodities up, or down. You could also just hunt various bounties in each system, or perform various types of quests for the different factions in the game, such as the militia or merchant guild.
Lastly, I greatly enjoy both the graphics and the sountrack. I often find myself staring at the various stars and planets in the game, even being mesmerized by the movements in an ice field. For the sountrack, the twangy rock style fits perfectly into combat or encounters whenever it is triggered, fading in and out at appropriate times seamlessly.
Overall, I would say this is an easy 8/10, with my only qualms being that sometimes long journeys in space can be a bit dull, with the only breakups being enemy AI that are far too willing to jump into combat they cannot possibly hope to win, and it is incredibly annoying to be halted from light speed because you came just BARELY too close to a stray rock in an asteroid field. Well worth the money I spent on it, and a truly great deal if you can ever catch it on sale.

At around day 8 I had 4 people. Marco, Bruno, and Pavle are the guys and zlata was the girl. everything was going well. Marco is my scavenger man so he was always out at night scavangeing. Then i decided to go to the center square of the city which is a place for trading. And my god did i find a♥♥♥♥♥♥TON. I had bandages to help Bruno because he was injured and a gun with ammo for defense. Plus just some other great supplies on marco. So i decided to check out an apartment building in the same center square and turns out i was not suppose to go in there. I got out before the guys got trigger happy. But I wanted some more supplies and went back in. A guy found me and pulled his gun. I started running. I got out of the door and was running for the exit. I was home free! But there was another guy who was with the guy after me. He turned around and gunned marco down. I lost all the supplies. the gun, the bandages, everything he had. I was shockd at how it went from calm to a♥♥♥♥♥♥storm in mere seconds. I lost a good man that day. But that's not even the part I'm still thinking about. After marco died, Bruno went int a depression because he lost his friend who he was with at the start of the war. So Bruno is on the verge of suicide and I don't knoiw who will continue to scavange. I decide to try out Pavle. He becomes the new scavange guy and we are ok on food. But not medical supplies. And we don't even have much protection at night anymore against raids by thugs. So eventually Zlata gets wounded and bed ridden. We have no supplies to make any bandages and I am being forced to steal from people just to help my friends. It's all going downhill. So then finally, on the 15th night, both Bruno and Zlata are bedridden and cannot guard the place while i scavange. I pray that we don't get raided tonight and that they don't die of their wounds. I then send Pavle off to the construction site. It has food, medical supplies, and snipers. Military snipers. Who kill anyone on sight.  My only weapon is a shovel. I take the chance and head in. I make my way to the top of the construction site. I am getting many supplies on the way up. But no bandages. The one thing i need to treat my friends. I go higher up the unfinished building. I can hear the snipers. Laughing as they gun people down. I am a floor beneath them. as well as a floor beneath the roof. I accidently make to much noise and one of them hears me. They come to investigate. My only choice is to fight. I can't turn and run because my friends will die if i do. I equipt my shovel and then the biggest action movie scene in any video game i have ever played happens. the first guy comes down and i ambush him at the doorway, me with a shovel, him with a gun. Luckly, Because i can swing a shovel faster than he can aim, I start to win the fight. But as this is happening, his friend comes down and aims at me. He is able to get a shot on Pavle. I turn around and hit him with my shovel. The other guy turns around and aims. *click* out of ammo. He starts to run. I turn back and hit him one more time. He is out. He falls to the ground, never to get back up. His friend, scared and also out of ammo, runs away and climbs up to the top of the roof. I follow. Pavle, now with less than half health, is slow and limping. He has taken a shot that could end his life. But he isn't out of the game yet. He came here for one reason. To get his friend's their bandages. He climbs, slowly but surely, to the roof, after the man who shot him and cost him valubale time. The man runs to the edge of the unfinished roof. He is petrified. He has no where to go. The man starts begging Pavle to let him live. That he can't do this. Pavle doesn't listen. He raises the shovel and hits the man. the man arches back. Crying, begging to live, the man pleas. Pavle hits him again. Sending the man closer to the edge. Before the man can regain his footing, Pavle slams the shovel into him, sending him off the side of the building. The deed is done. These men won't be hurting anyone anymore. I unequipt the shovel. I turn around to see a scavenge spot behind me. I open it and inside i find a single bandage. I laugh. I found what I was looking for. Sadly, it is nearing 5 o'clock. I don't have enough time to get home in the stealth of night. But I tread on anyway. The last I saw of Pavle was him limping slowly down the unfinished building. Trying his hardest to return to his friends with the supplies. If the player does not return to the exit of the map by 5, the screen will go dark and it will say that the character will take longer and may be at more risk on his return to the shelter. Bruno and Zlata didn't survive the night. The shelter was raided and their wounds were too fatal. Pavle never returned to the house. But it did not say he died either. I believe he i sstill out there. Making his way back to his lost friends. This game made me feel for the characters and not put the mouse down. I loved it. Even though I only lasted 15 days. This game is hard and, as i said, unforgiving. But it is an amazing experiance and hopefully you can get as epic as a final moment as I did. R.I.P Bruno, Zlata, and Marco. I still know you're out there Pavle. Somewhere.

I had heard, of course, that Bioshock 2 was the disappointment of the three Bioshock games. I played Bioshock: infinite  first, having got my gaming laptop right after it came out. And I loved it. It was amazing. So then I went back and played the original Bioshock--and while quite unforgiving when learning how to play--I loved it. Except for that awful escort mission at the end. That was the worst part of the original Bioshock. But hey, at least there was only the one.
.....
So I'd heard that Bioshock 2 was't very good but over Halloween, it went on sale for $5, so I grabbed it. I was prepared to be underwhelmed but I wanted to go ahead and try it and hope that it would surprise me.
Big Daddies are cool--but only from a distance. They were awesome in Bioshock until you became one--then all of a sudden, you were constantly attacked and no one was afraid of you. Same song and dance here--except now 75% of the game is one Little Sister escort after another.
I don't get why writers default to escort missions sometimes. They are not fun, they're not interesing and they are extremely annoying. Infinite was different--because Elizabeth could look after herself. So you got to focus on the fun parts. But here--it's all about the little gremlins. They aren't even individual. They all look exactly the same--which I presume is just laziness on the developers part.
And weirdly enough--all the splicers that are left seem to have a strange grudge against the Big Daddies--or rather, actually, just me. Because they say "Big Daddies" but the other BDs are never attacked like you are. They even go so far as the BLAME the BDs for the Little Sister program--even though that doesn't make any sense at all. In Bioshock 2 : Mediocrity Strikes Back, it's implied that the Alpha series of Big Daddy candidates came from criminals. In Bioshock 1--it's rather vague on where other BD candidates came from. So how can they blame Delta for the program when it was obviously around before he became a BD?
That's another thing--at the beginning when Delta is shot in the head--you presume that he's dead. In fact, he doesn't wake up for ten years. So was he dead? He was, right? How do you take a body that's been dead for ten years and suddenly bring it back to life? If the vita-chambers could reanimate cells that were decomposed to that extreme a level--why wouldn't everyone be throwing people in the chambers? And why did the Hypnotize Big Daddy plasmid suddenly make Delta do whatever Lamb said? In BIoshock, that just made the BDs protect you like a LS. It certainly didn't make them do whatever you wanted.
Sophia Lamb is ridiculously stupid. Her poor writing and weak story show the holes that this game was just intended as a cash grab. Her supposed policies don't make any sense--she talks on and on about how Adam can be used to....consume, basically, the memories of others. That doesn't make any sense. If every time the LSs or Splicers consumed Adam, they found themselves with memories from other people or from being a sea slug, I guess--people wouldn't use it. Not that it was ever clear what the LSs DID with the Adam after they collected it. And Lamb's bleating about how all these experiences bundled together would somehow make the perfect person---that's even worse. It's not like she figured out how to differentiate between 'good' traits and 'bad' traits. Any person could sit back and go, "Yeah, this is a stupid plan."
I could accept that Lamb is just crazy--but everyone seems to think that she's a genius. Everyone acts like this plan was totally plausible when it very obviously wasn't. Andrew Ryan's attitude at least made sense--it made sense--it just went too far in one direction. And you see him progress to becoming exactly what he proposed to get away from in Rapture. He made sense. Lamb doesn't at all.
And then you meet Tenenbaum at the beginning of the game. She claims she's going to help you. Claims she's there to stop Lamb from continuing to create LSs.....but then after Sinclair takes over as your Headset Jockey--you never hear from Tenenbaum again. She bugged off to escape with some of the gremlins--and then never reappears. So where the hell did she go? Dd we just leave her down in Rapture? Did she sink into the trench? And what about the Big Sisters? Who are supposedly grown up Little Sisters (that we either didn't rescue in the first game or belong to Lamb--I'm not sure). We just left the remaining down there? Didn't bother saving them?
Sinclair, I was actually waiting the entire game for him to betray me because he followed the same script and cues as Atlas. And I guess he sort of betrayed Delta...before the game? But then he ends up helping you? But it's not really clear why, I guess. So whatever.
Eleanor was just the Damsel in Distress to get the story progressing. She basically had no character other than "helpless girl to save" with severe daddy issues. Delta has no personality at all--so there's no reason to get attached to him. Their supposed Big Daddy-Little Sister father-daughter connection--he doesn't even seem to remember. He only goes to Eleanor cause he'll go into a coma if he doesn't? Or his heart will stop? Which is stupid--because if their LS is being drug away or something--then BDs wouldn't be able to efficiently chase and rescue them. And even then--causing Eleanor's heart to stop--or actually, just interupting it--retcons that connection entirely! So what's the point!
Bioshock 2 makes out the Big Daddies to be these odd berserkers---even that Grace woman--she tells Delta to just go ahead and kill her. If you choose not to, she'll say, "You chose not to kill me. That's what a thinking man does. Not a Big Daddy."
But that doesn't make sense either. Because no Big Daddy ever attacks you unless you attack him first or you get too close to his Little Sister. So even a normal Big Daddy would not have attacked Grace and killed her--because there was no Little Sister there and Grace didn't attack Delta. So ironically---a thinking man should have actually chosen to kill her. By not killing her--that's just the default Big Daddy state.
Also, what exactly does Delta have that enables him to rescue the Little Sisters? But then--that didn't really make sense in the original BIoshock either. If you have a plasmid that can return them to normal--than why all the wigging out about the girls? Bioshock 1 and 2 and event he DLC for Infinite---focuses a LOT on the Little Sisters. But they are just props. And the mythos surrounding them doesn't really make much sense.
That said---the coolest part of the game was when you got to briefly control a Little Sister. Seeing Rapture through their eyes was actually a new and interesting experience. I would have liked to have seen more of that. THAT was actually cool. Because the games focus so much on them--but we don't actually know hardly anything concrete about them. It was like a reverse Silent Hill--knowing they split back and forth between the real world and their beautiful fantasyland and not really knowing which one was real for them--that was really cool.
But not worth playing ten hours of game for.
I've replayed Bioshock and Bioshock: Infinite---but I will probably never replay Bioshock 2 : Big Daddy Fan Service. There's very little replay value because the story is so weak. As a Big Daddy, you're slow, clumsy, clunky and your drill is basically useless---seriously. No one gets close enough for you to use the drill efficiently. The only time I actually used the drill was when I had to clear that ONE section of rubble--that you can never do again, by the way. As soon as I got a gun, I switched to it permanently and spent all my weapon upgrades on the guns.
And by the time I was in the last area--I was cruising through--and didn't even need Eleanor's help. So, don't waste your money. Go get Infinite and the original. Skip this one

Note: This review, while for players as well, is mainly directed towards the devs.
Quite fun, I have almost no problems with lag or glitches, and I really enjoy the features involved.
That being said, the reason my computer can run it so smoothly is probably because my computer is a beast and hardly breaks a sweat running ARK: Survival Evolved on full graphics, and I've tried to play on my laptop and gotten the infamous "black-screen", so of course the programming could use some work, but what game out there doesn't?
As far as the gameplay and general features of the game, there are some things I'm not as fond of:
1. Once you make a deck with their deck wizard, you can only make changes through deck wizard, so customization is severely limited and in order to edit the deck fully you would have to re-create it through the advanced process.
2. Unless you know what you're doing, as far as the card game in general, you're going to have trouble trying to put good decks together with the cards you're given in the early game. Booster packs and experience help with that, but it is a (inevitable?) issue.
3. Earning coins can be a pain. In order to get a booster pack of 6 cards(150 coins), you would have to win 7.5 online games(20 coins), and you could just end up getting cards completely unrelated to any of your decks, which I guess is the nature of MTG in the first place. If you were given say, 35 coins, 5 more than the hardest solo mode, I believe that would make this game less grindy-feeling.
4. Unless you run through each campaign entirely, you will be severely lacking in useful booster packs, and therefore in power to win in PvP, and therefore cannot earn gold. This could be fixed if there was at least a consolation prize for losing an online match, maybe 10-15 coins.
5. This one is a bit inevitable, but when its your turn, if you have a spell you can cast with the mana you have, it will freeze your main phases until you hit continue, making it clear to your opponent that you have something up your sleve if you don't use the spell. Thus, sneak attacks are much more difficult. The only way I could think that you could reasonably fix this would be to make every player have to hit continue on every phase, not just when they have a spell available to use.
6. You never earn coins beyond the first time going through the storyline. I personally really enjoyed it, and I would love a reason to play it again. Maybe if you had a completion bar, and after you had gone through a full storyline for a second time, you could get 50 coins? Just a thought, though.
7. Specifically with the Jace plainswalker card, quite a few people, myself included, had difficulty figuring out how to actually cast a spell from the graveyard after activating his second ability, as you have to scroll down to the bottom of the card to see the option. Maybe if the option were put at the top of the card, instead of the bottom, this would cause less confusion.
8. No re-do button or request. Occasionally I find myself losing a match or making a bad move because I forgot to activate some ability or spell before the timer ran out, but if players could send a re-do request to their opponent, I feel it would be more enjoyable. Of course, they wouldn't have to accept, but I would love to have that option, as well as the ability to grant that ability to people whom I play against.
I should proabably mention what I enjoyed about the game as well. Here are some:
1. Excelent storyline, and the way they introduce each deck as you play farther through the campaign is excellent, with it all culminating in a final fight that generally summarizes the entire purpose of the deck, and often pits you against what would be your type of magic's arch-nemesis.
2. Mini-match tutorial style is a very interesting idea, very well done. It does an excellent job of teaching players each mechanic of the game as it comes up.
3. The variety of cards given to you and that you can gain makes for some rather interesting decks with some rather fun matches and combos, although of course you have to earn the rarer cards through booster packs and such.
4. The daily quests are wonderful for earning the coins that I feel the game lacks in regular PvP. This is partially negative, partially positive, as I enjoy the coins, but often find myself getting on just long enough to finish the daily quests, without feeling the drive to play PvP longer than absolutely necessary.
Regardless of the number of pros and cons, I actually enjoy this game quite a bit, I just wanted to point out several flaws and suggest ways to solve them.
Overall, I recommend trying this game out, expecially if you have a gaming computer or laptop, as you will hardly ever encounter the lag or bugs many people complain about. It's not the same as the card game, but it does a good job for what it is!

I honestly didn't like this game at first. I enjoy roleplaying in games, and it's important that I care about the characters I'm interacting with. At first glance, it seems like everything in Bioshock is either insane or evil, so I had a hard time feeling motivated to "save the day." However, the more I played, the more I began to enjoy Bioshock's engrossing story, rich characters, and engaging combat system. The powers and weapons are just too damn cool and fun to use. I also found characters I sympathize with -  McDonagh, the Little Sitters, and especially the Big Daddies. It may sound stupid, but a key moment for me was when I found out about Hypnotize Big Daddy. (Yay! I have one friend!)
Unfortunately, Bioshock's wonderful qualities make its one glaring flaw even more glaring. Bioshock crashes when you try to save. Not only that, but you may find multiple save files deleted post-crash. It kept happening over and over until I was afraid to save at all. I did some research, and it seems that many other people also have this issue, so it is a bug and not an issue with my rig (thank goodness!). Even with this issue, the game was so fun that at first I was fully prepared to grin and bear it, but the agony of repeatedly losing hours of playtime has put a damper on my desire to finish. I may finish it after all, but as of now I feel too cheated.
My recommendation is to play the original version. My understanding is that it has many fewer bugs and fairly good graphics even compared to the Remastered Edition. I also suggest that Steam make the original version purchasable by itself (ideally at a lower price, though $20 is completely fair assuming that the original does not bug out). Although it's too late for me, as a consumer, I want the opportunity to buy a great game without the price being jacked up because it's tied to broken features.
TL;DR: Excellent gameplay, but it crashes when it saves.
