It's basically a 3D platformer of sorts, where you push, pull and cut blocks with your tools and use them to get well, what appears to be your dead grandfather's underwear (or as the game describes them, "pants").
There's segments between levels with the odd characters of Tiny & Big. There's a narrator/game adivsor on their car's radio that tells you what needs doing on the level that's coming up. Tiny plays out the levels on what seems to be a Game Boy type device. Basically a video game inside a video game.
The unusual game concept and the so-far introductory puzzle/level designs are so far teaching me to do what I'll presumably be doing later on without its guidance. Something about this reminds me of the classic Lemmings games of the late 80s/early 90s.
Get it when it's on sale (or not), the price is right and it's got cards you can sell.

So, things are better now that Steam has worked with the publisher to move the saves over to Steamworks.  Kudos to Steam for helping make that change.  I'm absolutely certain that this will return some good will for people who felt ripped off that they'd paid for an unplayable game (BTW...doing the same for other GFWL titles, would be great).  I know that it made me feel a lot better about Steam's response to the problem, especially as a very long-time Steam member.
As for the game itself, I'm still pretty torn and can't wholly recommend it on PC.  It's a fairly clunky port from consoles, and honestly it probably plays better on those (which pains those of us who are PC gamers).  The save system is still very console-focused and pretty annoying, as a lot of checkpoints are set in an area where there is a high potential of death, and then you're stuck replaying quite a bit just to take another run at the same thing.
The reality is that other zombie titles play much better on PC...Left For Dead 1/2, Dead Island, etc.  If you've blasted through all of those and simply need another zombie killing game on your PC and this is on sale (like it currently is), then it's perhaps still worth it.  Otherwise, move on to stronger titles or at least wait until this one is on sale.
I the meantime, I reluctantly can't give the game a recommendation, even though it's decent.  I'd probably give it a thumbs-up on a console.

A rogue-like that doesn't feel like it. Neon Chrome oozes style, substance, and is insanely friendly to the player. Everything is simple and clean, with a great soundtrack, brilliant use of color and a firm grasp of the cyberpunk aesthetic. It's addicting and great fun, with the ability to pick up and play as you need to. You're not punished for needing to pause, minimize, or take a break and that really pushed it over the edge for me. It was a game that let me play it.
Despite all the pros, some of the cons are that some character classes feel definitively better than others, and that is the case with some guns, skills, abilities and modifications. There are a few I've never used and probably never would, even if I grinded to Overseer 100.0. Overall, when you find out what's good and what works you begin to enjoy the game three times as much as before and you're driven to starting from level 1 to make that badass character one that wipes the entire Neon Chrome megaplex.
I highly recommend this to anyone who enjoys rogue-likes and those who may be able to tolerate a unique take on one while diving headfirst into the rainy neon grit of a proper cyberpunk universe.

The truck controls decently well and the art is vibrant, though the sound is a ittle obnoxious. The game doesn't seem to have the same skill/strategy depth as Trials, but there is quite a lot to do, and getting through the harder levels can be very difficult. I found that this game is best played in short sessions (though, for later levels, a short session may not be enough time to accomplish much).
If Snuggle Truck looks at all interesting to you, it will be well worth your five dollars.

So far I'm digging this game. What initially drew me in was the aesthetic; this is a gorgeous display of cyberpunk. The gameplay itself surprised me: while most twin stick shooters I've played involve a lot of "run backwards and fire" strategy (and Neon Chrome certainly has its moments of that), many of the firefights involve careful use of cover and choke points. This is bolstered by the destructible terrain. Many objects and walls can be destroyed, allowing you to ambush enemies or flank their shields. The guns themselves have a decent variety, although I wish they dropped more frequently. There is also a nice assortment of enemies, each promoting different tactics. One caveat that this game has is, at least so far, it's not particularly difficult; the flip side of this is that I haven't had any moments where I felt the difficulty was artificial. Overall, I highly recommend Neon Chrome.

I have spent quite a few hours with this game now. I've played all the Civs, DLCs as well as the original SMAC plus add-ons. In one sentence; this is a rich game that is similar to yet significantly different to standard CIV. IMO it allows a fun and rich exploration of what the future could be like. Playing the affinities is fun and they require significantly different paths to victory making it varied and interesting.
I think a significant flaw is the lack of 'storification' or enrichment. At times it can feel like you are just clicking around making small choices without a realy sense of progress e.g. at one point you can re-connect to old Earth. This for me is  a pretty big moment in the game and should be accompanied by appropriate video, awesome graphics/visuals, something that really brings this big moment to life. Instead you just get some text. This happens consistently throughout the game, even on victory, and can make the experience feel hollow at times. My approach to this is to make more effort to imagine the game reality; don't just click through but take moments to connect and visualise to what is being described.
Many people say the units are not differentiated or the affinitities are not meaniningfully different. I strongly disagree; play the game on the harder or harest difficulties and you will see that every decision matters and the different paths are indeed very different!
Should you buy it? Yes if you want a rich, thoughtful game and cann accept the flas tthat it doesn't desribe its own story very well. Have fun!

So I have hap this game for about 3 years now, and recently I told my friend about that game because it was on sale. (not this sale,but the last one.) He sees it and thinks it's amazing, I tell him that it is. He gets the game and we immediately begin playing. After about 5 hours of teaching him how to play, he gets tired and leaves.
Now a little bit ago I say we should play again, he is hesitant, but he agrees to anyway. We start up the game and I set everything to faster so he can play a quicker game (faster training, mining, culture.) Everything is going great for the first 10 minutes or so, until we establish first contact.
Now since he is still learning, I have had to teach him up to this point and our technological advancements and colonization have been slow. Not to mention I had to help him learn how to play the Advent as I was playing the TEC. I expected that star to star jumping would be reached within 10 minutes, but they are already here. A couple scouts are not really an issue, so we continue to expand, then my friend is alof a sudden really scared because he had lost one of his colonies. I simply thought he accidentally scuttled it and he was paying attention to his (small) army fighting rebels. It wasn’t until the third colony that I went to investigate. There, I found a HUGE war party in his late colony’s system.
Im freaking out and Telling him to Bring his army back to defend his home world, and that's when I notice that the same this is happening to me. With an army of that size, they must have been expanding into the other galaxies without much trouble, and now we were paying for it.
About 20 minutes later, and 20 minutes of constantly defending our colonies, I have a great idea. I immediately start rushing siege frigates and my titan (the Ragnarov titan is personally my favorite, which is basically a giant rail gun, with engines and smaller guns all around it) and I tell him to do the same. Confused, he has to listen because he has no other ideas.
My idea is to win by sneaking 100 siege frigates and a titan into the enemy territory, and take their home planet before they can gets troops back from the front lines (our colonies). And very soon, the pan is under way. We have literally every single ship, which added together is only a fraction of our enemies army, and send them on a straight shot for his home world. During this time, he has taken almost all of our colonies(be both have about 2 left) and they don’t seem to care that our armies have disappeared.
5 Minutes later, we make the final jump into a heavily fortified system with gauss platforms and mines EVERYWHERE and a fully upgraded starbase. Note that at this point, all of his ships are flying back to save his home planet, but by then it's too late. we destroy his defences and being bombing the planet. Sadly, about half way through destroying it, my friend lost his Capital, and his ships lost all ties with me, but is was too late. The final nuke was fired, sealing his fate as the first of his ships jumped into the system. We had won in probably the most dirty and underhanded way, but we had won.

Man, eat your heart out Han Solo!  Space adventure and star-RPG action not seen IMHO since the likes of Freelancer.  Great soundtrack, lots of gratutious space battles, arcade-like control, plenty of alien races to blast into the next dimension.  The controls, while a bit awkward at first to me, after a while they became intuitive and better than I'd say Freelancer's was...  And I'm an old sk00l die-hard Freelancer fan.
The star systems are beautiful and actually laid out like a real star system, orbit paths shown and all,(via the map mind you) something I always wished Freelancer had done, instead of being static planets laid in a "small" star system.
The attention to detail of the ships is great and you can even see "scarring" of battle damage done to your ship in realtime.  These things really give the feel to the game to make it truly a space sim.
The dynamic economy and persistant universe features are also great features I loved from Freelancer are well done here also.  There are many many things done in Rebel Galaxy I had always wished Freelancer would be, but sadly it's no where near the depth and "size" of it.
So with that said, the game is not without flaws though, It's story line is interesting and engaging, but also very short.  There is only a total of 14 solar systems in this game to explore, last I remember vanilla Freelancer had about 40-50 of them, some mods had an upwards of over 150 systems! (Crossfire 2.0)  Far too small of a universe to explore IMHO.
While you do eventually upgrade to bigger and badder ships, sadly IMHO the name of the game is speed in these space battles and most of the big boys are far too slow to stay alive.  To me the only "big ship" to upgrade to is the Blackgate, (the biggest dreadnaught there is!) anything less and if you're overwhelmed, you simply won't be able to weather the assault or run from them.  Your upgrades, defenses and weapons are far more of an important factor in survival here as well as your tactics.(and hire a friggin' Merc fighter pilot!)
As far as the BGM, I did enjoy the soundtrack at the beginning it eventually began wearing thin on me and I finally ended up muting the BGM.  Don't get me wrong, I love Blues Sacrenro and the songs are some of the best on a game's soundtrack I've heard in a long time, but listening to it for weeks on end?  Ahhhh, thanks but no thanks...
In closing, the game has ALOT of great things going for it and I truly see it as a "spiritual" successor to Freelancer.  However, I can only assume due to the abbreviated schedule of the Double Damage team limited them to  what they were able to cram into the game is that sadly it's nowhere near of the likes of it's predecessors like Eve Online, the X series, Freelancer and so forth.  Therefore I feel you'll get your money's worth, but this is only if you're looking for something "entry level" in a space sim as this game is very approachable to casual gamers I'd say.  Try it for the space sim, stay for it's "arcade-like" action.

You find yourself on a beach, surrounded by the remainings of what looks like to be your ship.

Betrayed is an OpenWorld where you have no help of any sort, no tutorial.
What to do and where to go is up to you to find.
You will have to explore the world of the living and the world of the spirits to find clues and informations to help you rebuild the events.
Visually the game is really engaging; this odd black and white graphics where only the colour red is shown create a really suggestive scenery; as suggestive are the sound effects.
The fights are more or less hard, that's up to your skill as a gamer.
I've to admit that missing a destination or any kind of hint on the long way bores me; a risk that you have to keep in mind is losing a good amount of time wandering around (and dying by the hand of the enemies) without having a clue on what to do.

All considered I recommend it (maybe at a low price, why not?) for his originality and uniqueness.

Siete su una spiagga, attorniati dai resti di quella che presumibilmente era la vostra nave.
All'orizzonte si posso scorgere altri vascelli intenti a salpare.
Nessuna indicazione di chi o cosa siete; nessuno che vi indirizzi verso un particolare luogo; tutto quello che vi rimane è cominciare a camminare, seguendo il sentiero.
Qualcuno ha lasciato dei messaggi lungo la via; testi che vi mettono in guadia: "Questo posto è pericoloso, continuate a vostro rischio e pericolo".
Betrayer è un gioco OpenWorld in cui non vi viene fornito nessun tipo di aiuto, nessun tutorial.
Cosa fare e dove andare spetta a voi capirlo.
Dovrete esplorare il mondo dei vivi e quello degli spiriti per trovare indizi e informazioni che vi aiutino a ricostruire gli avvenimenti.
Visivamente è molto coinvolgente; questa grafica particolare in bianco e nero in cui spicca solo il colore rosso rende l'ambientazione suggestiva; altrettanto suggestivi sono gli effetti sonori.
I combattimenti sono più o meno impegnativi (dipende dalla vostra abilità di giocatore).

Rebel Galaxy is a story driven space exploration and battle game with a unque style and a firefly-esque feel. Above is a short video of me running through th first half hour or so of the game, below are my thoughts on Rebel Galaxy.
was provided a review copy by Double Damage Games and for that we thank them.
The opening soundtrack and just the music in general really gave that space junker, firefly, out in the verse where there is little law and less integrity vibe.. The following gameplay did not let this notion slip away. This is a fantastic western style space traveler and battle game. It's a great adventure game and I'll likely be coming back to it often to see what's next in the story.I'd reccomend this one to any fans of space games, especially those where players can outfit ships and fly around a massive galaxy.

Betrayer is pretty unique in terms of gaming experience. In fact, I'm not entirely sure it can even be categorised as a 'game' per se... I shall try to explain.
You begin shipwrecked on a beach in 1604; all you know is that you sailed from England to join a colony in the Americas. You are met with an eerie, black-and-white landscape, devoid of colour and, apparently, life. You make your way up the beach, and from there you must begin to explore your environment in order to work out where you are, and what has happened here. Things are clearly wrong in this unsettling place. Your only ally is a mysterious woman in red who doesn't know her own name. Your enemies vary from Spanish Conquistadors with demonic red eyes to bow-wielding natives who utter unearthly howls as they stalk you through forests and grasslands; you barely see them coming before they are upon you, attacking and darting away before you can return fire. When you find and ring the fort's bell, the world around you shifts; just when you thought the daylight was scary enough, the night-world is ever more terrifying with skeletons and ghosts to be found all around you, shrieking in the darkness.
So, scene set, let's start with the basics. The monochromatic graphics are brave and striking; the rendering is gorgeous and you soon get used to looking at this greyscale world, as items of interest are vividly marked in red. But don't be fooled, this doesn't make anything easy to see coming, as realistic wind effects keep the trees and grasses shifting, fooling the eye into seeing movement where there is none, or covering the stealthy approach of a foe. The wind is both your enemy and your ally; you freeze when it blows, for fear that you've seen or heard something moving, or you can dash through the gusts, knowing the sound and movement of the wind will disguise the noise of your approach.
As if this didn't make things tense enough, sound is extremely important. There is no background music and no vocal acting; all you will hear is the wind, and the sounds around you - some enemies can be detected by the clanking of their armour, distincive howls, or gutteral roars. Early on you gain the ability to listen, using your HUD to follow sounds to be led to clues, locations and lost souls in need of rescue. Ring a bell to enter into the night-world and the sounds are amplified; the dull clanging of the bell, the screaming of wraiths, and having to use your listening ability to pinpoint the next clue... Seriously, play this game at night, alone, with the lights off and no other background noise, and you will discover a whole new level of immersion in this terrifying world. It will probably give you nightmares. And PTSD. Especially if there's a sudden noise in the house while you're immersed... honestly, last night, my cat sneezed while I was creeping up on a heavily-garrisoned fort area, and I had three kinds of heart attack all at once.
One of the hardest concepts to grasp in this game is that for pretty much all of the time you will not have a single clue what you are supposed to be doing - or even if you are supposed to be doing anything. Think about it - most games you play will have clear cut objectives, quests and story lines to follow. Betrayer doesn't give you any of that, and to be honest, why should it? It's realism at its finest - in real life, a stranger doesn't approach you in the street and tell you that the answer to all you seek is in the next town, here's a map, speak to so-and-so and report back to me so I can tell you what to do next... Betrayer expects you to behave as you might if you really did wash up on a beach in 1604. Figure it out for yourself! Take a walk - look around - collect clues - piece it together - find scraps of paper - talk to the friendly folk - kill the ones that try to kill you - trial and error; you'll get there in the end. Hopefully...
...Which is why this game gets mixed reviews, it seems. Betrayer will frustrate you as often as it rewards you, because when you're missing a clue and you don't know where to look, then it's hours of map-trawling to try to work out what you've overlooked. There is no handholding here; once you get used to that and start to work things out for yourself you can really start to enjoy it, but this game probably loses a lot of players early on who don't like that style of play. However, the rewards for perseverance are exceptional; intense, involving play; clever use of stealth and strategy; incredible characters and a deeply shocking storyline that keeps you guessing until the end.
So when I said at the beginning that it can't be characterised as a "game", it is because of the incredible amount of realism involved, despite the supernatural themes. It is a media form in its own right; a cross between a game, a movie and a real-life action adventure where you have to work everything out for yourself. Betrayer will not even ask you the questions, let alone tell you the answers - you will literally have to suss everything out for yourself. The beautiful thing is that you will be vey pleased with yourself when you do!
One of my favourite elements of this game was in not knowing where the true evil was; in the deeds of the settlers you learn about, or in the shadowy realm of ghosts and monsters. The irredeemable acts that people do to each other in their own selfish interests and the ways in which those deeds come back to haunt them are intriguing, horrifying and tragic all in one go.
Betrayer is, essentially, a simple game that can be incredibly difficult at the same time. For example, the combat is apparently straightforward in a point-and-shoot manner, but the nature of the weapons and the environment makes tactics important. Stealth is essential in many cases and reload times for muskets, pistols and crossbows have to be taken into account. You can only carry a realistic amount of ammunition so being able to recover spent arrows from fallen enemies is a nice touch and saves your precious resources. You quickly learn the best weapons to use against each enemy, and there is a grim satisfaction to be had in being able to "stealth kill" an enemy silently from a distance using your trusty longbow (my personal favourite weapon in the game) or by sneaking up and throwing a tomahawk at them.

In fact, it is hard to pick fault with Betrayer. Any frustration at not knowing what to do is negated by the fact that it is simply part of the point of the game; you just have to keep searching until you find something that takes you forwards. If you don't like the greyscale graphics, you can adjust the settings of the game so that it is in full colour; personally, I enjoyed the atmospherics much more without any additional colours. If you don't like the eerie silence of the game, you can ruin it with your own background music or something.
My only real nitpick is that it would have been nice to have some voice acting - if the Lady in Red and other "characters" could talk directly rather than using text boxes, then it would have made the game feel even more realistic. The text boxes were, for me, a jarring interruption to an otherwise flawless experience; even the HUD has been carefully considered to be as unobtrusive as possible, and can be turned off for ultra-realistic feel.
Otherwise, I thoroughly recommend this game. This is definitely one for those with patience and tenancity who are looking for a real challenge. It is not something to be played through quickly or for light relief. If you invest some real time in working through Betrayer and give it - and yourself - a chance, then you will not be disappointed.

Before you buy any war FPS, try this game to see the real meaning of war.

At around day 8 I had 4 people. Marco, Bruno, and Pavle are the guys and zlata was the girl. everything was going well. Marco is my scavenger man so he was always out at night scavangeing. Then i decided to go to the center square of the city which is a place for trading. And my god did i find a♥♥♥♥♥♥TON. I had bandages to help Bruno because he was injured and a gun with ammo for defense. Plus just some other great supplies on marco. So i decided to check out an apartment building in the same center square and turns out i was not suppose to go in there. I got out before the guys got trigger happy. But I wanted some more supplies and went back in. A guy found me and pulled his gun. I started running. I got out of the door and was running for the exit. I was home free! But there was another guy who was with the guy after me. He turned around and gunned marco down. I lost all the supplies. the gun, the bandages, everything he had. I was shockd at how it went from calm to a♥♥♥♥♥♥storm in mere seconds. I lost a good man that day. But that's not even the part I'm still thinking about. After marco died, Bruno went int a depression because he lost his friend who he was with at the start of the war. So Bruno is on the verge of suicide and I don't knoiw who will continue to scavange. I decide to try out Pavle. He becomes the new scavange guy and we are ok on food. But not medical supplies. And we don't even have much protection at night anymore against raids by thugs. So eventually Zlata gets wounded and bed ridden. We have no supplies to make any bandages and I am being forced to steal from people just to help my friends. It's all going downhill. So then finally, on the 15th night, both Bruno and Zlata are bedridden and cannot guard the place while i scavange. I pray that we don't get raided tonight and that they don't die of their wounds. I then send Pavle off to the construction site. It has food, medical supplies, and snipers. Military snipers. Who kill anyone on sight.  My only weapon is a shovel. I take the chance and head in. I make my way to the top of the construction site. I am getting many supplies on the way up. But no bandages. The one thing i need to treat my friends. I go higher up the unfinished building. I can hear the snipers. Laughing as they gun people down. I am a floor beneath them. as well as a floor beneath the roof. I accidently make to much noise and one of them hears me. They come to investigate. My only choice is to fight. I can't turn and run because my friends will die if i do. I equipt my shovel and then the biggest action movie scene in any video game i have ever played happens. the first guy comes down and i ambush him at the doorway, me with a shovel, him with a gun. Luckly, Because i can swing a shovel faster than he can aim, I start to win the fight. But as this is happening, his friend comes down and aims at me. He is able to get a shot on Pavle. I turn around and hit him with my shovel. The other guy turns around and aims. *click* out of ammo. He starts to run. I turn back and hit him one more time. He is out. He falls to the ground, never to get back up. His friend, scared and also out of ammo, runs away and climbs up to the top of the roof. I follow. Pavle, now with less than half health, is slow and limping. He has taken a shot that could end his life. But he isn't out of the game yet. He came here for one reason. To get his friend's their bandages. He climbs, slowly but surely, to the roof, after the man who shot him and cost him valubale time. The man runs to the edge of the unfinished roof. He is petrified. He has no where to go. The man starts begging Pavle to let him live. That he can't do this. Pavle doesn't listen. He raises the shovel and hits the man. the man arches back. Crying, begging to live, the man pleas. Pavle hits him again. Sending the man closer to the edge. Before the man can regain his footing, Pavle slams the shovel into him, sending him off the side of the building. The deed is done. These men won't be hurting anyone anymore. I unequipt the shovel. I turn around to see a scavenge spot behind me. I open it and inside i find a single bandage. I laugh. I found what I was looking for. Sadly, it is nearing 5 o'clock. Okay, so as I write this I am currently only at eleven hours of playtime, not a whole lot really. And in the grand scheme of things? I've barely scratched the surface of this game. You're dumped into a solar system, with a few planets and maybe ten-ish? stations to visit and get some random missions from. Cool, great, awesome. Did I mention this is only one solar system out of a galaxy?
Sure it's in space, the game isn't really going to be absolutely teeming with life or a huge population, but whenever you find a landmark there's usually some miners, pirates, the Militia, or some traders that are around, and it's up to you how to interpret who is friend, who is foe, and who is prey.
Can you be a pirate in this? Absolutely. Can you trade and smuggle illegal materials from different stations? Of course, just be careful of Militia patrols - they're in bigger, and meaner ships than you are to start out with, and they tend to shoot first and ask questions later if you're on the wrong side of the law. And of course you can also play the role of a bounty hunter, chasing after Pirate heads to fuel your bank account and taking up odd jobs to buy a few new guns along the way.
You can also be a trader, taking supplies from one station, then going and selling them at another station to make a huge profit. There's a news-feed option in there to let you know what the latest prices are for each station, if you're patient enough. Just look out for the pirates. Or, if you're a wuss, you can just be a miner and shred through astroids with mining lasers, selling the metal ore for profit, and running the hell away from the Pirates who like your cargo, but don't like the work.
As far as the combat goes, there's nothing really all that complex about it. You've got Broadside weapons, Turrets, and Secondaries. Broadsides are pretty self explanitory - they're guns mounted in the port and starboard sides of your ship (Left and Right) that are your main ship-killing weapons. What's neat is you can just spray-and-pray with them if you want, or you can charge them up, take aim, and have a well-timed barrage that leads your target so it lands right into their hull. Although if you're point blank, sometimes the spray-and-pray is better for use as a DPS race.
Then you have turrets. You can have some pretty simple stuff... missile turrets, laser turrets, beam weaponry, and even some flak guns to take down those pesky fighters and bombers swarming around your poopdeck.
And lastly there's Secondaries. Secondaries are essentially up to you, and effect certain places where your craft will be effective. You can put... bigger flak guns, you can put mine launchers, dumb-fire missile launchers, heat-seeker missile launchers, and so on.
As far as the story goes? I haven't really gotten that far into it yet, but from what I can tell it's super simple and not really anything that you're gonna get lost on. Find some alien-tech doohickey and then go on an adventure to find out what the heck it is and what it does.

Saints Row: Gat Out of Hell is essentially an expansion pack for Saints Row 4, and not a particularly great one. Stick to the main game, and if you decide that you absolutely must have more Saints in your life, then
consider this one. It's hard to say it's a good investment of time or money though.
The only step forward from the prior game comes in the form of tweaked flight mechanics. Gaining or losing altitude directly affects your flight speed, and flaps of your angelic wings act as a secondary stamina system to add a touch of extra depth to the system. They're small touches, but they add up to make flight engaging in its own right rather than just a convenient way to get from A to B.
That comes at the cost of nearly everything else though. There's barely a campaign to speak of, homies have been completely cut out, music has been completely cut out, and even The Boss has been cut out in favor of Johnny Gat, the least interesting Saint by no small margin. There's simply a dearth of character, which is not a good look for a series that has always hung its hat on it.
Bottom line, the open world gameplay is totally serviceable. But that's pretty much it, and open world gameplay isn't hard to find these days.

Story: Now in this game we continue's on from Blood money. The game begins with Agent 47 detailing his relationship with his handler Diana Burnwood whom he had trusted until she, without explanation, betrayed the International Contract Agency (ICA) by sabotaging their funding and database, using the subsequent confusion to vanish. After the ICA is reformed, 47 is tasked by his new handler, Benjamin Travis, a high level official within the ICA, to kill Diana for her betrayal and retrieve an important Agency asset named Victoria from her mansion in Chicago, Illinois. 47 sneaks into her mansion and shoots Diana. Rather than finishing her off, 47 comforts the dying Diana and asks her why she betrayed the ICA. Diana reveals everyone has their limits over the bad things they have done and she discovered hers after learning about Victoria, a teenage girl who is genetically-engineered to be an Assassin within the ICA. Not wishing to see Victoria suffer the same fate as 47, she betrayed the ICA and escape with her. As her final request, Diana ask 47 to protect Victoria, and he agrees to do so. Because 47 refuses to return Victoria to him, Travis brands 47 a traitor.
Now this story revolves around Victoria, ICA and more other great story characters. It is certainly a very good story well done to. I enjoyed it.
Game Play: The game play takes place in America e.g. The United States. Which is different that around the world like the old Hitman games. But I will try not to compare it to the old ones. Now we have the addition of the online feature called Contracts which you can compete against other players around the world doing contracts and even make your own to challenge your friends and others. Also the addition of this instinct feature. Which you can see through the walls and the enemies followed by using it to distract the enemies. Shame there is no in story weapon customization of the weapons and the load out choice to.
Controls: Controls are simple to learn as always even for the new player which is good.
The Graphics: Just amazing. Such an improvement. You can see it in the game and the cinematic's to. The detail on the weapons to and on Mr 47 even the npc's. I can not see a fault in it.
Music: It worked well with the game, it set the scenes up great even in the cinematic's to. I did not even want to turn it off which I did with the old games.
Bugs and Glitches: Well as with any new game these years there is always bugs and glitches. But there was only one or two. First would be crashing in loading sections and the other where the save file is unable to sync up. Other than that I could not come across any other. Many people have said of corrupt save files. I wounder if its connected to the failing to sync up.
Reply Value: There is certainly replay value in this game. Going through each difficulty level and there is the contracts side.
Overall: Great story as always, Game play just gets better with additions of a new skill and environments in America. Bar the loss of the weapon load out set and story mode customization's of the weapons. Controls simple to learn and use. Graphics just amazing. Music in the game adds to the game suspense. As I said there is always bugs and glitches hopefully these will be sorted. So for this next great installment to the Hitman Series. I give this game 9 paws out of 10

This is an excellent game. Verging on legendary. The issue is that it is a very poor PC port. On release the game constantly crashed and was unplayable. Now we’re a few patches down the line, things have improved but aren’t exactly living up to the concept of a Bioshock Remaster.
My issues with the game can be boiled down to two main points. First, performance on the PC is poor for the supposed graphical enhancements on offer. The graphics are a little clearer and sharper compared to the original, but framerate suffers drastically and refuses to remain constant, especially during scripted events.
The second issue is that there is very little “remastering” on display here. Other than the minor bump in graphic quality, the game retains all the bugbears of the original. They’re still using the same crazy, sometimes downright inane physics engine. Portable turrets are still annoying as hell, getting in the way whenever they possibly can. I swear the AI has actually gotten worse, it seems pretty dead on arrival here, NPCs doing the craziest of things such as just standing there whilst being shot at and constantly going back and fourth on themselves. Big Daddies also have this issue and still occasionally crash the game.
Not only does this feel like a rushed port, but it feels like a rushed remaster, probably aimed to capitalize on the XBO and PS4 more than anything. If it wasn’t for the fact that I got this for free, I wouldn’t be playing it. Do not buy it. The original will no doubt run much better.

Take a trip with me, down memory lane.  This uses the Q3 engine as it's way of conveying the story.  You play as BJ Blaskowitz, a Nazi-killer extraordanaire.  He's breaking out of the German's custody, and you arrived just in time to watch him do this.  You start your adventure in a castle, then head to a village to meet with a guy who outfits you with information and ammunition.  Then you start your adventure machine-gunning apart zombies and nazi's.
How much better could life get, if we had games like this released every five years?  Back in the early 2000's, this was a wonderful game.  It offered you just enough, to make you beat it, and then start on a higher difficulty.
You go about your business, and you'll spend maybe ten hours to twenty hours looking for secrets in each level.  You'll scream as a boss hacks you apart.  You'll be frustrated because some attacks just dispose of you very quickly.
But these games are rare.  This is one of the finest games ever released, and you have an opportunity to enjoy it.
Vanilla RTCW is a windowed game, but there are guides out there to let you update this to a more modern look.  Even if you do not do such a thing, you will have yourself a good time blowing apart the Nazi's.  10/10, playing through it once again.

Neon Chrome is a top-down shooter with permadeath that you can play fast or slow, swooping in with guns blazing or picking off enemies slowly with stealth. That being said, using stealth is going to take a while. As you play through the procedurally generated levels, new enemies show up to keep things fresh, and there are four bosses distributed across the game. The bosses are okay, not frustrating but also not all that interesting.
The character progresses through weapon upgrades and biotech upgrades. The weapon upgrades are a simple level system, but you have to change your weapon to a different type to take advantage of the raising level. The biotech upgrades are gained from upgrade machines. When you find one of those, you get a choice of three upgrades of which you can pick one. Some are better, some are worse, but all of them are in some way relevant. As you play you unlock various new weapons, abilities and biotech upgrades that can from then on show up randomly anywhere, on the current and any future characters. Also, after you die you can upgrade various stats that make all your future characters stronger. And you can choose a starting weapon, ability and biotech upgrade for your next character, for a price. You can also enter the game at several checkpoints, but you will lack upgrades, so this is only really viable after playing for a while to upgrade your global stats.
It's quite a fun game, it looks cool, sounds cool, and doesn't waste your time. I recommend this for people who like top-down shooters. Due to the short game length I wouldn't pick it up at the current full price of 15€ though. I got it much cheaper from a Humble Bundle.

X:Rebirth is a fascinating mess.  I did not play the game at release or anything near to it, so my review is in regards to the game circa early 2015.
X:Rebirth is a many-headed hydra, where each head does not fit well with the others.  Presumably to reduce the reliance on menu's seen in previous X games, X:Rebirth features a 'walking in stations' system.  At no point does anything you do while walking in stations add anything other than a terribly looking character to your game experience.  As soon as you figure out how to do the same thing via menus, you will.  It is faster and more aesthetically pleasing.
The core of the game is an economic empire simulator with the player as a trader CEO who for some reason also engages in combat and exploration.  All of this is accomplished from one ship that has a paltry number of upgrades that only require vast wealth to acquire.  The control of underlings is accomplished through a terribly poorly designed ui that requires repetition of multiple clickthroughs to achieve even the most simple of tasks.  Reassign a fighter from one wing to another? Requires comms to the pilot, choose how to assign them, pick their new superior, and then you are actually forced to wait while their confirmation dialogue plays.  All this could be accomplished through a single drag-drop, but not in X:Rebirth.
The space part of the game looks great even without mods, but most of your time is necessarily spent flying around stations.  Although the stations have a wonderful diversity compared to say Elite:Dangerous, no one really wants to spend hours and hours flying around them.  Yet you must in order to discover trade opportunities, missions, and the discounts that make trade profitable.
Even with a fair amount of modding to reduce the tedium of things like scouting stations, I still found myself bored and frustrated by ~70% of the campaign.  I also ran into a game breaking bug that apparently others have not experienced involving a full stop in campaign progress due to a missing NPC.  I had kept hoping that at some point the tedious exploration, lackluster combat (I think 90% of my missiles missed no matter the type I used) and poorly voice acted story would evolve into a fun trade empire simulation, but, for me, it never happened.
Even at a reduced sale price, it is hard to justify the purchase of X:Rebirth unless you give Egosoft a lot of credit for aspirations rather than accomplishments.

Betrayer is a first-person game, where you awake on a small beach after your ship wrecked.
You are thrown into the game, without any explanation or a real goal first, so you'll start exploring.
Controls are basically like any other first-person game. you can jump, crouch, use your weapons and interact with objects.
So, until here, everything is quite the usual.
What makes it so interesting and unique in my opinion, is the visuals.
Yes, having a game being black and white and only highlight enemies and objects with the color red was a great move. It adds a lot(!) to the atmosphere (you can however play with the contrast, and color saturation yourself to make it  colorful again, though i wouldn't recommend it).
After you have made your first steps, you encounter quite mysterious happenings.
Enemies appear and will try to shoot you on sight, but they don't seem particularly human.
After finding and entering your first settlement, you'll find burned corpses and try to find out what happened to these poor souls and then, there is also that mysterious maiden in red, which appears out of nowhere and then there is also, what i would call, the "ghost realm" (after ringing a bell in a settlement, everything darkens and you'll end up fighting skeletons and talking to souls, which got murdered).
Together with the visuals, the great sound and the spooky atmosphere it makes a quite good game.
The world itself is divided into larger hubs, where you can roam and explore freely, though, there isn't that much to find (graves, some clues and diary-entries which will give you a bit of backstory and few settlements or smaller places of interest).
You will find (or buy) different weapons throughout the game, like bows, crossbows, pistols and muskets to fight of the enemies (which you should do stealthy in most cases, as you can't take much damage).
The middle part feels a bit stretched and sometimes, it can be a bit frustrating, not knowing exactly what to do and where to go, but if you like exploring and a rather stealthy first-person mystery game which doesn't take you by the hand, then i would definitely recommend this one!

Betrayer caught me by surprise. I heard good praises about it without querying for details. After completing the game, those praises are definitely warranted. The initial setting of being washed ashore with no knowledge of who or where you are shrouds the player in a mist of mystery. The black & white graphics provide a unique atmosphere. I actually didn't realize you could play the game in color until I was almost finished with the game, but after trying both settings the black & white graphics really adds a sense of creepiness that you don't get with color.
Stumbling upon the first fort location, armored figures can be seen pacing back and forth, standing guard. At first it's really unclear how to approach the situation. Are they friendly? While trying to be sneaky, I was quickly spotted by one who alerted the whole platoon and 12 enemies quickly descended upon me. Goose bumps filled my skin from head to toe as I just turned and ran, my heart pounding as I occasionally looked back only to catch a glimpse of the blood red eyes of my pursuers.
It soon became clear that I could not escape and one-by-one I drew my makeshift bow, adrenaline swelling, and aimed squarely for their heads. One down...then another. Soon, after what felt like an eternity of running and shooting, they all fell before my feet, their red outlines lingering. My heart was able to catch a much needed rest.
And this was only daybreak. More sinister lurkings are waiting in the night...
Betrayer is really a spectacular game, for the first 3 or 4 areas. Then it starts to feel repetitious because all the adrenaline expended killing your first squad starts to become routine after about the 4th instance. So while there is plenty of gameplay, its appeal is lost somewhat quickly. And while there is a grander story coupled with all the action, it gets lost in all the noise (until the end of course).
Overall, it is a fantastic game, although it could have been a lot better had there been more to explore.

The game play is fun. After awhile, I got used to the 2D/Broadsides combat, and it doesn't feel like I'm missing as much as I feel I should. But, it's not as fleshed out as it could be either. Otherwise, it's a great modern freeform space sim that lets you live the life of a spacer with a clear mission to work on in the meantime.
The best thing for me, though, is the soundtrack. It's rare to find a game that completely nails it to the point that the soundtrack becomes so crucial to the game that without it, it starts to fall apart. I made the mistake of trying to customize the soundtrack... I thought I could mix my own flavor of dirty-guitar, bluesy rock, etc, and I should have just left it alone. When you hear friends talk about how great the soundtrack of Fallout 4 is and how well it helps define the game... that's the level of audio immersion in atmosphere that comes to mind here. Parallels to Firefly have been drawn a thousand-times over already, and the soundtrack is as responsible for that relationship as anything else. I rarely care about game music, and often turn it off, but here... I'll never listen to a space sim the same way again.

Introduction
Rebel Galaxy is the space swashbuckling brainchild of Double Damage, reminiscing of arcade space games like Freelancer, and is supported by an excellent Firefly-like soundtrack. Unlike most space arcade shooters, the game has no pitch movement, instead opting for travel along a single plane. The main game is set inside a galaxy, although it does feature multiple maps, relatively large in size. Despite its similarities, it does a whole lot of thing in a slightly different manner, from combat style all the way down to the way you travel. What you see is basically a new breed of space arcade gameplay, and very much feels like its own brand of shiny new original IP. Prepare yourself for broadside battles and inter-faction negotiations, along with a whole lot of lighting effects to blind you mid-mining.
Storyline
This game actually has a rather interesting story line, which is something I didn’t expect. Basically I was expecting it to be like Freelancer in most ways, but be lacking in some department or other. Despite my previous disposition, Rebel Galaxy follows a decent storyline. Basically you’ve been sent a message from your old crazy Aunt, who actually turns out to be a swashbuckling badass space-pirate at the age of late 50’s early 60’s. You’re trying to find out where she is, and make some sense of this weird AI you’ve gotten a hold of. Needless to say you get backstabbed and used like no tomorrow, and very often end up murdering the people you started out helping. It’s all a bit up and down, but heavily broken up by side quests and random world events. It’s similar to Freelancer in that you really need to do side quests and random events in order to upgrade your ship between main missions.
Gameplay
Learning Rebel Galaxy initially can be a bit odd. I went in expecting one thing, and discovered it was something different. The key problem is I was expecting something akin to most space arcade titles. I wasn’t far off, but I was enough for the game’s management to throw me a bit. From scanning areas to turrets with AI, that and the fact that despite manual aim there’s still an aim assist – don’t walk into this expecting Freelancer/Freespace/X-Wing. Take portions of a number of space arcade games, and you’ll eventually have a recipe for Rebel Galaxy. The mystification lasted only a short while in fairness, it’s just something new you have to get used to, but once you do it becomes second nature. To clarify, this is a good thing. What we have in Rebel Galaxy is something that feels at least a little bit unique, unique enough for us to be learning something new, while enjoying ourselves at the same time.
I’d like to go on about how much I love this game, so let’s first get the crap out of the way. Two things disappointed me most. First and foremost is the aiming system. AI turrets are awesome, configurable, and there’s a whole bunch of them and they do their job. Manual aim however, felt consistently interrupted. When engaging in broadside battles the game is constantly doing what it thinks is best. I aim the broadsides at a ship, but there’s another smaller ship closer which the game’s AI thinks is a more important target. The catch is my broadside weapons are slow velocity projectiles, and quite frankly I don’t give a damn about that tiny piece of crap. My lasers will take care of it. Instead of simply aiming at the ship I want to kill (which is usually fine in most cases I might add), the auto-aim kicks in and starts shooting broadsides in a direction that is not where you’re pointing. I hate it when a game thinks it knows better than me, and is flat out causing issues for me in intense combat situations. This doesn’t happen all that often, but it’s enough to annoy me a bit. Freelancer had it right. Allow full manual aim, but add aim assist circles to shoot for to shoot ahead of an enemy’s flight path. Auto-aim is just plain interference, because if you want to adjust the game’s target, you have to go into scan mode and switch targets.
This auto-assist comes in a second form, with the game’s speed and travel system. I cannot abide it. I’m sorry, but throttling my sublight speeds and dropping me out of warp at the hint of a sparrow’s fart gets extremely irritating throughout the game. Basically warp can only be engaged when the game says so. Sublight can only be sped up to cruise speeds when the game says so. Give me control of my damn ship’s navigation, and stop farting about like my mother. Nothing has been more infuriating so far than travelling 6000 game-lengths and getting stopped three times between A and B because you skirted around an asteroid field. Freelancer solved it, but adding AI auto-avoidance around objects. You’d occasionally hit stuff and lose some shield, but no problem. Slowing me down, and then further slowing me down to the lowest sublight speeds, forcing me to turn ninety degrees and boost out of an asteroid field is immersion breaking.
Rant over. The rest of the game rocks. This game is not Freelancer. Stop right there. Take all those predispositions out of your head, and prepare to play an all new type of game. Movement is entirely on one plane, but that’s cool. It means you can focus more on your tactical (or woefully haphazard) combat with those big♥♥♥♥♥broadsides. Turrets have varying types of AI that can be programmed to fire at certain types of targets, and there’s so much variation in weapons it tickles me in all the right places. Combat feels punchy, it looks pretty, and quite frankly simulating space-pirates is an excellent idea. The easiest way to make money is to pick a mission and then do all the randomised events that happen on the way there. There’s tonnes to do, and an enormous solar system to do it in. You might think to yourself that after the first solar system you’re halfway done, but you’re wrong, there’s a tonne more, and each map is as big as the next. Quite simply put there’s an awful lot of content and a lot of sights to see.

*note this review assumes some knowledge of the previous Hitman games*
The first Hitman game I played was Hitman 2 back in 2005, after playing the first assassination mission I fell in love with the game. The freedom to walk around an area and kill a target the best way you seemed fit without getting caught, even discovering funny and interesting ways to kill a target or innocent bystanders. I’ve followed the series since then and haven’t looked back since.
Then Absolution came out, through the announcements I was excited for a new Hitman game, since I was playing through Blood Money constantly. I knew from developer interviews that the game was going to be more linear so I was prepared to expect the altered gameplay.
While playing the first level I was surprised to find they took out the save system they had in Blood Money where you can save during a mission (difficulty dictated how many saves you had) and replaced it with a checkpoint system where they had specific locations where you can get a checkpoint. This makes sense with the linear gameplay but were completely pointless in some of the sandbox assassination levels.
Absolution adds in a new feature called ‘instinct’. This allows the player to see the paths of AI and items of interest (e.g. electric box to turn off lights or TV). Eidos decided to get rid of the map for this system. It’s a great system that they added making the game more difficult for a player to simply abuse the map and also makes its quick to look at AI paths close to you so the player can decide quickly instead of going through a menu and stopping. This feature is a great evolution to the game and one that I did like added to the game.
‘Instinct’ is also needed for disguises. If you have a similar disguise to an NPC you have to use instinct to cover your identity from that NPC. The change to the disguise system makes it harder for a player to simply get a disguise of a person that is authorised to go to all locations on the map and walk around with free reign and no consequences. This change means you have to look for exits or locations that have the least amount of NPCs with likewise disguises. This system is still flawed in Absolution, making it possible for you to simply hide behind a low wall after losing ‘instinct’.
The changes that Absolution brings into the Hitman series are mainly isolated to the game itself and its new gameplay. Absolution is a more linear gameplay with a 50/50 split on sandbox levels to linear levels. This was mainly brought about because Eidos wanted a different storyline, one that isolates Agent 47 from The Agency.
Absolution doesn’t have a story that will have you on the edge of your seat but gives you enough to keep going forward. Following Agent 47’s defiance of The Agency and their enviable pursuit to hunt and try to kill Agent 47. I didn’t like a group of assassins that were tasked to kill him, because they over sexualised the character when in previous games they didn’t. In Blood Money during the later missions you were being hunted by the CIA and their assassins tried to lure you away so they could kill you or like one assassin place you in a room to have a duel with pistols, assault rifles or sub machine guns. That aside Absolution has the most story elements in all of the previous Hitman games and does make it fit into the Hitman world.
Overall Absolution is a game that I would recommend to play. It’s a game that has pretty good graphics makes you think before taking action and ‘sometimes’ rewards those who are silent. Absolution hasn’t taken out the funny dark humour moments like killing someone by changing hot sauce for lighter fluid. If this is your first time trying out the Hitman series its pretty good to get you started especially if you are used to linear games but I would recommend Hitman Blood Money first before trying it.
If I don’t consider the previous Hitman game into comparison of Absolution I’ll give it an 8.4/10 , but with my previous experience of the other Hitman games I’ll have to give it a 7/10, only falls short because there weren’t many sandbox missions where you are given a target and chose how to kill them.

Primary Objective: Survive.
Secondary Objective: Preserve your humanity along the way.
You control a group of civilians trying to survive in an urban warzone. They have different talents (or lack of talents) and differing tolerances of morally questionable actions you may elect to take in order to survive (such as killing and stealing).
The survivors must take care of their basic needs and protect their shelter. Supplies run out and each night a member of the group must go out scavenging for materials, food and goods for barter.
The game plays out as a 2D survival management sim; during daytime you'll manage your resources, trade and improve the shelter. During the night the game is a 2D stealth-action game: You search for useful supplies while avoiding or possibly killing enemies. Combat is determined by RNG, but heavily influenced by equipment and player timing. The game is hard, offering little help to the newbie and your first playthrough will probably go poorly. Doing better the next time is a great appeal of this game. In later playthroughs you can play as a different group of survivors and possibly start the game during the winter season (which changes the game economy in favour of fuel for heating).
You can only save upon exiting (essentially always iron-man mode) and death is permanent. This makes your choices and priorities much more relevant and engaging.
The game aethetics greatly complements the theme being gray-toned and washed out. This is not a happy game. This is a game about war and how far you'll go to survive. Will you risk getting shot by the soldiers or will you prey on those weaker than you, taking their supplies by force? You can imagine your own little stories about the survivors as you decide their actions.
I found this game delightfully addicting, providing a "one more day" (game time!!) kind of feeling. I highly recommend it!

I was very torn on whether or not to recommend this game. Don't get me wrong, BioShock is a game that everyone should experience; some of the game mechanics are quite dated, but once you're used to them the atmosphere and world of Rapture is something that begs to be explored.
The major niggle I have is with the Remastered version specifically; in the 12-14 hours it took me to complete the story, the game crashed unexplicably about 5 times, causing me to replay 30 minutes or so of gameplay each time it did so. You may think that saving often is an easy solution to this, but frustratingly 3 of my crashes occurred when I pressed save. These constant crashes meant that by the time I was around 3/4 of the way through the game all I wanted to do was rush through, which is frustrating because of how much I enjoyed exploring every inch of the submerged city. If you're an achievement junkie I say give it a go and try to perservere through the occassional crash, but if you're not too bothered in the way of achievements definitely play the original version, the game is no less enjoyable. By the time I'd decided on this I was too well invested in this edition.
TL;DR:
If you care about achievements give it a go and try to persevere, otherwise play the original edition. The updated graphics aren't worth the continuous crashes.

I am extremely positive about RTCW. And that is correct, the game is well, quite elegant and confident. It is an old game, but almost nothing in it really feels dated or old. It is pure and no-nonsense in almost all it does. There is NO such beast as a perfect game, nor a game for everyone and RTCW is no exception. But honestly, it is a title that understands what it is and what it wants to be. It is an action first person shooter that is proud of what it is, warts and all. One with stupid but at the same time glorious paranormal and science fiction elements. A mechanic heavy creation, but one that does not shy away from world building and gets the so far established tenants of storytelling in gaming surprisingly well.
Alternate WW2 is a setting it takes to its heart and it is definitely a game I’d consider being made with care, attention and love. And personally, at least for me it is one of the finest first person shooter titles of all time.
Presentation: Nothing bad here. It has a lot of options, runs well and was damn excellently optimized for its time. Very good art style that ties in all the game's environments. Excellent sound effects and great music are essential and the developers knew that. A fan patch can be easily applied to help the game use newer aspect ratios, but that is to be expected. It is a PC game and it shows. 19/20
Story: Surprisingly, the game understands how to use its genre and medium really well. Do NOT expect complex themes or characters or ideas (even by video game standards), but do expect a surprisingly involving and well thought out plot with solid world building that uses the medium’s strengths to boost itself. It knows it is an action game and is damn proud of it, unlike the movies we call FPS games nowadays. 14/20
Gameplay: Elegance, simplicity… unexpected depth. I can say only good things about it. Thankfully many good linear shooters like Metro have learned their lessons from RTCW. It is not extremely complex but it is very well balanced and thought out. Polished to a shine few games attain. 19/20
Audio & Visuals: For its time it was a Crysis or Doom 3 level event. Extremely good looking by 2001/2002 standards and very scalable. Pioneered some interesting lighting and animation techniques as well as many cinematic special effects. Even used an early form of tessellation. Of course it has aged, but the fact that the game’s atmosphere will not diminish even 15 years later is a testament to both the it’s art department as well as its tech team. 20/20
Lasting Appeal: It is a linear shooter, true, but the replayability due to the excellent level design is top notch and can potentially give a player a decent amount of extra content. A dedicated modding community as well as some excellent multiplayer (which is now almost entirely moved onto Enemy Territory: Wolfenstein ) does give the game great extra staying power. Lots of maps and mini campaigns exist for those who look for them. Some quite decent… others not so much. Still, it is a game built to feel complete and for PC Gamers. 18/20
Overall: 90/100, A classic of its genre!

Kind of a mix between Hotline Miami, Rogue-Like, and Roleplaying game.
The game game is a top-down shooter, with an "infinite" gameplay. That means that while there's an end-game, you can repeat the whole process with higher difficulty, and since every floor is procedurally generated, every single experience will be different.
The gameplay is really nice if you take off Vsync in the game's files, guns are really fun to use, there are a few different classes of characters (of which you'll be able to pick between 3 everytime you die), the music is synthwave and really addictive, and the graphics are well done. It's a refreshing title that doesn't need too much thought to play, and I really liked it in short bursts. Also want to mention that there are a few unlockables that you might find in your playthrough; special weapons, abilities, normal weapons. Unlock them once, and they'll have a chance to drop in weapons crates/abilities pods/augmentations pods, making every single character a different customization and making it not repetitive.
Regarding the game longetivity, the devs have said that the usual player takes from 7 to 14 hours to finish one playthrough. I finished it in 5, and while I'm a good player, I don't think I'm incredibly gifted. If you're good at hotline miami you'll not have a lot of troubles in the game.
To the point; you collect credits that you can use before starting another round in permanent upgrades or weapons/abilities for your next character, and only your next character. It's a fun way to make the game easier, though I spent all my money on luck.
This game is a great short game, really fun and addictive, it's a shame I have a great backlog of over 20 games, otherwise I'd play another playthrough. I'll probably do it in the future.

'A fun little platformer about lost pants." 7/10
'Tiny & Big' is a wonderfully original platformer, despite the fact that it takes more time to cook a Thanksgiving turkey than it does to complete the game. Yes, this game is very short and can be beaten in just  a few hours. But should that take away from the overall experience? No! The price maybe...actually definitely the price, but certainly not the experience. The artistic style is simple, beautiful and gives off a nice 'Playstation 2 in High Definition' feel to it, and the soundtrack is very reminiscent of 'LittleBigPlanet'; two of the most refreshing aspects of the game. And I don't know about you, but I needs me some good songs when I be platforming.
The idea of finding songs is also a great way of encouraging exploration; something most newer games still don't get right. There is no voice acting, only grunts and groans ike in the early 'LEGO' games, but this only adds to the overall retro feel of the game. And the whole 'cut-anything-you-want-to-get-to-where-you-need-to-go' thing also reminded me of the original 'Red Faction' game; which is a very good thing. So overall, for a game where you search for lost pants, it's definitely worth playing through, if only once. Fans of older platformers will definitely appreciate this one as well as there are several aspects from games long forgotten.

Below is a short review on why I recommend the game, but if you would like to read more about the game, you can follow
to read a more fleshed out and relatively spoiler free review of the game as well as how it compares to the original short story the game is based on.
------
I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream is a story that is relatively timeless, and has many psychologically terrifying and does well to exploit our deep-seated fears as human beings. Each character's psyche and story is unique, and the mechanisms that lead you through each of their exploits, as well as the final chapter, serve to not only deepen the characteristics of each individual as well as the lore, but lets the player learn more about these inherent fears, and possibly even something about themselves.
While the mechanics are fairly basic as well as the hidden "moral" system, it is still an enjoyable and interesting ride, especially considering the ability to have multiple endings. The point-and-click genre of games is fairly known for having obtuse puzzles every now and then, and this one is no expection, but taking into account that the ultimate "good" ending in the game was suppose to virtually unreachable, it serves a purpose. The pixel graphics are still very well crafted, and the music and sound design are to be expected from this era.

The thing about x-rebirth that i love is how massive the world is and the fact it is all rendered in real time with all of your owned ships, you can be just wandering around a station collecting stashes while one of your stations is receiving wares on the other side of the galaxy, or one of your patrolling ships encounters a xenon that wondered into the area. the world never stops and waits for you to finish a mission or to catch up to someone your following to continue like it does on so many other games and thats one of the things i love about it.
The other major thing i love is that you control all of whats happening from your one ship, the Albion skunk you can start as just a little ship doing all the work yourself to managing a giant fleet, or a trading empire or whatever you want and its so imersive in that sense because you don't just instantly get these things you have to find ways to get the money to buy a construction vessel to start building a station, be it slowly with missions moving cargo or transporting people, or by accepting missions from the pirate factions and getting several million by causing mass chaos (at the downside of turning factions against you) you can do whatever you want.
What i hate about the game
Honestly the only thing that bugs me about the game is how they haven't been able to go as far as they could of with the whole idea of the economy, yeah each faction has its own funds and stations and resources and stuff but theres still instances where it feels like ships spawn in out of nowhere instead of being built, like with some of the pirate factions in the game, they have their own stations yes but they are in now way capable of building ships or making money to supply the pirates? and the pirates don't actually raid trade shipments, they attack it then if they win they just fly off and look for another one. i can't help but feel that they could have done more with that so that pirates actually had to attack people to survive and if you fought them off enough or launched attacks on their outposts it would slow them down or eventually destroy that faction. since you can make giant empires and have fleets of 50 ships easily but you cant seem to stop a group of pirates.

Community
the only problem with the game changing so much is that when you search google for guides and stuff they are all for older versions of x-rebirth, or the wiki's are no longer up-to-date because the people who were working on them have long since given up on the game as have many fans because of how long it has taken them to get a nicely working version of it. it's also majorly effected the game's rating and put off a lot of new gamers coming to play it, but trust me this is not the same game it is a epic trading/empire/war simulation.
Mods
with the prospect of mods now aswell you can completely destroy people's stations and help some factions build more of their own, the mods have added a tonn of content to the game along with what there already is in it so i do recomend checking them out.
Overall, if you like actually thinking about a game then get this xD its whatever you wanna do kinda game and worth the cash, if you wanna get nitty gritty into working out different productions and sabotaging other companies so your's will be able to sell stuff at higher price you can be that kinda player, but if you just like flying around shooting stuff there is that too, whatever kinda playstyle you have you can make your way in x-rebirth

Betrayer amounts to a slow burn ghost story. Any expectation of a high suspense thriller, big set pieces, or even many jump scares should be set aside. Instead, the game focuses on a very deliberate theme of exploration and investigation.
In terms of presentation Betrayer uses a black and white palette with slashes of red and shimmering effects to call attention to objects of interest. An alternate reality may be accessed early on that changes the scenery to an even more bizarre inky version of itself. While there may be complaints about the high contrast or crushed blacks, it is likely a good idea to give the default setting a chance before tinkering with colors or levels. The intended graphical style is an impressive companion for the tale being told.
Similarly, the audio design deserves special credit. The player often hears an enemy or object before they see it. In addition a certain item allows for areas of interest to be "heard" from a distance and zoned in on. This helps to substantially reduce the potential of the game becoming simple meandering.
It quickly becomes apparent that combat itself is not particularly the point of Betrayer. It is often fast and brutal. Stealth tends to lend the greatest rewards and is quite satisfying. Death is only lightly punished (there is an option to make it more severe) making mistakes mostly a nonissue. The enemies, while limited, offer certain unique behaviors though all seem to resort to running straight at the player eventually.
As for the meat of the game - the investigations - they serve mostly as a vehicle to relate the story to the player. The writing paints a rather bleak picture that was compelling to see through to the end. That said, on a mechanical level, investigations left something to be desired. It mostly boils down to finding an object, then taking the item to a npc who tells you about it or an event involving it. There is no ability to make inferences or mistakes. The player is simply lead to an object (via sound) then lead to whom they should speak to about said item (again, via sound).
Another small annoyance is the map. While perfectly serviceable, a game with so much ground to cover would have greatly benefited from an ability to mark points of interest (chests and the like) to return to later. Another weak point is enemy designs. As a whole the creatures in the game simply come off as a bit flat and uninspired.
Overall, Betrayer is a worthwhile experience. If given patience, as well as a proper understanding of just how to play the game, it offers an interesting tale to slowly unravel. It is not without its flaws, but none of them are severe enough to drag the entire experience down.

As expected, anything with the name 'Civilization' on it is going to be a pride and joy of Sid Meier.  Civilization: Beyond Earth is no exception.  This is a very fun game as we have come to expect from the franchise.  Not only do we get the classic turn-based strategy that makes Civilization what it is, but Beyond Earth presents a slew of user interface enhancements that I think make this game play a lot better than what we've seen so far in the series.
Besides the obvious and classic qualities of Civilization: Beyond Earth (in addition to the newer, sleeker presentation), players familiar with the series will note that Civilization: Beyond Earth is more accurately described (in my humble opinion) as a modification (a 'mod') of Civilization 5.  The entire gameplay of Beyond Earth directly mirrors Civ 5, and that even includes some of the game text.  Changes are slight, such as having a "tech web" instead of a "tech tree."
In all, Civilization: Beyond Earth is a fun game that I would not consider being even a 'stand-alone expansion' - it really is just a Civ 5 mod.  However, it is a great 'mod'!  I recommend that you buy it and play it.  But for how much?  I would recommend that you spend $15 or less.  If they start churning out DLC and expansions for this title (and I can't imagine why), then I'd try to keep the whole thing under $20.  (Paying the full $50 for the base version of Beyond Earth might be more for the person who does not own Civ 5 and is glad to part with his money.)

Betrayer is a fantastic game. It combines elements of horror, mystery, playing detective, and discovery in a 1604 colony establishing itself in Virginia, tied together with a strong narrative. While investigating disappearences and unearthing the fate of the colonists, the player travels across a gorgeously designed world. Think Miasmata style exploration, with the stealth of archery, or the braziness of muskets and pistol combat should the player choose.
The engine runs very well, and looks stunning. The game features a black and white filter, the strength determined by the player, who can choose true greyscale or saturate the colours as vivid or dull as they choose. Certain elements of the world remain red regardless.
The combat is very well done, the weapons are very responsive, and the archery behaves exceptionally well.
Even just exploring the world makes this game the comfy simulator so many people desire.
To top it all off, the writing builds a world of characters so vivid and varied that you'd be hard pressed to stop playing, lest you not know what happens/happened next.
Absolutely recommend this game to anyone looking for a comfy experience, or a middle ages, colonial setting horror or mystery.

Cultural system in place meaning you can't just send a fleet to a place bomb it out of existance and take it over, you have to convince the existing population that you can colonise the planet. And lastly a diplomacy system that means you have to work to become another empires ally. You can't just agree with a 2nd guy to bash on the third.
All and all. Amazing strategy game that I would reccomend to anyone willing to spend quite a bit of time on one game.

Plentty of ships to customize, you have to grind to get credits and stuff to update your ship. You can hire mercenaries to improve your ship. The only difference from FTL is that this game doesn´t flip a coin when you start the game giving you a maybe chance to finish it. Which in my opinion was the stuff that i found really frustrating of FTL.

The Iron Law of Political Balance: "The answer is always exactly in the middle of whatever inane extremes you stake out on either side." Except the first Bioshock was pretty close to the Randian ideas it lampoons and this one is attacking some incoherent collectivist strawman with scarcely a mention of Marx or Lenin. This game tries hard to emulate Freelancer or Privateer, but sadly fails.
1. The look and feel
Looks ok, especially considering this is an indie title. Especially the spaceships have a cool touch to them.
2. Controls
Instead of freelancer or even EVE controls, they decided to do some strange console like UI navigation & flight controls on a 2D plane orientation (in space?!?). They felt clunky and unintuitive to me.
3. Combat and space gameplay
This is in my oppinion the biggest issue - the broadside combat might be a good idea in theory, but not how it is applied here - since the ships often behave more like fighter craft than behemoth ships shooting broadsides at each other, it is highly annoying to control. And most of it is strangely semi automated with snapping auto aims etc. - I get the feeling this was "consoled" down.
Why not just do something classic like freespace or freelancer? Free movement and skill aiming in a full 3D environment, not on a 2D plane with strange autoaim and clunky movement?
4. Strange camera behavior
Really annoying was the camera, which would zoom in and zoom out during screen switchens (and interpreting this as a warp)
5. Story
I guess 15 years ago, it was quite ok to receive storyline quests from some shady guys in a spaceport bar.  Transfer it to today in a slighly better 3D look instead of pixel characters, and it no longer is so cool. Especially since the writing does not hook you.

6. Who put the afterburner on "W" and not on "tab" - seriously :)
