I've played this game for ~32 hours, and am currently working on the third playthrough (aka. 3.0).
Initially, I bought it because I liked the game's premise, and the graphics made it look interesting.  What kept me coming back, actually,  was achievment chasing.  The game is fairly easy to play, but the some of the achievments were surprisingly difficult.
Consider that I tend to like easy-ish games because they're casual, but I obsess on challenging achievments.  Doesn't seem all that consistent, does it?  And yet this game has a good blend of both - and that's what hooked me.
These days, Neon Chrome should be fairly inexpensive, but I think it's still a better than average value.  The replayability is impressive (to me); you can choose a different style of play each time you boot it up, and yet accumulate statistics in the form of purchased upgrades, no matter which character you play.  After beating the game, you have the option of increasing the difficulty yo the next levelk, which increases dropped rewards, etc.
Overall, Neon Chrome delivers casual fun in a way that kept me playing for longer than I'd planned on playing.  That's gotta count as a successful game.

This game is fun, but don't expect it to be a game you will play for 100+ hours.  It'll last the hardcore main story mission runners about 15-20 hours.  The main storyline seems short.  Most side missions are faction based, but pay well for the time involvement.  Side missions have some variety and are easy to find the location of and execute.  If you like doing side missions and answering every distress call, you can expect 50+ hours of gameplay.
There is a variety of ships each with their own specific stats, but you are more defined by your ship's equipment.  Multiple options for defenses, weapons, and components.  Once you get the largest ship with almost all of the best weapons, the enemies don't really pose a threat and the large dreadnoughts can be melted in under 10 seconds.  Looting is easy and your cargo capacity is upgradable, to a limit.
Controls are easy to use and doesn't require you to learn and use 100 different keys.
The soundtrack is great and is a mix of Rock, country, and blues.  It includes music primarily from guitarist Blues Saraceno (Poison, albeit briefly) and others.
Achievements are easily attainable.  I finished them in 60 hours(all but one at 56), but I probably could have done it much faster if I wasn't meandering.
Graphics are good and have plenty of good effects.  You have many options you can turn off.
Minimum HW requirements are low, so it'll be playable on most people's gaming computers.
There are some things that could be improved if you analyze every aspect of the game.  This is not a sim, expect it to be somewhat arcade like.  The game appears to be aimed at combat and having a good time.  Don't get hung up on the trade system because it needs an overhaul.
Overall, it is a well polished game with good graphics and a good soundtrack.  Buy it for $19.99 and enjoy it.

The shortest possible way to describe the gameplay of Neon Chrome would be the following math equation: Neon Chrome = Rogue Legacy - Super High Difficulty (early on) + Hotline Miami + Cyberpunk Setting. That's a bit too basic, though, and not 100% accurate, of course, so I'll go into a bit more detail.
If you didn't already know, the big difference between a rogue-like and a rogue-lite, is that although both give you randomized maps and you start the game over if you die, rogue-
give you some form of progression/unlocks that is saved between runs. Neon Chrome is the latter, letting you keep the money that you picked up from enemies and loot boxes, and essentially letting you continue past bosses you have beaten, using the money you earned on your run to purchase persistent (permanent) stat upgrades for all future runs. This is much like the system used in Rogue Legacy, though I actually found this game to be a lot more fair and designed to encourage tactics more so than to simply abuse the player.
That leads me into the Hotline Miami comparison. No, you don't just die any time you're hit, but I'm referring to the real-time tactical aspects of that game. While some players may have run in like a screaming barbarian, clubbing everything and zooming around rooms trying not to get hit while taking on an army of guys and being shot at, I tended to be stealthy, going into a room and killing enemies before I was seen, thus reducing the odds of death and systematically getting myself closer to victory. You can do that in this game, too. It's unlikely you'll go unseen, but you can minimize the number of enemies who have seen you at times and use doors as bottleneck killzones, and corners with your laser sight to line up easy kills.
Playing like this helps to even out the deficiencies in your stats or in your gear, while the persistent upgrades give an enjoyable "vengeance" sensation while wiping the floor with enemies who used to make your life suck when doing another run. The randomized parts of the game consist of enemy placement, map layout, and per-run weapons and cybernetic implants. The former come in a variety of well-designed weapons you'll grow to learn the strengths and weaknesses of, while the latter give you amazing bonuses, such as 50% max health capacity bonus, +100% manual reload speed, immunity to mines, 35% HP recovery upon completing a floor (so good!), and many more. On each run, you get a new character (random 3 to pick from a la Rogue Legacy) with pros and cons to him or her (Hacker rocks when trying to make lots of cash!). Try several character classes and see which one(s) you enjoy most.
Did you find a weapon you like? Why in the world would you ever bother opening another gun box when you have the gun you want to finish the game with? Well, the developer was very clever here. At the beginning of the game, it's a level 0 gun, with pretty awful stats. If you open a gun box, not only do you get a new gun you can choose to take or leave, but
gun drops on that run are now leveled up higher, and thus have better stats! Why visit weapon upgrade machines if you're using a gun you want to ditch ASAP? More brilliance on the developer's part. Using the upgrade machine
levels up all future gun drops on that run. If you go visit all gun boxes and upgrade machines, max level guns should be dropping by end game, which really helps out. I could go on about the things you find to unlock more things, but it would just be rambling.
A successful run in which you kill everything and collect everything will probably be about an hour and a half in length, and it goes by pretty quickly. If you die and finished a boss, you can start over around level 5, 11, 17, 22, or 29 (I'm sure I'm off on a few of those, sorry!), by stepping into an elevator with the appropriate section number (1 through 6), with each one lighting up after you beat that chapter's respective boss. The bosses are pretty simple but well-designed in their attacks and movements (I love the second boss). Personally, though, I played from the beginning whenever I died, because it's so rewarding if you open all the gun boxes so you have higher-leveled weapons by end game, and you can breeze through the easier, earlier levels while unlocking more things for future runs and getting more cash.
An hour and a half long if you play it well? I'm sure most people will need a few attempts to win, but yeah, it's not a super long game. If you're one of those folks who sees value in game length, though, this is absolutely a "new game plus" game. The big screen on the right in your starting room says "Overseer 1.0" but if you win the game, it shows 2.0, do it again, and 3.0, etc. You can use a computer console in a room on the left of the starting room which shows you a bar graph of the various stats in levels, including enemy HP and damage, as well as loot amount. The loot amount goes reeeeally high when going from one difficulty to the next, giving you much, much more money per kill and loot box, letting you get your stats maxed in a jiffy.
But what in the world do you spend your money on between runs if you've maxed out all your stats? You spend it on per-run guns and per-run cybrnetic implants. At the top of the starting room are three consoles which let you purchase and level up certain guns for money, as well as take specific cybernetic implants of your choosing and a combat ability of your choosing instead of relying on randomness on future runs. Each successive implant costs much more money than the last, but it's really worth it to get the must-have ones for your playstyle (max HP and health recovery stuff for me because I'm pretty terrible!). The developer really thought this stuff through and clearly put a lot of time and effort into it.
Long story short, here we have a top-down shooter in which you can be somewhat tactical along the lines of Hotline Miami, with persistent purchasable stats between runs like in Rogue Legacy. It's got a nice cyberpunk asthetic, and the developer clearly cared more about making the game be fun than a pain in the rear. It can be challenging in your first couple of hours, before getting any stat gains, and before all of the glowy cyberpunk things in levels finally register with your brain so you know what is a decoration and what is something vital you need to interact with, but eventually your skill, even if crappy like mine, will likely allow you to triumph with some nice persistent stat gains between runs making up for your weaknesses.

A classic point and click loosely based on the short story by Harlan Ellison. The music is good, the voice acting ranges from average to excellent, with Ellison himself as the voice of AM. The game is very open-ended, with multiple paths through most of the scenarios, and multiple endings.
The puzzles are a mixed bag. The logical stuff is simple enough, but the metaphorical stuff can be cryptic.
Honestly, the worst part of this game is the sequence breaking, often happening to the point that progress will be hindered or the game will be outright unbeatable if something is done out of order. I noticed this most prominently in Nimdok's stage, with the watch, and in smaller cases during the other scenarios. At the least, it will cause confusing situations, such as having one event trigger another, unrelated event. At its worst, you could end up saving in a bad spot that requires starting the game over from scratch to have another chance. Of course, the game is short if you know what you're doing, so making up lost progess like that is a matter of minutes, but it's still annoying and frustrating.
Other than that, this is one of the finest translations of story to video game I've ever played, even if this version is changed, and quite embellished.

I Have No Mouth And I Must Scream is a bad game.
This 1995 point and click adventure, incredibly loosely based off Harlan Ellison's 1967 short story and co-designed by Ellison himself, shows its age and not in the usual way, though not in a way that marks it as the bad game it is. Those particular reasons are timeless.
Throughout the game, you're taken through five "psychodramas", which you can choose at your own leisure and each centering around a particular character with their own sordid history full of metaphor and mental allegory reminiscent of Psychonaut's own Dreamworlds (though obviously, this game came first), and an end sequence. There are a variety of actions you can complete in each scenario that either lowers or raises each character's "Spiritual Barometer", a basic morality system that, given the completely arbitrary and unsignposted actions that alter them, is thankfully nearly completely worthless on its own.
The art design is fantastic, with the intentionally ugly humanoid sprites laid thickly on richly detailed backgrounds that range from rusting iron plates to cerebral nightmarescapes, to one incredibly memorable locale that invokes the late H R Giger's biomechnical designs. The animation is negligible, which is more than acceptable given the time period the game was made in and the memory constraints developers had to work with, but does its job well enough.
Voice-acting and dialogue within I Have No Mouth And I Must Scream are executed very well, along with the noticeably good sound design in general, but have aged into campy and ridiculous conversations and reactions.
Playing as a tortured girl having a mental breakdown from confronting her [Hymen Highwayman] shouldn't be funny, but when the [Hymen Highwayman] in question is a Saturday-morning cartoon villain and the follow up is a sassy one-liner accompanied by a hilarious uppercut it's impossible to take seriously. This permeates the entire game. AM doesn't sound like a malevolent god going steadily crazy inside his suffocating shell, he sounds like the Joker phoning in his lines after a particularly strong hangover. The entire script has fermented into a vassal of ham and stifled laughter.
Only exceptions to this are Benny and Ted, the former who despite the massive overhaul to his character still comes across as a convincing racist military officer, and the latter whose entire storyline and character are just weak and forgettable. Despite the obviously unintentional retrospective of the narrative it's still enjoyable on its own.
None of the above remotely contributes to why I Have No Mouth And I Must Scream is a bad game. At worst it'll make you sad that, if you played it like my own playthrough ended up, you won't leave this game with the sense that you have truly managed to appreciate Ellison's narrative and tackling of themes that are usually not even whispered about in videogames, but with a steaming sense of frustration, regret that you ever bothered with the game, and a throbbing headache from having to replay the same sections over and over because you didn't managed to abuse save-states as much as they obviously expected you to.
"Unsignposted Dead Ends". Innocuous actions which lock you into an unwinnable state, that the game does not notify you about or otherwise point out at all. You just wander around until your ever-decreasing cup of patience runs dry, trying to pick up another loose thread on the game's already obtuse and thoroughly unenjoyable puzzles, wondering if you're just missing a vital interaction or you have truly just screwed over your playthrough and you don't know how, when or why. One of the most hilarious examples had me complete an action that locked me into a dead state at the beginning of  a scenario, but still let me get through almost entirety of of the scenario anyway, only locking out the last ten seconds of puzzle before the ending. It happened an average of once per scenario, each necessitating a complete restart if you've saved at the wrong moment.
Don't buy this game, folks, save your time, money, and the few non-aching brain cells you have left on something else. Anything else. It's not worth it.
And the game was designed like this on purpose. Someone sat down, and decided that assuming you had to pour water on the electronics a second time due to dialogue, or giving the pliers to the wrong starving victim at the wrong moment, was going to lock you out of completing the game and they weren't going to do a damn thing about it, not even update that otherwise useless hint book of theirs. Why?
I Have No Clue And I'm About To Scream.

Betrayer is a nice investigative adventure game that has some horror aspects and some aspects that can be similar to that of Skyrim's open world. I didn't mind the whole black and white color scheme but you can choose to give it color if you like. This game doesn't have any side quests but you'll never get lost during the story thanks to the "Listen" button you get that shows you pretty much where to go (I should note that you don't get this until the first town in the game so maybe not "never" lost). Below are some pros and cons I found about the game.
Pros:
-For once I enjoyed not having to farm enemies for better weapons that might just be 5 damage more or something like that. All weapons of the same name have the same stats so you can focus more on the story and if you want, hunting pages and chests.
- Inventory space will never be a problem because you can "scrap" your items in your inventory at anytime and gain money. Now that's convenient
-The gameplay for me was pretty smooth and incorporates drop when shooting arrows (not sure about guns because all I used was longbows.
-Collectables such as pages, key items and also treasure chests that are near will actually make a high pitches noise so that was helpful. Now only if my keys did that.
-There's also fast travel. Like, thank god. Seamless fast travel if you're moving around in the same map which is AWESOME.
Cons:
-Sometimes it will feel like there aren't really much enemies at all on the map.
-The shades sometimes hit you with a melee attack before they get in your melee range.
-Although it is listed as a horror game and I said it was, there wasn't really anything scary to me but this is just my personal opinion.
-After you beat the story, there's not really much replay value. Only to get achievements.
All in all, this was a great little indie game. However I don't think it's worth $20. I got in during the summer sale for like $5. If it was $5-$10 then go ahead and grab it!

So, Hatred. I stumbled upon this game having never heard of it before. The title is what reeled me, and the fact that it was at the top of Steam. I checked it out quickly. I love a game that flips common tropes on their head and is not afraid to push the envelope to the point of breaking. The fact that this is basically a mass-murder simulator when (in the US at least) there are mass shootings every day really gave this game a lot of "edge" for lack of a better term, which is what I like in games, whether that edge be due to controversy, difficulty, or in depth storylines. However, it is rare to find raw unadulterated controversial gore nowadays. I decided, despite the negative reviews to buy this game at its current price and play it.
Pay no mind to the negative reviews, this game is amazing. The black-and-white artstyle is amazing, the voice acting is amazing, the weapons, environments, enemies, civilians, executions, all contribute to a fun violence simulator. It is simple, easy to play, enjoyable in its brutality whilst still being challenging to the point of me damn near throwing a tantrum over losing a level 5 TIMES! The best part is, the developers and the game make no bones about what this game is: a mass-murder simulator, designed to simply and brutally explore in an arcade-like manner, the activities of a violent misanthrope bent on killing anyone in his path. Its simple, brutal, and violent, which is something that seems rare in today's gaming environment.
For god's sake even the credits are a heavy-metal music video of gore and death, showing the main character brutally killing both police and civilians alike.
It makes a good stress reliever, a good arcade shooter, and just a good game overall with great style and flow in the gameplay. 10/10

Betrayer is a curious game. It's a horror game, with a semi-open world to explore. It's a shooter, but it encourages stealth. It even shuffles some RPG elements in there for good measure. The end result is an experience that's quite unlike anything I've ever played.
The game starts off with you washing up on a beach in 16th-century Virginia. As you make your way inland, you discover the nearest colony has been overtaken by a mysterious force: one that turned the local populace into ashes and changed a Spanish invasion force into feral beasts. You meet the enigmatic Maiden in Red, whose past is tied to this place in ways she cannot yet remember. As you venture through the forests you uncover more abandoned settlements, each with their own history and ghosts left behind to tell it. You'll face a multitude of strange creatures, brought forth by the plague ravishing the Frontier. The combat can get a bit clunky, but the novelty of shooting monsters with muskets and crossbows makes up for that. Exploration can get a bit dull, since the world mostly looks the same. I had to resort to using an online map for each of the game's segments in order to get the full experience.
Each map of the game world is strewn with collectables. These range from journal pages left by the people to graves and clues you find in the wilderness. Speaking with wraiths can give you valuable insight into the tragedies that occured here, even before the world went to hell. There's some interesting stories to be found, and they all receive a form of closure. The way you handle them can also have an impact on the ending of the game, but don't expect the effect to be too great. The ending itself is also strange, and leaves a lot open to interpretation (and the inevitable sequel), but the game's climax is satisfying enough to overlook that.
Betrayer is definitely not easy. The enemies pack quite a punch, even on the lowest difficulty setting. There's not a lot of guides on there online, either, so you'll have to find your own way through the intricate maze of Colonial history the developers have crafted. Figuring it out is immensely satisfying, though, and I'd definitely recommend everyone to play this game.

After finally completing two full games on two separate maps and dabbling with a mod
a
total conversion mod), I feel qualified enough to write a small review.
+Lots of units with different abilities
+Pleasing aesthetics with diverse designs and shapes between the 3 factions
+Good sound effects
+Unique and pleasant soundtrack - the score here shies away from bombastic brass and drums and throws most of it's eggs into the stringed instruments basket, and it pays off nicely
+Brilliant mixture of real-time strategy and 4X - if a more well-known studio had done this it probably would be significantly more popular.
+Tantilizing lore
+Lots of mods for various franchises, including
(Dawn of the Reapers),
(Sins of a Galactic Empire),
(Sins of the Prophets - WIP as of September 2015), and
(40,000 Sins - WIP as of June 2015). I have only played with the Sins of the Prophets alpha a bit and had a lot of fun with it, not sure if the others are finished. The game also has what I'll call "native" mod support (there's a function in the main menu that allows you to load in and use a specific mods next time you start the game).
+A large number of units have at least one special ability, with capital ships having at least 4. To add to the fun, the units are able to intelligently use their abilities on their own - meaning you can build your empire and fleet, coordinate your fleet's travel logistics, prioritize targets, and then kick back with your beverage of choice and watch with sinister gratification as your fleet annihilates with intended precision your enemy's fleet and bases, followed by orbital nuclear bombardment of their colony until only ash is left for you to build a new world up on.
+Sense of accomplishment - I was trying to figure out where the enemy's homeworld was in the last game I played - it was just me vs. him - I had, in a slow, turtling fashion, annihilated two opponents - one who had apparently feigned interest in diplomacy only to turn around and attack me, and another from another star system who had made themselves an absolute pest with the continual streaming of tiny fleets into the uncolonizable planets in my system. In later mid-game, one of the AIs, who had begun to show diplomatic interest in a peace treaty, cleaned the clock of two AIs in relatively short order - as soon as the knocked down the one AI they shared a system with, they cut ties with me and started priming an experimental weapon to use against me. I got scared - what WAS this experimental weapon?! I kept sending scouts into their star system, but the AI killed them before they could make a second jump to a planet. So I marshalled the largest fleet that particular galaxy had ever seen, flew into their star system, and killed their titan and entire fleet guarding the system's entrance and left behind a rear-guard fleet of 12 heavy cruisers and 12 anti-fighter flak frigates. I took an educated guess and went off in one direction, hoping to find the experimental device before it destroyed my empire. Lo and behold, a massive, eerie-looking space station came into view in one of the gravity wells.
I said to myself. Then I zoomed out and looked at some of the planet's information.
I had my cruisers and frigates make mincemeat of the experimental device and had my capital ships bombard the wretched enemy's homeworld with nuclear salvos. I annihilated the planet and had a very satisfying victory after a long and mostly enjoyable 6-hour match. I look forward to playing on an even bigger map soon as well.
-UI isn't the most intuitive but compensates by being self-explanatory. I thought all the maps were tiny little 15-planet areas until I found the "change map type" button, whereupon I discovered maps could go in excess of 100 planets. Finding this was a huge reason why I came back to the game for another go.
-
-Noticeable to significant lag in end-game. I have not experienced this myself but it appears to be a widely acknowledged problem within the community - there are several mods that take different approaches to fixing this, including reducing the number of fighters present in a fighter squadron without changing the strength of the total squadron. This significantly cuts back the amount of pathfinding the engine is required to do and thus cuts back lag.
-Not a shining example of optimization. On that note, the game is more than playable on an Intel HD 4000 Chipset (yes, an Intel chipset). This is still counted as a negative because of the end-game lag players experience.
Overall I strongly recommend this - it's a really fun title. AI isn't shabby and 6-way matches can get fun depending on the difficulty. I haven't played multiplayer but I'm under the impression this is a largely-multiplayer title, especially in light of the lack of a campaign.
Buy it. ESPECIALLY if it's on sale (Winter or Summer).

An underrated sequel to one of the most atmospheric settings of its time, Bioshock 2 is considered to be the black sheep of the trilogy, and the only one that wasn't developed entirely by Irrational (Some of the members had a hand in with 2K Marin).
This entry is actually difficult to get into unless you've played and/or were well-acquainted with the first game, as it's confusing to understand why or how everything around is the way it is. While there is a reference guide to the first game within the help menu, it only touches upon the big picture and doesn't fill in the context needed for new players to relate to their setting.
This game was meant more for people who've already went through Bioshock 1, and it certainly shows in more than just the in-game lore. The gameplay in everything, from combat to customization, has been tweaked, rebalanced, and expanded upon.
Being able to use plasmids alongside your weapons (instead of switching between the two) brings more focus on doing more things within a given moment, upping the skill ceiling and letting you do some crazy things and combos. If you're not a reserved person and like to go wild and experiment, then this is a huge blessing and by itself made this sequel far superior in gameplay for me. You can't replicate how godly you feel when you smoothly juggle multiple plasmids and weapons in the midst of battle and mastering order out of chaos. Gunning down a Rosie with armor-piercing rounds while casting Incinerate 2, Insect Swarm, and Electrocute (in that order), then going in for the kill with Drill Dash while he's stunned with electricity and you're refreshing your EVE bar is nothing short of exhilirating.
The game streamlined some annoying mechanics from the predecessor that I appreciate. A much shorter and more twitch-based hacking system, and a more involved and less awkward camera research system go a long way to making the game more enjoyable and focused. A ranged tool for hacking solves the predecessor's moments of having to shock/freeze mechanical enemies to run up and hack them. Tonic selection is no longer bound by category, so instead of having 3 lines of 6 slots each, you now get all 18 slots without needing to worry what category you can fit a tonic in. This is really useful for players who don't care about hacking tonics at all, as they can now slot whatever tonic they want into those previously-categorized slots.
All weapons (besides the drill) can now zoom in, and it's a much more useful zoom that keeps the crosshair active and doesn't obstruct your view with terrible sights like in the predecessor. It's still only useful to a small selection of weapons though, namely the rivet gun and the spear gun, as zooming in disables your use of plasmids. Speaking of the rivet gun, that weapon is much more useful than Bioshock 1's pistol, as it has better alternative ammo that isn't outclassed by the machine gun. You'll see this weapon have more uses later on in the game than the pistol did.
Melee is a more balanced affair this time around. Bioshock 1 has a melee build that was overpowered in that it was easy to sneak around and one-shot splicers, while also having powerful confrontation abilities (such as stun-locking with the wrench when you equipped both SportBoost tonics) regardless of difficulty level. In Bioshock 2, your main melee weapon has a slower attack speed and disorients your camera a bit per swing. Not only that, but the SportBoost tonic doesn't affect melee swing speed anymore and the Drill Lurker tonic only quiets your footsteps when you're crouched. On top of that, you have less damage boost modifiers in general. In return, you get a melee attack that is a continuous form of damage through spinning, another melee attack called Drill Dash that is a powerful gap-closing charge against a target, and the ability to melee with all weapons (though weaker than with the drill). What you get is a melee system that still allows "backstabs" (though you better hope it one-shot or close), but is now much more engaging (and sensible) in the heat of battle against multiple foes.
Plasmids themselves now have additional functions and/or abilities when upgraded. Some of these are passive, while others give you different functionalities when charged, but it all comes down to providing more options and tools while you're in combat, and it goes very well with Bioshock 2's dual wielding. For example, Electrocute 3 sends out a continuous stream of electricity at your target, which essentially functions as Bioshock 1's Chemical Thrower with Electric Gel. This solves the main problem with the Chemical Thrower of the previous game, as while you are stunning your target, you couldn't do much else about it besides what a regular stun could afford you. In Bioshock 2, Electrocute 3 means that while you're stunning your target with your electric stream, you can now also have your drill out and continuously melee/drill them.
All of these changes and refinements to combat make Bioshock 2 much more fun to do battle in than the first game. It's all overwhelming at first, but if you have the patience and the initiative to experiment, it pays off in a gameplay experience that you'll sorely lament about the lack of in the first game. You're not playing as a human; you're a Big Daddy and the devs definitely know how to make you feel badass if you are willing to dive into it.
Little Sisters now have an additional option to them, where instead of determining their fate and getting your ADAM right away, you can have your adopted Little Sister gather from preset corpses to supply you with more ADAM before resolving them. This by itself is fleshed out and encourages a different playstyle while you're defending your gathering session. I thoroughly enjoyed this type of gameplay more than I thought I would, and that extended to the Protector Trials DLC. Though it's perhaps because there rarely was a defense type of event in the first game, and I feel like that kind of event is a good way to test your handling of combat options thus far.
One of the things I do hate though, is not being able to go back to previous levels like in the first game. From a story standpoint, this is understandable. From a RPG perspective however, this gives off a frustrating habit to completionists to find and do everything within a level before moving on. The previous game really shined in just letting me go back whenever I wanted to, without grinding the game's pacing to a halt.
The story is definitely where the fans remain divided upon. I personally don't find the story as atmospheric or surprising as the first game, and I would describe the exact reason why, but that'd be spoilers. However, the arc and pacing are much more consistent this time around, and it's easier to wrap things up by the time the credits are rolling as a result. There's also a more meaningful and gray theme playing in the background, and while I can't spoil too much, there was a moment in the game where I had a really difficult time deciding on. All-in-all, I find Bioshock 2's story to be more relatable and self-reflecting. And I think the devs intended for this, as I'm very sure it's difficult to create something comparable to Bioshock 1 in terms of the story. It seems to me that, rather than compete and risk being forever stuck in the shadows of the predecessor, the devs tried to strike out on their own and push the limits on a different kind of narrative.
Looking back, I always find myself aching to replay Bioshock 2 more than any other entry of the trilogy. And the explanation I always come back to as to why is simply the refined gameplay and the more servicable story (that is easier to replay with). Basically, I have more fun replaying this than the others. It's a game where I can tune out the story, and what's left is amazingly fun to go through. A personal favorite for me.

When I play Rebel Galaxy I am instantly reminded of the TV show Firefly. This space western feels like its straight out of a script from this show. You start off with a message from your aunt telling you to get her old spacecraft and meet her at Rust City, from there you are thrown into a world of bounty hunting, space piracy, blockade running, and much more than I can list in this review. Here is my breakdown of this space adventure.
Graphics – The graphics for this is not bad. However there were little annoyances like to much glare from some of the stars and nebulas. I have seen much better graphics from games like EVE online and Elite Dangerous. While not bad the graphics are average at best for a space game. 3 out of 5
Sound – I blame the soundtrack for the countless deaths I have had in this game. Just imagine you are cruising in your starter ship you get knocked out of warp because you came too close to the enemy. You see 1 capital ship and a handful of fighters, you decided to leave to fight another day and then the music kicks on and you suddenly you can take on the world and you say I can do this and end up as space debris……Yep sound is good. 5 out of 5
Controls – The controls are something you have to get used to, it is a mixed bag. First off the game is in 2D space meaning there is no up or down. The main way of space combat is broadside cannons like on an old navy sailboat. You have to pull up to the port or starboard sides and fire. Controls on the keyboard are a little tough to get used too. I do recommend a controller for this game. 3 out of 5
Story/Gameplay – As far as story goes if you watched Firefly or the movie Serenity and you enjoyed them than you will enjoy this game. As far as the people that have not watched the show or liked the show for that matter, than this game is a sandbox space adventure game. There are many games that are on steam that give you the same experience however the story of Rebel Galaxy sets it apart from the rest and personally it is a must play for anyone who enjoys a good Space Adventure. 5 out of 5
Conclusion – Rebel Galaxy is a wonderful game for anyone that enjoys space/flight adventure if you follow the main story the game is pretty short (10 – 15 hours) However with all the side quest on top of the extra missions you get during this game, for $20 it is a must buy. 4 out of 5

I bought all 3 Bioshocks in a bundle and played the first game and had an amazing adventure. The second Game I held off on playing for a long time because I wasn't sure wether or not it would be an enjoyable experience. A lot of my friends would tell me not to bother, I'm extremely glad I did bother. The game took a little while to truly grow on me, the entire beginning sequence felt a bit off. But once I got to Pauper's Drop I started to get into it, the voice overs are excellent and the atmosphere started to rebuild itself. The City of Rapture really took ahold once more as I met more characters and learned more backstory. Dionysus Park and forward just got better and better.
I think the biggest obstacle I had to overcome was the player character. I could not get into the role for a while because of my memories from the first game. Big Daddies were tough enemies, very tough and could tear out your chest in one go if you weren't careful. So playing one felt a bit unfair and also gave me a sense of false invulnerability, the only thing that could take them down in the first game was the player and since I was now playing one the only way I'd die would be my own folly. Well, I was wrong of course but it still felt that way for a good while and when Eleanor really started to converse with you and as you learned her and Sofia's backstory the more I wanted to rescue her from that insane psychiatrist that dared call herself a mother. I chose to rescue all the Little Sisters and spare all the choice characters, however, Alex the Great, man did I want to end him and I debated a while what was the right thing to do before ending the level. The story overall was satisfying, and the ending for being a Savior was very touching.
Gameplay wise, it isn't a great deal different from the first game but man is being a Big Daddy and doing the Drill Dash satisfying. The new enemy splicers and Big Daddies were a welcome addition and fit right in with the scenario. There were a few near useless tonics, but then it would fit someone elses' playstyle and not mine, the wealth of tonics really let the player play the game however they'd like.
If you haven't already played this game, do it. The story alone is worth it and provides great insight to Rapture post-Bioshock 1 as well as fleshing out characters you'd already met or known about in the first game.

The X games have always been close to my heart. X3 did so many wonderful things for the genre. It improved upon the issues of the previous titles while adding what seemed to be boundless possibilities for customization and replay. X3 was the “be anyone you want” of space sims. Beyond that, the games always had a robust following of experienced and talented modders that provided even more customization and options to make the universe more alive.
It was that consistency of greatness that drew my eye to Rebirth. I was captivated by amazing visuals and the promise of an even bigger universe than the previous games. All of this came crashing down, however, on the day of release. Steam comments flooded in claiming the game was nearly unplayable, and that the new features had drastically reduced the diversity of the gameplay.
There was hope, however, as Egosoft heard the public’s plea and promised to introduce fixes in the future. Additionally, the modding community could pick up any slack the developers left behind, right?
Wrong.
It is now more than a year after release and the fundamental issues that make this game such a poor installment in this universe are still going strong. What was once a complex and diverse universe is now nothing more than a light framework for a space sim. The degree of customization and control has been stunted to an awful degree. Control of ships is absurdly confusing and requires you to continuously jaunt through infuriatingly vague menu commands that ultimately lead nowhere. You are confined (piloting-wise) to one ship, which is not as big a deal as it might seem, but the lack of control makes it too much of a hassle to play.
Even the mods for the game are surprisingly unimpressive. There is no XRM or CODEA. That’s not to say there aren’t helpful mods out there, but they just don’t add the same degree of life as the mods of the previous X games.
If you aren’t a German speaking player, you are also subject to some of the most awful (often to the point of hilarity) voice over work ever presented in a game. It shouldn’t be difficult for Egosoft to find native English, French, or Russian speakers to handle the localization and voice work for the game. The arduously broken English doesn’t just pull you out of the game, it makes you feel like there wasn’t really any effort put into it. It honestly would have been better if there weren’t any speech at all, just text.
I feel very badly for those who paid full price for this. The game seems like it was made by children. Some of the “features” seem like something your 12-year-old nephew might suggest. The rest of the game is stale, lifeless, and oversimplified.
I get that this isn’t supposed to be “X4,” but does that really justify the release of such an lack-luster product?

I haven't played for long but I believe I have a good enough understanding to write a review. I will most certainly update this as I accrue more playtime. Thank you for your patience
========================================
Core Gameplay
----------------
The game plays like a more forgiving hotline miami but feels like your classic twin stick shooter, albeit with much more customisation and abilities. You choose a character from a pool of 3 (although later on you can choose weapons, characteristics and abilities that are certain to appear in your pool for that run) and they are your "asset" for that run. Your aim: destroy the overlord on floor 30. You must fight (or stealth) your way through while collecting weapons and abilities and upgrade your loot level/current weapon.
Items/Abilities
---------------
There are a lot of weapons and abilities to unlock. The unlock system is very balanced and you will find yourself wanting to start from an earlier section just to try and pick up unlocks that you've missed! Abilities are awarded by entering a chamber that gives you an ability that you've selected from a pool of 3 (4 if your class is cyborg) and you have to be quite tactical with your abilities as you can only have a set number of them
Gameplay (In-Depth)
----------------------
There's rarely a dull moment. Whether you're dodging turrets, fighting robot spiders or trying to get behind those GODDAMN RIOT SHIELDS you'll cherish the times you get to stop for breath. You can upgrade weapons by finding loot caches and you also upgrade your loot level which determines how good future gun drops for that run will be. Enemies do not spawn too frequently nor too slowly which is excellent. You always feel as though you are progressing as well which is excellent. Also, there is a save mechanic (although it's not obvious, exiting saves your progress). Also, the environment is destructible so that's pretty neat :P
*Overall Rating*
---------------
Gameplay - 8
Soundtrack - 7
Graphics - 8
Controls - 10
Story - 7
Replayability - 9
Overall - 8.5
Conclusion
------------
An excellent example of how top-down should be done. Even though the story is somewhat lackluster (although I can't really judge given my tiny playtime) it's an exceptional game that is worth the price!
TL;DR 8.5/10, worth the money, feels like Hotline Miami but better

Ok, so I bought this game over the weekend and haven't really been able to put it down. Why?, I will try to explain...
I am not familiar with the franchise or any games of this particular genre. I am also aware of the appauling state this game was released in and the plethora of negative reviews and dissapointed fans this game has racked up since release. I have not experienced the bugs to the extent of those that purchased the game on release, so I don't share the same experience. But as a modern gamer I can certainly relate to the extreme dissapointment that these fans have experienced in games like Rome 2.
But at the end of the day, I felt compelled to write a review, probably because of my contrarian nature in which I felt that this game in it's current state is not represented properly.
It's a real gem! The work the devs have put into revitalising this game has to be commended, albeit a year too late.. But the very fact that they are still fully supporting and working on the game vigorously shows commitment, which is a worthy trait in a developer in this day and age.
Ok, now for my review.
STORY:
You start off as a sort of space vagabond who comes across a ship which apparently has quite a history, and affectionately called the 'Albion Skunk'. Your copilot, a sexy space babe who coincidentally has some high up connections  and political ties stumbles into your ship and accompanies you throughout the game.
Ok that's more or less it for story. The rest is a sort of political/ factional scenario whose narrative has been built up over previous games. Think Star Trek/ Star Wars/ LOTR/Game Of Thrones typical factional allegiances and disputes and you'll come somewhat close. In other words it perpetuates the racial typecasting and stereotypes we have all come to know and love in todays society.
GAMEPLAY:
The thing I love about spaceships is the freedom of movement in 3d space. In my opinion it can't be fully realised with just a mouse and keyboard. I use a G13 in which the thumbstick controls my steering, and the x/y strafe movement is controlled by the WSAD keys on the G13. Gun aiming and general browsing through my ships peripherals is done with the mouse. Throttle is controlled by the rollerball on the mouse. This enables a deeper control which unwittingly adds another layer of immersion to the game. Again, coming from a background not familiar with these type of games it's all the more a savouring experience for me. Last game I played like this was perhaps 'Descent 3' way back when...
You really feel that you are a pilot and develop a bond with your ship. Every upgrade you purchase for your ship, be it engine type or shield type, you tailor towards your play style. The variety of upgrades to the ship specifically is somewhat lacking. But bare with it, as there are other dimensions and upgrades beyond mere shield/ weapon/ engine types.
Enter the drones.. Ok these wonderful little companions come in two flavors: URV (perhaps not the correct term for what these vehicles actually do in this game but thats what they call them) which you launch and they more or less go about doing their thing, and ROV drones which you personally control through a VR helmet from within your ship. There are Assassin drones, Shield drones, Hacking drones, Combat drones, Worker drones (for your cap ships or freighters).
Wanna be a space pirate? Load up a few Trojan drones, upgrade your scanning tech, skirt to the edge of the sector/ asteroid belt or mining colony/ or just near a faction you want to weaken or don't like, wait for freighters to loot, scan the cargo, send in your drone from a distance, hack the cargo doors on the ship so the freighter drops its loot. Have your freighter parked up nearby with a stack of collector drones, pickup the goods, sell them to your favored faction.
Want to be a raider? Load up a crew of space Vets, hire engineers/ captains/ marines, asssault an enemy frigate, board and hijack disabled vessels. Sell them off to your favored faction or add them to your personal fleet.
Want to be a trader? Scan stations and chatup NPC's for discounts and commisions, install trade agents onboard every station so you can keep up to date with buy and sell offers and bids. Build up a database of trade offers and identify defecits in supply and demand. Get yourself a freighter and automate trade between stations, buying low and selling high, cornering the market and running your competitors into the ground.
This sort of playstyle sits so well with me. It plays into the faction synergies and economics of the game so perfectly and  way better than any other game out there currently, it's almost a revolution in this genre.
Granted, the stations and jobs are rather generic and so are the NPC's which I hope the dev's improve upon, but it doesn't matter so much because of the METAGAME. The jobs themselves come in a variety which have been improved upon in recent patches. You can do taxi missions, station protection missions, special envoy missions, sabotage enemy billboard missions, and new relic and treasure hunt missions to name just a few.
Then there is the station/ fleet and empire building part of the game. WOW, this is immense. You build your corporate empire in which ever manner you see fit. You can build your own stations, construct your own wares, hiring your own staff, who through quite sophisticated AI manage themselves. You can assign budgets, delegate pilots and ships like freighters to managers who will then go on to use those resources you assigned them to defend themselves if attacked or to go and buy a resource they need from a station. The staff themselves have statistics and attributes that can be improved upon through recently added seminars.. Can you begin to fathom the scope of this game?
GRAPHICS:
Beautiful, albeit a bit generic in terms of stations and NPC's. The different space locals are quite impressive, be it near a sun where you can see the Solar gunk being ejected from the surface, or destroyed planets and moons, all make for different regions in space, and does not make it feel like you are in empty space all of the time.
Make sure your rig is sufficient to crank up anti aliasing or you'll be in jaggy town deluxe due to many structures popping up in the emptyness of space. Allot of outlines and silhouettes, so aliasing becomes a necessity. I run the game on full ultra settings with 4x anti aliasing and SSAO set to low. A trick I found to most games and this one in particular is that if you turn AA up turn AF down or off. Do this through your card settings and set the game to control af settings as it has none. This increases performance in many games at the expense of sharper textures which is sort of fixed by increasing AA in itself.
But yeah the ships look fabulous, and new ones have been added since release, so thats a positive thing. Theres rows of traffic near stations, queues to get onto the interstellar highways. Combat feels good, with pretty explosions and effects. Not an amazing array of different weapon types like some games but enough to keep it fresh looking.
CONCLUSION:
What this game attempts and somewhat pulls off is commendable. This game does combat and battles well, but that's not what it is. Information is so valuable in this game. You find yourself pulling up in a sector, looking at the radar and analysing ships and cargo, what they're carrying, which faction they belong too,  what class ships are accompanying, what kind of armament they are sporting etc.. Either just to get a trade or power picture or sussing out who's carrying a juicy payload worth robbing. All through your ships onboard computer. It generally touches base with everything you'd want in an open universe exploration game with an almost limitless scope, and now it seems in this stage to be in a working state. If you like these sort of games, wait for the next sale and buy it with no second thoughts.

Harlan Ellison is a weird guy.
Now I've said that, I wouldn't be surprised if he turned up at my door at 3am demanding an explanation... but it's true. No "normal" mind could have come up with this scenario, but that's a good thing.
Very loosely based on a short-story Ellison wrote back in the 60s, IHNMAIMS is a story about redemption, about bettering oneself, and about finding the goodness in everyone. I think.
I'd be hesitant to call this a game in the usual sense, as it's full of red herrings, illogical puzzles (especially in the end-game scene) and sheer unfairness - it's more of an exploration into man's darkside. Dealing with mature themes such as♥♥♥♥♥♥ murder, suicide, one's sense of duty, paranoia and trust issues, IHNMAIMS is more of an exploration into deep psychological issues. Perhaps not in the sense of the "human condition" (as in, things that everybody faces at some point), but it is refreshing to have something that deals with these themes in a thoughtful, introspective manner - not just for mere shock value.
I would have quite liked to see Benny as the original character from the story though. Perhaps in 1995 they felt they couldn't have a homosexual character struggling with his own identity and what it means in the wider scheme of things. Ellison had no problem back in 1967, so perhaps this means that literary types are better adjusted than gamers? Who knows. The game creators have mentioned in interviews they regret not exploring this angle, so I guess I'm not the only one.
You'll probably need a walkthrough if you want to get the "good" ending, but IHNMAIMS is an absolutely fascinating game to play through. After hearing Ellison himself as the voice of AM, you can't imagine anybody else doing it.
Now you'll have to excuse me. There's somebody at the door.

Return to Castle Wolfenstein is apparently the start of the third distinct Wolfenstein continuity, after the first one of the old Apple II games and the second one of the 2.5D games. This one has more of a focus on on Nazi occult dieselpunk stuff, and it's also a lot more fully fleshed out than previous Wolfenstein games, in terms of both story and gameplay mechanics. Here are my thoughts:
Like all id games (although id only produced this and built the engine, some other guys actually made it), Return to Castle Wolfenstein is technologically cutting-edge for the time it was made. However, as most basic technical leaps had already been made by this point, this mostly manifests as higher-quality models and better lighting & water, which is not as interesting as being able to look up and down or having lighting and water in the first place. Anyway, today it looks fine, if clearly dated.
There are lean buttons now, but you can't shoot while leaning, so I'm not sure what the point is.
The level design is...a mixed bag. It's fairly intuitive, and there are some secrets and hidden areas cleverly scattered around, but levels also sprawl and loop around back into themselves all over the place, which can get pretty goddamn confusing. It's best when it's simply a linear path, instead of a large, interconnected area that you're trying to figure your way around.
But none of that matters a whole lot of the shooting's good, right? Unfortunately, it's not. The weapons hold up their end of the deal, as there's a lot of them and all they feel good to use, but the enemies let the whole thing down. For most levels, you just get to shoot lots of identical human Nazi troops, which is just boring. Sometimes, however, they're complemented by undead (way too much health), female super-Nazis (way too much health and weirdly sexualized), horrible experimental monsters (way too much health, damage, and mobility—just try to stunlock them with the minigun before they flatten you), or bosses (all over the map in terms of how hard they are to kill). What's more, none of them feel good to fight. Bullets hit them and a little cloud of blood will come up or some armor will fall off, but they don't seem to feel the impact. When they die, they just fall over, or collapse (not explode—collapse) into gibs if you do enough damage. Nothing feels good to shoot, and in a shooter, that's a real problem.
However, Return to Castle Wolfenstein's main problem is that it's caught between being an old-school FPS and a more modern one. Like an old-school FPS, you can carry 15 weapons at once, shoot crazy monsters in underground Nazi laboratories, grab health and armor, and run through mazes pushing buttons, but you also duck behind cover a lot because you can't take a lot of damage, snipe unsuspecting enemies, and go through a really horrible stealth level at one point (that broke at the end, so I had to cheat to progress). The two genres don't mesh together particularly well, either, so a lot of the game can be fairly unpleasant to get through.
Overall, don't expect another DOOM or Quake from this game. Fittingly, this is more like Wolfenstein 3D: a sometimes tedious shooter based mostly around shooting identical Nazis with hitscan weapons in stony gray areas, one that's more interested in experimenting with new technologies and gameplay styles than creating the best possible experience. I don't think I'd recommend it on its own merits, but I do recommend it as an interesting, gawky example of shooters' transition to modernity.

Tiny and Big: Grandpa's Leftovers is one of the most unique games I have ever played.
Gameplay:
The main game mechanic, on which all gameplay is based off of, is slicing (with your awesome laser slicer), pulling, and pushing pieces of... well... stuff - statues, pillars, blocks, walls, floors, just about anything. It's super fun, fluid, and addictive, and what really defines this game.
Story:
The story is quite simple, Tiny (who you play as) is looking for his Grandpa's white, fine rib underpants - who Big (your arch nemesis) is wearing.
Graphics:
The artstyle in this game is unique and gorgeous, I've never seen a game with a similar artstyle, so I can't give you an example. Watching a video is OK to get an idea of what it's like, but when you're in-game is when the graphics really shine. So yeah, the art is fantastic, but don't expect Crysis 3-esque graphics, the highlight in the graphical department is the artstyle, not textures, lighting or any of that.
Audio:
The sound effects are satisfying, and are complimented with cartoony "BANG", "SMASH" and "FIZZLE" pop-ups. The soundtrack is fan-f*cking-tastic, you add to the soundtrack by collecting tapes in-game, and they're all (in my opinion) awesome. I would recommend getting the game+soudtrack version, but first search YouTube for some tracks from the game to see if it's your kind of thing.
Some other stuff:
I finished the game in almost 4 hours, but i have nowhere near 100% completion - the game is full with stuff to collect - tapes, and tons of rocks (yeah, you collect these special rocks). So if you take you time to enjoy the game, have fun with the slicing, and make an effort to find secrets (there are secret rooms with easter egg-ish stuff in them), you can probably sink twice the time I did into the game in one playthrough.
Also, I would say the game deservees a higher score than metacritic's 75, it's a real Indie pearl.
Definitely recommend! Have fun!

Warning wall of text ahead:
This review will be based on the game only as I haven't read the short story the game is based of.
It kind of makes me sad that I have to give this game a negative review. But there are some things in this game that just didn't cut it for me, seeing how hyped this game has been over the years, always being mentioned in "best point and click/adventure games of all time" threads all over the internet, I don't really see why. Sure the story is very unique (and the short story is probably 10 times better) but I really couldn't feel that dark and twisted feeling that most people did.
Ok on to the parts that made me give this game a thumbs down. Oh and like many others who have played this game, I live and breathe point and click/adventure games. I grew up during the 80's with the big 3 on the NES (Deja Vu, Shadowgate, Uninvited) and I played my fair share of the Sierra/Lucas arts games during the years. So no "trolling" here. This review will probably get down rated anyway :)
The first big turnoff in the game is "trial and error" part, don't get me wrong I love a hard adventure game (took me months to beat Myst without a walkthrough). But this game forces you to either pick up a walkthrough (which I dislike) or save your game every time you interact with something. Why? Because if you screw up even the slightest you can't complete the game. And the worst part is that the game doesn't even tell you that you screwed up. So either spam that save/load button or stick to your walkthrough as soon as you pick it up, because you will need it more than once if you don't want to go mad. In the end I think I were suffering more than the characters in the game due to this mechanic.
The second thing that really killed it for me was the overall atmosphere over the characters. I saw some other comments like this under the reviews and it feels good that I'm not the only one noticing this. But these characters (without spoiling too much) have been tortured for over 100 years, and they just seem so... full of spirit.. At least some of them, some characters even joke around when your play them (Ellen). This is why I didn't feel the "horror" and darkness in the game. I really didn't feel like these characters were suffering or anything. You might think that these people were walking disasters after 100 years of mental and physical torture, but nope! I didn't care for any of the characters, I just wanted to skip to the next one all the time and sadly it never got better, only worse. And the ending was a HUGE meh, giving me a feeling like I have been doing everything for nothing (yes I got the best endings).
One other small problem I had with the game is the amount of bugs, stuff disappearing and multiplying (you pick up a key only for it to reappear when you reenter the room). Doors you can walk through sometimes and sometimes not because you have to "use" the door. But hey it's an old game, I can let that one slide.

TL;DR  There are plenty of other horror adventure games out there with a more twisted and darker story (yes I said it) than this one. So save your money or buy a game like The Cat Lady instead and watch a complete walkthrough of this game on youtube.

... Well what is it? What will I get from it? and possibly the most important question of them all how much will it cost me, and is it worth my hard earned money? (for me yes) What is it... A PC game that will delight, astound and more than a few times have you jumping out of your knickers. . It's neither a FPS nor a RPG although there is plenty of your friendly Skeletons (blow them apart), Spaniard/Spanish soldiers with demonic eyes, spiders and weird floating beast's to kill. How about a FPEGA (first person exploration ghostly adventure game). Blackpowder regard it as a first person action adventure game (Indie). What-ever call this Indie Game it's well thought out and extremely pleasing to play. Once you clear the first map you're on your way to a rather pleasant and rather unique game (my opinion). Your playing field is forest, forts, Indian villages, settler cabins and more forest. You should not expect any-thing else, after all, the game is set around 1604 colonial America, and this is were settlers set up homes in them days (forest and farming land), and tried to live in peace with the local Indians. The expanse of forests is (what can I say) massive and very much like reality. The attention paid to the greenery. grass, trees, plants, worn pathways all tremendous detail... superb. Buildings, boulders, flags flying, forts very much what you would expect to see, if it was possible to time travel back to that era. The only gripes I have is the use of the sound director. When trying to find all the chests, which I did near the end of the game, could for me have had a greater range. It was like looking for a needle in a haystack at times, and voice over. These guys have still come up with the goods on limited funds. Me... I am a dedicated RPG fan known to sometimes play First Person Shooters, Action Adventures, MMO's and Multi-Player games. I found this game to be a refreshing change and will put these guys at the top of my list and keep my eyes open for their next release... May the force be with you

Yes its true that Absolution may not be the best Hitman game being that the Hitman formula was changed into a more linear stealth action game. Yet, I like it. They took it in another direction. They weren't afraid to try something new. I give them credit for it because at least its half decent and not butchered up. It still feels like a Hitman game in a sense that some levels still hold natural freedom that the other games have had, its true that it doesn't hold as many options but still, I found the experience, in my eyes, worth the change.
Not to say there is bad in this, the disguise system is unrealistic and unfair at times. Your whole face could be covered up and somehow the guards will still be able to spot you a mile away. Its frustrating to be stealthy when the disguise is next to useless because of a poorly implemented disguise system. If they do bring it back, they better improve it and make it more realistic. Like if you are facing away from the enemy or if you have a disguise that covers up your face then you shouldn't get spotted but even then, if there's like 100s of the same guard type, how in the hell are they gonna be observant enough to see you don't belong? Did each guard bond with one another before doing their job or something even if out of 100? I don't think so.
Pros:
-Best gunplay in the series. Easily.
-Stealth is not shoehorned and is done well (excluding the disguise system).
-Decent story.
-Very well done voice acting.
-Villains are♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and its satisfying to kill them......look at the 4th con below.
-Instinct isn't the worst feature and helps somewhat with the disguise system not being completely unfair. Though its limited :(
-Signature kills require some decent amount of thought to figure out sometimes and makes you feel like a boss when you execute them.
-Graphics are gorgeous!
-Contracts mode is amazing and challenging.
-Some levels are non linear and quite open at times.
Cons:
-Disguise system was poorly done.
-Majority of levels are linear.
-Scoring system. Makes you play a certain way so you can get the best score.
-Some villains are killed via QTE or linear event which is kinda stupid.
-Why is tipping your hat down or rubbing the back of your head while looking down slightly to hide your disguise against other types of the same people you disguise as require the special instinct skill?
-The melee system is awful! QTE ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t... that can get you killed if you want to subdue someone quietly but instead accidentally start a open fight with them ruining your stealthy run and maybe getting you killed since you didn't expect an open conflict to happen off what should of been a simple, quiet kill/knockout.
I think the main reason Hitman fans hate this game is because of the linear campaign and the disguise system. I love stealth games so it works for me. The disguise system makes the game a ton harder so I guess it can be looked at as a challenge. I wouldn't prefer it to come back though. Its not perfect but there's joy to be found here. If you love stealth games, give it a try I suppose. If you're looking for another Hitman Blood Money here, don't get it until you lower your expectations.

Gat out of Hell is the expandalone for Saints row 4, basically meaning it could have easily been a DLC release, but as always making money is the top priority. The title felt like a quick cash grab from start to finish, everything about it seemed rushed and short lived, the map is just a copy paste Sci - Fi theme to an underground Hell theme but the theme itself was actually very appealing to be in and I just wish there was more to do in this title in terms of gameplay.
The story is childs play, you get to play as either Jonny Gat or Kinzie Kensington and the end goal is to rescue the boss by shooting Satan in the face, anyone could have written it, while characters like Shakespeare, Vlad and Blackbeard where interesting historical figures with charming personalities they were short lived to the point of having 5 minutes worth of dialogue each, the story in general here is an utter waste besides the musical which did put a smile on my face.
The side activities felt short lived as well sadly but they were still fun while they lasted, things like collecting soul clusters while flying around with angel wings felt like a good sense of freedom. There were still things like trail blaizing and insurance fraud, and doing other basic violent things to stop satan's operations.
Overall the story and all side activities take around just over 5 hours to complete, if your a completionist like myself who wants to purchase all the upgrades for the new demonic powers which are actually worth getting because this is the new meat of the game, and they actually have a strong unique variety to them, it was just very shortlived.
In conclusion, pick this title up on sale, have it as a side game to play when your bored of all the major triple A products out there that everyone has heard of, play it to blow off steam and wreck havoc, even if its only for a short time.
Final rating - 2/5 for a mediocre experience.

Betrayer was quick to draw me into its world. It is a world that manages to feel, at the same time, both desolate and packed with intrigue. There are places to explore, mysteries to solve and threats looming around every bend. This is a game that isn't afraid to take some risks in terms of game design. The results are sometimes wonderfully successful and other times ineffective.
What first drew me to Betrayer was its artistic design. While it does look as good as the screenshots, the novelty of it does wear off over time. I eventually experimented with turning on full color and was pleased with how things looked that way as well. Just know that simply turning up the color saturation slider doesn't make for something pleasing to the eye. You'll have to change the light and dark intensity sliders as well. I had both of them moved most of the way to the left.
As eye catching as the graphics style is, the sound design is equally as good and is an integral part of the experience. Even though the only music is during the main menu and credits, I never felt like the game was missing a soundtrack. All the sounds of the forest and the way you "listen" for clues and collectables makes your ears as valuable as your eyes as you explore.
Hunting for certain collectables can be a chore due to your long range "listen" ability being restricted to leading you only to story related locations. That can make for a lot of aimless wandering for completionists like me, which gets frustrating when you're still missing something after going through an area quite thoroughly. This could have easily been remedied by a late game unlock to be able to "listen" for everything. It also doesn't help that there isn't a lot of variety in environments. In fact, around the halfway point in the game zones start to blend together and no new enemies are introduced either. The final zone is very cool and unique, however. From around 50% to 85% of the way through the game is easily its weakest portion. Contributing to that is that it is around this point that you begin to identify gameplay patterns, making things feel predictable and repetitive.
If you're into murder mysteries then I suspect you'll enjoy Betrayer. Each area you visit has its own stories to tell. Some of these stories offer clues as to what's happened in the larger region in which the game is set. Others simply flesh out the local histories. It is up to you to decipher what fits into the grander scheme of things.

I played for 45 hours and I definitely give thumbs up to this game. If you are a fan of Firefly, and if you like Star Trek - Star Wars style space combat, this game is for you. Although not being a masterpiece; the game has a nice atmosphere, wonderful music and sound effects, flashy explosions and lasers, detailed unique ship designs, in short: it has a %85 healthy body and mechanics.
Pros & Cons:
- The depth of space looks nice, however the colours are mostly vivid mostly and too luminous for space. Though it's less depressing :))
- Warp and Jump concepts are very nice.
- Thumbs up for weird aliens, their creative languages and weird ships (gets weirder further you play the main mission :)
- The game lacks of citizens living wandering around when you visit a station. When you visit a bar, you can only have the bartender and your hired gun, which is so unrealistic.
-Diplomacy needs to be worked on some more. And yes, I agree with the other guy: developers need to put a "reputation" system inside the game. When a guy destroys 100 capital ships and some 500 fighters, weaker enemies should run away from you on sight, or at least try ;) There is a "Hail-dialogue" system in game. Little bit impractical. You can choose to intimidate your enemy which I succeded several times. Still nobody says "Oh noo! it's the guy who eats destroyers in breakfast! We frakking need to disappear right now!"
- After 30 hours repeated side missions decrease the fun. Fortunately the main quest saves it from boredom.
-  The turret manual targeting sucks, it's pretty hard to choose your target in real time combat. You can of course "tab" and lock your target but I don't like wasting my time when i have 20 meteorites to hit around me (yeah you can do mining and sell the ore you extract)
- You have many options to outfit your ship with deflectors, shields, rockets, lasers and such and especially with useful components. The turret's locations are important, nevertheless you can't just drag and drop your weaponry on the ship as you like. You will need to know by trial and error which turret is which and install-uninstall the weapons until you find the right one (I have 8 turrets on my ship for instance).
That's it for now :)

Let's get this straight: For 15 bucks this is a scam. I got this during a sale or bundle or whatever, so it's "ok", but essentially this game has 0 missions and almost no story. Instead the narrative is to complete loyalty missions for your various "allies" in hell (1 for each district). The initial missions are kind of ok, but after that it's just side missions, side missions, side missions. At least you will not have to do them thousands of times, because by the time you've completed 3 of your 5 allies the game can be completed, since then you have caused enough mayhem to challenge the devil. There's a bit of fun dialogue and story with his daughter, but that's about it. You go on to fight the devil in a straight on fire fight and the game ends. You can then choose from 5 different 10 second endings...yay.
Apart from that you will spend your time collecting "soul orbs" just like in Saints Row 4. You will also be running up skyscrapers and flying around (instead of megajumping or whatever it was in 4, I forgot). Anyway, it's just way too much effort for what's in the package. If this was a 5 dollar DLC, maybe worth it.
Saints Row 4 was imho already stretching it, since it was still almost the same gameplay and even the same city, just transformed. Guess what, it's still the same city and hell looks kinda boring. Gunplay is as boring as ever of course, and your hell powers, I dunno, there was only 1 I ever felt the need to use regularly and that's the hell stomp, which, when upgraded, can just about kill almost anything with 1 hit and has an aoe effect. I spent way too much time running around completing missions and collecting stuff I didn't need to and I completed the game in 4 hours. I'd say you can do it in 2, possibly even 1 hour. So, if a bunch of side quests and a handful of story missions is worth 15 bucks to you and you need another Saints fix, go ahead, otherwise skip this or wait for a DEEP discount.

The best survivor / war sim I've had the pelasure of playing in a very long time. This game can be extreamly hard and emotional.
My take away lessons for newbies: Don't get attached to your characters, take small steps when exploring new sites, don't get greedy, don't go on a "revange missions" if you lose a member of your team, sneak in and out of each sites (snipers can be leathal), make sure you take care of them wounds and sickness ASAP, plan ahead for the winter: fortify your home base, build a vaggie garden and traps for food, make as much stuff as you can to trade later on (You will need it). Use the right character for the right action/mission.
The possibilities are endless, the replayability of the game is more than exellent. (Random maps, items, encounters, game lenght... AWESOME)
I love the dark, pencil-style graphic, 2 mode play system (day/night).. Oh and check out ALL the stations on the radio... Some cool tunes hidden in there!
Overall I give this title a 10/10 for story/concept, 9/10 for interface/gameplay (had issues with the combat system)
Personal notes: Combat/defence interface could be improved and the fact that I was still getting raided over and over even after i upgraded the reinforced security door and patched all the holes was kind frustrating, specilally with 2 shotguns and a pistol in my inventory.
Highly recommended.. I fear I will waste many more hours on this title.
