Exactly. I'm not sure why many didn't even give Bioshock 2 a chance. It's great to be back in Rapture and the gameplay is improved upon in every single way. Dual wielding plasmids/guns is fun, the new enemy types are great, the Little Sister mechanics are awesome, the level design is fantastic, and the story is solid enough. Tack on Minerva's Den and it's just icing on the cake. If you were a fan of the original and skipped out on this one, all you've done is a disservice to yourself. It's a great game, so would you kindly give it a chance?

I wish I could say Hatred delievered on it's promise to be a gritty dark look into the mindset of  a spree killer, however, I cannot. It feels more like a comic book interpretation of a spree killer. It's dark visuals would suggest that it's a dark game, however it feels more arcadey than anything else. Your character sprints everywhere, has a obsession with jumping over anything you move near, and police and civilians march towards whatever weapon you're carrying, or more often than not, into a corner. The AI's reactions to the character are just as comical really, screaming out for mercy as they run into the line of fire, followed by occasional quips delievered by the character that are somewhere between ironic, satirical, and a attempt at being dark. It's almost as if the game would be more emotionally impactful if every gun was replaced by ponies that shot rainbows into teddy bears that bled stars or something.
Is the gore or violence at least good? Not really, in fact, there's a older game that did it much better, and believe it or not, it actually WAS a comic book interpretation. It's a little hard to find, but The Punisher 2005 gives a better experience in shooting, gore, and even framerate. I'm not sure what is going on, but it seems that Hatred is locked to thirty frames constantly, or that it's just not animated to anything over that, I'm not sure which would dissapoint me more. The executions are all bland, just cutscenes of your guy shooting them again, or stabbing them. In The Punisher, a game from ten years ago, your options included, but were not limited to: Rhino impalement, Aztec sacrifice, toilet bowl drowning, wood chippers, and even good old fashioned visceral curb stomps. The curb stomp in Hatred: a singular stomp(or sometimes three) that all feel very light and whiffy, but then explode the mans head with a splatter sound. Curb stomp in The Punisher: With obvious and very well animated fear in the victims eyes, you must move your mouse up and down, the faster the stomp, the harder the stomp, with the cracking of bone on concrete punctuating every movement, and then you can drag it out too, by just moving the mouse down slowly, you grind the poor ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s head into the pavement slowly, but it doesnt kill them. Hell, even the low resolution models from The Punisher made me wince when I first found out some of the shotgun executions in the game. Sure you're killing obviously and very comically evil people, but they still felt more human than anything in Hatred.
One final interesting flaw to give you a idea of the polish to expect in this game: There are no bullet hole wound textures, just blood splattered on the model.

1: Game crashes when you alt-tab -- no fix
2: No FoV options -- has a fix
3: The FoV fix stops working when you aim down sights -- has a fix
4: The fix to fix the FoV fix crashes the game -- no fix
5: Mouse accleration is ALWAYS on. You can reduce the mouse acceleration, but never turn it completely off, despite what the options menu tells you -- no fix
I tried fixing this mess for an hour then gave up. I played it on consoles when it first came out, and I was looking forward to playing it again. This is a horrible port; it's like I am really playing it on a console!
If I wanted acceleration, the inability to alt-tab, and 75 FoV, I would just play the console version. PC gaming has spoilt me, so now when trash like this comes along, I just can't play it.
On the bright-side, the amount of time you spend in .ini files trying to fix this game will definitely introduce you to some basic scripting, and even a little bit of programming. The perfect game for little Timmy who wants to be a programmer when he grows up!
If you are willing to spend a few hours cleaning up the mess the devs couldn't be bothered to clean up, then you're in for the best Bioshock in the series! Personally, I would rather be playing another game than be playing "Bioshock 2: Can You Fix This Trash Edition".

On the whole this game is not enjoyable in the traditional sense.  It's not a fun game, it's not action packed, it's not instantly rewarding, and it's not fast paced, nor is it supposed to be.
What it is instead is gripping, suspenseful, and internally rewarding.  It is extremely difficult, and every decision you make will trickle down to other decisions in the future.  Do you eat today, or do you stockpile fuel for the cold weather coming up ?  Will you steal from the elderly couple down the road and ultimately condemn them to death just to feed yourself?  Are you prepared to allow one of your survivors to die to better insure the survival of the others, or will you waste medical supplies and sleepless nights trying against all odds to nurse a friend back to health?  Will you murder in cold blood for a piece of raw food?
These are decisions you have to make, and each one no matter how small can mean not only the difference between life and death but affect the emotional and psychological stability of your survivors.
Not only is the gameplay and strategy riviting, but the artistic style, RTS like controls, and musical score all together paint a portrait of a dismal life of despair and heartache with limited options and no end in sight.
Should you get this game?  Yes!  Definitely!  When was the last time you had a video game make you sit back in your chair, sip on your beverage, and look around and appreciate the home you have and the life you are living?  For me, it was just a few hours ago, and it was this game...

The game is nothing special. It was briefly given the same treatment that Wolf 3D and Doom were given over two decades ago by certain religious organizations and "family" groups.
The game is a isometric shooter like Crusader: No Remorse. You go around killing people, men and women. If they are wounded, then you have the chance to execute them. Doing so will trigger a short sequence where the

guy that looks a lot like Nathan Explosion gruesomly murders the terrified injured person begging for their life, or in some cases cursing or taunting their killer. Police, SWAT, and US Army will periodically be summoned to kill you. Civilians may also pick up weapons and fight back to a suprisingly high effect.
Most of the missions include at least 2 or 3 sidequests that you may complete at your leisure. Usually it involves something extremely bloody. To the game's credit, the grenades, molotov cocktails and random propane tanks and gas cans explode in a satisfactory way, cause a massive amount of property damage, and often set off chain reactons. You can also take control of some vehicles and military humvees with mounted machine guns. The driving is somewhat hard to control and the cars tend to blow up unexpectedly with you in it.
The graphics are alright. Sometimes it is hard to see some things. You can press a key to outline objectives and targets to help you out. The game really does not care how many people you wipe out in a target area or how badly you mess something up with explosives, so long as you mess it up and kill some people.
The models of your victims that you burned to death are have a relatively high degree of detail, despite the fact that you will not likely see them unless you execute someone among them and the camera closes in.
The controls take some time to get used to. They are not bad, but may feel better on a controller. The AI is somewhat subpar. The civilians sometimes run into your fire, although they could just be panicking after watching some dude murder hundreds of people. The combat AI isn't very bright either, as it bunches up frequently, but the bullets hurt a lot, so you can't really let your guard down. Aiming down and crouching are extremely useful skills to have as close range combat at higher difficulties guarantee death as combat NPCs are harder to kick down than civilians since they are shooting at you and will most likely only stagger for a moment before shooting you to pieces with help from their buddies.
The game has a habit of respawning you in bad places, and you sometimes get stuck and can't get out. This is rare, but it does happen.
There are quite a few weapons in the game. Most of them are just standard stuff. The game does have a flamethrower that is extremely fun to use against mobs of people.
The ambient music is suprisingly not heavy metal, but spooky ambient. In fact, it gets pretty tense at times. The author appears to be Adam Skorupa, the guy who did a massive amount of metal and ambient trackwork for the games Painkiller, Gorky 17, and The Witcher. There are a couple of metal tracks in the game that are not featured during gameplay. The rest of the sound design is alright.
The player character is characterized slightly more than the Doom Marine. His one liners, surprisingly, did not get on my nerves.
The optimization is pretty bad at release. I was able to play it with only a handful of stutters, but they were notably bad.
The game is OK. It actually isn't that edgy and seems to be fully aware of itself, which is a refreshing surprise. I don't know about $20, but I don't really regret purchasing the game. I had fun.

I play this game only 3 or 4 hours a month, but have done that for almost 2 years now. It hits a spot for me, and thought I'd write a review to say why I like it.
The graphics are low budget. You won't find asset loaded, busy graphics with James Bond like cut scenes, but the talented one man developer has given a picturesque touch to them. Its easy on the eyes and may actually be preferable for a fishing game where you'll be staring at them a lot.
The sound effects are 'spot on' as they would say elsewhere, a good mix of near and far sounds, adding to the relaxing immersive feeling of being on a lake.
The game seems to be going for a genuine fishing experience. From the time and date matching real life time and date, to the game telling you literally nothing about fishing strategies. But you can learn those strategies at your own pace (trial and error, internet searches, etc), the only consequence is you may catch less and smaller fish, but can still earn money and progress in the game.
Although I like this, it would be nice to add some general tips of those factors that are programmed in the game, yet without giving away the game. So non fishermen can 'catch up' some to the experienced fishermen.
Overall, its fairly immersive with a feeling of being out on a lake, and a low pressure experience while learning some fishing strategies. A new update is on the horizon, I'm excited to see what it brings.

As a huge fan of twin-stick shooters (even though I prefer to use the mouse and keyboard for these games), I saw this and got very, VERY excited, and imagine my excitement when I found out that these guys also made Crimsonland, one of my favourite games of all time.
I'm an 80's kid (born 1983), and I'm passionate about the styles that the 80's and 90's created. Neon Chrome takes the music and artistic theme from the 80's that many of us know and love (Think "Kung Fury" for an idea of the style I mean. Kung Fury nailed it too), handed us a gun, packed a top-down level with angry soldiers and robots, firmly pat us on the butt and told us to "Stick it to 'em".
The controls are tight and responsive, the gameplay starts out hectic but doable, and the upgrade system makes the difficulty curve your own responsibility!  If you loved Crimsonland but wanted more explosions and bright, hot neon pink, stop reading this review and go buy a copy of the game. You won't regret it.
The music is gloriously well written for the style of the game, and the title screen theme is now part of my soundtrack to life, so even if the game itself doesn't tickle your pickle, it's worth it for the music.

4k+ reviews on Steam - 3k+ negative - 1k+ positive.
The 'proof of the pudding' is with Teladi Outpost:
31 positive reviews.  1k+ people defended this game, but only 31 people have given a positive rating for Teladi Outpost - so how many of the 1k+ people who gave Rebirth a positive score are still playing it?

Go and get it's predecessor, Alpha Centauri.  It is a far more diverse, complete, and interesting game.  There is much more you can do with the technology than in Beyond Earth.
Categories where Alpha Centauri beats Beyond Earth:
Underwater cities.
Dynamic world.  Global warming and cooling, sea level, and mind worm aggressiveness is directly related to how much ecological damage is done by tile upgrades and quest / UN decisions.  BE is static.
air power (it's almost useless in BE.  come on, I can launch a satellite into orbit, but my airplanes have only enough fuel to fly to my city limits 4 hexes away?)
diversity in units, at least 100 different combinations more than BE.
More useful upgrades for veterancy.  In BE, for half of the veterancy choices and the building "quests", you'd have to be an idiot to pick one of them.  Were none of the developers / play testers a math major?  In what world is 1 energy as useful as 1 production?
Animations for world wonders.  BE has pictures.
City taking.  It takes 3-7 units to take a city in Alpha, in BE it takes 10-20.  The city bombards and kills one unit with one shot every turn, their aircraft and garrison kill one every turn.  It is really expensive to try to win militarily.
Areas where BE beats Alpha Centauri
unit vs unit tactics.  Hex based, non-stacking model means unit placement matters more and tactics can be used to protect weak units better and give more control to players over the combat.  Civ 5 has this too, but before this if someone had more than one type of unit garrisoning a city, it took stacks of units to take it again.
Graphics.  Duh.  But Alpha Centauri was what, 15 years ago?
1 extra victory condition.  Alpha had Transendence (Harmony), and Space Race (Unity), and BE adds the Emancipation supremacy condition, which is basically the same thing as the unity one but with more warlike flavor.  It has less victory conditions than Civ 5, which has Diplomatic (UN president) and Cultural victories, which aren't present in BE.
The game is rushed, and for me has a low replay value.  I am glad I was able to try it during the free weekend to confirm what most of the other reviews have said.

I never write reviews on steam games, but I had to do it for this one, so, this is my first review.
As a hard core WoW arena player, when game went south I didn't find any similar games that could give me the same feeling of arenas as WoW did. Back then there was a game by the same developers as for this game called Bloodline Champions (BLC). This is basically a newer and better version of that game.
- Games do not last long
- Everything is a skill shot (even healing and CC)
- You can always find a character that suits your play style and tweak it by cards (like talent system) that improve your characters abilities
- You have 3 game modes: 2v2 arenas, 3v3 arenas and Battlegrounds
- If you are good enough, you can do 1v3 and win a round/match
- There is no gear, so you're as strong as the other guy
- You have 3 currencies: Gold, Tokens and Gems.
With gold you can buy characters (if you didn't buy the game while it was in early access, if you did, you get all characters for free) and silver chests (rumor says that you will be able to buy additional services like name change etc. with gold). You earn gold by playing games and doing daily/weekly quests and achievements or by leveling characters.
Tokens are used for all cosmetic items (character skins, weapon skins, mounts etc) and you get tokes by getting duplicates from any chest type, by leveling your character or getting them as a loot inside chests.
Gems you get by purchasing it with real money. You can use it to buy better rarity chests (that give you better skins, mounts etc).
Community is fine so far, but sometimes you will come across some elitist players that will flame you for anything (I guess they have nothing else to do with their life), but toxicity levels are minimal, most of the people are friendly (at least in my case so far).
So, to sum it up. If you like brawlers or something like WoW arenas, and are not afraid of skill shots, this is definitely a game for you, and its F2P, so you have nothing to lose (except time I guess and maybe HDD space).
Learning curve can be steep, as a lot of players already have experience from playing BLC and early access, but if you're having fun, I don't see any problem :) in time, you'll just get better.
Have fun and see you in game.

Betrayer is kind of a neat game and unlike anything I've ever played before. It's got some good ideas going for it, but there's a lot of blandness and repetition that bogs it down in the end.
The stealth gameplay is pretty decent, feeling genuinely rewarding as you successfully maneuver around in the shadows and take down unsuspecting enemies. At least at first. Sometimes when you're in a hurry to do something, all this stealth can get kind of annoying. So instead you run as fast as you can, alerting the entire forest and hucking tomahawks at everything that moves. Which is kind of satisfying... but these are pretty much the only game mechanics, so it sometimes gets a little old. There are guns and such, too, but it takes so long to reload a musket that it doesn't get much use... more of a one-shot-per-enemy-encounter type of use.
There's lots of stuff to run around and find, but there's so much of it that you would never happen upon unless you search the entire forest. But who's gonna do that? Nobody. So you have to look up a guide and compare your game map to the guide map to slowly collect everything. And there comes to be a strange satisfaction in all the tedium, but you collect everything in one area, then move onto the next one and repeat, counting how many more areas of the game there are until you're finished. And when you start to look ahead at how much more of the game there is until you're finished rather than letting it unfold on its own, that's never the mark of a good game.
The story's pretty bland and uninteresting. It's made up entirely of meeting ghosts, asking them what happened to them, then finding clues around the area and confronting the ghosts about them to unlock their memories of how they died or whom they killed, etc. The individual stories that each ghost tells are somewhat interesting but don't amount to much. It's sort of the one trick of this one-trick pony. There's an over-arching storyline that tries to connect the whole thing, but it again ends up being just another story that's sort of amusing but nothing more. However, there is also the occasional note that gives a bit of story that seems to be completely unrelated to any other parts of the story. There are some genuinely neat little stories in some of these.
The game does have a decent atmosphere, though. Its default black-and-white look with the occasional stark red highlight on points of interest and enemies is pretty captivating. Though by the end of the game, it starts to feel a little lifeless. And wouldn't you know it... it wasn't until I finished the game that I found out there are color options to play the game in full color, which looks so much better... lol. The sound design is great, giving distinct audio cues for different enemies, allowing you to pinpoint not only when an enemy is close, but what kind of enemy it is and where it is, so you can get the drop on it.
I can't tell if Betrayer is trying to be a horror game or not. It's not scary. However, it does do some cool things. The presentation of ringing a town's bell to change the scenery from day to spooky night is startling and very well done. The ending's not very good, nor did I care enough about the story even if it was, but the very final moment of the game, although confusing, was actually pretty freaky. I have no idea what it meant, but I like freaky, so props for that.
Anyway...
4/10

Neon Chrome is honestly very good.  It succeeds as a twin-stick shooter and as a roguelite.  As a twin-stick shooter it steals many of the best mechanics and basic gameplay feel from 10tons' own much earlier classic Crimsonland, but adds destructible environments, special attacks, and rudimentary stealth.  Also your character is actually much sturdier than in Crimsonland, which is funny for a roguelite but it fits the format better since you don't heal up between levels.
As a roguelite, it has a gradual perk unlocking system that makes the binding of isaac look incredibly detailed by comparison, but actually, the high-level unlocks are obviously intended to allow scope for a little bit of a "build" aside from simple max dps.  Simple stuff like "shots have 15% chance to stun enemies" + "stunned enemies take double damage".  Between runs you spend the money you earned on permanent boosts to damage, or perk slots, yada yada rogue legacy upgrade your castle we've all seen it.  It's all done very well here.
If you enjoy roguelites, it's not as fun as the binding of isaac but currently, in my opinion, no roguelite is really trying to compete with that.  Short of TBoI, this one is about as fun as they get.  If you enjoy twin-sticks, well, this is crimsonland in roguelite form.

Betrayer is an excellent game and reminds me a lot of the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games (if they were made by an indie company). It has the same slow, tense atmosphere and requires you to think about each enemy encounter, instead of rushing in weapons blazing. Enemies do a lot of damage and your healing item is minimal for most of the game, so you have to attack from a distance or sneak in an backstab a couple enemies first. The variety of weapons is really useful for multiple playstyles: muskets. pistols, and explosives do more damage, and help you survive when you accidentally attract the attention of a mob, and your knife, bows, and tomahawk are *mostly* silent and help you get stealth kills.
The black, white, and red aesthetic was actually really engaging and improved immersion for me, but don't worry, there is a really simple option to play it in full color if that's not your thing. What's even more interesting about the atmosphere in this game is that it incorporates a Silent Hill-esque mechanic of dark and light "worlds" that have different enemies and quests.
The storyline is fairly good, but I wouldn't say it is amazing. The theme of "betrayal" (I see what you did there Blackpowder Games) is consistent throughout the game and there are many smaller stories interwoven into the primary narrative, however, after the first two maps, whenever I spoke to a character that had a quest for me, I could already predict what evil "twist" would occur in his/her paricular story. Furthermore, I feel that the player-character really doesn't have much motivation at all and ffter playing it all the way through, I don't even know why he's there! All that being said, the story is genuingely creepy and "messed up."
I only have a few criticisms for this game. The first is how repetitive it gets right before the end: the enemies don't really change much, so while combat is still fun, it's the same kind of fun, over and over. Even if the frequency of enemies increased, or if the types of enemies were mixed together in close proximity this would present new challenges. Ideally, I would have like to see three more enemy types: 2 for the "dark world" and 1 for the "light world," but I realize that this is an indie title, and there's onyl so much you can do. Also, there is a certain item that let's you dig up these rock piles you find throughout the game, and these piles have some of the best weapons in the game. Unfortunately, by the time you get these awesome weapons, you are near the end, so your need for them is really minimal. It would be nice to get this item halfway through the game. Finally, finding treasure chests and items is really tedious. You simply march out into the forest, wandering aimlessly, until you hear treasure (treasure chests emit a whistling sound). The problem is, you can literally wander around for an hour on one map to find all of the items! Something as simple as a mark on the map when you find a treasure would have made it go quicker, so I don't backtrack to places I've already searched.
All that being said, this game is still chock full of crazy, tense, scary, challenging, shooting, stabbing, sniping, sneaking fun! Get it now!

I just can't recommend this game for more than $20.
Essentially, it's a glorified Alpha Centauri mod for Civ 5, but packaged as a standalone.  Oddly, though, it isn't really an improvement on either.
Alpha Centauri had a much more compelling story and environment.  The miasma and the xenomass which generates it is just a lamer version of the fungus in AC.  The Annelida-esque creatures are replaced with Arthropoda-esque creatures that don't have any cool psionic abilities and aren't nearly as frightening (except maybe the first time you come across a siege worm which, contrary to its name, never bothered to attack any cities).
Beyond Earth replaces a few Civ 5 features and adds some things like favors.  Favors basically mean you don't have to have a resource at the time to attempt to trade.  You just owe someone a favor.  In practice, it just means that the NPCs (weirdly, even ones I had JUST tried to completely exterminate) will bother you for goods EVERY SINGLE TURN and only offer you a favor as payment.  If you turn them down, they get mad.  But if you pay them, they screw you.  For instance, I would accept a favor in return for 1 Energy per turn for 90 turns.  Later, I would try to cash in my favor for 100 Energy and the NPC would balk at my request.  Okay...
Many features are missing that I really enjoyed in the past.  Religion no longer exists.  You can no longer build interesting custom empires and are pretty much limited to the same cookie cutter factions with boring choices over and over.  Faction-specific units are gone and instead replaced with unique upgrades to units based upon one of three path choices you make (which feel more like constraints than anything else).
In the end, this game really feels like a half-hearted attempt at a game and the glaring vacancies in features feel like intentional voids left open for future paid content.  I really hope that isn't the case as I have always stood by Civ games as bastions of how to do things RIGHT in the gaming industry.
Basically, you can still have more fun playing the Fall from Heaven II mod in Civ 5 than playing this game.  It just doesn't have the grand feel of past Civ games and it isn't compelling enough to warrant the weekend-long marathons I used to put into Civ 5.

(Played offline so Steam wouldn't let me record hours. MFW)
Being able to play this game offline is already a great plus. Especially since a single game, even on the smaller maps with only a few sytems, can last the better part of a day, or even two.
Simply put, if you're looking for Civ 5 with a nice, space fantasy touch, then you've come to the right place. This game is a vivid mixture of fleet-building, sublime graphics, and engaging combat, though most of the time you'll have your screen zoomed out so far, all of your ships look like little blue pixels. Which is for the better, since you'll get a lot of ships, and planets are immense compared to the sizes of most ships, let alone stars. So unless you really admire spaceship combat (cue Star Wars), you'd probably leave your ships to it while you were busy upgrading your stats or diverting mining ships away from incoming pirates. Yes, there's a lot to worry about. Which is why a game can take ages.
Like Civ 5, this game is not for the impatient, aggressive type of player. You need to wait until all your resources are in place, then launch strategic offenses on enemy systems that may, most of the time, go to waste. Unless you've stumbled on a resource-rich system somewhere, in which case you'll ironically be rushing ships instead of saving resources up, just so you can go defend your newfound hoard of treasure, which is bound to attract pirates, corsairs, and sometimes other enemy players.
I haven't played this game in a multiplayer setting yet, but you don't have to - the AIs are smart, and they will always know more about the game than you do. They'll pin attacks on you when you least expect them. Leave a system undefended, it'll have become a pirate outpost by the time you return your attention to it. The universe is a big place, and playing this game means you have to be on the edge of your seat at all times, because unless you divide and conquer, you'll soon find yourself completely surrounded.
Ultimately, this is a game where the winner is the one who pays the most attention to their research and construction queues, and to the balance of power between systems and between factions. Intriguing backstory and stunning ambience aside, this is a game that invokes a special kind of excitement that no fighting or RPG game will ever hope to emulate.

Having played this game for over 40 hours, I can say that I was hooked right from the get-go. This game deserves a 10/10. The game puts you into the role of survivors holed up in a house, where you will be living/sleeping/eating and surviving in.
Everyday is split into a "day" portion and an "night" portion. During the day, you will be crafting things such as metal workshops, a stove or a herbal garden. If your characters are hungry, you will need to feed them in order for their condition to not worsen. In the earlier parts of the game, material and food collection is crucial.
At night, you select one of your characters to scavenge another building in the area while the rest of the characters guards the house or sleeps through the night. Each character has their own "special" abilities, such as having more backpack slots to store items that you have found in the buildings, or being a good cook. Once you have filled up your slots, you return to your home for the next day.
As you progress through the game, some buildings have thugs that reside inside and may attack you on sight, and if your character is killed, the game still continues on.
Some things to consider:
Each player has their own statuses and addictions. These may be changed as the game progresses.
The statuses include emotional ones (sad/content/depressed) and condition based ones(hungry/sick/injured)
The realism in this game is what made it playable over and over again.

I just finished my first playthrough of the game, and I can say that it was well worth the money, and I am not someone who buys many games these days.
There's no tutorial, but the games mechanics are simple, which means you fumble around trying to get everything together for the first few days as your initial supplies dwindle.  I soon got used to perpetual hunger, and was satisfied as long as my band of survivors was not starving as I tried to figure out how to navigate the city's wartime economy of barter and scavenging.
I get the feeling that if you know the city well enough after some playthroughs, and as long as the game doesnt start you in winter (which means you may forsake building vital security improvements to your shelter and focus on building heaters and stoves to melt snow and keep you warm) then a player could learn how to optimise their economy very quickly.  The problems come when you make mistakes (see the story below) or when you get very unlucky (which happens a lot) then the risks of death become very high.  You also come across people who need your help, for example a starving hobo in an old building who needs food bad, and if you don't have it, by the time you spend a day or two getting back to help him, you find him starved to death, so it's inevitable that you will see people suffer.
I desperately tried to keep all of my ragtag band alive through the war, and failed when, due to a misunderstanding at the hospital, I lost poor Boris.  Boris ate a burst from a rebel soldier's assault rifle when, after making one of them mad, he couldn't leave the building fast enough for them due to his injured leg.  Eventually they got tired of shouting curses at him and hitting them with their gun butts and shot him.   Somehow he survived and crawled halfway across the city to the house.  When it became clear that he would die of his wounds unless he recieved some real treatment, Katia, who was the most cheerful of the group, ran into the house of an elderly couple that lived across town and raided their medicine cabinet for bandages and medicine while the poor husband and wife begged her to stop.  Katia only took what she needed: two packs of bandages and a bottle of antibiotic pills, but for days after felt depressed by what she'd done while boris hovered on the brink of death.  Then the bandits came in the night.  And though we had some weapons, boris suffered a minor wound while in his bed, and died.  My heartbreaking robbery of the old couple had been pointless.  The rest of the group lost all hope after that, but somehow we pulled through.
Boris had been the strongest, and could carry the most back from dangerous forays scavenging the ruins, but then my group met Marco, a former firefighter, and although I almost turned him away because we had no food to feed him, much less ourselves, he quickly proved his worth.  With Marco's help we managed to scavenge enough supplies to keep from starving.  We also had more people to spare to help our neighbors, and even save a few lives when we were out scavenging before relief finally reached the city.  If that little story doesn't convince you that this game can be very engrossing, then this is not for you.  For me it's a great and wonderful adventure into human suffering that is more engaging than many games where the war is from a soldier's perspective.  8.75/10

I previously did a written review on Bioshock 1 in 2012 which can be found at...
That might help explain some of my thoughts on the basic premise before talking about Bioshock 2 itself. Now I know this game got a lot of flack when it came out. Both over the fact that it had multiplayer and that many felt it didn't live up to the previous game.
I actually have to say I disagree on the second point. I enjoyed the story MORE in Bioshock 2 then I did in Bioshock. At a first glance the idea of playing as a Bid Daddy, these hulking monsters seems a tad absurd. But when you stop to think about it, they're not really monsters. They used to be human. Made all the more clear and horrifying in that opening cutscene where the Antagonist mind controls Delta before making him remove his helmet and shoot himself in the head all while we watch the event through his eyes. No I don't consider that a spoiler, it is literally the first scene in the game.
The first game makes you stop and think about actions in games. How we just do what the game tells us. Bioshock 2 takes a pair we basically just saw as objects in the game previously A Big Daddy and his Little Sister, then put us in the shoes of the Big Daddy. But not just any Big Daddy, one who has had his Little Sister taken from him. His entire reason for living, not to mention being separated basically puts his life on a timer.
And while I won't spoil it, the ending did bring me to tears. I can't deny that. But much like the first game IMO this one also suffers greatly from all the space in between the major story sections. After the opening, there isn't much that happens that is very memorable until close to the end of the game.
I also found it weird that despite the situation your character is in, the game still expects you to kill other Big Daddies and take their Little Sisters for you own in order to make yourself stronger. Seems a bit contradictary to the main story.
I can't actually comment on the multiplayer aspect of the game, not for lack of trying. I literally could not get a match started, there doesn't seem to be much of anyone playing online anymore.
Overall I'd say it's an average game with an above average story. If you liked the first game and avoided this one because of reviews, you might want to reconsider IMO.

Probably one of the poorest games I have ever played.
I finally took the bait when it was on sale and update 3.50 was released.  The point being I bought into this at v3.50.
For me, the game is dead by default.
The whole idea of having to fly all over and around individual stations just to find a stinking missing is a game mechanic that is offputting beyond belief.
I'd rather not have to faff about to be able to find something to do.
To me the game was designed to be unfriendly and unwelcoming - I feel sorry for anyone who paid full price for this and lost their hard-earned money.
The stats show the game has failed beyond imagination.
4k+ reviews on Steam - 3k+ negative - 1k+ positive.
The 'proof of the pudding' is with Teladi Outpost:
31 positive reviews.  1k+ people defended this game, but only 31 people have given a positive rating for Teladi Outpost - so how many of the 1k+ people who gave Rebirth a positive score are still playing it?
Patching the game won't help me enjoy it - the gameplay sucks for me and (I guess) for thousands of others.
Gameplay is not slick - there's too much hunting around for something to do - too much pointless scanning stuff.
Previous X3 games made it easy to see missions as you flew through a sector.
Modders seem to have tried to save the game by releasing mods to try and overcome the train-wreck that the developers have created; however, will further updates to this game break mods that fix the game?

This games reminds me of Freelancer and the scenes in the new star wars movies where Anakin is chasing the bounty hunter through a very busy city highway. Since X4 has been announced for 2018 I'm super pumped and decided to get back into X Rebirth. I've been playing a lot of X3 Albion Prelude lately too.
Pro's
1) Boarding and capturing capital ships is very fun - highly recommended.
2) Flying around stations is also very fun, and can help you with trading if that's your thing.
3) Exploration is more interactive
4) Menu system is easier for players to remember (key sequences etc).

Cons
1) Whether you're an X veteran or completely new, some aspects of the game won't be obvious to you and you'll have to look around to find "How to..." whether it's a more common issue like crafting or something like long range scanning/hacking.
2) If you're expecting an upgrade to previous x games then you will be surprised. Not disappointed (at least I wasn't) but surprised. This might not even be a con for many people.
3) The "Tutorials" are more of a feature showcase than a proper tutorial. Space Engineers is a good example of a video tutorial combining feature showcasing and "How to do X" is noticeably missing from these vids.
4) Can only fly 1 ship directly. Being able to fly multiple ships has been a big part of the series (apart from the very first game) and if I didn't know I'd be limited to 1 ship before I bought Rebith I'd probably feel let down too. Another good reason to read reviews/check a game out before you buy. On the flip side your ship is a lot more customizeable than previous x games.
5) Only a few weapons with various tiers for each

This was one of the last games I bought on physical media years ago. But I’ve never finished it until now. The reason for that was that back then, I didn’t have a gaming computer, only a laptop. And the weirdest thing happened when I first played the game on that laptop.
I played through the first couple of minutes until you arrive in Rapture and get out of the Bathysphere to first explore the city. And then my screen went dark. Completely black. I thought this was part of the game, so I left it running for a few minutes until I realized that this couldn’t possibly be on purpose. So I tried to quit the game and even after that the screen stayed black. Booting up the laptop showed an image only for a few minutes and after that, same thing. The ♥♥♥♥ing backlighting of the monitor broke right in the middle of me playing a horror game. So I sent off the laptop for repairs (it was still under warranty) and after I got it back, I never tried to play the game again. Not out of some kind of superstition that the game would break my PC or something, I just never cared enough. Until now that they’ve released a remastered version. And since I got the Bioshock collection a few years back during a Steam sale, the remaster came free of charge for people who already owned the Steam version. Which is a really nice gesture. Ironically if I now read the Steam user reviews for the game, I see that tons of people are having issues with this remaster crashing on them and deleting saves. Weirdly, I haven’t had a single issue with it. The ragdoll physics sometimes act up a bit, but overall this was a really smooth ride for me in terms of technical aspects.
So what do I think of this now 10 year old game? I thought it was pretty ok overall. Not some sort of masterpiece by any stretch, but I mostly enjoyed my experience with this game. The plasmid powers are fun to use in a variety of ways that encourage creative gameplay and they tie in nicely into the lore and story of the game as well, so as such I feel that they’re a well thought out aspect of the game. More mechanics should be integrated this well into a game on a mechanical and narrative level. Unfortunately, there are some clearly better plasmids than others. The first two you get, electro bolt and telekinesis, are literally the most important ones to your progress. And after I got the third one, the fire bolt, I foolishly swapped that one with electro bolt and since you can’t swap out plasmids on the fly I got stuck using that one and realized my big mistake. And since I relied so much on these few plasmids as well as saving all the little sisters resulting in less ADAM overall, I honestly never got to play with most of the plasmids (and combat and engineering tonics as well) that seemed way to situational to be useful to use on the fly when encountering enemies.
The same thing is true for the weapons along with their multiple ammo types. I just used the pistol and machine gun for the biggest part of the game, rounding up the rest of the time with the shotgun. I only used the chemical thrower during the final escort mission and the grenade launcher for a few big daddies. The shooting overall leaves a bit to be desired. I don’t quite know how to describe it but it’s a kind of “Tighten up the graphics on level 3” kind of affair. It’s just a combination of sounds and general impact of the weapons that leaves me kinda cold.
One of the most annoying parts of the game though is the hacking minigame. I get that you want to be able to convert enemy turrets, hack security cameras and crack safes and locked doors, that’s all cool. But the Pipe Dream minigame got on my nerves. Especially since at times it’s literally impossible to complete one due to placement of broken tubes or alert tiles. And there’s no way of using your insta-hack tool after you’ve already chosen to do it manually. And since I chose to not harvest the little sisters, I haven’t gotten enough ADAM to unlock that many tonic slots to make hacking more bearable in the long run. Not that it would’ve helped because seriously, this minigame is just awful.
What’s weird is also that the game clearly had ambitions of being a role-playing game but these aspirations are severely underdeveloped. You can buy health upgrades and incremental improvements in firearm damage and capacity as well as upgrades for plasmids, but it all just feels perfunctory. There’s no inventory management and for some reason I never figured out if you can sort your weapons, because I hated how the game automatically relocates your weapons at points in the game where you lose them. Picking up craftable items is an entirely abstract process. I don’t know how many tubes or screws I had and I don’t know what I can craft with them until I arrive at a U-Invent station. Finding food means that Jack eats it right then and there on the spot, so the only way of saving up impromptu health regeneration is via medkits.
Not that it’s hard to find those. The game is littered with money, ammo and medkits and I rarely died so even without the really dense placement of the vita chambers I was almost never in trouble when I got into a fight. Overall the game is a bit on the easy side with you being able to tank quite a lot of damage while dealing out tons of it, so the whole horror aspect falls kinda flat because not a lot poses any challenge to you. Even the big daddies are fairly easy to get around and the final boss fight was hilariously easy.
The game also feels a bit overlong. And that’s saying something, because I beat it less than 10 hours. It kinda feels like the game really wanted to be a primarily narrative experience that critiques objectivist philosophy (which it does quite nicely, even though I personally think that objectivism has more merit than it’s given credit for here) but they ran out of steam at some point and had to pad out the game. The part leading up to Andrew Ryan was a great crescendo, but everything after that just feels like a tacked-on denouement. Because the story ends with the interaction between the player and Ryan. The twist is revealed and the message to the player is delivered. Everything after that is just done for the sake of concluding the story and it drags out way too long.
It’s not like this is some sort of open-world exploration game. Bioshock is aggressively linear. And I really don’t mind that in a game, but the amount of backtracking it makes you do to gather plot-necessary items is just boring. It’s the most basic way of designing quests and this is what you’re doing most of the time. Need to build an EMP bomb? Gather these couple of materials. Need to pose as a big daddy? Gather the items on this list. Need to just simply progress? Find and kill these three individuals and take pictures of their corpses.
Speaking of taking pictures: Researching enemies is boring too. I did it for the one time the game required me to do it (in another “Need to progress? Photograph three splicers” quest) and then never bothered with it again. The benefits aren’t worth sneaking around and trying to take good pictures when I could just as easily perforate their brainpan with hot lead.
So yeah, I’m as usual highly critical of a game, but I still enjoyed the majority of the experience. But I’d never consider this one of the greatest games of all time. It has a huge narrative ambition that most other games would never even attempt, but the gameplay is just kinda there for the most part. Which is a shame.

Well. Two hours might not be enough to write a decent review but I don't care much.
This game is, well, strange. It's a great 2008 space game, with its bugs, its huge pretentiousness and its very badly modelled story. But this is not an X game and I think it won't ever be until EGOSOFT developers will change their mind on a lot of design decisions. Let's start with a deeper review.
First thing I can notice is that the game is really really heavy hardware wise. That's kinda acceptable, it's the trend these days. What isn't acceptable is the huge lack of optimization:
1) Even on minimum graphic settings (no antialias, no shadings, 1280x720, very low textures detail) the game doesn't have solid fps, ranging from 20 to 50fps (most of the times it varies. 40-50 fps facing a wall, 38-45 while moving on a station, 20-30 while in outerspace with ships on screen) on medium end hardware. Most animations also doesn't really exist: in past games if a ship jumped away using a JD you would notice a warp animation and the ship's computer voice telling that it was gone. In rebirth you have no animation for JD and no computer voice. The ship simply despawns. This can be noticed in the second mission, where you take your new aquired female member to a corporation's ship. While flying really close to that ship you can notice that it simply despawns.
2) Ships' AI is very badly implemented if you compare it with older x games (taking away that weird bug present in all games from X2 to X3:AP where sometimes a cpu ship would endlessly bump on a station stuck on its way). Most of them will eventually bump on a station or another ship.
3) Stations' interiors are full of bugs. I landed on three different stations (and in multiple points of those stations) and 80% of the time I found bugged moments where you could just fall in the void and then respawn in your ship. In the submission where you hire a captain for your capital freighter you land in a sort of night club. After landing you go through a blast door and you find a robot "minding his business". If you bump that robot you'll eventually be thrown away from the station in the 3d void and then respawn. Same thing with the air conductures in that same corridor.
4) A lot of ships' 3d models are unstable. In example, while adding a captain to my capital I noticed another capital surrounded by Triath Vanguard fighters. While I was near those fighters I noticed that the left half of those ships was trembling.
Design wise this game has an awful lot of bad decisions and bad implementations of good decisions:
1) We were advertised that EVERYTHING in the game could influence economical, social and political situations or even the smallest situation in the game. THAT'S FRIGGIN' AWESOME.
Well, it would be if it was implemented better. In example: while flying in rebirth I noticed a capital ship blocking an highway. The strange thing is that nothing happened. I flew in the highway but that ship across the tunnel didn't even made me or other ships crash. This is not lack of eye candy, it's lack of a realism which should be the trademark of the game.
2) Station exploring would be an awesome eye catch (and maybe somehow useful to what you are doing) but there's a huge lack of life. NPCs stand still (that's kinda acceptable tough, I guess that making them move would be another huge weight for our poor cpus). You can hear them chatting sometimes but most of the dialogues are repetitive and without any caring. OST is minimal, not many ambient noises.
3) The inability to fly any ship other than the Albion Skunk is kinda a huge step back.
4) The story is told in a really superficial way. Even by paying maximum attention to every dialogue I found myself going to the next waypoint without even understating what's really going on.
5) UI is confusing if compared to the masterpieces UI that were in x2 and x3:R: menus are unclear (I did had a lot of trouble while searching for my cargo bay in the menus) and basic cockpit doesn't even show most of the informations (like speed expressed in numbers along with the usual bar). Maps are the most confusing things I ever seen so far.
6) The lack of fundamental features is really disapointing: monitors for targets and objects doesn't exist anymore. SETA is surprisingly absent making most of the first flights REALLY boring.
7) Voice acting is mostly bad executed (apart from two actors present even in old installments that are really top tier).
8) Highways are kinda ok but they could have been better.
9) Docking is a huge pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ searching for a docking bay is a long and boring process, many of the stations' points must be uncovered by yourself and most of the times is a huge time wasting.
10) Radio communications aren't useful anymore
11) NPC talking is really confusing.
12) Don't know if it's because I didn't play much but so far I found only one alien, a split in a station. Also his 3d model was kinda fun, a green man with moustaches. Totally different from the splits I'm used to see.

I never played an "X" game before, which will make this review of more use to those of you who also haven't and just want to know if this is a good game, and less use to those of you who have, and want to know how it stacks up to its predecessors. I thought I might start with an anecdote.
Tasked with building a space station in an ally's territory, I only needed about 60 fusion reactors to complete it. I searched every sector for it, but nobody was selling. I soon found out why: these were only being produced at 3 stations and my enemy, the Plutarch Corporation, owned one of those and was buying every reactor that came off the production lines at the others. So what's a poor rebel to do?
Raid their shipments, obviously.
I waited several kilometers away from one of the factories with my cargo freighter standing by. After seeing a Plutarch ship dock and then pull away, I scanned its cargo, revealing that it was carrying my coveted fusion reactors, I made my move.
I used my dumbfire rockets to quickly disable its engines and warp drive, then went to work on the main hull. This was a long process but I found a safe spot just behind the engines where I could go to recharge my shields. Woe to the unwary freighter that travels without fighter escort.
The freighter destroyed, I tagged the cargo for my own cargo ship to pick up. As a swarm of drones buzzed toward the remains, I spotted a Plutarch destroyer in the distance. Several seconds later it was apparent that it was headed straight for me, most likely in response to my little Space Pirate schtick. I had no means to fight a destroyer, but I did tangle with the wing of fighters it sent ahead of itself in order to protect my cargo drones. As the last drone made it safely into the cargo bay, the destroyer began to open up on my freighter. It's a hardy vessel but it wouldn't last long under that hailstorm of fire. I ordered the captain of the freighter to get us out of there, then swung my craft around to the front, briefly exposing myself to the destroyer's fire to dock. I watched from the deck as lasers streaked across the sky and missiles exploded against the hull, hearing the faint sound of the frieghter's jump drive charging up. Moments later, explosions were replaced by silence. The jump had taken me and my freighter hundreds of thousands of kilometers away, with our precious reactors safely aboard (and with no load screen in between).
I chose this little anecdote because it perfectly encapsulates X: Rebirth's interacting systems of trade, construction, and combat. But I neglected to mention a few details.
During this whole scenario, I encountered a massive drop in framerate that persisted until I left the zone and returned. The game crashed inexplicably some time after I transferred my wares. I originally tried boarding the freighter, but found that while 8 marines was plenty to take a destroyer in an earlier story mission, a full complement of 50 marines was totally incapable later on of capturing even a much smaller freighter than my target. The station repeatedly reminded me that my rash behavior "isn't tolerated in these parts," but apparently forgot to attach a consequence to their threats. Even now I can trade with that station as with any other. And the whole excursion was made necessary because my previous shipment of some 114 fusion reactors inexplicably disappeared from the freighter's cargo holds--the freighter made it, the goods didn't. It still had the order to transfer the wares to my construction ship in its queue. Upon deleting and reissuing the order, a message told me that it had no fusion reactors in its holds. Gone into thin air.
My point is this: At its best, X: Rebirth is the most full-featured, exciting, strategic space sim available that I know of. Though dogfights are a little awkward because the smaller spacecraft are so maneuverable, combat overall is exceptionally exciting. The game has made me think in terms of real logic (how can I acquire this good by any means available) as opposed to game logic (how can I exploit this system to get 1000x as much as I'll ever need). It appears, so far as I can tell, that the entire game is driven by a real economy: goods cannot be used until they're produced, and producing these goods means someone has to mine them, extract them, refine them, and manufacture them. This creates a living world unlike any I've ever seen before, and when I close my trade console and nudge my throttle forward (I use a Saitek X52 joystick) towards the next station, or merge into a highway and switch on the auto-pilot while I give orders to my fleet, I really feel like I am there, interacting with a real world in space. Seeing a station suddenly pop into view as I exit the space highway, or docking on one of my larger vessels while it jumps me across space (with no loading screens!) are experiences that just never get old.
At its worst, X: Rebirth continues to sport more bugs and headaches than are really excusable, especially with it being the fourth iteration in the series. You will encounter glitches. Your framerate will inexplicably drop to a crawl (only happened to me twice in 24 hours play though). You will experience crashes (save often). The story dialogue is fair, but most of the other conversations and text might have actually been written by a third grader (hearing a Marine Officer randomly chirp, valley-girl style, "Eww, slimy green lizardy things are everywhere!" is just bizarre, and some of the logbook entries are so poorly written as to be indecipherable). The game does not explain itself very thoroughly, and you will spend much time trying to figure out how many of its systems work (or don't work, as is occasionally the case).
I had great anticipation for this game's release, so I was very disappointed when I read that it was basically an unfinished product. The free weekend just recently spoke a great deal about the developer's confidence in the current state of their product, and I believe that confidence is justified. This is now a very playable, fully-featured game, and if you are patient and have a good tolerance for the occasional bug, it can give you some of the most fantastic gaming experiences you've had in years.

If the "Magic Card Shuffle" doesn't bother you...then this is a good game and I would recommend it....However....
What is the "Magic Card Shuffle" you ask?  It's how inaccurate shuffles are compared to having a deck of cards in your hand.
This is your typical Magic card game.  The duels are 100% based on the shuffle (or luck of the draw if you will), which is lacking at best.  If it was once in a while it would be understandable...however in 3 back to back games drawing 6 lands in a row or not drawing a single land is not what you would call a good shuffle and your only option is usually concede or restart duel (if solo).
The AI gets exactly what it needs 80% of the draws...it gets frustrating to have a good hand to start...then nothing but land, land, land while the AI manages to come from behind.  This is regardless of the "difficulty" of the AI challenger.
This holds true for the actual Magic The Gathering Online game as well...i've played all the Magic games since the originals came out and this has been an issue from the first game released.
I'm very well knowledged in how to build a deck, as i've been playing Magic for 20+ years now.  So those that might say you have an unbalance deck, you have too much land, not enough land...that's not the case.
Now I know people will say well that is the game and you only have X hours on the game, however in that short time I seen the same "shuffle" issue i've seen with all versions.
Installation was rough, didn't run well on my compter and crashed a lot. Even aside from that the game felt like it needed a few more months polish to make a solid game.

Return to Castle Wolfenstein is one of the classic Wolfenstein games, made on the Quake engine in the early 2000s. While a lot of people insist this is one of the best Wolfenstein games ever made, an essential FPS of the early era, and still holds up today, I disagree. RTCW has its high points, but also abysmally low ones as well.
(This review was based on a single playthrough, on what was basically medium difficulty out of three options.)
Let's start with the positives.
The atmosphere and level design are amazing. Having any sort of weather effect adds a lot to a game, and RTCW wasn't afraid to get a little foggy or snowy. This obscures your sight, just like real weather would. It also has complex but logical lab layouts, making them feel like it could be a real place. RTCW builds a world that seems just as possible as the WW2 we learn about in 8th grade history.
The story is also worthy of some praise, despite its slight cheesiness. It's just what you would expect out of a Wolfenstein game: Germany is researching the occult and enhancing its soldiers with robotics. Eventually they get mechanized soldiers and you have to fight them. It's formulaic, but effective. It gets the point across and while the German soldiers do have comically fake accents, they and the Allied Forces generals are well acted and are pleasant to listen to.
Unfortunately, the positives of Return to Castle Wolfenstein cannot outweight the negatives. While the first half of the game does not suffer from these problems, the ending levels are plagued with them.
The enemies are offensively bad in design. There is almost a sort of aimbot switch going on, where a single soldier can miss an entire magazine of shots but then land 20 of them in a row flawlessly (Even if you are strafing or peppering them with your own bullets), depleting over half your health and armor. Enemy snipers can also have the same problem, able to land shots at such a great distance that you can barely even see them, let alone snipe them back before half your health is gone. This "boosted" response time and accuracy is courtesy of the difficulty system, which isn't increasing the difficulty at all, just the omnipotence of the enemies. Notice how I do not say this game is HARD. It is just bad AI that leeches the enjoyment out of the game. While this is insultingly bad AI, it is tolerable through the use of cover and smart positioning. This goes out the window in the final three levels.
The final levels introduce Lopers and Super Soldiers. Lopers are incredibly fast moving enemies that can either attack by using a massive electric AOE attack, or by jumping at you at an incredible distance. This jump is fast, nearly unavoidable, and does huge damage in a massive area despite no attack being visible. I was killed by a Loper 5 meters below me while on a catwalk above just because he was jumping around on the ground floor, but somehow still hitting me. Super Soldiers are even more offensively bad, as the prototype soldiers are quite content to spam endless rounds of either RPG rockets or minigun bullets in your direction with no pause. The complete Super Soldiers also use a Tesla Cannon, which is an electric beam (With infinite ammunition, of course) that will not miss, has nearly unlimited range, pushes the player back and deals staggeringly high amounts of damage with absolutely no drawbacks. All encounters with the Tesla Super Soldiers take place in rooms with nearly no cover or way to avoid their fire. This is horrible, unfair and unfun enemy design, and whoever thought these enemies were acceptable for public release need to reconsider their career choices.
The biggest problem with this game is the massive difficulty spike the player faces if they are not constantly quick saving. I do not look down on save-scumming, but when it is close to the only viable way to complete a game there is something seriously wrong with said game. The Quake engine is not designed for stealth, many enemies have near endless sightlines and can see you and shoot you well before you even know which direction they are in. And of course when they see you, the entire enemy compound somehow knows which exact rock you are hiding behind and go on full alert. This near instant change in the situation makes quick saving after every twenty feet or bit of progress the only way to not ruin an entire mission just because an enemy partially obscured behind a bush two miles away saw you peek out from behind a wall, or turning a corner and instantly losing 50 health & 80 armor to a single man with a Panzerfaust. Return to Castle Wolfenstein is more of a trial and error game than a proper skill and positioning FPS.
The pinnacle of dissapointment lies in the bosses of the game. The first and final boss are hilariously easy, as they can only use melee and limited, easily dodged ranged attacks. The easiest and most effective way to beat them is to simply stand 10 meters away and pepper the walking sponges with bullets until they eventually explode. The final boss is even more of a dissapointment than the first, because after a whole 2 levels solely dedicated to padding the game length before the boss you get to face a heavily armored man that can ONLY use melee, and occasionally summons normal zombies to join the fight. The second boss of the game is more offensive than the other two simply for being one of the aformentioned Tesla Super Soldiers. The instant the fight starts, 8 out of 10 times he locks onto you with the Tesla gun and wipes out a solid chunk of your health before you can even attempt to find what little cover there is in the boss arena. It is a gimmicky dissapointment.
I specifically leave this here, not because of the game itself but because no matter where you go, any criticism of Return to Castle Wolfenstein is swiftly met with unending hate troll spam. Any forum you go on that talks bad about this game is met with thunderous dissaproval, let alone just this review. If steam hadn't removed the percentage approved feature on review ratings, you would see how many downvotes this review got. Not because its a bad review, but because the nostalgia blinded fans cannot imagine for a second that their precious baby is flawed in any way. You have no idea how many comments I deleted because they brought absolutely nothing to the table except troll bait attempts. If you want help in beating this crappy game, be warned. The community here is more likely to tell you to Git Gud than a Dark Souls player. No matter how good you are at games, they will INSIST you are bad and "can't handle a game that doesn't hold your hand". Not that you should get this game in the first place.
In summary, Return to Castle Wolfenstein is a gimmicky, broken piece of crap that happens to have a fantastic atmosphere and surprisingly good visuals for a game made in 2001. No amount of personal skill can help you overcome the bad AI and unbalanced weapons (I've been playing games for nearly 20 years now, you could not pay me to believe I have not "gotten good", especially when I have 100% completion in two Dark Souls games.) Do not believe the nostalgia blinded fans, many of which will downvote this review and prove my point (Even though the ratings are supposed to be "Is this review helpful?" not "Do you agree with this review?") No matter what the price is, this game is not worth your money. Go buy Half Life, which came out 3 years earlier and is somehow better in every aspect, and still costs about the same as this game.

This game has a lot going for it.  No, it is not Civ 5.  It lacks a lot of the complexities and nuances that developed with the expansions of Civ 5.  I hope the expansions are coming--soon.

That said.  It is enjoyable.  There is enough complexity with the new resources involved that it is interesting.  The way the wonders of this game are used, and that you can lose them without losing a city, is a nice twist.  I have wondered why that was never an element in Civ 5, even though you could see the wonder on the map, you had to take the city to take the wonder.
Was it worth the original price tag?  I don't think so.  There are too many things still needing to be fleshed out, or even just developed,  Do I enjoy the gaem?  Certainly.  If you remember this is not Civ 5, then I think it is enjoyable.  And, I can hardly wait for the expansions to roll out (soon, I hope.)

It's not an average FPS from your library. Muskets and pistols from 17th century acts like they should and your hero is not the commandos with magical autohealing.
It's not an average modern stealth action. If you can hear the enemy or see him from hundred meters away - so does he; they're not deaf and blind as it trended in stealth games nowadays. Enemies are smart but reckless, they'll track you down almost always, even if you'll run from them to the other end of the map.
I was sceptical when got heard about this "open-world horror action". But the atmosphere of the game is really great - mysterious and grim, even in the bright daylight. I highly recommend to play this game in original black-white-red palette - your eyes will bleed, but it's worth it.
Sound is also a big part of ambience and it's awesome: wind, birds, trees and grass, weapons, ****ed-up Spaniards, skeletons and wraiths. It'll sounds crazy, but lack of voice acting is not a flaw in this case - it makes the game even more surrealistic.
Totally worth the full price (but I grabbed it with -80% at Summer Sale). The game that you'll remember even after few years.

Yes, as a software service this product launched in a horrendous state, with some serious server connectivity issues. Most have been ironed out by now.
Technical problems aside, for new and casual players Magic Duels is a very, very capable computer game version of Magic: The Gathering:
- It is much cheaper than paper Magic.
- It features proper card collecting and deck building (although with an overall limited card pool).
- It does an outstanding job of introducing new players to the rules.
This is currently the most accessible way to play Magic in terms of budget and time.
Nevertheless, still lacking any support for cross-platform multiplayer gameplay is a significant limitation to the potential success of Magic Duels.

This is presumably the final iteration in a long standing series of flavored magic card games; the effort to consolidate the annuals into a single framework.
Compared to it's predecessors it's the closest wizards has come to creating the mtg experience online.
While I'm not fond of the microtransaction model, it's use to permit players to buy more cards has been a staple of the ccg since it's inception.
Sometimes this is a game where you command an unstoppable force of nature to demolish an opponent before they have the land to assemble a defense, let alone dream of developing a counter-attack. Other times, you've lost well before deciding if you should keep your hand or not, and no matter how much skill or luck you are able to command, you'll be losing a short game. Yet it's the vast swath between these that's truly rewarding; where a deck fully designed by the player contends with something just as good by someone else, where the balance of power is constantly shifting, and the whole game comes down to a single health point or two, and a single turn makes the difference between a win and a loss.
So, after about 100 hours or so in the game, I feel comfortable enough to say it's worth a round every now and again.

Having played this game for over 40 hours, I can say that I was hooked right from the get-go. This game deserves a 10/10. The game puts you into the role of survivors holed up in a house, where you will be living/sleeping/eating and surviving in.
Everyday is split into a "day" portion and an "night" portion. During the day, you will be crafting things such as metal workshops, a stove or a herbal garden. If your characters are hungry, you will need to feed them in order for their condition to not worsen. In the earlier parts of the game, material and food collection is crucial.
At night, you select one of your characters to scavenge another building in the area while the rest of the characters guards the house or sleeps through the night. Each character has their own "special" abilities, such as having more backpack slots to store items that you have found in the buildings, or being a good cook. Once you have filled up your slots, you return to your home for the next day.
As you progress through the game, some buildings have thugs that reside inside and may attack you on sight, and if your character is killed, the game still continues on.
Some things to consider:
Each player has their own statuses and addictions. These may be changed as the game progresses.
The statuses include emotional ones (sad/content/depressed) and condition based ones(hungry/sick/injured)
The realism in this game is what made it playable over and over again.

If I had to describe this game in one word, I would say it was 'ambitious.' A black and white, open world, horror FPS set in the colonial era from a virgin studio? Most indies would rather churn out another ♥♥♥♥♥♥ puzzle/platformer. But does the execution live up to it's premise? Nope! Does it matter? Maybe.
The stealth system is awful. Many of the later enemies have black and white color palettes, so you don't see them before they see you. Oh, and they can see you instantly from 50 yards away. There's a mechanic involving wind masking your sounds or something, but I never felt that it was worth the risk.
And the game is plauged by a lack of variety. There are only five different weapon types, with varying qualities. There are only six or seven enemies. You can find equipment, but all it does is give you passive bonuses that are hardly even noticeable. Each zone in the game plays out the same way: find everything in the light world, find everything in the dark world, talk to ghosts and move on to the next zone. By the end of the game, you're sprinting from point A to point B just to finish the game. I haven't felt this kind of repetition since Assassin's Creed 1.
Betrayer has a fairly solid engine. There's a myriad of graphics options and HUD options to choose from, which is always welcome from an indie dev. You can even skip the black and white aesthetic and play with color (recommended). That said, I did get stuck a couple times in the geometry, forcing me to kill my character and respawn.
But if you can get past these shortcomings, the game is really interesting. The sound design is stellar. I can't think of any game that has such a robust audio department, much less one that is so integral to the mechanics of the game. When the story comes together it can be superb, but the story elements are all non-linear. Sometimes the story doesn't have the impact it should have because of this, even when dealing with incredibly grim topics like filicide.
If you're a stickler for mechanics, I'd skip this title. 'Rough around the edges' doesn't even begin to describe my experience. However if you're more interested in atmosphere or story and you're not bothered by the broken stealth system, this game will entertain you for a few hours.

I just finished my first playthrough of the game, and I can say that it was well worth the money, and I am not someone who buys many games these days.
There's no tutorial, but the games mechanics are simple, which means you fumble around trying to get everything together for the first few days as your initial supplies dwindle.  I soon got used to perpetual hunger, and was satisfied as long as my band of survivors was not starving as I tried to figure out how to navigate the city's wartime economy of barter and scavenging.
I get the feeling that if you know the city well enough after some playthroughs, and as long as the game doesnt start you in winter (which means you may forsake building vital security improvements to your shelter and focus on building heaters and stoves to melt snow and keep you warm) then a player could learn how to optimise their economy very quickly.  The problems come when you make mistakes (see the story below) or when you get very unlucky (which happens a lot) then the risks of death become very high.  You also come across people who need your help, for example a starving hobo in an old building who needs food bad, and if you don't have it, by the time you spend a day or two getting back to help him, you find him starved to death, so it's inevitable that you will see people suffer.
I desperately tried to keep all of my ragtag band alive through the war, and failed when, due to a misunderstanding at the hospital, I lost poor Boris.  Boris ate a burst from a rebel soldier's assault rifle when, after making one of them mad, he couldn't leave the building fast enough for them due to his injured leg.  Eventually they got tired of shouting curses at him and hitting them with their gun butts and shot him.   Somehow he survived and crawled halfway across the city to the house.  When it became clear that he would die of his wounds unless he recieved some real treatment, Katia, who was the most cheerful of the group, ran into the house of an elderly couple that lived across town and raided their medicine cabinet for bandages and medicine while the poor husband and wife begged her to stop.  Katia only took what she needed: two packs of bandages and a bottle of antibiotic pills, but for days after felt depressed by what she'd done while boris hovered on the brink of death.  Then the bandits came in the night.  And though we had some weapons, boris suffered a minor wound while in his bed, and died.  My heartbreaking robbery of the old couple had been pointless.  The rest of the group lost all hope after that, but somehow we pulled through.
Boris had been the strongest, and could carry the most back from dangerous forays scavenging the ruins, but then my group met Marco, a former firefighter, and although I almost turned him away because we had no food to feed him, much less ourselves, he quickly proved his worth.  With Marco's help we managed to scavenge enough supplies to keep from starving.  We also had more people to spare to help our neighbors, and even save a few lives when we were out scavenging before relief finally reached the city.  If that little story doesn't convince you that this game can be very engrossing, then this is not for you.  For me it's a great and wonderful adventure into human suffering that is more engaging than many games where the war is from a soldier's perspective.  8.75/10
