Saints Row Gat out of Hell... the standalone expansion to Saints Row IV, though Saints Row IV was supposed to be an expansion of Saints Row The Third as well. I love the Saints Row series, it is surely one of the most fun open world game series of all time. While I mostly dislike Saints Row 3 for its crappy humour (sex jokes everywhere) and absolutely unfulfilling story mode (which heavily reused side activities), SR4 came out to be an absolutely amazing masterpiece - to me, at least. While it was downright insultingly easy (lol), I found it fun and the side stuff was the best part of the game. This game is literally SR4 in a new city. Well, shall we say, a reskinned SR4? But it ain't exactly that.
The gameplay in this game remains almost unchanged from SR4 though flying was added. Flying is absolutely amazing and feels like something that should have been in SR4 (you could only glide in that one). The city of New Hades is almost like a mixture of Saints Row 2's Stilwater and Saints Row 3's Steelport. Graphics are nothing special unfortunately, however it certainly doesn't look bad!! Saints Row IV looked better in my opinion. But in this game, it isn't as copy and paste as SR4 was from SR3. Car models are slightly altered, there are new guns, a whole new city, etc.
The game proved to be decently lengthy for the price, clocking in at around 7.5 hours to beat (main story and all side activities. Little collectibles.), and maybe a maximum of 10 hours to get all the endings, which thankfully you don't have to replay the game in order to get them.
I had an absolute blast, as I did with SR4. However this game is a lot harder, but to ensure challenge just don't upgrade health. Maybe 1 level maximum if you want a decent challenge. Hardcore is ALMOST brutal.
Other than that I would give the game a great recommendation. On a sale it is a great run for your money (£2.74), but for full price, I wouldn't really advise it. Get this only if you liked Saints Row IV, or if you like the SR series in general.

This will be a mixed review, but I’ll be honest this game was awesome. I played it non-stop, which is pretty rare for me.
THE GOOD:
I’ll start off by saying I don’t really like open world games. I want a straight path I can follow that leads through hordes of enemies you need to shoot or chop your way through until you get to the next cutscene. THIS IS THAT GAME! I was fighting and button mashing the whole time and I loved every second of it.
Aside from being a LotR game, this game hits all the right tropes: finding a missing wizard, enchanted forests filled with giant spiders, goblin ambushes, orc camps, ruined Dwarf mines overrun by goblins, treks through snowy mountains, delving into undead-filled crypts, begrudgingly grateful dwarves, super friendly and wise elves, and of course the classic trio of heroes (elf, man, dwarf).
Good♥♥♥♥♥♥
THE BAD:
First off, a major knock against this game is that the controller set up is totally wonky. I started the game and it said Press Start to begin, but Start was mapped to A, B was mapped to Start, and X/Y were mapped to RT/LT. Most of the other buttons did nothing.... so I had to open Steam in big picture mode and find a controller scheme to remap everything. That was super annoying. Also, once everything was remapped, there was still an issue with picking up loot. For whatever reason, I couldn’t do that without using a mouse. So we lose some points for the weird crappy port.
Next up, this game tried to be an RPG but it really shouldn’t have. You’re given dialogue options that are totally useless, since you can’t change the outcome. I would have preferred straight cutscenes instead of that half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥dialogue jumble.
You’re also given the ability to level up and choose your gear, which is cool at first, until you realize none of it matters. I started as a level 1 guy with like 16 STR doing wimpy damage against orcs. By level 21, I had 50 STR and weapons that did 1000+ damage, and those same orcs had been scaled up to being even harder to kill, making my leveling up totally pointless. If you’re going to scale up the same enemies, just don’t bother. Don’t level up anyone and make them the same throughout the whole game. It all amounts to the same thing, and doesn’t waste my time having to switch weapons.
Going hand in hand with that, while I love hack and slash games, it would take like 3 minutes to kill an enemy. Then I’d level up and get new swords and it would take 3 minutes to kill those same enemies. By the time I’m level 20, if I’m still fighting goblins, I want to turn those guys into goo just by looking at them. I did not feel powerful at all in this game. Every time my weapons got better, the enemies got harder.
Difficult enemies is fine, but THEY ARE THE SAME ENEMY! If I’m fighting goblins at level 1 and Uruk Hai at level 2, that’s totally reasonable to have them be stronger. But if I’m fighting goblins at level 1 and the same goblins at level 20 and my attacks aren’t doing anything, that’s just stupid. I wanna feel like a hero! Instead I felt like a guy smacking his sword into a brick wall over and over again.
Last but not least, breakable weapons. Ugh. Just kill me now. PLEASE DO NOT PUT BREAKABLE WEAPONS AND ARMOR IN YOUR GAMES. I’d leave town with a fresh batch of new gear and after hitting 3 of those invincible goblins my shoes would break and need repairs. So dumb.
THE VERDICT:
Ok, so this was a mixed review, but I really enjoyed this game. If you’re into hack and slash or LotR, you’ll like this. If you want a Skyrim style game, this isn’t going to be for you. Buy it when it’s on sale!

BioShock 2 is quite a good example of a game that didn't really need to exist. BioShock 1 was a self-contained story and ended nicely with any and all loose ends suitably tied up so what could a sequel to one of the best games of 2007 possibly bring to the table? The answer is quite a lot!
BioShock 2 is a First-Person Shooter game with stealth and horror elements and is set in the year 1968, 8 years after the events of BioShock 1. You play as a Big Daddy and, after an incident 10 years ago, have just been reactivated. You are tasked with finding your Little Sister and are caught in the middle of an attempted takeover of the decaying city. Since our last trip through Rapture, things have gotten much worse but you are not just any old lumbering slow Big Daddy though. You are Delta, a Prototype Big Daddy with the ability to use different weapons and Plasmids.
Irrational Games did not make BioShock 2. The duty was given to 2K Marin. The result is a pretty damn good game, it just doesn't feel as polished as the original does.
Right off the bat, the majority of the environments appear very nicely detailed and it is clear that a lot of work has gone into them. It is best not to look too close however, some inaccessible parts of some levels look quite bad. I have clear memories of one corridor ending in a completely black wall!
For the first three hours or so of the game, it's environments are less open than BioShock's levels. It goes through teaching you the basics of play, who the characters are, what your role in the world is and the game eventually opens up a little bit and gives you the freedom to explore.
Instead of BioShock 1's combat mechanics where you could only use either a weapon or a plasmids at any one time, In BioShock 2 you have control of both hands; your left hand uses Plasmids and your right hand uses your weapons. This makes combat a lot more fun and feel much more responsive. No more faffing around trying to find the plasmid or weapon you want whilst being defenceless.
Now you can try out different combinations with your plasmid powers when they are powerful enough. put a Cyclone Trap down and zap it with Electro Bolt or Incinerate and see what might happen. Get experimenting! And Yes, Cyclone Trap is still as hilarious as it always has been.
As for game-play and game progression, there isn't much difference to the first game. If you've played BioShock 1 then you will feel right at home for BioShock 2. The only difference is, being a Big Daddy, you get to interact with the Little Sisters a bit more. In order to get Adam, you'll have to get yourself a Little Sister who is usually being protected by another Big Daddy. Once dispatching of the Big Daddy, you are free to gather Adam for yourself or Harvest the Little Sister.
The whole process of gathering Adam for yourself is one of the game's better points. Building up a defence and watching it all go off while your Little Sister does her thing is quite satisfying. But you better be careful... not everyone may appreciate you taking the Adam for yourself...
BioShock had an extremely tense atmosphere to it; the levels were dark, the scares were genuinely scary and the music really helped to enhance the tension. In BioShock 2, this scary fun is largely missing and when the game does attempt to unnerve you, I found that it just fell flat. Slightly disappointing. I do believe that the music may have been broken in a few places as, upon reloading a previous save one time, music would start playing where there previously had been nothing playing at all.
And, while the story isn't ever going to meet that of the first game, it really does pick up towards the end with some incredibly beautifully created sections and environments to match. I wont spoil anything but it really did impress that they could do what they did with the technology.
They did a better job with hacking though. Instead of a 2 minute long pipemania style game, the player can now simply time button presses correctly in a much quicker and simpler hacking minigame.
While the key-bindings work fine, they may break when given on-screen prompts. I was given a choice of adopting a Little Sister and, with no updated bindings on-screen to tell me what button did what, had to just kind of press a button and hope that it was the right action I wanted to take. Luckily it was.
And now, its time to talk about all that DLC that came along after release. I remember 2K thinking and delaying and rethinking about whether or not to release this DLC on PC at all. Thankfully they did and it should not be missed! Here's a run-down.
- This DLC is exactly what its name sounds like it is; Take the process of protecting a little sister from splicers and turns it into its own mini-game!
- Absolutely incredible from start to finish. Take BioShock 2's mechanics, BioShock 1's darker horror-themed and better constructed environments and triple the size of the levels and you have Minerva's Den, a self-contained story with about 12-16 hours worth of entertainment to it. It's almost impossible to say anything about anything inside this DLC without spoiling things but trust me... you need to play this if you have BioShock 2.
At the time of writing this review, I have not played the multi-player. I do know that it was made by a separate studio as to give the single player team the time they needed to create the single player without any distractions. It has an interesting side-story to it; It is set prior to the fall of Rapture and you are a plasmid test subject for Sinclair Solutions. A Civil War is breaking out and it's your job to go and smack some of your fellow citizens around a bit. I'll update this review later when I get around to playing it.
Overall, BioShock 2 does the combat better than BioShock 1 but the story never really had a hope of matching. It is a game that is definitely worth playing though and the DLC is up there with some of the best Single Player DLC I have ever played. The Shock series of games continues to be of a high standard of quality even if BioShock 2 does falter in a few small places.

Game is pretty darn good and stable, even with alt-tabbing repeatedly like i did while writing this review.
Cockpit detail is far better than previous incarnations. You can partially swivel to look around inside the cockpit very smoothly. External view is fully rotatable and zoomable plus there is a tactical view (edit: well not really; it's a close-up view of the enemy, useful for identifying Beyond Visual Range enemies so that you don't bite more than you can chew) There is also a built-in game recorder just to mention. Space stations scale is humongous, they are also very detailed. Because of the gigantic scale of the space-stations, landing and taking-off has an added sense of immersion.
Trading items are expanded over previous Xs as there seems to be many miscellaneous non-functional items whose only purpose seem to be just to add content (edit: for trading purposes) BUT addition of items also added a new feature; crafting. Crafting allows the forming of new higher value items or special purpose items, like gifts or hacking tools. Incidentally nearly everything is tradeable, ship equipment, missiles, even the marines. The one thing that isn't is the cockpit configurations; it's an expense. If you don't like the cockpit layout you can buy a different one. There's no functional difference in gameplay; just a visual preference. Not sure if crew is tradeable though, 'coz i might want to trade my co-pilot for a more ...erm interesting conversationalist.
Finding the best prices is not difficult, even in the beginning, it's only a bit tedious as it requires repetitious page flipping between the various vendors offers. You can fly to the vendor to make the trade if they are not in the same station or you can simply use the menu but there is a shuttle fee for the extra convenience. It's quite easy to make money once the trading interface is fully understood. You can be a smuggler dealing in contraband or be a smuggler simply because you don't have the licence to deal in restricted goods. Licences can be purchased provided you meet the minimum faction rating.
Game is completely open-world and non-linear even in the campaign mode just like Freelancer but it does it much better as the economy is dynamic and affected by cargo ships moving throughout the universe (like Space Rangers). Can't comment about the story though as i've barely begun the story missions.
NPC: Pilot, come and get some bargains from me.
Player: Show me your wares please.
NPC: Sure lets get to it.
NPC: Can i show you anything else? And i mean... anything. ;-)
NPC: You all have a nice day.
So far the one thing that is so annoying about this game is the bar music or is it music in a bar? No regrets with this one, game is soo good, i couldn't wait for 75% off like always. Music in space though is awesome; one of the strongest reasons i couldn't wait to add it to my collection.
Generic NPC monologue is limited and therefore repetitious but that is a minor fault. Nothing like the dynamic dialog between NPCs in Fallout 2 or in more recent games like Skyrim.
There are no minigames; if those arcade machines you see in the bar can be operated by credit tokens, that would be it. What seems like a minigame - small talk is but an option during interaction with NPCs in the stations. It's a useful, easy and fast way to increase faction rating in addition to trading and destroying pirates. High faction ratings mean better discounts.
Perhaps the single biggest advantage this game offers over previous Xs is the option to save the game at any time, free without the need to buy salvage insurance, even in space like in the middle of trying to capture a capital ship or in a bar, when the NPC starts talking. It's a very useful nifty feature that helps you backtrack to rectify a colossal mistake, i mean who doesn't like an on demand savegame feature right? Incidentally you have up to 10 save slots in addition to a quicksave slot and 3 autosave slots making a total of 14 slots. Be warned, the savegames are quite big, when all slots are used it can reach about 500 MB or more. Too many games rely on a single savegame or worse a single autosave. IMO it's disrespectful to deny PC gamers multiple save slots, i mean it's a PC game not a console game. Here we have the best of both worlds; good old school multiple saves and autosaves.
Highly recommended if you can get past the little niggles. 8/10

Coming to the office block was a big mistake. The place was crawling with zombies. The walking dead perambulated throughout the premises as if in a somnambulant haze, a twisted parody of, but not a huge departure from, their former selves. So far I've been lucky and remain undetected, stealth was the right approach as the sound of battle would surely attract the horde.
My target had been the Stationery Cupboard. Successfully procuring most of the contents I would soon be able to craft a plethora of makeshift weaponry such as Submachine Guns, Autocannons and Pipe Bombs. It's amazing what you can make out of pens, paper clips, staplers and a few Stick-It Notes in a Zombie Apocalypse. Now all I had to do was get out alive.
Crouched amongst a clump of ugly grey office partitions I waited patiently for a nearby zombie to amble past. That's when I made the noob mistake. Moving backwards I inadvertently stepped on a plastic cup. One of those you find at water fountains, a popular congregation spot for malingering employees feigning thirst. The loud crunch it made attracted the attention of the zombie and it immediately began to lurch toward me.
As the zombie got closer I could see the ravenous look in its dead eyes. Its gaping maw a cavern full of fetid brown teeth. Its putrid breath reeked of decay and the unmistakable miasma of the walking dead. Initially I was paralysed with terror, then recognition struck. It was Dave, an ex-colleague of mine. A soulless Ginger, now just undead. Poor Dave, he didn't deserve this!
Dave stared at me, perhaps a silent entreaty for absolution. I would end his suffering but all I had was a clipboard. Clipboards whilst good for repelling Mall pedestrians are worthless against zombies who are not afraid of marketing surveys. "Get back!" I yelled as I brandished the clipboard menacingly. But Zombie-Dave was relentless. Suddenly it stopped and to my utter astonishment said, "What the frak are you doing? You coming to the meeting or what?"
Goddamnedsonofa♥♥♥♥♥! It turned out that the Zombie Apocalypse hadn't started yet and it's just another day at the office. Also, I may have had too many drinks over lunch. Dave's eyes narrowed suspiciously as he spied the boxes of office stationery I cradled protectively in my arms, "You stealing office supplies again?"
"No!" I yelled in protest. "It's for the Zombie Apocalypse. You'll see." Dave looked dubious as he ambled away.
"You really should get those teeth looked at," I suggested helpfully, but Dave just waved his hand dismissively without looking back. "Some breath mints would be nice too," I added
, but Dave was already out of earshot.
Dead Rising 2 is an open-world third-person action game set in a fictional casino town beset by a Zombie Apocalypse. The environment is detailed and very well modelled comprising shopping malls, food courts and casinos. A crafting aficionado's dream, there is an incredible amount of paraphernalia about that can be used to craft a veritable cornucopia of zombie-eviscerating weapons from Spiked Bats to Sentry Guns. Some of which are more practical than others, but almost all hilarious. Support items such as health restoring drinks can also be crafted.
The main disappointment in the game is in the use of timed missions to create artificial urgency. Each mission has a timer and if not completed in the time allotted results in failure which may end the game. This forces the player to dash from one mission to the next leaving insufficient time for casual exploration and 'playing' with zombies. An untimed sandbox mode would have been nice, but is only available in the standalone remake Off The Record. It is possible to stop the timer using third-party utilities such as CheatEngine, but a modicum of technical ability is required.
Being a console port, inventory management seems to be unnecessarily unwieldy for PC players, although overall it seems to be a good port. Definitely one of the better zombie games around and a worthy addition to the Zombie Apocalypse genre.

Harlan Ellison's "I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream"(1995) is an excellent example of how, when turning a story into a video game, you don't have to sacrifice anything. Ellison's direct involvement in the game definitely shows and his voice as AM, the machine God, is brilliant.
The storytelling in the game creates a very immersive experience, drawing you into each character's mind and torment.  You learn the deepest secrets and darkest fears, even the outrageous desires of these character's and the realistic reactions really put you in the character's shoes.
The premise of the game alone brings intrigue but the unfolding of this story in such a mysterious way is really what drew me in, I wanted to learn as much as I could about the post-apocalyptic world that was presented to me.  The idea of a super AI turning itself into a type of God is interesting indeed.
The story is so excellently encapsulated, the imagery is macabre and barren, and it's all brought together here marvellously.  Nothing is left out, in fact, in the gaming format you have an opportunity to explore beyond the main narrative.
Point and click at its finest.
I can also say, having played this back in the 90s, that this Steam version works really well and I believe the game has aged  nicely.

If Hotline Miami, Binding of Isaac, Smash TV, and Blade Runner all had a baby then that baby would be Neon Chrome. You might say to yourself: three video games and one popular sci-fi movie can't make a baby. OK, fine. Maybe Neon Chrome is more like an abomination unto nature.
Say what you will. At 15 bucks there's a lot to like about Neon Chrome. It's shiny. There's a ton of replay value. And the combat system rewards leveling via multiple-playthroughs without feeling grindy. That's a tough line to walk and Neon Chrome does some Fred Astaire ^#$@ on that line. What I'm trying to tell you is that the core gameplay here is great.
The boss battles are anti-climatic, the voice acting is Saturday morning cartoon level, and some of the graphics look like they were built from Lego knock-off brands.
But much like the beloved creme egg (or I guess...all eggs) the quality center of rougelike gameplay awaits you. If you like top-down shooters or any of the other baby-making stuff I mentioned earlier then this game is for you.

Hoo boy, what happened to this game? Prior to this one the X series had been rehashed an absolutely ridiculous amount... This time Egosoft decided to try something completely new it seems. Of course they only have like 20 people, so that may not have been the best course to take even with 5 years or so to work on it. As a fan of the X series I can tell about 30 minutes in that they tried to change way too much in one game and it really didn't work out for them. Does it deserve the metacritic it got though as of this writing? I can't speak for the release of the game but in its current state absolutely not. The game is playable and better than a lot of space sims I played, it's just not up to the standards of the X series.
First things first, the interface. X has always had a god awful interface that was the number one driver of the learning curve, so for Egosoft to make it even worse really is quite a something. This game isn't quite the menu hell that the others were, which really is shocking considering the number of complaints I see calling it that. There are plenty of menus, but I'd say overall it is fewer than prior entries to the series. However, even so everything is FAR more clunky. Far, FAR more clunky. The most glaring thing that stands out is that menus are no longer popups. You turn to the side and look at a screen as your ship comes to a complete stop. Greaaaaaaaaaat. No more multitasking allowed. One thing at a time only. And docking... goodness. Docking is even worse. You autodock now but you have to find the port since you can't lock on anymore. Then you get to walk around in the terribly optimized stations to do lots of things if you want to save money. This is particularly bad when it comes to repairing or dealing with black marketeers as you cannot even comms the people in question. It's neat that they added walking in stations to contribute to the atmosphere... unfortunately it seems like most of them look like carbon copies of one another.
On the upside because of all the interface changes the game is actually legitimately playable on a controller. Quite playable in fact. For all the complexities of X they actually managed to fit enough on an Xbox controller using every single button. That is impressive. You're still crippled as far as targeting goes but targeting in general seems very poor anyway. Space sims have always been a rather relaxing genre to play, so I would count being able to use a controller without a keyboard backup as a major plus. Just chilling, relaxing... flying... Don't expect to sit far away from your screen though as the fonts are incredibly tiny and a strain to read even sitting at the desk. For a space sim and especially the X series you need to play a lot more actively than usual too. It's pretty clear this was an intentional design decision as early on in development Egosoft had stated SETA (up to 10x speed time skip) was going to be going away. Although I recognize and agree that it's not the best of design mechanics, I don't really agree with the design changes they made to fill the gap. The space "zones" are smaller and focused, with green streams along them called highways. While you are in a highway you basically play Andy's Asteroids from Earthworm Jim, either going really slow or dodging ships. It's kind of neat at first, but it gets old rather quickly. The autopilot is also completely and utterly unable to do this, so it never ever goes away. It also means no more autopiloting to distant sectors. You have to fly ever single kilometer on your own. I can't think of a single decent spacesim in recent history where this has been the case. Not necessarily a bad thing, but its definitely a major detractor for me when I was sitting in a capital class transport just giving orders to my massive fleet near the end of X3TC.
Other smaller problems are the performance and a glitch. X3TC was quite difficult to run so this is nothing new, but this is for so little! The graphics are better but not by much. All the humanoids of the X Universe have awkward animations (most of all your lovely co-pilot whose comments you cannot turn off), poor quality models, bas voice acting... The aforementioned space stations run absolutely horribly for a narrow hall, worst I've ever seen. In space the stations are big and there really can't be a draw distance limit in space, but seriously? What happened to LOD?  There was only two sectors that had mega fps issues back in X3, but it seems ever present in Rebirth which is a real shame. As far as glitches go... Based on everything I heard about on release it must have been way worse on release. Now it seems relatively bug free, save for one thing. The combat. I still see enemy ships just frozen in place about 40% of the time. Once was even during a story mission where the objective was 'Survive' and I was horribly confused... The game is not bug free, even now, over a year later. Not terribly surprising given the fact that Egosoft never fixed a bunch of simple things in their older games, like the landing music being five times as loud as everything else.
Even with its issues it's better than a lot of space sims out there... but if you compare it to its predecessors in the franchise it simply is not up to snuff. So much is gone for so little gained; I've tried to be objective in evaluating it as its own thing but it's very difficult to do so when you look at how much you could do in prior games vs. this one. On it's own, X Rebirth is mediocre. As a franchise that has built on itself incrementally, it is easily the worst entry. The thought that I may never get X4 or that it'll be similar to Rebirth makes me very sad.

Return to Castle Wolfenstein is a blast, offering a variety of locations and some decently sized levels to explore and usually get lost in. Chewing up enemies is fun, with punchy weapons and great animations.
Enemy AI is generally great, with them retreating, throwing grenades and such. They are deathly accurate, though, which can start to grate especially when the draw distance fog starts to conceal distant snipers. There's not a lot of enemy variety, which honestly I was grateful for later on as the few unique enemies thrown at you are annoying at best, outright infuriating at worst. You won't miss the shield guys, or those bloody jumpy ones. God, the jumpy ones. You'll mostly fight soldiers and given how great their AI is, it really doesn't get old.
There's a decent arsenal but honestly I found myself just using the automatics most of the time, and the sniper rifle in open areas. There are no shotguns, which is a shame, and a few cool weapons like the flamethrower which while neat take a second or two to ignite enemies (in which they almost always get a shot or two in, making it entirely counter-productive). Weapons feel punchy and the feedback is great, so again didn't get bored of chewing through guys with the MP40 level after level.
The story is entirely forgettable, but servicable enough to set up travelling to new areas and giving you a motive. The missions themselves shine on their own, particularily covertly infiltrating a V2 missile base and blasting through the titular castle. The plot wont suck you in, but you don't seek out an old school shooter like this for the story.
In short; generally great, few sucky moments like the Crypt and X-Labs but many more great misssions and yeah, would definitely recommend to fans of old style shooters.

10 Reasons why "I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream" is awesome and you should totally buy+play it before your next birthday...
1. Starring ... HARLAN ELLISON
For those unaware, this P&C Adventure game is based on the dystopian post-apocalyptic sci-fi short story of the same name, written by Harlan Ellison in 1967. Nearly 30 years later, a team of game devs decide to make the game, and they contact Ellison for permission to make the game, and not only do they get permission, they *get him to voice the villain* (who is, in some sense, the story's chief character). "AM" wouldn't be half as awesome without Ellison. He was about 60 at the time and about 80 now ... yes, still alive ... and it'd be great if Steam players newly discovering the game wrote him fanmail about how the game inspired them to read his work, etcetc... ^_^
2. Aged Gracefully
For a 1995 PC game, the game's graphics are decent, the audio is of the same variety as (but in many ways superior to) the first two Elder Scrolls games, and the engine is surprisingly stable. Based on other reviews I've read, your mileage may vary, but I had exactly zero crashes in a multi-faceted playthrough (testing different fail-states and endings, etc). As a huge Adventure buff, I can assure you that there are dozens, perhaps hundreds of games released in the past two decades that won't be as valuable 20 years down the road as this one turned out to be.
3. Not just full VA ... *good* VA
I'll have to take exception to Dr. Nimdok, whose slow, aged German accent sometimes misses the mark, especially as to which words or syllables to stress. Other than that, the character VA in this game is leaps and bounds beyond its 1995 peers. I suspect this is because the actors were getting to read lines either directly from, or inspired by, the original short story, which is quite well-written. So good.
4. "Dude, that's not PC!"
Real characters have flaws. Real characters don't give a crap about whether they're being politically correct or not, especially when they're on their own and have survived 100+ years of torture by a mad machine. I'm not praising this as though it's something to be cherished: rather, I'm saying that the surly nature of Benny, the rugged trucker-ness of Gor, and pretty much the entire Nimrok scenario make for a pretty provocative game. I suppose the open talk about Ellen's plight would also apply.
5. Fail-States exist, but they don't over-punish
Because this game is paced out *just right,* if you accidently off your character and lose progress, it's not a huge deal. The five scenarios are each short enough that you'll a) remember the puzzles well enough to quickly recover progress if needed or b) you'll have saved like 2 minutes beforehand and then it *really* doesn't matter. That said, there are ways for characters to die -- some more easily than others. And in the end scenario, it gets really tricky...
6. Endings galore
There are, in fact, five bad endings and one good ending. It's in the end scenario that the game takes the strongest departure from the short story: the latter offers a fight scene between two of the characters that, due to the way the game is structured, simply wasn't going to happen. However, the five bad endings of the game combined make up, in essence, what Harlan Ellison originally wrote. Each character will deliver those famous words after describing in wretched detail what AM has done to them for the rest of eternity after their failed assassination attempt. BUT, should you get the "true" ending (not at all in Ellison's story, but apparently Ellison-approved since he voiced his dialogue for this ending), there's something horribly fascinating waiting at the end, including some excellent philosophy that fits very much with this and Ellison's other tales.
7. Click what where with what, oh it's too much! -- No it's not.
One thing I've found in the Adventure revival of the past 5 years is an over-abundance of items in my inventory. It gets to be a bit *too* much. In IHNM, however, the standard view of the inventory shows only 8 slots. This will actually expand (and has to in at least one scenario). Yet, in another scenario, the number of items only goes as high as three. As for interaction options, you have the basic set: Walk to, Talk to, Look, Use, Take. Give, Push, and my favorite, Swallow. And that's it. That's all you need to get around, and with the narration and a little bit of clever thinking, you'll find many of the puzzles solve themselves. That said...
8. Walkthrough-friendly
Should you need to turn to a walkthrough (GameFAQs has three at present), it's pretty easy to figure out where to look. Most people won't need it until they reach the end, and if they find themselves exasperated (especially by which character order to use) then a walkthrough can spell it out. Quickly, and painlessly, without the pain of a thousand qualifications ("if you've done this, don't do that" etc). The complexity of this game is in its narrative. The mechanics and puzzle-solving are less dense, though they can still be tricky even on that surface layer.
9. Did I mention the length?
This game is of the perfect length for most 21st-century gamers. The devs were ahead of their time in this regard. Its peers were often packing in filler content to brag about how many hours the player could get out of it. And then, on the other hand, there are a handful of P&C Adventures so pathetically short that they're hardly worth calling a game. This one fits just right: 2 hours with a walkthrough, 5-8 without (that range I'd give based on players' range of problem-solving capabilities and/or desire to skip voice acting with right-click spam).
10. We vote with our dollars
If the other nine points have convinced you that this game might actually be *good,* let me remind you here at the end: Steam notices what kinds of games we buy. How much of any given title is purchased will mean something to them. Financially it also means something to the rights-holders of this game. And while it could crash and burn miserably, I'd not be opposed to a huge overhaul / HD remake of this very game -- sometimes the risk pays off. Or, perhaps, it would inspire other developers to do decent P&C adventures with weighty/heady sci-fi short stories from other great authors. This game proved it could be done, and done well.

I've enjoyed Betrayer so far, having played quite a few hours to get a feel for the atmosphere, mechanics and enemies. I recommend it strongly if spotted on sale, and a warm recommendation at regular price especially if you are a cheap ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ like myself.
The game isn't hard to figure out or learn to play, though the introduction scene is short and is not comprehensive. I would have liked to be able to practice more sneaking and using the bow before moving into the game world proper, as this is the majority of the gameplay.
Betrayer relies on text in scraps of notes or with NPCs to transmit the details of the world. If reading a sentence of exposition or a super-short paragraph of dialogue isn't your thing, you've been warned.
I appreciate being able to piece together ghost stories by finding clues with the 'listen' mechanic. Finding treasure chests and other goodies while stumbling through the wilderness adds to the experience.
As I said, sneaking and stealth kills are the majority of the game. How stealthy you are to the enemy is not communicated to the player besides simple simple video game common sense. Crouching and walking are near silent, walking is loud, running is right out. Being in shadows seems to help tremendously, though if you are within line of sight of an enemy looking in your direction you are likely to be found out regardless. Detection distance is irregular. Sometimes I'll be spotted across a flat field with little ground cover, sometimes I can get away with it. This isn't terrible, but it forces the player to be cautious, especially since it is easy to be overwhelmed.
All out combat isn't preferable because the player is fragile. A group of enemies is deadly, and it is best to pick them off with stealthy arrow kills. (You deal more damage when the enemy has not detected you yet according to the tutorial.) When hard combat becomes necessary, it is difficult enough to survive that you learn quickly not to charge into any group of foes.
Progression is measured in areas you move into, as well as what items are available in the shop (which also become available as you move to new maps). The weapons handle distinctly and feel great. Charms add passive bonuses to actions (musket reload speed, run speed, stealth, etc) and most everything you need can be found or purchased. Broken or shoddy versions of weapons can be found on enemies and sold for currency right in the field from the inventory screen. Ammunition is picked up from enemies or purchased from the shop. The game also allows you to conservatively retrieve arrows and other thrown weapons' ammunition from dead enemies. If you miss, sometimes I've been lucky enough to find the arrow in a tree, bush, or in the ground far behind the intended target. Ammo bought at the shop is cheap, but money is better spent on fancier versions of weapons to start, and this encouraged me to pick shots carefully.
The intial black and white visuals are what I heard and saw first about Betrayer. While it was a nice introduction to the game and set the tone appropriately, I eventually turned up the color to saturate the natural environment. This also grew tiresome because the bright red of clues and enemies was easily lost in the woody greens and fields. I opted for a medium saturation, and the game ends up looking washed out enough to know that there was color, but still allowing the red signals to catch the eye and keep the bleak, lonely feeling of the game world. This setting becomes moot in the shadow version of the world, where everything becomes black and white anyway, so I don't feel like it changes too much of the experience.
Sound, particularly listening to the environment, is
important in Betrayer. The primary 'listening' mechanic allows you to locate plot clues in the area by briefly adding markers to your compass HUD. The marks change width and brightness when your heading to the item is true, then fade out until you 'listen' again. It's an old idea, but I like the system because it is not as precise as a simple waypoint on your map and allows accidental exploration. Simply listening to ambient noise is incredibly helpful because item caches and enemies will make sounds at a distance as well. This gives the player the opportunity to explore, avoid, or maneuver around these opportunities. I appreciate that different enemies will make different noises. For example, I did not figure out until the umpteenth ambush that Naturals have a birdcall idling sound; I previously thought it was an ambient bird sound from the forest. Again, this is an old idea, but it fits well with the gameplay and setting, and is executed very well.
Mystery, suspense, horror, paranormal activity, and good old-fashioned, New World mysticism are all wrapped into one tight package. Hours of fun were had combing the woods, listening tensely, and hunting Spaniards. I'd give it a solid 9.2/10, an A-, a 4.7 out of 5. Play it, especially if it goes on sale again.

I'm on the fence here.
I like civ games. I'm usually horrible at them.  Even on the simplest difficulty, restarting is almost always a must until the background of the game can be figured out.  But not this one.  In my mind, that's not a selling point.  It's just out of place for the genre.
More often than not, civ games boil down into some form of rock paper scissors that only escalates with time.  CivBE doesn't really have that aspect.  Ranged units are aweful until they're not, at which point going toe-to-toe with someone is relatively meaningless.  Everything seems to be about a culture and tech race - escalate culture to escalate progress, which fuels the system.
The game is just too simple, which is sad.  More reminiscent of a RTS than a 4x.
I've got one other big gripe, which is that there is no predictable way to flesh out affinity.  If affinity were a resource which could be gathered or built up like their other strategic resources, I could understand.  The "questing system" only rarely offers bonuses to affinity (and does it far too early), and some planning is required until mid-game to make sure units keep up.  Then everything just stops mattering, and becomes a 20-30 turn research run for wonder requirements.
That and politics is a joke.  It might be nice if I could actually get some help in a war rather than just fending people off because I don't want to give them energy for favors which aren't usable until after they're worthless. But it's kind of expected with a Civ game launch.

Saints Row Gat out of Hell... the standalone expansion to Saints Row IV, though Saints Row IV was supposed to be an expansion of Saints Row The Third as well. I love the Saints Row series, it is surely one of the most fun open world game series of all time. While I mostly dislike Saints Row 3 for its crappy humour (sex jokes everywhere) and absolutely unfulfilling story mode (which heavily reused side activities), SR4 came out to be an absolutely amazing masterpiece - to me, at least. While it was downright insultingly easy (lol), I found it fun and the side stuff was the best part of the game. This game is literally SR4 in a new city. Well, shall we say, a reskinned SR4? But it ain't exactly that.
The gameplay in this game remains almost unchanged from SR4 though flying was added. Flying is absolutely amazing and feels like something that should have been in SR4 (you could only glide in that one). The city of New Hades is almost like a mixture of Saints Row 2's Stilwater and Saints Row 3's Steelport. Graphics are nothing special unfortunately, however it certainly doesn't look bad!! Saints Row IV looked better in my opinion. But in this game, it isn't as copy and paste as SR4 was from SR3. Car models are slightly altered, there are new guns, a whole new city, etc.
The game proved to be decently lengthy for the price, clocking in at around 7.5 hours to beat (main story and all side activities. Little collectibles.), and maybe a maximum of 10 hours to get all the endings, which thankfully you don't have to replay the game in order to get them.
I had an absolute blast, as I did with SR4. However this game is a lot harder, but to ensure challenge just don't upgrade health. Maybe 1 level maximum if you want a decent challenge. Hardcore is ALMOST brutal.
Other than that I would give the game a great recommendation. On a sale it is a great run for your money (£2.74), but for full price, I wouldn't really advise it. Get this only if you liked Saints Row IV, or if you like the SR series in general.

It's fun to feel godlike when firing 20 broadside cannons and killing ships that used to give you trouble in a couple of shots. This wears out pretty quickly though and I find myself wishing they would throw more at me to match the level of my ship.
Once the storyline is finished I don't feel there is a lot of replayability, there's no real "other" way to play the game except as maybe an outlaw, which will severely limit the number of stations you can visit and missions you can take.

Although the learning curve can be a bit steep at first, the interface is actually quite helpful and easy to use once learned.

There are many types of ships at your disposal to conquer your enemies with, from the humble scout frigate, used to explore and find new planets, to the Titan, capable of taking on entire fleets at once. Micromanagement and fleet planning is definitely reccomended to get the most mileage out of your ships during battle.
The only true downside to this game is the sheer amount of time that multiplayer games can drag on for, depending of course on the skill of your opponent(s), and the map size.  The ability to have a vote to change the speed of an MP game, similar to Empire Total War, would definitely reduce the drag of playing online matches.
Have you always wanted to rule the galaxy, and have a blast while doing it?
If so, this game is for you!

It's good. Really, it is. It's not, however, amazing.
The short:
The storyline is... cursory, at best. The game would lose virtually nothing if it weren't there at all. There are some annoyances in missions and travelling, and you need to be comfortable with the need to grind for gear, but all in all it's a very enjoyable space shooter.
The long:
As I've seen mentioned in other reviews, there's an almost consistent misrepresentation of the mission risk. Low? It could be, then again you could also barely make it out with an inch of hull left. Other times you end up against a ship you literally do not have the damage output to even touch the shields on. High? It could be. It could also be a milk run. It just doesn't make any sense.
You do learn to recognize them, though. Some mission types seem straight forward, but will always end with you having to deliver something to a station that's under siege. Skip those. Escort missions are a pain, as in pretty much all games, Fancy waiting 2-3 minutes while your ship lines itself up for the escort? Fancy doing that numerous times as the journey is interrupted along the way? How about inside an asteroid field, where your ship keeps getting stuck on rocks, adding another few minutes. At first, I learned this was a perfect time to go fetch something to drink. Or check email. Or read a page or two of a book. Later, I learned to just save my sanity and skip them. Eventually I did learn a set of mission types I could reliably predict the difficulty of, and I just stuck with those and ignored everything else.
There's a fair amount of travelling required, which is to be expected. Space is big, after all. What isn't fine is how often your travels are interrupted. There are countless asteroid and junk fields littered about, and odds are you'll be pulled out of warp a handful of times on most journeys. Which means you then need to crawl along to the edge before you can get back up to speed. If you pay attention you can spot some of them and go around. Not going in a straight line from one place to the next, also seems to help. Then there are the random enemy encounters, which have the same effect of slowing you down. You can spend time fighting them (if they are ship types and numbers you can handle), for loot worth next to nothing most of the time, or turn your tail and boost out of there. In most cases that'll have you on your way again in 30 seconds or so.
So why the heck am I recommending it? I guess I must really like spaceships. And lasers. I had great fun, despite the above mentioned drawbacks. Enough so that I put 40 hours into it. After finishing the story, I kept going until I had the best ship fully upgraded. I then went back in a few more times to just fly around enjoying being invincible. For entertainment value, it was a bargain for the price.

Once again, you return to Rapture in this amazing sequel. BioShock 2 is absolutley outstanding. With better gameplay and graphics, BioShock 2 is an insanely fun ride. The only thing BioShock 2 is lacking is in story. Don't get me wrong, the story in BioShock 2 is one of the best I've ever played in a video game. It further fleshes out characters including Andrew Ryan, Tenenbaum, and even Jack (the main protagonist for the first BioShock). But, BioShock 2's story is in the shadow of the first BioShock. Most of the new characters you meet aren't all that interesting (besides Sofia Lamb and Sinclair) and some of the story feels like filler to make the game longer. For example, you need to get through a door but you can't so you have to go find something to open it. But when you find what you need to open the first door, you can't get it because it's behind ANOTHER door that won't open. So then, you have to find something else to open the second door. AND THIS KEEPS HAPPENING! While the story gives a little something to be desired, BioShock 2 more than makes up for it with it's INCREDIBLE new gameplay. Unlike the first game, the player can use BOTH plasmids and weapons at the same time. This can lead to devastating attacks on enemies. Some new upgrades for plasmids have also been added into the mix as well. You can go from just setting someone on fire, to shooting a constant stream of fire out of your palm. The revised gameplay is easily the best thing about BioShock 2. While BioShock 2 does have its flaws, it is still one of the best FPS' out there. I highly recommend this one.

I recommend Rebel Galaxy, but you've got to know what you're getting into.
Rebel Galaxy initially has far more personality than many of its peers in the "randomly generated open world space game" genre.  Unfortunately, the space cowboy facade wears off pretty quickly and the game still boils down to being the same sort of soulless mechanical grind as every other open world space game. The only thing compelling you to play the game is getting the next bigger ship, until you finally get the biggest one, and then you're left only a bit of a hollow feeling at having wasted so much time doing the same things over, and over...and over.
So why the thumbs up in spite of these gripes?  Because it's priced right and I knew that's what I was getting going in.  For what it is, it's quite fun to play; it strips away some of the unnecessary complexity of similar games and lends itself to being played in short bouts - which makes it far more palatable to me than some of these games which require an hour just to make one profitable cargo run (you know which ones I'm talking about...). It scratches an itch for space shootin' without being particularly cumbersome to play. I've had enough fun with it for the price that even if I had stopped playing before getting the biggest ship, I would have been satisfied.
Just go in knowing that there's a "honeymoon" period with this game that eventually wears away before the raw mechanical nature of it is laid bare and if you start getting bored.  After that, I recommend treating it as a "filler game" you play in short bouts between doing other things and you'll enjoy it.
I do have a couple specific nitpicks that I will list only in the event that they could be taken into account for future improvement:
The soundtrack is great...but it makes me realize why some other space games have "ambient" orchestral soundtracks.  The game can easily sustain many, many more hours of gameplay than there's soundtrack to cover and the 10th time you hear the same song, it will start to drive you nuts.  There are simply not enough songs in the game.  You can import your own custom soundtrack and that's good, but requiring a player to go to the effort of cultivating his own soundtrack just to avoid being driven insane by the hearing same steel guitar alt-country song for the 65th time is a problem.
Regarding the ship models, it became a little too apparent that some were done via contract work or perhaps even just bought off a content store.  The first few ships were very clearly designed to fit the game.  However, some of the later model ships have designs that don't really gel with the visual design of other ships in the game (even accounting for them coming from different alien races). Some have turrets in spots that don't really make sense for the game's mechanics (which ends up in the turret being fairly useless because it's often blocked by the ship's own geometry), or the broadside fire coming out of parts of the model that don't look like they were designed for that purpose.  I wish every ship in the game was as carefully designed as the starter ships.

As someone who played a lot of X3 years ago, which was my first and technically only X game i've ever played (also Terran Conflict), I cannot recommend X Rebirth, unless you can get it on sale.
It feels clunky and unpolished in every way, compared to the previous game. There's some new features, and you can clearly see how ambitious Egosoft were. For example, you can walk around your ship, see the crew compartments and stuff. You can also walk around the stations when you dock, and talk to weird german aliens and loot crates like some kleptomaniac RPG hero, also you can hack things to make the station vulnerable to attacks or something. All this walking around stuff didn't look very functional, but it's kinda cool, i guess. Even if your ship and the stations look like crap on the inside. Also the denizens don't look too good. They look horrible, actually. It's like Egosoft pulled their models out of some weird european FPS from 2003.
Me myself, i was fine with being locked up on my ship all the time back in the X3 days of yore, staring out into space even as i docked into stations.
Voice acting never was the strongest part of the X games, i suppose, but this game, which heavily depends on it, because it brings you closer to the actual people aboard the stations and your own ship, has some terrible, god awful english voice acting. Everything except for our smarmy space trucker hero talks like a robot, trying to communicate in what it thinks is English language.
Oh, and there's supposedly only one ship you're piloting for the entire game, which you got from the beginning, which is some sort of an argon corvet (i guess?) called the "Albion Pride". It's not a big deal, having only one ship for the entire game, considering that corvets are probably the most flexible type of ships and most players stick to those. You can also upgrade it in some ways to suit your needs, from what i've seen.
Even after two years, as of patch 3.50, it's horribly unoptimized. My rig is i5 3570, GTX 660 and 8 gigs of RAM, and since NVIDIA Expirience doesn't support X Rebirth, i thought i should keep the graphics somewhere in the middle. And it still lagged like hell, somewhere around 30 fps most of the time.
Egosoft were very ambitious with this game, and i respect that. Unfortunately, X Rebirth doesn't feel good to play and i couldn't bring myself to play it for more than 0.8 hours.
Some people say that the germans can only make crappy point-n-click adventures, and i strongly disagree. There's a company called Egosoft, which created some of the best games i've ever played. I'll be waiting for the next X. Good luck to you, guys.

As a player who can barely get into the other X games, I was kinda worried about getting this game on release day. 1 year and a half later, this game goes on sale for 15$ and they even offered a free weekend period for the skeptics. I decided to jump in, and I was extremely pleased with what I found:
-The most immersive space game I have played, second only to Freelancer ( I miss you Freelancer :'I )
-Actual effort in the soundtrack!!!! (God, I can listen to this all day)
- U.I. that is more friendly than past X games.
- Hiring and assigning employees is easier than ever.

- Combat, while not as creative as Starpoint Gemini, is still satisfying and epic!
Sidenote: The fact that you can control only one ship might♥♥♥♥♥♥off a few people, but I find that it contributes to the personal side of the experience.
Other than framerate issues, I haven't experienced many negatives in this game (yet). I will update this review accordingly.

-Ram leak, which forces me to restart the game every 2-3 hours (not too bad, but I have 8 gb, I can't imagine those with 4)
-Having fleets is quite awesome, but capital ships seem to collide with each other WAY too often. I personally fixed this by making  2 capital ships follow another, and that other follows me.
-Be careful what mods you put, it might prevent the trigger of important story events.

Some people have complained about the time restrictive format of this game. It can be off putting at first, but once you understand how everything works, it gets less frustrating. I highly recommend this game and look forward to playing it again sometime in the future. I rate it 8.5/10.
Anyway, thanks for reading and don't forget to like this review if you found it helpful ;-)

Original text: This isn't a bad game, just not everything it could be, and not worth its current price of $20. I also feel it didn't deserve the hype or the AO rating from the ESRB. But it's technically not the dev's fault about the hype, only those stupid media outlets.
There are 7 levels and most of them take place in an open outdoors area. The primary objective in most of them is simply to kill X number of people, then usually after that X number of some kind of law enforcement. Most levels have "side-quests" but really it's just going to the icon on the minimap and killing more people there. Completing these side-quests gives you a respawn point aka extra life. Once you run out and die you must start the level over.
The only way to gain health is to do executions on dying or stunned people. An interesting mechanic. By my count there's only about 8 guns in the game and 3 grenades. You've got a pistol, a machine pistol I only ever saw once on the train level (EDIT: It's an uzi and you do also see it on the next level),  3 different types of automatics, a shotgun, a flamethrower, and a bazooka. You can only carry 3 weapons at a time.
Pros:
+The AI for the cops and such are simple yet very effective. When you get to the later levels and there's more than a couple they will always endeavor to flank and surround you. Makes it quite challenging.
+Environmental destruction is really great! You can shoot/blow up walls to create new passages in a house if you want, or even drive a car into the house.
Neutral:
+-The aesthetic style of everything being in black and white except blood, explosive items, and anything lit by fire is interesting and not that bad, but I still would have much preferred everything to be in color. Because of lack of color everyone looks the same which ups the repetitiveness factor.
+-The executions aren't bad, but with the exception of the foot stomps aren't particularly gory. What makes this neutral is that I wish there was a lot more executions to see.
+-The main character is basically emotionless. Yes he has Hatred but it's always controlled. I feel they missed out on a lot of opportunities to up the fun factor if they gave him emotion and had him screaming and yelling at people, which would also enable him to be more emotionally involved in his killings and especially executions. All executions are silent regarding the main character, though sometimes he will say a line afterwards. I feel he should've had a wide variety of phrases to say during an execution such as brutally yelling "Die!" among many other possibilities.
Cons:
-What is afflicting the vast majority of people including me is incredibly bad stability and very poor optimization resulting in terrible fps. Apparently it's a very common problem with Unreal Engine 4. The devs appear to be quite willing to work on these issues so kudos to them.
-I hate how enemies can and will start shooting at you from off screen. In order to counter this you have to hold the right mouse button to do a fine aim which also let's you see further in the direction of your mouse pointer. Only problem is it doesn't work too well on areas below you and you can't rotate the angle (which is fine to me). What we need is a more zoomed out perspective, or enemies with shortened firing range.
-Not enough screaming or reactions from the people you kill, especially civilians who I would expect to do that more. Sometimes they plead but it's much too underplayed I feel. Not enough emotion here either.
I'm not a huge player of twin-stick shooters but this was one of the weakest that I've played. If this still looks interesting to you then I recommend waiting for it to get a nice discount.

Cards and Castles is one of the best free to play card games I have ever played. It is simple, easy to learn, not pay to win, and honestly doesn't have any crazy gimmicks to try to keep you playing, because its just good enough without them!. There are six deck factions, each with there own building, unit and spell cards. The factions are Vikings, Ninjas, Pirates, Warlocks, Crusaders, and Neutral. Each deck can only be comprised of neutral cards and one factions cards. as you play the cards in game they become playable pieces on a grid like board for you to command and move around your units for battle. The goal is to try to lower your opponents castle health to zero.
The game doesn't really have much more to it than that, but the gameplay is so simple and effective that it makes you want to not stop, something that for me personally is hard for a card game to do. Id recommend it to anyone who is a fan of free to play card games, and wants one they can play with pretty much anyone.

I am really up in the air on what to rate this, but since I've decided not to finish it, I suppose it's a thumbs down; however, if you like really good stories and don't mind using a walkthrough, this game would probably be a good choice for you.
Here's an example of what's wrong with this game *The following contains a small spoiler*
So when playing the doctor, you are going around and gathering items, interacting with people, etc.  At some point you have a jar with eyeballs in it and a box, along with a bunch of other stuff.  If you don't put the jar with the eyes in the box (but not any of the other stuff you're carrying), you will fail that character's story and be unable to complete the game.  I want to emphasize that there is no reason to actually combine the jar and the box.   There's no hint.  Nothing.  You just have to randomly decide to do it.  And this is not the only seemingly random action required to complete the story.  That's just the careless way the game was designed.
So after fnishing a section incorrectly, you can either reload a save a try again--though you likely won't get it the second time either without the walkthrough--or, if you were careless with your saving, start completely over.
It's just a potentially great game that suffers from the odd design choice to let players fail with no ability to retry and little direction on what went wrong.

Sid Meier's Civilization: Beyond Earth is much like the previous Civilization 5. You get thrown into a world where you rule a civilization and compete, barter, go to war with and befriend other civilizations on your way to conquer the world. This is a turn based strategy game on a hexagonal grid. When all your units have taken a turn, you let the next civilization have its turn. You start with a home settlement that increases in size over time. With each settlement, you select a unit or facility that will then be complete after X amount of turns. During your turn you'll also pick a technology to research that results in new facilities that can get unlocked to build in your settlements. Its all streamlined so you don't have to hunt for the next city or unit to move, you'll already have them selected.
It looks like plenty of people are complaining that this is too similar of a game to Civilization 5, and they're right. However, it still feels like a good fresh sci-fi version of the game. The previous Civilizations made good use of historic characters, but this game lacks those characters and that personality. They still manage to put in all Earth's nations into this game without any sort of alien races. The real hurdle for me was the game crashing every time after the opening cinematic. That seems to have gotten fixed.
No matter what randomly generated world you play, its a hostile one, full of insect aliens that will oppress you. They spawn from nests, attack your troops, and cities. It can be difficult to even get out of your cities to grow and thrive. The game has a combat edge to it. There are combat troops, both melee and long range that can fight on land, water and air.  The insects are there to grind and train your troops, to give them experience, get them leveled up with selectable perks for each level.  Melee units can only attack the tile next to them, while long ranged can attack up to two tiles away. Each unit has its own movement distance and you can set up a unit to move far away and it will get there over X amount of turns without you having to move it each and every turn.
Each unit has a wide array of commands, move, attack, explore, alert so they wake up if an enemy comes in range, fortify to heal themselves, and more. When you have a combat unit selected and hover your mouse over an enemy, you can see the likely outcome who will do more damage. Its a nice system.
Its not all combat though, there are worker units that will gather resources and build things. Thankfully you can assign a worker to work on his own so you don't need to control him. Explorers can find and mine resources. Colonists can go out and make a new settlement as long as its three tiles away from any other settlement. It is best to have an armed escort go with them, since they aren't meant for combat.
When a new settlement forms, it controls a few tiles around it, making that your territory. As the population grows, so does the radius of tiles. So you can connect your settlements into one big territory. Since its your territory, other civilizations need to ask for your permission to travel freely through it. They will offer you tributes for the rights and you barter back and forth with them to make a deal happen. Do you want energy (currency) each turn for their travel? Do you want rights to travel through their land as well? Do you even trust them to travel through your land? They could be setting up a siege to conquer your settlements.
The civilizations can be both nice and hostile. Some civilizations feel that your rapid expansion near their territory is a cause for concern and they'll warn you to stop. The game keeps track of your promises too. If you say you won't build another settlement, you might risk a war if you do. Then at some point the game will tell you that your promise has been kept and you can build another settlement at your leisure. Some will even warn you that you've slaughtered too many people or insects and you need to stop. Its all a delicate balance.
You can make alliances with countries, ask them if they'll go to war with another civilization. There is a lot of depth here, but some are justifiably unwilling to budge. Just because someone declared war on you doesn't mean one of your allies will help save you. There is a nifty diplomacy tab to see what is going on politically. Who is at war with who and your relationship to other civilizations.
If combat isn't your thing, there are covert ops. You can unlock the ability, build a facility, train your agents by defending your cities from spies that will steal your technology or energy. Then send your agents abroad to other cities and do the same to them. It also becomes a political issue, when agents are found or killed. Do you let it slide or declare war? Its all a way to get around combat. I did find a giant covert ops breaking bug. When an agent was idle, the covert ops panel was just black and empty.
Beyond Earth feels like a race to see who can decimate the other civilizations. A tranquil, relaxing game can turn very stressful when your neighbor picks a fight and declares war. I would say the game lets you play how you want, but like other Civilization games, I felt dragged into war, bullied and unable to stop it. If someone declares ware, you can always make a peace treaty by offering them up resources or things like cities. Yep you can give them your cities, because they'll take them anyway.
Settlements can defend themselves, but they'll soon get overwhelmed. Its really a competition over land. Who controls the most land. Who has the most settlements to generate things. There is a problem though. Sometimes the civilization outgrows its energy consumption. If energy consumption dips below the reserve energy supply, the units will begin to disband one per turn. This balances out the energy consumption, but makes units disappear and leaves you vulnerable. That is the risk you run having a grand civilization.
Sometimes there is not enough food in your cities and it will halt their growth. To compensate, you can unlock trade depots and trade convoys, then set their trade routes between settlements to distribute food, energy and resources.
For those that need goals, the game does have quests, but I found myself ignoring them to do what I wanted. Competing a quest, gives you a choice between two perks. It was always a real toss up. I never felt like any perk offered was that much of a game changer.
The game feels excessive when it comes to frills. There are civilization perk trees, technologies to unlock and even troop upgrades. The upgrades change every troop of that type. You even get to select a permanent perk for that type. The choice and the random worlds make for huge replay value. The excessive frills are useful for marathon games. You'll always have something new to unlock thousands of turns into the game. With different difficulties and different sizes of planets to inhabit, one game could go on forever!
Beyond Earth is still a good game, its just like Civilization 5 and its expansion with a sci-fi twist. I would have appreciated alien races other than insect fodder.

Metacritic is waaaaay off on this one.  Unless blackpowder has just made a ton of improvements and optimizations since it was released (or the review sites couldn't figure out how to enable the color instead of playing in black and white the entire time) then I just don't understand the low score.
Betrayer is awesome.  Huge, lush natural environments (some of the best graphics I've ever seen -- especially when the wind blows through all the bushes, grass and trees) with intelligent enemies (love the haunted Indians) that hide behind trees and crouch in bushes and hear your footsteps.  Solid story with depth in the gameplay.  Betrayer is a convincing, surreal world that I enjoyed losing myself in for the 12-14 hours I played it.
In fact, the only complaint I have about the game is that there's only one save slot.  My power was knocked out on my first play-through after I was already 9 hours into the game and my save corrupted on the outage.  Maybe it was for the best, though, as I honed my skills enough the second time through so I was able to progress even more smoothly to the end.
Ok, just one other complaint.  What were you thinking, blackpowder.. the game should default to color instead of black and white.  I don't know why anyone would want to play this beautiful game in black and white.  The color and lighting needs a little tweaking to get the right saturation, but once you do, wow, you have better looking natural environments than Skyrim does--and everything moves.  If you turn the draw distance up all the way then even the grass on that hill 1/4 mile ahead of you will lean when a gust of wind comes along.
Bought it on a 9.99$ sale here, but it's well worth $29.99 or more.  Get it.

Betrayer is much a game that doesn't hand anything to you and after your starting items and explanation of how the world works, it's much a game that leaves you on your own to fight for everything you have.
To be clear for those who are unsure if you like the visual style the game is going for, there are some very flexible options in the game that let you play with the color levels of the game so yes, you can play the game entirely in color even if you feel it might take away from the atmosphere.
That being said, Betrayer isn't some big game you should go into expecting a horrorifying experience. Betrayer has a serious level of atmosphere, but it ISN'T a horror game. There's ghosts abound, enemies that can be somewhat unnerving or startling but it is not a horror game.
It's a game about fighting off ghostly spaniards with the voices of hunting dogs and other ghastly creatures while trying to find clues as to what happened to this place that left it so lacking of life, a CSI Roanke if you will. That being said, some of the emotional punches of the game are lacking given that for likely budget reasons the game lacks voice actors.
I see you running away at the sight of those words, and please don't. Betrayer is a rather interesting game, a great game to get a break from the norm you're used to. You're stuck with colonial era weapons like single shot pistols, bows, rifles and tomahawks (all with their own upsides and downsides) which in addition to the health system at play which gives the intertwined combat and exploration a feel closer to hunting or carefully managing your supplies so you can stay alive longer and keep going.
Fights will often turn into an affair where the roles of the hunter and the hunted switch constantly as you and your mostly spaniard persuers trade rather high damage attacks. This is one of the few games I can think of where stealth isn't just a way to play that the game gives you if you for some reason don't prefer going guns blazing, but rather a rather sensible way to lessen your chances of getting seriously hurt and having to head back.
That being said, as atmospheric as the game is, and as cool as many of the concepts behind the game are, it can't hide it's budget for long. As cool as the location is and as tense as the combat can be, this is not a game I'd reccomend marathoning.
There's about 1 or maybe 2 if you're lucky new enemies every area you progress and after a while the gameplay mechanics can rub you the wrong way after having to listen to the wind and run toward the next clue for the 6th time with the same tricks employed over again. I'd personally reccomend taking breaks and playing something else every area or two just to keep things feeling a tad more fresh.
That being said, if you've liked the hunting feeling bits in games like Far Cry 3 or Skyrim, like atmosphere and exploring strange places and want to see a game that's not afraid to put you into a situation where a stand-up fight is not only a costly idea but one that might get you killed later down the line, I can't see a game that would give you a better breath of fresh air.
