Betrayer put me on quite an emotional roller coaster. The first few hours filled me with enthusiasm and excitement and the well known wow effect that arises when starting to explore a new world. The atmosphere of the game is fantastic and the black and white setting strongly supports that.
After reaching my first outpost, fighting off a few foes and making contact with the first supernatural elements in the game I found myself completely stranded. I was about four hours into the game, had searched the first map several times and was completely frustrated because I had no idea how to carry on from here. I had missed something important, but I was not aware of that and so the only way to carry on was to search the net. And I really hate it if a game leaves you so helpless that you have to search the net for help. At that point my frustration over the game was as big as my initial joy. I even thought about stopping to play Betrayer altogether.
Once I found out how to continue I learned the general pattern of the game and what is expected of you. A huge part of the game is exploring big forest areas in search of clues, chests, weapons, hints. Besides that you meet quite a number of wraiths, lost remains of British settlers that all have their own story to tell. Naturally, it is up to the player to uncover the secrets behind these stories.
This part of the game is actually fun. Either if you have a masochistic urge to search every square meter of huge forests while taking the chance of missing the clue that will allow you to carry on, or if you found some maps, like the ones provided by CrispyCrisis in his 'Betrayer Map Guide'. Even if you follow the maps you will have a lot of search to do and it is still possible that you will miss something- at least I did. But that might just be me. You may disclaim using a map but be aware that you can not finish the game without finding all clues. The game allows you to always come back to continue your search at any point of the game though.
So do I recommend playing Betrayer?
Yes I do, but this verdict comes with mixed emotions. The game has some pros and some cons.
Pros:
- great atmosphere
- nice graphics (the blur effect in the distance is intended)
- good story, or should I say stories
- quite addictive, you find yourself coming back until you reached the end
- nice ending, I can still feel my heart jump
- good sound effects, wind, distance screams, fearful grunts
- enemies, some reviews claim the enemy AI is dumb. Well, it is, but I like the fact that as soon as you are detected your foes attack you very aggressively. While it fits your enemies nature, it increases the pressure on the player. Enemies are hard to beat in the beginning and rather easy in the end because your equipment improves. You can sneak around to prevent detection.
- all achievements can be reached, the game never becomes unfair
Cons:
- can be extremely frustrating at times. The biggest downturn of the game is its lack of in-game support. As a player you are simply left to yourself to find out what to do and this can be a very frustrating experience. So you will need patience and endurance.
- Big Picture – Forget about it!
The game has controller support but it's quite buggy.
While the general game functions like running, fighting, aiming and interacting with the surroundings work perfectly, controller support sucks in the menus and in the inventory. If for example you scroll through the list of your weapons you can not move upwards once you reached the end of the list. You then have to close the inventory or move to another section of the inventory to get out of the list again.
The controller also does not work in the main menu. I always have to click on the button 'Continue' with my mouse and after that I can use my controller.
If you intend to play in big picture mode you can forget about that. For the first four hours I played the game launching on my couch. My TV is about 4 meters away from my couch and it's simply impossible to read anything on the screen because the font size of the messages and the menus is simply too small. I had to stand up and move close to my TV in order to read the text. That sucks!
But that's not the only problem in big picture mode. The game strongly depends on audio signals. If you move close to items, that you can inspect or pick up, a certain sound is played. Playing on my stereo TV did not allow me to determine the direction in which I had to move in order to move closer to the source of the sound. For the daytime mode that's not a big problem because you already are very close to the item when the tone appears. But for the 'dark' sections it is a huge problem because you have to follow sounds miles away.
After moving back to my PC I could clearly indicate the directions I had to move to and certainly had no more problems with the font size and the menus because I could use the mouse where necessary.

This War of Mine provides a unique look at war. Instead of being the heroic soldier, you are the victim, forced to make horrific life or death decisions. Every choice you make is morally questionable. For example: Some children come to your door, they ask for medicine for their sick mother. Do you give the kids the medicine? Even though you know, your people may become sick soon, and if they do, will have you have enough supplies to save them? Or do you keep the medicine? Do you let the little children's mother die, and as a result probably them with her, just to save yourself? This is only one of the many choices you will have to make in this game.
As far as gameplay goes, it fairly simple. Think of it as a Sims type game. By this I mean, you have 3 or 4 surviviors, and click on each one to make them do tasks. Such as cooking, sleeping, eating. The game only gets "real" gameplay at night. This is when you have to go to other locations in the city and scavenge for supplies. You click where you want your character to move, but have to silently navigate around, so as to not alert any possible enemies. All this while looting piles of rubble, and stealing from peoples cabinets.
In short, this game is incredibly difficult an depressing, while at the same time, fun, and rewarding if you manage to save the lives of your crew, and others. Get this game, or you will be missing out.

Every saga has to have a fitting epilogue, and SR: Gat out of Hell is a decent final chapter in wacky, crude, zany, filled to the brim with cultural references, emotional and bloody fun adventures of the Saints Row gang.
Everything that you loved in third and fourth sequel is here: one last outrageous campaign where after fighting the corrupt ULTOR Corporation, Killbane and its associates, and Zinyak the alien conqueror of planet Earth, it’s time to settle the scores with forces of Hell for kidnapping the President of U.S.A. If you were more of a fan of the first two games that were much more serious in tone, Gat out of Hell is going to irk you the most. This time you play as a fan favorite Gat and his trusty, psychotic sidekick Kinzie as you wreak chaos in ole Lucifer’s domain, by doing main missions and side activities while making as much havoc as possible. While for me personally, Saints Row 3 was the best game in the series, this one is the least exciting, due to the overall shortness of the game and its buggy nature. As an expansion, if you focus only on the main story, it’ll take you around five hours to beat the game, but with all the side activities you will have fun most of the time with clocking at around 20 hours max.
The impressive engine Volition has used in the last three games is finally showing its age, and while it still manages to look fine, the graphics wow factor is gone and the overall bland art direction coupled with washed out color palette makes Gat out of Hell visually forgettable and underused, especially if you consider the hellishly delightful look and style the game could have due to its themes. Also, the game is very buggy this time, with frequent flights to Windows or hard-crashes.
Story is the highlight however, and even though it’s short, it is still fun and exciting as it was in the previous SR games. The best bit: a surprising musical halfway in the game. A musical… in an action, open-world game! Singing of any sort is in extremely short supply in games overall, but when I found out there is a short musical in Saints Row title, I was grinning like crazy from joy. There are multiple endings this time, and all of them feel satisfying and complete, leaving zero chance to any possible sequels. This is it, one last love letter from its developers to the fans.
Action is still fun and hectic, like in previous SR games, where along great driving and shooting mechanics, coupled with super-sprint power from Saints Row 4, you have one more amazing addition: the power to fly. I cannot describe enough how good it feels to reach the brimstone skies and fly over the entire city of New Hades in a matter of minutes. It has to be experienced to be believed. Side activities unfortunately feel the most grinding this time. There was always an aspect of optional grinding for those who wanted to complete 100% in every previous SR game, but due to extremely low number of main quests and almost zero side quests, getting everything in Gat out of Hell for completionists is going to be an infernally repetitious task.
Sound is excellent as before, but I presume due to budget constraints and the game’s relatively low cost, there is no radio music to play and add to the atmosphere and enjoyment as with previous games. I wish they added the option to play music from hard drive like GTA 3 did. Travelling around Hell and creating chaos is going to feel underwhelming without some music to kick in.
Overall, Saints Row: Gat out of Hell is a mostly positive experience, as reviews right now suggest and gets a single thumb up from me. It is still crazy fun and one of the rare open-world GTA clones that doesn’t take itself seriously. After GTA Vice City and San Andreas, new GTA games became a bore to me, but Saints Row series carried their lost spirit and evolved enough to stand on its own feet. For that Volition, you have my thanks :D

Aiming to misbehave is not only rewarded but maybe even required to survive in Rebel Galaxy. Your goals are simple in the black, live, make money, and take care of anyone who tries to stop you from doing the other two. To help you is your trusty vessel of death and destruction, which can be armed to the teeth with guns, missiles, hull upgrades, shields, and gods know what. Along the way you will meet some interesting folk whom may or may not have your best interest at heart. While the main campaign does an okay job of expanding the universe. The meat of the game lies in combat, random events, and upgrading your vessel. The game itself is gorgeous, you can almost feel the sizzling heat of your cannons firing. The explosions of missiles rocking across your ship, and satisfaction of watching your enemies explode in a fiery death. All the ships look unique, the weapons have the proper amount of oomph behind them, and the soundtrack is a homage to Firefly. On top of all that sweetness, the game is really easy to get into and start playing. The game really reminds of AC: Black Flags naval combat, just this is in space. Same level of simplicity with more customization in weapons. Now Rebel Galaxy does have its occasional black holes. There are times where repetitive missions come into play and are required for equipment advancement. Lack of cosmetic customization feels like a miss in an outstandingly done game. The games story itself does feel like it could be a bit more exciting as well. Occasionally during combat it does feel odd you can't move up or down in space. Despite these issues, the game is still extremely well made. No bugs ever interrupted my gameplay. As far as replay goes, there are multiple factions to pursue an allegiance with and multiple play styles you can choose from. Be a bounty hunter, cartel member, or trader, the choice is up to you what role you will play in Rebel Galaxy.

Needs polish but I can forgive its sins since it was only $20.  Great space cowboy soundtrack, graphics, gameplay.  Yadda yadda.
What rustles my jimmies though is that it suffers from escort mission hell; something I'd hoped gaming had put behind it a long time ago.  Escort quests are quite simply, broken.  Slow, tedious and prone to utter disfunction.  Escorts will charge the nearest enemy capital ship and hump its broadside.  To proceed, you must endure the synchronized lumbering of both ships as they sluggishly array themselves for a joint warp jump constantly broken by dozens of random junk gravity wells and meaningless random hostile encounters.  More synchronized lumbering, jump, stop, fight/lumber some more, ad infinitum.  THEN you might not EVER reach your destination anyway as the pathing seems to bug out; I had one escort mission start/stop over 15 times before it broke entirely, seperating me from the escort mid jump and causing a mission failure on what felt like a half hour pain test.  A shame that the broken escort quest system was pushed out the door.  The whole sync-jump thing needs to go.  Have the damn escort follow YOU, not the other way around.
And upon first installation I had some random crash-your-pc bug going on.  A suggestion from the dev to turn on the vsync and swith the render engine to dx9 seemed to fix it though.  Kudos to the dev for quickly helping people in the forums with tech problems.
If it was a $60 game, I'd be angry.  I'm more forgiving of a budget title, especially since the rest of the game really is very nice, even the characters in the space stations and voice work.  Found amusement in just listening to the wierd animated alien jabber they came up with for some species rather than just clicking through it.  Despite my griping I have truly enjoyed my time with Rebel Galaxy and look forward to finishing it.  Better than many $60 titles I've picked up in my time.

Simple. Lonely. Desperate. Sparse 80s decor and lots of rain.
Ghost in the Shell + Frozen Synapse + F.E.A.R. + System Shock + NeuroVoider
With bossfights imported from Metal Gear but with the serious character of an Angband throwdown.
This is a game is a twin-stick shooter about the ballet of CQB. You manually push a cybernetically enhanced pawn across a Frozen Synapse-like landscape after some sort of bizzare robot uprising / AI mental takeover. Some of the pawns are great, and here is a game where you can play a cyber-ninja in thermoptic camo, equipped with seeker rockets, a super-sword and a repeating shotgun with 24 rounds in the mag.
It is about the long and lonely road through a very large building, one room entry at a time. It is intensely repetitive but never boring. The enemies are kind of dumb but that does not make it easy, and there is a good justification in the setting. (It's pretty questionable if they're fully themselves. You are a brainjacked meat puppet yourself, so it's got a certain abstract game-within-a-game aspect to it.)
The way the enemies behave makes it almost a procedural puzzler at points, then you mess up and it's wild gunfire and swinging monokatanas. Bossfights are mostly positional puzzles / position control challenges, however, the bosses do have attacks that will insta you so don't get complacent.
Worth your time if you wish you could take part in a lot of infantry combat in the milieu of Ghost In The Shell.

: 10tons Ltd
: 10tons Ltd
==========
I honestly don't remember where I got this game from, but I am so glad a friend mentioned it to me. Once I gave it a try, I was hooked for several days straight! I usually don't binge rogue-like games, but a very select few have managed to grab my attention. Neon Chrome is one of them.
==========
Neon Chrome is a cyberpunk top-down rogue-like twin stick shooter. You are an operative trying to take down a corporation called Neon Chrome, that's run by a ruthless Overseer. The premise revolves around sending your operative's consciousness into an "asset", sort of like in James Cameron's Avatar film. You then use this asset to navigate through the many floors of the Neon Chrome building, fighting your way to the Overseer at the top. There are a variety of weapons and enhancements to help you mow down the hordes of robotic enemies and guards that you'll ve facing.
As this game a rogue-like, expect to die. A lot. However, the money and experience you gain each run will help you progress further and further each run. You'll learn how certain enemies move and behave, their attack patterns, and the best tactics/weapons to use against each. Money collected can be spent on permanent stat upgrades, or even to pre-equip yoru next asset with weapons and enhancements of your choice. Every so often, usually at random, you'll come across special pods that bestow cybernetic boosts. These boost gives you special abilities or increase your stats by a large margin. For example, there is one that increases your HP by 50% and your speed by 25%. You keep these boosts for the entirety of each run once found (and they can be unlocked and found again later!), but they are lost if you die.
The Neon Chrome building is full of procedurally generated levels filled with traps, locked doors, and things that go boom. Almost everything you see can be blown up or destroyed....including precious loot boxes. Thin walls can be destroyed, but thick walls cannot. Locked doors can only be opened with keys, and these keys are either hidden in a room or held by a special Keymaster guard that must be defeated in order to obtain the key. You'll find all sorts of loot boxes, which usually contain money or energy tabs, which replenish your store of energy that is used on special attacks. Every 5 floors you'll unlock a "checkpoint", where you can start your next run from if you die.
==========
The overall look and feel of Neon Chrome is amazing. Very vibrant and colorful. Cyberpunk influences everywhere. I love the art direction. It's not super detailed, but it's good enough. The game works with what it has, and excels at what it aims to do. However it can sometimes be hard to keep track of your character amidst the explosions and ammo flying around. Different weapon types (laser, plasma, etc) have different colored projectiles, most enemies get a new color when you meet a new variant, and power-ups/collectibles are very well defined and easy to spot. Keymasters are clearly labeled with a big red "KEYMASTER" over their heads, and later on stronger, more dangerous guards have their names over them as well, some of the ones I remember seeing were "CHRIS", "SCOTT", and "LENNY".
==========
I love this game's soundtrack!!! There's a few different tracks, and they all have a different feel and energy to them. Boss music gets you pumped (like it should). Each floor has a different theme to it, and it changes when you move to a new floor. Overall the rest of the game sounds great. Explosions are awesome, even if they are your latest cause of death (and they will be quite often). Your different weapons types all sound different as well, so you can oftentimes tell what kind of weapon your opponents have just by listening to the sound and the rate of fire.
==========
I have no complaints here. The game runs nigh perfectly. I did not experience any problems whatsoever, even when there was total chaos on-screen. No dips in performance, freezes, or FPS loss. I played the game with my Logitech F310 controller, and it felt great. Left stick to move, right stick to aim, R2 to fire my gun, L2 to use my special ability, and L1 to break walls or smack things in the face with the butt of my gun. Simple, right? It's an effective control scheme and works very well.
==========
Neon Chrome is an excellent rogue-like/twin stick shooter. Challenging, fun, and in my opinion one of the better games to come out last year. I could kick myself for not having tried it sooner!

I've been a fan of this series for a long time. I held off buying Rebirth due to the very poor reviews it got on first release. So I was pleased to try it out for free this weekend on Steam. And I'm afraid that after 2 hours of playing time it is a firm thumbs down. I know 2 hours is not long, especially for a game like this which requires a lot of practice and perseverance. But 2 hours is long enough to know whether the basics are right. To decide whether you want to spend more time with it. And I don't. At the end of the 2 hours I am bewildered at the direction the studio has taken and the way the game has been implemented. Frustrating flight controls, mystifyingly pointless time consuming elements (highways, scanning, wandering around stations), uneven graphical quality (some aspects are good, some are appalling). What did the designers, developers and testers think they were doing? The studio should be embarrassed that it released this after a string of increasingly engrossing, enjoyable games. Yes, new ideas need to be dreamt up and encouraged. Games need to grow and develop. But ideas should only implemented if they add to the enjoyment of the game. This feels like a vanity project. Like someone important at the studio came up with a bunch of second rate ideas and no one else had the guts to stand up and say "No!" Well I am saying no - you are not getting my hard-earned cash for this nonsense. Terran Conflict wasn't without its challenges and frustrations but it had the basics right. What was being reborn here? A brain dead shuffling zombie, banging it's head against the cockpit door? This game is high on frustration, low on fun. Very disappointing.

As its core, Hatred is an interesting game because it reminds us how narrow, formulaic and claustrophobic gaming narratives can be. Imagine cinema without Scarface, Hannibal Lecter or even Mike Leigh's Johnny. Moral ambiguity is essential to the silver screen but remains only a distant hope on our monitors.
The game certainly has its limitations. The core mechanics are those of a middling-quality isometric shooter with some fine destruction physics. Moreover, no significant narrative is provided for the orgy of destruction. This could either be viewed as serving the nihilistic atmosphere, or be considered as a narrative failing when compared to cinematic anti-heroes.
However, considering that the utterances of Hatred's anti-hero are not especially inspired, it's perhaps for the better than the minimalistic approach has been taken - we are free to each craft our own reasons for the violence.
Positives:
- Good atmosphere; cold, grim visuals
- Surprisingly good physics & destruction via UE4. It works well when backed into an Apple Store's bathroom and gunning down soldiers, who finally bring the entire structure down, forcing a hasty run-and-gun exit through the rubble.
- Good concept
- One of the best flamethrowers since Return To Castle Wolfenstein.
Negatives:
- For a game so rooted in gunplay, the actual gun sounds lack punch.
- Something of a manufactured controversy - not really as violent or drastic as people might expect,
- A fundamentally simple game that would struggle to justify a higher price point.

- Speaking about the authors' commentary... they contain HUGE spoilers not only about this very game but also about the future ones! So my advice is to avoid them until you have played the whole saga, DLCs included.
- Last but not least, many Achievements are too difficult to unlock, in my opinion - and I am not a newbie.
All this being said, I want to repeat and underline that "BioShock Remastered" is simply fantastic: it has amazing scenes, cool characters and most of all a really intriguing story.
So yeah: I do definitely, totally reccomend it! I will play it again myself for sure...

Beyond Earth is certainly a game that takes a different aproach than previous Sid Meier's Civilization titles. However, this change is one I think they executed very well.
The largest of the changes I noticed was a completely different overall feel to the gameplay. In Beyond Earth the civilivation you are tasked to build is much more, say, you. You make many small quest decisions that give small boosts to certian areas, building up over time; tech progression is much less linear; there are many more types of military units; and you affinity level alters the appearance and fuctionality of nearly every unit. Add to these the new affinity victory paths, and the choices you make are suddenly much more important.
Overall, I found Beyond Earth massively entertaining and very worth buying.
(TIP: Aliens on normal settings will become provoked only if you attack them or a unit stops within two hexes of an active nest.)

Tiny and Big: Grandpa's Leftovers is a quirky little game I received through a Humble Bundle Indie Games bundle and it sat on my "To play" list for some time. Like many things involving Steam and the Humble Bundle, your games library can increase almost exponentially and like many others, this game was buried until a song from the soundtrack came on while I was driving home one day and I immediately put the whole album on and listened to it, especially the highly catchy track, Little Pretty Thing by 3typen featuring Bryan Kessler. I also logged onto my mobile Steam app and began downloading the game remotely (How many people forgot that you can do that?). Developed and Published by Black Pants Game Studio.
Gameplay: 86/100 B
The basics is all that exists here, in the world of Tiny and Big, with three added mechanics, a grappling hook to pull stones and statues around, a rocket gun to push stones and statues out of the way, and the main "weapon" of choice - a laser powered stone cutter. A majority of the game involves literally cutting your way through levels of stone in order to get to the next part of the stage mixed in with some platforming, that can be a little frustrating as your character, Tiny, does feel just a tad loose in the controls, but nothing a little adaptation can't fix. The niche mechanics are really nice for a good portion of the game, planning ahead in some cases as you try to figure out if you cut a platform, will fall in the direction you plan and land where you want it to. It can be really satisfying to watch a pillar fall and come crashing down to form a bridge for you to cross, makes you want to yell "TIMBER!" every time it happens. Unfortunately, at least for me, the charm wore off around 3/4ths of the way and I found myself just wildly cutting away, creating a pile of rubble to climb upon instead of a carefully crafted structure, but there is a deterrent to this strategy - wildly cutting around may inadvertently remove the support structure of something next to or above you and, much like [SPOILER WARNING] Clayton madly slicing away at vines in the climax of Disney's Tarzan, it will most likely become your downfall. That said, it's probably best to be careful when cutting away at a wall, because almost everything you can see is able to be cut by your laser tool.
Story: 83/100 B-
The story of Tiny and Big is silly at best, but I don't mean that in a bad way. It's charming and even cute at times, but make no mistake, it's not for children. The occasional curse word will remind you of the target audience. The basic premise of the story revolves around Big taking Tiny's underpants. Though there isn't really anything in terms or talking, it is all text driven, much like a comic book in motion. There's even "Bam," "Fizzle," and "Boom" word effects when stones crash to the ground ala Adam West Batman, further adding to type of story the game is presenting. It's simple, starts in the middle, and ends in the middle. It is not a plot meant to be taken in anything, just as it is and with that, it delivers. It's not crude, but it's also not classy. It's almost like a toned down Borderlands.
Audio: 95/100 A
The music of Tiny and Big is broken into two parts: there's the ambient game music and then there's the "Buckets full of Indie Music" to be collected and found by "hardly known, but genuine indie bands." While it may sound like a disingenuous advertisement for the music, a little tongue and cheek has to be taken, since the game itself doesn't take itself too seriously as well. The gameplay music is composed masterfully, invoking emotion and matches the environments perfectly, much in the same way Borderlands did, but much like Borderlands, Tiny and Big makes you long for something more as you gaze out into the horizon. At times, the soothing music makes you want to just wander off to see what's out there instead of fulfilling your mission.
Visuals: 93/100 A-
Much like the music, the art direction mirrors that of Borderlands, the heavy black lines and vibrant color schemes makes it stand out and is very easy on the eyes, a welcomed break from the bleak gray and brown color schemes that is so overused in video games these days. As mentioned before, Tiny and Big even has "caption" effects like "Crash," Splat," and "Pow" and adds to the effect in a charming way, although there was more than one instance when the words got in the way of a pillar falling in my direction and couldn't see it. Not really a problem, but it did make me slap my forehead on occasion. The design of the game is also very consistent, even though you only get to explore a small portion of the world you're on, you are given a fairly good idea of what it's like. That kind of direction, not just in art styles, is what builds a fan base and community, and with that, often sequels and support.
Content: 75/100 C
Like most indie games, they are designed to be taken in small doses, played as a relaxant or in between major sessions and Tiny and Big is no exception. One could easily finish the game in an hour or two if they wanted. There is a motive to explore, finding hidden items, mini-games, and music tracks and despite the general length of the game, exploring is often worth it in this case. Finding the mini-games especially was fun, going into a hidden room behind a wall or turning a corner to find an old coin operated arcade machine is a pleasant surprise.
Design: 88/100 B+
Like I stated in the Visual aspect of the game, everything is consistently designed, from the characters, to the tools, to the environment, definite thought was taken into account and not just tossed together based on someone's cool concept art.
Verdict: 87/100 B+
Tiny and Big is a nice little distraction and a wonderful first game by Black Pants from the choice of music to the art direction. It is another sign that the indie market still has a lot to offer which the AAA market won't risk or toy with. Goofy story telling, basic mechanics and a swagger of being just itself gives it enough of a push to be shared and recommended to all your friends. Yes, it does have some problems, but like with many indie releases, the ideas and games overshadow the flaws, something AAA can't seem to get right, especially when the flaws are so simplistic, makes you wonder how they ever went unnoticed.

Turn-based strategy games require a high degree of balance to maintain even a basic level of enjoyability. Incorporating cards, this game ran a particular risk in that it could easily become heavily P2W, require too much time to attain necessary game elements, and/or botch its game board element by way of card abilities.
This game avoided all of the vices.
Cards and Castles upholds the virtues of its genre(s). As of its most recent patch, it is highly balanced and increasingly so. It lets you jump in head first without stripping the player of all merit-based reward. And perhaps most importantly: The game is FUN. With my first 100 hours of gameplay, I can safely say that the game has lots of steam left in it. You can  enjoy this game in passing moments via Asynchronous play, in short sessions to test new decks via friendly mode, or grind it out over time toward the heralded Rank 1 in ranked mode. Each option grants the full Cards and Castles experience in its own way.
I look forward to continued improvements. Slight bugs persist, but they are addressed quickly. Connection issues have improved rapidly. Never before have I messaged about slight issues and had the lead game developer personally respond about the status of the fix toward the issues I had brought to light.
This is the work of people who know what they are doing and anyone would be wise to jump in early and grow alongside the game.

The most accurate description I can think of for BETRAYER is “FAR CRY 3 meets SILENT HILL by way of ELDER SCROLLS.” It applies some of the mechanics and structure of open world action games to a survival horror game, or at least a really dark and atmospheric adventure game.
The game has you explore the ruins of 17th century English Virginia colonies, piecing together the sordid tales of the people who lived there while fighting off monsters. The combat might be a love-it-or-hate-it affair, but BETRAYER’s main appeals are definitely the detective aspect and its atmosphere.
The most immediately striking things about BETRAYER are obviously its monotone color palette (which is actually optional) and that its unusual (for video games) setting. Both work together, along with the paper map by which you navigate, to create a great sense of being in another time and place.
It’s not just the lack of color that creates the style either, but the high contrast Blackpowder games employs (along with the reds that stick out to facilitate gameplay), particularly the very deep blacks which accentuate shadows. Blackpowder lets you adjust the contrast and bring color back into BETRAYER. Setting everything to “1.0” makes the game look much more “normal” and realistic, but also less interesting if you ask me. At some points you have to travel into an “otherworld” where the monochrome scheme inverts and thick, SILENT HILL-like fog is prevalent. Oppressive would be a strong word to describe it, but it manages to feel sufficiently moody.
The meat of the game is exploring the world to track down clues and eventually interrogate ghosts to put the story together. The ghosts all make for diverse and interesting mini stories that eventually connect to the main mystery of the game, though Blackpowder didn’t have the budget for any voice acting.
Even though the main mystery is fairly directly told once you gather the necessary clues, BETRAYER manages to vaguely allude to other mysteries behind the scenes. These culminate in a highly ambiguous ending that’s already ignited various interpretations from players.
The combat is probably BETRAYER’s most polarizing aspect. Of course it can’t be a normal first person shooter when you’re dealing with 17th century weaponry. What Blackpowder ended up with is something I find rather challenging and skill-based but others might just find to be a crapshoot.
As you fight monstrous Spaniards, skeletons, and other creatures, you mainly use a bow which feels nice and takes a bit of practice for figuring out when to loose arrows. Stealth definitely helps for starting or avoiding encounters but isn’t always an option. The knife, crossbows, muskets, and pistols are suited to different kinds of enemies and situations which all have patterns to learn. Dodging enemy projectiles is particularly tricky but learnable. If you want you can turn on a feature where you drop your equipment when you die and have one chance to retrieve it a la DARK SOULS, but the game as of this writing has it turned off by default.
BETRAYER probably takes between five and 12 hours to finish due to much of its content being optional, but also desirable because of its affect on the ending. For fans of survival horror and adventure games who miss investigating dark, mysterious places, this isn’t only a nice first person game to chew on, but also a unique application of open world game design. From there it’s just a matter of whether or not the combat holds you back.

New Review:
It's been a few months since I've played (and beaten) this game... and I find myself passing up probably-good games because it just doesn't seem like they'll compare, even remotely. And here's why:
Music: I fell in love. The sound of it, the timing, intensity, flow and quick pace is utterly perfect. When I'm working on something I'll still do a youtube "Rebel Galaxy music playlist" search and let it take over. I've recommended the same to friends and they all LOVE it.
Combat: I thought it would be bland and I would hate it. I honestly only played for the capital ship combat. I wanted the biggest, baddest ship and that was my sole goal in the game. Somehow, and I'm still scratching my head, RG made corvettes and frigates astoundingly fun to play. I've gone from my big dreadnaught back into a corvette for no reason other than I wanted to zip and boost around a larger ship or through groups of enemy ships and spam broadsides to my heart's content. It's... satisfying..
Dialogue: The trailer makes it seem cheesy. The game just confirms it. But it had a good story, I liked the characters, and nothing felt pushed, forced or too "whut." Great job by the voicing staff!
Ships: A very broad selection to choose from, almost all with their own benefits (speed and size or firepower in terms of broadside ports, turrets, or a mix of both (I always preferred turrets.. pew pew all over). You couldn't own multiple ships at once and cycle through em at will, but the process of going from ship to ship (buying the next size one or trading in for a smaller one) was effortless, and smooth. On top of that, the "grind" was perfect. You look at the prices and think "no way in hell can I ever reach that" and before you know it, you're two tiers below it and it's within a day's reach. Great reward/price scaling!
That's all I can think of for now, but DEFINITELY get this game, sale or not. And if you see that a friend wants it, get it for them, too.

As its core, Hatred is an interesting game because it reminds us how narrow, formulaic and claustrophobic gaming narratives can be. Imagine cinema without Scarface, Hannibal Lecter or even Mike Leigh's Johnny. Moral ambiguity is essential to the silver screen but remains only a distant hope on our monitors.
The game certainly has its limitations. The core mechanics are those of a middling-quality isometric shooter with some fine destruction physics. Moreover, no significant narrative is provided for the orgy of destruction. This could either be viewed as serving the nihilistic atmosphere, or be considered as a narrative failing when compared to cinematic anti-heroes.
However, considering that the utterances of Hatred's anti-hero are not especially inspired, it's perhaps for the better than the minimalistic approach has been taken - we are free to each craft our own reasons for the violence.
Positives:
- Good atmosphere; cold, grim visuals
- Surprisingly good physics & destruction via UE4. It works well when backed into an Apple Store's bathroom and gunning down soldiers, who finally bring the entire structure down, forcing a hasty run-and-gun exit through the rubble.
- Good concept
- One of the best flamethrowers since Return To Castle Wolfenstein.
Negatives:
- For a game so rooted in gunplay, the actual gun sounds lack punch.
- Something of a manufactured controversy - not really as violent or drastic as people might expect,
- A fundamentally simple game that would struggle to justify a higher price point.

A fantastic title if you're looking for a robust starship sim. You select your craft from a wealth of options that range from a speedy corvette-class vessel to a dreadnought bristling with a dozen turrets. Combat is reminiscent of naval warfare, where you try to position yourself to blast your foes with powerful broadside weaponry and the options for arming yourself are truly staggering. You can arm your ship with particle beams, mines, flak cannons, missiles, anti-matter cannons, pulse turrets... there's an option for every playstyle and you can sink hours into perfecting your unique ship.
There's a wealth of content to be had but the downside is that a lot of it can grow repetitive. Upgrades for your ship don't come cheap and as difficulty spikes can be quite jarring you'll find yourself doing a lot of the same basic missions over and over again to get yourself up to snuff. The mechanics themselves are a joy, though, which really helps to ease this shortcoming and the moment to moment opportunities for profit allow you to choose between piracy, mercenary activity or just plain honest trade.
All in all, if you're looking for a space sim that will spoil you for choice, Rebel Galaxy is the game for you.

Like many people I was really excited when I initally found out that there was going to be another X game.
The reality is quite different, a friend of mine bought X-Rebirth before me and was so disappointed by it he wouldn't even show it to me. So after the launch debarcle and the console revelation I have seen the regular patching to try and stem the bleeding. Then the free weekend comes along and I get to try the game I had such high hopes for without having to dip into my wallet, and what did I find? A very poorly executed mash mash of badly married ideas and concepts which in no way resembles the X games I have loved playing in the past.
There are a couple of things that I like, one is the general look of the stations and the second is the fluidity of the ship movement, after that the only real redeeming feature is the fact that the total redesign of the interface meant that on my first two plays ended abruptly for reasons I cannot explain.
Some of the things I don't like; what is the point of the useless room at the back of your ship, you can't do anything in there so why have it? why has the entire interface been redesigned again and not for the better? Why do we have a story that after such a long time since the gates have shut down nobody has worked out how to restart them? (Think what it would have been like to get to explore how each race coped during the time the gates stranded everyone, an opportunity missed there I think). The rendering of the people, they all have a weird distorted look about them, its very odd and unsettling. After all the patching it is still a deeply disappointing experience.
Maybe this is one rebirth that should be allowed to quietly die.
As an object lesson in how to destroy the fanbase of a popular franchise this is an epic success.
As a functioning game that is fun to play and full of engaging gameplay, like its predecessors, it is an epic fail.
Would have been much kinder to never have released this travesty which in no way deserves to be associated with the family of titles it claims to be part of.
Steer clear of this, go for X-2 or X-3 instead.

I would suggest to  buy the Egosoft Colledtion. I sunk hundreds of hours in X3: Reunion, X3: Terran Conflict and X3: Albion Prelude. If you are interested in space sims I can recommend them all as good games.
Concerning X Rebirth I must say the space looks gorgeous but the interiors of stations seem very generic and repetitive and I'm sorry to say that this Yisha person - my copilot - would be best thrown out the airlock. I personally don't like the cockpit view as it is taking away part of the beautiful scenery. Thankfully you can buy different cockpits but why not leaving the choice to the player?
The X series never was very friendly to beginners and X Rebirth is no exception. I think of myself as a not especially dumb person but it took me some time to figure out how to dock at my freighter in the campaign. The fact that you're limited to one ship - the Albion Skunk - is also annoying to me as it is a ship not very good at skirmishes with small fighters and for trading you have to use your freighters which require a captain and optional other crew members.This could arguably be a good thing if you get rid of the micromanagement involved with trading but it doesn't work for me. The experience of former X games in mind it could be solved much easier with something like trade software Mk 3 to establish a sector or galaxy trader. So in comparison to the GUI in former installments of the series the menu in X Rebirth looks to me more like a regression than a progression. You feel not anymore in control of a large trading empire or a mighty battle fleet.
All the above said I think that X Rebirth in itself is not a bad game and if you are new to the X universe you should definitly give it a try especially for the asking price. I also want to mention the dedication of the dev team at Egosoft to improve the game and adding content  which I think deserves to be supported.

Let me start by saying, I'm not recommending this game at full price.
If this is your first Saints Row game, don't start here. The game was incomplete because of the closure of the studio, so the game is not a complete experience. If you're already a fan of the franchise, read on.
The game's humor is so good. I got it for $3.75 or so, and it was well worth it. The depiction of Satan is wonderfully done, and I can only imagine how much cooler it could have been if the game had been finished.
If you didn't like Saints Row 4, you might not bother with this one. Personally, the addition of super-powers hurt the franchise for me. Suddenly, I was dis-incentivised to try out the myriad vehicles in the game, or the cool weapons. There are a lot fewer vehicles in this one, and the sensation of being able to run at lightning speeds and flying becomes a stale sandbox experience after a while, especially if you played #4.
The quests are nearly non-existent. The quest-givers were in place already, so the developers opted to make their quests hinge on completing challenges instead. (Fly through the bubbles, capture this control point, defeat 3 waves, etc.)
In summary, if you don't look at it as a full game, you'll enjoy it if you like the others. The way I see it, for three dollars, I got to play a game that would have just been shelved or lost to time. The bits that I got to play of the game that might have been were fun.

Stick to the duels of the planeswalkers series instead of trying this game. You'll get way more value for your money that way. This game may be free, but its wayy more pay to win than dotp is. In this game you unlock cards WAYYYY slower, so you'll be at a disadvantage for a MUCH longer time unless you pay for cards. The cheapest you can get all cards in the game is about 80 bucks. Spreading out those purchases will make it cost more.
The duels of the planeswalkers games have pay to win too, but it's hardly as necessary as unlocking cards in dotp takes a fraction of the time it does in this game. In dotp you pay one small fee for the game, maybe one more even smaller one for an expansion, then just have fun for several hours learning the starting cards and after a day or 2 you'll already have them all. In Magic Duels Origins, it'll take weeks.
EDIT: Also the story mode forces you to use premade ♥♥♥♥♥♥ decks, with no customization. So even if you play perfectly whether you win or lose a match is 100% chance. Sometimes (or rather, most times) there's just nothing you can do because your deck sucks, making the story take longer than it would otherwise simply because you're forced to lose at random. This also makes the card rewards from the story mode hardly worth the time.
TL;DR:
Duels of the Planeswalkers is a small one time fee for the game and you can quickly unlock all cards.
Magic Duels Origins is free to play but unlocking all cards takes way wayyy too long to encourage you to spend AT LEAST 80 bucks to unlock all cards instead.
As with any TCG, it's going to be pay to win. Skip this scam of a game and just wait for the next duels of the planeswalkers game, where you can avoid pay to win by simply playing for a few hours with the cards you start with.

If your looking for a realistic fishing experience then this it i dunno if you have ever been fishing in the real world or if your just interested in the sport but either way this sim is for you. Il get this outta the way nice and early the title is "Carp Fishing Simulator" the sim focuses on Carp so dont expect to reel in some big bass or a beasty Tiger Shark or something because that aint gunna happen, its not just carp though there is other species you can target such as Catfish. Pike and Perch. You start out with 3 rods you can setup each one using a variety of stuff like hooks,rigs,line etc its completely up to you. Theres plenty of baits to choose from and an optional bait creator tool you can download (For Free) theres a bait boat and spod rod (for feeding the fish) and theres also real world weather effects and time of day. Once you reel a fish in and admire its beauty you can then put it back and i dont mean press a button screen goes black and the fish just disappears i mean you actually get to put it back in the water and watch it swim away. Its really satisfying and is one of my favourite features, if you have ever been fishing in real life you will no what im talking about. You dont need to be an expert to play this sim but having a little knowledge will help you catch and thanks to the Internet that informations only a click away.  Now this is early access so itsgot bugs that need to b squashed but its very enjoyable and worth supporting its development.

As a long time Civilization fan I was wary of another Civ game after what I what I considered the bad route they went with for Civ 5, and I unfortunatelly was not surprised. One unit per tile drives me nuts. I understand that being able to squeeze 80 units on a tile is not terribly fun either, but why has no one thought of a simple supply system? Each tile has supply, say up to 100, and units take up supply. Infantry might be 20, cavalry 25, artillery type 30, tanks 40. You can only get so many units in to any area at any time but no more of this game destroying 1 unit per tile bull plop.
The tech tree is interesting, reminds me of other space game tech trees though, not super original.
Units look ok, but it can be easy to lose sight of some on the very colourful map, some can really blend in. Combat looks pretty cool. I like the way you upgrade units, but am confused on how you GET to the point where you can upgrade, was it from a lot of combat, tech upgrading or time spent playing? It didn't seem to explain that very well, if I missed it well I did only play for so long.
Health was another thing that drive me nuts. I built every + hea;th building, took + health ideas/quest decisions, and didn't let my pop grow TOO fast, and yet I was almost always at -10 or more health by the time I had 3 cities.
The factions are also just AWFUL! I really didn't want to pick any of them, none looked appealing to me. There are huge areas of earth that seem not to be represented in the game (can anyone say DLC?) and some of the ones that are are very confusing. The Slavic Union? Slavic countries are not known for cooperation. The African Union seems just as silly honestly. I understand peoples need to think all countries in Africa are the same/can get along, but they really aren't/don't. Overall the factions are a very, VERY bad joke.
I fully expect I'd get better the more I play but I really have no desire to play any further, I ended up uninstalling with some 12 hours left on the FTP weekend.
In general it feels like the game has been...streamlined seems like a bad work but it sort of fits...down to the point where much of the challenge of pre Civ 5 games is just gone. Aside from having issues with health, the AI was pretty dumb and harder difficulty just seems to let it cheat, not get HARDER.
Thank you for the free weekend, I know not to buy this. I'll just go back to Civ 4.

As a huge fan of Alpha Centauri, I was longing for this game, hoping it would recapture that magic and bring it back to us with updated graphics and an UI that didn't suck.

The general atmosphere does a decent job at imitating SMAC: SciFi Setting, fictional tech quotes, aliens, and so on. Beyond Earth even goes - well - beyond Civ 5 by adding the orbital layer, covert ops, quests, excavations and the affinity system.
Compared to the version at launch they've ironed out most of the UI issues that originally lead me to give this game a bad review. Trade routes autorenew now. No more UI blur in managment screens. The help system is decent and the various search options do their job.

Certainly no replacement for the custom unit design in SMAC. It does however automatically upgrade all your existing units for free.
All in all I'm not sure if I'll be playing this all that much. It's a competent game now but it lacks the spark - the courage to be different - that made SMAC such a gem.

This War of Mine has been an extremely difficult game for me. Getting attached to my little pudgy chef, my adorable little running boy, and my grumpy old scientist, all for naught. It was a fateful night. Like the fool he was, the poor little chef ventured out into the hotel. He wanted to save the people there from the atrocities of the psychotic killer on the loose. Armed with an AK-47 and iron will, he moved in. Too late did he realize that he had no bullets.
The runner came next. He ran in, knife in hand, and was shotgunned mercilessly.
The poor old scientist was last. With no way of scavenging, no weapons, and no food, he slowly starved.
All of my chillins died...
In all seriousness, This War of Mine is a brilliant game. It outlines the all too serious issues of wartime effects on civilians, ever present in this day and age. It also runs paralells to the violence in Ukraine, as it is set in a slavic country with a good deal of conflict between a rebellion government and an already established government.
The game also allows you to make a pretty awesome bomb shelter, and gives you crippling morality decisions. As you take on more members for your party, you increase the likelihood of starvation, but at the same time, turning away starving people is almost too much to bear.
This War of Mine does not simply tug on your heartstrings. It pulls them out and mercilessly beats you over the head with them, then for good measure slaps you about the cheecks a few times before jamming them back in all haphazardly.
Now my heartstrings are spaghetti....
I would recommend this to anyone looking for a great game theyre willing to invest some time into.

As most reviews say, this is not the Hitman you know, this is very different. The levels are not as big as some of the previous games, but if you ask me, they are way more detailed and more options than the previous Hitman games. You don't get to much of an open world anymore, but more a, get from point A to Point B style. i was skeptical about this at first, but grew to love it, even though it's a From point A to B, you still get alot of diversion and ALOT of choices on how you wanna get there. The new disguise system is 50/50, i love how it adds to the realism. The cop will know you are not one of his colleagues, but how is the civillian to know that you are not a cop? It is a bit to sensitive though, even though you are standing with your back to a guy who is 6-7 meters away he will still notice that you are not one of them, and that is a bit to much. You don't get to choose what weapons and equipment you wanna use anymore at the start of the game though, but i think this adds to the fun, and it works well with the story, this also means that you don't have a pocket filled with thousand coins anymore, instead you gotta find objects around the world, that you can use as distractions/weapons, this is also a welcome change.
The story is also a big part of Absolution, in the previous games. You got your mission and then you executed it, however you felt like and that was that, and that was good, cause that's why you played it.
I felt alot more motivated to keep going in this one, cause of the story and what happend in it, and even though i mostly try to do it stealth with none or a few extra casualties , there was just places where i went in guns blazing cause i didn't think the ones i was up against deserved to live. I also had some really heartpounding moments, cause i was so focused on killing my target for one reason or another and that rarely happens to me.
On that note, it also alot funnier to do fire fights in Absolution: When you empty your 45 cal. UMP magazine into a guy and you see him spasm all over the place as he falls to the ground, feels really awesome.
All in all I will give this game a 9/10 it is a great game, but with a few things i would like tweeked, but these things are so minor that they can be looked through pretty easly. Don't expect the next version of Blood Money, but a deeper more involved game

Play this game. You won't regret it.
So, I took the time to read the negative reviews before I wrote this one. Their chief complaints were the repetitive nature of the game and the randomness of events causing you to survive or fail. They also complained there wasn't a sense of "accomplishment" or "achievement" to it.
See, this is what I think-- this game isn't designed to be like most out there. Yes, it can be repetitive. Yes, the combat system sucks. Why? It's a survival game, playing as civilians. You don't have skill sets or weapons. You're just a small group of frightened survivors trying to scavenge your way through a civil war. The combat isn't supposed to be the focus. The whole idea is that you can't take on the world by yourself.
No, it's not ridiculously immersive like some games available on the market-- but it gets the job done. It's gritty. It's well-designed. It will frustrate you, because you can't just tank your way through it.
In a game about the horrors of war, should it be any surprise that beating the game comes without a great sense of accomplishment?
If you want a FPS survival genre game, go play something from Bethesda. This is an indie game, designed more as an exercise in thought than it is an exercise of your trigger finger.

Tiny and Big: Granda's Leftovers has several good sides and bad sides to it. I'll start with the good sides.
------------------------
Good Sides
------------------------
#1: The graphics overall are outstanding. It gives you a feel to the game, and it lets you know what he's feeling. It's hard to explain, but I'll just say that it gives atmosphere to the game, and I like that about it.
#2: The gameplay is fun. It's always a mystery as to what's next in the game, and it is extremely action packed.
#3: The equipment you use. Oh my gosh. I love them. The laser is my favorite. Oh, you wanted to cut that mountain in half? Guess what! If it's small enough, you can. Bam.
-----------------------
Bad Sides
-----------------------
#1: The game itself is extremely short. It has 6 levels. SIX. LEVELS. It seems unfair to spend 10 or more dollars on this if I can't atleast play more than 15 levels or so! Sure, they may be complex, but still. Six levels.
#2: The game is hard. And I mean HARD. You make one wrong move, you're dead. It does make it exciting, but it never gives you a break unless you're in the first level, which is essentially the tutorial.
#3: At some points in the game, if you don't get it just right, you won't make it past the first part of the level. I spent almost 2-3 hours on one point of the level in which I almost got a sledgehammer to smash my comuter open with.
#4: It's laggy as crap. You have to turn down the graphics at some points.
----------------------
Altogether, the game was interesting. It's fun, but it just wasn't good enough for me to recommend. Sure, it had good graphics and gameplay, but I just wasn't feeling it. I liked the laser though.
Overall Rating: 7/10

Especially for that pricetag, it´s definitely worth a shot.
The game is very neatly done.
Though the story seems dull after some time of playing.
First of all: There are many settings that allow you to adjust the game to your taste.
I suppose the developers intented people to play this game in Black and White (while the colour red is the only colour that is always displayed... in colour - yeah sorry about that) BUT they have added the option to increase the colour saturation in this game.
So people who dislike the black and white gameplay, can switch to coloured gameplay as well. +1 for that, even though I like it in B/W.
Further, I recommend to tick the box where it says that you lose all of your loot when you die and that you have to pick it up before your next death, otherwise it will disappear forever.
Might sound harsh and too difficult, but really isn´t. I died three times so far, and each time I was able to pick my loot back up with ease. It just adds to the games atmosphere.
The enemies are... weird. And deadly.
They usually carry bows, knives, pistols or muskets. (so far - I haven´t completed the whole game yet)
If you see an enemy carrying a musket or knife, kill those guys first. It´s quite easy to dodge arrows of enemy archers.
(If the guy with the knife manages to get close enough and stab you, you´re likely going to die. Because they don´t just stab you, but right after they stabbed you and drained about 45% of your HP, they will very quickly draw their pistol and shoot. And that shot will drain the rest of your HP)
The game offers quite nice stealth/sneaking tactics. You can hide in bushes, as far as I understood, you also need to try to not stay in the wind as it carries the sound of your footsteps. So if you have an enemy in front of you and the wind is in your back, he is more likely to hear you.
That is accompanied by a ton of vegetation that indicates the direction of the wind. So that´s pretty cool as well.
Enemies receive increased damage as long as they didn´t see you. So that is quite helpful for players who prefer stealth, as well.
Arrows can ricochet off of the enemies armor (luckily not all enemies have armor) so be sure to either hit the optics in their helmets (basically try to hit their eyes) or other unprotected body parts.
The arrows have close to no dropoff, so most of the times you can just aim directly at their head.
Last but not least, before I say something story-related:
The developers left an email adress in the main menu where you can directly send feedback to them.
That is pretty cool, in my opinion.
+++ SPOILERS BELOW +++
So at this point I want to point out some things in the story, that I have witnessed so far.
One - the story seems very interesting at first, but becomes dull after your first sidequest and talking to the first main NPC.
So there´s that mysterious woman in a red cape right after you leave the beach. And she disappears again after a few seconds. And then she later appears in an abandoned fort and when you talk to her, she says that she wasn´t that first woman in the red cape you saw, but that it was her sister.
Okay.
Further she tells you that she has no idea which enemies you are talking about, because she can´t see anybody besides you on the whole island.
Okay.
So why can´t I bring her with me and actually SHOW her the enemies I am talking about, because all she ever does is, stay in the stupid fort? It could have an actually logical story related reason, but that´s as far as I am right now.
The sidequest I had so far, was basically a ghost that was missing his wife and son. And you are supposed to find out what happened to them.
And here comes a really cool thing.
In Fort Henry, you will find a bell. Upon activating the bell, you can switch into the other world. The black and white colours invert and the whole game suddenly becomes really scary. (Note I´m scared easily)
The game further adds to the scary atmosphere, because you have to "listen" to be able to find quest relevant places in the darkness. And the listening involves hearing ghostly whispers and screams.
-----
There´s more to say about this game, but just go ahead and give it a shot. It´s not the best game, but it definitely isn´t bad. And for that pricetag, you don´t lose much, even if you dislike it.

Stick to the duels of the planeswalkers series instead of trying this game. You'll get way more value for your money that way. This game may be free, but its wayy more pay to win than dotp is. In this game you unlock cards WAYYYY slower, so you'll be at a disadvantage for a MUCH longer time unless you pay for cards. The cheapest you can get all cards in the game is about 80 bucks. Spreading out those purchases will make it cost more.
The duels of the planeswalkers games have pay to win too, but it's hardly as necessary as unlocking cards in dotp takes a fraction of the time it does in this game. In dotp you pay one small fee for the game, maybe one more even smaller one for an expansion, then just have fun for several hours learning the starting cards and after a day or 2 you'll already have them all. In Magic Duels Origins, it'll take weeks.
EDIT: Also the story mode forces you to use premade ♥♥♥♥♥♥ decks, with no customization. So even if you play perfectly whether you win or lose a match is 100% chance. Sometimes (or rather, most times) there's just nothing you can do because your deck sucks, making the story take longer than it would otherwise simply because you're forced to lose at random. This also makes the card rewards from the story mode hardly worth the time.
TL;DR:
Duels of the Planeswalkers is a small one time fee for the game and you can quickly unlock all cards.
Magic Duels Origins is free to play but unlocking all cards takes way wayyy too long to encourage you to spend AT LEAST 80 bucks to unlock all cards instead.
As with any TCG, it's going to be pay to win. Skip this scam of a game and just wait for the next duels of the planeswalkers game, where you can avoid pay to win by simply playing for a few hours with the cards you start with.

This is a pretty poor attempt at a Magic game. It's pretty sad when you have inferior TCG's like Yugioh or Pokemon put out better products. Here is why Magic Duels sucks.
1) Next to no cards in the game. You would think that with a game like Magic that is 20 years old that a game about it would have tons of cards right? Wrong, this game only has about 500 something cards, and that's including the new Battle for Zendikar set. It would have not been hard for them to add in at least everything from M10 to M15 and some Duel Decks, but no, instead you get next to nothing. All is in the game is Magic Origins, Battle for Zendikar and a few random cards from random sets.
2) Its very difficult to get new cards in the game. You only get 15-20 points if you beat someone online or the CPU and it takes 150 points to get a 6 card booster. What a joke, it takes winning 6-8 games to get 1 stupid booster pack that might be total trash. I dont get why boosters only come with 6 cards when in real life they have 15.
3) No drafting. Drafting is one of the fundamental signature formats of Magic, yet it's not in the game. How is it that the new Yugioh game has drafting when Magic, a game that has had drafting as a format for over 10 years, doesnt have it in it's own game?
4) Stupid deck restrictions. You can only play 4 copies of any common, 3 copes of any uncommon, 2 copies of any rare and 1 copy of a mythic rare in your deck. I dont get why they invented this rule since real Magic isn't anything like this and having this random restriction in the game makes no sense.
5) Next to no content. All there is in the game is the crappy storyline, battle against the CPU and battle against people online.
6) Campaign is such a waste of time. All the matches are scripted and the storyline is pretty boring. The CGI is pretty cheesy and boring.
This is a pretty sad excuse for a video game for a game with a ton of depth and strategy such as Magic. How it's competitors are doing better is pretty pathetic. I dont know what Wizards of the Coast was thinking with this game, but it sucks hard and I would not get it. Even if it's free, to have a decent deck that doesnt take you hundred years to get, you have to pay a decent amount of money. Stay away, stay very far away from this pile of garbage.

Imagine you go to McDonald's to order a meal.  The meal costs you around $5, so as you wait for your meal to finish you aren't expecting anything exciting.  Actually, you assume the meal will be dry and boring.  But, still, $5 for a meal!
At this point, you still aren't expecting anything more than a drab way to satisfy your hunger.  As your name is called for the meal, you take it almost grudgingly, thinking back to other meals you could have bought with that $5.
However, you begin your meal being mildly impressed with the soda selection.  You fill your cup to the brim with the best choice and turn around to find a table.  There, in the far corner is one far away from the habitual customers.  You go to the table and find that it is still clean.
Your hopes suddenly begin to flare and you you eagerly open your bag.  Inside, you see a nicely made burger with seeds still attached to the bun (a delicacy at McD's), pickles are placed neatly on top of the patty, and the burger has a perfectly round and symmetrical shape to it.  You even received extra fries!  What more?  You turn to look at the counter and see the attractive employee who made your burger is smiling and winking at you.
This, of course, shocks you immensely as you only paid $5 and expected something much more bland than this satiating meal and even enjoyable experience.
From now on, you make a promise to yourself not to judge cheap meals too harshly and know that, in the future, choosing a cheaper meal may be the best choice you make.
These feelings I have described below are precisely how playing I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream is like.
Bonus: you are given the short story the game is based on!  Just check the steam folder for this game.  Very similar to finding an attractive employee is winking at you, I'd say.

This is a difficult review. I don't usually finish games, so generally to get to the end they must have something that grabs me.
I remember playing the first few Hitman games and enjoying them enough, so seeing an improved new version on Steam I bought it on an Eidos sale.
I finished the story mode for Hitman:Absolution and one of the core reasons was that there was something that drew me back. However overall it's not enough for me to recommend the game, or to want to play it again. Essentially I just ended up grinding it out.
Pros:
1. Graphics and audio.  Reasoonably well done. A little too much bloom, and the cutscenes are jarringly sub-par compared to the in-game graphics but nonetheless it looks the Hitman part. For the record, I have a medium rig.
2. Some of the Gameplay. I think when it works, this was the games strongest point. When playing in crowds or having lots of easily accessible hiding spots Hitman was quite enjoyable. Not unlike watching a guilty pleasure B-grade action movie.
Cons:
- When it doesn't work though. OMG then it's obvious;
1. Cutscene story inconsistency - what's the point of being a super-assassin (the story says you are), and playing like one (making sure not to make stupid mistakes), when the protaganist just throws it out the door at every cutscene? It was like a slap in the face whenever he kept making rookie mistakes and then you, have to get him out of the predicament.
2. Recon - Ugh. So I said that it had areas that worked. But overall, it was just bad. Instead of being able to survey the location, choose the best option(s) available and to prepare (with costumes, weapons etc) you were simply just dumped at the beginning of each location in full assassin uniform glory.
3. Disguises - So you can grab a disguise, that's great! Problem is that the second you do this, any NPC who have the same uniform are onto you. So you spend more time hiding from them. (also, can't he afford a wig or beard?). Which leads me to;
4. NPCs - The game makes you spend all of your time hiding out of the line of sight of any NPC. They just have a preset walking path (you can see that from your flames of hell vision) and all you end up doing is trying to walk between these paths. What's the point of disguises or stealth then? In addition any NPC that catches you, immediately notifies everyone else. How can that be? Wouldn't some NPC (like janitors) be slower to do that? Wouldn't they need to actually  take the time to call someone (not just a generic soundbyte while you're strangling them).
5. Dumping bodies - So, you can hide bodies in lots of containers and boxes around the locations - but what ever happened to just being able to hide them in dark areas that NPC don't walk through? If you don't hide them in a box, then they're always found. In addition, if I'm an assassin and I make an NPC bleed, can't I mop up the blood instead of leaving evidence?
6. Control - The amount of times I pressed the wrong button or my character did the wrong thing was way too numerous. Hold Y for this, but press Y for that, Hold A for this, but press A for that. Why make it so convoluted? And when it's such a fine line in getting the timing right. This got really frustrating fast.
7. Agent 47's voice - OK not such a big one, but still I didn't like it. I never really liked his voice originally but now it really doesn't seem to match with what he looks like. No hate at the actor, more just the older articulate voice was mismatched with the bald angry so and so. Especially when I'm used to seeing Michael Chiklis, Jason Statham, and Bruce Willis where their voices actually match their looks.
So the whole game just feels like you're constantly waiting for an NPC to pull the trigger on you. What kind of stealth game is that? There should be an element of getting caught but not to that extent (and maybe only in more difficult levels). If I was a real assassin wouldn't I be good at this by now? My disguise solid enough not to draw any attention because I'm great at not standing out?
I'm really hoping that the next iteration will play more out like a proper recon game. Something like GTA V heists as the right way to pull a job. So you get to check the place out first and determine entry points. You then get to get (steal?) the devices and uniforms you need, and finally you then have to pull the job.

Quick summary: 4/10
A funny thing about the positive recommendations in the reviews.  A large proportion of the positives actually end up saying it's not so great now, but just give it a little time [until the modding community finally makes the game interesting].  They're being optimistic.
I played the free trial this weekend, and put in 22 hours.  Which indicates that the game definitely speaks to the OC gamer in me.  But it was very mechanical.  I still play SMAC, and in that game I find a vested interest in eliminating certain factions - I take their attacks on me personally.  In other words, that game has personality.
This game, OTOH, is a mechanical grinder.  Nice graphics, the affinities concept is nice, and so is the tech web.  But the other factions are as featureless as the plastic manequins that pop up every so often with ridiculous trade offers and unreliable deals - the diplomacy system is same frustrating one from CIV V.  A talking head would be much more effective than the animated barbie dolls that gesture their disapproval with a hackneyed wave of dismissal.  For Empress Theresa in CIV V it might have been appropriate.  For "modern leaders" it is anachronistic.
Ultimately, playing this game feels like computer chess rather than dealing with people.
Note that I did not try MP mode.  That might be different.
Other issues: it needs more flexible upgrade options.  All that's available are various power-ups.  How about something interesting like the upgrade options in SMAC?  Or different types of air units?  [This is not the 18th century after all].
The holdover of the lack of stacking is frustrating, occassionally requiring towers-of-Hanoi busywork .  No spy satellites?  No way to harness the alien wildlife?  No stealth?
Ultimately, this is a reskin of CIV V - medieval concepts and units - with some interesting new window dressing.  I'm going back to SMAC.  I'll take another look at this in a few months.
