There's a core mechanic at work in Tiny & Big and it's the ability to cut, pull and rocket-propel huge pieces of your surroundings. It's highly original and in the early stages of the game it's applied really well. You're left mostly to your own devices to get to grips with your toys.
Unfortunately it's not long before you're subjected to something akin to an overly long, drawn out boss battle with 'Big'. He's a 2-dimensional, uninteresting nemesis who has one main trick up his sleeve; he throws things at you while standing on columns or ledges. It is then your place to dodge or slice those (increasingly huge) projectiles or get smooshed.
The problem is that due to the fiddly nature of the tools and the random nature of your attackers projectiles you'll often find yourself getting hit with whatever's left of the original projectile or you won't even get chance to get your shot off. Sometimes an identical technique that got you killed on your first go will be successfull on your 20th. There's little consistency.
After being pelted seemingly endlessly across the level, there was a brief reprieve to take part in a more platformesque section but once this was completed it was straight back into ducking/splitting giant projectiles again as another wave of Big's boss scenarios kicked off. There's literally no other enemies besides that one guy so there's not even the satisfaction of eliminating smaller guys for target practice/hilarity's sake.
Ultimately I just felt fatigued by the same old attacks happening on a larger and larger scale. The tools are a great idea but you're swatted too frequently to ever really get the best out of them. It's a shame because the art style is really nice (think a sort of roughly-drawn Adventure Time) and this would otherwise have a lot of charm.
Very good game, it really makes it to turn on feelings while playing the game, this is thx to how easy it plays with your sense of morality and depression.

This review comes after my having played a little over 12 hours of it and in all honesty, there is a year's gap between playtime. When I first purchased this game, I was playing on a computer that was nearly 6 years old and it was starting to show in performance. I only got a couple hours of play on record for this game before I gave up on it temporarily. My moving on from "War in the North" was due to the game repeatedly closing unexpectedly and at the time this was occuring, I was experiencing this with a host of programs and not just certain games I was playing so I chalked the issue up to the performance of my computer and not the game itself. A year later, I am playing on an up-to-date machine and all of my other games are running flawlessly. Then there's this one. It is worth noting that I am a dedicated fan of "Lord of The Rings" and all things Tolkien so my motivation for purchasing this title didn't really go beyond "takes place in Middle Earth". When this game went on sale during one of the frequent WB Games sales here on Steam; I bought it eagerly.
Before I go into the flaws and the criticising, I do want to point out the things I really do love about this game. The first appeal is the graphics, the very look and feel of this game is supurbly detailed. From a rainy night in Bree dropping into the Prancing Pony to the ruins of the Third Age in Fornost and even the outfits and features of the heroic trio, the detail of this version of Tolkien's world is impressive.
One of the things I appreciate having learned from playing the first time is to take my time exploring the areas I was in. I ended up getting stuck in the boss fight at Chapter 22 of the first part of the storyline because I had been in such an excited hurry to see what was next that I did not take the time to level up my character and properly spend skill points, improve gear from loot, etc. This was 100% my mistake and when I started the game over, I made sure to fully explore each area as I worked through it and smashed everything up looking for loot and secret hiding places. By the time I had arrived at Chapter 22 again, I was better prepared and more learned in the mechanics of combat and character enhancement that I was able to beat it easily and move on to Part 2 of the storyline.
My excitement about advancing further into the game soon turned to disappointment however because Part 2 is where the bugs and glitches started happening. In Part 2, the heroic trio is sent by the Rangers into the Barrow Downs outside of Bree when two of their own go missing. The goal of the first couple chapters is to explore the Barrow Downs and begin clearing the tombs of risen wights and skeleton warriors enslaved by Sauron. This is when the trouble starts.
If you get too caught up in a mob in the Barrow Downs, the game shuts down or even worse, it starts glitching and falling apart until you have to force a shut down. During the numerous times I attempted to clear this part of the storyline (sometimes succeeding in clearing 2 of the 3 tombs in the first zone of the Barrows, other times not even clearing the first tomb) I found that the game simply could not hold up to its own chaotic action. During battle in the tombs, I started noticing the walls and floors of the tombs were flickering and fuzzing like an old TV that needed to be smacked or antenna readjusted in order to improve the signal. Then enemies would start vanishing and then the heroes would freeze in place, unable to continue combat. Sometimes, I'd be able to Alt+Tab in and out of the game and let it square itself away in a minute or two, other times, I had to force the game to close becaue the lockup and increasing decay of the zone would not stop until the whole screen was an abstract work of colors and vauge graphic squares and bars.
After losing my patience playing this part of the game over and over with no increased success, I took a break and started just searching the web for info about "War in the North". Not looking for cheats really but just a better understanding of whether or not this was as big of an issue as other Steam reviews had gotten me to thinking it was. All I needed was Wikipedia's collection of gamer magazine reviews on "War in the North" at the time of its release. Here's a few gems to take into consideration:
"There are times when War in the North shows you the game it could have been [...] But each time the game starts to hit its stride, it soon stumbles and falls on its face".
- Carolyn Petit for GameSpot
"The Lord of the Rings: War in the North is a soulless cash-in that has little to do with its license, and nor is it much fun in its own right. If you're lucky enough to not encounter any game-breaking bugs and if you have a friend or two to play with, then it can be pretty entertaining for a few hours. But that's a lot of "ifs" for so little payoff".
- Jeffrey Matulef for Eurogamer
In November 2011, IGN rated "War in the North" to be the fourth most disappointing release of 2011.
To bring up the Eurogamer review for a moment, I agree it would be more fun with friends...if that part was not seriously defective as well. I played for about an hour with a friend of mine and did it entirely online rather than in the same room with each other. We barely managed to get through the introduction at the Prancing Pony and make our way to Fornost without one of us constantly getting kicked out of the game and having to restart it. It got annoying after awhile and we gave up and moved on to something else. So even though "War in the North" is categorized as a multiplayer-capable game, it is entirely unable to function as such.
The year 2011 is worth noting because that is the year of another big game release: "Skyrim". This only shows just how much potential "War in the North" had to be an amazing game and yet no one involved in its development seemed able or willing to make it happen. There is an open world look to this game (as I mentioned above, the detail is stunning) but the feel of it is actually very confining. You cannot go wandering off anywhere you choose without running smack into an invisible wall as soon as you leave the designated path towards your next destination.
If its open-world Middle Earth you are looking for, turn to "Lord of The Rings Online". Celebrating 10 years of play, LOTRO was (until recently) a WB Game but is now entirely in the hands of an indie studio that has a better working relationship with Middle Earth Enterprises than Warner Bros. currently does (Hobbit Slots, anyone?). I have played LOTRO for 6 years as of the publication of this review and it remains my absolutle favorite game and I cannot and will not stop steering people towards it because it is a true gem of an MMO. Even Atlas Obscura praises it.
Going back to the point of limitation in "War in the North", the destination you are forced towards in your not-so-open-world will more than likely not have a save point. Saving in the game is automated but the points at which it does so are few and far between which means if you and your two companions are killed, you have to start over farther back than you think and have to go to all the trouble of re-investing skill points and scrunging up gear if you recently made a switch that also didn't stick. This is something that can quickly lead to frustration and loss of interest if all your effort and planning and restrategizing ends up being an epic waste of time.
I sincerly wish I could recommed this game as a Tolkien-esque treasure but I think even he would be dissapointed by what the final product is. I'm left scratching my head over how a studio could release a game that was broken from Day One and not do a single thing to rectify the situation. I think "War in the North" could easily be given the "Skrim" treatment and be throughly revamped and re-released if only it was put in the hands of people who actually cared.

Upfront I have to say, I am a huge fan of the X³ series and X Rebirth is a different game, as was and is always claimed by Egosoft. So, I will try not to compare the two.
TO UNDERSTAND WHY I RECOMMEND THIS GAME, YOU HAVE TO READ THE WHOLE REVIEW (or at least the last abstract :)
Rebirth looks great! Stations and ships are detailled to a level that could be even considered not even necessary in a space game. Even the surrounding scenes in first person mode look great! The station layouts are a bit weird, though. All of them feel a bit crammed, even when they are huge on the outside. Textures and room are unbelievably repetitive. I don't get it why Egosoft did not simply include large windows in the station's interior sections to watch the beautiful scenery outside. They could use the same station layout over and over again, but you would still have a great sense of individualism. Add some simple ambient lighting effects depending on the outside scenery and you are there.
Speaking of the interior: Here seems to be the biggest problem. The first person view is currently clearly a kind of elaborate placeholder. There is simply not much to do, but you could imagine it being used for close-quarter fire fights, boarding and similar missions. Why I say placeholder? The potential is there, but it is not being used at all. Other characters are boringly static, sitting around on their beds in their BORING 3rd class dormitories, for crying out loud. Whenever I have a bunk in a hostel, I will be sitting in a close bar, restaurant or even outside, or be somewhere either working or having fun. In Rebirth, the AIs sit, looking depressing as hell in their shiny helmets (helmets in bed??) and space suits. In the end, hiring one of them to drive your slow big freighter feels good. In the sense of freeing a pet from the animal shelter. I actually wondered if they would hug you!
I don't even want to criticise the character models or animations. They are edgy and look clumsy, but that would not spoil the fun as much as the lifelessness of the stations. I want to buy a drink, change the music in a bar etc. Small, simple stuff. It's nearly all there anyway!
Your ship looks so nice, you actually want to wander around in it and play with it. I am not a fan of the jerky cockpit entry animation, but my bigger issue is: Why make a ship you can walk around in, when you cannot walk around in it whenever you want? And why can I not enter the cockpit in first person view and look around and only have a pre-animated move to the seat itself. Also: I want to interact with the ship. Simple things: Have a music player somewhere. A TV set? An ingame browser, or SOMETHING! PLEASE! A coffee maker. A bed, or at least a light switch. Oh boy, you only have this one ship to play with, LET ME BOND WITH IT!
There is so much springing to mind: Since I have a second character in my ship, why not allow her to "autopilot" the ship somewhere and go to sleep for the trip? Have her wake you up if anything happens? Nice and easy roleplay option. Thank you.
Flying the ship feels a bit clumsy, especially when in close quarters around a space station. Forward and backwards should be as controllable as traversing left, right, up and down in that situation. Having forward and backwards only via throttle does not feel good. Also I want to be able to look around properly in my cockpit.
AND NOT THE BIGGEST ISSUE: Let me walk around in my ships. And let me fly them. It is a space game, for gods sake! I can understand this might be an addon. I could live with it. I was feeling especially confined when I landed on my freighter (MY freighter!) in the beginner's missions and was not allowed to leave the landing pad. I want to go to the bridge and look out the huge windows. THAT woudl be awesome.
The winding of the space highways is utter nonsense and feels idiotic. Why not make them straight energy beam kind of accelerated ways, from gate to gate? This winding nature seriously offends me. Sorry.
I can see where Egosoft would like to go and, having lived through similar ups and lots of downs with the X, X² and X³ series, I actually think they will be able to pull it off, but the way there could be quite long and rough.
Before I forget it: THANKS FOR THE LINUX CLIENT!
To sum it up:
I think this will be an awesome game if Egosoft has the stamina to improve it to meet their vision, they are known to work on their games for years to come! I guess I will buy the game, even if it is only to give them the financial means to do it. But so far I will gladly wait to actually play it until it is more complete and does not feel like an elaborate tech demo.

So, I've finally bought this game (v4.30) on sale. Can't say I'm finally happy with everything, but at least I can recommend it now.
After playing it again on free weekend with mods I've come to conclusion: X-Rebirth is a remake of X-Beyound The Frontier with focus on more realistic and immersive gameplay. A step away from great and feature rich X3 series. (They also could be called as space sim of Excel. hehe)
Some things are done better in X3 series and some are better in XR.
It takes some time to get used to GUI and controls, to setup everything, to learn new mechanics and differences in features between X3 series and XR. A few in-game tutorials are available.
Previously disliked "highway concept" and sector layout is ok now, after mod installation that removed highway traffic. Now after I played the game a little, I began to see the reason behind this concept and stopped being too fixated on jump gates.
"Scanning stations" is now less painful with mods that basically remove most of this tedious mechanic from the game.
Illegal goods are now marked as such in game and allow player to discard them before returning to ship.
"police-car ship" is still looking laughable, at least now it without sirens thanks to "No Sirens" sound mod.
Basically, almost every problem I had with this game previously now fixed with MODs from Steam Workshop and NexusMods. Without these MODs I'd never bought XR.
Probably I will create some mods too in the future.
Also I have to say that I play it on GNU\Linux Debian 9 and Linux port is very stable and works without any issues.
Sorry, EgoSoft, but this game still requires many patches and possibly redesigning some aspects of the game so it will be worth a buy. Probably will try it again on next free weekend and after a few major patches..
I've played for only 2 hours on free weekend and have seen already why this game got so much negativity.

Space combat never was one of strong points of X series, but in X Rebirth it is just awfull. Even in "X - Beyond the Frontier" and "X2" combat was good. Best space combat I've experienced was in game "Privateer 2".
Getting information from stations is such a hastle. The requirement of flying near every point of interest marked with icon is a way too much. Why can't we have communications from a distance as it was done in previous X games?
Docking to stations and spending time onboard is overal good concept. It creates more immersive experience. But station insides are all the same and looks lifeless. Neon Chrome is pretty good top-down shooter with strong cyberpunk theme and procedural levels.
The core gameplay is extremely solid, the controls are tight and the fights are often quite fun, especially the bosses. There's also a decent variety of weapons and several different classes that feel fairly different.
Each time you die your current character is gone, but you keep all the money you have collected and can then spend it on permanent stat upgrades and loot for your next character. While a good idea in theory (similar system was great in Rogue Legacy), in practice the upgrades are extremely boring and simply make the game feel needlessly grindy.
The game could have also used more variety with both the levels and the enemies. As it is, I had fun during my first playthrough but felt that there was little point progressing to Overseer 2.0 or higher difficulties as the game starts feeling quite repetitive.
Despite these issues I'd still recommend Neon Chrome to fans of top-down shooters. It's great fun for a few hours, even if the experience grows stale after a while.

Stuffing the game with collectibles can't disguise the shortness of the main plot and the formula has become so familiar by this point that even the charm of the characters doesn't do much to alleviate it.  An anti-climactic ending (you straight-up get told by the narrator,"There are 4 endings, choose one") and a sense that a lot got left on the cutting room floor adds to the sense that this was made more out of a sense of duty/for the cash than as a labor of love.
All that said, the charm of the characters remain from previous games, there are some nice callbacks, the powers are as fun to use as they were in SR4, and I did enjoy playing it for the short time it lasted - I just felt like there could have been a lot more, and that I would have preferred something a little more original.  If you are just looking for roughly 5-10 hours of more of the same from SR3 and 4 that is exactly what you're going to get.

So after a five day binge play of the BioShock franchise, here are my thoughts about the second installment. And though I'm going to recommend this title, I want to caveat the fact that it is by far, the worst in the franchise. It's well worth picking up on sale due to the fact that its story line reflects on the other two titles, but not worth it's asking price. Lets get into why....
I was warned by a friend that this game was sub par to the original BioShock, but at first blush I was confused as to why. It looked like a vast improvement, with brushed up graphics, new weapons, new enemies, and the ability to play as a Big Daddy. All things that should have made this a block buster game, but are handled so poorly that in the end it actually leaves you very disappointed.
Where to start..... The brushed up graphics at first seem to be a big improvement over the original. They fix one of my gripes about the first game with plenty of new Splicers, each with different voices and outfits, they even added new types of Big Daddy. The problem with this is that you eventually notice that what they've done is remove the glassy, 40s stylized look from the first game, and made everyone look more "realistic". This is a huge disappointment, as it damages the mood the first game set and the surreal look, setting Rapture as far away from ordinary as a city at the bottom of the sea should be. And though they did an alright job making the Splicer's look deformed, it's not the same feeling from the first game where things were bulbous and misshaped or looked out of a 40s pulp comic. The Big Daddy suffers from this problem too as they even out its proportions and turn the Little Sisters into just normal girls with headlamps for eyes.
Weapons are improved from the first game, with things like a rivet gun, .50 Cal, drill, things a Bid Daddy would carry. However, these guns seem to pack less than the punch you would expect. Splicers are brutal and manage to eat tons of rounds with only hits to the head seeming to do anything. Rather than hacking like the first game, they give you a wrist mounted tool, that fires remote "tubes" that allow you to hack from a distance. This sounds amazing till you discover they nerfed the hacking  from the tube puzzle, to a Pre-Skool metronome color match game. This does nothing to solve my gripe from the first game, where hacking stops being a challenge and becomes a chore that you dread. And to remove ANY challenge from this process is worst of all, patronizing the player and making it more busywork. Ammo is dropped in a frustratingly random way, always seeming to give you rounds for every gun but the one you need, and the first half of the game is so stingy with drops that you will run into the red if not out of almost every round by the time they toss you up against your first boss. Money is also unbalanced, leaving you dry when you most need it, and like BioShock, the limited wallet space is so annoying that it makes you want to punch a kitten in the neck. Also, the game seems to throw a lot of "junk" at you in boxes and dead splicers, that seem to do nothing! In the first game, drinks, smoking, and eating would give you bonus and detraction in stats depending. But in this game, you get swamped with odd food items, tons of drinks, and random objects that flash by you so quickly that you really have no idea what they do or what they're for. You find yourself slamming the "loot all" button and pray that it's doing something beneficial.
Next, is the fact that you're playing as an original design Big Daddy, or Delta series. Naturally, this unique and should be an enjoyable adventure, but sadly it isn't. And why? Because for some reason I can't seem to figure out, you are as weak as wet toilet paper. Yes, the massive Big Daddy from BioShock, that can kill you in one shoulder charge, is reduced to something a Splicer can kill with some errant gun fire. And don't give me the excuse that it's because he's and older model, as the game shows in the open that he can crush Splicers with hardly a thought, but once the game starts, all that power is gone. In fact, it feels like you have LESS health than the protagonist from the first game! This is utterly insane. As a Big Daddy, I should be able to swat Splicers like flies, and of course, the other Big Daddy have no problems doing this, yet even though Delta uses Plasmids as well as eight unique weapons, he's still weaker than just about everything. And this really blows, because they could have pulled a huge contrast to the survival aspect from the first game, by utilizing the massive size and armor of the Big Daddy to wade through huge amounts of smaller enemies and larger, more brutal "boss" situations. That's not to say it's all bad, as you can "adopt" Little Sister's from fallen Big Daddy and protect them as they collect ADAM from bodies littered around Rapture. This is rather enjoyable, and creepy as the Little Sister's vocalizations are just bizarre.
Another glaring problem with this game is the plot.... The story line to this game, in a word, stinks.... except in winter, when it stinks on ice... It makes little sense, and doesn't do a damn thing to try and sell it to you. The concept is beyond weak, where a character magically shows up to take over after Ryan and Fontaine are dead, and SUPRISE, is an integral part of Rapture though no one deemed her important enough to mention in the first game. And believe me, this woman is so utterly annoying that you'll want to drip poison into your own ear, rather than have to listen to a single word Sofia Lamb has to say. If the first game was trying to covertly extol the Communist agenda (which it didn't), Lamb picks no bones about being a tree hugging, collectivist, self serving, commie pinko ♥♥♥♥♥. This woman is the thing that never shuts up, and she verbally assaults you non stop through the ENTIRE GAME. And truly this is a major problem, because again, all the updates in the graphics department can't save a game with faulty plot. Another huge problem is, after making Delta out to be some long lost dare devil that stumbled onto Rapture they simply drop any explanation of his back story, and even worse, kills him at the end for NO APPARENT REASON! Can you say poor plot device?! Somehow I feel if they hadn't wasted time building a crappy PVP Multi-player mode where adolescent boys can cross♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and brag about how many kills they have, we would have had a more rich single player story.
With all that said, there are some very good points about this game that in a way save it. Again, despite the realistic graphics, Bioshock 2 still manages to build a fantastic mood, with some of the visuals giving me chills. There is a large glass window that overlooks the ruins of Rapture that simply made my blood cold, as well as a fantastic scene of a "Rosie" Big Daddy doing something other escorting a Little Sister. There was also a great section where you got to see out of a Little Sister's eyes, where Rapture appears to still be a heavenly place filled with satin drapes, pillows, and rose petals. Sadly, this is mismanaged as well, seeing as the scene is short and serves no more purpose than to be a gimmick to extend the ending. They also do a great job on making you feel Delta's weight, as the floors creek, jumping is limited, and movement slow and methodical. Plasmids are improved and bugs fixed, but again it seems you use the stun ability of the Electric Plasmid more than any other. Voice acting is again is phenomenal despite Lamb, though the mapping suffered because the game is formatted for console rather than PC.
To summarize, the game has many faults and at times feels unworthy of being the successor to the original, but still manages to be a good play at the right price. However, if 2K ever decides to pull a mulligan, this game deserves it far more than the original.

Many reviewers expected Beyond Earth to be Alpha Centauri 2, which it is not. Neither it is a Civilization V mod. It IS a new game, which, although share some features of Civ5 (hex grid, battle system, unit classes, wonders, resources, neutral units) and AC (ideologies, sci-fi techs), is played differently.
The main focus in BE is on affinity (ideology) choices. As you specialise towards a particular victory type, you need to focus on specific technologies. Each next progress level gives you an affinity point, which in turn provides you with useful perks (upgrades) for your units + bonuses. These specific perks will radically change your units as you progress on specific affinity path (alien-like units, machine-like units or human units).
The culture works in a similar way as in Civ5. After certain level of culture is reached, you can acquire virtues (4 virtue categories – Might, Prosperity, Knowledge and Industry - in 3 tiers), which work in a similar way as social policies in Civ 5. There are synergy bonuses for focusing on same category virtues or same tier virtues.
Also, there are quests, research pods and exploration areas, which substantially can boost your progress over the time. As well as the destruction of aliens and alien nests, especially with certain Might virtues.
The victory types are following: Domination - conquer all other players; Contact - contact alien civilization; Transcendence (requires Harmony specialisation)  - civilization fully adapts to the new planet and becomes enlightened; Promised Land (requires Purity specialisation) - bring Earth population to the new planet; Emancipation (requires Supremacy specialisation) - conquer ("free") Earth.
So, it's a completely different setting in Beyond Earth. And you require a different approach from what you're used to in Civ5. Although, the same basic rules are still in place: e.g., a) food is population, population is everything; b) science is progress, progress is victory.
When I played Beyond Earth for the first time, there were certain innovations that annoyed me, but after playing a while, I got used to them and they started to make sense for me.
For example:
1. Technology tree is replaced with technology web, which makes it hard to find things, unless you haven't played few sessions. However, with filters and search option, it becomes quite easy to find what you're looking for and to plan your strategy.
2. Miasma - spore clouds on some tiles that damage human units. This was really annoying in the beginning. However with right technologies, it actually is kind of cool way to have something to transform. And besides, it makes sense, that alien planet is initially hostile towards humans, but as human population adapts to the new habitat, it learns to use the nature for its own good.
3. Aliens – very hostile, very procreative and (some of them) very strong. Initially, it is very hard to avoid them or kill them, so it might be annoying experience for beginners, but, again, with right technologies and strategy, there are ways to overcome this problem and turn it for your own good. After you have the right technologies and units, it's a great opportunity to gain XP for your army. You can have neutral relationship with aliens (by not destroying their nests), but I have never tried this option, because they are always in your way and threaten you on each turn.
4. Colour balance - blue and green are dominant colours, it's hard to distinguish miasma and resources. By turning resource yields and icons on, it's possible to minimise this problem, but, still, why couldn't they make miasma red or purple?
5. There is a radical shift towards agressive playstyle compared to Civ5. It's almost a must to constantly build units and to defend or attack somebody. It's not something I was used to in Civ5. And at first I didn't really like it. But then again, the overall gameplay is more versatile and balanced and the player gets to use and enjoy all of his strengths in a versatile way. It really freshens up the TBS feel in this game.
6. AI behaviour. AI players are either nasty or stupid or both. The diplomatic relationship and deals do not make any sense. There is no solution for this. Just forget about reasonable trade offers, when playing Beyond Earth. You're on your own. I hope Firaxis will change this with future updates.
So, with that said, I think Beyond Earth is really a great game. Not perhaps as good as Civilization V, but it certainly feels fresh, runs smoothly and each game session offers a different experience.
I would recommend it to all Civilization fans, not perhaps for its full price, but with atleast -40% discount (30 €), it's worth the price even in its current Vanilla state. However, I do hope there will be new expansions, scenarios and maps.

Bioshock 2 is not as innovative, cohesive and thematically sophisticated as the original. That being said, it plays just as well, if not better, due to some much needed design modifications. And the game looks markedly better as well. Its problems lie in the storyline and how it progresses. While the communism v.s. objectivism theme sounds fantastic on paper, it is not as convincing as Bioshock's treatment of objectivism and capitalism. Perhaps it reveals that Ken Levine knew what he was writing about, whereas Bioshock 2 better resembles a summary of Wikipedia pages on the subject. But, if you're there for the gameplay and experience itself, you'll be happy. Combat is smoother; the environment is more detailed and traversing it is more challenging. However, the means to obtain Adam soon grows very tedious.
Remember that section in the first game when you protected a little sister against waves of enemies? In the second game, you don't have a little sister until you defeat another big daddy and take his. Naturally, the combat here is very challenging. However, if you harvest the little sister right then and there, you'll get very little return. Instead, you must let her extract Adam from three designated corpses in the area; each time, you are beset at all sides by enemies who only become stronger the further you advance through the game. Of course, after doing this three times, you are met with the same binary choice as in the first game: harvest or set-free. But don't forget, each area has three big daddies and three little sisters. Once all little sisters are harvested or freed in an area, you'll be forced into an immediate fight to the death with a big sister.
This is what I mean by 'boss battle overload', and it's all the more confusing that the character you're playing should, by all means, BE a boss! It certainly doesn't feel so, as you die just as easily as any human. So, unless you LOVE this gameplay mechanic, you might come to hate hearing the words, "look daddy, it's an angel!" That being said, certainly persevere with the game. You just might like to save the expansion, Minerva's Den for a while later.

“I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream” gives an interesting take on the mythos surrounding mortality and consequence. The game plays as an adaptation of the short story written by uber-famous sci-fi extraordinaire Harlan Ellison, onto which humanity is put at an ultimate test.  Those who are familiar with titles such as “Eternal Darkness: Sanity’s Requiem” will feel well at home with this title; as each game not only amasses a variety of time pieces, but contains different stories that in some ultimate fashion fasten together for a grand conclusion.
The game kicks off in a pseudo “System Shock 2” manner in which a supercomputer named AM—reminiscent of “2001: A Space Odyssey” HAL—selects five members on which to do his bidding… namely torturing these poor souls to relive their greatest guilt in an unending cycle in such the style of Hell. Each character only remembers bits and pieces of their past, but do not remember what terrible offense they had committed to deserve such cruelties. Later exploration consists of a psychological exodus where they slowly come to a moment of realization; it is normally at that moment where AM—in one final and desperate tactic—lays out an ultimate torture for each subject.
“I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream” is accompanied by a sharp script that is borderline twisted and amusing; it defines dark humor amidst a tale of tragedy and desperation. The script is elevated also by the unique performances of the cast, including none other than Harlan Ellison who voices AM. There is an array of emotions by each character that not only draws a gamer deeper into unraveling the mysteries, but at some moments also feel for the character, as if accompanied. The subject matter in all its seriousness provides a great contrast to an otherwise campy story that, had it been crafted in any other manner, might not have been taken as seriously in other games. “I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream” not only knows the balance between comedy and tragedy but does a flaming knife juggling on unicycle act. There are very few science fiction writers that have accomplished such things—the closest to come to mind is Philip K.♥♥♥♥♥♥ who wrote countless short stories including “We Can Remember it for You Wholesale” which inspired Paul Verhoeven’s 1990 sleeper hit “Total Recall,” basically another story that balances itself between tragedy, comedy, and campiness.
The gameplay as a whole is decent for the most part; not the lengthiest or most challenging of adventure games in the market. Seasoned adventure veterans could go through this title in a solid 2-3 hours; casuals, add at least 2 hours to that notch. The game is more story-driven than anything, and the locations aren’t incredibly large. The game does call for a great deal of backtracking, but on a plus note there is very minimal handholding. There is a consequence system. Consequences are measured by the actions gamers take: whether they completely miss a step, mess up on a puzzle, choose the not-so-nice conversational responses, reflects on a character portrait. The more you do a faulty job, or the wrong choices you make, affects the colorization of the border in a character portrait, leading to a different outcome endgame. It is basically your average in-game report card before stats started lingering the gaming market. Some would argure that the system mandates are unjust, that the game wants you to basically follow a set pattern and offer very little room for freedom of choice. In the contextual realm of “I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream” it fits very well with the philosophical nature of the game.
If there were any complaints to be made, it was that I wanted more. Each chapter offers small episodes for each character, and they are each original in their very nature. Some romps are more amusing than others. But when the grand—and I mean grand—finale of the game comes to a close, I was left as much satisfied by the delivery as I did emptied. On a positive note, the game does have multiple ways in which the game can end, depending on which character you would choose to perform the final actions. The puzzles remain the same, but any prior knowledge one particular character has effects certain situations in the final stage. While such a variety was interesting, there still remained little to no difference in other departments outside of the story. Does that sour the overall experience I have had with the game? Not in the least. “I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream” does  contain a very interesting story—filled to the brim with references to other literary works and historical moments—outside of its rather primitive and linear level designs, but it is a game that has switched enough mental gears to make it an overall unforgettable experience, especially for those who have an appreciation for older titles. The game is ultimately affected by its concise duration, even for a game made right after the transition from DOS/floppy disk titles, which can stint game completion (by those who have memorized the game full and through) to under an hour. While it may thematically reflect the length of a short story, "I Have No Mouth, and Must Scream" painfully makes me wish it were rather the length of a novel.
Presentation: 8.5/10
Gameplay: 7.5/10
Graphics: 8/10
Sound: 8.5/10
Replay Value: 6.5/10
Overall: 7.8/100
Final Analysis: “I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream” provides an entertaining adventure through the ages. While the adventure is cut short by content value, it more than makes up for both story, originality, and personality. Adventure fans may find some interest to be had from this title, anyone else regard it with caution—albeit it has aged fairly, “I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream” requires patience, persistence, and a sense of appreciation for games of yesteryear. Definitely worth discount price; anything more than 5 dollars is a swindle.

I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream is a fascinating piece of work. It's one of those games, much like Scratches, that works wonders with atmosphere, but not so much when it comes to the actual gameplay. Although where Scratches had a really tense, frightening atmosphere, No Mouth is more mysterious and depressing. I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream works more with fridge horror, I feel. Yeah, it's creepy, but it's only truly scary if you sit back and think about it. And you will, because it's a tale that provokes thought.
I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream was originally a famous short story by one Mr. Harlan Ellison. If you get the chance, I recommend giving it a read, as there's a reason it's so famous. Actually, that's a lie. I don't recommend reading it. I really recommend
to it. The I Have No Mouth audiobook, read by Harlan Ellison himself, is truly a treasure of audio. Ellison is hammy and over-the-top, but man does he
it. The man gets completely into his story, and it benefits immensely from it.
If you've done the above, then I think you'll be more than pleased to hear that Ellison also plays AM, the maniacally hate-filled, torturous supercomputer who serves as your antagonist and tormenter for the duration of this game. He's every bit as hammy and over-the-top, and it's hard not to hang on his every word. The other voices in the game vary in quality, but you won't really notice the dips as you'll be too focused on the unfolding storylines, and also on WHAT DO I DO
So let's start with the story. You play five different characters, who comprise the entire remaining human population of Earth. AM, a colossal supercomputer which resides beneath the crust of the Earth, more or less got frustrated with his lot in life and unleashed the world's supply of nukes at... well, the world. But it kept five human beings alive to be his playthings for the remainder of eternity. For over a hundred years, these five humans have been subjected to ungodly torments, and now AM would like to play a little game.
Each character is thrown into a scenario built especially for them, expected to be horrible and miserable for AM's amusement. The true goal before you is to fail AM, and prove yourself above his petty games. It is in these scenarios that you will learn about each character, their faults, their history, and a little bit about AM himself and what's going on behind the scenes and beyond your view.
This obviously differs from the original story, as these scenarios never existed. They were created (with major input from Ellison) especially for this game in order to give more backstory on the characters. Things change. The story as a whole changes. But it's still very much I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream.
Let's talk about the gameplay.
It could be better.
IHNM is presented in a classic SCUMM format. You have a list of verbs and an inventory at the bottom of the screen, both of which can be used to interact with the world around you. You will talk to characters, solve puzzles, find objects. All the familiar trappings of a good point-and-click adventure. So far, so good. The first major hitch is that eternal adventure game hellspawn, the unrelated event. You know what I'm talking about. When you do a thing, which triggers an unrelated thing to happen somewhere else which you have no way of knowing about and no reason to think might have happened. So many point-and-click adventures have fallen prey to this design flaw (Myst IV and Hector 3 among them, just thinking off the top of my head, here), and I wish it would stop.
I had one point in the first scenario I picked where I didn't know what to do. I looked up a guide, and it didn't help. I thought maybe my game was glitched, as I had done everything the guide had ordered. And then I saw it. A very subtle thing. A line in the guide telling me to exhaust a certain character's dialogue. All I had skipped (for reasons that we'll get to in a moment) was an entirely unnecessary rude line that doesn't actually help anything. But lo and behold, when burning off that one useless line of dialogue caused an unrelated character to appear in a different location, freeing progression from the devs' icy cold grip.
There are some other annoying bits, here and there. Some items and interactables that aren't exactly obvious on the screen. Two scenarios allow you to progress past important items or before doing mandatory bits. It's problematic, and very confusing when it happens. Luckily, it's possible to die after this moment in one of the scenarios, bringing you back to the character select where you can choose to try again. For the other one... well, just keep multiple saves, is all.
In addition to simply making through each scenario, every character has a personal spiritual meter. The better the spirits they're in, the lighter the background behind their portrait in the lower-left becomes. Practice good morals and make progress to lighten it. Screw up, be corrupt or evil, or just cause your character to freak out to darken it. If the meter turns white as the scenario draws to a close, you've perfected that scenario. This is not always easy to do. I only managed it in two scenarios.
They say you need to get a white meter with each character in order to see the best ending, and that's going to require either a guide or multiple playthroughs. I wonder, though. I'm pretty positive I did in fact get the best ending, despite not having all whites. I think it's probably possible as long as each character has almost a white meter, or a couple characters have white meters and everyone else is close? Or something? Though don't quote me on that, I really don't know, and there's a surprising lack of entirely helpful documentation on this subject.
Anyways, my advice is to not worry about it. Do your best and get an ending, whatever that ending may be. Give the finale a few tries, though, because you'll probably screw it up a couple times.
Anyways, point is, the game looks great and sounds great, and the story will draw you all sorts of in. Just be aware that you may need to consult the Internet at times, and be sure to rotate your saves. Or do what I did and just make each save a new one, because this game seems to have infinite slots. Which is a nice feature.
For all its faults, I still enjoyed the majority of my time with I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream. And if you're a fan of the original story, or games which not only don't shy away from adult themes, but walk straight through a minefield of adult themes and take it all in stride with a sly grin upon their lips, then I think you'll enjoy it too.

So despite my lack of hours in this game, I feel I can give it a review. It is a well built game, with a decent AI, decent gameplay, decent just about everything, except map choices.
The AI is tricky. I had a 5v5 battle last two days due to AI that could resist a full frontal assault. Got most of the achievements for capital ships in that period of time, destroying and building and leveling. 5 titans died at that star. The AI in this game is by far the best out of all I've seen, even on easy. It knows when it should retreat, and when to sacrifice part of its fleet for the greater good.
The gameplay is beautiful, nice artwork, little bummed that there aren't any collisions. Would be fun to ram a ship through another. I've also had some lag issues when playing multiplayer, when someone I can see phase jumps. Sort of bad for a rts, since tides can turn in seconds.
The races are pretty boring in diversity, but are also well balanced. There really is no 'better' race/group. One faction may have high shield points, giving up some HP, while another has less shield, more HP, but either could destroy either. Of course, research can make that not true, but everyone starts out basically as powerful as everyone else.
Map choices are slim, in my opinion. I like having more maps than I can count to choose from. Also dislike that, despite being in space, and everything being 3d objects, the game is still played in a 2d form. Would be neat if I could swing ships under and above enemies.
That is all I really have to say about this game. The price is slightly unsettling for me, with DLCs, but I'm not regretting the choice I made to buy it, either. Arguably one of the top of its genre. 9/10

I have a difficult time writing about I Have No Mouth and I Must because of my personal attitude towards this game. While I consider “The Longest Journey” the paramount of an adventure experience and believe that everyone should at least try this game, in case of IHNMaIMS is more complicated since, clearly, it is not a game everyone can enjoy.
First off all, IHNMaIMS is kind of The Elder Scrolls of adventure gaming, and for more than one reason. Firstly, hardy any point and click adventure gives player such freedom of choices. Secondly, much less on a positive note, this is possibly the greatest bugfest in the history of adventure gaming. When deciding to play this game one has to be prepared to face game breaking bugs that will inspire either restarting one’s adventure or a ragequit. Still, while IHNMaIMS forums are choke-full of bug reports ,  I was lucky enough to finish at least three different versions of this game without any problems.
Secondly, people who prefer solid mechanics and comfortable gameplay may (and probably will) completely disdain this game. In IHNMaIMS everything seems to be secondary to narration. If you prefer story over anything else, then that is not an issue, but if you want to play comfortably know this: this game has a nasty habit of playing with the gamer. Not to spoil too much, it often may look like you have to do something bad to another character (kill is such a nasty word…) or a group of characters to gain a particular item or simply progress a story. And when you finish that chapter you discover that said item was completely useless. On the other hand, the character’s alignment / sanity is of great importance in this game, and it is affected all the time, exactly by this kind of choices.
Thirdly, it needs to be said that to fully appreciate this game, some basic knowledge of Freudian psychology is needed. Especially the ego, superego and id and the dream symbolism may come in handy.
So, what does this game give in return ? Probably the most emotionally engaging experience in the history of adventure gaming. The world (or worlds) within this game is rich and congruent, storylines are brilliant and characters are captivating ( The game goes to great lengths to make one feel compassionate even for a sadistic scientist of a totalitarian regime). Also the way the puzzles fit into the storyline is truly brilliant. For example (not much of a spoiler, since that’s the very beginning of this particular chapter), the first day of the Benny’s storyline. Benny’s body has been completely mutilated during the years of merciless torture, his bones have been shattered and forced to grow together in a bad way, his vocal cords have been torn out and he is generally a mess. Consequently, first he has to learn  how to eat, walk up the stairs and how to communicate with others.
Finally, for the game that’s nearly 20 years old, the graphics are still pretty impressive. The backgrounds are dark, moody and full of detail. Still, It should be appreciated how authors made almost every important item clearly visible.To conclude, let me just suggest running this game on ScummVM, a free tool that enables many graphic and sound options as well as some bugfixes – which in this particular game helps a lot.

Pisanie o I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream (dalej IHNMaIMS) przychodzi mi z trudem ze względu na fakt że jest to jedna z tych gier które zdefiniowały moje podejście do przygodówek. Inaczej jednak, niż w przypadku „Najdłuższej Podróży”, która niezmiennie jest moim „numerem jeden” w świecie point and clicków, nie mogę IHNMaIMS polecić każdemu.
Po pierwsze, można powiedzieć  że ta gra jest swoistym „Elder Scrollem”  przygodówek, i to z więcej niż jednego powodu. Podobnie jak seria Bethesdy daje wolność wyboru niespotykaną u innych przedstawicieli danego gatunku. I podobnie jak „Scrollsy” jest aż po same brzegi napakowana bugami wszelkiej maści i kalibru. Odpalając IHNMaIMS trzeba być przygotowanym na błędy które mogą uniemożliwić jej ukończenie, zmusić do restartu całej historii, albo spowodować ragequit. Inna sprawa, że ukończyłem co najmniej trzy różne wersje tej gry, nie natrafiając na żadne poważniejsze bugi, więc da się też „zaliczyć” ją bezproblemowo.
Po drugie, ludzie ceniący sobie solidną mechanikę ułatwiającą rozgrywkę na każdym kroku prawdopodobnie znienawidzą tą grę. Jakie problemy można mieć z mechaniką w point and clicku? W IHNMaIMS wszystko jest drugoplanowe względem opowiadanej historii.  Osoboy ceniącym sobie w grach przede wszystkim angażującą narrację nie będą miały z tym problemów, niemniej ta gra potrafi momentami być bardzo złośliwa. Zamierzenie. Żeby uniknąć spoilerów wspomnę tylko że nieraz może wydawać się że jedynym sposobem zdobycia jakiegoś przedmiotu czy popchnięcia historii na przód jest wyrządzenie mniejszego bądź większego zła któremuś z bohaterów pobocznych. Kiedy już gracz zdobędzie dany przedmiot, okazuje się że nie jest on do niczego przydatny, podczas gdy poczytalność bohatera –którą tracimy bądź zyskujemy, zależnie od dokonywanych decyzji – odgrywa kluczową rolę w opowiadanej historii.
Po trzecie, żeby w pełni docenić IHNMaIMS, przydaje się podstawowa znajomość psychologii Freudowskiej – ego, super ego, id, symbolika snów. Bez tego niektóre fragmenty gry mogą wydać się niezrozumiałe.
A co ta gra może dać w zamian? Prawdopodobnie najbardziej wciągający horror science-fiction w historii gier przygodowych. Świat (czy raczej światy) przedstawiony tutaj jest bogaty, mroczny i fascynujący, historia ciekawa, a postacie wielopoziomowe i wzbudzające sympatię (nawet sadystyczny doktor z obozu zagłady – bo i kimś takim przyjdzie nam grać) . Jeżeli zaś chodzi o zagadki które stawiane są przez graczem, uważam je za szczytowe osiągnięcie jeżeli chodzi o łączenie narracji z mechaniką rozgrywki. Przykładem niech będzie początek historii Bennego (nie jest to wielki spoiler – pierwsze 5 minut rozdziału).  Benny jest uroczą postacią – jego kości zostały połamane i zrosły się w paskudny sposób, struny głosowe zostały wyrwane z jego gardła, twarz ma pociętą w drobną kratkę – ogólnie Benny nie jest okazem zdrowia. Oczywiście ma to wpływ na zadania przed jakimi staje  – na początku musimy nauczyć go jak komunikować się bez używania głosu, jeść (!) i wchodzić po schodach (!!).
Mógłbym o tej grze napisać wiele więcej, ale kończy mi się miejsce więc słowo o oprawie: po prawie 20 latach grafika ciągle robi wrażenie. Tła są klimatyczne, pełne szczegółów i wspaniale kształtują mroczny obraz gry, budowany również przez klimatyczną muzykę. Warto wspomnieć że autorzy dokonali niemal cudu sprawiając że na tych pełnych detali tłach prawie każdy istotny dla fabuły przedmiot jest widoczny. Na koniec wspomnę jeszcze tylko że najlepiej uruchomić tą grę przez ScummVM, darmowe narzędzie udostępniające w starych przygodówkach wiele opcji graficznych, dźwiękowych i naprawiających wiele błędów – co w przypadku IHNMaIMS ma niebagatelne znaczenie.

This game is very strange, maybe that's what I like about it, but what is Betrayer?
Betrayer is a game of survival and exploration steeped in mystery and a spark of the paranormal. You wake up on a beach, don't know who you are or what's going on, as you pick up scraps of paper that are scattered throughout the landscape which give you clues as to what happened in this place in your absence and your role in it. You discover locations from the initial coastal shipwreck site by exploring on foot and unlocking landmarks as you happen upon them (and there's a fast travel system so you won't turn into Walking Simulator 2014) which makes up smaller parts of a greater world map. You are discovering the new world after all.
It needs to be said that the atmosphere in this game is quite possibly my favorite aspect of it. You're in a constant state of being a little on edge. You might find yourself feeling a little more at ease when you get the mechanics down but there's still this fleeting dread I feel when I'm playing. Especially when you're in the otherworld.
The supernatural element is interesting but it hasn't been clearly explained as to why you're able to tap into the spirit world to talk to ghosts/wraiths and collect from them what I would call side quests. The how happens very early in, the why is a mystery to me.
If you care about graphics, it's a pretty looking game too. And if you don't like the black and white style, there's a saturation option to add the color back in. Spirit world is always black and white however.
The only issue I have is with the intuitiveness of this game. There is a listening mechanic that gives you a clue as to where you need to head but never tells you whether or not it's necessary. The same sound is used for graves, chests, mounds, totems, etc. And it's not always clear as to what needs to be done to proceed. The sound of enemies spotting you is great and kind of shoots a little shock to your system if you're skulking around and suddenly hear the telltale ring followed by a mild panic until the target is in sight. Furthermore, it should be noted that I'm not one who needs to be led by the hand by my games - this is beyond non-linear, it's just a bit confusing at first.
Broken down:
Pros:
+ Very creative
+ Great artistic direction
+ Control are tight and responsive
+ Movement and weapons feel great (Thanks Unreal engine)
+ Heavy atmosphere
+ Exploration never gets dull
Cons:
- Vague sense of what needs to be done
- Listening mechanic, while creative, isn't always helpful
On the whole: 9/10. Especially if you can get it on sale.

First impressions say a lot to me, so this review is based on about half an hour of playing. Do with that as you wish.
The short time I played this game in its free weekend left me frustrated above anything else. If one were to ignore the terrible dialog and voice acting, the game just plays horribly. The first mission is supposedly a tutorial, but it was probably the most unintuative mess I've ever seen. Nothing is explained properly. The entire UI is utterly confusing and your current goals (if any) are not easily found, let alone marked. I had to travel to a station and then dock.
Firstly there is apparently some sort of highway system that acts as a 'current' through empty space. The way things are marked in space I first tried to go around this because I thought my objective was behind it. Eventually I figured out I had to go into it.
Arriving at the station is where the real fun began. It took me absolute ages to figure out how docking worked. It took Google to explain to me that mousing over a service and pressing F comes up with a contextual menu. Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥how hard would it have been to explain this in the game? And even then it works like absolutely♥♥♥♥♥♥ Why can't I click on something to get that menu?
Once I was docked the mechanic needed parts to fix my ship. Parts that were stored in a cabinet. His own cabinet, which he was standing right next to. But for some reason it was still MY job to get the parts from HIS cabinet. This is where I said '♥♥♥♥ it' and just closed the game. The game reeks of bad design in ever corner and playing it any further would have just left me even more frustrated. Maybe if you get past all this it could be a fun game, but it's just really badly designed. Certainly not something I would spend any amount of money on with the first 30 minutes of gameplay being this bad.

This weekend, Steam had a free weekend which included X3 Albion Prelude which I had not previously played, so I gave it a go and going back to the X3 series has just highlighted to me how rubbish X Rebirth is. I have tried to like X Rebirth, I really have, but Egosoft seem to have ripped out or messed up everything that made X3 enjoyable.
No longer do you have a range of ships and weapons to choose from that you can buy and fly. You are stuck with one ship that has a few upgrades available.
Trading has been completely messed up. There is remote trading, which is almost completely unfathomable and never seems to offer any profit or there is station trading with half a dozen stock lookalike characters on each station. The best way of making any money in this game seems to revolve around crawling around in air-ducts on the stations and selling the stuff you find there to the locals, which becomes completely boring very quickly.
Combat is another botched up mess. It isn't really clear who you are fighting and I found that destroying Red 'Enemy' ships lost me reputation and unable to dock at the vast majority of stations. Then there are drones. I am yet to figure out what the point of drones are. There is a tutorial in using the spy ones but it failed to explain why you would want to do this.
Factory building was great fun in the X3 series and you can build individual or complex factories anywhere you fancy. Not in X Rebirth though. You are limited to a few, game dictated spots and have to hunt high and low for the stuff to make them. The economy is such that it is almost impossible to know what to build where.
The transport system has been completely changed. No longer do you have jump gates with the option of jump drives but highways and super-highways to transport you around the universe. This means sometimes you have to go around an entire loop just to move one system.
The only good thing I would say about X rebirth, and you would expect this considering the age of the X3 games, is that the graphics have improved.
I really looked forward to X Rebirth and perhaps I expected too much after the X3 series but this new incarnation really has torn the heart out of the enjoyment of the game. If you are looking for a good space sim try the X3 series.
If you have already, like me, tried the X3 series and liked/loved it, do not buy X rebirth, you will only find dissapointment.
To Egosoft - Please think about ditching this disaster and moving on to X4 - X3 with X Rebirth graphics perhaps planet landing options, better fleet controls and even multi-plsyer. You have got it badly wrong with X Rebirth and the reviews on steam show it.

For new MTG players, this game is reasonably good, mostly because it is free. For veterans, I'm not sure this is really worth your time, but I've been playing to get a taste for some of the new cards. This version of Duels brings some nice new things to the table over previous games, but not all of them have been done well.
The tutorials are better than they have been in the past (for newbies), but you are forced through the initial set. Vets do get some coin for suffering through them, though, and they are quick little game chunks. The story mode is very different than in the past, in that you do not BYO deck.
They added freeform deck building with the complete set of cards available in the game. This is wonderful, although as many have noted, the cards are generally less powerful than previous Duels games. With the new rule of mythics only being singleton, rares capped at 2, and uncommons at 3, it seems like they could still keep power pretty well in check without making my constructed decks feel like they were built in a sealed tournament.
The deck wizard is a great addition to Duels in concept, but the choices it presents you don't even offer the optimal choices among your available cards. I'm not sure if it is much better when you only have the starter cards or a full set of everything, but in between, it doesn't always follow it's own stated purpose very well. Not only can you not adjust the land count in these decks, though, you can't even choose which of your lands go into it, which gets very frustrating as you start to unlock the colorless lands (I don't want Counsel of the Foundry in every deck, nor do I want 24 lands in my ramp decks!). Hopefully, this gets more refined in the next Duels or as this game is patched because it is incredibly helpful for newbies. Fortunately, they have either abolished or greatly reduced the frequency of the daily quests that required you to use a wizard-built deck instead of one of the freeform builds.
When it comes time to play your decks, there are some noticeable setbacks compared to previous games. They did bring back the beloved 2HG multiplayer mode, but somehow decided that chat should no longer be part of the game.
They made it so the AI takes over in a game when someone concedes, which irked me at first, but it does allow you to concede in style. I like to pump my opponents creatures up or lightning bolt my own face to let the person I can't chat with know that I am conceding without them having to finish against the AI. But about that AI...I honestly cannot tell the difference between the three difficulty levels. The easy level still has access to all the mythics you don't get at the start, and the difficult makes dumber mistakes than the previous games ever did at the Planeswalker difficulty. They are still painfully predictable, with little sense of board state or no clue what your untapped mana could mean given your colors. The mulligans use the first one is free concept that was passed over in favor of the scry 1 rule, but that is okay. What isn't okay is that the AI will sit there with 0 or 1 lands in hand and not bother mulling. It's never a fun game when you are totally mana-screwed, but it's also not fun playing solitaire against the AI while they discard every turn with just one lonely land on the table.
At any rate, free in this game gets you farther than the demos do in the previous Duels games. The free grind is certainly helped along with the daily quests, but many people, only get new daily quests every other day (EDIT: this bug was fixed, at least for me), significantly reducing the amount of coin you can earn in a short period of time. If you're thinking of paying money for coins, though, I cannot recommend that. For playing against AI, you're probably better off putting that money into one of the previous titles. To play other people, you can do enough with that money in MTGO/MODO to make that a far better choice, although the learning curve is quite steep, so newbies would be advised to at least play around with a Duels game first or maybe consider going to play on paper at your local store.

I passed on this game when it released, thinking it was a poor imitation of previous Hitman titles, ruined by attempts at modernising the series. I was very wrong; the game is excellent. To briefly cover things that most reviews touch on: in the mini-sandbox assassination levels, the core gameplay is very much intact even though the levels are a little smaller; there are multiple paths through each level and targets can be eliminated in lots of ways. I've finished half of the story missions and so far stealth is an option in every single level, down to the 'boss fight'-type confrontations—sometimes it is bitterly hard, but it is doable and built into the game. The cover system does not ruin stealth at all, but the new disguise system can be infuriating sometimes.
All of these things together make a
game, but I honestly think Absolution is more than that. There is more attention to detail and atmosphere-building here than I have experienced in any of the other Hitman games, more humanity and humour. NPC exchanges are varied and regular: you will hear the usual tough-guy talk between police/thug characters, but in the adjacent room a group of the same thugs are frantically stealing prescription drugs to sell under their boss's nose, and down the hall a junior hired gun is laughing nervously, clearly uncomfortable with the violence. Every level is full of these little exchanges that add up to create a really unique entry in the series. And when a wistful anecdote syncs up with the music so the instruments swell as a character falls into silence, and sunlight through the window lights up clouds of dust, the whole experience comes together in quite a special way.
I've gone on for a bit now, but I never see any reference to these little touches in games press reviews; IO definitely deserves more credit for Absolution than they initially received.

I'll get straight to the point and say that if you are a fan of older First-person shooters, Return to Castle Wolfenstein is  definitely a worthy purchase. Considering the fact that the game is 16-years-old, it is quite impressive to see how well this title has aged. Being priced at $5, there really is not much reason to not purchase this gem. Hell, you could even wait for a Steam sale and snatch it for even less.
Pros:
+RTCW has an enjoyably unique storyline set in WWII, but... (See first con below)
+Environments are relatively varied and levels are usually large enough for multiple approaches to combat
+Enemy variety is solid (You are not only fighting Nazi soldiers, but also the undead, mutated experiments, and more)
+Each section of every mission is a perfect length. None are too long or too short
+Every weapon feels powerful and useful
+The game manages to be unnervingly creepy, but also humorous with it's drunk Nazis and exaggerated German accents
+Awesome level of violence
+Visuals are great for the time
+Not the longest game out there, but still longer then the average FPS
+(Mostly) Provides a fair challenge
+The base price is already a steal!
Cons:
-...Many of the cutscenes progress the story in a mundane way. For instance, when you complete a mission in the game, most of the time the story is progressed with just some of your commanders talking to each other about what you just accomplished. Since these conversations were used as a vehicle to progress the story, the overall narrative became less intriguing to me
-More or less every boss requires the same strategy to defeat
-If you go back to a quick-save during combat, it seems that the enemy A.I. get a tactical headstart and are therefore able to pinpoint you quicker then usual. In other words, deaths can feel cheap at times especially when you are low on health
-Besides the useful secret health and ammunition you find, you can sometimes find treasures and gold which have virtually no use in the game. I would not be surprised if the developers added these in just for the sake of giving the game some more replay value for completionists
-Repetitive soundtrack that is fitting, but honestly forgettable
-No widescreen setting since it is old. However, there are mods for that
Overall:
Return to Castle Wolfenstein is an immensely enjoyable FPS that has aged quite well. Do recommend.

The game is visually impressive, with great animations and effects, and a decent number of cutscenes for the execution kills (which I never turned off because even when you're rapidfire kidney-stabbing some dude to death for the 20th time, it still hasn't gotten old). The game is difficult. I found myself replaying the army base level something like 6 times on easy mode before I managed to make it through successfully. Only part of the difficulty feels legitimate, though. A lot of it comes from being unable to set up executions to restore health on later enemies, as soldiers cannot be kicked to the ground, and have guns that will quickly tear you apart if you're not shooting them from a full screen away. I probably should've been far more liberal with grenades, but the animation time on them is slow, and it feels more natural to just shoot enemies one by one.
I would have really liked melee weapons to be included, since most of the weapons play too similarly, and being right next to an enemy and waiting on the reload to finish before I can shoot them was frustrating. That being said, it's an indie studio and the features they did include were pretty solid overall. The flamethrower is a bit unwieldy, and the driving sections are mostly pointless because of how wonky the controls are, but everything else controls pretty smoothly.
Honestly, I found it worth the price of admission just from how fun and violent it was. The first few levels are mostly just spree-killing hordes of innocent bystanders and maybe some cops and SWAT guys, which is fun. Once it starts introducing soldier enemies I think it gets a little weak. The ending was too funny, though. This was clearly just a game made by a bunch of dudes who wanted to make something funny, gruesome, and tasteless. I get the feeling they probably enjoyed making it, and I look forward to seeing more of this type of stuff in the future.

Return to Castle Wolfenstein is basically THE “I borrowed this game from a friend.” Game.
You once again play as William “B.J.” Blazkowicz, sent in to stop those cuhraaaazy Nazis from messing with the occult and probably summoning the dead or something.
RTCW is another game I had a lot of experience with back in the day, especially the multiplayer. The single player starts out in the same vein as Wolfenstein 3D, with Blazkowicz escaping a prison cell before torture with nothing but a Luger and a knife.
Return to Castle Sniffenscratch runs on the Id Tech 3 engine, the same one they used for Quake III: Arena and Star Trek Voyager: Elite Force. It still looks good, especially for the time, and you get a bunch of neat little effects like shading and dynamic shadows.
Oh baby those 2002 dynamic shadows.
You have an assortment of weapons to play with, ranging anywhere from standard WW2 pistols and sub-machine guns, to more wacky Nazi super science like a chain gun that blows people up and a testla gun. There isn't much for crunch when shooting at enemies, however, unless you get a chance to blow them up. You do, however, kill most things with a well place head shot, so you can at least start pulling off some rootin' tootin' trick shootin' if you got the aim for it.
One of the big draws to Return to Castle Chocula was the multiplayer. Which is funnily, deader than Hitler. But back in the day it was pretty poppin'. You played as either Allies or Axis and had a set number of objectives to complete, ranging from escorting an important item or destroying a defensive structure. The Allies would attack and the Axis would defend. It was also surprisingly enough a class based multiplayer instead of the usual arena deathmatch style like Quake III or Unreal Tournament.
It actually reminds me of Conker's Bad Fur Day's multiplayer, or at least the Tediz vs Squirrel High Command mode. I'm pretty sure Return to Castle Dog Mug inspired the multiplayer for Conker's Live and Reloaded, but I have no way to actually confirm that. Mostly because lead designer: Chris Saevor won't return my calls or answer his door.
There are more ways to play Return to Castle Huff'n'Puff than this version however. There is also an Xbox port that was ludicrously popular when it first came out, it also came with an extra chapter where B.J. went to Egypt. There was also a PS2 port but I don't care.
If you're like me, and hurting to play the multiplayer, however, then you're looking in the wrong place. Most people who played Return to Castle Nintendo moved on to Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory, a free multiplayer only spin off to RTCW.  It's still kind of sort of active, so you can at least get a half decent game going to quench that mighty need and go back to playing puzzle pirates or whatever it is you do on your free time.
Go play RTCW, you'll probably like it. Or don't, I'm not your dad.  It's aged well, or at least to me, but I haven't really left 2003 mentally, so you shouldn't listen to me on the subject.
Actually, do listen to me, I'm great.

I don't feel that games in general should be judged on their own, but up against their peers.  In the case of Beyond Earth, Civilization V is a monster game in the same series from the same publishers, and my personal experience with Civ colors my impression of Beyond Earth immensely.
--Negative Atmosphere
My personal feelings are that the user interface and world are too dark in general; I know it's space-themed, but that doesn't mean the planet I am exploring should feel as black as space.  Similarly, the soundtrack consists of whimsical beeps and boops that are gratingly undefined and stagnant; the ambient soundtrack which I feel is reaching for a sense of futuristic wonder is lost on me and leaves my mind dulled rather than excited.
--Negative Map Readability/Damage
A major factor early in the first single-player game I tried was the presence of a toxic 'miasma' on tiles.  If units ended their turn on the tile, the miasma would injure them significantly.  While this might add a level of complexity or difficulty in a game with little to AI power, it is poorly executed because the miasma tiles are difficult to distinguish visually from the regular non-toxic tiles where I would want to station units.  I found myself looking toward the tooltip on the right side of my screen rather than at the map itself while hovering my cursor over places I might want to move, a time-consuming and tedious task that could have been solved with an icon displayed by default.  Similarly, when I first ran into the planet's 'siege worms' I foolishly attacked them and did about 4 damage out of 100HP, while the worm took nearly all my life, then in the following AI turn, the worm killed the unit.  Again, while worms may add complexity by adding map elements that can kill, it doesn't solve the classic Civ problem of poor AI in single-player games.
--Negative Multiplayer Performance
There are problems with Civ; the game habitually crashes or disconnects players even over stable connections.  Also, the developers keep introducing new bugs into the game with patches, and then take a year to fix them.  The notorious trade glitch, for instance, allowed anyone in multiplayer receiving an offer to create a counter-offer and then accept it, potentially allowing a person's cities to be stripped away when offering just a simple declaration of friendship.  Here, despite even reporting the bug myself, it took 2k/Firaxis a year to fix this game-wrecking bug.  In that intervening year, since no one could be trusted, it killed multiplayer diplomacy in a game where diplomacy was already weak.  The reason this gets mentioned in the review for Beyond Earth is all the multi-player glitchyness of disconnects remains present in this rendition of the Civilization universe, and I don't expect any patches to help fix this problem since they didn't fix it in their flagship Civ V.
--Negative Uniqueness
Beyond Earth feels like a re-skinning of Civ V where all the menus and tech tree are changed and I have somewhat more customization options of my civ.  If I wanted a prettier interface or a new experience, I would play Endless Legend rather than this darker twin of a much cheaper, more successful, more complete game like Civ V.  I feel that if this had been more an Alpha Centauri remake than a Civ cloning experiment, things would have gone much better because we would at least have something new to this generation of gaming.
