Hatred got a lot of press and I fell for it. I picked it up because of all the hype, but looking back, I likely would have passed on this game based on looks alone. However, I pass on a lot of indie titles because they just don't appeal to me the way they once did.
Hatred's theme is dark, just like the media played it out to be. To that I say, "Who cares?" What really matters in a game is whether or not it's fun to play, innovates at all, and sticks to its core theme or strays somewhere along the way. I will say that Hatred took a theme and stuck to it, but not at a loss.
The plot, if you can call it that, feels too familiar. We all remember that mission in GTA San Andreas where we infiltrated an army lab, stole C4, and blew some stuff up. Hatred isa  re-write of that mission. In this version, instead of some straight up hood stuff, you're a troubled 20 something who feels he's been dealt bad cards by life and likely spends most of his days browsing "teh Ch4n."
Hatred plays like an 80's style shooter with updated graphics and little else. The weapon selection is subpar with only a few solid choices, an artificial difficulty with sending in hordes of enemies and a limited amount of respawns, and no story to grip you in. To anyone thinking this game could possibly spawn another tragic Columbine, I think we're safe for now. Hatred doesn't connect you to its character in the slightest. (Later identified as Clint Westwood)
Color me stupid, but I hoped that Hatred would connect me to a troubled character and try to make me feel the things he felt. I'm no psychologist, so maybe if just for a few minutes I could be inside the head of someone so disturbed and see what makes them tick, that would have made the game more fun for me. There are no scenes where he's picked on in high school, no bullies, no oppressive parents, or mentally abusive relationships. It's just some low-life, alcoholic 20 something with no life who goes on a rampage.
If you really want to play a 80's shooter style game, I recommend Bunch of Heroes. At least it has multiplayer!

I thoroughly enjoyed this unusual game, despite a few flaws that became apparent along the way. I can't speak highly enough of the aesthetic - a black and white world peppered with red, incredible use of sound, and an atmosphere that gets creepier as the game and story progress. While some of the game mechanics do become repetitive, I found the story interesting enough to want to make it all the way to the end. The "otherworld" - an alternate version of the world filled with spirits and obscured by a thick grey fog - felt quite unique and added to the mystique. The sound of that bell is just incredible, and it's still ringing in my ears. There's a good progression of items and weapons over the course of the game, even if you have to work to find them, and I also found the level of enemy difficulty increased in proportion to the size of my arsenal - it never became too easy or too hard. I absolutely loved using the bow, and upgrading the weapons over time was very satisfying.
On the more critical side, it is unfortunate that the shovel isn't available until later in the game, when one has already passed over many items that only it could dig up. Returning later with the shovel, I could hardly find any of those places without running aimlessly all over the maps again - though one is well rewarded for their diligence if they do so. When moving back and forth between areas, I frequently found myself facing the wrong direction and having to wait through two extra load screens. And the "listen" feature does get quite repetitive after a while, in time I ended up feeling like a supernatural courier with increasing lack of investment in the stories of the wraiths. I will say that I thought the story ended well, even if many questions are left unanswered and the overall ending was a bit bizarre. Room for a sequel? Unfortunately, a bug prevented me from finishing one of the final battles, so I had to watch the ending on YouTube as I really wanted to finish and wasn't willing to wait for a fix from the developers. It seems this game is still being developed and I came into it after many bugs had been fixed and improvements had been made, so I'm grateful for that at least, but I hope to see that last bug fixed soon so I can properly finish the game, and find the rest of the unique weapons and loot.

Not actually a horror game despite what it looks like. It's more eerie, alienating, and often tense. There's no soundtrack, no voice acting. This game is all about sound. You use it for locating both enemies and objectives. And it delivers the most authentic feeling of creeping through a forest I've tried in a game yet. It's dense with varied amount of bushes and tall grass. There's bushes that can't simply be walked through as if they weren't there, creating a varied terrain of obstacles. There no sounds but the sounds of nature. Gusts of winds stirring the whole scene.
You try to uncover the mystery of the unknown lands you've stranded on. Why are there beasts in Spaniard armor roaming the forest? Why do you suddenly see ghosts when ringing the camp bell?
All the weapons carry enough punch to be satisfying. Enemies recoil and slump to the ground, while letting out a growl that echoes through the forest when hit by the finishing blow. And usually it'll be a calculated shot, allowed by careful creeping and observing.
Instead of giving you HUD markers guiding you, you have "pinging/listening". The points of interest emit a ghastly sound, and you point yourself towards it. It can be quite unnerving looking into the blurred-out distance, knowing that sound is telling you to go there.
Definitely play this game with a good stereo headset, the 3D sound is great and immersive, and big part of the gameplay.
The black&white visuals are pretty cool, but can become tedious. Luckily there's sliders for colors and black&white intensity levels right on the pause screen. So if you really want to, you can play it in color.
Not really worth the time or money. Needs to be balanced better, might be worth it at a later date not right now.

Sure, i don't have thousands of hours on pc... But i do on console (PS3).
Summary wise: It's worth the money and to play the game. Don't let these other reviewers persuade that the game porting sucks or that the game is laggy or giving them low frames.
Storyline: 9/10, I really like it. There are character developments. Each characters have their own personalities, and you'll grow fond of them.
Gameplay mechanics: 8/10, a bit different than what you're used to, but it's really designed for you to use "auto-battle." Sure, at times you'd rather have 100% manual control over what attacks you do, but it's a great game if you're going to just spam mouse1 or "x" to ok all your auto  attacks.
Gameplay visuals: 9/10, almost no graphical improvement over the console. Sure there is V-sync enabled by default, and i dont think you can change that either. But it gets better, because your PC may be "better" than a ps3's hardware specs, your gameplay won't drop FPS simply because of its hardware limitations like the PS3.
Graphics setting: Now, people may over do their settings because they want the best qualities, but in shadow resolution, you should remain with what your hardware is most efficient, not capable. SHADOW RESOLUTION: should be set around 2048x2048, no more than that. Even if you have a gtx 1080ti, stick with 2048. There are port and coding limitations on how graphical information can be processed. (Don't be like one of those people saying "I have a gtx 1080, but i only get 20-30fps," Those people are just going by "brute force," rather than understanding and going with the flow of nature).
CPU: You need at least 4 cores, minimum. Something equivalent to ryzen 5 1500x (not 1400), or i5-7500. Make sure that your cpu is running over 3.4GHz. It is required to maintain high frequency rates. I overclocked my cpu and gpu to 10-20% to run this game smoothly. Don't let others fool you into thinking that this game (made in 2014 and ran on old gen console) be under-estimated.
FYI: low frames in this game is NOT DUE TO HARDWARE/PORTING ISSUES. This is all about the coding within the game itself. Historical information: console games are coded to run based on console specs, which are all about the same. But when you port them into pc, there are hundreds of different specs. PS3 has like 2-3... Because of coding based on console, an i7-8700k will run the same as a ryzen 5 1600, this game is not a gaming pc coding, console coding works differently both in concept and application.
Don't over do the settings, keep it medium or low. going high won't do anything but lower your frames.

This review was written 6/24/2014
Betrayer is an interesting experience to say the least. With a combination of mystery puzzler, and survival elements (tough enemies and limited offensive capabilities), Betrayer provides a unique middle ground between the fps and the now popular "run and hide" horror games. This is not to say the game is scary (unless you're a tool) but it can be quite suspenseful and you might find yourself detouring around some of the larger enemies, this is especially true if you're running low on supplies.
Gameplay (disclaimer: I only have 7 hours clocked in at the time of this review) consists mostly of walking around searching for clues, completing fetch quests for ghosts, and slaying enemies for loot (beware of the skeletons). For some this might seem rather... basic, well that might be true, everyone has different taste, but what Betrayer lacks in variety it makes up in... you guessed it, atmosphere (yeah I know, overused). All jokes aside, the ashen color pallet (adjustable) and intriguing minimalist radiant story elements provide a convincing sense of foreboding, which increases your immersion and the mystique of the cursed land you tred upon.
Betrayer is still in early access, so it does have an unfinished quality to it, e.g. trails that lead nowhere, a very basic inventory and quest menu. Despite this, I haven’t run across any major bugs and the game seems well put together. Graphics settings are pretty standard, as mentioned above you can adjust the color saturation and view distance.
In its current state, those who enjoy faster paced action packed ego shooters might not find Betrayer to be worth its non-sale price (about $20). Those who enjoy atmospheric interactive stories with some extra challenge thrown in would be well advised to give this one a shot, especially if it's on sale.
Thanks for reading.

This War of Mine is an excellent survival game that shows off a different aspect of war. You are not a health-regenerating god with the skill to shoot enemies in the head with a pistol from 100m away. No. You control a group of survivors that are facing the hardships of war: having to scavenge for supplies, fend off bandits, beat the chill of the winter, etc. And trust me, it is HARD!
The controls are simple: click here to walk, click there to search through some trash, click on that guy to punch them, etc. And it is well done too as I never felt like that controls were inadequate or dodgy, so props to the developers on that one. The gameplay is simple too (there seems to be no tutorial, but after 5mins of playing you will surely figure out what you're doing): build up your base with furniture, create weapons, manage your survivors health and hunger, trade with other survivors that approach your shelter, and more, throughout the day. When night comes around, you get to decide who sleeps, who guards (or have no one guard, which is risky due to the possibility of being raided), and who goes out on a scavenging run (e.g. search an abandoned house for materials, or go all out into a military outpost looking for food or medical supplies).
The soft pencil aesthetic is very pleasing too over the top of the 2.5D look of the game. The music and sounds are all well-done too, although the variety of music on the radio is limited (probably due to the war, which is justifiable). The different characters you meet along the way all have their own bio, which changes depending on how they're feeling (e.g. if they have just killed 3 people on the last-night's raid, they may be feeling quite depressed about it). Because of all these factors and the fact that the war could last only 30 days or over 40 days, the potential for replayibility is high.
If you're interested in seeing the side of war that most modern-military shooters don't often portray these days and want to play a rather difficult survival/management game, then definitely pick up This War of Mine. It is truly brilliant!
Enjoy! :D

Short Review:
One of the most astonishingly beautiful pieces of crap you'll ever see.
Long Review:
I really wanted to like this game, I loved all the other games in the series and played the hell out of them, in spite of their massive learning curve they were extremely enjoyable because learning to play them felt like discovering how to play them.
Rebirth is a glorious looking game based on a flawed development plan. Were they making a game where you control lots of ships or just one ship? What was the point of walking around on a station, was this supposed to be like a shooter or something? Everyone looks the same and trades different wares, but all this serves to do is make the simple act of buying and selling enormously tedious. The previous games had a relatively simple interface for trading, managing your ships, and viewing the map, these things are all convoluted and cluttered in a series of menus which aren't really explained.
Beyond that, there's really not a lot of fun. The main quest for example has you build a URV forge at one point but the build process requires materials you can only buy from a hostile faction. Okay so go pirate and steal what you need, right? Well not exactly, in my game Fusion Reactors just weren't being traded anywhere, I guess if I let the game run non-stop over a period of several days the economy might right itself, but I ended up just altering my save file to get on with things. What ended up happening is the URV forge completed but required me to provide a mining ship. I go to purchase a mining ship which must be built first, so I build my mining ship and nothing happens because, again, it's missing some resource to finish building it.
If you fell asleep during the description of gameplay in that last paragraph I wouldn't blame you, the quests are just that boring, I wanted to love this game but it finally occurred to me that I wasn't having any fun playing it. It's a beautiful game no doubt, but honestly if they just took the previous X games and slapped these graphics on them that would have been great, it would have been released sooner, with fewer bugs and higher reviews. You're given very little instruction about how to play the game and you'll find yourself spending more time in Google looking things up than you will blowing up badguys.
As far as the combat goes, well you have the option to auto-aim at everything which makes it boring OR you can turn off the auto aim and try to manually aim but the weapons don't track very smoothly and you'll find the simple act of killing an enemy a frustrating endeavor. Adding to this, some ships like corvettes don't even have a lead indicator but maneuver like fighters. There are some great mods out there, the capital ship bridge mod for example is so wonderful that you have to wonder why it wasn't included with the game, but overall I've noticed that modders tend to abandon their work due to frustration with the limitations of the game engine, This can lead to corrupted save games and having to start over but more often having to make do without mods you had come to enjoy.
I really wanted to see a better end-game played out, the possibility to conquer whole sectors of space and wage huge intergalactic wars, I wanted to see a smoother interface and tighter fleet management, the ability to control my wings of fighters and carrier groups against large scale invasions, the ability to lead a squad of commandos in an exciting, if rudimentary, boarding action on an enemy starbase or capital ship. Maybe those things exist somewhere to some degree at some point in X Rebirth, but I don't have the stomach for all the endless tedium one must endure to reach that point.

Tiny and Big: Granpa's Leftovers is a good game. TL;DR version below.
You control Tiny going after Big who stole his pants and he wants them back. With you have the Radio and some tools that cut, rocket and pull rocks and mountains apart. It's a platformer where you can create your own paths and destroy almost everything in the levels for fun, or for exploration. Some fun pysichics and mechanics, when you stand below a mountain and cutting it off, just to see this movie like seen where the mountain falls over you, trying to run away from it. It looks great. You find your own music, which is a fun mechanic, they are not hard to find, so don't worry. And the soundtrack fits and gives that little extra feeling to it. The stages can be a little to linear and you can't redo cuts, this can be a little trick, let's say you cut a bridge you need to cut, and the checkpoint first comes when it's cut, then you have to restart the entire map. But the stages are interesting and fun to maim about, and still a lot of secret things to discover here and there. Though even well designed stages, there is only one way to reach the goal. In a game with mechanics like this, where you cut your own way through mountains, there should be multiple ways to reach it. There is, but not to that extend it was intended and you go through hell if you mess up and try to make another piece of mountain fit has a bridge.
The game is done comic book like, with textbubbles and grunting for speech. It has humor and done well. I don't think I have much more to say about that... Oh, the game also needs workshop, this game has so much potential for that.
What is also good about this game, is does something more games should do. The game is enjoyable at all times, nothing in it seems like a chore, at least not to me. The puzzles could be a tad irritating in a good way (You know, the way you just need to do this and the satisfaction when you suceed). Even the tidious tasks as collecting boring stones, opens up for exploration and secrets. This game makes you want to explore, destroy that mountain and see what's behind it. So it's a huge shame that the maps were as linear as they were and short.
TL;DR
PROS:
Exploration and destruction of everything
Good humor
Great Soundtrack
Fun psychics and fun to play around
Well made stages that are fun and challenging to play
Nothing seems like a chore
CONS:
I bit tad short
Maps are a bit linear for what the game offers
Can't create to many of your own paths to progress
No workshop :(
Conclusion: A really enjoyable game. Even though you can complete the game 100% in 13, it's a really fun, enjoyable way to spend 13 hours. So for 10 euro, this game rocks. I am hoping for workshop and or a sequel that is even more ambitious. If you like platformer and exploration, this game is for you.

Sid Meier's Civilization: Beyond Earth, you want the short reason as to why I wouldn't recomend it? It feels like a re-skin of Civ 5 with to many of the core features pulled out.
The long reason?
The aliens are an annoyance, they don't add a fun challange they just zip around eating your units while you can't do anything to defend them. The research is a pain, half the time you've got no clue what it is you're researching. Take the "transgenics" research for example, it gives you a gene smelter. Great. Somebody mind telling me what a gene smelter is or what it does before I waste my time on this research? Also the research is a mess, people can end up with aircraft before you have any form of anti-air units that can defend you. basically meaning that your units get bombarded by cities twice. Finally, and most annoyingly is the lack of explanation of how to do anything with the trade routes. I, wrongfully, assumed that as every other unit in the game can embark onto the water the trade convoy could as well. Nope! It's the only type of unit where you've got to build a differnt unit to travel across the sea. So to summarise a ranty review, the reasearch is in a stupid order and you generally have no clue what you're doing, trade routes make no sense and aliens are plain annoying.
Are there any good points? Sure, the affinity system is a great addition in my opinoin and the unit upgrades that come from this system are relly cool. That's about it for the good though. Apart from that, lazy re-skin of Civ 5.

Played it for free, and as an old Alpha Centauri veteran, I wanted to like this game, but I just couldn't. It just feels so bland. There's very little to discover, and pretty much all of it is just recycled assets from Civ 5. The gameplay is even simpler than in the mother game. There's no happiness, there's just health. That means there are also no luxury resrources. There's just natural resources that add food, production, science, culture and energy, and strategic ones which I have no use for even by turn 200. The AI wants them, but I don't know what it does with them. It keeps offering me favors in return, which sounds better than just asking them for free, but the difference is cosmetic. The AI still has nothing I'd want, so I just keep stockpiling favors I can't use.
It feels like an incomplete game. The pacing just isn't there. Outside of warfare, there isn't a lot to do. As a peaceful player who would very much like to coexist with the aliens, the experience is disappointing. It's cool that the aliens will be mainly peaceful, but defend their nest if I stray too close. But even with a relatively high Harmony Affinity, the aliens still keep attacking, and I don't know if I should be exterminating them. The game just doesn't tell me. Though Alpha Centauri's storyline was common for all factions, very basic and always the same, it sucked me into the game. It told a story of me, getting to know this new planet, my new home, and dealing with its own rules of nature. Beyond Earth does none of that. It just drops you into Civ 5 with some reworked rules and tells you nothing about them.
There is a cool idea where you can specialize your buildings once you build them. You are given options to choose from that add extra functionality for the rest of the game. But the choice feels rather thin, especially if Health is one of the choices. My first game failed, because even though I was doing pretty good, my Health was plummeting as my cities grew and as a consequence, city growth and culture began to stagnate. The game didn't tell me how to fix it. It didn't even seem to think it was important to notify me that I should do something about it. Instead, it kept pestering me about stuff it had already told me dozens of times. "Do you want to create trade routes?" Still no thanks. "Your explorers have found something." Yes, I know, thank you.
If you compare this to civ 5 mods that are freely available, I really could not justify a full pricetag. It's basically a reskinned Civ5 with a few alterations. And I have this nagging feeling that it feels incomplete, because it was incomplete on purpose to gradually improve it with expensive DLC, just like Firaxis did with Civ 5. I think I'll just wait a few years until the game is really finished and buy it on sale. Firaxis, get your act together.

text:
Most video games attack tough moral questions and present important life lessons with the grace, subtlety, and objectivity of a BET comic performing in Austin, Texas on the anniversary of September 11th. Ham-fisted political opinions draw you right out of a game, and just about any sort of perspective from the developer is only worthy of an eye-roll and a groan. This particular game is not of that variety.
This game, based on the post-apocalyptic sci-fi short story by Harlan Ellison, is the paragon of point-and-click 90s adventure games. If you fondly reminisce about these kinds of games, you will not be disappointed. This is just about the perfect game you can purchase to satisfy your nostalgia kick. If you aren't familiar, this is the perfect way to introduce yourself to a piece of video game history.
In this game, you play as five deep characters with different issues and personalities. To complete the game, you need to solve a series of problems they encounter in scenarios presented by the main antogonist, who you'll surely be introduced to soon enough. The puzzles require a sharp eye and creative mind to complete, with the endings entirely determined by how well you performed each chapter. Although some parts are not very intuitive, vigilance is key and well worth the effort.
More important than the puzzles is the setting, which becomes an integral part of the story. Each character's setting is incredibly important to understanding the character themselves, and the effort put forth to creating such a deep game is apparent from minor details to the themes themselves. Some of the topics covered seem to have pretty obvious "correct opinions":♥♥♥♥♥♥is wrong, infidelity only leads to heartbreak, Dr. Mengele isn't someone you invite to your twins' birthday party, etc. With this comes important themes contingent throughout all stories, ranging from forgiveness to perseverance and chivalry. To appreciate all of the effort the developers and original author put into every intricate piece of the software, I would highly suggest taking your time and not rushing from one decision to the next. Carefully move forward, because like a lot of 90s games, this game will punish you for failure as harshly as it can.
This game has a few minor flaws, and appeals to a certain demographic of players. These things can really turn some people off of a game entirely, but I would wager 75% of people who purchase this game will love it and 24% of people who purchase this game will at least appreciate the experience. It is worth every cent.

Summary:
This is a nice, action-ladden space opera. Decent presentation, virtually bug-free and quite a lot of fun for many hours.
Further Info:
Think of Starpoint Gemini 2 done right. It has nice (albeit cheesy) music, pretty nebulas and explosions and Laser Beams. Like, a lot of beams. And missiles. There are a lot of spaceships that you can customize with different type of weapons to accomodate your game style. Whether you prefer to attack from afar or get in melee (including ramming), there is the right equipment for you.
So if you like to blow up spaceships of all kinds, this is your game. However, if you like a realistic space sim, stay away from it. There is nothing realistic in Rebel Galaxy. Flight physics are very basic and very forgiving. Space in the game is only 2D, at least for you. There are objects and enemy fighters that can fly above or below you, but you cannot. To me, this is a great design choice. But this means that you will not really do any dog fighting. Instead, combat feels like seaships battling with the sea removed. This impression is supported by the fact that ships in Rebel Galaxy have their most powerful weapons mounted at their sides and not the front.
And by the way. While you can mine in this game and trade, you will likely spend most of your time blowing up spaceships. Mainly because mining and trading is very rougly implemented. I guess, if you make a space opera, you have to allow people to mine and trade. Because people expect it to be there. Even if it is boring as♥♥♥♥♥♥
There are a couple of negative points I would like to mention: the loot system is very basic. There are a few weapons you can only get from destroying other ships, but these are very rare and not really special. So upgrading your ship is mainly done through spending credits you earn through missions. And while the ship customization options are fine, I would have preferred still more options. Like putting extra power into weapons by sacrificing shield strength. Or installing an extra tower while giving up a support module. Also, the story is sort of generic. No big surprises there.
Still, this is another game that revives the space opera genre, which was believed dead long enough. And if you are actually still expecting Star Citizin to be great, this might be a game that shortens the long wait.

Rebel Galaxy is a space game set out to be the next “freelancer” a pretty lofty goal. They failed.
Not to say the game is entirely bad. It’s got pretty 2005 graphics a great soundtrack and decent ship upgrades. But when you get down to it, It’s a shallow sort of game.

It feels as if they outsourced the game to India, asked for a pirate sim and got a space game with a Wild Wild West theme. The game tries so hard to fit all these roles and just falls flat. I believe it would have been a fantastic game had they made a few changes.
For weapons you have variations of turrets and Navel Style broadside cannons. They wildly shoot unless you hold L2 for a focused aim. The turrets auto aim and take out smaller targets. Autonomy is a nice thing.
What I will say though, is the game has a lot of depth in ship configurations despite being pretty shallow and simplistic. It’s like the best of IOS games ported to a PC. (hint: IOS/mobile games mostly suck due to microtransactions)
Essentially the game plays itself. you steer the ship, everything else is done for you. Now granted you are in a bigger than average ship, but it’s also a game. I want to actually feel like I’m doing something beyond controlling the direction.

The men who built Rebel Galaxy, Travis Baldree and Erich Schaefer, have a damn good record when it comes to making enjoyable games. Diablo, Fate, Torchlight; these guys seem to make games for gamers. With Rebel Galaxy they have proven to me that they just flat out understand how to make a good game.
The sci-fi atmosphere is a mix between Star Wars and Serenity and the ship pilot gameplay fits in perfectly to the overall feel of the game. The story missions are interesting and voice-acted pretty damn well, though you can ignore them for the most part if you wish and start your own trouble within the local system until you're ready to get back to it.
The ship buying and customization is implemented in a way that everything you do is working towards your next upgrade, so you do not feel like you are wasting time or money on anything. Your upgrades either transfer over to your new ship, or can be used as credit towards better weapons and ship parts, so your progress actually feels great the entire time. The trading and smuggling aspects of the game are well made and rewarding with a lot of care and attention put into them. The combat feels like a naval combat game and serves its purpose well. While primarily taking place on a 2D plane, the combat mechanics certainly takes advantage of the 3D environment with action and attacks happening all around you. The weapon variation is nice and even some of the basic weapons feel heavy-hitting, so I am sure that the badass factor on the later weapons will be awesome.
If you're looking for a fun space sim with satisfying progression and rewarding mechanics, Rebel Galaxy will scratch that itch. For $20 it is definitely a steal.

It may not be the most flawless of its kind, but it is a landmark in point-and-click storytelling.
Pros:
The adaptation of Ellison's story is creepy, depressing, and enjoyable all at once.
The design of each scenario is dark and beautiful.
John Ottman's soundtrack perfectly reflects the scenarios you play, and the theme is unique.
Cons:
The animation can be clunky and at times awkward.
Though functioning well, there are glitches aplenty, and the point-and-click controls tend to be tedious.
At times, the audio quality can be extremely poor, and the options do little to fix that.
Nonetheless, this game is an amazing and terrifying adventure that I recommend anyone to give a shot.
Also, I hope one day for this game to be remade!

Alright, let's face it, most of this game boils down to being a giant fetch quest. But the beauty of it, is that they always felt like they had a purpose. Thus, I never got bored. There were an awful lot of ghosts whose skulls had been stolen from their graves. Like, a lot. But it never felt stale, because the entire way through, I kept asking 'Why? Why are their skulls missing?'
So, the presentation of this game is spectacular. I've noticed there is a mod that colors the game up, but if you get this mod, you're a savage. This game is almost enirely in a black and white hue. Why this is so nice, is because they then use the color red in a very interesting way. A lot of emphasis on the color red. Twisted Spaniards roam the land, and they wear bright silver armor, with red cloth wrapped around it. Bright red. Stuff like that.
The story is essentially a big 'Who done it' story. You land on the coast of the newly discovered American shores, and find a town. But it is utterly abandoned. There is one other living person on the island, so it seems. The Maiden in Red, who also knows nothing about herself or her past.
The delivery is excellent, forcing you to listen to find new clues and locations... As well as making you use stealth to eliminate your foes. The game is incredibly unique and different, and I would highly suggest it.

I wanted to give this game a good review, but I just can't. I only played the main campaign, but I found it to just be too flawed. It is a typical space-game campaign where they have you build alliances and then they make everyone your enemy. Sounds alot like Freelancer. There will be plenty of missions where you are tasked with simply flying through enemy territory to reach the next objective. This would not be a problem if your boosters didn't draw their power from your shields. Needless to say, you will need to make frequent use of the save system. This becomes even more annoying when you consider that the game does not have any real checkpoints. If you die you have to sit through annoying load times. It is even worse, because sometimes your objective requires to loiter in enemy space while the main character casually chats with some NPC. I had to jump in and out of a highway just to survive the conversation.
Another thing I did not like about this game was the station information system. Basically, if you want to build up your map and business associates, you have to fly up to stations and scan them manually. Piece by piece. I looked at the game clock and realized that 4/5 of my game time was simply scanning stations, which is boring.
I know that this game could be improved with mods, but I feel that the base game should at least be fun as is. I don't feel compelled to play this game any further because I got it as part of the free weekend. I already don't like this game, so just imagine how much I would hate it if I had to pay for it. Even when it is free, I can't stand it anymore at around 7 hours.

As a space-sim enthusiast, I went into this thing open-minded, ready to disregard X Rebirth's abyssmal review scores and give the game a fair chance thanks to the free weekend promotion.
Sadly, it only took about an hour to see that all the bad reviews were not only justified, but still relevant as well, despite all the claims that a myriad of patches have somehow "fixed" this train wreck into some sort of release-worthy state.
You see, the problem isn't stability (although I have read several reviews that would suggest otherwise) - the problem is fundamentally flawed game design. This is immediately evident during the introductory mission, which ends with you destroying some hostile drone crafts and reclaiming your freighter, which the main character in his infinite wisdom seems to routinely leave floating around in empty space unguarded and unmonitored. And this empty space is swarming with armed rogues and thousands of hunks of floating debris, mind you. It's like leaving your space Ferrari on the side of the space road in the space ghetto. Who does that?
Anyway, there's absolutely no way our hero could have seen this coming (>_>), so your only recourse is to set phasers to irritate and plink the drones to death. This is not nearly as straightforward as you'd think, thanks to this game's controls being the absolute worst I have ever experienced in any flight game in any genre, bar none (and no, Battlecruiser 3000AD doesn't count, because that thing does not qualify as a game). I don't care if this game is "meant" for a joystick - there is no reason that W, A, S, and D should not control pitch and yaw BY DEFAULT. Instead, the game pushes you to toggle flight controls - that's right, TOGGLE FLIGHT CONTROLS - with the Spacebar, which causes your ship to follow your mouse cursor. This needs no explanation to those who have experienced mouse-driven flight before. For those that haven't, all you need to know is that having to manually put the mouse cursor PERFECTLY back to the dead center of the screen to stop turning is absolutely terrible. I suppose you could disable the cursor by tapping Space to disable flight controls, which would stop turning as well, but COME ON.
The obvious side effect of this is that hitting targets is ridiculously frustrating even when they're not moving. When both you and the target are moving - ha. It's nothing more than an exercise in frustration. How this passed focus testing is beyond me. I don't even know if the control scheme can be changed. The simple fact that this crap is the default is all I need to know.
Your pitiful weapons can barely hit the drones at 300 m. However, the drones have no issue at all accelerating to 2km and beyond in seconds. Going back to Wing Commander 1 levels of AI complexity, the drones then proceed to stop, turn around, and rush you from 2km, firing all the while. They have no trouble at all hitting you non-stop, with laser precision from 2km away, even though you can't hit them. You can kill your thrust and sit there like a turret trying to do the same to them, but nope: eventually you'll lose your shields, individual components of your ship will start to break, and then you're dead.
Why even include "combat," if this sorry mess is the state of it? You get spanked mercilessly by braindead AI at the very start of the game? You're trumped by what I assume are supposed to be throwaway DRONES?
I've got plenty of other complaints. Don't even get me started on the "hyperspace lanes" nonsense, which is essentially a long-winded, boring, irritating teleportation mechanic. I'm just going to stick this game in the rear-view mirror and have done with it.
Do not recommend.

This War of Mine is an emotionally distressing experience every gamer must play at some point in their lives. It is very much a Schindler's List of video games, reminding us of the horrifying reality that lies outside our favorite form of entertainment, and best experienced by us through it. Though stylized and simplistic on the surface, it pulls no punches in its gut-wrenchingly realistic depiction of survival amid the unforgiving chaos of war. Inspired by the personal account of a survivor of the 90's Balkan War told on a survivalist forum, the development team clearly did their source material justice. You won't find awards and points here, but you will be challenged emotionally, objectively, and morally. The real puzzle in this game is you, the player. What will you do to survive?

I remember getting this game on the 360 awhile back and it took me 1 year and some change to actually beat the game due to lack of interest or other games coming along to distract me and by then I had forgetten most of the story. Well I saw it on sale and figured I'd give it another try after playing both FF15 on PS4 and FF10 on PS3 as I've been digging the series more. This one definitely is my least favorite of the FF games I've played, but it's holding my interest so far. I'd like to punch about 90% of the cast with the only excpetion Sazh because he reacts to things kind of normally, Hope is probably an irredeemable moron and I think Snow is supposed to be some hero type but I'm not really feeling it. Graphics look pretty good, but then again the game is kind of a bunch of glorified hallways. There's slight exploration, but it's mostly just going down one hallway to find an item before having to turn back and go down the correct way. Combat is intially pretty boring and gets slightly less boring about 2 hours in when you get to start assiging roles to people and upgrading their stats. I don't know why I like this game, it seems like there's a bunch of bad things about it but I just keep playing it anyway.
Now for the less favorable: I read online about the port and saw people claiming that it was near perfect after some patches. I have no idea what those people were smoking but this port is far from perfect. I think I have a pretty good system (i5-6500, GTX 1070 certainly above the recommended specs) and I can't keep a stable 60fps, which is what the game is capped it. It's mostly stable but there's times where I'll just be walking down a hallway and drop to like 30fps and this game has crazy agressive Vsync. Dropping a few frames will result in microstutter and it's kind of annoying. Cutscenes are also actually worse than the PS3 version as well, you can look up pictures of it. It also has no in game option to cap the FPS to 30, so if you want to do that you'll have to use 3rd party software. This port also has very few options to fiddle with, you basically get antialiasing, shadow resolution, and regular resolution. Not much to mess with if you're getting unfavorable performance. I'd say it's playable for me, but if it is for you will be something you'll have to decide.
It's kind of a bad game, but have a soft spot in my heart for bad games. Music is also pretty good, not that it makes up for some of the more boring and stupid things about the game. For $16, there's a lot of game here but the port makes it unfavorable in a lot of ways. It's crazy to me that the cutscenes are worse dispite the game being a 50gb download and takes up 58gb after it decompresses. I guess if you're interested go in knowing that this is a sub par port and you might enjoy it.

The equivalent of sitting down and smoking a sub-par joint but everywhere else is dry.
Hatred takes place in the outskirts of New York City, where you play as an unnamed man named The Antagonist (DID YOU SEE WHAT WE DID THERE?!). As the Antagonist, your goal is to murder as many human beings as possible, be it by fire, firearms, knife, grenade, or old fashioned curb stomping and kicks to the head.
The gameplay itself is below average. The controls are functional, but it runs into the Assassin's Creed problem of being able to run into walls very easily. Hit detection can be a bit dodgy as well, and it is entirely possible to fire a shotgun point blank and miss due to visual difficulties.
Which ramroads us to the next point in the visuals. Thematically, it's presented a bit like Sin City: all dismal greys and blacks and whites with some splashes of Red for blood or Blue for police lights. Your crosshairs can be different colours as well (which is hilarious when its green), but even then it's difficult to tell at the best of times where you, or anyone else, currently is, or what's hitting you to begin with.
The weapons are satisfying enough. You point guns in one direction, bullets fly out of them, and they interact with civillians in obvious ways. AI's dodgy though, so more often than not you have policemen completely missing where you are and civillians who run screaming -towards- you, for some reason.
Despite this, Hatred is fun in the sense that you are not playing it to beat it, nor are you playing it for a good story experience (especially not that, dear god the acting...). You're playing it because Dave at work flipped all your buttons, Sasha was able to emasculate you at the company meeting that day, and Darryl was busy being Darryl, the self centered idiot. So, you come home, flick on this murder simulator, and just blank out for a few minutes.
Hatred is a game that exists to unjudgementally help you relax and unwind after a long day until you're ready to do something productive, like playing a far, far better game. Postal 2, the GTA series 3 and onwards, Manhunt 2, they all accomplish Hatred's job better than it does. But Hatred itself accomplishes what it set out to do regardless; here is you, here are some guns, here are people who can be shot, go have fun.
Maybe get it on sale, but I'm not upset at paying ~20$ for this.

This is more of a first impression than a review, and I'm basing it on years and years and generations of Civ games.
Like a lot of people, I have followed this series for a long time. There have been a few bumps along the way, and some ideas that could have been fleshed out a bit or kept as options that disappeared.
I have logged quite a few hours on Civ V, and have several expansions. It hits a lot of the right notes for me, although some of the AI behavior seems to be a mystery on occasion.
I waited to play Beyond Earth primarily because according to the Mac specs, it's incompatible with my video card. I downloaded it during the free weekend just to try, and it ran beautifully!
I'm still digging in to my first game, and so far I like the concept. I enjoy the visuals of the planet, I enjoy the tech tree, and I enjoy the various quests that come up and the fact that on occasion, a decision made could impact the game later. I kind of like the idea of favors. I also like the various new reasons another civ can become displeased.
That having been said, I feel like outside of some of those nice changes, it's essentially a Civ skin, and in the spirit of appearing futuristic, some elements were left completely bland. Dialog boxes are just plain black. The dialog itself is directly lifted from Civ 5. Every sentence is the same. Every response is the same. The leaders are ... well... just people.. I have no Mouth, and I Must Scream is one of those Good Old Games on Steam. This Good Old Game uses DOS emulation to run on modern systems, meaning that there are naturally some problems with the emulation (this is also present in the GoG version). I have no Mouth, and I Must scream is based on the short story by the insane genius writer, Harlan Ellison, who plays the insane genius super computer, The Allied Master Computer (or A.M.). Your goal is to be free from A.M., while preserving your humanity and this game gives you a many chances to ♥♥♥♥ it up. Unlike modern games with multiple stranding choices, if you screw up, you will not get a good ending, but a different ending.
Gameplay wise, it's a standard Good old point'n'click PC game. It plays like many of these games, and without its atmosphere, IHNMAIMS would be an average game of its era, however, due to its theme, it stands out. There isn't rally too much to say about its gameplay, as it is really extremely standard for its genre.
Visually and sound-wise, it's solid and really stands out for its era. The themes it goes across throughout the story are made all the more memorable by the use of visuals and sound. The sound is not perfect mind, some of the voice acting is very... odd, and seems almost out of place in a game that appears to take itself so seriously.
The story is what the game is all about, and for the most part, it tells the story of the short story very well. The plot is centred around how far you'll go to maintain your sanity and morality in some very unique game sections. However, some themes that define the characters are poorly represented in some places, but despite this, there are moments in this game that many other games never quite meet.
Despite these flaws, this is one of the highlights of the classic PC games on Steam. I have to recommend it to everyone who wants to try something different, it may be massively niche, but the game itself, outside of these weaknesses, is a great, cheap title that I have to recommend, and its great that Steam and GoG can allow games like this a chance to be discovered by a newer audience, such as me, who missed this the first time around. This is Cyberdreams finest hour.

While I do recommend this game, do not think that there are not some things that are less than acceptable =
Story- The story is a bit more dumbed down then the first one. The gist of it is you’re a prototype Big Daddy who got resurrected and you need to find your little sister (now grown up). On your journey, you go through misadventure to misadventure. Overall, not the strongest out of the Bioshock series
Gameplay- Gameplay is more polished and improved from the first game. While there are very few new plasmids, the old ones are improved and have more development than the first game (For example, Electro Bolt at Level 3 can shoot a stream of electricity and chain lightning) Gunplay is also very fun, but some weapons are better left untouched at a Power to the People station than others. Overall, solid and entertaining
Graphics- The models are a step up from the first game, now more polished and scary looking. Environments are similar to the first game, but with improved textures and a more abandoned feel. In sum, an upgrade from the first game.
Control- The controls were fine. You can now duel wield a plasmid and a weapon. Switching weapons and plasmids in a fight could become tricky, but isn't a major fault that affects the game.
Difficulty- Identical to the first game, with the added challenge of being limited to 5 medkits and 5 EVE hypos. Most of the time it’s a fair incline, but be prepared to gluttonously consume medkit after medkit during some fights.
Polishes- Hacking is improved (Replacing long boring tube puzzles with quick button pressing) Plasmids are fun to use and they defiantly spice up the gameplay. Research is also more innovative, making the player contribute.
Low Points- Games for Windows Live (GFWL) sucks. There, I said it. I recommend finding a way to disable it and adding -dx9 to launch options (Oh and stay away from multiplayer if you don't want a sour taste to be left in your mouth). Also, you can't go back to previous areas, so better scavenge the area well.
Final Verdict: 7.5/10

However, when we got wind of Battlerite's upcoming launch we were incredibly excited. We played the beta together and since then I have played it consistently from last winter to the present. After my extensive time with this game I am continuing to enjoy myself, every game is a learning and growing experience in a fast-paced, action packed brawl with fantastic and lovable (or unloveable c:<) characters. I purchased Early Access to this game via Steam. It has since seen its full release (a lot of you bought this while it was on sale yesterday, so I guess you all are aware of its full release, lol).
Anyway, I have put about 4 hours (maybe a bit less) into the game so far and my impressions are as follow:
It is a disturbingly beautiful game. The sharp contrast between the black and whites in the black and white world are compelling. The way they did this was pretty amazing IMO. The world truly looks living and breathing, and yet at the same time, there is a forlorn sense of desolation that comes with it. Really an amazing setting. The use of red to highlight things of importance such as items, enemies, and even allies just adds to the stark contrast between beauty and horror. You can also enter a spirit world version of the same world (basically, your perception of the world around you is changed) wherein enemies are highlighted in blue instead, and everything seems quite surreal. The developers use of sound really brings all this to the forefront. Every sound and sight has a reason and noting seems out of place.
The interface has notably improved from the early versions of the game. The item/quest menu is pretty simplistic and easy to navigate. The map has also improved from its early state. Key areas show on the map as you find them and become fast travel spots. You can also see pretty much exactly where you are on the map. Other than that though, you really have to rely on the in game compass to navigate. In fact, this game doesn't really hold your hand at all. I think in many ways, they got their inspiration from Morrowind, especially in the way quests are presented. For example, you may meet the a guy who is looking for signs of his wife. Last he remembers, they would sit together on a hill overlooking the fort. That is all the info you are going to get. Now, it's on you to try and figure out where that location is. However, there aren't a lot of hills overlooking the fort, so it isn't a needle in the haystack type scenario, and when you get closer to the spot, it is highlighted in that eerie red and certain sound become more evident in the surrounding area.
The use of stealth is very important in this game. In fact, I knock a little off my overall view of this game due to an issue tied with this, because....once you attack something, it aggros and knows exactly where you are regardless of how fast you run, how long you run, or how well you hide. In addition, if it (or you) use a weapon that makes a lot of noise, and other creatures within earshot also aggro. That is a real flaw in the game in my estimation. So, stealth becomes ever more important to try and either get the best position to take down an enemy quickly, or to just completely bypass them altogether, undetected. The use of movement during wind gusts to mask your sound is particularly brilliant in its application and wind gusts happen often, so being stealthy is completely do-able.
The combat itself is fairly forthright. You have missile and melee options. Your missile options include one launched/fired weapon (bow and arrow, musket, so on) and a thrown weapon as well. Your bows/guns can be scrolled through on the gamepad and you can have up to three assigned to slots for this. The enemies can take some punishment,so again, the element of surprise is crucial as is upgrading to better weapons whenever you have the option. Healing is accomplished by drinking water and you carry a waterskin with you.
The story itself is pretty intriguing so far, and is both surreal and haunting. It and the environment suit each other quite well.
The gamepad interface, which was a complete wreck in early stages has also become a pleasant alternative to k/m. Some real thought went into how to key the various actions to a gamepad, and I personally prefer it to k/m for this game at this point.
So....those are my impressions so far. I think it is easily worth people trying out due to its unique qualities and amazing backdrop. Just know that the combat can be quite unforgiving for the reasons I outlined above. Hopefully (at least in my opinion), the developers nerf the enemies aggro a bit so you can at least flee a battle if need be without the certainty of being hunted to the ends of the earth unerringly.
I will update this later after I have either finished the game and/or found things worth mentioning here.

I bought this game during early-access back quite some time ago and now just started playing again last week, after not having much time due to private reasons.
Honestly, Stunlock Studios fixed almost all of the few issues that existed earlier in the EA. Right now, I really enjoy playing it and I think, that anyone who liked WoW Arena, Bloodline Champions or any other "Arena-Brawler" back in the day will really have a blast playing it.
At the moment there are already over 20 different characters with 9 abilities each, which offer tons of different ways to play the game. Moreover, Stunlock Studios has plans to release tons of new characters in the future, with, according to a devpost, like 6 in the next 6 months.
There is also tons of different outfits, weapon-skins and victory poses for all characters, which are, for the most part incredibly well done. Moreover, they also changed the way "talents" work, (these are 5 perks, which enhance your abilities in different ways), which you can choose prior the each game, but when you already know what enemy "heroes" you are playing aginst. Personally, I really enjoy this new way of choosing these, as it lets you customize your Loadouts(=talents)  according to the enemy teamcomposition, which is able to give you a huge advantage, once you fully understand how the enemies' characters work.
Just a quick side-note: Do not get discouraged if you don't immediately succeed, feel a bit overwhelmed and lose a lot of games, as it is a quite difficult game at first. It may sound weird, but having your own 9 abilites to use and also needing to at least kind of know what each character is able to do, in order to use your skills accordingly, really can be a bit overwhelming at first. Especially because one mistake can quite easily cost you a round (Each game in arena is played as a best of 5, meaning, that the team, that wins 3 rounds wins the game.) Each round takes about 2 minutes, so at most, 1 game takes roughly 10 minutes, most of them are shorter though.
But the great thing with that is, that the game gets more and more rewarding and fun once you have the basics down and it also gives you a reason to keep going, which sadly, at least in my opinion, a lot of other games these days lack.
One last thing, there is this thing called "Odeum", which is a pretty much fully functional replay system (even though the devs are still working on improving it even further), where you can look at, edit, and upload your own amazing plays and watch tons of replays from other players in the game client. This was especially helpful for me at the beginning, as you can see how other players, who play the character you enjoy most, and have already mastered them to some extent, play them.
With all that said, I definitely want to give everyone a recommendation to give Battlerite a try, as it is an incredible game, which just recently reignited my passion for pure, non-luck/gear dependant PVP, a kind of game, I had been looking for a long time.
The F2P version is released on the 8th of November 2017, so there is nothing to lose in trying it out as well. I don't quite know how the new system for unlocking characters will work, but if it is anything like in Bloodline Champions (which was also by Stunlock Studios) it does take quite some time after receiving the initial free character(s). So buying the package, which unlocks all current and future champions may very well be worth it for you, at least if you find yourself enjoying it after playing it for some time. I defniitely do not regret buying the early access bundle, which is essentially, for the most part, the same as the new character bundle.
Hopefully, we will meet in the arena one day and engage in some challenging, unadulterated PVP action!

Do I even need to write a review? Old as♥♥♥♥♥♥ rebellion comes as complete and adds mirror rebel versions of the 3 base factions (giving you 6). Awesome game if you're into space empire building from the leaders seat, ala civ.
Very enjoyable for a hardcore-but-also-simple 4X Real-Time Space fleet strategy game. Base building is done inside a planet gravity-well / static defence, planets themselves are your strongeholds. they are capped not destroyed, but similar to lowering a flag and raising a flag, or controlling points (of a galaxy map).
Civ in space, in real time, with space ships and planets, pew pew!
Maps can be randomly generated and theres already a spew of hand crafted offical ones, there a few map editors (I believe an official one as well) can be found online, some give you way more control then others. Players can choose from 3 base races, 2 variations of tech paths per race, giving you 6 different choices (6 different factions).
Ships start as frigates, work up in class/shipsize to mega-capital ships. Capital ships are Hero units (inc. mega-capitals), and cannot ressurect XP once killed/destroyed (obv. can rebuild). Common/Regular Ships themselves come as types, some types are grunts (swordsman/rifleman feel), some are support types (Medic only abilities) some house fighters/bombers of your choice(how many of ea.), obviously there are dedicated carriers as well. Each base race has different ships avialable to them, most mirror one another to create simple balance mechanics.
Credits and materials are generated based on a gather rate / time unit. Tech trees are fairly big, espeiclly at first but you learn short-cuts, what you need/don't need pretty quickly after a couple of games with your prefered race. Each race also has different tech options, with different effects- but the rebel factions (mirror factions) have slight modifications to them, mostly for different ships that are available, or a niche tech that really bennifits them and sets them apart. (I mostly play Terran (Traders) and the above written is more so the observed comparrison between the two (traditionalists and rebels))
Pirates / Bounties on other players are a thing, can hinder the game, some times break it depending on how aggressive other players don't want to get♥♥♥♥♥♥on at the last moment and how much money they have, and you have, and obviously how much your both willing to rappidly 'dump' by clicking the bounty button, each click ensuring more pirates, and grow a horde (rapidly) thats seconds away from dropping on one another (You'll know exactly what I speak of first game, if you and your enemy have the cash!). The resulting mess of pirates can wipe multiple players out on the way (if in the way) as well as decimate the player who just happened to have the timer close on him (almost like musical chairs!). You CAN DISABLE PIRATES before you begin a match. And also, Pirate come from specific 'homeworld asteroids', if you conquer or wipe out these planets, the Pirates will stop coming- because they are 'much dead'.
Matches can last anyware between 1 hours - 12 hours+ (I've never played more then about 12 or 13 hour matches at most). And of course matches can be saved.
Depending on number of players, AI, and your system; performance in late game CAN and most likely will take a hit, at least until people start getting wiped all over the space-floor. If you get games just too big for your system though, you can quickly find that in 45 minutes of gameplay your frame rate just peters out and the matches can become 'unplayable', which can become quite suprising if you're just getting into a match  / having 'a blast'.
It should be noted that there are quick gameconfig.ini to tweak different effects, max ship numbers, etc. etc., all to boost or lower your performance (If you have some sort of "Mega-Rig" and you just want 100X more ships then the initial release suppored, it's do-able quickly by editing your INI's, but it's mostly on you to figure out what your system can do!).
Apparently theres also great mods (Starwars total conversions, etc) available as well, though I haven't had much luck getting them going myself.

Tyd wag vir Niemand is an Early Access indie platformer/puzzle game by the South African studio SkobbeJak Games.
Tyd wag vir Niemand translates to Time Waits for No One, a beautiful and philosophical saying that is contrary to the premise of the game. You control time in a world that is stuck in the Mirror Dimension of Doctor Strange. Your goal is to traverse through the strange world, using your abilities to control time to your advantage.
Much like SUPERHOT, you control time and use it to your advantage. Unlike SUPERHOT, however, you have direct control. Your time control isn’t limited to whether you’re moving or not, however, you do have unlimited time control. You have to use time control in order to successfully make a difficult jump or solve puzzles. From what I have seen so far (I am on the third stage), there is no combat. The closest you will come to actual combat is fleeing speeding metal balls on a farm.
The world of Tyd wag vir Niemand is beautiful in it’s own sense. Some of the textures aren’t so pleasant on the eyes, but the grandeur of the maps is quite impressive. On the second level, you are in a crystal cave that makes you feel like an ant. The levels are massive and beautiful. The first map is by far my favourite with a beautiful sky world that you have to see to believe. The textures on some of the obstacles do leave much to be desired, however.
Each level has it’s own unique soundtrack, which is quite nice. However, I spent quite a long time on the 2nd and 3rd level, and the song became quite boring once after it looped a few times. It may be different depending on the amount of time you spend on one level, but if you’re not the best at platformers (aka me), you will find yourself listening to the track looping endlessly. When you slow down time, you hear the tick tock of a clock that speeds up as your time control runs out, which is a great way of planning your next move. I quite like that mechanic and I tip my hat to the developers for including it.
I am about an hour into the game, and so far, there is no story as to how and why the world is how it is. It looks like Doctor Strange’s mirror dimension scene, but there is no exposition as to how. If the developer was able to piece in an extravagant story, the game would be so much better. I see great potential in the story aspect of this game, but at it’s current state, there is none.
Besides the storyline, I only have one quarrel with this game. The developer has said in previous posts that they are considering adding a sprint functionality. I support that idea. Whenever you fail a section of the level, it teleports you to a certain distance from where you are supposed to go. Sometimes you will be in front of the puzzle, but sometimes you’ll have to walk a great distance. Of course, sprinting while time is slowed down would be quite over-powered and broken, but if you separated the two and made sprinting only available when time is moving at it’s normal speed will solve the problem.
I enjoyed my time playing Tyd wag vir Niemand and I applaud the studio for making the game. South Africa isn’t exactly known for its gaming scene, and I fully support the developers who are based in the country. Tyd wag vir Niemand is innovative and quite tricky during a lot of the levels. If the developer incorporates a storyline into the game, I can see myself playing this more in the future.

"The War is Over." That's the phrase that pops up when you survive the war, and frankly after playing this game that's all the satisfaction you will ever need.
This game is indie. It's not funny, it's not known for its fighting mechanics, but it sends a message that can be summed up in three words "war is bad." But of course we already know that right? 9 out of 10 people you ask will probably say that war is bad. They might say support our troops, let the conflict in the middle east end, or hold a moment of silence as a sign of respect. But talk is cheap, actions are what define a person.
By actions are what define a person I am not suggesting a call to action that every single one of us quit our dayjobs or schooling to go rally and achieve world peace. What I am asking is that you experience a very accurate simulation of what war is truly like, because after this game trust me, you will have a whole new understanding of what war is. Playing this game won't suddenly make you relate to the horrors that the REAL victims of war have seen. But it will make you feel like a human being and if you do it right, you will get some strong emotions in the mix too.
If you do get this game, I suggest you try to play it as realistically as possible and as humanly as possible. What I mean by that is that you keep in your mind that these are real people you are controlling, because eventually there will come a point in the game where you will simply forget that. Everytime your character helps someone, you will feel happy. Everytime you turn away a neighbor asking for help you will feel bad. You will see things in the game that you are powerless to stop. Your morals will be questioned all the way until you either survive or perish. Will you steal from an elderly couple? Will you stand up from those who are being abused even if it means putting yourself in danger? Will you barter with the very people who are responsible for♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ looting, and taking advantage of ordinary citizens like you? You won't know who you really are until you play this game, until you realize that the game is sad for a reason, until you realize that all of the things that happen in this game could and have happened to other people in real life.
You know war is bad. Now experience it for yourself.
TL:DR I was feeling inspired and emotional. War is bad. Get this game if you have a heart and want to learn at the same time that you have some fun. :)

It really amuses me to read all of this so-called reviews about this game, made by people who didn't invest at least 10 hours into the game and not recommending it to anybody.
I am a Magic player, and despite not playing that much past couple of weeks, you can trust me when I say that this version of Duel Planeswalkers is the best implementation up to date. It is an expandable (Battle of Zendikar is live now on PC) free-game (which alone is very rare, regarding Magic: The Gathering), in which you are finally able to play with Planeswalkers and make your own deck to play versus others, or AI.
The game has microtransactions (you buy boosters with in-game money), but you can earn that in-game money playing for free (like other games out there), by doing quests or finishing storylines events.
And to make the story short here is a list of PRO and CONS:
PROs:
- expandable free-game with microtransactions (like other games popular right now: see Marvel Puzzle Quest for instance).
- enough methods to earn free money in game (If you play regularly, you can buy a booster every 2-3 days).
- expandable storyline
- unlockable cards according to the real set of cards (as of now: Magic Origins and Battle for Zendikar).
- planeswalkers (you can play with them, and the current creature-planeswalkers are a great fun to play with)
- battle others online
- make your own decks with Wizard and Advanced Deck building (in other variants you could only play with certain decks or make 1 color decks. Now you can make any deck you want with the cards you have in your collection)
- gives you motivation to gather the cards needed so you can improve your decks.
CONs:
- the archetype deck-building (Wizard) can be improved. It limits you to choose between the first 5 possible cards at a certain time in the building phase, and only when you chose one of them you can choose other cards. It should let you choose from all the cards that are available for the restricted archetype build in any order and amount you want to "draft" them.
- It lacks the ability to play with friends (battle versus specific opponent or play 2 Headed Giant with a friend).
The game has lots of potential to grow, and it certainly has more room for improvement. It maybe is an 8 out of 10 right now, but it's going in the good direction, and with more expansions it can look better and better.
I am very glad that I now have a way of playing Magic for FREE with most of the cards in the real core sets and I think all of you Magic fans should be.
I recommend this game to any Magic fan. It isn't as high as Magic online yet, but in some areas it really is doing a better job.

This is like the Jupiter Ascending of video games. I actually feel dumber for playing this even a few hours. The game obviously wants to be a live action game but for some reason refused to be one, a fundamental design miscalculation. It tries to have its cake and eat it too, and not surprisingly nobody ends up with any cake.
You get neither the joy of strategic tactical turn based combat nor the visceral fun of real time action fighting. The game's odd combat isn't that fun when you are focused on the text menus of chaining attacks up and swapping paradigms, and not really getting to see the flashy fights. Like Horizon Zero Dawn, there's also the weird dissonance between realistic looking character art design yet having oddly bloodless violence.
Obviously a lot of money was spent on this game's cut scenes to make it look and feel like a cheesy over-the-top caricature of a Hollywood Blockbuster. Unfortunately the actual roaming mechanic between cut scenes is very rough and plays like a cheap MMO. Jerky animations, invisible walls, silly loot chests, tap-shoes obnoxious footstep sound effects and other absurdities make it feel very cheap.
Games can skate by with mediocre parts if they make up for it in other ways, such as with interesting story and characters. If this game has such things they are buried way beyond what I have the patience to find out. There's no hook here to make me care what will happen and keep going. It's just not fun or interesting in any way. Voice acting is fine but half of the script is made up of gasps, groans, sighs and so on to a oddly ridiculous degree.
Performance wise I had no problems running this port at 60fps, but I only tried at 1080p even though the launcher offered higher resolutions. Worked perfectly fine with a wireless Xbox 360 controller, all I needed to do was set the display prompts to show controller buttons in the settings. The lack of any sort of haptic controller feedback though made things feel kind of cheap and non-AAA.
I'm still recommending it because there's still something likeable about it, and seems like it may be good game for very young children, and as a console port it behaved well enough on my PC. But I was bored stiff after just a few hours and could no longer endure the tedium.

This is a very polished blend of roguelike arpg and top-down shooter. Unlike some roguelikes, this has persistant unlocks and stat upgrades, which allows for a feeling of progress even when restarting. The different classes offer a nice variety of playstyles and the wide range of cybernetic upgrades effectively allow you to customise your character (or 'asset') throughout a game.
It's also a lot more immersive than the screenshots suggest. I think that this is largely due to the excellent sound design. There is an impressive attention to detail here, eg different weapon types have a satisfyingly distinctive sound and the pitch of a weapon will change when the clip is running low, the synth soundtrack changes to elevator music as you get close to an elevator etc. There are also some great graphical touches, such as being able to see the falling rain in the Bladerunner-like city outside.
It has a similar atmosphere and look to the excellent Brigador, but my impression is that Neon Chrome is somewhat more polished and definitely more accessible to casual players (but of course it's also a different type of game). Unlike Brigador, Neon Chrome automatically saves your progress if you have to leave mid-game (hint: use the 'Exit' option, not  'Disconnect'), which is an essential feature for casual players.

There comes a time in every AAA addicts' library when everything starts to feel samey and me-too. When hunting variably nonsensical objects around a gorgeously produced, big-budget-world starts losing its' flair. A time when the easy infinite death->rebirth of most modern games begs the question: if nothing happens when i die, then why try to stay alive?
All of these issues are solved with one simple, indie, twin stick shooter. This game will make you remember why skill matters in a single player game (though it's got co-op here too, if that's your speed). Though you'll quickly find satisfaction in the simple design, the geniusly paced levels and excellent boss encounters; it's the inclusion of the roguelike feedback loop of progression that sells it for me.  That loop involves levelling aspects of your randomly rolled, cheekily named and classed character that are permanent to the game regardless of how far you made it last game, the cash you had upon death and the unlocks you discovered during your play will carry onto the next avatar.  All of this happens automatically while blasting fools and leveling your weapons (which happens per run), and while the levels seem to be 'seeded' in such a way, they still manage to feel designed by hand rather than tossed together by a ruleset.  All of this makes each play feel fresh and accomplished and satisfying, and every tense moment worthwhile.  Reaching another checkpoint between "chapters" automatically unlocks access to warp at the beginning of your next run from that level or any other previous level, these chapters at first last first 5 levels, then get longer as you get further into the game.  Just a few days in and i can already feel myself becoming more strategic in my approaches.  If you have played roguelike games then you know what i'm talking about, but if not,  the important takeaway is that you never feel like you start from the same spot essentially, in addition to the levels rerolling the sense of progress carried from one playthrough to the next is tweaked so that you can always have another leap in levels within reach, all the while managing to communicate via simple skill improvements that you're always getting better and more capable.
Being one of those AAA addicts that i mentioned in the first paragraph, it's so refreshing to find an honest, skill-based shooter that leans on the generous side of rewarding, keeping things lively from the first moment until you realize you've spent half a day playing one game.
Bought it on sale, had i known it was this well designed and downright FUN, i would've gladly paid double. I know it's a small game, I know it looks a little silly even in some of the screenshots, but believe me none of these things matter once you get into the game, it harkens back to a standard you probably completely forgot, tasting overall a bit like the cyberpunk offspring of 'Gauntlet' and 'Smash TV'.  After a handful of unexpectedly engaging marathon sessions, you'll still be asking yourself: "why is it that some great games are barely on the radar, while other bloatedly shiny yet mediocre ones hog the limelight so often?"
Check this game out if you're a fan of rewarding arcade-style twinstick shooters that keep you hooked.  Best budget purchase in my library in YEARS.  Highly recommended.
