Absolution neither lives up to the hardcore roots of its past nor makes up to be a fun ride for the present. As such, I cannot recommend this game. It simply isn't about a hitman. Agent 47 is not given the respect he deserves; he no longer functions as a perfect contract killer. Read on and decide for yourself whether Absolution is worth your time and money.
Absolution is the first ever Hitman game that is a console to PC port. It's an above average one. Graphics and textures are good and the new game engine runs smooth on a solid PC. By smooth I mean the game has minimal glitches and the third-person OTS is not too bad. Keyboard rebindings and a number of visual (but not many game) settings are also included. And a new Instinct Mode is also there for those who need a 'helping' hand.
Well then. Now to the bad. Keep in mind that these are all my opinions, and as I have 70+ hours devoted here I've tapped into pretty much all Absolution has to offer. I also have no ill will towards the game itself; this is just an honest review on my part. But the truth hurts.
First off, I guess I need to describe the 'feel' of Absolution as a hitman/stealth hybrid. Previous Hitman titles always had solid control layouts (eg. in Blood Money hold the right-mouse button for the inventory/action keys for situation events etc.) and for every level a simple list of targets to kill. Absolution however, is a mess.
What you get at the start of every single level are a bunch of tedious, unskippable cutscenes. There is no inventory for items. There is no map. Whoever decided to replace the map with one of the worst minimap/radar systems in the world should be shot.
The new cover system also feels slow and unresponsive. Absolution demands you to rely upon walls and benches on your every move (it's the only way to achieve silent assassin). Similar modern PC titles such as Arkham Asylum, Deus Ex: HR, or heck even Gears of War handle their cover systems much better - swifter and tigher. The cover system encourages you to play more stealthily... but remember, this is a hitman game. You're not Batman, or Fisher, or Jensen. Hugging walls and benches reduces the many ways you would want to approach your target; the creativity and degree of freedom you had from previous Hitman titles is now all but gone.
The way 47 moves is just so aggravating; with this strange lethargy. Again, the very act of moving around is ust slow and annoying. And for a game that demands both precision and intuitive decision-making as fundamentals to master, the new movement system sure doesn't help.
This along with the terrible cover system often causes you to bump directly into an enemy from cover. And most times it's because 47 does not turn at a specific angle/move three inches/find cover properly that you immediately get caught rather than it being your decision - you judging the right time to move or to act. In a good stealth game it should be this decision-making that should define whether you succeed or fail. But here it's the other way around; here it's almost always the movement system that brings you down.
You'd then want to think, "..okay, I made a mistake, why don't I try it again? I'll just reload my last save..." Only there are no saves. Just some really messy checkpoints that respawn all guards, or for you to restart the entire level. Terrible, just terrible game design.
Speaking of guards and NPCs, you know how to get them silently out of the way? Well as the disguise system is just... bad (I won't go into specifics, it'll take too long) the only way to distract guards is by throwing an item in a corner, getting them to move and stare blankly where it hit, and then you move past them. Rinse and repeat. This is essentially 40% of the thrills in Absolution, the thrill of getting from A to B without getting caught. The rest are some pretty uninspired ways of killing targets. I don't want to play some stealth or thief game. Neither do you. I want to play hitman. There's a difference. The game should encourage me to play as hitman. But for some reason it doesn't. Absolution is a real let-down because of this - it plays as a poor man's stealth-action game.
Absolution is a perfect example of tasteless gratuity in modern gaming. Violence, sex, profanity - it's all there. None of it works. Previous Hitman games have always approached these subjects with a dark and twisted sense of humour; the result was a more meaningful and mature payoff. You really had to explore the levels to find the sick details. Absolution's sense of humour is anything but dark. It's uninspiring, and constantly bombarded in your face.
Often as you run past NPCs you will hear some of the most inane dialogue spouted towards you. 47 is a silent assassin yes but to make everyone else around him louder doesn't make him more silent. Soon enough I found all dialogue in Absolution just annoying; forced into a world that feels less realistic and less mature than any previous Hitman game.
At it's core, the story is just so damn silly. After a life that has revolved around killing people, 47 does a full 360 and is now having to run from it. Oh and save a little girl. Everyone is after her. For this reason 47 brings down 'absolution' ("assasinates") just about anyone he sees as having a bad influence on the poor child. I mean, in one level you are killing a crew of young punks for no reasons whatsoever. Just.. cause you can?
This is a story-driven game and as such goes against much of the hitman mindset. In previous games characters never drove the story. You were just a simple hitman. Each level was a contract and you were given a simple list of targets to kill for money. You were not meant to feel any real sense of glory or remorse in killing them - you were a hitman. The real meaning came from how you handled each contract - how you killed your target and got away - the 'sandbox' element: your creativity. I mean the degree of freedom on how to kill was and is still amazing - second to none. Absolution is the opposite. The game wants 47 as some sort of anti-hero; killing tons of goons, not targets. Genocide over any real 'absolution'.
So does the new Contracts Mode (online) redeem this mess? Please. It really has nothing to do with the perfect hit. I cannot understand why people praise it. There is no glory or justification in killing a random innocent or a policeman walking down the street. No context given at all. Just some bizarre sadistic complex, all just to get a high score. Contracts Mode simply has no meaning, it's just there. I don't really know why.

REVIEW:
When I had the opportunity to buy the Hitman franchise, I actually wanted to skip this game. I just felt it was a slightly watered down version of the real Hitman titles, as I saw from videos and reviews. Nevertheless, I decided to just give it a try, since it was on sale.
It was a little weird to understand the mechanics of the game, especially if you are used to the old games. It came to a point right in the beginning of the game, that I felt I had wasted my money for nothing, until after a lot of trial and error, you begin to grasp the idea of it. And then, this game just grows to you.
The "instinct" mechanic is pretty awesome, the shooting and cover system is very well executed and the environment feels very much alive, albeit linear, unlike  the open-world feeling in the previous titles. Assassinating targets is very fluid and the option to subdue or kill them is way better than the use of Sedatives in "Blood Money". Still, where the hell are poison syringes?!
Finally, while I still have a lot to explore, the "Contracts" concept just makes the experience much enjoyable. Being able to compete with others for your assassination skills is captivating, in a twisted way. Hopefully the sequel will add more modes.
What I find slightly questionable is the rating/scoring system during gameplay. On one hand, to keep a higher score, it encourages you to discover other methods and unlock new challenges; on the other hand, it feels like it kills your joy about choosing your methods of progress, making you feel judged for every step and mistake that you take. Maybe, we could just place it in the end of the mission, just like the previous titles.
Last but not least, is the linear style of missions. While the environment is still wide enough to move around and explore, it doesn't have that depth that previous titles did. The next installment will actually bring back the open-world setting, so I guess this will be quite an improvement.
Overall, this game holds a special place in my library and would definitely play again. 9/10

I've rented Dead Rising 2 on Xbox 360 before and thoroughly enjoyed what I played. BUT BOY WAS I WRONG!
This game is plagued with installation, client update and registration issues. Honestly just Google "Dead Rising won't start in Steam", I wish I had done this prior to purchasing TWO copies. The game doesn't launch straight off the bat, It has issues launching Microsoft Games For Windows Live (GFWL) - Which is understandable considering no manual or company actually informs you that this needs to be installed until you've purchased the game and are frantically searching the web for answers. The problems don't end there, once GFWL is installed it requires you to log in about 3-4 times over and over as it has to do multiple updates, I experienced different outcomes for each of the two copies I installed. One updated fine and then threw constant errors trying to connect to XB Live. The other computer failed to install the second update then suggested I check the error logs buried deep in my User/Appdata folder. The troubleshooting and manual fixes just keep coming beyond this point. After finally logging into GFWL I managed to start a game only to have it Crash on me in the first cutscene. This is as far as I've got, I'm frustrated having paid $20 for each copy but after the many hours I've spent troubleshooting this game before even playing it I'd be annoyed even paying $5 for such an experience. In fact I'd put money on the fact that I would probably have a smoother ride getting a pirated game to work.
There is a fundimental problem plaguing PC gaming these days and if it weren't for hardcore PC gaming fans I doubt anyone would stick around and put up with this problem to support PC gaming.
All thanks to Pirating there now are OODLES too many third parties involved in the licensing and registration of games now. Long gone are the days where you could just buy a game on DVD, insert the disc, type a CD Key and 15mins later DONE! The game is ready to play, with maybe the exception of a minor patch.
Now days EVERY godamn company involved with the games development or distribution has to clip the ticket and request you sign up to their own Game Client Service just so they can mine your personal information and gaming habits. Now I know this is somewhat designed to stop pirating but at what cost? This makes buying a legitimate game such a slow and painful process when you have to download multiple game clients, register multiple accounts and download multiple updates. Keep this up and people WILL pirate more! What makes the whole process even more painful and flawed is that none of these Third Party services seem to actually communicate or co-operate with one another, so when one link in the chain fails they all point fingers and the poor man in the middle (US GAMERS) seeks advice or support we get shunted in the opposite direction everytime... Extremely enjoyable game. I've been playing it for a year now and though the game has had its ups and downs (like any other EA game, tbh) the studio always delivers. You may see people compare Battlerite to games like League, but the two games differ greatly. Battlerite feels completely different to other mobas, mainly because of it's focus on fast reaction time and mechanics. There are no lanes or minions, and there´s only one objective to fight over.
However, there is still a lot of depth. Each character has 8 skills (excluding basic attacks), and fast reactions, CD and energy management and the high skill ceilings of the characters prove it. This game will cause adrenaline rushes REALLY often, especially when you are left alone to fight 2 or 3 foes (you can actually 1v3, and it feels great to win one).
As I said, I really recommend this game. I bought the EA and I don't regret it at all. I introduced over 10 other people to the game through the use of Battlerite Lite Keys, and though not all of them fell in love with the game, they all really enjoyed it, and are allways up to play a couple of matches if asked.
P.S.: The community of this game is great  too. As in any other competitive game, there are toxic individuals, but I rarely (if ever) encounter one. There are helpful and funny people, and a bunch of really good artists.
TLDR: Good game, high skill ceilings, fast paced and entertaining combat, and a wonderful community.

Based on the classic dystopian sci-fi short story by Harlan Ellison, this has some of the best writing you'll find in an old-school point-and-click adventure game. Ellison also provides some truly fantastic (especially for its time) voice acting as an insane AI.
The gameplay suffers from a number of glitches (though none that I saw made it un-beatable) and a very rigid, archaic game design. For example, a number of progression events will only occur after you say or do things that are completely unrelated to the event.
Unlike most adventure games of its time, there are multiple solutions to many puzzles...but usually only one "good" way. You'll have great difficulty getting the best ending (and yes, there are multiple endings) without a walkthrough. Of course, given the underlying subject matter, it's rather fitting that the (relatively) happy ending is elusive.
All that said, it's worth playing for fans of adventure games and especially for fans of the short story - as the game's plot is very different.

(Really original and fairly unpredictable too)
(It was a 3D Puzzle game with a physics simulation that allows you to create your own paths through puzzles by cutting objects down and moving them around, almost every object in the game could be cut)

The attention to detail in this fairly compact game perfectly articulates the atmosphere of its creepy post-apocalyptic science fiction plot. The point-and-click system may throw some gamers off (This is a very old game, and I had the same problems configuring the game for playable quality as I did for the 1990's X-COMs) and the stream of thought needed to figure out some of the puzzles is not as intuitive as indie sci-fi adventures with bigger budgets. Regardless of the issues spawned by IHNMAIMS' age, this is an excellent take on the famous short story and, in the world of videoame storytelling, parallels the influences of Ellison on techno-dystopian fiction. The game itself is an intriguing point-and-click that offers the player a peculiar menagerie of tension, fright, curiosity, and apprehension for the PCs. The story is akin to a visual novel, an interesting perspective for the modern gamer looking back into the history of storytelling in videogames (let alone science fiction games). I would suggest this game to anyone with a campy, sincere love of science fiction, the post-apocalyptic/dystopian genres, and/or supercomputers.

If you're looking for a challenging and deep action brawler to play and master, look no further. Battlerite brings all the intensity and fast-paced action of MOBA teamfights when they're best, and cuts out the (to some people) tedious MOBA aspects of farming gold, rotating around the map and shopping for items between fights.
It is smooth, balanced and every single ability has to be aimed manually which makes it so rewarding to play, as you slowly but surely learn more and more about the various champions, how they work together and how they're countered as well. You may think to yourself that there are few heroes to choose from if compared to games such as DOTA or LoL, but you must understand that the champions of Battlerite have 8 abilities (and an ultimate) and a surprisingly complex Battlerite system (hence the name) which lets you customize their playstyle to your liking. This system recently got overhauled and improved even, which just goes to show how committed Stunlock Studios are to making changes in order to make the game as good as it could ever be.
It's quality over quantity in the case of Battlerite, and i really hope you'll check it out and try overcoming the initial struggle of getting used to the combat and fast-paced nature of the game. You may feel underpowered, that the other team has "broken" champions which cannot seem to be beaten. But you'll find that eveyone has a weak spot, most actions have an appropriate reaction to counter it, and once you learn how to use these mechanics in your favor it's the best god damn multiplayer brawler you could hope for. It's so polished and well designed that the newly released free-to-play edition simply DEMANDS you give it a try if you're feeling competitive and regular MOBA's fail to get your blood pumping anymore!
A solid 9/10 from me, would give it 10 but Stunlock has proven this game still has so much potential and they're working hard to make it better always, so perfection still lies in the future!
Hope to see you in the arena for glorious Battle!

Most games released nowadays are a dissapointment to me. This game has been the first, in a long while, that I've enjoyed thoroughly. While this game isnt a 10/10, its damn near close.
The first thing I want to talk about is the choice of lighting. When you start the game, the default lighting scheam was b&w with really dark shadows. Even with my computer's brightness turned up fairly high, many of the paths were too dark to see for me. I perfer seeing the detail in the shadows and like the game with colors, so I lowered the darkness and turned those on. The nature of the game changed a bit with just that. This is neither a good nor bad point; I mention this because some reviewers had "struggles" with the default settings but they are easy to change.
For starters, this game is very intunitive, but doesn't spell everything out for you. There are hints and messages to tell you of completed sets of notes and chests per map, but it doesnt take you by the hand and play for you; something a few indie games do that puts me off. The "listen" feature is really cool to me and definitley a must "over there." The things you pick up and learn are concisely recorded in a journal that is easily managable and well marked.
When I first started playing, the game quickly got creepy. Strange sounds, insane enemies, odd shifts in lighting and crazy mysteries, came at me in unison. The game isn't scary, and it doesn't try to come off as such. However, many of its spooky/creepy aspects add to the action of the game to make it more enjoyable to play.
There are a few things I don't like about this game. Most notably, this game has an eerie loneliness about it. The red maiden that you barely interact with doesn't help too much either. It still feels like a pointless you-vs-world kind of situation that I don't enjoy and, while I don't know how to solve this issue without ruining the atmosphere the game trys to create, it is an issue I have while playing it. Another problem I have is the bow. I've probably missed more arrows than I've hit. I was expecting this game to have drop or sway or at least SOME kind of innacturacy in the bow, so I'd always try to lead my shot or account for the distance, purely out of habit. Instead the arrow would go right where the cursor was aiming every time, unlesss I was a huge disstance away. I read that the devs used to have drop and took it away, which I think is a mistake and takes away from the integrity of the game.
The audio for this game is phenomenal. It feels like it just fits. The only small problem I have with it is that the ramping isnt really gradual on the listen sounds. I would listen and hear just a small abnormality and then run over 10 feet and it would be echoing around my room. This is a very minor detail and doesn't really bother me too much.
Another small thing I'd like to mention is the poinlessness of the tomahawks and explosives. It might just be me, but I haven't found a point to acutally use either on enemies so far, and I don't see myself using them in the future. In any situation I've had so far, using my guns/bow just seems like a better idea.
Overall, this game leaves a unique impression, and is definitely very fun and intense. I'll update this review if I come up with more stuff as I play through the rest. So far, this is definiely something I'd recommend diving into.

This game has a special place in my heart. When I was about 11 or 12 I got this game, and I remember never being able to get in to it. Finally one night I ran it on local co-op (on my Xbox 360) with a good friend and we played all night. In fact, we never beat the game. Each time we'd start it up we'd begin a new campaign, and never got to finish what we started.
Regardless, nostalgia definitely paints this game in a good way for me.
Analytically, I think the game is incredibly unique. It blends the classic gameplay feel of console action games (for some reason the 2003 Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles game for PS2 comes to mind), utilizing both co-op teamwork as well as the gratifying beat-em-up style of early 21st century fighter games. The uniqueness comes when War in the North manages to incorporate RPG elements (quite successfully) into this style. The ability to full customize your character's inventory, alter their appearance and define your playstyle through three branching skill trees makes War in the North a game that sits on the precipice of the change in interest of modern video games.
My description may be a bit confusing, so let me summarize what I'm trying to get at:
Lord of the Rings: War in the North lends in equal parts to the classic co-op fighting games of the 2000's, and also to the mainstream wave of RPG games present post-2010.
I should also address some negatives, which lie mainly in the writing and graphics.
The graphic issues are not necessarily in gameplay, as when you have your settings cranked to ultra the game looks stunning, but rather in the animated cutscenes. There's almost an excessive amount of film grain in the cutscenes, and the animation looks like the developers tried too hard to make the characters look real - which, as is time and again proven, only makes the characters look less real. Apart from this the game doesn't lack much in graphics, so long as the player keeps in mind that this game is from 2011, not 2017.
The second issue I have is with the writing. Perhaps the writers adhere very closesly to Tolkien's style and I'm just not a fan of it, but to me (having long forgotten the actual Lord of the Rings books and films) the dialogue seems a bit awkward. It's almost as if someone asked the writers to write in Old English (you know, classic medieval jargon) and they implemented it at every chance. Ultimately I'd just say it feels cheesy, but again I think this could be a result of J.R.R. Tolkien's writing style: he essentially invented the fantasy genre as we know it, so I believe what I see as 'cheesy' could just be the game's writers mimicking Tolkien's style and because so many others have done it, what was once original now seems like a trope.
Again, I'm rambling a bit. Hope this helps someone make a purchase. I snatched this game up for nostalgia purposes and still can't get enough of it, whether I'm playing solo or with friends.
Finally, a deathmatchy FPS that I like! And now I feel like I don't have to go see Jurassic World.

tl:dr: If you are looking for a simple, fun space game with loot etc in the vain of Freelancer this is the best choice at the moment. The 2D limitation of movement seems annoying at first but it actually simplifies navigation a lot and combat still feels dynamic enough. Voice acting makes the universe feel alive.
The main framework of the game consists of typical space sim quests a la "kill those guys" "bring that there" "protect this ship" etc, nicely packed into flavour text and a fully voiced main Storyline which after 6 hours is fun enough to follow while not very original.
While most space sims focus around dogfighting and smaller ships this one is all about capital ships and broadside combat. Different sections of the ship can be controlled manually while the remaining turrets fire automatically, mercenary wings can be hired to offer additional support.
Aiming is secondary to navigation and tactical ship placement.
The universe is made lively and colourful by voiced cutscenes and radio chatter.
A nice amount of very nicely designed ships in various sizes is available
All in all this is a great game for people who don't have enough time for Elite:Dangerous (or simply find ED to be too boring and monochromatic) but still want the Space Exploration experience.
Also the soundtrack is very nice and the game makes adding custom music very easy.

"The War is Over." That's the phrase that pops up when you survive the war, and frankly after playing this game that's all the satisfaction you will ever need.
This game is indie. It's not funny, it's not known for its fighting mechanics, but it sends a message that can be summed up in three words "war is bad." But of course we already know that right? 9 out of 10 people you ask will probably say that war is bad. They might say support our troops, let the conflict in the middle east end, or hold a moment of silence as a sign of respect. But talk is cheap, actions are what define a person.
By actions are what define a person I am not suggesting a call to action that every single one of us quit our dayjobs or schooling to go rally and achieve world peace. What I am asking is that you experience a very accurate simulation of what war is truly like, because after this game trust me, you will have a whole new understanding of what war is. Playing this game won't suddenly make you relate to the horrors that the REAL victims of war have seen. But it will make you feel like a human being and if you do it right, you will get some strong emotions in the mix too.
If you do get this game, I suggest you try to play it as realistically as possible and as humanly as possible. What I mean by that is that you keep in your mind that these are real people you are controlling, because eventually there will come a point in the game where you will simply forget that. Everytime your character helps someone, you will feel happy. Everytime you turn away a neighbor asking for help you will feel bad. You will see things in the game that you are powerless to stop. Your morals will be questioned all the way until you either survive or perish. Will you steal from an elderly couple? Will you stand up from those who are being abused even if it means putting yourself in danger? Will you barter with the very people who are responsible for♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ looting, and taking advantage of ordinary citizens like you? You won't know who you really are until you play this game, until you realize that the game is sad for a reason, until you realize that all of the things that happen in this game could and have happened to other people in real life.
You know war is bad. Now experience it for yourself.
TL:DR I was feeling inspired and emotional. War is bad. Get this game if you have a heart and want to learn at the same time that you have some fun. :)

As with Civilization 5 before it, Beyond Earth needs a couple of years of patches and probably an expansion before it will offer really compelling addicting strategy gameplay. As it is now, there aren't quite enough interesting decisions to be made, and there are some annoyances that should be ironed out. For example, there are so many useless buildings and pointless "quest" decisions. Diplomacy is lacking. Civ 5 was the same way, but now with Brave New World and several years of gameplay/balance/AI/UI patches, it's really compelling. But still, Beyond Earth is a new Civ game, and if you like the turn based 4x strategy gameplay, you could do worse. It's both the most similar sequel, in that it reuses the underlying Civ 5 Brave New World engine (hexagonal tiles, one unit per tile, trade routes) and the most different, in that it explores futuristic alien technologies. It makes some nice simplifications over Civ 5, such as simpler promotions, simpler city conquering (no Courthouses), removal of Great People (which were more fiddly than they were worth in my opinion), a more gentle happiness/healthiness statistic. So my advice is to buy Beyond Earth whenever it's heavily discounted, but don't play it until late 2015, after they've made more improvements.

As i'm making an effort to finish every single final fantasy game, halfway through the franchise i decided to go for the lightning storyline, i felt it wouldn't really spoil anything so i went for it...and almost quitted on chapter 11
So, would i NOT reccomend this game? Nah, it's not really a must have but it's not a total disaster really, yes, combat is weird but it still can be fun, it presents you an interesting gameplay, quite unique combat and tactics, i liked it, however, the game feels like it's hell bent on wrecking itself up, the game felt like a constant battle against itself, for every great character there is a whiny emotional grey haired little b*tch to counter, for every good piece of plot, there is a massive hole on it, for every cool mechanic there is a lock on progression that ruins it so it balances off as mediocre.
The main thing that i need to talk about this game is it's genre, RPG, many, many, many times i asked myself "Am i actually playing a RPG?", it has no farming, no real item shop or variety, enemies are sometimes recycled and the encounters and everything are pretty much linear, there is not really a world to explore (untill the damn endgame!!!!!), there are 5 weapons AT MOST for each character and you pretty much get all of them in a linear way, accessories have way more variety but you pretty much earn every one in order too, levelling up items can be wasteful since you can't farm for more material, again, for every RPG mechanic there is a feature that kills it, the game keeps on fighting itself.
Now the story, it made me say "what,,,the f*...is going on?" from start to finish, there is the l'cie and pulse fal'cie because the gods battled and so pulse fal'cie made l'cie because the fal'cie is actually a conspiracy and the pope kills l'cie because fal'cie told l'cie to do stuff so the purge...i BARELY got some few things right and the game kept plot twisting the whole thing, i can't even remember half the names they made up AND WHY ARE ALL THE NAMES SO SIMILAR??? IT'S CONFUSING.
I can't say it is a bad story, it was just way too complicated and poorly explained, i was barely making something out of it but i was quite in it to be honest, the characters are somewhat well developed and you will most likely end up loving some and hating other with all your guts, i loved Sazh's character and his development was great for me, he had a thrilling story arc and his backstory with another character is by far the part i was most interested in the whole game, his parts kept me going hard to keep discovering his story, however, there is Hope..let's just say i hated him with all my heart, still, maybe someone liked Hope's character and hated Vanille for instance, it's a thing, not great, not bad but worth a taste.
Alright, my main point against this game isn't really it's contradictions but chapter 11..after tenths of hours playing, when you feel you're reaching the endgame and after you managed to go around the game's mechanical flaws and finally unlock powerful magics and actually useful abilities, the game branches off to multiclassing and boots you on a final fantasy 12-esque area system to complete hunts and sidequests...WHAT THE F
I am one of the weirdos liked that system from final fantasy 12, that quirky sandbox-ish linear-ish...thing...it was enjoyable and i have no problem with 13 doing the same, the problem is that it locks you off anything near that, it gives you no branching, explorable, backtrackable map or sidequests and all of a sudden branch off like that, i felt like everything i did before was just some 25 hour long tutorial and only now through those i could actually grow to a good level, i called it quits there and came back months later, i played 35 hours total outside that, wishing the game gave me some sidequests to get those 200 points that remain to get a good magic before a boss but it kept things going linear and only now that i don't feel that need anymore it gives me what the whole game mechanic needed? Nuh-uh
I did not understand why that was thrown there, neither why it was so horribly timed, i see no point in it and it just shows that if this game had more thought behind it, what could have happened before, why didn't the game give me chapter 11 on the other motherf*cking forests and mountains i was in before????? Huh??????? I surely could use some farming before fighting Enki and Enlil, the Havoc Skytank or Barthandelus and i'm sure more casual players could use that to make those and other bosses easier or faster.
Some other minor points, this game is by far the most mechanically weird game i have EVER played, nothing really fits, things kinda just fall in place instead of progressing, if quirky games tick you off, steer away from this.
Also, what the hell is wrong with this game's size? IT'S SIMPLY COLOSSAL, not even the later final fantasy 13 games are so HUGE, in fact, every other final fantasy game i have is under HALF it's size.
So, is it bad? No, not good either, it's a cool graphic experience and if you come in without too much expectation, this is worth a taste.

Civilization Beyond Earth is a great opportunity wasted. While the core base still fun, it has many mid and late game issues and very short sighted decisions/mechanics which is really sad to see from Fraxis this late in the franchise.
While the game plays safe by incorporating most of the gameplay feeling from Civ 5 (as well as the engine) there are numerous things removed and just don’t work out well. The biggest issue is the game however that it’s missing the soul and life which previous Civ games had. It’s just “boring” and I was keep asking myself “why should I care” over the course of the game. Your “nation” has no real personality.
In short the Cons:
-	Terrible and Boring UI with underrepresented and uninteresting assets.
-	Terrible Computer AI who are very passive
-	Game got relatively slower (compared to other Civ Games), there were many turns where I was keep clicking the “End Turn” button.
-	No Great persons, Faith or interesting policies.
-	Good Early game, but bad and relatively boring Mid and End game (due to AI)
-	Very bad decisions with Trade routes and Covert Ops overall (literally unlimited trade routes – 3 per city – will drive you mad late game for micromanaging each)
-	Same bugs from Civ 5
-	Same quests over and over again in your games with no brainer quest decisions.
Pros:
-	Affinities are cool and good ideas. Affinity affects your cities and your society also making a unique look.
-	Units look cool. Orbital units are innovative and welcomed.
-	Victory conditions are interesting.
-	Alien AI is much better than Barbarians
This game is not “terrible” it’s just a wasted opportunity for something to be really awesome. It feels like a re-skin for Civ 5 with little effort put into the actual work. If the goal is to fix the problems with DLC-s later than I cannot support that kind of company policy.
At this current State I cannot recommend this game. Buy Civilization 5 Complete instead, it’s a very-very great game, and certainly better than Beyond Earth.

Gat Out of Hell is an expansion of Saints Row IV, following after the events of said game, where at a birthday party for Kinzie, the team uses an JuJu board and asks if the boss will ever have a partner. It is then suddenly the boss is sucked into hell.
Your mission, whether you play as Gat himself or Kinzie, is to retrieve the boss' soul from Hell.
The gameplay is nearly identical to Saints Row IV, with the same design as well as a few challenges which are similar. Although on my part, the keyboard/mouse controls for actions such as 'Flight' are very tricky and unfortunately irritating.
The extension is mainly focused on the story rather than being able to run around killing demons, and it could be pretty much finished around 5-6 hours if you don't collect audio tomes and every cluster. Activites in this game are also more challenging than in SRIV, so if you felt a bit empty of a challenge in SRIV, give a go or two at Salvation maybe.
There's not much to say about the game on my part for now, however I recommend you use a gamepad if you have one, because the game seems to be much easier with that rather than kb/mouse.
The game does not fail to deliver entertainment as you complete musical numbers, rally with club DJ/prolific bard William Shakespeare and help Vlad the Impaler out of the trance that is The Wheels on the Bus.
Despite control issues, I definitely recommend it if you have the time.

This game is beyond awesome, I almost regret buying it on sale for 1$ because I'd value it at 15$ (same as soundtrack edition costs, which is what you should be buying as the soundtrack in this game rules!) if it was a bit longer, I'd value it a lot higher than that.
I played it on (Arch) Linux, it took me 3 hours to finish, and it ran flawlessly from start to finish, It also supported X360 controller just fine on there. I'd say the game's length is going to be roughly 2 hours if you rush through it, 3 hours if you fool around and enjoy it a bit like I did, and even more if you actually bother looking for the secrets and easter eggs which I very much missed out on in my first playthrough.
The game is highly replayable as there are many ways to solve most of the puzzles, and a lot of secret areas. The game can also be modded and custom levels can be made (although sadly no workshop support for that content) but most important of all, this game is fun.
It was probably the most fun 3 hours i've spent for a number of years, the graphics were (intentionally) really cartoony, and the gameplay was a lot like one of those 3D puzzle games in their early days (I'm thinking Gex: Enter The Gecko) and as a result, I was taken back a good solid 15 years to back when I was a child and playing video games for the first time ever. It brought me a lot of joy.
It is worth noting the game is also child-friendly as the most questionable part of it is a small piece of the world lore narrated through wall paintings late in the game, and basic slapstick/cartoon violence.
This game is like a breath of fresh air, it is funny, it is fun, and it is cool, for a hands down rating:
(Really original and fairly unpredictable too)
(It was a 3D Puzzle game with a physics simulation that allows you to create your own paths through puzzles by cutting objects down and moving them around, almost every object in the game could be cut)
(The environment delivered the intended effect, the shortcoming of graphics which dropped it a bit was the character textures and how simple the textures of everything else was, models were also simple but that was a necessity in a low budget indie game like this with the gameplay mechanics. I can say though that one thing I loved about the game is that it has no UI/HUD, all it has is a crosshair to help you aim which is all you really need, it creates a nice immersive feeling not to worry about health bars or ammo or anything, the text messages that followed up with sound effects when objects smashed into each other was also really cool in my opinion.)
(Hands down the best soundtrack (system) in any video game ever, it was an intergrated part of the gameplay, you would unlock new music tracks by picking up audio tapes and then you could switch between them whenever you wanted with just the press of a button, there were several music tracks fitting like a glove on each of the environments the game offers and if by any case you didn't like a track, you would just change to the next one! Apart from how the system handled soundtrack, the music itself was awesome and personally for me good enough to listen to outside of the game even, you can use the two trailers as examples, I'm a fairly harsh critique when it comes to music too, so me endorsing a games soundtrack this much is extremely rare, the only other game I can think of I would ever score this high is The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind)
(This is the games weakest point, the game is very well playable on a keyboard and mouse, but aiming the laser is sometimes a little bit annoying and unintuitive, especially since it is limited to the field of view of your camera, and playing it with a controller just didn't work very well for me at all, I couldn't aim for♥♥♥♥♥♥with the controller which was the main issue on there (using the right analogue stick, but maybe it's just cus I suck with analogue sticks, there's also no auto-aim.) but I also noticed it was a lot harder to control my character with the analogue stick than with the keyboard, using the D-Pad works great though!)
This would've been 9.5 out of 10 if the game had been just about twice as long as it was, but like I mentioned, it can be modded and players can share new levels with each other which I imagine would be really cool! if only it was more popular and had a few dedicated modders, this would go a long way.

"The War is Over." That's the phrase that pops up when you survive the war, and frankly after playing this game that's all the satisfaction you will ever need.
This game is indie. It's not funny, it's not known for its fighting mechanics, but it sends a message that can be summed up in three words "war is bad." But of course we already know that right? 9 out of 10 people you ask will probably say that war is bad. They might say support our troops, let the conflict in the middle east end, or hold a moment of silence as a sign of respect. But talk is cheap, actions are what define a person.
By actions are what define a person I am not suggesting a call to action that every single one of us quit our dayjobs or schooling to go rally and achieve world peace. What I am asking is that you experience a very accurate simulation of what war is truly like, because after this game trust me, you will have a whole new understanding of what war is. Playing this game won't suddenly make you relate to the horrors that the REAL victims of war have seen. But it will make you feel like a human being and if you do it right, you will get some strong emotions in the mix too.
If you do get this game, I suggest you try to play it as realistically as possible and as humanly as possible. What I mean by that is that you keep in your mind that these are real people you are controlling, because eventually there will come a point in the game where you will simply forget that. Everytime your character helps someone, you will feel happy. Everytime you turn away a neighbor asking for help you will feel bad. You will see things in the game that you are powerless to stop. Your morals will be questioned all the way until you either survive or perish. Will you steal from an elderly couple? Will you stand up from those who are being abused even if it means putting yourself in danger? Will you barter with the very people who are responsible for♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ looting, and taking advantage of ordinary citizens like you? You won't know who you really are until you play this game, until you realize that the game is sad for a reason, until you realize that all of the things that happen in this game could and have happened to other people in real life.
You know war is bad. Now experience it for yourself.
TL:DR I was feeling inspired and emotional. War is bad. Get this game if you have a heart and want to learn at the same time that you have some fun. :)

Aaaaah, I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream.  Now I must be honest, when I first played this game a few years ago, it actually made me scared and I stayed up because the bad ending scared the ever living s*** out of me.  But then again, I was big wuss back then so...yeah.  Anyways, IHNMAIMS is probably hands down my favorite point and click game ever...okay next to Gabriel Knight it is...because Tim Curry is a god among men....<_< don't you judge me.  Anyways, IHNMAIMS is almost everything I ever wished for in a Point and Click game; a good UI, an amazing storyline, well thought out puzzles and great characters.  IHNMAIMS follows the story of 5 people who have been tortured by a giant super computer built by America, Russia and China; known only by the name AM.  For over 100 years AM has tortured these people and has decided to play a game with them.  Each character must go through a series of tasks.  Now, this is where the game gets pretty unique.  As each character goes through their trials, each one must overcome something from their past that has troubled them.  The game also relies on something that I like about this game, it relies on actually doing right or wrong.  Each character will be faced with choices that will either reflect positively or negatively on their actions.  All in all, this game is probably something I could recommend to any fan of Psychological Horror or Point and Click games. Have fun :D

You could throw out the "battles" and make it one long cutscene, it would be less annoying then. Story would be acceptable, had the creators not spiked it with idiotic, unnecesary made-up words to make it seem DEEP. Cie'th, l'Cie, fal'Cie, f***'Cie them all, really. No FF before needed that babble. It just isolates you even further from the game world, preventing any level of immersion. Storytelling makes it even worse - you won't get what's going on unless you read the in-game encyclopedia/wikia. So - there's no storytelling there. In general, there's no there there. Easily one of the most contraversal entries in the series, does it deserve all the hate? No. That isn't to say that Final Fantasy XIII, and its' two sequels do not contain plenty of flaws, but one can easily find plenty of redeeming qualities.
Story
This game has one of the more iffy casts. I enjoy half of the characters, those being Lightning, Snow, and Sazh. All of these characters have their own archs and/or internal conflicts. Although he may be irritable, Hope does feature one of the most prominent and well executed character archs, and his evoling relationship with Snow was executed well. Despite what many say, Lightning does actually have a personality. Having played through the game several times, on different platforms, Vanielle and Fang (the other two party members) have almost no character development. The antagonist of this game is kinda forgettable.
The narrative is decent, certainly different than most Final Fantasy games which may be a welcome change for some. The writers of the game certainly deserve points for creativity. That being said, most of the story is told through exposition which is lame. In fact, dialogue in this game is kinda bad. No one talks like a normal human being. Imagine if a bunch of exposition that was written in Japanese, and then translated into English, and then that English script was given to Japanese writers again, so that they could try and translate that modern English dialect into Shakespearean English. Its as bad as it sounds.
Gameplay
Many of this game's detractors say things like, 'hurr dee dur, Its a haaalllway! Notice how this specific area is supposed to be a narrow walkway? See the entire game is a hallway! FINAL FANTASY DIED AFTER X.  R.I.P SquareSoft'.
The thing that many of these fans do not consider is the fact that nearly every Final Fantasy game is incredibly linear. Final Fantasy VII is incredibly restrictive with its linearity, and one could argue that Final Fantasy X is even MORE linear than XIII, but both of those games are considered absolute masterpieces. Unless you have the same criticism of the rest of the Final Fantasy series, then complaining about XIII's linearity simply isn't valid.
As many have stated, the game does open up late into the game, and this is where most of the game's content is located. I do think it is a problem that much of the gameplay experience doesn't come into play until super late into the game, although this isn't as big of an issue until one decides to do repeat playthroughs.
The side quests that this section features has an incredible amount of variety, and yet an extreme lacking amount of variety. Every side quest can be boiled down to, 'Go to the place, Kill the thing'. While that is the case, each quest provides a vastly different enemy to face, each with its own strengths and weaknesses. To take down each encounter, players will often have to stragize and try various methods until one successfully works. There are only a handful of these encounters that you could attribute to being the 'same'. There is certainly no lacking of potential playtime here.
Although there are some issues with the combat itself (such as having to rely on A.I), at the end of the day, the combat is fun, which is what is most important. It will certainly keep you entertained until the well into the post game.
Presentation
This is one of the best aspects of this game. As I mentioned, the dialogue in this game is awful, so the presentation of the plot is poor, but nearly every other aspect is excellent.
Each enviroment is vastly different from the last, and on a visual level, every area is beautifully crafted. While the graphical fidelity is partially responsible, the biggest reason this game still looks so damn good after all these years is due primarily to a strong art direction.
While there are stronger soundtracks within the Final Fantasy franchise, there is no shortage of excellent tracks to listen to. Music is used effectively to create emotional impact throughout the game, and often times the soundtrack adds significantly to the personality of each location. The general boss theme, 'Blinded by Light' is probably my favorite battle theme in the franchise.
Final Verdict
Despite the game's flaws, it is still one of my favorite entries in the series. Definitely buy it if you are a Final Fantasy fan. Even with its problems, the entire trilogy is one hell of an experience, and one you will want to have if you are invested in the series. If you hate linearity in RPGs, you should look for something else to play. If you are Final Fantasy fan who hates linearity, maybe you should get better opinions.

I feel like this is somewhat of a sleeper game that flew under the radar for a lot of people and for that reason I am writing a review. This War of Mine is an absolute gem and a game that deserves attention for exploring a part of war that is hardly ever seen. When playing triple A titles like Call of Duty or Battlefield or any other fast paced FPS I always noticed how there were never civilians around and rather than the cities or locales we were fighting through looking lived in, they looked like set piece ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t with conveniently placed cover.
This War of Mine puts you in the shoes of a civilian with one simple goal: survive! You and a few survivors (usually between three and five from a roster of about ten or twelve) are put in a house and need to do whatever you can to survive. During the day you can scavenge around your house or build upgardes such as weapons, stove, animal traps, rain catchers, beds and even a guitar.
During the night time you must pick one person to venture out into one of the locations where supplies must be scavenged. Early in the game you only need a lockpick or two to search for cigarettes, food, and building supplies. Yet as you start to exhuast supplies you must venture into areas where other people are living, usually armed and dangerous. It becomes a balancing act by ensuring the survival of your group and trying to navigate the tough moral implications of you stealing supplies from other or in extreme situations killing them.
It is a tough game and you must be prepared for members of your group to suffer quite a bit as the strain of trying to live in a warzone takes its toll. It is a visceral and somewhat brutal take on a facet of war that is seldom explored. It is definitely worth a try to see if you can last in This War of Mine.

As a long-time fan of the Final Fantasy series, I first bought this on Xbox 360 back in 2009. I remember playing a few hours and then, disgusted by the linear nature and overly convoluted battle system, I consigned it to the bottom of my 'to play' pile. Eight years on, I finally gathered the courage and patience  to reattempt it in this 1080p Steam version, and, happily I have found that it is a much better game than I initally thought.
The story is quite complicated even for a Final Fantasy game - after spending 90 hours on it I am still not sure what it's about. A group of kids get some wierd brands tattooed on them, and find themselves outcasts of society because of these markings. The game focuses on how they end up travelling to the heart of their world and ultimately facing a deity which results in them getting their old, unbranded lives back.
The big problem remains the linear nature of the storyline for the first 30(!) hours or so, and the limited characterisation and development of the main party, something which has always been a notable element of the Final Fantasy games. Once the game opens up and you can start battling the 64 monster missions, the flexibility and challenge of the combat system emerges, leading to some really interesting battles which require strategy and, at times, skilllful execution. Unfortunately there is little variety in the look of these monsters, though the graphics still hold up remarkably well.
This is a game which (just about) rewards patience, but demands lots of it. For those who enjoy Final Fantasy games, and can look past some of the limitations, there is a lot of fun to be had here. If you are new to Final Fantasy, I'd recommend starting with a more approachable entry, such as VII, IX or X.

Now this is there the PC port review comes in. I'm not going to lie, it's not good at all. I've got a powerful rig equipped with a 1080TI, and I've got FFXIII at max settings. PC can easily handle this as it does with current games at max settings but I experience a lot of frame drops.
Cut scence constantly run at 60fps, but while roaming, I can get anywhere from 30-60fps (mostly 60 though). During combat is where I see the constant drops. Sometimes battles will run at 30 and it just doesn't feel right. Then again, this is a game from 2010 and was ported over in 2014 so I don't expect the best results. It definitely doesn't effect the gameplay at all but it could hinder your experience ever so slightly.
Despite all that, a definite game to play. Love the story!
EDIT : After putting ~80 hours into this game, I felt somewhat exhausted and had no interest in playing the sequels. I will comment on them based on my experience from PS3. The combat is far better, with some cinematic/interactive battle scenes and slightly shorter of a game. With that said, FF13-2 has a somewhat complicated plot that can come off boring. Despite that, I would recommend going to YouTube and watching the cutscene movie. I did the same with FF13-3 but I wish I took the time to play that one. Collectively, if you so choose to play the sequels, prepare to put another 50-60 hours in total.
TLDR : I only started my FF playing career at X but I can say that this is probably my favourite story line. Best story line, but least favourite combat system. Definitely play the first, watch the second on YouTube, and if you have the time play the third one.. otherwise you can catch that one on YouTube as well.

I spent about 12 hours playing this game/stand-alone DLC because i spent WAY too much time looking for collectibles, and seeing as how I most likey bought this when it was on sale for probably $7.50 I'd say I got my money's worth (1hr=$1).  I didn't enjoy it as much as Saint's Row IV but I didn't hate enough to not finish it; while it feels a little shallow I finished it, which is more than I can say for most of the games I own.  You can probably get through it in much less time than I did if you don't worry about getting 100% of the stuff done. (a streamer could probably get through it in one or two sessions).
Pros:
*Super Powers
*Flying (not just gliding)
Cons:
*No player customization (Hell has no clothing shops)
*Not as many weapons as SR4
*With less Saints available there's not as much of the interactions that I enjoyed so much in SR4, this one is for the gameplay not the story or characters.
There aren't that many "misisons" other than the main questline that unlocks itself as you complete challenges (spend 20 minutes flying, kill 1000 demons, ect) where a bar fills up as you complete challenges and unlocks forced cutscenes - not like new missions but it takes out out of the game and plays it for you; one of which happened while i was flying around looking for collectibles (soul clusters for upgrading powers and audio logs) which was annoying. Until you unlock all of Satan's attention and you get a final Mission unlocked; after that happens you can take your time doing all of the distractions (mayhem, insurance fraud, ect) and they Loyalty missions for your buddies in Hell (which I think is just for colour because doing that doesn't actually help you in any way but might unlock a bonus cutscene after the credits)
So basically you just run around causing havok until you get the devil's attention then confront him; there isn't much more to the story than that.
Aspects from SR4 that carry over to this stand-alone DLC are the super powers (blast, stomp, and aura) with the addition of "summon" instead of the telepathy power.
Blast consists of turning enemies to stone instead of freezing them, there is an ability that creates a vortex that slows them down and does damage over time, and an ability that fires a target-seeking soul that does damage over time and can chain to multiple enemies once upgraded.
Stomp has the same default blast, a vortex ability that sucks enemies into a black hole and pulls in health and money drops, as well as a Holy Light power that can stun enemies if it doesn't outright kill them.
The aura ability has a flame ability like the one in SR4 with a slight twist (the "cold fire" can freeze enemies as well as burn them when upgraded), as well as an ability that causes enemies to worship you which grants a damage bonus and stuns them (they don't attack while they're worshiping you) and a vampire ability that saps health.
The new ability is the ability to summon demons to fight for you.  It starts with imps that grab onto an hump their target before exploding.  You can upgrade this ability to get more imps as well as making them burn the target as well with cold fire and the ability to trigger their explosion when you want it to happen.  You also gain the ability to spawn a spire which acts as sort of an immobile turret; upgrades add firing missiles and a wider attack area (i didn't think i'd use it as much as i did).  The last power for Summon is the ability to summon a Titan. this is a large hulk of a demon (the wardens of SR4) that will run around and melee enemies; they're strong, tough, and mobile.
Super-running returns with an upgrade that allows you to run across lava (if you hit a bubble you'll still burn but not from touching the surface) but you will most likely never be in a situation where you're in lava because most likely you'll be spending all your time flying.
Flying in Gat Out of Hell is much like the gliding in SR4, you jump into the air then dash forward and glide, but with your wings you have the ability to climb, dive, and turn-on-a-dime (with agility upgrade) instead of being in free-fall as it was in SR4; you upgrade yourself to have move flaps available to increase your speed in the air (as you climb you lose speed and if you lose all your speed you fall.  I spent A LOT of time flying around, and instead of the speed-running races they have flight-based races this time around; which were a lot of fun.
There is a sort of fast-travel system for teleporting from node-to-node (like the gateways in SR4) but the map isn't large enough to necesitate fast-travel; just fly up a little higher and you avoid all the roads and buildings.  Though there is a reward for unlocking all of the teleports, so there's that.
All things said I don't feel like I would spend $15 on this game/stand-alone DLC; $10 would be tempting, but I don't feel like I wasted my money buying it for $7.50 (just remember that it feels more like a stand-alone DLC than it's own game; like if Far Harbor was sold without needing to have Fallout 4)

I bought this game during early-access back quite some time ago and now just started playing again last week, after not having much time due to private reasons.
Honestly, Stunlock Studios fixed almost all of the few issues that existed earlier in the EA. Right now, I really enjoy playing it and I think, that anyone who liked WoW Arena, Bloodline Champions or any other "Arena-Brawler" back in the day will really have a blast playing it.
At the moment there are already over 20 different characters with 9 abilities each, which offer tons of different ways to play the game. Moreover, Stunlock Studios has plans to release tons of new characters in the future, with, according to a devpost, like 6 in the next 6 months.
There is also tons of different outfits, weapon-skins and victory poses for all characters, which are, for the most part incredibly well done. Moreover, they also changed the way "talents" work, (these are 5 perks, which enhance your abilities in different ways), which you can choose prior the each game, but when you already know what enemy "heroes" you are playing aginst. Personally, I really enjoy this new way of choosing these, as it lets you customize your Loadouts(=talents)  according to the enemy teamcomposition, which is able to give you a huge advantage, once you fully understand how the enemies' characters work.
Just a quick side-note: Do not get discouraged if you don't immediately succeed, feel a bit overwhelmed and lose a lot of games, as it is a quite difficult game at first. It may sound weird, but having your own 9 abilites to use and also needing to at least kind of know what each character is able to do, in order to use your skills accordingly, really can be a bit overwhelming at first. Especially because one mistake can quite easily cost you a round (Each game in arena is played as a best of 5, meaning, that the team, that wins 3 rounds wins the game.) Each round takes about 2 minutes, so at most, 1 game takes roughly 10 minutes, most of them are shorter though.
But the great thing with that is, that the game gets more and more rewarding and fun once you have the basics down and it also gives you a reason to keep going, which sadly, at least in my opinion, a lot of other games these days lack.
One last thing, there is this thing called "Odeum", which is a pretty much fully functional replay system (even though the devs are still working on improving it even further), where you can look at, edit, and upload your own amazing plays and watch tons of replays from other players in the game client. This was especially helpful for me at the beginning, as you can see how other players, who play the character you enjoy most, and have already mastered them to some extent, play them.
With all that said, I definitely want to give everyone a recommendation to give Battlerite a try, as it is an incredible game, which just recently reignited my passion for pure, non-luck/gear dependant PVP, a kind of game, I had been looking for a long time.
The F2P version is released on the 8th of November 2017, so there is nothing to lose in trying it out as well. I don't quite know how the new system for unlocking characters will work, but if it is anything like in Bloodline Champions (which was also by Stunlock Studios) it does take quite some time after receiving the initial free character(s). So buying the package, which unlocks all current and future champions may very well be worth it for you, at least if you find yourself enjoying it after playing it for some time. I defniitely do not regret buying the early access bundle, which is essentially, for the most part, the same as the new character bundle.
Hopefully, we will meet in the arena one day and engage in some challenging, unadulterated PVP action!

I decided to change my review of this game to offer up points of why the game falls short. I'll summarize this as much as possible. If you want a very short review it is posted below.
The super short review :
6 out of 10 ( Good for fist timers and the younger gaming crowd )
Anyone expecting a game with depth in story line and ship functionality will be disappointed. The story line is predictable, the benefits are minimal, everyone wins gaming.
Would I play this game again? No, probably not unless the developer added many more features and vastly improved the game AI.
The good:
Overall a good looking game.
Runs well, smooth.
No crashes.
Great sound track.
Multiple paths to follow to end game ( Merchant, Pirate, Combat, Miner )
The Bad:
You "fly" on a single plane and cannot go up or down. While this is a space game I feel ike I am driving a tank or playing a FPS.
The weapons systems on your ship shoot through your ship most of the time.
It is a race to get Mark 5 / 6 items, you could do without but then you may have a harder times with the game.
You simply follow a simple path to the end game.
There is never a bounty placed on your head for the waves of AI you slaughter, your participation is not recognized in this game at all, this includes news stories.
Between Story line missions upgrading your ship is essential to completing the next mission you will not know this until you jump in and have a WTF moment.
There is no communication between stations for commodities ( minerals and goods ) thus what you buy for in one place might not be worth anything in another or one system over it is double in price.
You will never know unless you go there.
Ships and ship components are at 100% trade in and up value.  Thus switching out weapon systems is never a loss nor is it better from one place to another.
The AI never recognizes you. Sure while you can slaughter pirates whole sale in the hundreds, save countless traders or conduct crippling raids against the AI at no point does the dialog or your player presence change anything in the game. It is one dimensional.
There are always more AI, Going to a pirate faction station and eliminating everything in sight does nothing. The stations cannot be destroyed so eradicating a system of pirate activity is impossible.
Random encounters with AI fleets are pointless. Unless there is a bounty loot drops will not even pay for your spent missiles or damage you may take. Best to just avoid them.
The face you see of the AI are all the same. Pirates will taunt you and well this is the 100th time you killed that same pirate. Aliens all look the same also. Even some side characters look just like the random pirates as well as the Militia.
The lines for the AI or NPCs are the same and repetitive.
Trell the AI the story line revolves around makes some minor upgrade to your ship. These are nothing amazing just some sensor and defensive bumps. The only time you interact with Trell is when she wants something ( typical woman ) For an AI with vast knowledge you would think she would tell you how to boost your weapon performance or make some great weapon system or a new type of ship.... nope.
I came here to save Criminal Aunt Juno. However the dialogue with here does nothing to tell me why it would be worth it. No back story to tell me why I'd risk my♥♥♥♥♥to save this woman from the crap she got herself into.
Random AI gotcha moments, taking on a merchant mission with a low threat level was not really low at all. This was a game breaking moment for me because it made no sense what so ever. Enemy ships appear out of nowhere, surround your ship and disable it thus killing your mobility. This continually happens while fleets ( from fighters to dreadnaughts ) of AI pop up randomly. To sum it up the game mechanics cheat. You can attempt to run or if you have the right ship component ( so I am told ) nullify the effects of the disabling missiles.
The end game moments are really nothing special. I never got attached to Trell, she did nothing but get me into trouble, heck her upgrades were minimal at best. The was no big glorious end game movie clip or anything special for saving the galaxy from a deadly invasion. After all this Juno buys you a drink and that is the game.
The end game:
I wanted to finish up achieving the end game in the most "advanced" combat ship with a decent fitting. There was a level of satisfaction at that point because annihilating even a super dreadnaught AI at the end was easy.  Completed with mark 5 / 6 equipped Black Gate Dreadnaught 54,000,000 credits, 1498 enemy ships destroyed. This tacked on another 5 hours of game play before I took on the end game mission. The threat level went from Very High to Low.
Wasted time, I spent a couple of hours sorting out the AI "cheat issue" with the Merchant mission before walking away from the missions. Ironically the combat missions were less dangerous. Exploration, mining and other activities burned up a few hours also. So in 20 to 24 hours you can complete this game with a solid kitted out ship.

I just got this game 2 days ago when it went on sale and i must say i feel awesome i did. This is a great game and will probably grow to be one of my favorites among Endless Space and Master of Orion. Unlike the previously mentioned games, Sins is much faster paced, and leans more to the RTS side of the imaginary "game-type spectrum" i just created in my head, with a healthy dose of 4X-ish thrown in, rather than a full-on 4X game (such as Endless Space and/or MOO). You can research military or civic techs, you can send other people and/or pirates on missions or take some mission another person put up for some extra cred's, you can send afforementioned pirates after someone by posting a bounty, you can create massive fleets comprised of smaller units or smaller fleets of massive capital ships, led by your faction specific GIGANTIC Titan craft, or a mix of both. Your choice. Create trade ports and boost your income, and weaken your enemie's defences by means of expanding your faction's culture. Or blow a planet up.
The interface is very slick, the music is awesome and the feel when playing this game is great. Also it can run even on a toaster.
However the game is not without a very obvious weakness, that TotalBiscuit managed to identify first and i completely agree. In singleplayer, once your faction becomes an unstoppable force of death and destruction (or, you know, a cultural splendor, bah) the game does tend to get somewhat boring towards the end, where you just steamroll on everyone and the fights are more of a mechanical nature rather than an exciting dynamic thing.
I believe that the main intention was the multiplayer, of which the game has an active community with enough players online at any given time to start a match with. Also local LAN is nice. Since i haven't been able to play online yet i cannot comment any further on the issue, but i am sure it will be a whole other game when facing a human player.
If you like what you read, i can promise you, the game offers this, and much more. As i said before, it'll probably end up being one of my favorites and i hope you like it too.

Oh boy... This is by far the first (complete) game in my backlog that appears to have... no passion behind it. I don't think the artists who put it together are the issue, but the director/writers. This game is nothing more than a business transaction. Just another work day to be finished. It saddens me at how much it feels like whoever was put in charge of this game just... didn't care.
I could be wrong in my assumption, but that is what entered my mind as I played through this game. Let's just start everything at 10 points each and see how many points remain by the end. This is going to be more of a critique than a review.
Graphics: starting at +10
=================
Game came out in 2011, and this review is being written in 2017. However.. other games that came out 2 years prior to this one (e.g. Batman Arkham Asylum 2009) actually have great visuals that have aged very well. The graphics could've been much better. -2
How do I know the graphics could've been better? Because the CGI cutscenes look flipping fantastic. It appears that's where all the visual work went. +1
Bland boring environments for each and every level and region. -2
Animations for abilities are weak and uninspiring. -1
Pixelated user interface on menus and inventory system. -1
Needlessly confusing title screen. -1
Final score: 4/10
Sound/Music: +10
=============
Musical score appears to be orchestra, just from the sounds. While this is a good thing, the music in place doesn't really fit with the setting. It's boring and uninspiring (two words I'm going to use a lot it appears). The music should certainly help pull me into the game. This one does not. -2
Horrible horrible sound mix. You have music overbearing the (probably expensive) voice acting being done in many different conversations, to where you can't even hear the actors talking. Hopefully you enabled subtitles! Some characters will sound VERY LOUD while others will sound very soft (therefore you can't hear them). -3
Sound effects for abilties are dull and uninteresting, and there's no weight behind them. When I say weight...each sound effect should have a "heavy" impact to whatever it's complimenting. The ONLY acceptable sound effect is the final kill sound effect. THAT one should've been the Hero to match the other sounds with. -1
Voice acting is actually decent (too bad it's complimented by awful writing). +1
Final score: 5/10
Performance: +10
=============
Performs well. No lag and no crashes throughout my entire playthrough.
Final score: 10/10
Story: +10
========
Story takes place before and then during the events of the Lord of the Rings trilogy. Three heroes have joined up to stop one of Sauron's big bad guys named Agandaur.
Boring characters throughout (-2) with the exception of Beleram the Eagle (+1). With how much effort was put into the voice work, it's sad that the characters are never brought to life. -1
Overall writing and pacing is attrocious. -3
Final score: 6/10
Gameplay: +10
===========
Hack n slash gameplay with some RPG elements thrown in. You can also used ranged attacks (either magic, or a bow/crossbow).
Combat doesn't really grab you or entertain you from the very beginning. It's far too repetitive with almost the same exact enemies throughout the entire game, with slightly adjusted skins. -2
Abilities are almost entirely useless with the exception of knockdown abilities. -1
Final kill slowdown cam and sounds attached are actually pretty cool. +1
Getting knocked down in this game is about as annoying as getting knocked down in Lost Planet. If there is ever a time to get knocked down in a game by something or someone, it should be few and far between, not almost every encounter in the game. -2
Dual wielding enemies are a cheese fest. A dumb and frustrating enemy design. -1
AI is dumb as nails. -1
Revive mechanic is silly and needs a massive rework to be relevant. -1
Final score: 3/10
Overall: 5.6/10 (28/50 = 0.56)
=====================
Poor leadership will lead to poor results. This game is a shining example of what NOT to do not only in a video game, but any creative material whatsoever. Don't be lazy. If help is needed, then ask for it. There is no shame in getting advice, and this title needs a lot of advice.

I've played a lot of hacking sims over the years, (Hacking Simulator 2016, Dark Signs Online, hack_me), and while this game is in a very rudimentary state, if it realizes into what it could be, this could be the game that sticks around.
First Impressions + Gameplay here:
As far as most games in the genre go, Grey Hack is very technical. Focusing primarily on terminal gameplay, the game is a lot harder to start out in, because of the lack of graphic interfaces for a lot of the functions, which could possibly turn less technical players off. Still, with enough practice, it's easy to overcome these hurdles, which are likely temporary until the game is fully developed. The promise of procedurally generated missions is great, if it's done well. Already, I like the subtle variations in the actual missions, and that they don't really devolve into the same button clicks each time--a problem with a lot of the genre. It's also great that the game mimics real life Linux, using the same commands and file structures, and also has some of the same features that it does (placing commands in /usr/bin and /bin will let you use them anywhere, and passwd is in /etc, etc). There's a lot of placeholder spots in the game's features, but it's better to see implemented placeholders than it is to see bullet points on an intended features page. However, the game at its current state is still a little simple, but should flesh out over time.
Grey Hack isn't a visual-arts masterpiece, but it's also not ugly. The game doesn't have god rays or dynamic shadows, but then again it's a simulation of a computer, so I wouldn't expect it. It certainly looks and feels a lot better than much of the genre, actually mimmicking the aestetics of an actual operating system, as well as the functionality. The only draw back in the A/V department is the silence. There isn't any sound or music in the game, which makes it a little awkard to play at times. It's not a major feature, but having something there would make it feel more complete.
Overall, Grey Hack is one of the better hacking games I've played in a while. It doesn't quite beat the genre in functionality just yet, but within the near future, it'll likely develop into something above the most. If you're not technically inclined, it's going to take some time to learn, but it's not impossible. If you're looking for a nearly-developed game, come back in a couple months. If you're looking for something to scratch your Hacking Sim itch, but willing to stick with the weirdness of initial development, I'd reccomend picking up this game.

This War of Mine is one of the most moving examples of interactive storytelling I've ever seen. I cannot recommend this game highly enough.
