Before you spend any $ ask yourself these questions:
1. Are you a major LOTR fan who likes/knows the lore of this universe?
2. Do you have at least 1 friend to play through the game with?
3. Did you like the old hack and slash LOTR games such as "The Two Towers" or "Return of the King?"
4. Do you need a game that can be beaten in a good weekend session? Maybe even replayed again for fun at more difficulty?
If you answered yes to these 4 questions, this game is a great value. THREE ANNOYING THINGS THOUGH YOU MUST KNOW IN MULTIPLAYER.
1. There is an in game voice chat that can't be turned off. HOW YOU GET AROUND THIS: You plug in another mic, tell steam to use that mic, turn the steam mic volume to 0, and then have your chat program such as Discord use your main mic plugged in to your rig. You'll never hear it again, though you'll have to set this up quick every time before you play
2. Anyone who is not the host will not get some of the story achievements which is annoying, but their achievements... who really cares ;)
3. By the end of the game on your first playthrough on Normal (highest difficulty you can play without beating it first) you and your friends will be a little too strong, and so the game's difficulty really tones down which is a shame :( this is fixed in repeat playthroughs on New Game + where you keep your gear and start over but everything is harder.
This is a really fun game with a few quirks, but had me and a LOTR fan friend of mine pretty interested to see what would happen next during the story. Overall I'd give the game outside it's quirks an honest 7 or 8 out of 10 WITH AT LEAST ONE FRIEND. SOLO THIS IS BORING AND GRINDY AS♥♥♥♥♥♥SINCE FRIENDLY A.I. IS GARBAGE.

I wanted to try to write something nice about this game and recommend it to others who might be interested in it. ♥♥♥♥ that. Let me darn my fanboy garments right now!
That game! THAT game!
Yeah, it's your typical procedurally generated dual stick shooter surfing the Isaac wake. Yeah it's got that retro 80s look that's all the craze, up to the (spunky) synthwave soundtrack.
What is not captured by the screen grabs is how great the weapons feel. How cool they sound. How their pitch goes up when running out of ammo, so you don't have to look down at a counter to evaluate your situation. How the same is true for your adversaries. How the action will escalate to mind-blowing levels of mayhem as you progress in the later levels. How you can build up your own class through skills and weapons you pick up. How stealth is an option. How the constantly rewarding progression makes you feel like you didn't waste time, even doing a terrible run. How the game saves your progress transparently.

Rebel Galaxy is a great game that has plenty of good balance to it, though granted I had to remind myself it wasn’t Freelancer* with all its similarities. With the constant reminder that your piloting a 2 dimensional ship through 3 dimensional space that makes use of primary functions for broad fire tactic’s while combatting fighter vessels that can fly in any direction was easy to notice the uniqueness Rebel Galaxy Possess in standing out from the rest of the space games to hit the market.
One thing that would keep me engaged as a Gamer is the really good work with the Music Que’s between combat and Station Menu navigation. Yes you still get the option to customize your own music to the game, but speaking as an Audio Editor, there was some really good work into allowing the music to que into the combat scene’s. The music is so good that I even had the pleasure to find the list posted by Travis Baldree on the dev’s website Sound Track List**.
Granted I enjoy my gameplay and found myself wanting a bit more in the way of controls, but I constantly found the fact of the simplified combat and turret options in ship to ship combat well simplified. I partly wished I could have been able to explore the stations or board the ships that constantly threatened me to get sucked into space, so as only to just see that I could do it, but still we wouldn’t have had such a well-planned out 2 Dimensional controlled 3D Space Combat game.
Pro’s:
•	Short but worthwhile story
•	Simplified Ship controls
•	Great Music Selections
•	Persistent Markets when selling commodities – even gives a history on the price of the item, and system average for the entire System you’re in.
•	Great Map Design and navigation assistance though lacks a little in cross coordination with other implemented features of the game.
Con’s:
•	Not Exactly Merchant Friendly: Always a hassle trying to find a price for a single item between all known locations that buy and sell commodities of a certain type. Would have like an option that allowed seeing at a quick list of last known prices at all stations for a single commodity.
•	Stellar Mass often times stopping warp while not even in the way of the travel.
•	Not all ships are available, can’t truly pilot a fighter or gunship.
•	Not able to change direction up or down to evade Stellar mass in a direct collision course
•	Not able to properly map Cone of angles for the turret systems being applied to the ships. (Kinda handy when attempting to do mining to know where the laser fire can reach.)
•	Limitation to the Components that can be installed on all ships.
•	Not able to easily pull up the map when needing to make a quick reference to a station or asteroid mining location when getting info or finding merchandise while in space.
•	Limited to a single Mercenary Hire, can’t recruit an armada of Mercenaries.

-All Aboard the Cyberpunk Train!-
Get ready to climb ladder of the future! You play as an asset, here to stop the evil Overseer - A controlling AI that is the mind of Neon Chrome. In this future, complete and absolute trust is required to have the luxury of residing in said Neon Chrome. Once the Overseer caught wind of your sentience, well, you're simply marked for 'removal'. Teams of baddies, not to mention their robot machine-gun counterparts will stop at nothing to carry out exactly what the twisted leader demands.
There are no two ways about it, Neon Chrome is absolutely visually stunning. I cannot express how gorgeous and sleek everything looks from the start up screen, to the actual gameplay. The menus are slick and make you feel like you're completely immersed. Loading times are notably fast too--some of the quickest I've ever seen. If you're like me, and are just waiting in line for your next go at dying, this softens the blow and starts to desensitize you. Coupled with the safe room, where you get to upgrade, tweak and choose your next character, the game makes sure you start with confidence. But the higher you climb the cyberpunk rungs, the more expensive it all becomes.
-A Different Experience Every Time-
Neon Chrome has a unique level loader that randomizes every situation. Unlike Hotline Miami, where you can master every move and learn to own a level down to a centimeter--this game will move it all around and switch layouts up to keep you on your toes. As Neon Chrome is the towering skyscraper of Neon Corp, this special randomization feature makes you feel like you really are climbing your way through a never-ending building.
After Guardian of Light, I became a massive fan of the twin stick shooting genre. This is a game that makes sure you get all the fun squeezed out of it too. It's fast and reflexive. I won't lie, I'm not very good at this game, but it doesn't change the fact that I enjoyed every minute of playing it. Perhaps the Overseer got the best of my assets time and time again, but I can assure you good reader, that this little engine that could will keep coming back for the pain. Since every new turn is such a drastic change from the last, the monotony of playing the same thing over and over is completely broken up. Your assets are different people with endlessly different abilities. Each level is packed with exploding bits of environment, locked doors, keymasters and upgrading stations. No shortage of weaponry here, they've clearly strived to make nothing seem repetitive, which is a huge win for any game.
-The Future Is Well-Maintained-
Aside from it's being a great game as it is, it seems like the developers are constantly listening and improving on what is already something amazing. Being in touch with their fanbase, they've lowered the difficulty of the bosses, giving everyone a fair fight with more health pickups and tweaking the upgrade system to better suit our needs. Something neat that was also mentioned was the use of mods and how they're very actively supporting them (at your own risk!) to the point where it's easily accessible through the main menu. It's been mentioned that support could be implemented to make them more stable, but this would be pending on the sales of the game itself.
From the mind melting visuals that will leave your brain salivating, to the haunting, hallow voice of the Overseer--this game will satisfy your lust to take down an evil corporation of the future. You'll enjoy tailored gameplay that runs like a well-oiled machine with this one--it's not to be missed!

Another entry in the main Final Fantasy series that distances itself from earliest Final Fantasy games but is still filled with enough of the early final fantasy bloat to bring down an otherwise good game.  I'll start out by saying that I still recommend the game, even with its flaws but if players are looking for more of an open world traditional RPG, they may want to look elsewhere.
I'll start off with the positives.
First the Story/Characters/World.  I loved them for about 2/3rds of the game.  From meeting the characters, to finding out who they were, to learning about their motivations, to their conflicts and their eventual resolution to those conflicts.  The game also moves pretty quick in the early going and sends you to various and varied locations pretty quickly throughout the early part of the game.  The fact that this game is mostly on-rails/linear wasn't that big of a drawback with how the story played out.  Everything that happened had you wanting to move forward in the story and keep moving to learn how things work going to play out.
Now to some of the okay, but could been better.
The combat was a nice change of pace from previous final fantasy games I've played, gone is the slower turn based style and in is a more action oriented type combat system.  There are 6 different roles, physical/magical/tank/buff/debuff/healer, the playable characters will be proficient in 3/6 of those roles, so you can mix and match with characters to create a group that fits your style or is the most optimum, however since each character is proficient in so many you can always go with the characters you like, didn't seem to make much a difference to me who was in the group, so I just went with who I liked best in the story.  The problem with the combat was that 98% of the fights could be done with 1 physical and 2 magical characters, only for some bosses and late game harder enemies did you need to put some serious thought, the reason for this is the way the stagger gauge works, magical attacks quickly raise the gauge, while physical attacks make the gauge drain slower.  So with one physical and two magical, the gauge would charge quickly and wouldn't fall off before your next round of attacks. Based on the sheer number of enemies in some groups sometimes you'd need to switch your classes around mid fight through the paradigm system, but I would revert back pretty quickly.
There is a good variety of monsters in this game, though it ends up in the same class as many other Final Fantasy games where many enemy models just get recoloured in later areas.
And now to some things that just shouldn't have been in the game.
If your lead characters hits zero health in any fight, the fights over, that's it, if one of you the other characters in battle die, you can revive them and continue on like nothing ever happened.  I have no idea why this is, you should be able to switch paradigms and if you have another healer and they have raise, cast it and continue on, or maybe it auto switches lead in battle.  And its not tied to one character, later in the game any character can be the lead.
Also, SE could do well to get rid of instant death mechanics, they aren't fun, they never have been fun and combined with the fact that if you lead character dies the fight is over, means they are extra bull♥♥♥♥♥♥this time around.  There is a couple of fights where you have a countdown timer to death, I'm not talking about those, those are mostly fine cause the game is designed in a way that those fights are winnable.  I'm talking about some of the very late game enemies that use them and for some reason, those mechanics are thought of as 'challenging' when they are just a lazy way to make something feel more difficult.
The Final Fantasy series also needs to do away with useless battle animations that are either unskipable or completely useless outside of the first time they are ever used.  So with the battle/paradigm system, you get 6 preset paradigms you can take into battle with you.  The first time you switch your paradigm in battle you are greeted with a useless/unskipable animation showing you that you changed your paradigm.  This happens the first time you do it every battle, any paradigm changes later in battle thankfully skip this animation.  The worst part is that while you are animation locked, the enemy is free to act, like do damage.  So if you are trying to switch to a paradigm with a healer and need to get off a clutch heal, NOPE, got to watch that stupid animation first so hope the enemy doesn't kill you mid animation.
Also this game features a tank role in the paradigm system.  The role is designed to attract an enemies attention and be the focus of their attacks.  The problem is that whoever designed the battle system didn't think through what happens with AOE attacks.  You would think that any tank type class would be smart enough to move to a location where it can take those attacks without harming their party, but nope, the other members of the group for some reason get closer to the tank so they can also get hit by the AOE instead of letting the tank do their job.    So the healer and tank decide to get hit by all the AOE attacks together instead of the way it should be, neither of them would move out of the way of each other.
The only other thing negative for me was the last 1/3rd of the story.  Once you get the whole group together, kind of figure out what your goal is, you get dumped in your first 'open world' location and you kind of just stumble around for a while, there are challenges to do, but none of them feel rewarding.  You fight a few bosses as part of the story but I never felt like the story really progressed like it did in the first part of the game.  The resolution was nice enough, but damn does SE need to stop with the "This isn't my final form bull crap", just give me a boss to fight.
Overall the game was good but it stumbled with a lot of the filler that Square Enix just seems to love to fill their game with

This game has potential, but in its current state I can not recommend it over other games in the Civ series.  As it stands, it is just a poor man's Civ 5.  If you don't have that game, go get it now, the complete edition with all the core DLC is both cheaper than BE and wil give you almost the same experience (if not a better one).
Some Positives
-I like the Sci-Fi setting, lots of potential down the road
-The tech web, while taking some getting used to, is a cool new edition that adds variety to different playthroughs
-Affinities add even more replayability than ideologies in Civ 5
-Is very much like Civ 5 in look and feel
The Negatives
-Is very much like Civ 5 in look and feel.  Besides the Sci-fi setting, it is almost entirely a re-skin of Civ 5.  I feel this can be both a positive and a negative.
-AI characters have no personalities, will often not even talk
-Building a wonder is very unfulfilling, unlike Civ 5 which gave beautiful looking art to show what you built, all BE wonders provide samey looking blue schematics.
-Trade is pointless, there are no luxuries, and very little else  trade with other civs.
-Victory, like building wonders, is unfulfilling, with nothing in the way of fanfare or art.
-It is not better than Civ 5
Perhaps after a DLC or two this will start to feel like a totally new Civ game, but as of now it only feels like a glorified expansion.  If you have played Civ 5 for hundreds of hours and want something new, you can get this game on sale and enjoy a few more hours of new content, but otherwise, wait for some DLC to flesh out its potential.

I got the entire FFXIII series hoping to play through all three in one amazing sitting.
This game is all about pros and cons.
Pros being great character design, graphics, decent story, decent combat
Cons being that there is literally nothing to do but run down a hallway and fight monsters.
That's a dealbreaker for me. There is no NPC interaction whatsoever, the entire game feels constrained, almost claustrophobic because there is actually not a lot of space to move around at all.
This game might have made it as a mobile game, but as a full fledged rpg it fails to deliver the core of what RPGs are supposed to be: exploring and levelling up through battles and quests.
FFXIII-2 suffers the opposite problem: the characters have no life, there are port issues with the audio sync, the story is pretty bad, but the world was open and you could explore to some extent.
Square has forgotten the cardinal rule of rpgs ever since FFIX: Immersion
In conclusion, I can't say I dislike the game itself as there is really nothing to hate, but I find it very hard to recommend this game to anyone expecting an rpg. It would be much better served if the buyer views this as a visual novel or an interactive movie.

It's very different from most games around, and even different from most space sims around too. Complex and indepth, the game clearly has potential for those who have interest, but the learning curve and rough edges can be initially offputting (or entirely).
It is and isn't my sort of game; it looks like the sort of game you invest a lot of time into over a long period of time, versus the sort of game that throws you straight into the action - a game that potentially requires that you have a lot of free time on your hands, both for playing and possibly for learning stratergies and initially the basics.
My initial impressions were good and it appears that most of the reviews are due to people A. not being able to launch the game or B. due to problems and bugs I haven't yet experienced or were long fixed in previous patches.
Haven't had any issues at all after my very limited playtime (I did play an hour or two which isn't recorded in offline mode due to my internet going poof), though the game does seem very slow with quite a lot of mechanics - probably a very good game, but not the sort you can sink into casually without some effort and learning. Probably the sort of game you play for a good few hours before you can really begin to enjoy it as the ropes seem a little difficult to get the game of.
Some notes:
- Voice acting is terrible. There is literally only a handful of lines for generic npcs and overall the quality of the voiceacting is off (characters all seem emotionless and repeat the same lines).
Not sure why they did not settle with text instead of voice acting. Would have (in my opinion) improved the game if they just stuck with text chat in windows for communication (think Stalker, where only specific unique characters have voice chat, generic characters are just text).
- Playing through the campain - pretty tedious as you mostly move around doing one job or another. I wonder a little if the game is built more for free play than story. That, and whilst looking for crew members, a swarm of hostiles keeps taking out my ship & capital ship...
- Seems to be some performance issues. Probably related to my crappy CPU. AMD FX4100 & a GTX770 - can't run above medium without the game turning into a lag fest.
- You can walk around stations. Initially cool, but very quickly lost interest in the concept after a few times -- they all basically look the same inside and have the 'same people' in the regard that each and every npc has the same tiny set of voices and conversations (please oh lord, quit with the '40 years we didn't even have highways!')
- The GUI is terrible, in my honest opinion. Often lacking visiblity and ease of access, the GUI/UI overall is a right mess - it has strange ways of functioning and has made me accidently shoot stuff I intended to communicate to/interact with.
= Slow paced  gameplay. May or may not be your thing - it depends on how much time you have available. For example, I started and escort mission and half an hour later I was still escorting a ship. Got bored in the end and quit, but that is because of impatience and lack of time.
+ Atmosphere seems overall good. Well, bar the poor voice acting. Combat is typical space shooter, so nothing special in that regard, which I have no issue with.
+ Mods. Always a plus for me when a game has a modding community.
I won't recommend it to people like me, but I can see exactly why people
like it, which is why I'm giving an overall recommendation. The game is good for what it is, but I currently don't have the time and patience to sit down and learn the ropes and immerse myself - in the future I might, but for now I do not.
I don't care if you like it or not.

Second, this game only supports one device at a time, meaning I can only use my joystick, my throttle, OR my rudder pedals. This is absolutely a complete turn-off for this game and is the primary reason I decided I didn't even want to play it for free.

To all the nostalgic fans out there: no, this isn't Blood Money. And I'm a nostalgic too, but hope isn't lost. On the contrary, with Absolution you'll get a very mature and engaging plot, you'll see an Agent 47 driven, probably for the first time, by human feelings. And that's what makes the story so strong. With stunning graphics, of course.
The Contract mode is quite fun, if you have some friends to compete with. Not that the contracts created by other users are boring. It really makes you discover every little thing of every level. Every detail, every weapon, every situation that can be used to your advantage.
There are downsides, though. I would have liked to hear a little more variety of voices. You'll see my point after a few missions spent walking through crowds of people.
You can hide a sniper rifle in your pants? This is supposed to be Agent 47, not Guybrush Threepwood! I miss the old sniper rifle case, it looked so cool!
The disguise system surely has been improved, but it's far from perfect. Chicago is quite a big city, how comes every damn cop knows each other? And how can a normal cop be suspicious about me when I'm wearing a SWAT disguise? Seriously, my whole face is covered by the ski mask! He can only see my eyes!
In conclusion, it's not perfect, but it's a damn good comeback for 47.

Great twist on a FPS. Unlike most derivative FPSs, the setting is not burst-fire-full-metal-jacket but rather a period where you'll be armed with bows, crossbows, powder pistols, and powder muskets. And they will take time to load, including pouring powder and ramrodding. Again unlike most FPSs, there's a story you engaged in; not just riding along a cut-scene-driven story, but one where you need to collect clues and things and fill in your knowledge of what's been going on in the various areas.
The use of sound to help you locate PoI in the game is highly novel and clever, and the sounds are eerie & suitable for the setting. Pays to be listening carefully as you explore. Surround sound headphones were highly valuable. There are visual indicators to augment the sound if you need a little assist. The gameplay & environmental sounds are excellent as well.
For collectors, there lots of stuff to find--much of it quite helpful, especially if you're not the greatest twitch player--and it will pay to revisit old areas of the map.
The length is appropriate, but do note that you're looking at perhaps 12-18 hours; I'm not OCD on the achievements, but I sneak around somewhat (not to assassinate, just not to get injured in battles) so I took 17 hours. This length is very suitable for the investigations and degree of variety in the game.
There is just one save, which you can trigger yourself or let the game auto-save at key times and on a schedule. Normally I hate the single-save option, especially in games with ~RPG/story choices; I feel I get less value with no insta-replayability (no, I never want to slog through a game in order to make a different choice 11 hours in). However, in Betrayer it works out just fine and I didn't get that annoyed great-this-checkpoint-again feeling at any time.
All-in-all a quality game that was quite a bit of fun, had a unique settings, had novel use of sound elements, was interesting to complete, was suitably challenging, was engaging, and which didn't overstay its welcome. Refreshing change from the big console-catering publishers!

UPDATE: I upgraded my machine and installed Win7 x64 and was able to complete the game.
This is an interesting game- what I've been able to play of it, anyway. If you have a 32-bit OS, this game crashes like crazy. Wait until you are on a 64-bit OS.
The plot is simple- you wash up on shore in the New World (early colonization of America- like Jamestown). The land is drained of most color. A young woman in a red hood soon appears, telling you she doesn't remember much other than her twin sister is missing. You will have to explore during the day and the night to figure out what happened, and each has its own set of dangers.
The atmosphere schtick with everything black, white, and red works for me. It's hard to explain why I like it; best I can do is to say that it is easier to take in the setting when you know things in red are important and the rest (for the most part) is scenery. The graphics are solid- nothing amazing, but nothing bad beyond some of the typesetting, which is a bit sloppy and hurts immersion a bit. If you really hate the lack of color, you can opt to change it to a more "normal" color setting, but you'll lose some of the game's charm in the process.
Sound is well done. There is a type of enemy in the third area that, if you listen carefully, communicates via animal calls. One kind means they are near, another one is heard when I step into the open, and a third is the signal to attack. I have learned to fear bird calls, because they mean I might get jumped by multiple fast enemies shooting arrows aplenty at me. You can sneak up on foes more easily if the wind is blowing through the branches, too (though I have not been able to pull it off). There are a few enemies that are basically a skull and skeletal hands with dark vapors for a body- I mention this because killing them is punctuated by a rather funny "PING!" sound. On one hand, it doesn't fit the creepiness of night exploration, but on the other, when you nail that elusive Thief, it's very satisfying to "ring its bell", so to speak.
Gameplay is a sort of cross between an exploration/find and click adventure game and a first-person shooter. Combat is short and deadly; at first you can only take a couple of hits at one time (you do have a means of healing, but it is limited to undoing one hit per use, give or take). The bow, musket, and pistol feel like you'd expect such primitive firearms to feel (though if you're used to Skyrim's bow like I am, there will be a small adjustment period). Enemies often travel in packs, so proper attack plans and dodging are a must. Gung-ho rushing in will get you killed. The enemy will press the attack if you seem vulnerable, but you have a tomahawk to throw if they get too close. The melee attack seems best used for stealth attacks or as a last-ditch desperation move. Since my initial review, a new enemy, giant spiders, were added- while they are a nice addition from a pure gameplay standpoint (hard to hit and fairly fast), they are a bit incongruous to the setting.
During the game, you have to search for clues as to what happened, which will lead in turn to finding restless spirits to interrogate and/or lay to rest. You will find items early in the game that will make it easier to spot clues via visual or audial cues. Lots of people who suffered horrible deaths, and a fair number that probably deserved worse.
This game won't be for everyone. If you want another traditional FPS, Betrayal won't do it for you. However, if a blend of light clue-hunting and investigation, short but brutal bouts of FPS combat, and a setting/theme that keeps the player on edge much of the time sounds like it's worthwhile, give it a shot (and don't forget to dodge while you reload that musket).

I have no problem giving a thumbs up on this title.  A lot of people say it has a "Firefly" feel and they are right.  The soundtrack, universe and choices you make are what gives it that feel.  Will you stop for that distress call?  Or is that cargo too important for you to be a big damn hero.
The games story has been decent so far.  Combat feels like "Star Trek Online" where space is....flat.  Naval style broadside battles make you manage your sheilds as you try to stay on an enemies weak side.  Mercenaries are waiting to be hired at every space station for a price.  They'll fly with you until you dismiss them or faithfully until they die.  You can outfit your ship with a fair amount of upgrades or buy bigger ships.  Each ship has its own benefits depending on what you want to do.  Do you want to smuggle and run trade routes to make money between missions?  You'll want cargo space and speed?  You want to hunt down bounties?  Better go with weapon hardpoints and hull strength.  It's pretty open.  The game has an economy that is ever changing so goods might be cheap here but are selling higher on the otherside of the system giving you a chance to make a buck.
I've read people giving a thumbs down because it takes too long to travel from A to B on occasion.  All I can say to that is "Flying through hyper-space ain't like dusting crops, boy..."
My only complaint is that the pirate dialog is pretty skimpy.  You hear the same "well, well.  You most be lost..." quote too many times.
If you're a sci-fi junkie and want a space game that's not overly complex but still has substance then pick this up.  $20 you can't go wrong.  You'll get your $ worth.  You can be a leaf on the wind too!  Just watch how you fly...

I'm not sure why the reviews are so mixed.
Are there bugs?  Yes
Is the transition to microtransactions annoying?  Yes
Is the matchmaking sketchy at times?  Yes
But the AI players are better than ever, you have access to a breadth of cards, and can finally make your own decks.  I hate the "up or down" system.  On a scale of 0.0 to 10.0, this is about a 7.5.  If they could fix the bugs and make matchmaking not so sucky, we'd go to about 8.9.  If you could eliminate (or up) the number of decks you can store from 30 to at least 50. that would bump us up to around 9.4.
Read other reviews and draw your own conclusions.  If you feel strongly about other elements (like microtransactions) then stay away.  On microtransaction -- if you play the game a lot, you get a goodly number of "free" coins to offset, in my opinion.
The mechanics and the ability to play a decent AI are important to me (I can't always play with a human because I get interrupted).  Those work pretty well.  If you understand how complex M:TG is, this is no small accomplishment.

Blacked out. Time's passed, but I can't tell how long.

Also I have to say that to me Final Fantasy was always about the revival. Trying something new, not be the same. A lot of people hated VIII because it was not VII, it was different (but VII was also something entirely different and groundbreaking compared to VI). And you can say the same about IX or even X (which preceded XIII in terms of linearity, and X-2 and X-2 The Last Mission was once again totally different than the main game). XI was also something new and the list can go on with XIII and XV. To me this is Final Fantasy. Always trying to be different and trying something new.
Just makes me wonder how people who say they are "long time fans" can't accept that a mainline title is different when the whole franchise is basically about that.

After a weekend pushing through CivBE to win a Purity victory, I wavered between being totally engrossed - I did spend a free Steam weekend on it, after all - and wishing for more. The new affinity systems are fun, Firaxis did put some measure of backstory in, and the enemy leaders encouraged me to destroy them by being jerks.
I do like the new orbital layer - it's pretty clever, and using orbital lasers to bombard your enemies is fun. Also a good way of sending in 'space cavalry' to a corner of your empire when you don't have ground forces handy to take out local aliens.
The aliens are a fun threat. Milking them for science points (by killing them) is very satisfying. Also fun to see the competing civs take the opposite affinity (say, Harmony) and send in giant evolved aliens. Nothing better than then bombarding those as well with your super-powered Purity units. Note: unless you mod the game, there's an experience cap on killing aliens? Lame! As much as I'm glad they highlight mods on the official Civ site, it's pretty sad that some of the features listed there aren't included by default.
Things that mess up the experience:
- (common to all recent Civ games): as noted, the AI leaders are jerks. I liberate two of your cities, and you still won't sign open borders with me? Come on, I might as well not help you at all. They added a "favour" mechanic to make their begging for favours act like something useful, but I don't think it works that well. Or maybe I was too stingy with favours:  I sure didn't see a way to call them in though!
- the health mechanic is annoying: better than Civ 3's super-corruption, negative health immediately hits you, positive health only gradually benefits you.
- the 'unhealth' warnings for annexing a city (vs creating a puppet) are buggy. Annexing will say there's a '"0" point negative impact. This is not actually true.
- call your friends and family in when you expect to get victory. Do warn them it'll be disappointing because it is. A little screen with a voiceover. Meh.
- There is a "replay" of sorts, but it's not a classic Civ "repaint the map with your colonies" replay. Just a series of bar graphs. Way to phone that one in.
- You have to manually click to bring in Earthling settlers EVERY SINGLE TIME. Bad UI choice there - you have to play settler whack-a-mole to finish the game. Annoying setup.
- it's January 2015, the game's been out for months, and the advisors are still broken. I don't want to be told every few turns that I can build a trade route. Don't see any way to shut that off aside from completing disabling advisors, which I did.
Aside from that litanty of issues like that, the game is stable and didn't crash on a moderately powerful system. I'm not going to recommend it as a full priced purchase because there's clearly a need for more polish to justify it. A severe sale, on the other hand, makes sense - plan accordingly. I'd seriously spend more time playing Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri despite having killed it with hundreds of hours of play, if they released an updated version of it instead.

It is a niche game in the aspect that you need to love in order to get hooked;

2) Extensive Carrear options (Trade/Pirate/Hunter)
3) Telling Aliens where to put their hat (hint - not in a kind place)
Having sunk a lot of hours into the game, I have found myself hooked. It has a good wave between getting easy to frustrating and back to easy again, it doesn't fall off either cliff completely and I find the grind to be rather well balanced, which is an absolute must in this genra of game. A good perk to it is that the AI isn't derped or broken like I have seen in simular games (where a ship plants itself into a wall and doesn't get the IQ to turn around).
My only big knock against it is that the camera angles are at times borked out pretty badly, and requires its own learning curve to figure out and compinsate for. I would like if the broadside gunner views were pulled back by double to give a better line of sight, or give an option to have a gunners-seat POV.
For its price point, it is a must for any Space-sim action game junkie!

Pros:
-Civ gameplay
-Futuristic units and buildings
-Aliens and miasma add a new element of strategy
-Other factions not overly aggressive
-Choice option quests make you feel in control of your factions future
-Streamlined military units that automatically upgrade with enough affinity
-Can launch satelites to enhance your land or units
-Can be entertaining
Cons:
-UI is horrible. It looks cheap, nonintuitive, clunky, and actually hides info you will really want
-Diplomacy might as well not exist. Do not expect to use it ever except when other factions want your resources
-Military strength depends solely on affinity (a faction with more affinity WILL crush you)
-Affinity is largely gained by spending enourmous amounts of time researching things you don't want/need
-Aliens and miasma are nothing more than annoyances
-Killing aliens to make room for your people makes the other factions hate you
-Clearing miasma is very time consuming
-More powerful military units are locked after research until you have enough affinity
-No story beyond "flee earth to settle new world"
-Too often your entire turn will consist of pressing "Next turn"
-Tech web feels thrown together by a blind child with no prior Civ experience
-Does not feel like a complete game
-Perfect example of a game released too early, incomplete, at full price, with DLC needed to complete it
Verdict? Don't buy incomplete games from lazy dev crews looking to cash in on a franchise name.

I listen to his dialog for clues, and slowly, a deep tale of misguided masculinity and once good intentions gone astray begins to emerge, as the protagonist struggles with a world gone mad. The gameplay is solid, as you run around, guiding his wounded soul on a journey of healing and catharsis.  Sometimes the terrain is difficult to navigate, symbolic of today's confusing world. Its a steal for a mere $20. In short, its an amazing action game filled with gun play, explosions, and fully destructible environments, but on another level, it is a deep emotional tale of old fashioned masculinity searching for a place and self expression in a modern world of over indulgence and leisure.

After completing the piece of art that is the original BioShock, my expectations of the sequel was high - but not too high, since I doubted it would be better than the original. What I got, I didn't like. The story and athmosphere that the original game had, BioShock 2 completely lacked. I understand that it's hard to make a sequel to that kind of game, but playing as a Big Daddy wasn't as fun.
And let's not forget to mention the controls - they were awful! Almost no button corresponds to the original game's, and I was so used to where the buttons were, I constantly had to go to the options menu to try and make the buttons correspond to the same commands as the first game. I also found controlling the protagonist difficult. Something was so icky about the aiming of the gun, and I managed to miss my shots all the time, wasting ammo. And let's not forget the drill! The drill that ran out of fuel after using it 4 times! I ran out of ammo and fuel all the time, the hacking was never working. The controls never responded in time, and I preferred the old hacking system.
The splicers were far from intimidating, and instead of thinking "Oh♥♥♥♥♥♥ here comes those damn splicers," I thought instead "*Sigh*, not this again... -.-" Everything I loved about the original BioShock was gone. And why the Big Daddy? Why couldn't we play as, say, Tenenbaum instead? And after spending a long time struggling my way through a floor, my game crashed and I had to do it all over again. I came to the same spot - the game crashed again. I ended up quitting. Granted, that was probably my PC causing the problems, I couldn't bring myself to restart all the time.
But my main problem with BioShock 2 is that I could never get myself to play the game. BioShock 1 made me WANT to play the game, but the sequelt I felt I had to force myself through to eventually get to BioShock Infinite, and I didn't enjoy it at all.
BioShock 2 gets a 3/10.

C:\Users\[YOUR USER NAME]\AppData\Roaming\Bioshock2Steam\

I started playing this game not knowing what I was getting myself into. I just saw the video on the Steam store page and figured it was worth a try. I'm really happy that I decided to get it. All in all it is a rather solid game. What got me interested were two things. I thought it looked amazing and I liked the idea of using the wind.
I wasn't disappointed with how the game looked (especially when I maxed out the settings). It was so immersive to just wander around the different settings and marvel at how pretty it all was. The windwas more enjoyable on the asthetics side of things. As far as using it for stealth it was really only handy when I was going for the backstabber trophy. Beyond that I just did everything I could to keep my arrows on the mark. The plot was interesting too. I like that I needed to piece everything together. This game doesn't do any hand holding, and that was very appreciated on my end. It helped me feel more like I was exploring a new world, rather than feeling like I was being shown a new world. I will say though, that if you aren't the type to dig into every single nook and cranny and pick up everything in this game, EVERYTHING, then the plot could end up feeling more shallow.
There is a draw back to the game though. The combat is pretty bad. The enemies are dumb as bricks, and that might be offensive to the bricks. Once you figure out where they usually are on each map, and what the different sounds mean, the game becomes much easier. For most of the game this aspect didn't really detract from my experience too much (well except when I looked a conquistador in the face, they just look weird). It really didn't become a chore until I started going for the combat achievements. Then this game became a slog. All because the enemies aren't interesting at all. If they could figure out a way to fix that this game would be amazing.
If you're like me and you love games that let you explore this is a very good one. If you want a game that you can crank up to max settings and just be in awe of how pretty it all is (I recommend playing in color to get the full enjoyment) then this is the game for you. If you're looking for something that hands the plot to you in a direct manner, or if you're looking for solid combat, this is definitely not the game for you.

The gameplay, however, is amazing! Dual wielding, more passive upgrades, and being able to customize your playstyle more than ever before makes this game soooo much fun! Won't be hard, but finding something that does it great and looks great too (equal or better) if you are into "oh I want to get into the space sim genre and this game might be good for me", DO NOT BUY THIS.
It is broken from the first to the last feature. The AI is completely dead, which is unforgivible and utterly destroys the whole pure sandbox economy world. Ships are running into each other, local forces are made to be weird (anyone shooting at you is fine, if you shoot back 6 cops are shooting you to death without question). So it was the "superhero never dies" kind of ship, until it was nerfed back to "just one from others" level. Good luck doing story stuff that was designed for the original and puts you up against 6-10 other hunter ships. Attacking other people you were supposed to help, so they can just stand there and watch you die while nobody shoots at them the moment you show up.
The controls are terrible. They DESPERATELY wanted to make it work with a controller. Imagine using an Excel table with controller. 5-6 circle menus and submenus in a row to find ANYTHING. Illogical, uncomfortable, weirdly working features accessible from even worse menus. And on top of all this, it is the most poorly optimalized game of the recent years more broken than AC: Unity was at relase. No joke.
Whatever you want from this genre, whatever you look for in space sim games, get Elite: Dangerous instead. Or anything else but this. It took the devs several YEARS of patching to make X3 titles good. May be worked back then, but the genre   is starting to live it's second golden age and there are PLENTY of other titles to choose from. No matter what is your goal with them, I can guarantee NOTHING of them can be fulfilled with X: Rebirth. It takes a few hours of playing to understand why and how disfunctional and hopelessly broken it is, so belive me (and countless negative reviews) when I say you better throw that money out of the window than spending on this.

If you're looking for a challenging and deep action brawler to play and master, look no further. Battlerite brings all the intensity and fast-paced action of MOBA teamfights when they're best, and cuts out the (to some people) tedious MOBA aspects of farming gold, rotating around the map and shopping for items between fights.
It is smooth, balanced and every single ability has to be aimed manually which makes it so rewarding to play, as you slowly but surely learn more and more about the various champions, how they work together and how they're countered as well. You may think to yourself that there are few heroes to choose from if compared to games such as DOTA or LoL, but you must understand that the champions of Battlerite have 8 abilities (and an ultimate) and a surprisingly complex Battlerite system (hence the name) which lets you customize their playstyle to your liking. This system recently got overhauled and improved even, which just goes to show how committed Stunlock Studios are to making changes in order to make the game as good as it could ever be.
It's quality over quantity in the case of Battlerite, and i really hope you'll check it out and try overcoming the initial struggle of getting used to the combat and fast-paced nature of the game. You may feel underpowered, that the other team has "broken" champions which cannot seem to be beaten. But you'll find that eveyone has a weak spot, most actions have an appropriate reaction to counter it, and once you learn how to use these mechanics in your favor it's the best god damn multiplayer brawler you could hope for. It's so polished and well designed that the newly released free-to-play edition simply DEMANDS you give it a try if you're feeling competitive and regular MOBA's fail to get your blood pumping anymore!
A solid 9/10 from me, would give it 10 but Stunlock has proven this game still has so much potential and they're working hard to make it better always, so perfection still lies in the future!
Hope to see you in the arena for glorious Battle!

The price tag seems a bit steep for such an old game and I'm pretty sure I came across a (non-pirated) free DOS version somewhere on the internet. It is however patched more regularly than most 2000's games so from that point of view the price could be justified. I certainly didn't regret my purchase!

Betrayer is a bit weird, I think it's a finished product and there's no rough edges left, but it still feels like it's incomplete.
The game works in all respects and has no problems, I've got 100% completion (apart from 2-3 grindy achievements) and I didn't encounter a single bug. The UI is minimalist and the gameplay is interesting but eventually starts to become repetitive towards the end. It pulls off a decent combination of RPG and FPS, but I feel certain aspects could have been made better and others weren't really relevant (upgrading your weapons for example feels tacked on and doesn't actually contribute to gameplay, you just get more powerful weapons that do exactly the same thing as the game progresses)
The story is interesting and makes you think, the setting is unique and one I've seen in virtually no other video games and the mood and tone is excellent, I had cold shivers for a lot of the game and it brought me back to the creepy feelings I experienced in F.E.A.R.
The sound is beautiful in the game and the graphics are amazing for an indie title, but I highly recommend tweaking the contrast and color settings to bring a little bit of color back into the world, because the monotone black and white detracts from the lovely visuals. The only caveat is there is no voice acting whatsoever, and the game is heavy with dialogue. I myself didn't mind this but it is a shame to see a complete lack of voice acting.
The dialogue and storyline are solidly written and some of the conversations were heartbreaking while others were downright hilarious, so the writers have done an excellent job, I won't spoil the ending or the plot but I do feel the main plot was a little underdeveloped and not explained as well as it could have been, however the overall storyline and setting are leagues better than most story based games I've played, so if you want a story with as much depth as a decent novel or film, give this a shot.
Betrayer isn't amazing, but it shows lots of potential and is probably one of the better indie games to be released recently.

Dead rising 2 is a  good zombie slaugthering time, even with it's annoyences and issues.
The game takes place a few years after the first one and follows chuck greene, a motorcycle rider/father, who is framed for the zombie outbreak on fortune city. Story is fairly decent, but it's not the game's strongest aspect. There is multiple endings, but ending A and S are the only ones worth getting.
Describing the type of game dead rising is, is rather tricky since it's in a league of it's, however what I can call it is that it's a beat em up hack n slash third person shooting open world rpg, or you can just call it an action rpg.
Combat is slow and kind of annoying, but somehow in the end it's so fun slicing and bashing zombies. You can use anything as a weapon from knifes,guns (which are quite fun to use), brooms, to wheelchairs even. However each item breaks, which makes the game kind of refreshing.
One of the elements of the game that makes it so much fun is the combo cards, which allow you to take 2 items you find. You need to go to a maintenance room for it.
There is an rpg element in the sense that you will level up with PP. How do you get PP? Kill Kill and Kill, and also completing side missions which involves Rescuing survivors(which is kind of annoying, but tolerable if you find the leadership magazine) and fighting psychopaths(Optional boss battles that are generally enjoyable to fight).
the game also has a Timer which will turn a lot of people off....on the first playthrough, on the 2nd since you are at a higher level it's no big deal.
Dead rising 2 may not be technically impressive, but the game is never afraid to show something visually appealing and the animations are fairly good.
Sound is good, the music is ranges from lounge music, rock, to atmospheric music which fits well with the goofy nature of the game.
Dead rising 2 may not appeal to everyone, but what it does it's does it quite well.

Year is 1600. Emty hostile island. Spirits. Weapons. Ghosts. Empty forest, and a strange switch into darkness (same forest except creepy as hell) whenever you chose. Betrayer has more or less this atmosphere.
The game reminded me of STALKER in a way. You are put on a hostile environment with lots of nature, beautiful natural sounds mixed with some dark ambient and horror audio. No quest markers and pointers, you have to figure out what to do yourself.
For max atomsphere and immersion I advise to turn off the crosshair. It's pretty easy to learn how to shoot without the aiming help. Betrayer has a mix of exploration and first person shooting (which works fine). It has a classical horror story, which you will read in the game (no spoken stuff).
Game is normal in difficulty if you just follow the story. If you set out to find all secrets and hidden stash, it's difficult. Map navigation is realistic, although it would be awesome if the game allowed to set notes on it. To illustrate the difficulty of finding treasures: it is still hard even if you have a copy of a map in a Steam guide that shows where the specific hidden objects are.
It's definetly a different game, and the switch between light and dark world is very interesting (don't misunderstand, both environments are pretty hostile). One thing to note: Betrayer can get repetative after some time, I wish there were more unique environments and places put here, since 60-70% of the time you will be exploring. Still, I gladly suggest it to anyone looking for dark thriller kind of game, with appropriate atmosphere.

The game lacks however in content. I found myself spending most time in the opening starting area, which is like a huge valley of desert to rock. I completed the game in 4 hours, though I could of done it in 1 or maybe 2. That's how short the game is.
All in all I will give this game a 7/10.

Be sure to check online videos to see what this game has to offer, but if you like even a little bit, what you see, than you should definitely get this game!
It is a top-down shooter with clever mechanics and CONSTANT PROGRESSION! For me, it is the most important quality. Whatever you do, even if you manage to survive only a few levels, you will have the chance to upgrade your skills.
The upgrades to your character on every run also add spice to the story.
The gameplay is not reflex-based, more tactical, it is about knowing your enemies and types of weapons and secondary weapons. The bosses are also become less and less difficulty as your character improves, but they still stay challenging.
It is also good either for short bursts or for longer sessions.
The levels are procedurally generated, and that keeps the replayability basically endless. They are not too small (like in Forced: Showdown), not too large either, so there is enough place for tactical movement.
In overall: it is a great game for casual gamers, who would like to see their efforts not in vain (I look at you: roguelikes with lose-everything permadeath), also has a nice soundtrack and atmosphere.

This game is a blast!  It feels like Smash TV in something like a Shadowrun futuristic dystopia, with cybernetic implants, 'hackers' and 'techies'.  The variety of weapons is nice, and I can trade off accuracy for damage depending on my mood.
I needed a shoot 'em up like Smash TV, and this is a responsive dual-stick shooter with destoyable walls, which adds a dimension to the tactics.  The great game element that I've not seen in this style of game before is that whenever you die, you get money to buy upgrades, so you do not get stuck without enough power-ups to beat the next boss.  Similar to RPG's, you can just grind and power-up, then try again!
You discover new weapons and upgrades as you delve higher into the tower, and similar to some of my favorite rogue-likes, you then have the option to buy your initial load-out for your next attempt through the levels.  There are also checkpoints so you can skip the easy levels once they no longer provide you with enough benefit for the time you would spend there.
This is very well thought out and solid game for the price, and if you are interested based on the above, then I strongly recommend this game!

After playing the game for about 11 hours I grew tired of a Covert Ops bug (where you cannot redeploy your agents, and this is a known bug since October and hasn't been fixed up to now.) -Auto redeploy trade route check mark.
-Queues for city builds (set up your own preferred queues and let the city follow one of your setups) or even a mayor who can auto build the things for you.
-An option do auto replace a satellite when the old one comes down or even some option to relift it higher in orbit at a cost.
-An option for your workers to upgrade all your roads. (Instead of having to do that manually.)
I'm also missing some chances they had to make it more fun, perhaps some real terraforming where you can change the actual terrain, lower it, raise it and so on.
Basically the game is a lot of fun, but it could be so much better, but with all the unneeded micromanagement there is now it's simply not my type of game. I will probably pick it up again though after a few patches and perhaps some dlcs if those bring the game to a more complete package like civilization.

I am a big fan of the Saints Row franchise and have been a fan since Saints Row: The Third. Saints Row: The Third and Saints Row IV. The two aforementioned games had great humor and lots of action. Gat Out of Hell is an expansion of the franchise that is much shorter in content, but has some entertainment value.
Those who played Saints Row IV should feel quite familiar with Saints Row: Gat Out of Hell. The open world design and gameplay mechanics are very similar in Saints Row IV and Gat Out of Hell. All the super jumps and gliding in Saints Row IV turns into flying with wings. You can buy wing flaps as a way of upgrading your flying abilities. Given enough practice, you can gain exciting speeds and it feels quite different than gliding in Saints Row IV. Flying also makes collecting soul clusters exhilarating. The soul clusters are similar to those clusters in Saints Row IV and are necessary for upgrading your arcane powers which are similar to Saints Row IV’s super powers.
The story takes place in the portal of New Hades, a city that is hell, of course. There are activities in the game, but many are like those activities found in Saints Row IV. Some weapons are like those in Saints Row IV, but there are some nice, new additions, including the seven weapons that represent the seven deadly sins. One of the deadly sins weapons is an armchair containing a Gatling gun and missiles. The weapons upgrade system should be familiar to those who have experienced previous games of the Saints Row franchise.
The story is quite short and it is about Johnny Gat going after Satan and there is Jezebel, Satan’s daughter.  The Boss, the President of the United States, is kidnapped by Satan and forced to marry Jezebel. There are very few main quests, so it is possible to go through the main story of the game in five hours. The other returning character is Kinzie Kensington, an alternative playable character. If you want to play Kinzie, you can simply go to the Ultor hotel and switch characters. The plan set up by Johnny and Kinzie is to rescue the Boss from Satan. The story presents itself in cutscenes in the form of a book and I think it is done nicely. There are some guys assigning quests to you such as Blackbeard, Dane, and Shakespeare. Once you finish those quests you can simply reach the end of the story to battle Satan.
If you want to enjoy more time in the game you can play all the activities and diversions. You can also complete challenges which would require you to start trouble on the streets of hell by attacking either demons or husks (citizens of hell). Activities such as Torment Fraud are derived from the Insurance Fraud activities. Mayhem makes its return requiring you to cause as much destruction as possible. Survival also makes a return as a diversion. The newest activities are Hellblazer and Salvation. Hellblazer tests your ability to fly through checkpoints and having upgraded flaps for your wings leads to fun flying. Salvation requires to save as many dying souls as possible before they reach the bottom (hell) or the top (heaven). A type of diversion called Pledge Rush requires you to use a paddle to strike demons into the various circles, similar to Genki’s Mind Over Murder activities. I thought that the Hellblazer and Salvation activities are the most entertaining of all activities and diversions.
Simply starting trouble on the streets of New Hades to complete 100 challenges can be fun at the beginning, but it can get a little repetitive over time. You can find armored vehicles to conquer after blasting it enough times to bring the demons out of these vehicles. You can then drive them to a drop off point for a big payday in cash known as Wages, the currency of the game.
Gat Out of Hell is a game that is short on story and substance, but it is fun if you play activities and diversions, complete challenges, and participate in other forms of entertainment. It is probably short because it is an expansion, not a sequel. For a price of $14.99 it is not a bad buy. Just don’t expect to see the greatness of the gameplay and sense of humor Saints Row fans experienced in Saints Row: The Third or Saints Row IV.
My Score: 7/10

“What exactly is HATRED?” some might be asking.
Well, after some hands-on time with the game, I can tell you exactly what HATRED is and what it isn’t.
HATRED is a Twin-Stick Shooter with an angsty angle, placing the player in the role of a pale, black-haired, trench coat-donning lunatic with an axe to grind with humanity en masse.  His objective?  Kill everyone.  Literally.  Everyone.  Including himself, once the job’s done…and armed with a Knife, Shotgun, Assault Rifle, Pistol, Frag Grenades, Flashbangs, and Molotov Cocktails, it’s not too hard to start the blood a-flowin’.
Of course, there is no attack without riposte, you will be sought after by law enforcement of varying degrees, and even the civilians whom you are out to kill might arm up to attempt taking you out.  It’s very easy to become overwhelmed, and suddenly find yourself in a nasty pinch.
“How does one restore health in this mad, mad world?” you might ask…well, there’s only one way:  Executions.  When you’ve injured someone to the point of “Agony”, you’ll be able to perform a quick execution on them, be it smashing their skull with your boot, feeding them a 9mm Sandwich, perforating their chests with a 12-gauge, or going stab-happy on their kidneys (Or throats…or skulls…or gut…), and fully regenerate your much-needed health.
Ammo can be found in random places, obtained by killing the citizens who take up arms, or by killing law enforcement that comes after you.
And when all else fails, you can always put the boots to ‘em.  Medium Style.
HATRED is, in essence, a spiritual successor to the original POSTAL.
Man with a genocidal mission?  Check.
Lots of Run-And-Gun style gameplay?  Check.
Lots of people running around screaming?  Biiig Check.
¾-View perspective?  Check.
While the “story” of HATRED makes it look like “Captain Edgy’s Edgecapades Across The Edgiverse”, It’s really just a POSTAL clone with shinier graphics, and a few layers of paint.
Now…what isn’t HATRED?
Well, it’s not a sexist, racist massacre simulator, as the 3rd-Wavers and SJWs wanted everyone to think.  The game’s Protag…No.  He can’t be called that, let’s face it.  You’re the Bad Guy.  The Antagonist’s goal is to kill EVERYONE.  BAR-♥♥♥♥ING-NONE.  Everyone gets a shot at killing him, and everyone gets shot at by him.  ‘Nuff said.
PROS:
-The Twin-Stick mechanic is very smooth, but then again, that’s usually a normal standard for TS games.
-The buildings can be destroyed by gunfire/explosives/vehicles, which can lead to some interesting ways to change the flow of a struggle.  Pinned down by gunfire?  Use a grenade and blow the wall out from behind you…hoof it outta there.
-The action itself is pretty fluid, and the gameplay is moderately challenging the more you progress.  Keeps things from becoming too easy too soon.
CONS:
-The graphics, while very nice, have a bad habit of hiccuping and stuttering.  This can cause the game to bog down to very few FPS…which is pretty bad when you’re in a heavy firefight.
-I would’ve preferred if the game utilized the knife in more ways than simple executions…but alas, we cannot have it all.
-The one-liners uttered gruffly after executions and objective completions can often be…well…phoned-in, let’s just say.
What I think overall:
HATRED is a decent game, for all that it’s worth.  Granted, it’s bound to get some nasty press due to the ever-so-honest gaming media we have to deal with these days.  But, hey, this is all just my view and my say on the game.  If you’re a fan of twin-stick shooters, I’d say give it a whirl.  It’s honestly not as bad as the whiny brats of the internet make it out to be.

I've got a soft spot for cyberpunk, and more for roguelikes, and Neon Chrome does a great job of hitting the sweet spot between the two. It's an enjoyably difficult top-down shooter with some rogue-like elements and enough variety to keep coming back.
The graphics are solid, no difficulty in spotting enemies, (though to be fair, if it's moving and it isn't you, it's an enemy).  Plenty of neon-drenched plastic and chrome to fit the setting, and it all runs quite smoothly on an older laptop.
Gameplay, again, is very solid.  I haven't tried a gamepad yet, but the keyboard/mouse controls are smooth and responsive, although I did end up rebinding the reload key for easier access.  While there's permadeth, you can earn persistent upgrades (health, damage, etc) and each run gives you a choice between multiple "classes", each with different perks.  There's a decent variety of weapons with more than enough differences to make them have some impact on play.
In terms of replayability, this works well as a coffee break game or for an hour or so of blowing stuff up.  The persistent upgrades help push the "just one more run" feel, but it's shallow enough that you can jump right back in even if you haven't played for awhile.
Definitely a recommended game for good, old-fashioned mindless arcade type fun.

When originally released, this edition felt, played, and crashed like a shoddy console port, because to be honest that is what it was then.  After a bit of attention (still should have more!), this edition has become something else, and Recommendable over the original.
Therefore I will review the Remastered edition in its current form in comparison to the state it was in when first released.
:
The classic political satire FPS is back, looking much, much better than before.
Some more graphics options seem to be in there now, and work better.
Holy ♥♥♥♥ is Rapture beautiful now.
:
After the Dec patch, then going back into the game on a fresh install, there seems to be few of the original Remastered edition's problems of random save crashing, but there are some things that should be noted.
Some still report some issues with crashing around saves - this may be the engine taking a barf due to resource bottleneck somewhere.  IIRC the original engine had something of this problem regarding VRAM, so that is my suggestion for any likely culprit to start looking at if you experience these problems.
For best stability and experience, the Recommended specs are now quite spot-on and should be regarded as Minimum.
The system RAM required should be around 8GB for best smoothness and lack of crashing/save corruption.
VRAM should probably be around 2GB for the same.
Quad-Core CPU 2,5GHz or higher, though I've had it run fairly well before on the 2.2GHz QC toaster.
Still, Save Now, Save Often, Save Five Minutes Ago may apply given your experience, but there has been enough attention to make this worth a more worthwhile try.  Use multiple save slots.
This edition may still require OS update packages to overcome crashes on startup, but after that it appears to be fairly stable now.
This may seem like a lot of Negatives compared to the positive, but mostly serves as awareness for a better experience than what was offered before.
Thank you, 2K Games, for doing well on addressing the concerns of your community, and would you kindly continue giving more attention towards the technical troubles that do remain?  Treating classics right is a great thing to see from publishers/developers.
This is now the edition of BioShock I would recommend for anyone to consider as introduction to the series.

I could play this game forever. I mean, really this is the first game I've ever put so much effort into with such little time. Do what I did and just DIVE into this game reading no WIKI, not watching any gameplay videos, nothing. Complete and utter sink or swim experience, and trust me you'll sink. But it's not the kind of defeat that has you frustrated that makes you want to quit this game.
No.
It's the kind of frustration the festers when you know you made a mistake. I shouldn't have robbed those people, because my survivor is broken and now I can't go out and scavenge for food. I shouldn't have tried to take on those armed thugs because now someone has died. I should have boarded up my house sooner because I thought I could push my greed and make some animal traps and survive the night with just an axe.
That's the kind of frustration that we love. That lingering sense of victory behind the shroud of misfortune that this game keeps pulling you into.
You've read all the reviews before you, you know it's features. You know about the sense of immersion that game has, so how about replayability?
TWOM's replayability is limited ONLY by your imagination. That's right. Play the game after you have danced with your 25 raw food, your armory of 10 Assault Rifles and 8 Shotguns and make it harder for yourself. Challenge yourself: "Can I beat this game without killing a SINGLE person?" Then you have something refreshing. Can you defeat winter... with no furnace? "But that's impossible!" Shh-... It is possible, once you pick apart this game and find that it's real gem is you.
This game brings out all your colors. Your mechanical decision making-side that rushes animal traps so you can float raw food. The emotional shade that tugs on your heart when you kill Emil leaving the widow there to cry. All of that and more.

To start: I normally add a header to these reviews describing my ethos on scoring a game on the four criterion I chose. Since I've been running out of space more and more, I'll just keep it on my Backloggery page.
Gameplay: I'll just start off by saying that this game requires GFWL. If GFWL is enough to turn you away from buying this game, there ya go. If you haven't been, allow me to give my opinions on this game. Dead Rising is based around on an idea that I think every single budding game designer has had at least one point in their lives: use anything and everything in the environment to take out the enemies. This game does a pretty good job with that, although you generally end up using the same few weapons to clear out the hordes of zombies (my favorites were the Broadsword and the Defiler; easy to get/make and very effective). The combat is very dynamic, and you often find yourself going through at least two or three weapons per outing. Weapons do degrade in this game, although I would've liked more information on the condition of the weapon rather than the icon flashing red when it's about to break. There are guns as well, but I found myself sticking almost exclusively to melee, with the exception of a few bosses.
Speaking of bosses, there's a lot of bosses (aka Psychopaths) in this game. A lot. They're usually fairly fun, but there are a few bosses in there that seem like they deliberately cheat; Antoine and the Final Boss being the two that come to mind first. The reason why bosses don't always feel too terribly fair is because they get a LOT of invincibility frames; primarily when they are attacking you. For a boss like Antoine that recovers health, this gets to be quite the issue. Fortunately, there are a lot of very fun bosses in the game as well. Unfortunately, apart from zombies, there isn't any other enemies in the game until the very last hour or so, but by then it doesn't matter. The zombies themselves are, as one might expect, quite dull and very easy to mow down. Mowing down hordes of zombies does get a little dull after a while, and towards the end I found myself just rushing and dodge rolling my way through the hordes. Of course, since I stuck to just a few weapons, this may be my fault.
The gameplay runs in a semi-Majora's Mask setup where you have a limited amount of time to do various things within the game, It's never too big of a deal, and oftentimes, I found myself running out of time for missions just because I didn't care enough about them. These missions are all pretty much escort missions, which certainly doesn't help for the somewhat repetitive nature of the game. Your escortees are usually smart enough to keep themselves out of harms way, so you don't have to worry too much about them getting eaten alive. Completing missions gives you levels, or a way to phone in grinding. Really, I don't understand the purpose of levels in this game other than menial replay value. The game itself lasted me about twelve hours, but since the game is so repetitive, I don't see myself coming back to this game for quite a while. There is co-op, but once again, GFWL.
Overall, though, the game itself is pretty fun. I don't regret my time playing the game, but I do wish it had done a little more with it. It is fairly well-paced and there's always stuff to do, but again; most of what you do are either escort missions or bosses that end in escort missions. 7/10.
Story: It's pretty much Deus Ex. No, I'm not joking. However, unlike the masterpiece that is Deus Ex, this game doesn't have anywhere within a galaxy's reach of good writing as Deus Ex. The characters themselves are forgettable, although Chuck gets some Dante points for terrible one-liners after each boss. At least cutscenes involving psychopaths are fun to watch, even if they take themselves a little too seriously. It's enjoyable enough, but Pulitzer-prize material this is not. 7/10.
Graphics: This game takes a sort-of cross between cartoonish and realistic that I quite like. Unlike a lot of "mainstream" games (even though I loathe the term), I can see this game looking pretty good in ten years time; presuming the damn thing will even start in ten years time due to GFWL crippling it so healvily. Most everything is very vivid and colorful, without crossing the road to Toon Town. It's just silly enough; just like the game itself. It does run quite well, running at an average of 60degC at 1080p Max Settings on my GTX 760, with some dips beneath 60FPS here and there at certain, strange locations. You don't need too powerful of hardware to run this game at its maximum potential, but it does help. There is also some texture clipping here and there, but it's not enough to make too much of a difference in your playing experience. 4/5.
Audio: Definitely the most "port-y" category. Basically, the audio has quite the tendency to cut out whenever there's lots of zombies around. It's something that I've been trying to figure out for a while, and I do have an idea; perhaps the game is just running out of sound channels? I really can't say. This can get quite distracting after a while. There is apparently a fix for this, but it didn't work too well for me; it actually made things worse. As for the music, a lot of it is from other artist (yes, intentional) such as Celldweller and Celldweller. I do however quite like Celldweller, so it's not too big of a deal. The actual original music is forgettable. The voice acting is also forgettable. Truthfully, the only thing keeping me from giving this a one (due to the technical issues that haven't been fixed to this day) is the Celldweller music. It really shouldn't make me do this, but it does. 2/5.
Overall scores are: 7/7/4/2; cumulative score of 6.7/10. Another weird issue on the technical front is that I couldn't get my 360 controller to work with the game. Period. It's worked for every other game that has 360 controller support, and even other GFWL games, but it just didn't work for this one. I don' get it.

First things to know:
-I started playing at version 3.20
-I know it had a bad launch
-It is not X4
That being said, it is a great game!
Like I said, I have not experienced the game-breaking bugs that most player experienced at launch.
Egosoft really worked hard to make this game better, and are still releasing patches to fix/add/polish content.
I remember playing X3: Reunion years ago. It has tons of problems, but they fixed them in later patches. Then Terran Conflict came out: very similar to Reunion but way better. So I knew that a bad launch was not going to be a problem in the long run.
I understand the frustration of early buyers and fans, but now it is a great game.
You still see on forums the usual "is the game still broken?" posts. To those people I say: it is perfectly playable.
I had one crash to desktop, but it was my fault (alt-tabing during screen-resolution changes on a dual-monitor setup, the game did not like it).
I run the game at maxed out graphs, on a 1920x1080 resolution: no slow-downs in fps.
So here are my pros and cons:
Pros:
+Beautiful game
+Nice micromanaging
+Lots of options to choose from
+Great gameplay (altho different from other games in the series, again: not X4)
+Constant improvements from the dev team (thanks!)
+Good music & sound effects
Cons:
-Repetitive dialogs
-Some few-years-ago character models
-The interface needs a little getting used to
So for all space-sim fans out there: I recommend the game. If you read reviews of the game, be sure to note that old ones might be from older states of the game, which was indeed bad, so for those who never played the game, at version 3.20 (3.50 soon!): it is a good time to start. And for those who bought the game when it was bad: now is time to give it another try!
