Betrayer is the debut effort of Blackpowder Games, a company of which I've learned consist of former members of Monolith Productions, in other words, guys who worked on FEAR. Naturally, since FEAR is one of my all-time favorite FPS games, I decided to give this game a try while it was in Early Access stages. Unfortunately, it did not stay in Early Access for a large amount of time, and because of apparent time constraints, Blackpowder did not manage to reach further potentials this game could have had.
Pros:
+ Very nice effects. The game's biggest feature in terms of visual splendor is wind. Oftentimes when you are treaded the island, you'll notice that gusts of wind pass by and affect all the foliage around you. At once, this left me in awe. I could've sworn I've seen things like this in other games, but in this one it was done so well. I was surprised at my own bated breath.
+ Fun combat. It's pretty simplistic and straightforward, but combat was a surprising amount of fun regardless. You'll acquire an assortment of olden time weaponry that function well enough, ranging from pistols to muskets to longbows. I found all of them to be quite useful and satisfying. Fighting the spainards was especially fun for some reason. I liked hearing my arrows sometimes bouncing off of them with a humorous metallic clunk.
+ Deep and shaking mysteries! This island has been inhabited by a lot of pretty screwed up people! Throughout the game, you will be solving a plethora of mysteries around different settlements, encountering wraiths and lost souls and helping them figure out who they were and what role they played in the sick situations that had taken place in the past. This is the thing that really kept me going. I've seen a few misspellings here and there, but the writing for the most part is exquisite. It just really makes me wish the game had voiceovers.
Cons:
- Betrayer is quite repetitive. Seriously, as neat as the mysteries are, the gameplay is quite repetitive. There is no real section that stands out, and everything you see from the third level is what you've already played before. I wish there was a little more variety in gameplay, but again I feel this squandered potential was because of time constraints, plain and simple.
- Lack of real immersion and empathy with characters. This is mostly due to the lack of voiceovers. It may be because of tight budgets, but potential for immersion was really lost with the lack of a voice here and there. The dialogue and writing is for the most part excellent, and it makes me sad that Blackpowder didn't make more ambitious pursuits in this aspect.
- Ending segment. I will not spoil the game here, but the ending segment contains an optional task that might as well be mandatory since it makes the final fight easier (and it was already pretty nerve-rackingly difficult). This requires you to scour across all the maps you've been through to the end point, which means lots of annoying loading screens. I have really mixed feelings about the ending segment; on one side, it was really interesting and well-executed, but on the other, the gameplay aspect somewhat fell flat.
Closing: Even if Betrayer stumbles upon a couple pitfalls and doesn't feel as good as it could be, it is still very much a solid, spooky, first-person mystery/action that will find a way to engage you one way or another in its harrowing tales. I hope that Blackpowder will pursue greater projects in the future and continue to deliver us unique experiences not unlike what they've lovingly crafted into this mystery romp.

So I have 3 near-complete playthroughs and 24 hours of playtime behind me and I have to say, my first and lasting impression of this game is great. It is remarkably lore-friendly and goes very well together with tales and characters from the Silmarillion as well as the three books. It is definitely visible that the makers of this game knew what they were doing.
Unfortunately though, as with any game, there are a couple of relatively big downsides to the game.
For starters, the game lacks a good amount of fast-paste and varied gameplay. The core mechanics are spamming your base attacks until the yellow market pops up and you can pull off a critical strike, often killing the enemy or leaving them unconsious. Also, there is little to no possible way to effectively fight two or more enemies at once, except for using special abilities once in a while and changing targets quickly.
Also, in my opinon, the game is too claustrophobic. You fight your way through pre-made dungeons and arena's, and no matter what you do you're going to end up doing the same thing as every other player. For my personal liking a more open-world aspect should have been implemented instead of a silly, low quality map with various locations in middle earth.
To be honest, the problems I have gone over above are not at all that big of a deal. All in all the game does a great job at letting you experience just a little more of middle earth than LotR games before. It covers the stories about the ancient Angmar kingdoms quite well and I cannot deny it is fun to play. But the sole reason why I do not recommend this game is it's incredible amount of bugs and crashes. It's actually so bad, that I couldn't finish my first playthrough simple due to the fact that the game kept crashing at the same point even after I restarted it for the 12th time. It took me a total of 4 attempts to finish the entire game, praying I could reach every next checkpoint without the game crashing for some unknown reason. Despite the overwhelming amound of negative feedback regarding these bugs no hotfixes or updates have been released at all since late 2011. Also, there is no workshop for this game leaving the community helpless, as people aren't even aloud to fix the problems themselves.
All in all the concept of this game is great, that being the reason why I got it in the first place. But it is simply due to it's overdose of bugs and shortage of varying gameplay that  I could not play it for more than 24 hours. The only thing that can awaken my interest for this game again would be a total remake with modern-day graphics and game engines.

Ever wondered what has been happening in the northern regions during the Battle of Middle-Earth? Well, this game will certainly show you just what's been up. You ferry along three characters; a dwarf Champion by the name of Farin, hailing from Erebor. an elf Loremaster by the name of Andriel, hailing from Rivendell. Lastly, a man (Dunedain) Ranger by the name of Eradan.
Through this adventure, your quest involves engaging a dangerous and powerful black numenorean named Agandaur. He has been tasked by Sauron himself to conquer the northern regions for his lord. It is with your combined strength and the assistance that may come across you, to accomplish this quest.
Fun fact to everyone who doesn't know - this is the actual first real LOTR game. Because, the rest of the LOTR games were mostly based on the films, hence the many licensed titles you saw for PC and consoles. This game is not just loosely based on the films itself but it does base itself off from the books. What does it cover though? it tries to cover some of the background events in the books while being parallel to the main events of the story.
Story out of the way, I do like what it's trying to tell. It brings a little more expansion to the LOTR lore on it's own which is all well and good.
As far as the game is concerned, it plays all right but the combat system and leveling isn't something to behold. Just copy and paste type of hack and slash you'd normally expect. Gain a level, apply points to skill - blah, blah, blah, you know the whole deal. I only have a couple things to point out; it's one of those games again where you're in a bit of an animation lock and things have to be timed precisely so you don't get into a jam. I'll also add that the combat is, sluggish when you're swinging around your weapon. I picked Champion Farin for my playthrough and it really shows when you fight as him as to how slow the combat is.
I do like the scenery in this game and everything looks rather pretty for LOTR standards. Probably one of the few things going for it.
I'll recommend this title simply for the curious and core LOTR fan that wants some story that will cover some bases. But, to anyone else, when you take the LOTR name off and the influence, what you could've had is your generic RPG hack and slash game and I'd stray away from that if I were you.

***************
Review of Battle for Zendikar expansion
***************
This expansion is cool seeing as how it's Zendikar based and yet there's a lot missing. There's so much they could have done to make this worth the wait but sadly they didn't.
I don't want to sound ungrateful but the campaign for Zendikar was so short that I had it done in an hour or so max. While I greatly enjoyed the short "story," I had hoped there's be more to it. The DotP titles had much more in-depth expansions, will more content be coming out for Battle for Zendikar or was that all? A few landslide cards and Eldrazi don't do the block a whole lot of justice and yet it's still fun for a free game.
The brief campaign followed a group of heroes as they took on the dark forces of the Eldrazi (literally a metastory, failing to dive into any particulars or anything expanding on the block's awesome fluff).  I liked the storytelling and beautiful art/effects and yet I wish there was more to it.
Of course Magic Duels Origins is about the multiplayer and not the single player campaign. But the two decks unlocked at the end of the campaign aren't terribly awesome, the boosters yielded some decent results but nothing to rival my Zendikar paper magic deck (paper magic themed starter decks are probably more fun, at least as far as the Ally deck goes).
The Eldrazi-based preconstructed deck and Ally deck are decent. At least with Magic Duels you can create your own decks and many of the newer cards do work well together. Although I only unlocked a few boosters, I'm sure a varied playstyle can be supported by unlocking more. I'm actually fairly surprised that there wasn't more unlockable content, this definitely didn't seem like an "expansion" to me.
If anyone was expecting to actually use a Planeswalker during the campaign, you'll sadly be at loss. While Jace is in an Ally mission (on the opposing side), his role is minimal. I was able to remove him from the game entirely within a few moves (by reducing his loyalty to 0, of course). Are the boosters supposed to yield walkers? They didn't for me and I suspect they usually don't for others.
This game gets a decent "Positive" review from me. While the expansion falls a little behind the expectations of those on the community mailing list, the Battle for Zendikar is still enjoyable and both fun and rewarding for free. I probably would have been happier with the inclusion of Commander and Planechase but those pipe dreams are highly unlikely.

It has been a long time since I was addicted to a game like I am to this. I've played a lot of space simulator type games since I first discovered the genre in the legendary game: Freelancer - all have fallen short of my expectations. This game however is the anomaly - the one that given enough time and attention could very well rival it one day in my opinion.
The biggest problem I originally had with this game is the fact you can only move on a 2d plane - I've gotten used to it and it isn't a big deal - it is part of the charm now. The other issue that I've found is with mining - it doesn't seem to be very profitable - though I've not tried it much since the starting system, I was always getting worthless materials with a few valuables mixed in. Trading was vastly more profitable and completing mission reasonably better - this means I never mine, which I find ashame as it could be interesting if it were more profitable.
Sometimes I think the danger levels given in some missions is a tad "off" so to speak - doing a delivery of cargo mission with an "average" to "below average" rating and getting ambushed by what seems dozens of enemies - them ripping through my ship in seconds and dampening my engines so I can't escape or dictate the fight - after you've run a few of those types of mission, you expect it and are maneurvering and ready for it - isn't such a big deal then.
On the plus side - the music, it fits so perfectly, I'd like more tracks but the ones they have are really good. I like the fact I'm not forced to go down the main story line, I'm off in different systems doing different mission and buying bigger ships - that is the freedom I expect (but sometimes don't get) in open world games.
Combat is fun, the broadsides and turrets seem to be equally useful. The progression is great - though I find it a tad odd I can equip level 5 (which is what I'm up to) turrets/shields/engine etc on the smaller ships - surely they have to use more power or something? Meh doesn't really matter. All in all I'm very happy I bought this game and don't see myself stopping for awhile.

Fantastic space fairing action.
The trailers caught my attention with nice colourful space battles some time ago, but nothing prepared me for how fun this game was. I went in cautiously as it breaks one of main rules for space battling games, thou shall not restrict motion to a 2D plane, but I needn't have worried.  Combat is fast and tactical and full to the brim with laser beams and tracer fire and trailing missiles while surrounded by explosions, while you're led along either by your own need (to gain bigger ships and guns) or the story that lies within.
The story was reasonably interesting and lifted up by some surprisingly competent voice acting but woefully under developed, but with this game's price point it would be daft to expect more than what was already crammed in, I just lamented that one of the characters in game was not pushed more to the front along side the player in a MasterChief / Cortana style relationship.
Graphically the game takes its own style and runs with it, with some of the ship designs varying from interesting to inspired, though I would've liked to have seen more of the fighters and gunships. With player control being restricted to larger ships (frigates up to drednaughts) there was a missed oppurtunity for building a squadron of fighter level craft to follow you about. Perhaps that's something the developers could investigate for DLC or a sequel.
This game was a surprise in terms of quality. If you want a space game in the vein of Elite that makes with the action and less with the simulation, you will find a home here for some time. The 40 hours I've spent with this title will attest to that.

I used the opportunity to play Beyond Earth during the Free Play Weekend with a total of 12 hours gameplay. It was two sessions, each with another faction. Neither finished. The reason for this was boredom.
I have played Civ 5 (with all expensions) some time ago and had a total of 480 hours or so. I am also a diehard fan of Alpha Centauri and Alien Crossfire, which I played for several 1000 hours. And that is not exaggerated. Beyond Earth, on the other hand, bored me after so little time despite the fact that it is supposed to be something more like Alpha Centauri than a Civilization.
The main reason for this is that the game is almost a perfect copy of Civ 5 with too little changes and improvements. There are some minor changes. For instance when I build a facility in my base I have to chose between two mutually exclusive options, like a single boost to my reasearch or a permanent change of the facility's output.
Also, instead of barbarians like in Civ 5 there are now indigenous lifeforms. They are not hostile from the beginning and only when you keep attacking them, they will eventually become aggressive toward you. However, from what I have seen so far they are not as much of a threat as the mind worms of Alpha Centauri (nor have such a complex background story.)
The other factions behaved much like in Civ 5. Unfortunately, there are only 8 factions in total and they lack a bit of characterization. To me, they all seemed the same. A little stiff and dull.
The maps are very, very similar to Civ 5. One could almost say it is only new textures. (actually, some ice floes are exactly the same in Civ 5) But it is not all bad. There is now some kind of fog called miasma, which benefits the alien creatures and deals damage to your own units if you have not unlocked certain abilities. It is a nuisance compared to the fungus in Alpha Centauri, which could be really dangerous or really helpful. Other than that there are new (and some old) resources, crash sites of satellites and ruins of an unknown alien civilization. Resources can be harvested and the remains and ruins can be examined for little bonuses.
Then there are satellites which you can send to orbit and which will bring benefits in a certain area underneath them, like +1 food per square. A nice addition, though I have not used them that much.
The biggest change are the three affinities. They will actually change your faction in appearance and abilities and other factions will react to the chosen affinity as they also pick one for themself. It improves the gameplay but the change is not revolutionary. It feels more like the next logical step after ideologies in Civ 5. The game lacks social engineering like Alpha Centauri, where you had benefits but also had to keep an eye on the downsides of certain politics or values.
The game also has a quest system which is a very nice addition. It gives you missions over the course of the game and keeps things more interesting when playing for a longer period of time.
Instead of a tech tree there is now a tech web. You start with a technology in the middle and then make your way outward. It is a cool change and makes research different. Nothing major, though.
The interface is futuristic and minimalistic. Unfortunately, it also looks very monotonous. The tech web, for instance, contains tons of stuff. Technologies, abilities, facilities, improvements, etc. They distinguish in minor details like wonders in a faint yellow and facilities in a faint blue. My first impression as I looked at it: everything looks the same. This monotony is as dull as it is unhelpful.
In short, it is Civ 5 with a few minor changes. I would say it is more like an expension than an entirely new game. I would only recommend it to somebody who did not play Civ 5.
And it still lacks the complexity of Alpha Centauri, just like Civ 5. No social engineering, no drone riots, no atrocities, no planet council, no probe teams, no ecological consequences, no vulcanos, no meteorites, no quotes from Nietzsche, Machiavelli, Einstein and the many others, no videos for wonders, and many, many, many other things. It is a pity. Sid, what the heck are you doing?

Okay, the TLDR verison of this: You'll either like it or hate it and little I say matters.
Now on to the meat!
Graphics: 9/10 The artwork is beautiful, the scenery is gorgeous and the fight sequences are a thing to enjoy.  My only complaint would be that sometimes there are TOO MANY things to look at in a fight or a scene, so you lose out on seeing that ONE AWESOME MOMENT.
Music: 10/10.  Hell yes, it's great.  You can find yourself listening to it time and again if you're not careful. (Personally, I have those tracks to listen to outside the game.)
Characters: 6/10.  This is one of the weaker elements in the games.  While the art designs of the characters are excellent and fit the world they're in, personality-wise...the characters are heavily troped.  While I'm not against using a trope, they could have built up the characters a bit more, added in some side-quests to let you see more about the people.  I mean, Lightning is a female "bad♥♥♥♥♥with a sword" in the motif of Cloud from FF7, which is almost a shame.  It's not hard to LIKE the characters, but really loving them is a challenge.
Story: 3/10.  If the characters are pretty troped, this is nearly a straight up copy of most games.  "A bunch of folks are driven to otherthrow authority" runs most of the time, and it doesn't seem to have that much of a ticking clock on it.  A bit more drama would have been nice, and MORE CHARACTER DEVELOPMENT (see Character reviews).
Gameplay: 7/10.  This game differs from most other Final Fantasy entries heavily in that it presents most of the story as a "playable novel" with you wandering along the corridors or triggering scenes.  Not that unheard of from a majority of games nowadays, but it does it somewhat better than others.  Yes, the open-world concept that is a hallmark of the Final Fantasy series is missing from this game until near the end.  Yes, you spend a lot of time moving between checkpoints and scenes.  But if you think of the game as a novel, then it makes more sense.  They had a story they wanted to tell, and this is how they chose to do it.  The combat sequences aren't too bad, with the active system requiring some more thought (and fast reflexes) to how you use the characters provided to you.
Overall: 7/10.  It's a good enough game with its advantages and flaws.  If you're not a die-hard fan of the Final Fantasy series, it's worth the time to play it.  But if you're expecting the usual things from a Final Fantasy game, you will end up being disappointed.

I finished the game, and it's time to write a love letter to Travis and Erich and all the people they contracted out for ship modeling / designs / voiceovers, etc.

From the bottom of my brown coat pocket, this is a game that immediately put me in what I could only imagine before ... something resembling the Firefly universe. I think you hit the absolutely sweet spot of fun / progression / story and artwork. I sometimes lost myself flying around, you made it really feel like I was out in outer-space, with the wide variety of planets / nebulas / junk fields / ice fields / asteroid fields, what have you. The sheer number of stations and objects you would run into while out in the cold really made it feel great.
The care & thought you put into the simplified UI design was nothing short of brilliant. Simple & elegant.  I thought you had thought of everything and once when flying, my UI popped up and said "It's been a while since you saved, you should dock at a station to save your game" or something - then I knew you HAD thought of everything.
The story was engaging, and the missions were enough of a large variety. Trade missions, assasination, protection, dead drops, the game really gives you a lot of options. So many cartels to see which one's you'll join / fight. The emergent game play - the distress signals (and ability to trade with the merchants was again a wise design choice as it reinforces saving their butts ;-), the un-identified signals, getting popped out in a junk or ice field, you made what should be a very empty space interesting while travelling around.
For two guys and a small army of outside contractors / agents that you employed, this game rocks. I'm so glad that you decided to make this game.

It is unfortunate the series has never been able to shed the annoyance of having a time limit. Why must I play a game with time constraints?
It is not necessarily a problem should there be a game mode where this can be turned off. But there's none. I know once you're done with the story the game offers a sort of unlimited game mode for the purpose of just eliminating zombies, still, I would prefer the gameplay Dead Island has. You can go around and look for lootable items and complete side missions and you can also trigger the next main story mission if you want. There are no time constraints here and everything can be done at your pace.
I know there was a deliberate reason for not going ahead with this when Capcom came up with the series. It was decided with a purpose that there should be a time limit so that players cannot feel completeness - I think somewhere in a forum on the internet a guy put it right when he compared this game to the fun park experience of a child: the kid cannot really try out everything but must, instead, make a decision as to what to do and leave the rest for the future. It is all about making a priority list.
So, while the game feels rushed it seems you should set a priority to the list of things you want to do. And those you fail (including a lot of side missions where you need to save people) can later on be dealt with in your next playthrough. So, yes, I really understand what they were trying to pull off, still, I did not like it.
If you are not bothered by time constraints and you are OK with maximising everything throughout several playthroughs then Dead Rising 2 is clearly for you.
As for me: I like taking things at my leisure so this game felt too fast-paced and I was annoyed how many side missions I failed due to not being fast enough. Dead Rising 2 is not a bad game, though! And instead of "not recommending" it I wish there was a button of neutrality but since there are only 2 options available I am inclined towards the thumbs down.

There is frustration around every corner of this game.
To start off, you are not welcome to play this game at your own rate. It juxtaposes a Majora's Mask-Like mechanic around a leveling system. You level up and unlock recipies and special combat moves (most of which you can more easily unlock by inviting someone who has already beaten the game to your session) But you are also required to do the main missions in the time it gives you for each of them (Which ranges between more than enough time, to just enough time, to ridiculously slim time, to a lot of time, but you have to wait until the nick of time to actually show up, and that pisses me off the most) When you die or get a Game Over, you are given the option to either return to your last save, or the less popular option to keep all levels and experience in hand, but start the story over from the beginning. You have no other option, and your last save may as well be miles behind your grinding, and this is a VERY grindy game.
Next, the fairness aspect is divided between the game and the missions. They worked hard to make the zombie combat realistic and fair, however the "psychopath" bosses deal and take unreasonable amounts of damage, and you have no way of avoiding them when they attack. On top of that, bosses stick around, so when you discover them (which, at many times can be completely by accident) You have to either fight them with your current equipment and health, or wait them out until the mission requiring you to off them eventually expires. Whenever you enter the area, they will immediately hunt you down until you either beat them or leave. This flip-flop of realism completely ruins the flow of the game, if the story-save mechanic didn't do that already, as you switch between a game where proper headshots or hard hits kill zombies and Tekken with chainsaws.
And I neglected to mention that this game never autosaves. You can only save it on the spot after an important mission, which at most times is near somewhere that you can save. The save mechanic revolves around visiting a restroom (this game includes a lot of sex and toilet humor, but unlike games like GTA or Borderlands, they aren't nearly as endearing, as the story goes between a drama and a horror-psycho approach), which requires precise planning allthewhile battling the clock, which is a war you will ultimately lose, as it is borderline impossible to achieve every side mission in the game with the unforgiving times they permit you.
And finally, it is very buggy, you sometimes lose things you have already unlocked by going back, and there are plenty of other bugs to spare, which stick out like a sore thumb as the game is generally attractive and persistent at most times; and they aren't funny when they occur, they are just annoying, as this isn't a true sandbox game, it's a story game with a limit where every damn second counts. (Although, the levels always reset and anything you've left behind gets wiped)
I am very dissapointed in this game, especially since I bought the complete pack. Besides the graphics and animation, it's really lazy with voice acting limited to story scenes and unmanageable press-a-to-continue interactions that are all labeled "interact" in-game. It's still a fun play, though repetitive, unlocking new weapons and getting through those tight zombie fending scenes and kicking♥♥♥♥♥with an overpowered combo weapon is sure a hoot; but the mechanics that top it off totally limiting what would be a fun experience into an uninteresting story with a generic traitor plot that you are forced to put before all else to avoid having to reset in said story.
Unless you don't mind the restrictions to freedom and want to play an otherwise okay zombie game, I would NOT reccomend purchasing this game.

Horrible game. It sucks too because I really wanted to like this game but it just wouldn't let me. Betrayer is the debut effort of Blackpowder Games, a company of which I've learned consist of former members of Monolith Productions, in other words, guys who worked on FEAR. Naturally, since FEAR is one of my all-time favorite FPS games, I decided to give this game a try while it was in Early Access stages. Unfortunately, it did not stay in Early Access for a large amount of time, and because of apparent time constraints, Blackpowder did not manage to reach further potentials this game could have had.
Pros:
+ Very nice effects. The game's biggest feature in terms of visual splendor is wind. Oftentimes when you are treaded the island, you'll notice that gusts of wind pass by and affect all the foliage around you. At once, this left me in awe. I could've sworn I've seen things like this in other games, but in this one it was done so well. I was surprised at my own bated breath.
+ Fun combat. It's pretty simplistic and straightforward, but combat was a surprising amount of fun regardless. You'll acquire an assortment of olden time weaponry that function well enough, ranging from pistols to muskets to longbows. I found all of them to be quite useful and satisfying. Fighting the spainards was especially fun for some reason. I liked hearing my arrows sometimes bouncing off of them with a humorous metallic clunk.
+ Deep and shaking mysteries! This island has been inhabited by a lot of pretty screwed up people! Throughout the game, you will be solving a plethora of mysteries around different settlements, encountering wraiths and lost souls and helping them figure out who they were and what role they played in the sick situations that had taken place in the past. This is the thing that really kept me going. I've seen a few misspellings here and there, but the writing for the most part is exquisite. It just really makes me wish the game had voiceovers.
Cons:
- Betrayer is quite repetitive. Seriously, as neat as the mysteries are, the gameplay is quite repetitive. There is no real section that stands out, and everything you see from the third level is what you've already played before. I wish there was a little more variety in gameplay, but again I feel this squandered potential was because of time constraints, plain and simple.
- Lack of real immersion and empathy with characters. This is mostly due to the lack of voiceovers. It may be because of tight budgets, but potential for immersion was really lost with the lack of a voice here and there. The dialogue and writing is for the most part excellent, and it makes me sad that Blackpowder didn't make more ambitious pursuits in this aspect.
- Ending segment. I will not spoil the game here, but the ending segment contains an optional task that might as well be mandatory since it makes the final fight easier (and it was already pretty nerve-rackingly difficult). This requires you to scour across all the maps you've been through to the end point, which means lots of annoying loading screens. I have really mixed feelings about the ending segment; on one side, it was really interesting and well-executed, but on the other, the gameplay aspect somewhat fell flat.
Closing: Even if Betrayer stumbles upon a couple pitfalls and doesn't feel as good as it could be, it is still very much a solid, spooky, first-person mystery/action that will find a way to engage you one way or another in its harrowing tales. I hope that Blackpowder will pursue greater projects in the future and continue to deliver us unique experiences not unlike what they've lovingly crafted into this mystery romp.

A game you can truly lose yourself in. I won't lie, neither the story or the gameplay are spectacular, but the atmosphere and general aesthetic of the game are what keeps you playing. I haven't felt so immersed in a long time, a lot of other games just lose my attention quickly, but Betrayer kept it long enough to finish it all in two sittings.
Story? It did have me curious, but there was a lot of filler keeping you from what you want to really know, but it isn't thrown in your face so I can't complain, most of it is optional. The ending did feel kinda cheap, but had shock factor at the same time.
Gameplay? About 80% of the game is following your ears to move from one objective to the other, essentially one huge fetch quest, but the journey is riddled with enemies and the combat is actually really damn satisfying. You'll be using bows, firearms and my personal favourite: tomahawks, to dispatch opponents that get increasingly difficult. It felt like playing Far Cry 3 with the bow and having to be stealthy.
Design? The graphical style is amazing, I'm in love with it. The unique style may take some getting used to, but it really adds to the atmosphere of the game. Don't like it? Then you can disable it and go full colour in the settings. The sound is stunning too, really had me on edge a couple of times and genuinely sent shivers down my spine.
Performance? Some of the best optimization I've seen in a game. I never went below 60fps which is a rare thing for a laptop gamer to say. I used to crash frequently, but they patched the problem causing that and my second play session went fine without a single crash or bug.
I'd say this is worth the experience, as long as you're prepared to lose yourself.

Battlerite is a Team Arena Brawler that is a hybrid of fighting games like Smash and MOBA games like LoL or Dota. The best part about BR is it keeps the fast paced action of fighting games without the slow laning phase and objective dance of MOBA's.
What really got me addicted to the game is the addrenaline in sudden death. When the timer on the round hits 0:00 the round doesn't end immediatley, instead sudden death starts and the map begins to shrink around you. You go from having a whole screen to kite to having a space the size of a penny, which eventually will disappear. This game has some great adrenaline moments, while sticking to the simplicity of a fighting game where you don't need to memorize builds or leveling trees like MOBAs.

My least favorite addition to the series, Absolution is not without its merits.
Pros/Cons
+ The original voices of 47 and Diana come back for the fifth installment
+ The graphics are the best in the series so far, sometimes it looks really gorgeous
+ Fiberwire is much more efficient
+ Story is decent, with great voice acting for the most part
+ Ambient activity in levels is refined, people act more like people and they even talk too
+/- Story driven gameplay (as a side effect) often deters from the usual Hitman vibe
+/- 47 can actually participate in some decent hand to hand combat, but it's all quicktime events
- Assistance from the agency and predetermined weapons drops are gone
- Many of the levels are not focused on taking out a target
+ Maps have a lot going on and often many ways to approach situations/
- but they don't feel as open or sprawling as they once were
In my opinion, Absolution is worth playing through if you're either completely new to the series (and want to try the most polished but least 'Hitmany' first) or if you've already played the entirety of the other hitman games.
If you're only going to play one hitman game though, choose either the second, third or fourth installment.

Let's just start with looking back to first Bioshock which was by the way great gaming experience for me. Splendid idea of underwater city Rapture built with vision of free mind for artist/scientists and other types of creative people that might get limited by their surroundings in world, but not in Rapture.
As all previous utopistic societies that went straight into hell - new genetic improvements so called plasmids enhances your physical/psychical abilities in cost of ruining your body and mind (as drugs). But as every addict - you want more... but supplies are limited, so you start thinking about taking some from the others. In Rapture there were two major fractions - people listening to Andrew Ryan (man who built this "paradise") and Frank Fontaine(Ryans rival). After civil war, city was in ruins and people who survived this became weak-minded mutants (splicers) demanding ADAM (genetic material for plasmids).
In Bioshock 2 not much really changes from that - except city is more ruined and remaining splicers are uglier and desperate more than ever. Story of Bioshock 2 happens many years after first Bioshock. Power vacuum was filled with new visionary - Sophia Lamb.
You play as Big Daddy (subject Delta) whom was taken a little sister (Eleanor) years ago. You wake up revived by vita chamber years after death. And because you are genetically bounded with your little sister, you must find it or you'll die.
Your journey begins here...
I must say I enjoyed discovering new locations, newly refined plasmids, improved combat system (now you can hold plasmid and gun simultanously) and mainly fact being a big daddy, that giant monster in metal diving suit wearing drill, rivet gun and all...
Unlike first Bioshock, this one experiments with multiplayer and I must say it ended half-way to success. It have same atmosphere as Bioshock 1, game modes are fun, gameplay is challenging and entertaining same time, you have a lot of singleplayer elements here (hacking turrets, vending machines etc.), but lack of dedicated servers is biggest problem here and no matter how good gameplay you can offer, absention of dedicated erver bound with horribly coded network code ruins everything.
And I don't even mention GFWL and so called "DLCs" with overpowered third gun upgrades, new maps that you could play only if everyone owned that DLC (almost imposible) - I had to struggle with that until I stopped play it from frustration. Finally after some time GFWL closed (hurray for that) Bioshock was moved to Steam platform with all multiplayer expansions for free to all! So I could finally play some nice multiplayer... until people stopped play it so much, well at least I had some quality games before that.
It's a must have for every Bioshock 1 fan, but I would recomment it for people who likes interesting FPS shooters with some STORY (not pointing at any bad-story games (lies... lies..))

Before reading this review i should note that i played this game in a co-op mode with one other person. Meaning that we had one NPC companion being the elven mage. Also i have been playing this game on a game PC that runs almost every game perfectly fine on high settings. Also i've played this game for 20 hours.
The Lord Of The Rings: War In The North is said to be an RPG and Hack'n slash game. Though i'd rather consider it being a dungeon crawler. Its set in the mystical fantasy world created by J.R.R.Tolkien, called Middle Earth. And thats where the company that made this game took quite the risk. As this world is known to be very extensive. Full of lore and beautiful history. And it is therefore pretty difficult to make a game that completely follows the lines of Tolkiens Lore. But with a bit of research it should be possible right? Well this game does prove different but you will read more about that later in this review. Lets first talk about the aspects to this game and rate them all.
Story:
As i said before this game is set in Middle Earth. In the northern region to be correct. three friends that (without explaining) found each other and together took on the dangerous "right hand of sauron in the north". Agandaur this creature is called. And trough the game these heroes go to multiple places and meet a veriety of people on their journey to stop agandaur. This story is definitly not horrible. but not great either. Its not a very special story with a few fun plottwists. The story keeps the same basicly all game. Wich does get boring. But the story does meet some things that aren't completely logical to Tolkiens lore. Now i dont know all about this lore and i'm sure some things im saying will be incorrect, but some things that happen in this game tend to be pretty unlogical. Now i'm not saying i can't happen, just that it doesn't fit the style of fantasy that Middle Earth is. for instance the fact that Sauron teached Agaundaur how to use magic. And that agandaur teached the orcs. Meaning that there are actually orc mages in this game, together wich suicide bombing orcs too. I do understand that this is done because otherwise the enemy's would get boring after a while of killing the same orcs time after time. But also (correct me if i'm wrong) the elven lore master/mage tends to activate actual spells with her staff, BY USING HER VOCAL SKILLS TO USE THE SPELL?!?!?! it seems very unlikely.
Overall the story beacuse its a Middle Earth game gets a rating of 4.5
Gameplay:
The gameplay in this game is actually pretty fine. It has some fun fights and it doesnt really feel like repetetive gameplay. The fighting system works with basic attacks, heavy attacks and abilites and doesnt require that much of skill. there won't really be an enemy where you will feel like you cant defeat it once you get the hang of the whole dogderoll and attack situation. most enemy's do have a standart routine of fighting and you can see whats comming for you if you have seen what it does. But sometimes it does get annoying when an enemy attacks in a way that you can't see it coming. but overall the gameplay is not very repetetive and could be enjoyeble for a couple of hours. Meaning that its "alright". Also i do not realy have to talk that much about the gameplay outside of the fighting because as i did mention before i see it as a dungeon crawling game where you fight a lot and gather loot, and all the little conversations besides that don't realy matter.
I would give the gameplay a good 6.5
Bugs/Servers:
The bugs and servers in this game are pretty (let's say interesting). The game does have some bugs here and there trough the levels but thats no major issue. Things like trolls that just dead that just turn into a stiff body that stands there and then immediatly dissapears. or bod'y that dissapear right after you've killed them. But that doesnt really effect the gameplay that much. It just gets annoying when bugs come to path where the game crashes as you alt tab, or they look like its gonna crash but it doesnt. Also there are levels where the game just doesnt run as smoothly. For me that was in the pretty dissapointing chapter 8. where the level became almost unplayeble due to crashes and bugs. And at the end of the fight where the bossfight should be, the whole boss wasn't even there. he finally reapeared after a few times of restarting the game. The servers with that are okay. I didnt have too much trouble playing online co-op with my gaming buddy. One thing that did get in the way ALLOT and even made us play half the game OVER. when your game crashes and your partner loads a new area, the next time you join it will say that your partner is further in the game wich makes you unable to save and earn Steam Achievements. When this happens you can just start your solo story and play a few seconds/minutes trough and then when you've loaded the same area you can rejoin your partner. but in my case the solo story was bugged so i could not move on there either.
The bugs and servers get a rating of 3.5
characters:
There are three main characters in this game that all seem a bit boring. There is a ranger called Eredan that is mainly based arround the bow and arrow and does have a pretty normal feel to him while he talks and socializes.
There is also a dwarf called Farin that uses mainly two handed axes/hammers and a crossbow. Because he is dwarf he does tend to make more jokes and feel a bit more funny, wich made him the most interesting character of all also tracking his lore back when reading it online.
The third main character is an elven mage who uses staffs and swords. She is freaking boring to be honest. she doesnt say much and when she does its always kind of usless and captain obvious stuff.
also the charaters meet some other charaters that are known from the books and movies. these are recreated pretty nice and its also allot of fun to learn about the relationship between your charater and the famous books and movie characters.
the characters get a rating of 5 from me
environment and graphics:
The graphics for this game where actually pretty nice. the game dates back to 2011 and therefore looks pretty nice. not only ingame but also in some of the happening cinematics. but something i did very much enjoy is the view at some points. the few had moments where it was absolutely stunning, Beautiful mountains or an army of orcs marching in the background that feels great. and the same is to be said about the loading screens. The music with that really gave the game a beautiful and fantasy like feeling. though i wouldnt actally give it the Middle Earth felling in my oppinion.
the graphics and environment get a rating of 7 from me
By taking the avarage of all these ratings i can give it a rating of 5.3 and therefore higher then 5 wich means i DO recommend this game. as it is indeed a fun game to ruin about 12 hours of your time with. the only thing that really did annoy me from time to time where the bugs. but thats something you'll have to sit trough

Bashed by most critics for its lack of explanation and  repetitive gameplay, Betrayer is a game that completely drew me in until the goosebumpy ending (at least I felt that way).
It is a semi-open world action-adventure with lots of first-person shooting (or throwing), exploration and (text-)talking to ghosts, with a unique graphic style (you can change the high contrast black and white if you like), punishing difficulty (that you can set easier in the options) and, which is my personal favorite, an audio clue system that makes sense when you come to the end of the game (headphones or a quality sound system should be used while playing). The bleak atmosphere derives mostly from the visuals and the superb sound effects (no musical soundtrack). I recommend playing it in B&W if you can take it, important stuff is highlighted in red.
Personally, I never experienced any technical issues or bugs. It took me about 11 hours to see the ending, but I have not found every little thing there is to find.
You should play Betrayer if you like to explore and figure things out on your own, care for a mysterious story, are prepared to do some ingame reading and don't expect a typical FPS just because it's made by some ex-Monolith guys. Its a fine, but sadly misunderstood game by a small studio. I thoroughly enjoyed it and urge you to give it a chance.

Although Lord of the Rings: War in the North is a fairly enjoyable game, with a mediocre storyline and acceptable gameplay, the PC version contains many fatal technical flaws that sometimes even make it unplayable. Try this game on another platform if you really want to play it, just for fun and not for the story or great gameplay...
GAMEPLAY: Basic hack-and-slash action game, very little tactics. The skills you acquire throughout the game are handy in later levels, but offer very little variety and leveling, this game can therefore hardly be called an RPG. Enemies are often copy-pasted from earlier-chapter variations and offer little in terms of tactical variety. The bosses are sometimes tough, but more often than not easy. The most unfortunate thing was the last boss in the game, who was extremely easy to beat. The stores and interfaces are clunky, and often do not work as you would want them to, even crashing or having to re-open sometimes.
STORY: From a video game/fantasy perspective, the story is average. From a Tolkien-reader perspective, the story is horrible. Orcs and humans who use dark magic, goblins who blow themselves up with bombs, an entire never-heard-of timeline? J.R.R. Tolkien would turn in his grave if he had ever seen this game, and I can imagine heir Christopher isn't too happy with this either. A typical example of licensing gone wrong. Had this been a generic fantasy game in another setting, I would have judged the story as average but fun, but since this is misuse of the "Lord of the Rings" name, I have to be angry with it.
BUGS AND FLAWS: I played through this game via online multiplayer with my younger brother (we live in different cities). He has a medium gaming PC that plays most of the newest games at good settings, yet during a few levels, notably chapters 2 and 8, he experienced severe lag. At first we thought it was our online connection, but it turned out this is a well-known flaw that many players experience during this game, especially with ATI/AMD graphics cards. Secondly, if you join the game of a player that is farther ahead than you, you cannot save or gain achievements. One time, my brothers game crashed at an inopportune moment (chapter 2, right during the cutscene before the boss), while mine saved when the boss battle started. I quit, but alas, we had to retry everything. When he tried to get to the same point in a solo game, it turned out his save was corrupted and the game wouldn't load the boss into his arena. Therefore, we started the ENTIRE game again from the beginning. This time, when we got to the final boss battle in chapter 8, the boss wouldn't load into the arena. After the second time rebooting the game and reloading this save, he finally loaded and we could finish the game. By this time, my heart was already pounding, fearing we would have played through the entire game and not be able to finish the last battle.
In all, if you don't care about the most beautiful of worlds that J.R.R. Tolkien has created, if you don't care about variety in gameplay, and if you don't care about repetitiveness and some easy bosses, you can play this game for a bit of fun. But please, PLEASE play it on another platform. Unless you also don't care about major crashes, corrupted saves and restarting from scratch halfway through a game, of course... ;)

I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream is a classic adventure game. It resembles your typical point-and-click adventure game. I believe it is a different kind of adventure game due to how dark and disturbing the story is. You play as five different characters who have spent the last 109 years trapped with an insane machine with a serious megalomaniacal complex. You are tortured over and over by the God like machine. You are given a chance to finally end your suffering by completing a personal scenario that is unique to each of the characters. Most of the game consists of you playing these scenarios before reaching a sixth scenario that makes up the end game. Each of these scenarios can be completed in a number of different ways with one ideal way which will bring the character to his or her moral salvation. This is fairly limited by todays standards, but was impressive at the time and really results in "do something noble or do something cowardly".
The gameplay is fairly reminiscent of a Lucasarts SCUMM interface, clickable verbs are what allows you to interact with the world. The puzzles are quite complex compared to other adventure games with some really tough sections which can be frustrating. The graphics are impressive from a game published in 1995. It's a dark and gloomy setting that is suitable for the macabre subject matter. It's depressing and that's what makes the game quite special. The music and sound effects also contribute to this feeling of dread.
The game explores concepts that aren't really covered in many other games. It's unsettling, but entertaining. It can be tough if you aren't used to adventure games. If you are an adventure game fan and haven't played it then, I highly recommend it.

Primal Carnage is a game I can entertain myself for hours on end. Whether you're in it for the killing or just to mess around and role play (rp). I
this game. It's true this game hasn't been updated in months or maybe even a year now but even so it makes a great game none the less. If you want to feel a realistic dinosaur game then this one should be on your list of games to try.
The gameplay is quite smooth if you have a decent connection to the internet, it only gets laggy if there is a player with a high ping or your internet is just slow. It's a very smooth game and this is why I prefer it over Primal Carnage Extinction. The "improved" primal carnage (Extinction) is just too choppy for me and it just doesn't have the same feel that Primal Carnage gives. When I fly as a ptera I feel free, I could spend hours just flying around a map doing tricks and going under/over hard to reach places.
Pteras can actually speed up in this game by diving, wheras in Extinction you're basically just looking to get killed if you're a ptera. The movement of the dinos feels realistic, for example the raptor pounces at what seems within logic (in game it looks to be around 15ft). The rex doesn't vacuum you up into it's mouth, you actually have to aim to eat the human. Dilos are a much harder class to play, so if you like challenges then you should play that class and try to get atleast 5 kills without dying. Another thing that I like about the gameplay is the accuracy in aiming, it seems very realistic although the bullets don't slow down, they shoot the same speed as far as you want. Even still this game is quite fun.
One huge thing I love about this game is the community. Most people I have played with are reasonable although there is arguements on kill servers about weather a person is using "aimbot" or not. All in all most people understand the rules quickly and don't usually spam. I find there is less trolling in this game then in Extinction. Generally the people you meet will want to connect with you and soon before you know it you have a new best friend or someone who is very dear to you. I highly recommend getting to know the people you play with, you'll find out that they aren't so different from you and a lot of them share common interest along with you.
In conclusion, I would recommend this game to anyone who likes an intense and fairly accurate game. If you like it from the beginning chances are you'll get hooked just like I did. I am a die hard Primal Carnage fan and I will never forget this game. So if you want a little competition try new things in this game and push yourself to see how good you can really get. Before you know it you'll be the top killer on your team. I hope some of you will consider this game and give it a try.

Well, after finally beating it, I have to say this is the first survival game I've really liked. Perhaps because instead of zombies or mutants or whatever, this is a real thing that happens on occasion (and is probably happening in one particular country).
Gameplay:  Well, it's survival. You start out in a house with a number of people decided by the start you choose (no more than four, so far). You manage their happiness, hunger, wounds, illnesses and exhaustion. During the day, you play what's kinda like Sims Hardcore, where you watch your ever-dwindling stock of supplies vanish as you try to keep everyone alive and happy. You build upgrades to the house, things like stoves, a moonshine distillery (no better trade material than booze or meds) and defenses among others. At night, you post guards, figure out who gets to sleep and go on scavenging missions. These missions go to a wide array of places, where you can either loot the place (which will depress your survivors if you steal from innocent people) or trade with the inhabitants there if it's noted on the description. As loot dwindles at these places, you'll find yourselves making difficult choices with your supplies.
During the summer months, you're more concerned with keeping your food and construction supplies well-stocked. During the winter, vermin traps fill quicker (for obvious reasons) and give you more food while you toss every bit of construction supply you own into a heater to keep everyone from getting sick.
If they get too sick, too hungry, too tired, too whatever, they'll die. Yes, even if they get too sad, they'll kill themselves. Were there a problem I had with the game, it's lack of variety. Throughout my starts (to be fair, I've only had the first four characters unlocked until now) there have only been two ways the entire scenario goes down, with everything from house visits to unlocked areas being the exact same along those two starts. Also woulda liked more house models, but I'm being nitpicky here.
On the play I won, I endeavored to NEVER get into combat. There's something odd about the fact that on another play I snuck behind a would-be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥who had cornered a scavenger, slammed an axe into his head to save her, and he recovered quickly enough to shoot and kill my character before I could take another swing. Combat is incredibly awkward, is what I'm saying. I don't know if that was by design or lack thereof, and if it is by design, I get the point they're trying to make but I'd at least like a sneak attack from an axe to be a one hit kill, like the enemies' bullets typically are.
As much as it tries to encourage you to build and utilize everything, there were so many aspects of the crafting system I never bothered to use. By design, you have to play the game very conservatively, so wasting resources to grow vegetables, craft armor, craft higher level weapons, craft bullets, make coffee and make medicine is pointless, since you can just set up a moonshine distillery and keep making that to trade for anything that's more expensive to craft freeing your inventory up on salvaging missions so you can go after heaps of the bare necessities. Still, these are just minor complaints about very solid gameplay.
Aesthetic: There isn't a lot to speak about here, and I don't mean that in a bad way. The music is gloomy as hell (and also, is free DLC [Thanks, 11-Bit]), the art style is this kind of washed-out pencil shaded graphic of muted dull colors that really draws you into the game and makes you sufficiently miserable. Which again, is good, as it assists in giving the impact this kind of game needs.
Story: The game has no real story besides: a civil war has started, survive. That's all it needs, though, because you make your own story. Will you donate expensive and very valuable meds to the hospital or rob it blind while they try to help people? Will you rob an elderly couple for their medicine because that young journalist with you is sick and her only hope to survive are a few pills(I did)? Will you turn a blind eye to a soldier who's about to♥♥♥♥♥♥a scavenger because you don't want to get hurt? The story's all on you.

If you love space battles, strategy, management on both large scale and small scale then this game is for you. Keep in mind that the game can take hours to play a single round and days to master but the feeling of winning a challenging match is almost akin to chess in its joy. For those new to the game first take the tutorials and then play against an easy computer on a small map with each faction, then play a free-for-all against multiple AI on a larger map, and by then you should have an idea of how you want to play the game and with which faction you want to play with. Challenging ai only begins at hard, and unfair should give you an idea of how hard human opponents are. This game is best enjoyed with a group of friends but it is just as fun with a challenging AI opponent. Overall, the only reason that I believe that somebody shouldn't play this game is if they just don't like the RTS genre as this game captures almost every aspect of it while being like chess in being easy to learn and control but hard to master.

Just think Firefly + Cowboy Bebop = Rebel Galaxy.
Didn't know what all to expect when watching the trailers, so I thought "What the hell, I'll give it a shot."  Then I gave it another...and another...and another, and before I was done, pirate fleets were torn asunder and floating lifeless in the cold, empty void of space.
Overall:
+ Put in close to 12 hours so far and still in the first system.  In many AAA-titles released these days (I'm looking at you CoD), the main part of campaigns can be completed in 5-20 hours, depending on how much content there is. It isn't terrible by any means, but after hearing the same 6-7 songs repeated over and over again in some sequences, I disabled the music in the settings and began listening to music downloaded from YouTube. The gameplay perfectly recreates the setting of hell: It is torturous. While I love the Saints Row series, this installment takes the worst elements of IV and multiplies them. While the mini-games were ok in that, it was because of their brevity. The same minigames are drawn out here, just too long for it to be enjoyable.
The ragdolling is seriously out of hand. I spent equal amount of times being thrown around than actually playing the game. Similarly, they thought that the addition of anti-air defences to a game where flying is the only way around would be a fun addition. It is not. When trying to get from A to B you have to choices: (a) Stop and fight each of the 30 something AA towers or be shot down constantly and you guessed ragdoll and be interrupted.
The story is entertaining, although the actual story portion is pretty short. There is an intro and a loyalty mission for each of the 5 allies, but it hardly gives a lot of personality them. The musical number is true Saints Row fun though.
Overall, this is a DLC that is let down by the fact that the developer tried to stretch it into a standalone game. While I enjoyed the story, by the end the character's repetitive grunts when ragdolling (all the time) or being on fire (all the time when not ragdolling) is matched by my own. It is also not a good sign that it runs out of story content before the arbitrary level cap for the final mission is reached (which the game seems to be smugly aware of) resulting in contextless side activity grinding.
Get it on sale if a huge Saints Row fan. Otherwise don't bother. And the developer thought you would want to play this 5 times to unlock all the endings. Sigh...

Hatred is an isometric shooter where you play as a psychopath who's out to murder thousands of people. The premise is simple, but also the very thing that garnered the game so much attention. The game plays well enough, and it's quite violent, but at the same time, I feel the media has made the game out to be worst than it actually is.
Each level of Hatred will provide it's own challenge and goals, many are quite linear, but there are missions where it takes a more open world sandbox approach. As far as gameplay goes, it's your standard issue isometric shooter. You can run, perform executions to replenish your HP, crouch, pick up new weapons, etc, basically, standard fare. One thing Hatred introduces to this genre is the idea of killing innocent NPCs. In other games where the option to kill innocent NPCs are made available, they rarely give the player any incentive to partake in the action, but Hatred doesn't just give incentive, it makes it the main point. The issue with this is, shooting NPCs that can't fight back is really boring! After a while, the police, swat, and military will show up, which makes the game a lot more enjoyable and interesting, but there are some missions where a large portion of it, is rather dull, gunning down hundreds of unarmed NPCs that offer no challenge what so ever.
Artistically the game has it nailed down. It's heavily stylized with it's black and white aesthetics. Pops of red and blue are the only colors that line the game. The lighting and environments look great, brooding and gritty, very appropriate to the atmosphere. Hatred also features a low, brooding sound track, that never over powers, but adds a ton to the mood. It also features a physics engine that is sure to impress, as gun fire breaks away the walls that surround you. It's a great looking game! But be aware, the game can be buggy at times with NPCs flipping out, cars floating in the air, and other weird oddities.
For all it's controversy, Hatred is not the worst on the market. Mortal Kombat is gorier, Hotline Miami is more violent, and Postal 2 was more psychotic. The ONLY thing that set Hatred apart from the other games mentioned is that you play as a the villain that takes place in a (some what) realistic world. Basically, Hatred is controversial by concept only, the content of the game really isn't even a quarter as disturbing as the media would have you believe.
Overall Hatred is a competent isometric shooter that has an edgy theme to it. The gameplay itself is nothing special or revolutionary but does the trick. The controversy surrounding this game is way overblown, and dosn't deserve the AO rating (M would be appropriate). At the end of the day, Hatred isn't bad, but it's nothing special either.
Pros:
- Great looking style
- Competent gameplay
- Challenging (Once the police shows up)
Cons:
- Does nothing new or special in terms of gameplay
- Shooting NPCs that don't fight back can get boring.

This is yet another game where I wish I could give a middle rank, neither a yes or a no, but a "meh" rating too, however since the game is cheap, and has very good production values, and is fun for a little while, Ill give it the up vote.
Anyway, you can watch some videos to see what kind of game this is about, however, Ill just get into some of my gripes with the game design.
Some minor issues that annoy me:
1.  Missions are over scripted and in a way are not realistic.  For example, every time you have do a trade-guild mission to ship some specific cagro from point A to B, you will ALWAYS be intercepted.  There is ALWAYs trouble.   Now if this were the only problem, I could overlook this.  The actual problem is that the REAL trade mission is to actually destroy the guys who intercept you.  Case and point, I took a very lucrative delivery mission that took place in  the same system.  It was rated as HIGH risk.   I figued I could run away.  My mission is to deliver something, not kill things?  RIght?  Oh no, quite wrong.   So I am getting close to the station I need to make my delivery to, and as usual, the trap is sprung and a bunch of ships appear from all directions and they pull you out of "warp".    So what do I do? I escape, I use my after burners and get enough distance and jump back into warp.  I make it like 5 clicks and the same trap happens again.  I do this 2 more times and each time the trap is reset and sprung again which is just terrible game design.  The only solution is to kill the ambush.  All mission types that are not supposed to be directly about combat workout the same way.
2.  You can have missles as weapons, the problem with them is that you do not have a lot of ammo, which makes sense.  However, if you are an NPC, then you have infinite ammo.  I once had a ship that shot waves of missiles the killed my engines.  The didn't do any damage to my ship or shields, but I couldn't move.  It just sat there for like 10 minutes keeping me pinned.  I had to Alt-F4 to recover because if you exit normally, it would save your game and I would have been stuck forever.
3.  No quick save.
Ok, enough of the small sutff.  Why did I stop playing this game without finishing the main story?  What is the big thing that is wrong with the game design?
Basically it is repetivie and boring.  Combat is boring.  Flying around in space warping everwhere is boring.  Each star system is randomly generated, but they are all very generic and you can't really tell the difference other than this sone might have a yellow sun and the other one has a blue sun.   There is nothing to explore or find.  Its all the same, everywhere.
Now maybe if you LOVE space games you may get a lot more milage out of it then I did, but after about 20 hours the game felt more like work then fun.

Over all the game is quite good and addictive. The graphics, while not top of the line, are well done and pretty to look at. Gameplay overall is fun. There are some problems however, the first is difficulty. The game is quite hard, even on easy mode. Now normally difficulty isn't a problem with me; I like a challenge. The problem is the nature of the difficulty, it isn't because the game itself is difficult, it's because of some design flaws and coding issues. For example, you regularly get stuck on doorways and small objects. Many times this leads you to getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by the cops and military as you get stuck on the edge of a door when you're trying to escape. Secondly, enemies have pinpoint accuracy and will hit you virtually every time. Thirdly, the soldiers are quite overpowered, they can literally 5-6 shot you on easy, and they always come in squads of 20 or so, so it's hard to do anything against them, meanwhile they take 8-10 hots to kill each. The color scheme is noir and red, with occasional other colors in the mix. It's a great visual effect, but sometimes makes every thing look the same, especially when there's a lot of fire and chaos on screen which results in it being hard to determine just where the hell you're shooting. Lastly, and my biggest issue with the game is the camera often works against you. Enemies can shoot you perfectly from way off camera and you have no way to see them or shoot them because the camera restricts your view. This is the number one thing that makes the game quite too difficult. One thing I will say is the AI is quite good in tactics. I've noticed it will use flanking maneuvers in small squads on you. Well done there devs. Besides the difficulty because of the above mentioned issues, the game is quite good and I'd recommend it if you don't mind over the top violence.

It belongs up there with the other top shelf 2d shooters.

Crimsonland - Neon Chrome is the successor to the cult-hit Crimsonland. A new environment of rooms and corridors, similar functions yet better AI, looting and quests to it's predecessor.
Monaco: What's Yours Is Mine - The ambience, movement, the use of weapons, hacking, this plays like a shooter version of Monaco. Stealth is used more here to determine where and how to engage the enemy.
Hotline Miami - This is the base comparison for 2d shooters in close quarters. Neon Chrome is less frantic and has a larger view of the kill field. It's not as visceral but to me that makes it less jarring. The screen is busier and there's more to do with a destructive environment around you.
Rogue Legacy - Game difficulty curve, upgrades at castle and death cycle are similar to Rogue Legacy.
8.5/10.

I'm giving this product a recommended rating because I personally enjoyed it, mostly as a way of wasting time when I'm bored (Which I am right now, so, beware, this reviews going to be long). However, there's a lot of bad to go with the good here. Now, to be fair, let's start with the good...
Combat: Fighting in this game is entertaining enough, and you face a pretty diverse amount of enemies. I only played on normal difficulty because combats not usually the main draw in a VN for me. But still, it's fun and challenging enough for a casual player on normal, or a hardcore player on nightmare difficulty.
Characters: One thing WW consistantly gets right in the VN's I've played has to be the characters. They're entertaining, diverse, and a lot of fun. There's only one main character that I personally didn't like. Romances in this game aren't as prominent as in other WW titles, which is either a pro or a con depending on what you look for in the game.
Art and design: The one objective improvement from this games predecessor (Loren the Amazon Princess), has got to be the art. They clearly put a considerable amount of effort into drawing new characters, and it shows, nothing more needs to be said.
Bad Blood DLC: I've only just started playing it, but so far it's everything I wish this game was from the start.
The bad...
No description: For some reasons, this game is all dialogue with no description. Which really hurts the game whenever they're doing something that requires you to know what's going on. It also makes the scenes feel rushed, especially before and after boss fights, where the villain just dies instantly without a satisfying send off. There's rarely even dialogue from the villain before their death, someone else just tells you that they died. In summary...
Villain: Grwar! I'm going to kill you!"
*Boss fight*
Ally: Welp, he's dead.
Not exactly very interesting. This issue makes the final boss of this game so stupidly anti-climactic and rushed, that I almost face-palmed.
The story: Ugh, the story, let me give you a brief overview, spoiling as little as possible (Not that there's much to spoil).
Act 1, Winter: Starts off with you picking your character and learning the basics. Exploring your hometown Ninim while your overbearing father's sick. It ends fairly well too, with your character being betrayed by the village, and their father (who, as the hero puts it, 'seemed happy that you were paying a price for disobeying him, for once in your entire life'),
But unfortunately, nothing comes of this, no, really, the hero just gets over it immediately and wants to go home, with no ill feelings towards the village or their father. I would've been perfectly happy with the hero slowly learning to forgive and forget, but that's not what happens, they just forget about it, and hope you do too.
Overall rating: 6/10 (Would've been 7.5/10 if not for the hero getting over it so quickly).
Act 2, Spring: Personally, I think this is the best act in the game. For starters, there's actually an antagonist, and you meet all the characters that'll be with you for the rest of the game. While a lot of it is filler, the characters manage to save it. The ending is also pretty cool, minus the boss fight (for aforementioned reasons about description).
Overall rating: 7.5/10
Act 3, Summer: Barely a story here to critique, you just bop around having silly little adventurers and possibly starting a romance if you choose to do one. The adventures themselves were fun and all, but it becomes evident that there really is no character development or drama in the game at all.
Overall rating: 4/10 (Would be 3/10 if not for a good chapter conclusion).
Act 4, Autumn: Begins with boring filler as you return to Ninim, who, upon you returning, don't react at all, nor acknowledge the fact that they betrayed you earlier. As I said, the game simply forgets about it. This is followed by two boring quests that desperately attempt to insert completely new plotlines and threats that are promptly defeated. Whoop de doo.
But that's got nothing on what happens next, after you save the ungrateful Ninim, you reunite with your deadbeat father, who barely reacts to your return, and ignores how he let you get dragged off into slavery. He also reveals that both you and your twin are actually shapeshifters, which was actually pretty cool. But you know what would've been a better place to reveal this twist? The end of chapter one.
At least then we could've used our cool shapeshifting abilities, as opposed to learning about them minutes before the credits roll. It also could've added more conflict into the game, as shapeshifting is considered forbidden magic. But instead, you learn about it right before the credits, making it pointless.
Last and least, comes another "surprise" twist where a character that kept warning you that they'll betray you, betrays you, and you kill them. A cringe-worthy conclusion if ever there was one.
Overall rating: 1/10 (I promise, I'm not exaggerating)
It's a shame too, this game had a lot of potential story-wise, if only they'd put a little more effort into it. Oh well,

This is a tough review to write. I don't like this game, and I'll be refunding it after this review is written.
That being said, I think many people will like it, so I do recommend it. I'll try to explain the game, as well as why I don't care for it, then you can make your choice based on the kind of player you are.
So, I love twin stick shooters. All the way back to playing Robotron 2084 in the arcades as a kid. I also really enjoyed 10tons last twin stick shooter as well, Crimsonland, which I've got on GOG.
My thing is, when I play a twin stick, I want something fast and frenetic... something like Robotron, Crimsonland, Geometry Wars, Enter the Gungeon, Nuclear Throne... "my problem" with this game is pacing. It's almost like this just happens to be a twin stick controlled game, but isn't really supposed to be what you'd generally think of as a "twin stick shooter."
In this game you're in cramped hallways and small rooms, and it often-times feels more as if it should be a top down stealth game as opposed to what it is. Although many times the AI is so dumb, stealth won't matter. A few times I've shot a soldier standing beside another, and his partner doesn't even react. Or missed and bullets fired right past them, but they just keep "guarding".
The easiest way to sum this up is: Take Crimsonland, give it a neon, Bladerunner-esqe ambiance, an awesome soundtrack, and put it into cramped, mazelike quarters, shake in a little "rogue-lite" and you've got Neon Chrome. It's got the powerups and guns you find like Crimsonland. The bit of humor in their written summaries. Even the menu screens remind me of Crimsonland... The only thing this game doesn't have is all the fast action fun.
If you want a bit more thoughtful, strategic twin stick shooter as opposed to your typical fun run 'n gun, definitely give this a try. It's got slick graphics, a GREAT soundtrack, and decent controls (I used an XBOX One controller while I played). And in some ways it does make you think a little more than probably any other twin stick I've played (how to navigate the levels, etc.) but be aware that may ruin the pacing of the game for you as well.
All in all, I personally found it to be... not bad. Just not fast, not firing out both barrels... and not fun.
