I Have No Mouth, and I Must Scream is based on the novel of the same name by Harlan Ellison which I wasn't aware of until playing this game. I have since added the book to my Amazon wishlist to read in the near future.
The game is a horror-themed point and click adventure released in 1995 and has various elements that classify it as a weird type of horror game. The title alone should raise interest in almost everyone who hasn't played the game and since it is quite hard to find a physical copy of the PC or DOS versions of the game, Steam is the easiest method of acquiring it. For those thinking of purchasing a physical copy you will need a copy from around 1995 or an IBM compatible PC as stated in the game's specs. However, the Steam version is the DOS version of the game and runs through a software emulation called DOS Box which can be used to play other DOS games(such as System Shock). This means that the game ran seamlessly on my Windows 7 Professional 64-bit machine.
The game allows you to play as each of 5 players which I will briefly describe. Benny is a mutilated brute, Ellen is a professional engineer who has a hysteric phobia of the colour yellow, Nimdok is an old man with an amusingly voice-acted foreign accent who is conducting a sadistic experiment at  a Nazi concentration camp in 1945, Gorrister who is a suicidal loner haunted by what happened to his wife, and finally Ted who is a cynical paranoid. The basic story is centred around these 5 beings who have been held captive against their will for the past 109 years or so by a very creepy computer name AM (Applied Mastercomputer) who was implanted by nations into the centre of the earth. AM wants to play a game with each of the 5 and tests them in a way as to the decisions they make during their adventures.
Each character has a unique adventure with some of them such as Nimdok's being considerably short. The adventures presented by each individual will present the player with puzzles and clues which they will have to figure out by using their brains or through a walkthrough. The game can be quite unforgiving based on the choices the player makes and will force them to restart the character's story. However, the save system implemented in the game allows you to overcome this by regularly saving and loading. The game's save icon represented by a floppy disc starts to spin when the player hasn't saved in a while which is a neat feature. The game exhibits the standard mechanics of a point and click adventure game with a range of options to choose from and being able to explore through just clicking either left or right mouse button. Using all the options you can concatenate sentences together which will command the character and depending on the context make them interact with the world.
My personal favourite of the 5 character's stories was Teds due to the setting of a creepy haunted castle and its relevant themes. Least favourite was Benny's story but this is just my personal opinion.
The game is not very short and can be finished in possibly 5 hours, even though I took 16 hours because I play games slowly and explore as well as replay things to see other alternatives. It is a very weird game that will give you the creeps. I must check out the book which I've heard is nearly similar to the game if not for a few differences regarding the characters.
Already, the game at its normal price (£3.29) is a giveaway, but wait for the Steam sales to get it even cheaper. Thoroughly recommend trying this game but it is not going to be for everyone.

If the smile on my face told me anything when I got back to Ninim in Act IV, it was that I've thoroughly enjoyed this game.  Ah, it was good to be home, back where it all started (plus: new winter outfit art!).  With over 40 hours of gameplay under my belt, I definitely recommend Aravorn: Seasons of the Wolf.
Initially I was skeptical.  The specter of resource management wasn't something I wanted, and I did not like the idea that I would have to ration my power every fight instead of fighting hard like I did in the predecessor, Loren: Amazon Princess.  Nevertheless, I stuck with it, and I'm glad I did.  The game gave me enough tools to be somewhat incautious on normal difficulty, including talents that refund power points and taverns for resting.  I was rarely able to really cut loose, but I was able to slip into a sustainable rhythm in each area's fights after a little experimentation--and still use my powers (which is more fun than auto-attacking).
The game is packed with content, and just when I started to tire of an area, there was something different to do, new enemies to fight, new storylines to pursue.  I definitely grew more powerful and that power was tested, and my teamwork was and remained important for the entire game.  There's lots of loot to get and to shop for, and many options for how to approach the various challenges, including different flavors of combat,  stealth missions, and sometimes avoiding combat altogether.  This isn't a blow-through visual novel... it's a real, get-into-it game if you want it to be.
The characters are both well-drawn and well-written, and I had time to experience their depth and to get to know them.  Romance options were fewer than I would have liked (and what's more, the game lets you go down false starts) but the romance I did pursue was satisfying.  I also enjoyed the ending, though it felt a little abrupt.
The DLC added more closure and I was more satisfied with the ending after playing it.  It made my romance matter more with various scenes, including a nice CG at the end. It explains the romance ending you saw at the end of the original game, too, though it's strange seeing it out of order (why not move them both to the end if the player has the DLC?).  The DLC also changes up the gameplay flow and adds some different style content, so that was fun, too.
I'm looking forward to the next entry in the RPG+VN genre from Winter Wolves.  Keep it coming, guys, these games are great!

The crafting, sneaking/infiltration, trading, etc., seems much more realized in this game than in others in the genre.  The overall mood of the game and the constant sense of dread as you finish a night and wonder what happened while you were away - this, and more, ups the emotional stakes as you play and really makes you think about the choices you will make going forward.

When Egosoft's X3 first came out, I learned first-hand that it installed Starforce malware, so I complained on the Egosoft forums.  They were offended by my complaints and gave me a warning, so I swore off any future Egosoft purchases.  X Rebirth made me change my mind.  (Plus there's no Starforce this time!!!)
When Rebirth first came out I did a lot of research and learned that it was a big mess.  So I waited for over a year, did more research, and found that it was faring much better.  This got me to finally buy it during a Steam sale.  Man I'm glad I did!
I'm a big sci-fi fan.  I played Freelancer in the past, and am currently playing Starpoint Gemini 2 and Elite Dangerous off and on.
X Rebirth is one of the best single-player space experiences I've ever had.  I can see what Egosoft was trying to do with this game, and I think it shines.  Are all the negative reviews warranted?  Early on I'd say absolutely.  But they've patched it up and added to it quite a bit since then.  In my 106 hours of playing I've only had one glitch, and that was getting stuck during docking.  I simply undocked and redocked to fix it.
I played the campaign up until the point that I came back to Albion from DeVries and was hostile to everyone.  It was then that I restarted in free mode and have never looked back.  I've upgraded my Skunk to the MK5 shields, the MK3 weapon, and only have 2 more pieces until I have my MK5 engine.  I have the Skunk and 1 Fedhelm freighter, so the plan now is to learn capturing to expand my fleet.  I'd also like to dabble in station building.  There's so much more to do.
I've spent a lot of time just travelling around mapping my way and doing missions.  Sightseeing in this game is visually rewarding.  I've gotten used to the flight physics and combat and can hold my own very well.  I've been playing vanilla with no mods the whole time.  I tried changing my cockpit at one point, but none of the others appealed to me.  I've grown used to the clunky large one that came with the Skunk.  I also have no issues with just the one ship.  If I want to get somewhere quick I can dock with my freighter and jump away.
Could it be better, sure.  But I think what I've gotten so far for my dollar has paid off in spades.
PROS
- Visually stunning.
- It's as immersive as you allow it to be.
- Keyboard/mouse controls are very easy to master and fluid.
- Has a decent campaign from what I've played, although I preferred sandbox mode instead.
CONS
- NPC skins can be horrendous.
- Station skins are too repetetive.
- Repeating conversations are irksome.
- Inability to drop freigher inventory is just plain silly.
- Ren and Yisha.  Being able to choose other characters or customize would have been great.
Thanks Egosoft!

Betrayer is a game I have been waiting for awhile. It has been a very long time that a first person game has filled me with such dread and I am fully decked out with bows and arrows, crossbows, flintlocks, and tomahawks! It is amazing what a small team was able to accomplish especially with regards to the audio. The hisses of restless spirits, creaking of the walking dead, the groans of marauding Conquistadors, and the whistling of "naturals" create a soundscape where every encounter is filled with great risk and peril. Exploration can be very rewarding resulting in the discovery of loot of all types.
The art style is excellent. While the graphics aren't gorgeous, what's there is impressive be it English log cabins, native straw huts, varied geometry in the terrain, and well animated adversaries. I felt like I was taking a hike in the twilight zone, even using rocks and foilage to hide from my foes to ambush them with throwing axes and a hail of arrows. Heck I'd channel Natty Bumpo and fire off one of my many muskets to draw attention to myself. The AI is decent even if simplistic. Enemies will try to turn you into a human porcupine, hack you to bits, rend flesh with claws, lodge razer sharp bones into your flesh, or blast you with unholy bolts. Trust me, they're not trying to hug you!
What I didn't like was how annoying it was to go about discovering chests. Sure there's a chiming sound when you get close to an object of interest and they glow or blink red form afar, but in all seriousness I often overlooked things. An enterprising player collaborated with other explorers to take a screen shot of the map of each region with a legend of points of interest like loot. I love treasure! Even though I love the audio, the game is best played with headphones or a good surround set up. Even then I suggest on turning on visualization of audio cues. Running around spamming the "listen" button wasn't too much fun.
Combat is simplistic and felt suprisingly authentic. Except for the ultra accurate smoothbore flintlocks. Yeah their range was relatively far, but the dude you're playing as fires accurately and loads like a man possesed (or on drugs). Not that I'm complaining too much, in RL (real-life) it takes roughly thirty seconds to get your muzzle loaded musket ready for firing and that's if nobody's shooting at you, there's no yelling, or people trying to stab you with bayonets (which weren't invented yet). A lack of spear toting and halberd wielding enemies was a bit suprising, but a dagger is still plenty deadly. Things get easier with the discovery of new weapons my favorite being the crossbow. If you get decent at leading enemies and catch them before they enter melee the game isn't quite a breeze, but it's rewarding to keep cool under pressure.
All in all I'd give the game an 8/10. A bigger budget and more staff would have made this diamond in the rough into a gem.

Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion is one of the most versatile space based RTS games produced; the vanilla game offers three distinct factions and each of those has a sub faction you can choose; loyalist or rebels, each with different tech and construction options. The research trees are fairly comprehensive and cover everything from civilian, military, diplomatic and defence branches each with 30-40 techs in each branch. Therefore there can be different strategies each playthrough to some extent. But the combat is fairly satisfying as well as visually pleasing but the real beauty of Sins is the vast repository of mods available for it on sites like ModDB - Sins of a Galactic Empire (Star Wars), Star Trek Armada 3 are probably two of the most comprehensive you could check out, but there are many more. Therefore as well as the great base game you also have access to whatever particular science fiction genre you want to simulate with the solid game engine. What I would suggest for those familiar with them are programs like large address aware; but more for the mods as opposed to the base game as they tend to crank up the population capacity of ships compared to vanilla. (Due to engine constraints it only utilises the old school 4gb of ram limitation even if you have 16gb; LAA or similar will remedy this problem and allow for late game battles on a massive scale.)

Even though I haven't beaten the game or even come close to, this game isn't about story, more of roaming around and just exploring the world of Betrayer.  (Sorry if this review is a mess, tired, and not in the best mood)
Betrayer starts off on a beach and far off in the ocean is a wrecked ship. You came from that boat. The time is the 17th century and you are pretty much abandoned on this island or whatever. You are a misterious character with no name but, we shall call the character Betrayer.
In Betrayer, you can help dead and confused spirits by going into the towns of each area and ringing a bell which takes you from the light zone (Life) to the dark zone (Dead), where you meet people called Wraiths. They are lost and confused spirits that don't know how they died, what happened to loved ones etc. You find clues that may hint at where to go or that might trigger the Wraiths to remember what happened. Of hand, you can explore and sometimes help spirits in the light world. But, in each world there are people or monsters that attack you. For example, in the dark world, skeletons attack you and in the light world, conquistadors attack you. Knowing that, you might be able to find out where you actually are.
The games graphics are amazing, even though the game uses a black and white color scheme, with some red to highlight important objects, enemies, NPC etc. I'm not a fan of black and white, since I can fall asleep during black and white movies but, I enjoy this color scheme, it works well with this game. So all and all, this is a great game, everything about it is great, I haven't beaten the game yet, but people predict (that have beaten it) it's around 8-9 hours. For 20 bucks, that's not bad. TLDR: It’s awesome, but I have some nits to pick.
I finished the campaign in an Arcturus with level 6 defenses, a mix of level 5 pulse turrets and particle lasers, and level 6 neutron beams in about 21 hours (net worth just under 40 million). My equipment level was such that the final set of missions was pretty easy (I don’t think I lost shields once during the final battle, and the mission itself was listed as low risk).
Liked:
Combat: I read some comments before purchasing the game lamenting the fact that it didn’t allow full 3-D motion. While I initially held some of the same concerns, I very quickly fell in love with the navel style combat system, which would have been difficult if not impossible to pull off well in a fully 3-D environment. From the carefully aimed long range broadsides to those exhilarating moments when you slam the side of your ship into your opponent and scream “Fire at Will!” as you pull the trigger as fast as you can, combat is an absolute blast.
Movement: As an addendum to combat, the movements system in battles, especially when you reach the higher levels of boosters, is amazing as well. The sudden acceleration you see while surging along the side of a much larger ship trying to avoid its broadside feels like it should by squeezing you into the back of your seat. This, plus the broadside mechanic, combine to make combat absolutely enthralling.
Ship Design: I really like the types and variety of ships available to captain and kill. From the industrial ships of the common citizen to the more refined combat ships of the militia to the strange and futuristic designs of the alien races, there is a very nice variety of ship designs in the game. There hasn’t been one ship that I’ve looked at and haven’t said “Oooooo, I wanna fly THAT!”
Ship to Ship Scale: I really like how ship scale progresses in the game as you earn enough credits to purchase larger and larger vessels. You start off as a small ship trying to make it in the big leagues, desperately firing your boosters in an attempt to avoid a larger vessel’s broadside while keeping him under fire from your own. Later on you become that larger ship, trying to turn fast enough to keep that pesky fly in your sights before his constant fire wears through your shields. Seeing ships I used to pilot seem as gnats compared to my current ships really hammers home the progression I’ve made in the game.
The 'Risk' System: It may seem minor, but I really like the risk announcement. Hearing "Threat Level: Red" made my booster finger start to itch almost uncontrollably.
Music: Makes it feel like I’m playing Firefly the Game. Enough said.
Didn’t Like:
Warp Inhibition: Warp inhibition by stellar mass seems to be a bit finicky. I often found myself being inhibited by smaller asteroids when I had a clear path through a field, getting back into warp, and then later in the trip having to jerk to the side to avoid a much larger asteroid whose surface I would barely skim while remaining in warp without a problem. I overall like the inhibition system, but it seems it could use some tweaking.
Emptiness: I wasn’t exactly sure what to label this one. Basically, it felt that systems lacked traffic where you would expect it to be, and as a result the game felt a bit emptier then it should have. For example, I never encountered another ship around a jumpgate (except for the last story sequence, of course). Freelancer had a very good system in this respect, in that jumgates always had traffic moving through them, sometimes even enough that the player had to wait in line! Some of my best memories of that game were running from an enemy I couldn’t defeat and hoping that I would avoid the dreaded “entering queue” and be able to complete the jump sequence before my hull failed. Speaking of which…
Ease of Escape: I felt it was a bit easy to escape from enemies that outclassed you. Shields recharging under deflectors combined with the fact that broadside don’t fire forward by nature meant that it was trivially easy to escape any situation. I think I died a total of twice in the 20 hours I played, and that was only because I made a conscious decision not to run when I knew I should have. I really feel that there is a missed opportunity in dramatic escapes here.
Story: The story had an interesting premise but fell too quickly, in my opinion, into ‘save the world’ mode. I had hoped the story would focus more on “space wild west” type themes, like the conflict between the civilized core worlds and the wild frontier or between an expanding colonial power and those resisting that expansion. I could see hints of the latter in the story, but it ended up feeling more like a mass effect type overarching plot, which I felt fit the lore and feel of the game less well.
With all that said, I want to reiterate how much I really like Rebel Galaxy. It’s a fun, fast paced game with an awesome soundtrack and even better combat. I’m really interested to see where the developers take it from here and will almost certainly be purchasing whatever they create next.

IMPORTANT: This review is about "Magic Duels: Origins" itself from the perspective of a newbie to the Magic: The Gathering game. Therefore, it may be invalid for (returning) veteran players.
Magic Duels: Origins (a.k.a. Magic Duels) is the digital version of famous TCG (trading Card game); Magic: The Gathering. Unlike previous digital versions of the game, this game is designed as free to play (f2p). There is in-game coin and booster pack store. Booster packs can be bought with coin. Players can earn coin by winning, completing daily missions or buy it directly with real money. I find the store and amounts earned fair enough, because TCGs are based on spending money on new sets and booster packs by nature. Also, all cards are unlockable, so spending money is not mandatory.
Game’s most noticeable part is its tutorial. It has an extensive tutorial showing the player every rule and beginning level gameplay of Magic: The Gathering. Its design is also nice. Unlike showing all aspects of the game in one go, it teaches the basics at the beginning and sends the player to the story mode. During story mode, if a situation arises such as a new type of card or an ability on a card, a notification asks the player if he/she wishes to play tutorial for it. Playing that tutorial pauses the current game and starts the tutorial. After tutorial is finished, interrupted game continues. It is possible to skip these tutorials and play them later from the menu. Every tutorial also gives a small amount of coin, so it is a good idea to complete them all.
First “basics tutorial” and first story mission are kind of mandatory. Because most features are locked until they are finished. After that, the game sends the player to create his/her fist deck and lets the player to have a solo battle. When solo battle is finished all features are unlocked. This way of unlocking the features is not a problem for newbies. Actually it can even be considered a good choice to prevent newbies from losing in multiplayer too much, resulting them dropping the game. But for veterans, it is a big problem. They already know the game and want to jump right in multiplayer with their custom decks.
Other than the story mode, game has solo battle mode which is against AI, versus mode which is against another player and two-headed giant mode which is 2 vs 2 mode against either AI or other players (The player needs to invite his/her friend to able play against AI).
Solo battle can be played against 3 different difficulties. Interestingly though, “Hard” difficulty feels the easiest. These battles give coins depending on the difficulty (5 to 15 coins).
Versus mode can be played against either a friend or an opponent that is ranked the same as the player. The rank of the player changes depending on the result of the matched battle. Battles against friends and AI don’t affect ranking. Also battles against friends don’t give coins. Matched versus battles gives 20 coins.
Two headed giant mode is the only multiplayer mode where more than two players play together. 4 players split into two teams of two players and battle. Team players share the life and a player can block an attack against his/her teammate. A Player’s teammate’s hand is visible but interacting with it is not allowed. This also apply cards on the board. Players can’t use abilities on their teammates cards. Two-headed giant mode doesn’t affect ranking. It also doesn’t give coins.
UI is good and clear. There are no unnecessary animations or information bombard. Most of the in-game actions (such as attack animations of the cards) can be toggled in the settings. That said, I read veterans don’t like this UI. Until “Magic 2014” it was different, and indeed there are big changes. When I checked 2014 version myself, I realized that both button locations and general information design had big differences. For a newbie, it won’t matter. Actually I like the new one more. In the old UI, it felt weird not to be able see how many cards my opponent had in his/her hand. For veterans though, it will feel like switching from Mac OS to Windows.
It appears that previous editions had also chat feature and it was removed in this version. There are mixed opinions on this subject. Personally, I don’t think it is a must have but it certainly could be useful, especially in two-headed giant mode. it is impossible to talk to teammate if the player is playing together with a
. That said, if the player is playing with a
, he/she can use steam chat to overcome this.
Booster packs contains 3 common cards, 2 uncommon cards and 1 rare or mythic rare card (total 6 cards). Also packs can’t drop the cards that reached its deck limit so eventually every card is unlocked. Every booster pack is 150 coins. Winning against hard AI gives 15 coins and winning against a player gives 20 coins. Daily missions and weekly mission give 40 coins (there are up to 3 daily missions and one weekly mission). It is said that about 80 booster packs are required to unlock all cards. But there is a daily coin limit (400 coins) so players can’t grind coins (note that daily missions are not counted towards the limit).
During my gameplay, I came across one serious and one minor bug. Serious bug was that during my solo battle against the easy AI, it played 5 of the same card which is clearly against the game rules. (Note: a developer responded to my screenshot of this issue and wrote that they were going to investigate it). Minor bug was that the coin amount was not being updated after completion of the daily missions. It required (and still does) a restart to be fixed.
I didn’t have any issues finding opponents in both versus mode and two-headed giant mode. Also my test for steam friend invite worked without any issues (I need to note that I tested friend invite with only one of my friends, so it might be just luck).
This is very good for newbies to Magic: The Gathering game.
Thanks to this limit, all cards are eventually unlocked.
All menus and buttons are cleverly put together in a clear and simple manner. (Although, there are big changes)
This is only a con for veterans. As a side effect of the tutorial, some single play elements must be finished before multiplayer modes are unlocked.
Normally this is not a very big issue. But because of the ability to buy coins with real money, this creates a “pay to win” side.
I can safely assume that Magic Duels is designed to make new players interested in Magic: The Gathering title and not as a solo product to make money. Due to its extensive tutorial, it is very easy to learn the basics of Magic: The Gathering. As a newbie to the title myself, I can recommend this to everyone who wants to learn (or at least try) Magic: The Gathering.

Saints Row: Gat out of Hell is a fun, relaxing, and satisfying game. You start the game on the ship, with the characters from Saints Row IV, having a birthday party for Kinzie Kensington. Then Matt Miller bring out some sort of demon-summoning board out to tinker with. All of a sudden, The Boss is kidnapped by Satan to marry Jezebel (Satan's Daughter). Then without thinking about their actions, Johnny Gat and Kinzie Kensington jump into the gateway and find themselves in Hell. After you go to Hell you see the Ultor Building and go towards it to pay Dane a visit. He then gives you the ability of Super Jumping/Flight and Super Sprint. You then go to meet Blackbeard, Shakespeare, Vlad, and the DeWynter twins to receive your four supernatural superpowers (Summon, Stomp, Blast, Aura). You then can start doing loyalty missions for each of your new friends. All of a sudden there is a sceen when Jezebel leaves her room and heads out to hunt for Johnny Gat so she can help him. Then the game kind of cools down after you rescue all of your new friends from Satan's goons. You then do all your missions, challenges, etc. to fill your Satan's attention bar to finally take down the devil himself.

Saints Row: Gat out of Hell is a standalone expansion for the action adventure series. The game was developed by Volition Inc and published by Deep Silver, releasing in January 2015 on PC, PS3, Xbox 360, PS4 and Xbox One.
The gameplay is almost identical to the rest of the games in the series. Playing from a third person perspective, you are thrown into the middle of a humorous and absurd sandbox world; and you take part in missions with the common aim of taking down Satan, of course.  Your character, Johnny, will receive some new superhuman abilities, such as the ability to fly, and one of the more memorable weapons to be found in the game, is the Gatling gun arm chair, I know it’s almost as ridiculous as it sounds.  The missions vary from one mode to another, none of them have any real story potential behind them, there is just pure action throughout the game. It almost felt like all the missions were sided activities from a game’s main element, but the ease and speed at which the game was taken at from beginning to end made the lack of any real story side of the game forgettable as you are having too much fun to realize it.
Gat out of Hell relies on the same game engine as Saints Row IV; so we are going to have a decent looking game on our hands. The environments which you are able to explore definitely give you that feeling of being in hell; although they aren’t as interesting to explore as say that of GTA V, it is still a somewhat bustling city with thousands of collectable items to find and smaller side activities to take part in. The voice acting is pretty good here too, with a lot of the main characters from the previous games making a return.
This game is by no means hard at all; I only died once throughout the whole playthrough. The only really challenging aspect of this game is the platforming element which is always going to be my virtual enemy since I hate it so very much. Getting a hang of the controls and the fact that both inverted controls and regular control systems are used quite a lot throughout too left me confused as to when to use which. Some of the missions don’t give you any explanation as to how to complete them too which isn’t always a bad thing, but after ten tries or so it would be nice to get a little hint to stop the embarrassment.
I played through the story mode as well as working on collecting the majority of collectables and completing all of the side activities and targets across the city and still only managed to clock in just under ten hours; now this may not sound like much but this is a stand-alone experience so I have come to believe that a shorter amount of gameplay should be expected. I felt pleasantly filled up with my fix of Saints Row once I reached the game’s conclusion.
Throughout the whole play through I only ever had one crash to desktop and I wasn’t able to find the cause of that and never happened again so I’ll put that down to luck. I was able to play with settings maxed out and kept it running at 60 FPS the whole time whilst streaming too. This is a really well-optimized game for most machines.
Saints Row Gat out of Hell is a really good introductory game to the series if you are little on the fence about trying out some of the longer and more expensive titles. You can pick this game up for just £10.99 when not on sale, and even then this game is worth it. Such high production values on the genuinely fun gameplay make this a highly recommended game for me.

This game is a Visual Novel/RPG Hybrid. If you like games with good narrative and also happen to like RPGs, this might be a good game for you.
STORY
The game develops in a fantasy land called Aravorn. The main characters are a pair of snow elves that have to endure a series of hardships due to a twist of fate. In their quest, they will meet allies and friends that will join them to help them, but they also have their personal problems which you may want to tackle or just ignore them. The story is well written and the characters are deep and coherent (all the coherent that Rowinda can be…) and the main story as well as the personal stories of each character are quite good. You also have a few romantic interests to choose from and allow you to dig deeper into the personality of some of the characters. The story is probably the best aspect of the game.
ART/ANIMATION
As a Visual Novel, don’t expect high quality graphics and 3D animation obviously. However, the art is quite good. The character design is pretty nice, and a lot of the backgrounds are gorgeous. On the other hand, animations are scarce and simple, especially in combat where you would expect something else maybe.
MECHANICS
The game follows the usual Visual Novel system of make your decisions, combined with a map where we can decide which place to visit next. The combat mechanics are pretty nice, with each character having an array of skills which allow the player to develop diverse strategies depending on how you develop them as they level up.
MUSIC AND SOUND
The game soundtrack is quite good. It blends perfectly with the tone of the story in almost every scene and the combat themes are quite catchy. The SFX are nice too, although the number of combats and the abuse of certain skills might make you hate some of them.
OVERALL
Good music, memorable characters, an interesting story and a quite entertaining combat system make this game worth it. Don’t leave the mysteries of Aravorn unsolved and go for it. Furthermore, if you played Loren: The Amazon Princess and liked it, you can’t miss this one, and if you haven’t, then I really recommend you both games.

Being a huge fan of the X series I was shocked by the state X:Rebirth was released in:
The performance was terrible, the game crashed constantly, you couldn't even play through the main story because one of the first quests just bugged out and kept you stuck. The game was a frustrating mess.
My experience with Egosoft however was, that they usually continue maintaining their games over a long period of time and so I kept following the development of things as they rolled out one patch after the other.
Now, with version 3.20 I can finally say, that the game is now in a proper playable state.
They fixed most of the performance issues, the story quests work as intended, station building and fleet management works fine and the AI is starting to improve as well.
Finally they added more ship models, don't force you to walk around stations anymore to trade your inventory and upped the threat that pirates pose.
So, if you were thinking about getting this game but weren't sure if you really should because of the bad stuff you heard from frustrated early buyers, I think now is the time to pick it up without having any regrets.
I expect Egosoft to improve the game for a long time now, so there should be something new going on every once in a while that will keep me coming back to it and thus never removing it from my hard drive for ages.

Well, after finally beating it, I have to say this is the first survival game I've really liked. Perhaps because instead of zombies or mutants or whatever, this is a real thing that happens on occasion (and is probably happening in one particular country).
Gameplay:  Well, it's survival. You start out in a house with a number of people decided by the start you choose (no more than four, so far). You manage their happiness, hunger, wounds, illnesses and exhaustion. During the day, you play what's kinda like Sims Hardcore, where you watch your ever-dwindling stock of supplies vanish as you try to keep everyone alive and happy. You build upgrades to the house, things like stoves, a moonshine distillery (no better trade material than booze or meds) and defenses among others. At night, you post guards, figure out who gets to sleep and go on scavenging missions. These missions go to a wide array of places, where you can either loot the place (which will depress your survivors if you steal from innocent people) or trade with the inhabitants there if it's noted on the description. As loot dwindles at these places, you'll find yourselves making difficult choices with your supplies.
During the summer months, you're more concerned with keeping your food and construction supplies well-stocked. During the winter, vermin traps fill quicker (for obvious reasons) and give you more food while you toss every bit of construction supply you own into a heater to keep everyone from getting sick.
If they get too sick, too hungry, too tired, too whatever, they'll die. Yes, even if they get too sad, they'll kill themselves. Were there a problem I had with the game, it's lack of variety. Throughout my starts (to be fair, I've only had the first four characters unlocked until now) there have only been two ways the entire scenario goes down, with everything from house visits to unlocked areas being the exact same along those two starts. Also woulda liked more house models, but I'm being nitpicky here.
On the play I won, I endeavored to NEVER get into combat. There's something odd about the fact that on another play I snuck behind a would-be♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥who had cornered a scavenger, slammed an axe into his head to save her, and he recovered quickly enough to shoot and kill my character before I could take another swing. Combat is incredibly awkward, is what I'm saying. I don't know if that was by design or lack thereof, and if it is by design, I get the point they're trying to make but I'd at least like a sneak attack from an axe to be a one hit kill, like the enemies' bullets typically are.
As much as it tries to encourage you to build and utilize everything, there were so many aspects of the crafting system I never bothered to use. By design, you have to play the game very conservatively, so wasting resources to grow vegetables, craft armor, craft higher level weapons, craft bullets, make coffee and make medicine is pointless, since you can just set up a moonshine distillery and keep making that to trade for anything that's more expensive to craft freeing your inventory up on salvaging missions so you can go after heaps of the bare necessities. Still, these are just minor complaints about very solid gameplay.
Aesthetic: There isn't a lot to speak about here, and I don't mean that in a bad way. The music is gloomy as hell (and also, is free DLC [Thanks, 11-Bit]), the art style is this kind of washed-out pencil shaded graphic of muted dull colors that really draws you into the game and makes you sufficiently miserable. Which again, is good, as it assists in giving the impact this kind of game needs.
Story: The game has no real story besides: a civil war has started, survive. That's all it needs, though, because you make your own story. Will you donate expensive and very valuable meds to the hospital or rob it blind while they try to help people? Will you rob an elderly couple for their medicine because that young journalist with you is sick and her only hope to survive are a few pills(I did)? Will you turn a blind eye to a soldier who's about to♥♥♥♥♥♥a scavenger because you don't want to get hurt? The story's all on you.

I came worried that Rapture would lose its magic second time around, and left realizing how much of a fool I was. The city is more amazing than it was in the first game, characters better fleshed out, story more focused and generally everything feels significantly improved. While during the first game I spent the first hours just understanding what the hell the setting was about, this time Rapture felt like bleak home and I could appreciate everything from the beginning without that slow learning curve. Obviously, much of the mystery is diminished since it's not the first time. But you're compensated with better mechanics, stunning environments and a deeper story.
Tonics and Plasmids are still a great joy, improving the FPS with light RPG elements of character customization. The variety of active and passive abilities allows you to choose between an impressive range of playstyles. Sneak? Melee? Guns ablazing? Setting traps? Hypnotizing enemies to fight by your side? Use machines to wreak havoc? You name it, you have it. Combined with an unparalled atmosphere and unique setting, using the foundations of the first masterpiece and building upon them, BioShock is 20-some hours of pure fun of the best kind in computer games.
I recommend playing the first before the second. Otherwise, you'll have a hard time enjoying the most of the plot. You'll miss out on a lot of characters and spend too long trying to fill in the gaps by what you understand from the events. And this is a game you want to delve into the plot. If just for Rapture, its history and its imaginative premise.

TWOM is a great yet soul-crushing experience wherein you have to come to terms with what it means to survive in a state of war. It's not easy and most decisions are definitely not black and white.
You are tasked with controlling a group of survivors (I've heard you can unlock a solo variation) who are simply trying to make it in hopeless situation. Along with the variety of moral dilemmas that you face is a bit of mildly challenging resource management. When crafting, not only do you have to consider the materials needed but also the time it will take to accomplish goal x/y/z. The game also features a rich amount of dialogue from not only your characters (check out their cool biographies) but the places you visit at night during your looting runs. It adds a lot of character to the game and makes some decisions even harder to make.
There's a lot more to this game but it's honestly better to just take a look and see for yourself. If you want a meaningful survival game then I strongly suggest you pick this game up.

In 1992, id Software released Wolfenstein. Which later became known as Wolfenstein 3D. And it became known as one of the grandparents of first person shooting games and one of the first person shooting icons back in the day, such as DOOM.
Later in 2001, we received another title for the series, known as RTCW. Return to Castle Wolfenstein, for the full title. Now whether it was expected or a needed sequel to the original game, Idk. I don't know if it was expected. But I can say that it was a good treat from id, that year. More Wolfenstein, more nazi shooting and also some supernatural as the icing to this cake.
Centuries ago, Heinrich I was imprisoned on the battlefield by a wizard who dared to face him and to put an end to his reign of terror. Later in 1943, nazis from the SS Paranormal Division, led by Himmler, find themselves at the exact same spot, digging for Heinrich's final resting place, hoping to rely on his power in order to win the war. This reaches the OSA's ears and they send in two agents to investigate and report their activity to the office. Unfortunately during their mission, both agents are captured and taken to Castle Wolfenstein to be interrogated. One of those agents is the same character you played before, if you played the original Wolfenstein. You're once again, put in the shoes of B.J. Blazkowicz (pronounced "Blaz-ko-vitz") with the starting objective of escaping from the castle and contact an agent from a german resistance group called the Kreisau Circle. After your escape from the castle into a village near the castle, your contact tells you to head to the graveyard, where the nazis are also doing more excavations. That's where things start getting out of the ordinary for both the nazis and yourself as you have to deal with the undead.
The game will take you through various places as you foil the SS Paranormal's plans, aside from Castle Wolfenstein. You'll also go through places like a rocket base, an airfield, catacombs, even the ruins of a city in Malta in order to reach a weapons factory.
The game will also provide you with a wide variety of weapons, from a knife and the classic MP40 to guns like the flamethrower, the Panzerfaust and crazy stuff like the Venom Gun which is like this smaller yet just as powerful gatling gun and the Tesla Gun, which is like an electricity cannon.
The game's graphics... even for a 2001 game, they could look a little better. But if you wanna make the game look better, there's an HD graphics mod in the Steam forums. And trust me, the game looks like it's from 2010's, with that.
As for how long it can take you to beat the game, I'd say about 12 hours. Probably less if you manage to die as little as possible. Probably around 9-10 hours.
The soundtrack is also on point and it doesn't really deviate from the atmosphere the game tries to create for you.
And with that, I think it's time for the final score. I give Return to Castle Wolfenstein a 7/10. It's a good experience. If you're one for graphics, you're gonna want the graphics mod I mentioned, because with its original graphics the game looks kinda outdated even for the time it came out. It keeps you engaged as well and does a good job at it. I recommend you getting this game and if possible, the rest of the Wolfenstein games. At least up until the 2009 title. I still have yet to play The New Order.
Enjoy!

A competent, compelling and sometimes stressfull survival-platformer. I'm not a huge fan of platformers, but in this game, it feels right. Although, combat is quite clunky to say the least, once you get used to the fight sequences with your scavenger, its relatively smooth sailing. Be careful who you kill as well because all kills have repurcussions with your survivors, so make each kill count and be sure to wash it down with some moonshine :P!
If you are looking for a challenging, single-player survival game, then one could definitely do worse than picking up This War of Mine. It'll definitely earn its money back (in terms of time-played) and may even hold a special place in your collection. The game is not without its problems, however. -It has trading cards and Steam Achievements
Cons:

Overall, this game is witty and funny. Worth a look if you can get it on sale

Final Fantasy XIII is a tough case. Let me first state that I am a huge fan of the FF-13 trilogy- I think they are overlooked games that really shine in some areas but could use some work in others. None of the games in this trilogy exhibit this more than FF 13. It is a shame, too, that many people play FF 13 and then won't even try FF 13-2 and 13-3 - which are both vastly superior and really good games.
FF 13 tells the story of Lightning and her companions as they try to find a way to save her sister, Serah, from a crystal doom and save a whole world besides. The story is convoluted and barely told at the beginning, but over time really evolves into something special. I think it's very good, but takes some time to get going for sure.
I personally absolutely love all the characters - they exhibit great personalities and are likeable (or unlikeable) in their own way. There was so much potential to let their stories shine, but the game suffers from one big, grievous problem - it's linearity.
For about 60 % of the game, you will walk through one hallway, fight enemies, get items that are either on the hallway or on a very small sidepath, return to the hallway and fight some more. This continues for 20 hours; 20 hours full of linearity, be it in the combat, the freedom of movement or the character developement through the crystarium, a kind of developement system that lets you distribute points you earn from combat for attribute bonuses and new skills. All of it is VERY linear for 20 hours; more than enough time to make anyone quit the game way before the 20 hours are over.
It is sad, too, because what comes after these 20 painfully linear hours is great - a somewhat open cluster of maps, different missions you can do and get rewards for, you now always fight with three party members instead of only two, like for the majority of the story until then (and the fighting system is painfully boring with only two characters), you can develop all party members in all classes instead of only a select three and change the party leader and makeup freely. It becomes a WHOLE different game then and, at that point, it really starts to shine. Then it doesn't even matter that, shortly after this section, there are another few hours of hallway waiting for you (though you can return to said cluster of maps at some point during that).
The graphics of the game are great for it's time, though the port is somewhat mediocre. 30 fps are the norm no matter what setup you have, but some are lucky enough to get 60. Even so, the game is beautiful to look at and there are a few graphics customization options available. Music is good too, albeit repetitive at times since some areas have the same music.
In summary, the game has great characters, great plot and great gameplay - all of which is sadly very fragmented, slow and linear for the first ~20 hours. That is not to say there isn't fun to be had during that, but sometimes it becomes a real struggle to get through. Linearity itself isn't bad, but when you can't do anything else besides walk through hallways for 20 hours, it becomes very repetitive. Stick with it, though, and there is a wonderful and fun game waiting for you past that, as well as a story and characters that really feel, well, real, but take so long to develop. It is certainly a game that rewards you for sticking with it, both for the "endgame", and because it also makes the events of the two successors easier to follow - the question is if you have the patience to do so. I still upvote it because it has a special place in my heart if you look past all the (partly valid) criticism it gets.

As a way to play a subset of Magic while away from your computer, I'd say it's usable.  But it has a way to go before I'd strongly recommend it.

It would be easy to write a negative review of this game if you forget for a moment what you are buying.
This is a inexpensive game that does not proclaim itself to be other than it is, a space shoot-em-up.
The gameplay is simplistic in style, the learning curve is small and the fun factor is high.
There are not a huge amount of choices when it comes to ships and equipment, but they cover all the bases so you can play the style you wish to play. Laser boats, missle boats or whatever floats your.. well, boat.
The background music is great until it becomes repetitious after many hours of play. It can be turned off.
The missions are fun until they become a grind, naturally. But I must admit there are enough variations of them to keep that from happening for many hours of play.
Flying is a blast and fighting in battles is always new as there is not one technique that seems to stand out that will give you advantage in every battle. Each one is different in some way.
If I had one major gripe it would be the act of simple space fight between point A and point B.
Space is vast and cluttered with junk. Asteroid fields, nebulas, ice fields, literal junk fields and whatnot.  On average you can fly about 7 or 8 seconds before you will encounter yet another pile of something that you must fly around.
If you can fly from A to B without being kicked out of warp at least twice, count yourself lucky.  Interesting at first, enough to make you scream in rage the hundreth time. I've been to 12 systems and they are all the same. Couldn't at least one system be clutter free and pretty?
Many other pro's and con's have been covered by other reviews and I won't reiterate them.
In a nutshell, it's a blast for the price. How can you go wrong?

Overall, Neon Chrome is a hidden gem. I had my doubts at first, it being a small game, but let me assure you, it's well worth the price.
GAMEPLAY: Typical twin stick shooter action in this one. It is a roguelike, so there is an additional exra element of difficulty involved from the get-go. You have a variety of classes with different starting perks, and randomized weapons/assets to pick from before diving into the levels. Each one is randomized as well, so you never play the game the same way twice. Combat is intense and grabs you by the face and forces you to pay attention. You can choose from a variety of ways to play, whether tactical or guns'a blazin' and you can pull off wins either way, depending on how you fight. The level of creativity this game allows was quite a treat for me.
The item that stuck out most for me in this game, is that the difficulty is not impossible, but not a walk-in-the-park either. It's just enough to challenge you, and make the game fun. Boss fights in particular make sure you don't get too uppity and feel too good about yourself.
GENERAL: Graphics are very good, and definitely catch the eye. As the title somewhat suggests, there's a lot of bright neon lights thrown throughout levels and just as added detail to make the environment enjoyable. Audio is amazing. Music is nice (can get repetitive after a bit, but I find it useful to just turn off the in-game music and play my own in the background), and the combat sounds (such as grenades exploding and guns firing) are top-notch. Very satisfying to hear.
CONCLUSION AND EXTRA NOTES: All in all, an amazing game, that will be sure to get you to waste a lot of time on. I didn't expect Neon Chrome to be all that great, in all honesty. However, I was very pleasantly surprised. The devs went above and beyond for this one, and really highlighted on all the gameplay and audio stuff that really gets me into the feel of the games I love. 9/10 cannot recommend enough.
NOTES: Multiplayer is kinda funky. The game apparently supports up to 4 players, but I have only managed to get 2 player co-op on my PC, as only one of our controllers is recognized by the game. However, the co-op experience is very good as well. I personally prefer using the mouse and keyboard to play, but controller works just as well.

Alpha Runner is a very RELAXING ... RAGE QUIT game. Two words I never thought I would put in the same sentence. This is all thanks to its groovy musical score that drowns you out in the background, while you die a quad zillion amount of times. The story is you’re an Alpha runner and your goal in life is to be a Beta runner. Get it Alpha, Beta, bad joke I know, but I couldn't resist. Being serious now, it's a platformer where you’re biggest and hardest achievement goal is to try and get 200 squares which appear on platforms that will eventually disappear as you stand on them. Also you must avoid spikes, rotating saw blades and dropping hammers.
Unfortunately the game still feels like it is in Beta and this is because the developer (
) never seems to have a clear vision of where he was going with all this. It more looks like a product of a person who just wanted to make a game for the sake of wanting to make a game. For instance your character after a minute or so of traversing platforms will start to hold a umbrella which will spawn in, this is because there was a mini game where you had to avoid rain drops as well as continue to traverse the landscape of disappearing platforms and spikes, but the developer received a LOT of backlash about this concept and removed it, but kept the umbrella in for no reason. Also each time you die you get a different character, some characters have different abilities, one character can double jump, another character has greater speed, another character has an exaggerated jump, but some characters have no abilities what so ever and seem to be a product of a developer out of ideas.
Options are really limited. For instance you can only mute sound, not turn in game sound down which can be bad for those that want to record. There are also three different modes...
1) Normal: As described above the objective is to try and get 200 squares. This took me a long time, there is an xp levelling up system and the more you level up the harder the traps get and the quicker the platforms disappear. Eventually at level 22 I was able to achieve the 200 mark all thanks to the red system which usually only gives you spikes and the Astronaut guy which has an elongated jump and allows you some time to plan ahead. The higher your level the more complicated the two mini games are in normal mode. One mini game involves you being a spaceship destroying all the other spaceships by shooting at them in the opposite direction until you come across the Mother ship which requires you to shoot at it travelling in the same direction. The other mini game requires you to hit one of three keys at the same moment the prop tells you to alas a saw blade spawns in. You must keep doing it even though it gets faster and faster until the exit door appears. These are the only two mini games in Alpha Runner and again seem to be a product of a guy only wanting to make a game for the sake of making a game and someone who didn't have a clear vision of what he was trying to achieve.
2) Speed run: Here you get a certain number of platforms and traps to try and get the quickest time on. Problem with this is that even though the number of platforms are always the same. Their layout and traps aren't each time you log out and log in it. So one lay out which allowed me to do it 28 seconds another lay out would not allow it. So what is the point of it all if it isn't consistent?
3) MLG: It's the same as normal mode but after a minute or so it will flip upside down, it flips upside down even in the mini games. No one plays this as it is too hard and the game does not give you any time whatsoever to adjust. A poorly designed mode that does not favour the gamer, hence no gamer is really ever that interested in it.
4) There is also a practice mode where you can turn traps on or off, but again this mode never adds to the achievement scoring and seems rather pointless in practicing in it.
So why do I give this a thumbs up then in comparison to a weak envisioned platformer slaphazzardly put together, because in normal mode it is a really challenging and rewarding experience when you eventually are skilled enough to get your little guy to that 200 mark, and as stated before it is the most relaxing rage quit game I have ever played all thanks to a soundtrack which is the most fitting soundtrack I have ever heard for a game.
Below is me showing you the various modes. Notice my best score 247! Are you game?
Suggestions for developer...
* Each character should have a different ability.
* Get rid of the Umbrella.
* More mini games.
* If I’m able to opt out of the space mini game I should be able to opt out of the saw blade mini game.
* MLG give the gamer more time to adapt to the world flipping upside down.
* Background should change more the further you go, trees, waterfalls, comets, fireworks etc.
* Speed run should be consistent in its layout.
* A mode with an ending.

First it's a neighborhood, next it's a sewer/pier, then a train, etc.  One sad thing though I must say, there isn't a actual destroyable city, which I would have loved, yes there is the politician place which is IN a city, but there didn't seem to be much to really destroy, at least from what I could find anyway.
Civis use weapons:  The civilians will actually defend themselves by picking up cops' guns and fighting you with them, I actually thought this was really interesting since most games don't actually have anything like that.  Although they aren't all that smart and can't really aim at you unless they're in a HUGE group, then you might be screwed.
Barely hit if crouching:  I figured this out over halfway through the game, if you crouch down you're incredibly hard to hit by EVERYONE.  Apparently no one can figure out how to point their gun 30 degrees downward or something.  But you do have much better accuracy as well so you can save some of your ammo.
Good for stress: I've been very stressed over my own work and I figured this game could help ease some of that off, it did actually.  Maybe just seeing everyone run around screaming while I get to shoot at them all gayly, it's kind of like the Pyro from TF2 with his Schizophrenia or something.
Postal references: Remember when I said it's like Postal? Well there are even references to it, which I think is pretty cool.  I've only found 2, one is a achievement called "Postal dude would be proud" And a in-game voice from the character that he says "Only my weapon understands me" I got a little giddy from that, I thought this was pretty cool since Postal 2 is my favorite game or one of them.
BAD:
Terrible Optimization: This game is terribly Optimized or something, the framerate goes everywhere, it wont' even go above 30 frames even if I turned everything on it's lowest setting, which I didn't really mind cause it looks good at the 30 framerate, but even when I turned stuff back up it tanks anywhere it feels, it'll go from 30 to 20 in some areas and won't go past 15 half the time.  Then when the Execution Cutscenes show up they go everywhere, it could be 30 frames, could be 10, it's never consistent enough.
Game is pretty difficult: This game isn't easy, it's pretty hard later on when you've got a lot of cops swarming you in every single direction and you may/maynot be trapped in a corner of a building with no way to get out.  This isn't a con because I hate it, it's a con because this game later on can get on your nerves on hard difficulty.
Hard to see everyone:  This game is in a black and white art style with red, blue, yellow, etc. sticking out to be obvious, which is a neat thing for a game such as this but the problem with it is that, I CANT EVEN SEE ANYONE HALF THE TIME.  All the enemies and civs are black and white as well so they're hard to see.  Thankfully though, they do give you a button to show your objectives and it even lights up all the people on the screen including yourself, so you can see where they're all at.  But you're the exact same color as them, so it can be frustrating to figure out where you are at at times.  Maybe add a option to change your outline so you're obvious? I don't know.
Swat/Soldiers: God I hate these futhermuckers, they take forever to die with assault rifles and can hit you really hard, it'll take half a clip of ammo for a m16 to just kill one of them when you have to kill around 40.  And if you exploded all of the barrels and have no grenades laying around you're in for a treat.  Although that "Crouch down" thing works very well with these guys, so atleast you have a decent chance of killing them.
Hard to see where i'm aiming at: Even though you can change the crosshair and it's color, it's still really hard to see it and where you're aiming, I wish they'd make a option to enlarge the size a bit or something so it's more obvious to see where i'm actually pointing at.  One time I was fighting soldiers and when I went into a execution scene I ended up pointing the opposite direction from where I thought I was and was just shooting a wall while they stared at me all confused.
Pretty repetitive: Yes this game can be pretty samey if you don't have a imagination of blowing people up with explosions and watching their heads blow off with shotguns, so you kind of have to have a bit of a open mind with this game otherwise you're gonna get really bored really fast.  HeII I got so bored at one point I actually played a game with the cops which is to see how many cars can be piled up in the coffee shop without them blowing up.
CONCLUSION:
If you want a Postal clone and a damn good one at that, this is the game for you, sure it's a little more grim but I kind of like it, maybe that's because I like Manhunt so much and seeing all the detailed murder scenes I don't know.  It gets a 7/10 from me, it isn't really bad but it isn't really good either it's a hard balance of anger and fun but repetitive at the same time.  I gotta give them credit for putting a lot of detail in the game though cause holy s^*t there is a lot of it.

Very enjoyable VN/RPG.
Both genres are well executed - it is a full-fledged RPG, with VN storytelling instead of usual to a genre cinematics.
It feels very solid, much more than it's predecessor, Loren The Amazon Princess. In some way we get only a subset of content from LtAP - less classes, less monsters, less fights, less towns - but at the same time it is a right subset, it gives more details and variety. Like, for example, you don't fight hordes of same demons, you only encounter them several times, and each encounter is interesting. Regular monster packs change just as you are accustomed to fight them, but before they begin to annoy. Fights are now less about buff-spam and require some choices and timing. Especially on Hard!
Speaking of solid - characters and game world seems to be more worked on. Dialogs are no way cheesy (which was sort of a problem with Loren), every scene is executed great, with a good script and immersive visuals. And some scenes were really stunning. It was a great experience when lighthearted story was turning into something more serious.
Art is definitely a game's strong point. Yes, you are getting what you see on screenshots. And it may be missed, but the game doesn't reuse content much. Many locations and NPCs are getting appropriate graphics instead of generic ones. Followers have a great variety of costumes they wear. CGs are not numerous, but timely. And those unnoticeable small things really add to immersion.
Can't miss out the romances, since it is VN and Winter Wolves' VN. Personally I haven't enjoyed them. Possible partners are not really appealing. Straight choice for Althea conducts himself like a haughty idiot, and following that storyline feels unnatural and cheesy. So romances weren't a part of a game for me.
By the way, had I said that Althea is absolutely fascinating character? It is just drawing and some lines of text, but she does seems fleshed-out, and she is amazing. With her kind heart and openness there is no wonder she became the leader of the group. And for a runaway slave she has quite a taste for pretty costumes!
Bottom line. If you liked Loren The Amazon Princess, what do you want? It is the same but more. Grab at the nearest sale! If you like the art, get it, the gameplay doesn't let down game art's quality. As a VN, it is one of the best you can encounter on Steam. Not much a competitor with major RPG titles, though - but a good one for indie tier.
If you decide to buy it, consider buying DLC as well - ending is quite rushed and not impressive without it.

Here's the short version of this review: Tales of Aravorn serves as a solid update to Loren the Amazon Princess mechanically, but falls short of its predecessor from a narrative stand point. It's still a lot of fun, and fans of the Aravorn universe and Loren will love it all the same.
Now for the long version. The combat got much better with an updated layout and some much needed streamlining, and the choice system was enhanced with actual dialogue options and what felt like more meaningful impact (despite the fact that choices once again really only influence character reputation). More stats and much better skill trees for each class were also added, really amping up the RPG gameplay. Also worth noting, the game is huge for a VN RPG. Easily one and a half Lorens, probably more.
As for the story, characters, and game world, it feels as though they were secondary this time around. The cast is not nearly as colorful as they were in Loren, and the overall story arc was much less compelling. That, combined with the limited and arguably worse romance options made me feel disconnected from the characters and story, and in turn the awesome universe Winter Wolves created in Loren.
All that being said: if you enjoyed Loren the Amazon Princess, you will probably enjoy this game. I may have a lot of negative things to say about the characters and story, but the fact of the matter is that I'm only being so hard on them because the first game was so good in that respect. Tales of Aravorn is still exceptionally well done overall, and a lot of fun to play, even if it will likely just make you nostalgic for Loren. The writing is good, the gameplay is good, it's just really solid all around. Maybe not $25 solid, but solid.

Winter Wolves really went all out with Tales of Aravorn: Seasons of the Wolf; it's a huge game packed with well-written dialogue, and featuring a much deeper combat system than its spiritual predecessor, Loren the Amazon Princess. The whole game feels like a hybrid of a BioWare-style Western RPG and a Japanese visual novel, taking place over four “Acts”, corresponding to the four seasons of the year.
At its heart, Seasons of the Wolf is all about its characters – a diverse group of individuals, all fallen on hard times, who are forced to work together to survive. Difficult themes like betrayal and slavery are juxtaposed with a surprisingly lighthearted tone in the way the characters talk; it can feel a little odd at times, but it makes for a lot of fun moments.
If there's a problem with Seasons of the Wolf, it's that the game is perhaps a little TOO long. Some scenes drag on to the point that the game loses its focus. The ending in particular, while still good, doesn't quite have the “oomph” you'd expect from such an epic experience.
All the same, I love how Winter Wolves attempted such an ambitious project, and with so small a budget. Overall, Seasons of the Wolf has the appeal of a visual novel while still feeling like a full-blooded video game, loaded with great combat depth and customizability – and with a free demo available, it's definitely worth a look.
(Rating: 8/10 “Very Good”)

Tales of Aravorn is a hybrid RPG/visual novel.  The battles are all turn-based, with each class having unique abilities, and I felt that the game, much like Loren the Amazon Princess, was very well-balanced.  Normal is fair, while Easy and Hard live up to their names.  The story, while interesting, is a bit predictable at parts, but the characters are generally a lot of fun.  There's a decent amount of content: probably about 15-18 hours for a first playthrough, with some replay value due to the ability to play as one of two main characters and the various romance options.
To address the current one (1) negative review (by the user durandyl), I understand that he or she went into it expecting a much different type of game.  To be clear, Tales is NOT meant to be a hardcore dungeon crawler or anything of that sort, and you will be very disappointed if you buy it looking for something in that vein.  There is a decent amount of combat, and it's pretty well done, but there is a large focus on the story and characters.  As a result, the game is very text-heavy.  As I mentioned above, this is definitely part visual novel.
It's also important to note that, despite all of the constant mentions of and comparisons to the previous game in this universe, Loren the Amazon Princess, it is not necessary to have played that game to enjoy Tales of Aravorn.  All of the prominent characters are new, the story is not a direct continuation, and the game even takes place in a different part of the world (like entries in the Elder Scrolls series).
For those interested in how this compares to Loren, though...

Tales > Loren (things ToA does better then LtAP): I really enjoyed the addition of an overworld map and some of the refinements made to combat.  The overarching story is probably a bit stronger and less generic, as well.
Loren > Tales: The character classes in Loren felt much more distinct.  In Tales, all of the mage-types, for example, were largely interchangeable in combat, whereas in Loren, each mage subclass had a unique niche, which made it more important to choose your party composition strategically.  Also, I wasn't as fond of the romance options here, but to be fair, I played Loren with the DLC which added some additional love interests; Tales may get DLC later that will do the same.
Overall, a lot of fun, and a definite recommendation to Winter Wolves fans.  For those unfamiliar with Loren or with Winter Wolves games in general, Tales of Aravorn is a well-made game, and will be very enjoyable **as long as you understand what kind of game it is (i.e. not a hardcore RPG, but not 100% visual novel - you will be expected to do combat).**

This was a very good, fun game, but I'm going to approach the review assuming people have played its spiritual predecessor, Loren: The Amazon Princess, as there are some notable differences even though they take place in the same world.
The developer was upfront about making this a departure from Loren--less emphasis on romances (they're still there, just not as many options for all the PCs) and more emphasis on tactical combat. And resource management, at least on Hard or (I can't imagine) Nightmare difficulty. I played on Hard, which would not have been my 1st choice, but did it b/c, oddly enough, a great # of the Achievements you only get by doing so.
Pros:
1) Fun, likable, interesting cast of characters to switch in and out of your combats.
2) This is the 3rd RPG (after Loren & Planet Stronghold) that I've played from WW, and I enjoy the writing a lot. There's humor, there's pathos. Good mix.
3) Art. I really like the clean, anime-like (or is it comic-like?) art these games employ. YMMV.
4) I can only speak about Hard mode, but tactics are everything for a large # of battles, and certain boss battles will have you tearing your hair out trying to beat.
5) Good mix of tactical situations thrown at you (e.g., an underwater fight that robs you of fire-based spells and ranged attacks) throughout the game.
6) Turn-based combat. I find I gravitate towards this in my RPGs more and more. I'm no longer a twitch, Diablo-style player I guess.
Bad:
1) I wouldn't say anything was bad, but I thought some design decisions were questionable. Which leads to...
Questionable/Not sure what to think:
1) As far as I can tell, there's a location (3rd of 4 acts) that's only accessible via a very brief window of opportunity. Once that window closes, it's gone. And w/ it, a reasonable chance for an Achievement that shouldn't have been that hard to get.
2) You can't consume potions, use scrolls, etc. outside of combat. I understand the decision to force you to choose wisely between upgrading gear and using consumables (essential for Hard/Nightmare difficulty!), as money is tight in this game, but I can't understand the rationale for this. Sometimes you have multiple rounds of fights, ending in a boss fight, and if you're beat up from the last round and the new enemies go 1st...you could be in trouble.
3) If you're an Achievement junkie, which dovetails w/ people who like RPGs I believe, be warned this game will require multiple playthroughs to get most of them. For example, you'll only unlock 1 romance + 1 special skill (applies to 1 of 2 PCs). Make the wrong choices, and some boss fights you might have been looking forward to...never happen at all.
4) Not sure I liked a small minority of the art (animals looked crude compared to other foes).
5) It's a constant balancing act for spending what little $ you get, for most of the game. Consumables or better gear? Just accept you'll be able to purchase very little gear and make sure they're decent (not just +1 this, +1 that) choices. You will get some "keeper" items from solo quests. Which reminds me...
6) solo, flashback quests can be a b*tch. Make sure you have liberal amounts of saved games! Also, you don't necessarily need to recreate skills you chose for your PC; some skills I never chose or got later were perfect for solo quests. In addition, you will not be able to get all solo quests, I think, unless you skip certain romance options in the 3rd act.
Alright, don't want this to be TL; DR material. I'm looking forward to the DLC for a 2nd playthrough.

While the first Bioshock had the element of surprise on its side, Bioshock 2 is still very much a game that delivers. The combat has been revamped to flow nicer through things such as duel-wielding plasmids and weapons and a new real time (but sometimes still equally as frustrating) hacking mini-game. There are tons of new tonics, plasmid and weapon upgrades to experiment with, as well. On the story side, I found the father-daughter relationship that drives the plot as compelling as the first game's story. Obviously, Rapture lost some of it's survival horror feel, but it's still creepy, messy and twisted as ever. Bioshock 2 expands upon the setting in the first game and they've done a great job on that. Each new revelation and progression in the story keeps you playing, and while it might feel a bit "been there done that" it's still a lot of fun.
It's a shame that there were so many technical issues though. The sound skipped, stuttered, or otherwise wouldn't play when I was in combat, crashing due to Dx10, and a bunch of jaggys because the engine doesn't support AA. I had to fix a lot of these issues by myself (time consuming as well), when stuff like that should be looked at by the dev team. it didn't change my perception of the game, but it would've been nice if there were patches.
Having said that, Bioshock 2 is a great follow up to Bioshock 1. Reccommended.
