Betrayer is a rough diamond, its beauty and value unmarred by its unpolished edges.
You play as a sailor, stranded somehwere in New England in 1607. As you set forth to reach the nearest colony you realise that something is amiss: deserted colonies, deranged conquistadors and scattered corpses are a gruesome welcome for our protagonist. He soon finds himself a companion of sorts, a woman all clad in red, that will not fight his foes, but will be what little solace he may find in such bereft land, offering a chance for interaction and some sort of guide that helps you remember, to some extent, the humanity of your character.
That is not to say that she will be the only opportunity for interaction you shall find, for there is the "Other World", a parallel, twisted alternate reality of our world is there for you to access; when you are in there you can find lost souls, astray and forlorn. It is your job to help them remember their identity, and make them relive their last, darkest of hours, to piece their past and get to understand what destiny befell the colonists.
And that is where Betrayer truly shines: in order to piece together the various clues and information you must make various forays into the other world, as well as in ours. It is so seamlessly integrated that you go back and forth without ever feeling like it is being imposed in any way, rather, it feels as a logical path. The non-linear and open world nature of the game does help in this regard. Moreover, you find totems scattered all over the place, some of them corrupted; approaching these in the Other World triggers a fight with some guardians, and upon completion will leave the area less populated with foes, making your exploration easier.
As for combat, the Other World has its own share of creatures, creepier than their real world counterparts, and deadlier. In there you may fight spectres, skeletons, and some other creatures. That is not to say that the real world is easy by any means. You have to employ stealth, cunning and skill to survive in the environment, hiding in the bushes, waiting to strike at unwary conquistadors and indians, using the sound of wind to cover your footsteps.
Weapons are SERVICEABLE; they are the game's weakest portion by far. They  feel half-finished, lacking the "oomph" of a proper weapon. No crossbow thud, no arrow whoosh, no musket/pistol detonation feels powerful enough. They do decent damage, though, they just lack the right feel.
Graphics are alright. The game uses the unreal engine, and it does show in the grass and some textures. Yet the character's hands seem taken out of some 2007 game. They are alright, just not what you would expect of a 2014 game. It is worth mentioning that the game is in black and white by default, and it plays beautifully that way, far more immersive. That being said, you can tune the game and give it as much colour as Oblivion's palette, but it will lose its grim charm.
To sum up, a compelling story, an excellent and captivating gameplay and a charming (and eerie!) atmosphere are sure to make Betrayer a game you shall not soon forget.
All in all, I would highly reccomend this: 8.5.

Very good game. AAA.
PROS
1. Multiple choices
There are so many different choices to play the game. You are literally spoilt for choice. You can choose to go pure stealth, go in guns ablazing, disguises and signature kills. Lot of thought put into this. E.g. Turning on the gas and killing in the smoke, putting flammables in the hair gel, setting off the explosive chamber.
2. Sniper Challeng
I love it. All the Easter Eggs, planning + timing, signature kills/hiding the body.
Suggestion :
Co-op Sniper Challenge
4 different maps. 4 directions of a building/camp. 4 snipers at different locations. Work as a team to eliminate the objectives. You can have timed shots. E.g. 2 players snipe 2 guards at the same time. No suspicions raised. Potential problems include lag over the Internet.
3. Cool ways of Killing
Tanto knife is interesting. Signature kills are extremely interesting. Kudos to the developers who had to think of the scenario. E.g. Crushed by weights, electrocuted at the sink, getting police officers to kill the target
4. Detection
Even blood stains can give you away. Dogs can react to your presence. Most realistic.
Suggestion:
Radio Communication
If a person does not respond over the radio, AI sends people to investigate.
5. Prediction
The fire which shows where is a person is going is most useful for planning purposes.
CONS
1. Linear
No matter what method you use, the outcome is still the same. If you have to kill target A, you have to kill target A. It's part of the fixed storyline. While the methods you use to kill can differ, there is only a marginal benefit to killing a person with a bomb or a tanto knife. Compared to altering the entire storyline, it is most minor.
Suggestion
Force a choice. Go to mission A or mission B. You can only choose one to do. The other mission fails by default. Story continues.
2. No interactive multiplayer
Contracts literally fails at this. While you have such a great assortment of weapons and skills, you don't interact with another person. Replaying another person's puzzle isn't that fun.
Suggestion :
Co-op Contract
Imagine a scenario where 47 has to kill multiple targets at different locations. If you kill one, the other(s) run and you fail.
4-Players, 2-4 targets, you can choose to how you want to take out the targets. Add in a non-canonical storyline for flavour. Allow for signature kills. E.g. Assasinate a dictator-general and his right-hand man, if you fail to take them both out, the living one escapes and conducts painful vengeance on innoncents. Signature kill : One temporarily turns off the power generators and the lights (30 second window since there are backup generators), the other puts poison in the food (can't be done normally with the lights on). If your partner is a psycho, and goes in guns ablazing, back him up.
Genocide / Clean up Crew
Let no one escape. Leave no man standing. Kill every last witnes. Instinct will not work in multiplayer. This is similar to the Sisters/Nuns in Hitman Absolution. E.g. Killing a town, killing a camp of mercenaries, wiping out the Agency.
Co-op Sniper Challenge
As above.
3. Mostly physical killing
Where do you get to see the intelligence of 47? Only instance was of psychology was in the Chinatown mission with 3 targets where you get the police officer to kill the target. How about the psychological aspect? E.g. Bribery, misinformation, interrogation.
It's pretty unique. I like it.

I suspect that, in the mid nineties, this game got a lot of attention and attained a certain status because it's an adaptation of a short story that has a bit of a following, but really, it isn't that good.  I mean, taking into account that it's nearly 20 years old..and that the graphics / sound are going to be a bit limited, it still seems that it got more praise than it actually deserved.
Don't get me wrong, I'm all for games that make you think, wonder and want to find out more but the story and challenges in IHNMAIMS really don't do that; they're not intriguing, just frustrating..and it gets worse as you go along.  How do I enter this other area that I need to do so to complete the game?  Well clearly you need to flush a toilet three times!  That must be so obvious as to not need any kind of hint or relevant dialogue.  Further on, I need to inspect this pixel clump with this recently found item (that was another hidden pixel clump) so I can solve the mystery that I didn't realise was a mystery.  Easy!
It's moon logic, but the bad sort.
As I said, I can't really criticise the game for not using modern sound playback - this is mostly limited to parts that are voice acted, but, to be honest, I'd preferred if they'd saved those megabytes and kept to text.  Really, it goes between barely acceptable to cringingly awful.  The main antagonist (voiced by the actual author of the short story) is so bad as to be laughable, the only female character is a horrible stereotype who sounds like she's having *so* much fun.  The nazi doctor is just 'no' - I can only guess that there's a lack of germanic sounding people in the world.  The voice acting / scripting is so bad that I found myself just clicking through it as soon as I realised that it was something that I'd heard before, lest I gnaw my knuckles raw.
Midi music was so badly done that I thought that I'd messed up my midi settings on my PC (I hadn't) and the much talked about 'dark themes' weren't dark at all for one of the characters..and for another were made so ridiculous as to have me giggling in serious scenes.
Lastly, I got stuck on some of the challenges, not because I hadn't worked out what needed to be done, but because I hadn't done things in the exact path that the game expected.  Seriously.  Either allow multiple paths to solutions and trigger off the next event or only allow one path.  Making it so that you have to reload an old save or somehow backtrack does not make for fun times.
On the plus side, it's fairly cheap, it does actually work and it may encourage people to read so to find out why people were so excited about the game.  Oh, and it does come with the proper digital soundtrack, but just not in-game for some bizarre reason.

Forgotten, very (very, very) unpolished gem. Co-op action-adventure with RPG elements, equipment management and items sets, turrets sections, hub towns, side-quests, dialog trees, arenas with high-scores and canon characters like Gandalf or Elrond, but without oryginal voice actors. Potpouri with a surprisingly good and lore friendly story about human, dwarf and elf trying to stop one of Sauron lieutenants shortly before War of the Ring started. I would say it's more faithfull to the oryginal trilogy and Silmarillion - at least they spirits - than many other LotR related products, that came after the movies, like Battle for Middle Earth or Hobbit trilogy.
On the first glance the game is kind of a mess, mixing elements from various genres without greater idea in mind. There are levels, stats, skill trees, boxes with random content and gems for upgrading items, cause RPG. There are combos with streaks and special abilities, cause slashers and spectacle fighters. There is shooting and reviving allies, cause Gears of War. None of them creates greater whole. They just are, trying to do their job and the final result is quite effective. Combat is simple and very button-mashy, but satisfying with it's bloody slo-mo orcs decapitation and exp rewards. Finding secrets is hard (every character can uncover only one type of them, which makes playng with bots kinda stupid), but rewarding player with rare equipment. Levels are basically corridors with a lot of invicible walls, but with some nice looking vistas and big open areas from time to time. Dialogs can be performed only by one player, but writing is good and voice actors are trying their best.
It's also a product, that came one or two years too early and without proper budget. There are hub towns, but only with handfull NPCs. There are 30+ important places on Middle-Earth map, most of them arenas, but only handfull are playable (content of expansion packs that never came?). There is voice chat, but ♥♥♥♥♥♥ one, that can not be disabled. On top of that game have tendencies to crash, and returning to dropped game is hard at best. Oh and you can roll, but can't jump.
But if you can get past low budget, clearly unfinished content and somewhat basic gameplay with almost zero interesting and original ideas you will find satisfying experience, created by competent people, who put their heart into their work, but did not have enough time and resources to deliver something greater than strong 7/10. Worth picking up on sale, especially if you have someone to play with.

This game scratched an itch in me that I didn't really know was there until I played it. It isn't your traditional fare, and the game streamlines the experience of being a space captain. That said it plays like Firefly meets Pirates of the Caribbean. If you never have enjoyed playing games where you line up broadsides and enjoy the sweet victory as your enemy crumples under your withering fire...you might not like this game. If you do, and you like your universe dipped in hard whisky with plenty of grit on the side this game might be just your thing.
Ship combat is fast and furious, with most engagements and missions being over in a couple of minutes. Swarms of fighters, dancing beam weapons, and volleys of missiles light up the fights; all coming at you and maybe the poor sap you hired to protect you. Meanwhile you use a deflector (timed extra shield), main shields, and your armor to protect the innards of your ship while trying to line up a broadside as your turrets pick away at your opponent's shields. Because once someone is down to armor, it doesn't take that long before they are nothing be space dust.
Trading, while simple, is still deep enough to enjoy. There is also mining, bounty hunting, distress calls (and ambushes), dead drop missions, and more to enjoy. You can spend hours alone in the first system building up reputation and your ship before stepping out into the wider galaxy...and you just might.
As much fun as the combat can be, it sometimes falls a little heavily on your gear as to whether you can engage in that fight or not. Thankfully the game does a good job of tracking the threat level as to your chances of pulling off the fight or whether you need to pass or run away. Which even with a medium frigate all in top gear for the first system I'm finding I'm doing more running then fighting...yet. Mission boards also give you a threat level when you take them so you know you aren't walking into a complete curb stomp, but you will feel the sting of defeat if you don't pay attention and especially if you aren't willing to run away until your ship and equipment is more up to the task.
The other issue some might take is that this is all on a 2-D plane. So you don't go up or down with your ship, however fighters and objectives such an mine-able asteroids can be go/be off this plane. Turrets can handle these threats, but only if they can fire in that arc. As I discovered in mining however, you might need more then one of the expensive mining lasers to reach an asteroid depending on the turret placement and ship. They have a decent reach and make excellent short range beam weapons, but mining can be a pain and for as much investment you have to put into your ship to set it up to do right that can lead to some frustration.
Unfortunately the game doesn't feel like it's fleshed out ship wise. There are 21 ships you can supposedly fly over the course of the game, and about half of those will be available to you from the start, a few more unlocked by leaving the first system, and a handful unlocked by faction reputation. It would have been nice to see some heavy armored and fast gunships, or some lighter armored glass cannons. There is a class of ship called 'strike craft' which seems to drop off by the end of the first system.
The fighting can also get a little formulaic over time. I find running while my turrets pick off the fighters before engaging the larger ships to be the best road to success. Trading also can be a pain until you stumble upon the transponder that allows you to see the commodities of stations across the map without having to first dock at them.
If you enjoy broadsides and want a new type of scenario for your space faring adventures, this game might be just what you are looking for. If being a captain of a capital class ship isn't your cup of tea, then you still might want to pick it up on a sale. I recommend even at full price.

Cannot recommend any game that gets stuck in a .NET Framework failed installation loop.
For anyone that doesn't know what that is basically the game tells me it needs to install Microsoft .NET Framework version 4.  Unfortunately the install always fails if you have a newer version of the framework (like 4.5) This causes your system to force restart in a minute.  And when windows boots back up, you're greeted with a message... That installation failed again and that your computer is going to reboot in a minute....
To avoid the loop don't click the close button on the error message.  Instead hit Ctrl+Shift+Esc to quickly pull up Task Manager.  under the processes tab find 'Setup.exe' and click on that and then the end process button at the bottom of the window.   Sure you wont be able to play the game because of the failed non-installation of Framework, but now you won't need to go crazy trying to fix your computer either.
Strangely enough if you boot the game directly from your steam folder you avoid this nonsense altogethor and can hop in the game.

Final Fantasy 13 attempts to fix problems with the franchise that it never had. Unlike previous entries, thirteen follows a very linear structure to create a game with a dynamic combat system where storytelling can become a much larger focus. This works ultimately to its benefit and detriment as Thirteen starts very strong with an intriguing premise and a turn based system that feels very fluid and organic. Mixing and matching roles creates some interesting dynamics. Even enemies that would be considered push-overs can still end your team if you aren’t focused enough.
But it runs out of steam rapidly, beyond the first 5 hours you will rarely see any new gameplay elements beyond unlocking more abilities. Even with how interesting the story can be at times it ends as a grind to the next area/cutscene. For a 40+ hour game it isn’t a nice feeling for players. Personally, I believe this to be the critical flaw of the game. It really could have used some more side content to break up the pace.
However, there are still things to enjoy. While unnecessary the streamlined controls are rewarding to pull off, knowing that you’ve managed to overcome a tough challenge because you knew what to do feels great. The music is amazing, the art style is beautiful and while a bit odd and corny at times; The story has unusual yet touching moments that keep you wanting to see what happens next.
It’s not perfect, but upon finishing the game I can’t find myself able to dislike it. It’s something that must be played to be understood properly. Even at its most frustrating there’s something special about it that kept me going long after I would have stopped many other games for the same reasons. If you’re a big RPG fan I think it’s worth your time to see what this game has to offer.

In Neon Chrome you are a hacker that uses cyborg "assets" to wage an internal war inside of an archology. The game is a top-down roguelike, and thusly things are randomized quite a bit. The player progresses through floors full of enemies, upgrades and containers to loot looking for cash and weapons on their warpath to the top of the tower.
Each time a "run" is started, you pick a character out of three, each with a different role, weapon and ability. Weapons and abilities can be swapped out during your run if you find something more suitable, but roles will determine quite a bit of your playstyle. For instance: hackers can open purple boxes and use purple terminals that will allow them to possible collect more loot, while assassins are able to hide in the shadows and go unseen. A lot of weapons fall under the SMG/assault rifle/burst rifle/shotgun heirarchy, but there are also grenade launchers, rail guns, rocket launchers, heavy pistols and some other fun toys. As you loot more weapons, the weapon "level" increases. You will always find better guns up until the point you reach the top, or, less desirably: die.
In death, however, not all is lost. Your asset is left behind, a stain on one of the floors of game's namesake. The cash you earned is the real prize. This cash can go into upgrading your assets' health, damage, luck, energy and how many cybernetic upgrades they can have, along with puchasing previously found weapons and upgrades to have them from the start of a fresh run. These upgrades are never lost, and you eventually become a powerhouse.
The floors are randomly generated, and while sometimes you will recognize some "tiles", the placement is often pretty well done and I didn't get a "samey" feeling that tends to creep up on roguelikes that make use of tiles for map generation. One of the more interesting mechanics is that many walls, "thin" walls, are able to be shot through with any weapon. Some weapons will take a few shots, but there's nothing quite like firing a rail gun through a wall, nailing three or four guys in the process. In addition to this, there are some special levels that are accessed by taking an alternative exit. These levels are hand crafted mini challenges that are a fun way to break up the randomized mayhem, some of them even being puzzles of sorts. The goal of the top floor takes about an hour, depending on how thorough you are and how many special levels you take on.
Once you reach the end of Neon Chrome, all is not as it appears. The cycle continues, only this time enemies are harder, the layouts are more cluttered with mines, and the loot is more enticing. Your character, which seemed powerful, is now no longer shredding enemies, and the quest to upgrade even more starts anew.
The music and sound design are very good and fit the cyberpunk theme/artstyle very well. There is some voice acting, and it's not bad. Overall, it's a tight, well-made experience.
There is local coop, but I didn't have a chance to try it. There is no plan to include net multiplayer, so if that's a dealbreaker I would skip out on it (though NVidia's gameshare may be a way around that).
TL;DR: I highly recommend this game.

The Last Remnant is one of those games that could have been a fun & innovative title, but ultimately comes up short because of some poor design choices. There are quite a few things that this game did will, but the gameplay and story simply become too frustrating to make it worthwhile.
Pros:
+Fantastic art direction, especially the architecture of the cities.
+At max settings, the graphics are surprisingly good for a game this old
+Combat is fun when it actually clicks, particularly in large scale battles
+Music is very good
+The fetch quests are done in a way that makes them very convenient to do.
Cons:
-Protagonist is incredibly obnoxious and unrelateable, to the point of ruining almost every scene he's in
-Gameplay mechanics are completely inscrutable and unintuitive
-Overarching story is just not very interesting
-The interesting parts of the world (different races, politics of the different cities, etc.) are completely shafted in favor of more screen time for the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ annoying protag
-Difficulty ramps in a way that kills any desire to finish the game about halfway through
This game may be worth checking out for a few reasons, namely the gorgeous art direction and stage design in most of the urban hubs - I seriously cannot understate how impressed I was at the detail put into all the little architectural flourishes. And the game actually is quite fun in the early-mid game, when the characters have few enough skills that the battle systems doesn't collapse under it's own complexity. But it inevitably reaches a point where it requires so much time and effort to actually get the combat mechanics to work in your favor, that it's just not worth the effort. This is compounded by the really horrible MC and lame story, but it's sad that in an alternate universe this could have been the Next Big Thing in RPGs/

So, I have to say that I changed my mind over this game, at least a bit. I first I reviewed as a boring, overpriced and overhyped game but after trying it for a litte while I reconsidered it. I still think that it lacks a lil bit of more violence (guns, knives, fire, nothing new), that is overhyped and somewhat repetitive, but in its repetitiveness I find it fun and challenging.
Let me list its pros and cons.
PROS
-Good graphics. The black and white palette creates a beautiful contrast with the red of blood and explosions.
-Full environment destructibility. Being a major mechanics of the game it's really well done. Every wall can be demolished, every car can be blown up and everything can be shredded into pieces like if it was thrown in a blender, if you have a high caliber machinegun. Everything except saplings. Everything except the f***ing saplings.
-Challenge. If you tought this game was all about shooting unarmed civilians, think twice. I lost hours trying to finish it at Insane difficulty.
-Nice shooting sistem. You can really "feel" the bullet hitting the target (can't explain that really well, sorry) and the weapon roster is wider than I expected.
-Explosions. They're just so gorgeous that they take a place for themselves on the list. And on top of it there's plenty of red explosive containers just waiting to be shot.
-A survival mode. A good (and free) addition the devs made to the game.
-Good developers. They fixed lots of the major graphical issues, plus, they added a free survival mode to the game, which they could have sold as a DLC with no problem. From what I saw it seems that they care about their community and feedback, which is always nice, even if the game is mediocre.
-Fun. This is a very personal point, since I often enjoy violence in games or movies. Keep in mind that this made its repetitiveness waaaaay more bearable.
-Steam workshop. Mods. Pretty self-explanatory.
-Coolest credits ever.
CONS
-Overhyped. This game's fame is almost completely based on the controversity of its trailer. It was supposed to be a middle finger to every moralistic tv service against videogame violence but it just turned out as a pretty shallow work. All smoke and not very much fire.
-Gore. Or rather the lack of it. I expected much more violence, to be honest, expecially in the animations. The goriest one  is just a American History X-style stomp on the victim's head (which pops like a baloon, even if the guy is wearing an helmet).
-Shallow and repetitive. It didn't bother me at all (and to be honest I didn't expected much from the trailer) but it's the elephant in the room. The game's pretty short, the plot is literally "A big bad misantropic guy hates everyone and tries to kill as much people as he can" and almost every side-quest is "Go from here to point B and kill x people/ blow sh*t up". However, if you can get past this you're golden.
-Annoying protagonist. I'm sure that it's all made on purpose but it was one of the most annoying things in the whole game. He's just a big crybaby with the mindset of a 14 year old goth tumblr user that whines about how much he hates the world and its inhabitants. And his lines ridiculously edgy and cringeworthy. I know, it's meant to be that way but a shallow protagonist can't do any good to an already shallow plot.
-Somebody would probably toss the bad driving system into the cons but it really isn't that much of an issue. I mean, it's a thing, but driving is not a major component at all. You find vehicles in every level but you never really have to use them, except for a single side quest.
FINAL VERDICT
Overall I think it is a pretty good game, I expected a bit more but wasn't let down that bad.
I think it's worth its price but I always recommend to wait for sales to buy games anyway. I suggest you to purchase it only if you truly find this kind of content entertaining, or if you want to spend a couple of hours of shooty-shooty bang-bang after a stressful day. In both cases you wont be disappointed.

I sort of like this game, and I sort of wanted to recommend it.  It's good action game in many respects.  I like the pace of the combat, the environment interactions, and things like the level length / difficulty curve seem just right.
However, at some point developers need to figure out that they don't understand in the slightest what roguelikes are all about, and stop trying to shoehorn in 'roguelike elements' that are really just stupid nonsense.  PERSISTENCE IS NOT ROGUELIKE.  Persistence is the very opposite of roguelike!
And on top of that, persistent unlocks that simply increase your damage and health by flat amounts or percentages across all playthroughs are a lousy form of persistence, and this game is chock full of them.   If you desperately needed to include unlocks in order to satisfy those weird people out there who play games for unlocks rather than the actual gameplay, the weapon unlock system is fine and could have been kept pretty much as-is.
This is not a roguelike/lite and the developers do not understand what that even means.  Just stick to making good action games instead of shoveling in bad unlock mechanics.

NEON CHROME:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~
The Neon Chrome tower is a stunning building where millions live under the trust and direction of the Overseer. You come across a slight hiccup in this relationship! You see, the Overseer believes that trust is a two way street, but it seems that you have been red carded and you have just been put on a Removal Status. There is only one thing to do; make your way to the top of the tower and tell the Overseer what you really think about your removal standing. Show him who you are!
Oh, just before you start, let me wish you good luck. . . I think you might need it!
Neon Chrome is top-down shooter set in a cyberpunk tower with some roguelike elements to it.  At the start of the game, you will find yourself in Lab 13 of the Neon Chrome tower. There you will learn how to play and what to look for. As you go through this small but comprehensive tutorial, you will end up in front of a massive screen where the Overseer will explain to you that there is no point to try to eliminate him! In this instance, he will be quite right, as you will be defeated in this hall by strong corporate soldiers.
Next, you will wake up on the immersion chair (a pod)! From here, you will be starting a quest to kill the Overseer. As you become familiar with your operation base, you will notice several options available to you while moving north. The first five options are all about upgrading your characteristics, such as your health, weapon damage, luck, energy and ability slots. The only bugger is that all of them cost money to increase your character levels.
The ability slots can only be purchased ten times, but the other four characteristics go all the way to one hundred. Need to learn how to save, I’d say! A couple of steps further north, and you can choose (pay) which weapons, enhancements and abilities you would like in order to start your next attempt. They will all be listed but you will need to find them during gameplay to be able to select them in your next turn.
When you are done with this, just make your way back to the chair. Sitting comfortably? Great, now three options will come up on the screen and you will have to choose the style of your character. Are you going to be a hacker, a techie, a cyborg or an assassin? Having chosen your character, you will enter the body via a neural link. The lucky winner will raised from his capsule, which is located in the nearby hibernation vault, and off you go!
What you have to do is to find the elevator to get to the next floor. However, it is not going to be easy as you will have to deal with robots, corporate soldiers, mines, pivoting laser beams and other obstacles. For your first couple of games, your weapons will not inflict as much damage as you would desire. So make sure to take as much money as you can. Money is represented by these yellow rectangles which drop every time you kill an enemy, but can also be found in crates with a blue or yellow circle on them. Crates with a purple circle can only be opened by hackers, and hold bigger loots. The blue rectangle will recharge your secondary weapons, so do not hesitate to accumulate them.

You might come across a weapons crate, which will give you better weapons. Weapon upgrade capsules are harder to find but if you do, try to reach them by any means. There are vertical capsules too; when you access them you can add a special ability to your character. If you need to regenerate your health, find a health table. They are quite rare and can only be used once. In some levels, you might find an elevator shaft, which is only for the use of the Neon Chrome military personnel. There are additional levels within a level, and they hold spectacular goodies, but are slightly more challenging. During the gameplay, you can destroy most things within each level, which is really fun! When you die, you wake up in your comfy chair with hopefully a great stack of money to spend, and additional weaponry, too.
In the solo game, you have 28 levels to clear and this is without the sub levels that I mentioned above. You can also play local co-op, up to 4 people.
In regards to the controls, either gamepad or mouse and keyboard are really responsive. The graphics could have been better, in my opinion.
I think the best aspect in this game is the randomised levels (with the exception of the bosses’ levels) which give you great replay-ability.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Randomized levels
-	Good selections of weapons and abilities
-	You can destroy just about everything in each level
-	Interesting enemies
-	Solo and local co-op modes
-	Great replay-ability
-	Good controls
-	Achievements and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Graphics could have been better
Neon Chrome is a really good, addictive top-down shooter - a really worthwhile game to own. Your turn to try to eliminate the Overseer!
9/10

This game belongs to a niche genre popularly known as "Visual Novel", a characteristic of the genre is a heavy amount of text and dialogue between characters that plays out with periodic input from the player which can result in different outcomes. Winter Wolves are excellent at this genre, and I have encountered several decisions that seemed to have little impact at the time, but came up later with unexpected outcomes.
This game, like other Winter Wolves games, also has Classical RPG elements, such as character levels, stat building, item shops that sell various gear and potions, traditional turn based combat, and some adventure elements like a world map that can lead to different battles, treasures, character encounters, and unlock additional conversations.
As you play the game you will meet a variety of characters with their own unique backstories, you can take them with you in battle and talk to them at various points throughout the game to unlock dialogue and build relationships with them that can grow into friendships, rivalries, and romance depending on choices you make. This can effect things as the game progresses.
I'm somewhat picky about the genre, but Winter Wolves is very skilled at it.
I recommend the game with the caveat that if you can't stand reading this game isn't for you, but if you've managed to read this far into the review there is a good chance that you will appreciate it. The game also has some really cool musical scores, so the sound track may actually be worth buying if you're into that.

Very good game. AAA.
PROS
1. Multiple choices
There are so many different choices to play the game. You are literally spoilt for choice. You can choose to go pure stealth, go in guns ablazing, disguises and signature kills. Lot of thought put into this. E.g. Turning on the gas and killing in the smoke, putting flammables in the hair gel, setting off the explosive chamber.
2. Sniper Challeng
I love it. All the Easter Eggs, planning + timing, signature kills/hiding the body.
Suggestion :
Co-op Sniper Challenge
4 different maps. 4 directions of a building/camp. 4 snipers at different locations. Work as a team to eliminate the objectives. You can have timed shots. E.g. 2 players snipe 2 guards at the same time. No suspicions raised. Potential problems include lag over the Internet.
3. Cool ways of Killing
Tanto knife is interesting. Signature kills are extremely interesting. Kudos to the developers who had to think of the scenario. E.g. Crushed by weights, electrocuted at the sink, getting police officers to kill the target
4. Detection
Even blood stains can give you away. Dogs can react to your presence. Most realistic.
Suggestion:
Radio Communication
If a person does not respond over the radio, AI sends people to investigate.
5. Prediction
The fire which shows where is a person is going is most useful for planning purposes.
CONS
1. Linear
No matter what method you use, the outcome is still the same. If you have to kill target A, you have to kill target A. It's part of the fixed storyline. While the methods you use to kill can differ, there is only a marginal benefit to killing a person with a bomb or a tanto knife. Compared to altering the entire storyline, it is most minor.
Suggestion
Force a choice. Go to mission A or mission B. You can only choose one to do. The other mission fails by default. Story continues.
2. No interactive multiplayer
Contracts literally fails at this. While you have such a great assortment of weapons and skills, you don't interact with another person. Replaying another person's puzzle isn't that fun.
Suggestion :
Co-op Contract
Imagine a scenario where 47 has to kill multiple targets at different locations. If you kill one, the other(s) run and you fail.
4-Players, 2-4 targets, you can choose to how you want to take out the targets. Add in a non-canonical storyline for flavour. Allow for signature kills. E.g. Assasinate a dictator-general and his right-hand man, if you fail to take them both out, the living one escapes and conducts painful vengeance on innoncents. Signature kill : One temporarily turns off the power generators and the lights (30 second window since there are backup generators), the other puts poison in the food (can't be done normally with the lights on). If your partner is a psycho, and goes in guns ablazing, back him up.
Genocide / Clean up Crew
Let no one escape. Leave no man standing. Kill every last witnes. Instinct will not work in multiplayer. This is similar to the Sisters/Nuns in Hitman Absolution. E.g. Killing a town, killing a camp of mercenaries, wiping out the Agency.
Co-op Sniper Challenge
As above.
3. Mostly physical killing
Where do you get to see the intelligence of 47? Only instance was of psychology was in the Chinatown mission with 3 targets where you get the police officer to kill the target. How about the psychological aspect? E.g. Bribery, misinformation, interrogation.

Imagine a turn- based old school style JRPG.  Now imagine that instead of giving orders to several characters in a battle, you are instead giving orders to several GROUPS of characters known as unions.  How you organize your characters and unions is up to you.  Want three unions of warriors and two unions of mages?  You can do that!  Each character has their own skill sets and stats like any other RPG, so you can select what role you want them to play and what union you want them in.  There are so many characters to chose from that you can't even use them all at once!
Aside from the main plot, there are also side quests that you can complete.  These no only provide the usual rewards, but you can often hire the questgiver to join your party, and be a part of one of your unions!
The only con is the BR system, but once you know how to level up efficiently, it isn't a problem at all on the PC.  Just make sure you mostly engage in meaninful, challenging battles, and you'll be fine!
Like any other JRPG, it doesn't hurt to have an idea of how you'll advance your characters.  It might be wise to read one or more leveling guides to get an idea of how to properly level and use everyone.  Have fun!

A thrilling sci-fi action shooter/rpg with glaring oversights.
The main segment of the game is fun. While the enemies lack variety (particularly early on) they make up for it with a good balance of tenacity, hardiness, and straightforward challenge that rewards pre-planning and quick wit equally.
But the bosses. Oh dear lord the bosses.
Killing a giant spider with three stages only to, without any real pre-warning that this would happen upon winning, have the boss self destruct in a blast larger than anything you've come to face beforehand, thus killing you and rendering pointless your victory.
Or how about a giant worm who's sole form of attack in his third phase is to fling homing missles out you in massive numbers. I counted at least 6 on screen at a time, all with fairly large blast radiuses, and all of which can and will be launched at you while the boss is off screen.
These aren't challenges because you aren't given any tools to overcome them exept to boost your health for the next run or boost your damage to kill it quicker than it can kill you.
Without these oversights, maybe I could leave a positive review but with them I just can't.
It simply makes the game too frustrating. I feel my time would be better spent elsewhere.
Edit: Going back in, I still believe the bosses are ridiculous, but the game still has some real shining points. While I think they could have been better designed, ultimately they don't destroy the whole product. 7/10

STORY
Each season definitely has its own feel to it and are connected to one another quite well by the story despite their vastly different environment from the previous one. One of my favourite parts was the choices and freedom Summer gave you when selecting which quest to do and how to approach it which was vastly different from the previous season and fed perfectly into the story. Overall I found the story to be very heart warming, amusing and sad at the right parts much like Loren The Amazon Princess which was also created by Winter Wolves and will be mentioned a lot in this review.
At the start of the game you chose to play as one of two Elf twins, the brother Shea or the sister Althea. While all four of the romance paths are open to you the two meant for the other twin will not end in a romance ending. Of the romances I have completed I find them to be well done and fitting for the characters, Chalassa's romance specifically sticks out as quite an interesting one which I enjoyed every second of.
CHARACTERS
All of your party members are completely realised and unique characters which dialogue between feels natural and fitting to their characters. Even once I thought I knew all the characters a couple of them had quite dramatic character development which made my opinion and feelings for that character change entirely.
GAMEPLAY
The game's turn based RPG elements are a huge step up from Loren The Amazon Princess. Each party member have different skill sets which makes the choice of the six you take into battle much more meaningful. Some of the skills require certain conditions on the enemy to be usable which makes some character combinations quite dangerous. Skills require Stamina to be cast and Stamina does not come back after each battle which makes skill usage more tactical but can get frustrating at times.
There is also now an overworld map for each season which has points of interest on them which you click to go to. There are also a couple maps which are used for areas of the game where you have to chose which point of interest to take to move across the map, these areas I enjoyed but I would have liked more of them.
ART
I personally enjoy the art style used for the characters and was happily surprised by the amount of different costumes each one has, Chalassa stands out as the character who I can't think of a single costume I did not like seeing her in. The backgrounds are well drawn just like the characters.
The CG has a different art style to the rest of the game which makes them feel meaningful, they stand out as something else, which they are, much like the moments in the story at which you get them.
SOUND
I usually turn music off in games but I realised as I was playing Tales of Aravorn: Seasons of the Wolf that this game, as well as Loren The Amazon Princess, are one of the few games I actually keep the music on for. I was also pleasantly surprised by the credit song which was fitting for the end of the game.
OVERALL
I very much enjoyed my time with Tales of Aravorn: Seasons Of The Wolf. Winter Wolves have perfectly created all the characters of this game and none of them seem dull, they also improved greatly on the RPG aspects of the game over Loren The Amazon Princess. I found the story to be heart warming in the end and it kept my attention throughout. While I consider Loren The Amazon Princess to be a visual novel with an RPG aspect, Tales of Aravorn: Seasons Of The Wolf is definitely an RPG with visual novel style storytelling.
If you enjoyed the story of Loren The Amazon Princess then I would recommend you get this game since it is just as enjoyable with some nice cameos including one which I feel gives us a taste of what is to come in Tales of Aravorn: Reign of War, which was previously known as Loren The Amazon Princess 2. I also recommend you buy this game if you like RPGs or quality storytelling in video games.

If you consider this game was preceded by some of the best games in the world, this game might look "worse". In truth it's a fun game which I wish I could afford and wish I had time to play. I'd recommend it to open minded strategy fans who understand small variations are what differentiate the whole genre. I'd also recommend it as a good place to start with strategy games. (and yes, civ 5 is equally recommendable, long lived, and cheaper, so you might want to get that first.)
Standing alone, it's enjoyable strategy game, which is well balanced, looks nice, and has an intriguing scenario. It's not new, but it puts a modern game-y-viewpoint on the "how do we live with our planet" questions. While the setting is an alien world, really these questions are all classic debate topics. Gives you something extra to mull over while playing.
Compared to civilizaiton's before... (having played only in the free weekend)...
- other colonies are more peaceful (I didn't get raided immediately by my neighbours)
- the landscape is more interesting - there are more terrain features to work with (impassable and almost impassable terrain, miasma)
- the quests sound idiotic but aren't - they just replace victory conditions. They make more sense.
- tech tree is hugely improved in favor of choice vs complexity. In civ 5, you _have_ to get most preceding techs to precede. In Beyond earth you can specialize, or more importantly you can skip technologies that aren't part of your strategy.
- it seems there's more ability to "specialize" in what you produce as well. Perhaps I've not mastered Civ 5's mechanics, but in beyond earth I _easily_ created a colony who generated a lot of culture and power, and had the virtues which meant a lot of those resources gave enough of a boon to support other resources which I'd sacrificed. This is certainly possible in civ 5.. but Beyond earth makes it clearer what affects your decisions.
Downsides!
- AI behave like idiots still when it comes to democracy (really... one turn they offer something and you counter offer, then the next turn they offer something less useful than your counter offer)
- Enemy turns seem to take a long time to process
- The game is a bit "slow paced" in decisions, possibly because the other colonies are less militant
Simply different
- less factions, and they are less "cultured" (no familiarity, no real history - I love the real history of the factions in Civ 5 and will often read more about them when playing them)
- UI. I'd say it's mostly better than Civ 5, through subtle changes and priotization. A few places seem rusty, but it's nothing unusable.

-Pure skill based gameplay, (almost) everything is a skillshot (some support abilites which can only target allies are "ally closes to your cursor"), movement is WASD

This War of Mine is like nothing I have ever played before. I thought going into it that it was a platformer of sorts, but it’s actually closer to being a real time strategy game. The whole game revolves around keeping a group of survivors alive for the duration of the war, which includes keeping them fed, rested, warm, treated for any sickness (meds) or wounds (bandages) and also keeping tabs on their mental wellbeing, which I learned early on is very important as I lost a character to suicide.
The gameplay basically revolves around activities in your safe house during the day, which include things like building beds, stoves, work benches, etc and then building and managing supplies like food, fuel for the heater, filters for clean water,  and ammo etc.  As night falls, you have to choose which characters will sleep, which will guard and which will go scavenging for supplies. You have to balance sleeping with guarding, as you can’t let your people get too tired, but you also run the risk of getting raided each night by bandits, which leaves you with supplies stolen and possibly wounded characters.
Scavenging at night, now this is where the real fun of it came in for me. You can’t go in guns blazing as you usually scored yourself a pretty quick death. In the end I found the most effective form of combat was to hide in the shadows, and bait each enemy close to me so I could finish them with my knife. But, you have to balance who you kill as killing can have huge consequences on your team’s mental health. In the end it was easier to only kill when needed, as I didn’t have to worry about anyone getting sad or depressed.
All in all I had a heap of fun learning the game, and after having just completed my first play through, I look forward to playing through again with all the tricks that I learnt.  I highly recommend this game for all fans of strategy or even just someone looking for something a little different. Even at full price, I think there is a lot of fun to be had.

Betrayer is quite extraordinary. Its atmosphere is amazing, with it's beautifully crafted black and white world. But it's an empty world, one that needed way, way more content than this, because the gameplay becomes quite repetitive after a few hours, even if the story is mysterious and intriguing.
You end up washed ashore and you have no idea how you got there or where you even are. Moving forward will act as a small tutorial and once you enter the next area the real game begins. Soon you'll find a deserted village, a village where you find a Maiden In Red (which the story is all about) and a bell. A bell that belongs to the village. Restore the bell and you can ring it, and it will instantly transfer you to an even darker world (please note that that's not quite true; the area remains the same, but the enemies and NPCs become different) where ghosts can be found. These ghosts tell a story and it's up to you to find more clues and solve the many mysteries this world has. You can switch between the light and dark world on the fly with the ring of the village bell and both of these worlds contain clues, found as letters or other objects. With the press of a button you will hear voices and sounds that will guide you in the right direction. Follow the sounds to find your next clue(s). An original concept that works very well, especially because it's an open world. I really liked it.
Of course, there are also enemies to be found and these are actually quite tough at times. But defeat them and they'll drop loot. Loot that you might desperately need later on, because the enemies become harder to defeat. Other ways to gather loot is by buying it from a digital salesman in the village or by find treasure chests scattered across the lands. However, if you get slain by an enemy you'll drop all of your loot and you have one try to get it all back. Die before getting it and you'll lose everything, with no chance of ever recovering it (Dark Souls anyone ?).
Enemies can be killed with stealth. Just use your bow to silently take care of them. Or you can kill them with help of the wind. It will mask your sound. Another original concept that works very well. Unfortunately, the AI disappoints from time to time so it's not always the way to kill off enemies. Enemies might never hear you even if you're only a few metres away from them, and other times they come running to you from miles away. It's all over the place and I was disappointed to see a polished game like this have such crappy AI.
There are several areas in the game and exploration is key for solving the stories. But like I said, it becomes repetitive after a few hours because all you do is look for clues, ghosts and treasure chests and kill enemies. There's not much else to do in this game. Now, I do have to say that it kept my interest all the way through (which lasts about 10 hours), mainly because there's no handholding. The lore and stories are yours to interpret. And this is exactly what also made Dark Souls so fun to play. You get small hints of what's happening or happened and it's up to you to think of what might have actually happened. Good stuff !
Betrayer is an excellent game and I'd love to see a sequel. But please, fix the AI and make the world itself a bit more interesting to explore. Recommended !

My understanding is that somewhere in the course of the game you find a way to  "heal" the world and make everything in color again but the game has no quest path to this goal, you just have to guess and hope you get it right.

This game provides you the thrill of controlling an empire that listens to every command you make. Whether it is wiping an entire race from it's existence, or building a giant cannon that shoots the image of god to an enemy home world, either way it's really fun.  You get to choose between three factions, each containing the Loyalists(True Empire) or the Rebels, with various ways of winning the game.
The factions are and contain the following empires:
T.E.C. : Loyalists and Rebels
Vasari: Loyalists and Rebels
Advent:Loyalists and Rebels
Each faction has their own personal upgrades that shared between the the two empires in that faction, along  with their own personal ships, star bases, culture, and more. And depending the empire you choose you have to use different victory options and strategies. And one common thing that all players have to deal with are space pirates. Although they are annoying, they can be dealt with pretty easily especially late game. Your currency for all empires are called credits, along with metal and crystals. In order to have a good functioning empire you need all the three in order to purchase ships, research new technologies, and to grow.
Positives:
Intelligent A.I. (especially in combat)
Detailed ships,planets, and structures
Allows mods (Star Trek, Star Wars, Battle Star Galactica,etc)
High replayability
Easy to learn with helpful tutorial
Negatives:
Ships and structures can sometimes use auto use (Which makes them use a special ability) even after disabled
Pirates generally attack only one empire the whole game, very hard to pay off
Constant connection and save problems when playing online
Constant supervision of planets, ships,etc
That is all I can really remember at this time, note that this review is somewhat incomplete due to my bias opinion and my inexperience in the game. I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys awesome space battles, hardcore strategy, and management.

Before I start I just want to say I am a big magic fan, and I play the game quite a lot.  If you like paper magic then it is probably an obvious choice to like this game, right?  Wrong, the game can be summed up in a few words, grindy, boreing, slow.  You will find yourself playing game after game for just a few coins, these games take the same amount of time as a regular magic the gathering duel so about 20 minutes, but when you lose you get nothing, when you win you get hardly anything.  Eventually you will get enough coins to buy a pack (150, 20 coins each win) to get just 6 cards and only 6.  (6 random cards from the Origins set).  If you for some reason wanted to spend real money on the coins you will be paying 2 dollars for 150 coins, so 12 cards will be 4 dollars.  While you are getting two rares when you do this why would it matter when you get the rares?  You cannot trade them or sell them for coins as far as I know, so rareity is just about useless in this game (my opinion at least, but that is what you are getting in a review).
I am at a point in the game where I cannot get any farther at all.  It takes a vary long time to get enough money for a pack just for the pack to be trash, in a card game like this 6 cards just don't cut it when you have no other way to get cards.
You can probably tell so far my only issues are due to the fact that you don't get enough/good cards when buying the packs and that is somewhat true, however; I also have issues with the interface as well.  Lands tap almost randomly it looks at your hand to decide what mana to tap this is nice for new players that might have trouble tapping the right amount of mana, but for someone that wants to tap mana in a certain ways to get tasks done is just not useble.  When decideing what mana to tap it will always tap the non-basics that have abilities first like Rouges Passage, If I wanted to play a creature on my turn and make thopters on their turn I am unable to do that because the game taps the non-basic before the other lands (I have no idea what the game does if you have creatures that tap for mana, I have not even seen any of them yet, they probably removed them so that they could make the game easy).  I should be able to tap mana how I want to, not how the game wants me to.
While not as big of a deal I also find the strange animations to be distracting, I just wish I could disable them to be more basic (while not quite as simple as MTGO), and often times a large pop-up window covers my oponent's field saying ">NAME< IS MAKING CHOICES"  and I can easily say without a doubt that this is un-needed and is annoying whenever it pops up, most of the time it blocks the choices they make not allowing me to respond even when I stop the timer.
All and all, do not play this game... at all, I do not reccomend it at all and neither will anyone else that is pationate about magic.  If you want to teach someone to play the game don't get this, Magic 2014 is way better for that reason.

A thrilling sci-fi action shooter/rpg with glaring oversights.
The main segment of the game is fun. While the enemies lack variety (particularly early on) they make up for it with a good balance of tenacity, hardiness, and straightforward challenge that rewards pre-planning and quick wit equally.
But the bosses. Oh dear lord the bosses.
Killing a giant spider with three stages only to, without any real pre-warning that this would happen upon winning, have the boss self destruct in a blast larger than anything you've come to face beforehand, thus killing you and rendering pointless your victory.
Or how about a giant worm who's sole form of attack in his third phase is to fling homing missles out you in massive numbers. I counted at least 6 on screen at a time, all with fairly large blast radiuses, and all of which can and will be launched at you while the boss is off screen.
These aren't challenges because you aren't given any tools to overcome them exept to boost your health for the next run or boost your damage to kill it quicker than it can kill you.
Without these oversights, maybe I could leave a positive review but with them I just can't.
It simply makes the game too frustrating. I feel my time would be better spent elsewhere.
Edit: Going back in, I still believe the bosses are ridiculous, but the game still has some real shining points. While I think they could have been better designed, ultimately they don't destroy the whole product. 7/10

I have yet to finish the game but I'm currently at the last quarter of the game:
The world of The Last Remnant is interesting with different species inhabiting it, giving me a feeling like embarking on a journey into the world like I have never seen before. The story on the other hand is generic story you can find from almost every JRPG with characters that feel mostly copy pasted in from other games, with few exceptions. Still, the story isn't actually bad, just dull, and the characters rarely come out as annoying.
Main difference to your average JRPG experience is the battle system. Instead of micromanaging every single member of your team in turn based battle where you can see the order in which each of the character will act, The Last Remnant places you in charge of units of several characters, whom you give more broader commands of either attacking, healing or some variation between these two and the characters act accordingly from there. After the initial shock the battle system turns out to be surprisingly easy to learn. Sounds like nice idea for step away from all the micromanagement you usually encounter in these games.
Unfortunately, once the encounters get little harder, the battle system wets itself. The actions available for characters seem to be randomized so if you end up losing and fighting the same boss twice, the available attacks will change, making learning and readjusting your plan almost impossible. If several of your units are in need of healing at the same time, commanding your unit to heal is turns into game of dice and too many times you will find your team members topping those who have taken only few hits while ignoring those that are at the brink of dying. Luck plays some part in almost every RPG I have ever played by adjusting how effective your actions are (dice rolls for damage or who attacks first etc) but rarely have I encountered a game where its a dice roll whether your team of heroes decide to do what you want or not. I have fought encounters that I have lost within two rounds and won within four turns right after my initial loss without changing my tactics and I can credit this to nothing else but luck that has way too great influence for the combat than it should.
Overall, at its best The Last Remnant is enjoyable, although generic JRPG. At its worst it is unfair duel where you lose your fight not because of a bad decision or unsuitable tactics but because suddenly the game decides that you have to bring knife to a duel with guns, and your second might stab you into eye with it instead of giving it to you when the duel starts.
You could enjoy this game, but there are way better games out there so why not play those instead.

Neon Chrome was published and developed by 10tons Ltd, with the game being a ruthless top-down shooter with some rogue-like elements. The game is set in a sci-fi cyberpunk structure throughout the game which really sets the mood of the game and the enemies also.
The game itself starts you off being chased through Neon Chrome, the mighty overseer doesn't trust you anymore and trust is what the society Neo Chrome is built upon. You get caught and you wake up in a Total Recall chair from your latest failed attempt to take down the overseer. But you have many more chances to get this overseer and kill him. The game itself revolves around you trying to kill the overseer, progressing through floors whilst killing enemies along the way and trying not to die as you get through these enemies. But if you die, it's okay because you can just reconnect to another pod and try again through the floors. After getting through 4-6 floors you will come across a boss room, if you are able to kill this boss without dying then you will be able to respawn at that floor with the pods.
The game follows the general rogue-like elements throughout, with the general arsenal assault rifles, SMGS, shotguns ect. All of these general weapons have their stats from attack damage to range. When you die and get reconnected to another pod, you will have a special randomly selected special active ability that you can use as you shoot through your enemies. One of these special abilities can be shooting a rocket at your enemies doing extensive amounts of damage than normal weapons, you will have to use these abilities in order to survive through the tower.
But the game really shines through the destructible environment and the amount of strategy that is included throughout the game. With the game having a sort of strategy side to it, you will have to take advantage of the destructible environment in order to shoot enemies from behind which does double damage as long as they don't detect you. Being able to destroy walls and take advantage of the this will make you be able to get through the level with minimal damage taken.
The enemy AI isn't exactly the smartest, you can kind of manipulate them to your advantage and kill them easier than you are intended to. But, with most of the enemies being fully aggressive they can give you some problems if they start surrounding you and hitting/shooting you. The game can sometimes make the game from slow to really fast paced sending in reinforcements making for some really great gameplay. These reinforcements aren't just some normal guys that come running at you, there is about 15-20 of them shooting at you and throwing grenades all at once making the game fairly difficult at times.
The game, as it is a roguelike, is suppose to be difficult and ruthless throughout. The smallest mistake in the game can cost you the current run especially when it comes to the boss fights and explosives that will make you lose quickly. The health is scarce throughout, as you will struggle to find health when you need it the most.
The game does a good job with the currency of the game that you will find as you play through each of the floors. Exploring through the floors will reward you with better weapons ect to make your characters more powerful. With the credits that you earn you will be able to up your stats by buying each of the upgrades, from your health to your attack damage.
This game seems to feature full controller support or keyboard controls. For me personally I would choose to use a keyboard and mouse, just for the better accuracy when you shoot enemies instead of a controller which doesn't have as much accuracy. The controls doesn't seem to include a invincibility frame such as a dodge roll, this also makes the game feel much better with keyboard and mouse.
With the graphic side of the game it isn't as impressive as it seems. The cyberpunk theme throughout the game does seem to get a bit boring after playing the game for a hour or so, everything starts to look the same with the same dark and light colour throughout. I think that more variety would really make the graphics look better.
+ General weapons
+ Respawning you will get a different special ability
+ Destructible environment
+ Strategy i needed to survive
+ Aggressive AI makes the game more difficult
+ Lots of replay ability
+ Ruthless and difficult gameplay
+ Controller Support
+ Steam trading cards and achievements
- AI could use some improvement
- The graphics seem to let the game down a bit
So the final verdict of the game, this game is a exceptional good roguelike cyberpunk game that has a lot of replay value and exploration value of the game. The game is ruthless and unforgiving at times, which just makes the game better all together making you need to be more precious with your shooting. The game seems to fall at it's kinda stupid AI and the same look of the graphics. Overall I would highly recommend this game to rogue-like/lite lovers!

Neon Chrome is an addicting top-down shooter with rouge-like gameplay, placed in cyberpunk, colorful world. Since the very beginning of a game, players are greeted by an awesome soundtrack that will introduce you to the pace of the game. At first, the gameplay might look a bit chaotic and maybe even overwhelming, but once you'll get used to it, oh boy - the only thing you'll want to do is spread even more chaos! Or who knows, maybe you'll decide for a more sneakier path? It's all up to you!
This game is literally excellent and perfect. I might have not played a lot of it
(I'm a busy man, alright?) but I can't wait for the next time to get in and play it. It's also highly addictive, so far, I can't find any serious cons. Literally perfect. The replay value is great thanks to randomly generated levels and all those abilities and unlockables. Surroundings are nearly 100% destructible, so the only thing that stands in your way to burst through the wall into a room full of enemies is a wall that you'll need to take down! A.I. is not stupid, so don't worry, it's not one of those slashers where enemies just run at you, doing nothing. Story seems pretty good once you'll listen to it, hopefully I'll get to its end one day. One thing that surprised me is the diversity of all add-ons like combinations of weapons and abilities, unique abilities to specific characters and tons of upgrades you get going along the game - believe me, you'll have tons of fun looking for the best combination that fits your playstyle. One thing that would be nice is multiplayer, co-op or versus, it would be fun either way.
Do I recommend it? Hell yeah, just get it and play, you won't regret it!

Overall, I'm pretty bummed that this game wasn't very fun/good.  I can't really recommend this to anyone because Civ 5 pretty much did everything this game does, but better (two exceptions being the tech tree, maybe, and then I liked the virtue system from what I played anyway).  The opening intro for the game is pretty sweet, though.
Admittedly I don't have much time in this game (I only played during the free weekend, and even that was only ~5 hours, because that's all I could stomach - and I have almost 700 hours in Civ 5, 230 hours in Endless Space, 1600 hours in EU4, etc), but I don't think I would pay more than $10 for this game - and even then I would have some hesitance.  Calling this game a mod may have been somewhat generous, as it's more like a watered down reskin.
The UI is pretty much horrible; they removed the demographics stats portion entirely; they literally just renamed the mechanics and changed the icons (happiness is now health, money is now energy); you just build the base unit of each unit type, which is then upgraded (automatically) to the next one that you pick when you raise your affinity (which is pretty much only raised based on what you learn in the tech tree); the alien mechanic is kind of weird(?), you can not attack aliens and do the Harmony affinity, but they still occasionally attack you and ruin your trade routes, so it's just best to kill them all anyway apparently; the diplomacy options are all copy and pasted from Civ 5 (except for earning favors I guess now, which it wasn't exactly clear how that actually works out in practice); and the whole premise for the game, mankind embarking off into space for their salvation...only to battle against each other and repeat exactly what they did on earth that they were trying to escape/fix - sure, I guess.
The only two somewhat redeeming parts of this game are the tech tree and the virtue system, of which I'm still undecided on the tech tree since it's seemingly not really organized any way specifically and different techs and affinities are strewn about throughout; but the virtue system is pretty cool, I like it (at least what I played of it so far anyway).
With all the space themed stuff and technological advances, it really just made me want to play Endless Space or Galactic Civilizations III. I wanted to like this game, but I'm not even sure expansions could save it without overhauling the UI and adding a little more depth. Not to mention there's no portraits for any of the pictures for units and buildings, just words and icons. The only other thing that was kind of cool was that cities start out at level 0 and have to gain enough influence to become a full-fledged city.
Also, for some reason, you see where the computers all start, for basically no reason whatsoever. Oh, and did I mention that Stations (the city-state equivalents that only work with a trade route now) just randomly spawn places? Like when you're ~2 turns away from settling that area with a colonist on the way down? Basically my reaction to the game as a whole, but specifically when that occured:

Massive Change of a Negative Review, BIG TIME!
I gave up after a good go at this game, maybe I didn't add enough salt. But now, this week. Wow things have changed. This review is based on 3.61 (October 2015)
The game is still fantastically buggy, still very Hardware Hungry. But in terms of content, ironing out the bumps and offering a load more. Its a very enjoyable game to play.
I delved straight into the Teladi Outpost gameplay, one that I pretty much didn't bother with when I got it free on release. Recommended. You start, like all gameplay modes with a few ships but in a very hostile environment. Do your thing of fighting off all the huge bosses from blowing up all your ships in a single swipe. More importantly its huge, its every sector all in one galaxy, it takes an half hour + to visit each sector in a loop. They mean it when they say its the biggest sandbox this side of the galaxy.
The game play is very very full on, you really need to think. From taking over ships with the reworked marine system (experience) to trading long term. You find a gap in the market, the economy is real and is effected by war. You stations take time, but again due to the nature of the game you can change this by picking holes in the economy or again starting some fight with a company you either don't like or can do without.
After a while you see your pockets filling up. You expand your power through might and logistics, buying bigger, better ships to defend your income. This is where the Teladi Outpost DLC really got me. Its such a profitable zone that needs exploiting.
All in all if you have free time (single) and enjoy a game that you need to work and develop. Sit at your PC on your day off ready with plans and ideas you want to work on this game is great!
The bad bits are still quite strong in the game, for me out weighed with the shear level of economic, graphical and challenge detail this game offers so im still happy and wont shelve it. But simple things like upgrading a ship that gets stuck inside a station. Or crashes (save save save). The game is a huge hardware hog, personally im happy with this, it means the games working. Lots of ram, big CPU and an okay GPU is all you need. I have an AMD 8350 @ 4.875ghz, the game uses that at 80% most of the time. And when a lots going on, a war in another system it struggles, as in fps will drop to 30/40. Not the worst thing in the world but needs to be noted if your expecting 60fps or go playing with the graphics settings (low low low) Its still CPU intensive.
If you read other reviews including metacritic, it seems everyone wants perfection. UI super simple, not ending up stuck inside a ship, no occasional crash etc etc. IMO a quicksave (like in olden days lol) is a lifesaver and common sense. Try to look over problems with (olden days) attitude. Its a huge undertaking, massive, but no other developer could have come close.
The next X game is in the works, from my experiences in this game and if I was in power this game would be local networkable. Have a second computer on a gigabit network dealing with a few things while my PC deals with the other half and the game stuff (draw calls etc). But with DX12 in the works, I think this game would benefit with an API that can do much more efficient calculations  via the GPU. This game has ships not just milling about but constantly conscious (brilliant).
Verdict.
Its not a failed game, its a big and surprising hiccup game  form a developer everyone thought would pull it off. Try it again if you have it. Try it if you don't, its very playable, slowly improving, frustrating at times but is still a very very good game. I cant wait for the next!!!
EDIT:
The game is still played a lot. Its far from dead. Looking forward to seeing what 4.0 will bring.

I heard this game wasn't very good, but after getting it in the 2K humble bundle I gave it a shot. It's much better then most people let on. The biggest real complaint that it is very similar to the first game in almost every way, and by that I mean Bioshock 2 feels more like a expansion then a full blown sequel. It keeps all the strengths and weeknesses of the first Bioshock.  The story is filled with plot holes, but it's still pretty good. The characters themselves feel well written, even better then the original.
Most of the new weapons work differently but fulfill the same purposes as their Bioshock 1 counterparts. Although some of them are really enjoyable (Especially the Drill). The plasmids and gene tonics have been rebalanced, althought they still end up with the same problems as the original, some just end up being way more effective then others, I'm looking at you Winter Blast.  The biggest improvement would be that you can wield your plasmids and main weapons at the same time. The research camera returns in a new improved form as well as the same weapon upgrade system. The terminals that had allowed you to build things seemed to have been scrapped however. The hacking system has also been redone, it's not really better then the original, but it works. While there are some new enemies, most are recycled from the first game. Difficulty wise the game is not hard, I easily beat normal without dying once on the first playthrough.
The engine appears to be beefed up a little bit, but its not a whole lot different. There is still a lot of graphical beauty in the game, the attention to detail was not lost in this installment. Unfortunatly without some ini editing or disabling directx10, the game tends to have crashing problems for a lot of people.
At the end of the day I had a blast with this game. Sure it could have been more, but it still provides a fun experience. I'd definitly recommend it if you liked the original and can pick it up cheap on a steam sale or something.
TL:DR Summary: If you liked the first Bioshock, this is pretty much more of the same and you will probably enjoy it.
