This War of Mine is like nothing I have ever played before. I thought going into it that it was a platformer of sorts, but it’s actually closer to being a real time strategy game. The whole game revolves around keeping a group of survivors alive for the duration of the war, which includes keeping them fed, rested, warm, treated for any sickness (meds) or wounds (bandages) and also keeping tabs on their mental wellbeing, which I learned early on is very important as I lost a character to suicide.
The gameplay basically revolves around activities in your safe house during the day, which include things like building beds, stoves, work benches, etc and then building and managing supplies like food, fuel for the heater, filters for clean water,  and ammo etc.  As night falls, you have to choose which characters will sleep, which will guard and which will go scavenging for supplies. You have to balance sleeping with guarding, as you can’t let your people get too tired, but you also run the risk of getting raided each night by bandits, which leaves you with supplies stolen and possibly wounded characters.
Scavenging at night, now this is where the real fun of it came in for me. You can’t go in guns blazing as you usually scored yourself a pretty quick death. In the end I found the most effective form of combat was to hide in the shadows, and bait each enemy close to me so I could finish them with my knife. But, you have to balance who you kill as killing can have huge consequences on your team’s mental health. In the end it was easier to only kill when needed, as I didn’t have to worry about anyone getting sad or depressed.
All in all I had a heap of fun learning the game, and after having just completed my first play through, I look forward to playing through again with all the tricks that I learnt.  I highly recommend this game for all fans of strategy or even just someone looking for something a little different. Even at full price, I think there is a lot of fun to be had.

While this game failed to match the quality of it's predecessor, it's still worth a playthrough. It was said that one of the reasons Irrational Games did not participate in the development of this sequel was because they wanted to do something different other than just a standard return to Rapture, and unfortunately, that's precisely what this game did.
The main villain, Sophia Lamb, felt like a weak attempt to re-create the sensational Andrew Ryan from the original Bioshock. I never really felt a sense of peril or impending doom while playing, I just sort of wandered through Rapture once more, waiting for something of any significance to occur. While the Big Sisters did prove to be a challenge, I would hardly consider the encounter with two of them simultaneously to be an excuse for the game's only boss battle.
However, I still recommend this game for a number of reasons. One of those reasons being the fact that playing as a Big Daddy (Subject Delta) is TONS of fun. In the previous Bioshock game (and in Infinite, for that matter) the weapons you start out with are fairly weak, and you will most likely discontinue using them quite quickly. In Bioshock 2 however, the Drill that you start out with (and obviously never lose) is incredibly powerful, and the Drill Charge maneuver is a fantastic way to off pesky splicers in one punishing blow. Additionally, playing as a Big Daddy makes you feel even more invested in the Little Sisters, because they constantly praise you and look up to you for guidance and protection, and this may only apply to me, but it's an uplifting feeling.
On another positive note, this game boasts a significant graphical improvement over the first Bioshock. Yes, it was released 3 years later, so improvements of this kind are expected and perhaps even thought to be a given, but one still has to admire Rapture with even more vibrant details.
One small thing that I wanted to add, and this is about as nitpicky as they come, but I'm curious if there was a potential voice acting change with the splicers you confront on a regular basis? For some reason a lot of them sounded as if they were from Jersey, almost like the cronies you face in the Batman: Arkham franchise. Again, it's an irrelevant thing to complain about, but I couldn't help but miss the sound of proper insanity that the splicers emitted in the previous game, it added an undeniable eery element.
Overall, I would give this game a 7/10. You're not going to regret it if you play it, and you're probably not going to regret it if you don't. However, if it's been your dream and intense desire to play as a Big Daddy since the first Bioshock, then this game won't disappoint in that department.

Betrayer: Action, FPS Horror, Exploration, Mystery, all rolled into one game.
You find yourself shipwrecked and go to the new english colony in the new world only to find all its inhabitants are gone.
Seek after clues to find out what happened here, in this survial/adventure/mystery/horror.
The most immediately obvious feature of note is the games art which is in black and white with red highlights, is visually striking and conveys information of note to the player though these visual signals. However it can cause the game world feel dull and sterile after a time and thankfully there is an option for the game to be switched to full colour.
The game is semi open and each zone is large with many thing to find, hopefully leading to the discovery of what happened to the lost colony, However most of these clues boil down to finding notes and objects, which when assembled automatically avance the story with out input from the player, as long as you have the relevant clues the mysteries auto solve as is too often the case with mystery games, the mysteries in themselves are however enjoyable enough to compensate for this.
But probably the biggest element you're interested in, is that of Horror. Monsters deal alot of damage and can kill you quickly, this is balanced by the fact that they in turn can killed quickly by the player. In fact the very first monster encountered in the tutorial is one shotted and this unfortunately kills that horror vibe as the monsters never seem threating afterwards.
Its a shame to because the period weapons are done well, the slow reload on a musket can add some genuine tension as the shot alerts all nearby enemies and they rush you, the fact that they are a one shot to most enemies is balanced by the large numbers in an area. The obvious strategy then would be to use stealth to thin the ranks with silent bow weapons before engaging, but bows are unreliable and can arrows might bounce off armour, which wouldn't be bad as it could again add tension to the moment, except for the comedic clang sound when this happens.
I had briefly thought that maybe using melee only would improve this but as it turns out its actually easier to slash with your knife that to shoot anyone.
All of this makes the game seem poor until you reach the dark world sections the sudden trasistion to this other world is startling and as the world breaths it adds a serious creep factor, monsters here are more accurate and deadly and could be a threat forcing stealth to avoid these creatures, but they tend to appear in unavoidable ambushes which encourages players to simply run about without worry. A similar problem occurs with future enemies who also seem to want to encourage stealth but end up encouraging the opposite.
All in all it seems like the bad would outweigh the good but theres still much here to reccommend, the art, the atmosphere and the weapons are enjoyable and the game is too, you just might not want to go all the way with this one, Play it until you're done rather than to finish.

I prefer Bioshock 2 to the first game.
The story is much tighter this time around, and doesn't suffer from all of the third act problems that the first game does. It develops its characters, themes, and setting much more naturally. Sophia Lamb is a great antagonist for the story and her worldview and history inside Rapture not only build her character, but develop Rapture and it's inhabitants--Rapture feels like a place people actually lived in. Motivations are still complex, but I found that they were clearer than the majority of those in the first game. The game also does a better job of weaving the choices you make in the game into the narrative. I found myself a lot more emotionally invested in the story of Bioshock 2.
The gameplay is more intuitive and the plasmid/gene tonic/weapons upgrade system has a better balance. For example, the oddly redundant Chemical Thrower is gone, and it's abilities have been integrated into the plasmids. In Bioshock 1, there were a series of weapon upgrade stations scattered across the map offering two upgrades per weapon. In Bioshock 2, each weapon gets a third upgrade that unlocks after unlocking the two previous upgrades. The catch is that there are far less upgrade stations across the game, so you have to think more carefully about what you choose to upgrade. No longer requiring the player to choose between having a plasmid
weapon equipped makes a big difference in developing strategy for new areas.
Graphically it holds up better, things are sharper and it looks like the textures have a higher resolution (or are simply optimized better). There are other small details that have been altered slightly from the first game but make a noticeable difference. The little sisters don't tiptoe the line near uncanny valley anymore and actually sound like children. There's more variety in the audio diaries you can find. Hacking is no longer a frustrating minigame. Colors are used in the art direction to greater effect be it the red glow of the Big Sisters or the pinks, blues and greens of sea life encroaching on Rapture. Just small things like this.
Additionally, Minerva's Den is a great short story and DLC with its own unique gameplay mechanics. It is also worth picking up.

If BioShock was a dumbed down spirital sequel to System Shock, then BioShock 2 is  yet another step along the "no thinking necessary" path. I still love it though.
The story picks up some years after the original but still takes you back to Rapture - I would say it is very much worth playing the first one before you play this one as there are plenty of references that you'll miss otherwise. There are loads of audio logs. The story is well done and compelling and whilst it's reasonably straightforward you do still get to make some decisions that will effect how it plays out. The combat system got an upgrade too, allowing you to integrate a ton of passives while you mix plasmids (think magic) fired from your left hand and weapons used in your right all at the same time. Plus higher level plassmid skills have some interesting interactions available to them.
This is very much more linear though with minimal off track areas to explore, no going back to previous areas etc.
One of the main mechanics in the game sees you protecting Little Sisters while they harvest ADAM. Because you can choose when you start you can set up the area you are in to be as lethal as possible but I have to say these did annoy me  on multiple levels. I mean sure, she gathers and monsters come and attack - that much is fine. But when they gather and they aren't with you... the hoards of monsters are notably absent. When you have cleared an area and set her down to gather the monsters do alway come from all directions and this will include things like hoards of monsters springing from a closet you already searched that has absolutely no acessways in or out of it other than the one door...
Logical fails annoy me. *sigh* And there are others. Some of the layouts are really weird and you have attacks like insect swarm which - okay I totally get insects everywhere stinging you is bad... but when you cast it on a creature encased in head to toe armour that is entirely sealed (they are waterproof at least) why would that annoy them?
This also is a game which delights in going "Surprise! We locked the doors and now we have a hoard of monsters coming, see if you can survive!" which is not really something I like in this type of game although that may just be wishful thinking on my part as to the exact nature of the game.
Nevertheless it's still ridiculously fun to play and remains one of my favourites.

The Stanley Pereble is a first person narrative based game that is centered around the art of choice. In the game, at first it seems like you have very little control over the game, there are no weapons or intense action sequences, but then after playing the game through multiple times you will see that there is much more that meets that eye. Over the course of the game you are presented with many choices that impact how the game plays out. One playthrough you might be trying to escape an office complex, another has you climbing through a glitched window, and another might end in the player killing themself. This is just scratching the surface of the game, and there are many easter eggs and seceret endings hidden throughout the way that you can play through the game several times and still not have a clue about their existence. Another strong point of the game are the achivements, the achivements in the game can range to anything from 'quit and reload the game', to 'don't play the game for 5 years'. I personaly have hunted down all of the achivements and it was a fun task, but I'm not going to linger here. Overall the game has a great atmosphere, great gameplay, and TONS of replay value. I would easily give this game a 10/10.

This is the most twisted game I have ever played, you start the game with 5 tortured prisoners being held by a psychotic computer named AM (he is voiced by Harlan Ellison, the guy who made this game with Cyber Dreams & the book version that he wrote), it's a choice driven point and click adventure game so you can pick any character or decision you want.
As you progress through the past of these 5 characters you'll feel what they feel about themselves like for example Gorrister's Guilt, Ellen's pain, Benny's ignorance, Nimdok's desires for torture & Ted's lust. The main goal of the game is to either satisfy AM by making the wrong choices or you can fix the past by making good choices.
The whole point of the game is to lose, there is no hope for humanity & overall if you feel that games aren't dark enough then play this awesome classic. (Warning if your sensitive to torture, murder, satanism, sacrifices, lust and other depressing subjects that the game tackles then this game isn't for you)

Alpha Runner is as simple and retro of a game you can get.  All you do is grab orbs (of sorts) and then the orb moves to the next platform.  The level is one continuous level that never ends.  It's all about seeing how many orbs you can collect while navigating your way through the procedurally created levels.  You are faced with spikes on the floor, circular saws, pounding "boulders" and of course the open space between platforms.  The game, again, is quite simple though it can fulfill that casual gaming itch you may have.  I wouldn't recommend this game if it wasn't for the dev taking my idea.  Originally your character would change, graphically.  However, the gameplay wouldn't change at all.  I offered that he give each graphical character a unique trait, and he took off with it.  Now you randomly get a different graphical character with a specific skill like double jumping, fast movement, etc...
If anything, get this game to support the dev for being open minded to suggestions and listening to those who play their game.

Essentially Firefly: The Game, if the Serenity was a frigate or destroyer. Or Han Solo: The Game, if he never picked up that farmboy on Tatooine, and if Jabba had never put a price on his head.
Rebel Galaxy is not a complicated game. It's restricted to a 2D plane, for one. Missions come in a few varieties. All systems look and feel the same. Combat is pulled straight out of Assassin's Creed IV: Black Flag, and is a far cry from the space battles in Homeworld.
All that said, it is an extremely focused experience. Space is a crowded place in the Rebel Galaxy, err, galaxy. The game itself is as recommendable as any of its obvious predecessors and inspirations, such as Elite, Privateer, and Freelancer. Load up a ship full of beam weaponry, and every capital ship engagement feels like something out of Freespace 2. And the main quest line, while not inspiring in any way, never outstays its welcome.
If you could never get into something like Elite: Dangerous, Rebel Galaxy is that game with all the fat trimmed off, and injected with some actual gorram personality.

Alpha Runner is a fun little platformer game. You have a few different game modes with different dificulties.
#1 Normal
Normal mode is an endless mode where you need to collect one point after another while jumping from platform to platform. You need to avoid getting hit by bad stuff and might encounter mini games along the way. Your character is random each round and might come with a bonus (extra speed, less gravity [...] ). You can play as long as you survive.
#2 Speedrun
The goal is to complete the stage as fast as possible while beating a certain # of platforms and avoiding death. Character is random!
#3 MLG
Basicly Hard Mode. Same as Normal mode but platforms disappear more quickly and there are some... extras. Character selection is random again.
#4 Practice Mode
You can play as long as you want, nothing counts.
There music is fitting the game and did not get annoying during my hours of gametime. The achievements are okay to reach with 1 exception - getting 200 points in Normal or MLG. That one is very hard, but still reachable.
I totally recommend this game!

*Lore, Setting, Environment: Best I've seen.  11/10
No seriously, this lore is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing, I highly recommend looking up on the internet all the Fabula Noval Crystallis lore you may not understand after you beat the game, there's a lot of great things to miss, and alot of villain motivations explained through the very rich lore.
This is a flaw of the game but you actually have to read the datalogs too (and avoid being overwhelmed by the event recap ones).
*Story: hot garbage in the way it is told, unlike the lore.  Some cutscenes are beautifully directed and done, most are not.  Simply put: don't expect anything to be too coherent as you playthrough.  Prepare to cringe.
*Characters: garbage for the most part.  Prepare for Sonic-the-Hedgehog levels of edginess and cringe.  I liked Sazh and Vanille at least.  Hope and Lightning grew on me and developed at least.  Fang is pretty detestable.  Snow had slight hints of depth but is mostly cliche.  Overall though, didn't play for the characters, they were mostly just "there", at least I enjoyed Sazh and Vanille.
*Gameplay: excellent.  I really love the way the roles interacted and battle mechanics.
Buffing, debuffing, weaknesses, role bonuses, defense penetration through stagger, paradigm shifting, it all mattered in various encounters and was very fun to master.
Some random enemies have a lot of HP so battles can take a little while, which sometimes was not fun.. and until you had significant customization which was around chapter 11, you were basically forced to play a certain way in fights if you wanted to do it quickly.  But this was also a good thing since it made the game challenging and worth figuring out.
*Graphics/Music: 11/10
*Game design as far as pacing and chapters go: poor.  10 chapters feel like tutorials, then the last 3 chapters are when things get good and suddenly the game decides to end lmao.
Also, the memes are real, 90% of maps are basically a linear hallway, albeit there is easily 60+ hours worth of content like this so it was fine. Hitman Absolution is a wonderfully done and fairly linear stealth based assassin game that can provide a lot of replay value.
As the name implies, Hitman Absolution has you taking out specific targets as you move along in the story. It’s split up into 20 chapters which you can replay and revisit at any time. The story itself is very easy to follow along and sets itself up very quickly. You are treated to a large amount of cut scenes throughout the game which helps flesh out the story greatly. They are really well done.
The manner in which you go about completing the mission is up to you. You can go in blazing with your guns or you can take a silent and indirect approach. The game favors the silent type of play-through but does not restrict you if you want to go around with your guns. It provides the means and mechanics to do things both ways which is
!
The detection, cover, disguise, sneaking and combat mechanics all work very well together. I really can’t remember any complaints. I will note that I wanted to use my guns a lot but had to force myself to go about it silently to get the most amount of points per level. Your points are based on a variety of things, including how you take out your target.
The graphics are very, very good. Textures are all very sharp and highly detailed. I ran the game on Ultra settings and maintained a constant 60fps @1440p. Fantastic.
Sound,music and voice acting are also very good Adding to the environment nicely and giving you nice audio clues when events happen in the game.
Replay value is huge on this one. Each mission has a number of various challenges you can complete. Don’t worry as you don’t have to complete them in one run. You can replay a mission to specifically get one challenge you need. Once you unlock it during gameplay, it stays with you forever. A very nice thing to do. You can also go into contract mode and play or create special contracts other players have created. The contracts are replaying a level specifically how someone did it. Marking whatever targets, using whatever weapon and whatever disguise they want. You then try to complete that. It’s a nice addition that will let you continue playing even after the campaign is done.
+Fantastic graphics 60FPS
+Sound and music are good
+Story is good and easy to follow
+All mechanics in the game are done well (a huge plus here)
+Replay value is high
+Anti-climactic ending. It tied up the story but was very quick
+No manual save system
If you enjoy games like Splinter Cell you should definitely pick this up. If you intend on using the games replay value I would definitely recommend it at full price. Hitman Absolution was a very fun game to play and had me testing my patience multiple times in order to complete the mission how I wanted.

I picked this game up for 3.99 €, as several friends said they liked it.
At first, it felt very avarage.
Clunky character animations with poor transitions, cheap sound effects, barely-interesting story, that feels disconnected from the gameplay itself.
But I can handle that.
The game ran very poorly, despite the fact that the graphics lack detail and enviroments are small.
Now I can handle playing a game on low graphics without complaining, it's okay. Gameplay is what matters, in the end.
It crashed twice during first mission, and I lost progress. Then it crashed later, somewhere around 2nd or 3rd mission.
Iam okay with that though. Few crashes at beginning, and one rare in the middle, I can live with that. No problem.
I continue playing, Iam getting more and more bored. It became very mediocre.
And as I played even more, I actually became frustrated because of certain game mechanics, I'll list them here:
1) Trespassing zones - most of the time, there's no way to tell that you're heading to an area that's restricted.
Worse, once you enter the restricted zone, the people around start getting angry very quickly. Too quickly, and there's no time to turn around.
2) Disguise system - great concept in general, but very poorly executed.
You've certainly seen tens of movies, or heard several stories, that involved a spy who masked himself as a guard/policeman/mercenary, and used this disguise to make his way through restricted areas.
In this game? It doesn't work, because when you are under disguise, people with same clothes as you will get suspicious very quickly and will attack you.
I find it ridiculous, because for example, when you silently snap the neck of a policeman, and take the police uniform and wear it, other cops will become agressive within seconds if you pass by.
To get benefit from the disguise system, you actually have to do the
, you need to find the rarest clothes possible - so the chance of meeting a person with same clothes is minimal.
3) Mission design - everything I mentioned above could be solved if this particular problem disappeared.
The design of levels, placement of characters, their routes and view angles, and the placement of flank routes, is just wrong. It feels as if the levels were designed for a first-person shooter game.
Did I mention first-person shooters? This Hitman game actually has a few Michael Bay scenes, and they are a complete miss. They don't match the pace of the game, they don't match the atmosphere, and they set a wrong type of mood for the upcoming mission.
In the end, I'd give this game 5/10, maybe even 4/10. For stealth, the Splinter Cell series feels better in every aspect.
I feel bad for this negative review, because it seems like everyone loves this game, but if I wanted to post a positive review, I'd have to lie.
If you are reading this review, and still decide to purchase the game - and you will discover that you like it, Iam happy for you, and wish I could say the same.

This game picks up sorta how the first Bioshock left off, you play as a Big Daddy, all big, all oafy and loud.  For fun make sure to play the game on the Hardest Difficulty, anything less and its just too easy.  This game is much shorter than the original but the pace feels good, it never drags, so dont let the length fool you.  The games mechanics are not as fun as the original.  Playing up until Dionysus Park a player can survive if they use resources carefully practicing ammo conservation, but on the Dionysus park level it all falls apart.  Enemies respawn real, real, fast.  Often times an enemy is killed then you walk around the corner and the same enemy respawns so fast and is shooting you in the back.  This is a HUGE problem because enemies dont always carry money to buy more ammo or supplies.
The lack of ammo or money to buy things is where the game breaks down due to this.  This broken gameplay of the weapons running out of ammo way to fast is compensated for by placing vending machines every 15 feet it feels like.  This could have been done less if either ammo was cheaper, or players could carry more ammo.  Being a big Daddy should be all about using the drill, but the drill requires fuel, fuel that evaporates way to fast even after upgrades making those vending machines every 10 feet useful.  The gameplay feels broken spending the whole game going to vending machines, the fuel should have lasted longer or there shoulda been an infinite fuel upgrade for the drill since its kind of the trademark big daddy weapon.  Hypnotize 3 is kinda useless, it lets you hypnotize big daddies which lasts for about ten seconds and worse if they throw a turret hypnotized or not it attacks you.  A good story and a fun game, def a must for bioshock fans.  Kinda thought this would suck and its nice that it isnt too bad.

Massive Change of a Negative Review, BIG TIME!
I gave up after a good go at this game, maybe I didn't add enough salt. But now, this week. Wow things have changed. This review is based on 3.61 (October 2015)
The game is still fantastically buggy, still very Hardware Hungry. But in terms of content, ironing out the bumps and offering a load more. Its a very enjoyable game to play.
I delved straight into the Teladi Outpost gameplay, one that I pretty much didn't bother with when I got it free on release. Recommended. You start, like all gameplay modes with a few ships but in a very hostile environment. Do your thing of fighting off all the huge bosses from blowing up all your ships in a single swipe. More importantly its huge, its every sector all in one galaxy, it takes an half hour + to visit each sector in a loop. They mean it when they say its the biggest sandbox this side of the galaxy.
The game play is very very full on, you really need to think. From taking over ships with the reworked marine system (experience) to trading long term. You find a gap in the market, the economy is real and is effected by war. You stations take time, but again due to the nature of the game you can change this by picking holes in the economy or again starting some fight with a company you either don't like or can do without.
After a while you see your pockets filling up. You expand your power through might and logistics, buying bigger, better ships to defend your income. This is where the Teladi Outpost DLC really got me. Its such a profitable zone that needs exploiting.
All in all if you have free time (single) and enjoy a game that you need to work and develop. Sit at your PC on your day off ready with plans and ideas you want to work on this game is great!
The bad bits are still quite strong in the game, for me out weighed with the shear level of economic, graphical and challenge detail this game offers so im still happy and wont shelve it. But simple things like upgrading a ship that gets stuck inside a station. Or crashes (save save save). The game is a huge hardware hog, personally im happy with this, it means the games working. Lots of ram, big CPU and an okay GPU is all you need. I have an AMD 8350 @ 4.875ghz, the game uses that at 80% most of the time. And when a lots going on, a war in another system it struggles, as in fps will drop to 30/40. Not the worst thing in the world but needs to be noted if your expecting 60fps or go playing with the graphics settings (low low low) Its still CPU intensive.
If you read other reviews including metacritic, it seems everyone wants perfection. UI super simple, not ending up stuck inside a ship, no occasional crash etc etc. IMO a quicksave (like in olden days lol) is a lifesaver and common sense. Try to look over problems with (olden days) attitude. Its a huge undertaking, massive, but no other developer could have come close.
The next X game is in the works, from my experiences in this game and if I was in power this game would be local networkable. Have a second computer on a gigabit network dealing with a few things while my PC deals with the other half and the game stuff (draw calls etc). But with DX12 in the works, I think this game would benefit with an API that can do much more efficient calculations  via the GPU. This game has ships not just milling about but constantly conscious (brilliant).
Verdict.
Its not a failed game, its a big and surprising hiccup game  form a developer everyone thought would pull it off. Try it again if you have it. Try it if you don't, its very playable, slowly improving, frustrating at times but is still a very very good game. I cant wait for the next!!!
EDIT:
The game is still played a lot. Its far from dead. Looking forward to seeing what 4.0 will bring.

Eek...
So who wants to go to a dark and depressing abyss where you don't end as a winner with lots of monies and cookies, but rather a worn-out survivor with varying degrees of psychological damage? If not, then I guess don't play this game. But you would be missing out, because you don't see games like this very often at all.
My closest comparison to this game would be Spec Ops: The Line because both take you into very dark places and when you finish it you are more likely to feel exhausted than jubilant. Unlike Spec Ops however, This War of Mine has no set storyline to follow. None of the countless horrible events you can come across in this game are guaranteed to happen for you, and everything you do in this game is entirely your choice. So in that regard it is a step up from that lovely adventure into a sand-storm ravaged Dubai. Because in this game, when you decide to have your characters do something horrible, it was your choice. Nothing forced you to do that. And you (or rather, your band of survivors) have to live with that.
This game is about as unpleasant as it gets, and yet despite that this game was necessary since it shows the often forgotten side of war: the civilians whose hometown ends up becoming a battlefield. I can't say you will have fun (you probably won't, even if the gameplay is quite good), but I can say that it will be an experience you will think about for quite sometime.
Enjoy being plunged into a world of despair and desperation. Woohoo! x_x

The most twisted game I've ever had the fortune of playing.
Based off the short story (of the same name) by legendary writer, Harlan Ellison-- this is a dark point 'n' click adventure game.
The writing is incredible-- again, the job has been done by Harlan, who chose to expand the story somewhat, giving the characters even more life.
It's got fantastic emotive voice acting, with AM (the antagonist, a sadistic Allied supercomputer) voiced by Harlan Ellison himself. I felt for the characters (and they do go through hell-- specifically, their own personal hells), and you get quite a few to play with.
You've got:
1. Nimdok - ex-Nazi physician stuck in a concentration camp; forced to perform medical experiments on innocents to find 'the lost tribe'.
2. Gorrister - man stuck in a zeppelin; suicidal over committing his wife to a mental institution; finds he is missing his heart.
3. Ellen - ex-engineer stuck in an electronic pyramid, wall-to-wall of yellow (a colour she is afraid of); is given an opportunity to sabotage AM, but only if she can confront her yellow-clothed♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥inside the yellow elevator.
4. Benny - ex-military captain who killed his squad, degenerated to a brutish simian who can't express his intelligent thoughts; stuck in a stone-age community that regularly performs human sacrifices to AM.
5. Ted - paranoid schizophrenic stuck in a medieval castle; his love, Ellen (alluding to the other Ellen), is slowly dying because of a curse cast on her by her wicked stepmother.
The gameplay goes beyond typical point 'n' click, featuring a revolutionary (for the time) morale system, where your actions and the choices you make dictates the outcome for the character. There are multiple endings, for each character, and for the endgame. Good and bad things can (and will) happen to the characters you controlled.
One of the best games I've played, and also one of the best point 'n' clicks.

Betrayer is a fun game.
What you want more to this review?
Reviews are meant to be longer? Fine.
You end up shipwrecked on a beach in Virginia in 1604, as you get up and proceed to work your way to the colonies and small settlements you realized everyone is ♥♥♥♥ing gone except for a girl with a red hood, and Spaniards. And form there you must unravel what happened to the colony and everyone in it, that's the story right there.
The game is classified as horror, and this appears as you unravel the story, the history, and even in the enemies. I'm telling you right now that when you think you've seen it all, the game pulls another punch that catches you offguard. You'll also find that the game is split between two worlds.
Gameplay.
Gameplay is fantastic, it's a mix between Dark Souls and STALKER. Everything virtually takes away 50% of your health, you drink water to restore your health and can carry two charges of water with you to use, and it gets tougher as the game goes along. If you die you drop all your loot in that area, it disappears if you die before picking it up. You can change it to easy mode though but why would you do that?
Moving around the map is also pretty damn nice, as you can run for as long as you want, no sprint bar or anything, and fast travel is an option, making traversing a breeze. Combatwise you don't get anything, you only get a knife for melee and that's it, you can stealth kill with it and you can upgrade the damage it does. Weaponry includes musket's (pistol and rifle), bows (short and long), and a crossbow, there are unique versions of it which overhaul how you fight, and the bows are silent for stealth killing, you also get a tomahawk, which you throw, also silent, it oneshots nearly everything.
As you go through the game you will find pages which explain more of the history, and areas that are buried, these hold clues for your investigation jobs, and items. Speaking of which, your investigations play a vital role in the game, seeing as how no one cane be talked to in the light world, they happen dynamically, as you find items or otherwise. They really help toward the end game as well as open up the history more.
Moving on from that, we move to various tidbits, you can buy and sell, and you don't need to be at a merchant station to sell, you can sell from your inventory, pretty convenient. You also can retrieve arrows, ammo, and tomahawks off of killed enemies, as well as various loot items. And speaking of loot items, there are chests everywhere, and some hold upgrades to items, these include and extra tomahawk, and charms.
And charms are the next part, charms are those items you apply for various additions to what you have. These include the ability to be harder to see, faster reload, and more health. The charms and weapons all come in various qualities, from crude to exceptional, there's also unique weaponry, which upgrades on a different scale. You can carry three charms, and three weapons, and all weapons are tied to hotkeys and of course, the scroll wheel. Oh, and I forgot to mention, you do get set amounts of ammo, such as 10 arrows, but your ammo count is also upgradable, ♥♥♥♥in' A!
There are also bells in every section of the map, that lead to the Otherworld/Bell World/Purgatory. This is also a major area in where the horror manifests, as well as a whole different map to explore for loot, enemies, and the story of course! It's shrouded in fog and everything else you saw in the video on the store page. It's fun! You can also hit X for help, no waymarkers are used, despite having a compass, and hitting X will give you some creepy audio which leads you to clues and objectives, it can't be used constantly though, mashing X won't give you a stream of the audio; it "recharges" after use which takes a few seconds.
There is a toggle button which does give you a subtle waymarker on the compass to help you.
Stealth.
Stealth is one of the biggest aspects of this game, occassionally in the overworld the grass rustles, this lets you run through it for the duration without alerting anyone, and running will bring attention, as will firing any gun. You can crouch, which hides you, and get close to enemies to shank them, or hit them with a tomahawk. An important note to take is that wind does not affect arrows or bullets, so feel free not to worry if you are aiming and the wind suddenly blows.
Enemies.
Oh boy this is fun!
I'm only gonna reveal two, because I can and the enemies are really something to see.
Spaniards: One thing you'll notice fast is that the Spaniards dotted around the map are not quite humanly, these are your standard enemy, and they stop at nothing to kill you, they come in numbers, and force. They will be armed with bows, muskets of both kinds, and they tend to run up and stab/punch you in your face. Remember! You can't take too many hits, so even four of them will require some kind of planning. Worry not though, as the game does not penalize you for choosing one combat type over the other, but running in guns blazing is still a risky move.
Skeletons: The common everyday grunt of fantasy games returns and wants you dead! The skeletons are not push overs, every bit as strong as the Spaniards, but at least five different kinds of lethal. Unlike the Spaniards they are mostly melee oriented, but a good number of them will attack at range, and seeing as how they don't have guns or bows, they fire energy blasts at you at a rapid rate, did I mention they also have good aiming? Also unlike the Spaniards, they pop up at random around the Otherworld, some may pop up no more than a few feet from you. Spooked solid? You ♥♥♥♥in' bet.
Non-enemies.
Wraiths, Shadows, The Red Hooded Maiden.
Wraiths and Shadows are there to tell a story, don't expect too much from them. They are the people to talk to do everything investigation related, don't expect them to be fully fleshed out, however their own histories are pretty interesting. Shadows however are there to tell a story like the Wraithes and give you sidequests and rewards. Both Wraithes and Shadows really really add to the horror factor, and the Wraithes especially make it seem like it's some kind of purgatory where they are. The Red Hooded Maiden is the person you'll be in constant contact with, she's the only person to talk to in the light world, not much more to say but to experience it for yourself, sorry for ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tting my way out!
Tid-bits.
The game is in an entirely black an white color scheme, punctuated with shades of red. This adds to the horror, and the red shows you something is not right with the world. You can change the color contrast, but why would you do that also? I do recommend playing through it the first time on black and white, it was the dev's artistic vision and it really makes the game. There's also no music, relying on ambient and various sounds, some superb audio if I ever heard any.
The game also throws punches in terms of difficulty, as you do progress your weapons do let you deal with the enemies more smoothly, but as you get better so do they, as new enemies appear and as they get more agressive in numbers and to ane extent, power. Did I mention arrows have a chance of deflecting off armor?
There is one problem, and that is a bug that makes you crash to the desktop. This is the only bug and it happens by accessing the menu and just rapidly moving through things. It's not the worst, but it does break the immersion when it happens; tread carefully around that. The game also saves often, so no worries if it does crash.
Overall, Betrayer is an unsettling game, that gets better as you progress, it doesn't get over complicated or lost in telling the story, the combat remains challenging and grows as you go along. The total game time is at least 8-10 hours, not bad for an indie game.

I was very pleasantly surprised by this game. I was expecting a relatively generic indie platformer, but what I got was a portal-like physics based puzzle platformer that really got me thinking and being creative.
You can utilize 3 tools, and I very much like that it gives you all three within the first minute of the game. There is a small tutorial bit explaining some of the things you can do with the tool before the opening scene, but it's very quick, and outside of that the game never really limits which of the 3 you can use.
Left click activates a slicing mechanic, which locks onto an object, but allows you to strafe around it zelda-style. I would be interested to see what a more point-to-point dragging variation would be like, but the center and drag outwards control works well, and I guess it does allow you to react a tad faster. Right click activates a stiff rope that can be used to pull just about anything. It doesn't retract, but only follows your movement. And finally, Middle Click launches a sticky rocket that will attach to nearly any surface, and a second click will propel the rocket and whatever's attached to it forward.
The great thing is, that the levels have such a huge sense of scale to them, and these tools can manipulate pieces of stone hundreds or even thousands of times the size of your character. You feel really powerful, and it's awesome when huge walls or pillars come crashing down next to you.
I'd very much recommend a mouse and keyboard. The platforming feels a bit better with a controller, but the speed of the mouse can really add a lot to the experience. You can catch objects mid-air with all 3 of the tools, and manipulate them in ways that require timing just too fast for a controller.
The game is very mentally stimulating, and there are tons of secrets to find and quicker ways to do things if you really think about the environment and your tools. And that's one of the best features of the game. There's a lot you can interact with, and you can go as far as chopping off the path forward. Don't worry, you can simply respawn at the generous checkpoints, but I just like the fact that it lets you do so much that it can be impossible to progress. It really feels like a genuine adventure, and not just some path that you walk down.
The visuals have a unique and interesting style, although the fidelity isn't amazing, especially the texture resolution. The soundtrack also feels very unique, and while I didn't love all of it, there were a few songs that I really enjoyed, even more so because the music tracks are actually hidden collectables. I found all but 3 on my playthrough. There's so little dialog that I think it could really benefit from voice acting, and it would be quick and easy to get done. Your radio  has a personality and talks to you, but it's easy to miss much of what he says because it's just a text bubble on the bottom of the screen.
Performance wise it should be very easy to run. It runs extremely well, and does support 120Hz. There's no FOV adjustment, and while wasn't the 100-110 I'm used to, it was definitely high enough to not cause any issues for someone like me who sits pretty close to my display.
Chances are you probably already own this game from a bundle so go ahead and play through it! It's not a long game, and even though I would have liked more, it's a concise and genuinely enjoyable experience. There's a lot of creativity both on the part of the developers, and on yourself and how you play because of how open it is. And if you don't already have it, you can pick it up for $2 on sales or less if you trade for bundle key. I completely recommend it for everyone but small children, only because of the thinking and platforming skill required to progress.

Betrayed is an intriguing title that is not without some flaws.

So that all said, what is it that keeps me coming back again and again for more? Is it the superb graphics and artwork? Is it the setting of a Shipwreck survivor in the 17th Century, or is it the intriguing and mysterious  sub plots clues and locations that build towards a larger picture of Supernatural proportions? It is all this that creates a sense of playing within a Ben Wheatley cult British film.
So flawed and frustrating, yes, but this is far outweighed by its moody and enigmatic magnificence.
Now I need to take my leave, for I must return to the trees and rocks and that damned wind. Who knows what may befall me around the next bend, or what grissly secrets I may uncover. Whateveter it is won't be nice, but I am compelled to go...

A tough and difficult review for this entry. I will do my utmost to make it concise yet informative.
1) Features: Graphic still looks awesome for current trend, music even though no longer composed by Nobuo Uematsu, it still holds up on its own accord though some of them are not really on my preferences, but some really do like the Gran Pulse main theme. Additionally, SEA region version only receives Japanese audio as compared with ROW versions. This is a big letdown to me, as I like to keep on switching language in different palythrough.
2) Gameplay: Battle system somehow quite similar with Chrono Chross yet active input is required without pause setting for ATB gauge to filled up. Might took some time to familiarised with this new system for established FF fans, yet it is an interesting system once you get to used it. Different strategic tactics can be applied, though I'm not really keen with this system. Customisation of equipments and accessories, and levelling up via crystarium are nicely implemented and deter players to keep on mindless grinding. However battle rating could be implemented better, not focusing too much on time and damage applied, and not really into the "doom" imposed if you are to be involved in a battle for a longer time.
3) Story: be prepared to keep on hearing these famous words; fal'Cie, l'Cie. Caccoon, Pulse, Focus, etc. Storyline is filled with interesting mythology but quite poorly implemented on my humble opinion. Direction is quite linear, but hang in there as reaching to chapter 11 will improve your experience better (for FF veterans).
4) Replay value: Quite high, considering many equipments require expensive catalysts and many gill (game currency) required. Second playthrough might change the experience drastically.
5) Optimisation: Slight poorly optimised, several drop in FPS experienced in several area such as in Gran Pulse, glitch in datalog text (enemy descriptions) apart from 1280x720 resolution. Audio is too low and unadjustable. Limited customisation on keyboard binding capabilities. Esc and Steam home keys sometimes unresponsive. Apart from that, cutscene and graphic as stated earlier, are looking great.
What I really like about this game:
Graphic and FMVs, certain music, development of certain characters, certain implementation on the paradigm, mythology of the game
What I really dislike of this game:
Quite linear storyline with less to nill interaction with npcs, most informations could be given indirectly instead of relying in conversation and datalog methods (especially mythology of the game), paradigm shifting/transitions could be better. Finally, I really dislike this game in SEA region is only restricted in Japanese audio as compared with ROW version.
Neutral:
Difficulty spike, action in combat, system concerning upgrading accessories and weapons.
Final remarks: I would like to give this a neutral since halfway of the game, since I forced myself playing this game on numerous occasions until I reached out at chapter 11. Nevertheless, this game is good, but not that bad either. So its a yes from me. FF veterans might not favour this game, but I do encourage them to try and hold on until reaching to the Gran Pulse area. I would like to replay this game from scratch with different language, as in certain language, voice actors may perfoms differently compared with the original voice actors. This might yield different personification of certain characters.

Sorry Freelancer fans, you're gonna have to keep going without.

Hello, I've recently started playing through FFXIII on the PC, but I have beaten it many times on the Xbox 360.
So to start off with, this Final Fantasy is honestly my favorite one and here's why. Ill tell you some pros and cons of this game buit overall I would still recommend it to anyone. So here we go.
Pros:(for me)
Graphics, This game was released in 2009, so taking that into consideration I believe it still looks pretty damn good. (Most certainly better that FFXV in my eyes) The animations arent too clunky and the controls are still pretty smooth standing next to more current games.
Story, This games story is phoenominal. It is a bit linear as far as missions go but that doesnt bother me, I get annoyed with too many side quests in a story based game. Of course it is going to be an emotional rollercoaster but what FF game isnt. Some people complain about it or about the voice acting but I think its great. Not just great, but amazing. The characters are more relatable than most in the fact that some of the earliest large battles are based around the emotions of the characters. Which leads me to them,
Characters: Each one has their own deal in the game and their own role to play. Each with very distinct personalities from the rest. They're great and none of them really get lost in the story.
Pulse: The lower world of the game, Its very open and you are free to run around and kill, grind, or do whatever youd like.
Turn based combat and paradigms: I for one love turn based combat done in this format. I dont understand why people complained other that you have no way to  truley dodge an attack, but neither did you in the other games. Each character has their "class" that they are better with than others and youre required to change the characters you play so it forces you to use them all at least a little. ie: snow is a good sentinal and Vanielle is a good medic. BUT you can make them and train them to be whichever youd like and switch it as often as you want or need( even in battle)
Cons:(for some)
Story and progression: As I stated above it can and at more times is quite linear in the missions. Its a dramatic and emotional story which some people may not be into. There is a lack of side quests but later in the game you are able to roam around some
The Maps: some more linear shenanigans as you are limited ( until later in the game ) to going from point A to point B with hardly much room
leveling: You have to fight EVERYTHING ( or nearly ) thats in your path or you wouldn't have leveled enough to fight the bosses.
combat: There is no way to dodge and sometimes the characters will just run right into a one-shot attack and die. Most bosses require stradegy and multiple paradigm shifts throughout and it can get annoying one from A to B to C to A again all withing a minutes time.
and you still cant jump without the prompt

Rebel Galaxy is a fantastic spacefaring game for those of us looking for something more arcade-like than the hardcore sims available elsewhere.  I grew up with titles like the original Elite, Freespace 1 and 2, Freelancer, the "X" series, and my all time favorite Independence War 2.  This game is perfect for scratching that starship battle itch I get now and then without having to spend hours and hours (that I don't have anymore) grinding.  Sure, you get to follow the genre-typical gameplay loop that requires you to mine, trade, or take side missions in order to earn credits for better equipment.  None of it really feels like grinding, though, as even the most basic missions are varied enough to keep you entertained, not to mention the random encounters you may face on the way to said mission.  The 2D flight mechanics, though strange at first, fit the capital ship style of the game perfectly.  It really does feel like naval combat in space!  To tie it all together, the grunge-y outlaw rock soundtrack is the badass black cherry on top of the cake.
In short, if you're looking for surprisingly fun space combat with all of the open world goodness, but without the depth or complexity (or price tag), of an "X" game or Elite: Dangerous, Rebel Galaxy is perfect for you.  This game is absolutely worth every penny of its modest $20 price tag.

Neon Chrome was a game that I expected to be a bit bland when I went into it. To my elated surprise, it's actually pretty fun and addicting.
The cyber punk atmosphere actually succeeds at bring somewhat cyberpunky (a word? now it is). Not very many games a have succeeded in that, so hats off to them for that. It even keeps to the generally grey morality of many cyber punk games by having you play as a person who seems to
.
The gameplay itself is solid. There are a few classes that can be chosen from at the beginning of a run and, with money from previous runs, you can get premanent upgrades or purchase equipment for your next run. The combat is fun and there is a decent variety among the enemies.
The best part about the gameplay is the permanent pregression. (I personally think that) A rouge-like needs to have some form of permanent progression between runs, and Neon Chrome gets it down pat. The upgrades that you can purchase between runs is important, but everytime you beat a boss you will also be able to start from just after that battle. This negates the slough that so many rouge-likes have of fighting through earlier, weaker levels and repetative bosses.
Neon Chrome feels like a nostalgia trip to old, top down arcade shooters. It retains the greatness of a bygone era while still using some key features of modern indie gaming. If you like top down shooters or rouge-likes, this is a game to consider.

Futuristic games built upon worlds of dystopian despair, ruled over by malicious men of evil intent have always fascinated me. And it is because they tease a deep-seated fear within us on some primal level, in that such a scenario could plausibly occur at some point in our lives as technology rapidly advances in the wrong hands - with the only hope remaining for humanity resting upon the wits of techno-savvy rebels who desperately seek to undermine & overthrow such a diabolical system of rule.

And so it was with great anticipation & delight that I took the opportunity to review this latest offering in the top-down twin-stick shooter genre, Neon Chrome, from the very same developer, 10tons Ltd, who brought us Crimsonland...a very laudable title in its own right. But were they able to capitalize on past experience and improve upon the formula by taking it to the next level with their newest title? My answer to this question is a resounding yes, on all counts, and so let's now further explore why this is actually so.
Upon starting this title up with a grin of anticipation, what immediately struck me was how artistically gorgeous it all was. Aesthetically, the game is spectacularly stylish indeed, exuding richly vibrant neon colors which seamlessly blend into each other very pleasingly...delighting the senses and imbuing a great sense of immersion within these scenes of both illuminated and shadowed areas...itself perhaps a meaningfully subtle metaphor in describing this battle of both light and darkness. Coupled with its atmospheric ambiance, there is a true feeling of depth below you, letting you know in no uncertain terms that you are gradually ascending higher & higher within this frightfully towering colossus for an epic showdown with the evil overlord who rules over all that is - the inscrutable Overseer.
Essentially, your prime objective is to navigate your upgradable & cybernetically enhanced player around each floor with its many walls and maze-like paths, methodically sabotaging their defense systems and obliterating every ruthless minion or sophisticated robot you encounter, of which there are several uniquely different kinds to engage in battle with. The progression system here was rather well executed I thought, because there were numerous clearly defined challenges & goals to be achieved - complete with both bosses & mini-bosses found throughout. I felt a tremendous sense of accomplishment after each floor was reduced to rubble and no further enemies were left remaining to mercilessly hunt me down. It was both addicting and exhilarating to reach the next one higher (31 levels spread across 6 large floors incidentally) as I eagerly wondered what would be awaiting me to contend with when I arrived there.
The gameplay exudes a wonderful cadence, with moments of relative calm and strategizing as you consider your options, interspersed with sudden bursts of absolute mayhem as reinforcements mercilessly swarm you with incendiary explosions dancing all around your feet...inducing incredible adrenalin rushes as you desperately attempt to stave off this onslaught of malicious intent. And make no bones about it, the enemies in this game can be rather aggressive indeed...so planning is absolutely crucial for success here. And therein lies the true beauty of Neon Chrome, you must actually think ahead and plan your movements accordingly as opposed to mindlessly running & gunning around aimlessly. Thus a thoughtful strategy for attack is the key to success here, as opposed to impetuous and impatient tactics being employed, making for a vastly more enriching experience upon its floors of procedurally generated levels.
On a side-note, I must say that the enemy AI is neither superior nor wholly inadequate in my opinion - instead being found somewhere in between at the decent range. It can be exploited somewhat, but only to a limited degree since they tend to relentlessly hunt you down sooner or later.
Another positive attribute to be found here was the bountiful number of both powerful weapons & cybernetic abilities (unlockable) as well as diverse character classes (selectable) that could be deployed, each with their own specific strengths and weaknesses, ensuring that every single run-through was a deeply satisfying & uniquely memorable experience. I greatly enjoyed testing out their inherent abilities against my foes, continually dialing in the optimal setup for each challenging situation that I was presented with.
And to further expand upon this point, the environment is actually destructible which beneficially helps the game. And so for example, if you are unable to enter an area from the front entrance, then why not blast your way in from the side and make your own pathway forward utilizing brute force. This is yet another definite plus in the gameplay, injecting an additional layer of fun possibilities to the equation.
Now in regard to the background music, it was perfectly matched to the look and feel of the game, and consists of an edgy yet gratifying electronic tune that is endlessly looped...masterfully evoking a brooding tension in the air.
I did however have a very minor gripe with the camera height, in that it seemed to be quite a ways above the action...sometimes making it a bit tricky to discern detail. Of course, it's always a trade-off in that a lower height would reveal less of the gameplay area. Nonetheless, at times it did seem a touch too high up I thought. Ideally, it would be fantastic if it were dynamically adjustable in-game, so as to allow the player to set their own preference at any given moment. But again, this is a relatively minor quibble overall as the current setting is still very much within the limits of what is acceptable.
Thankfully, this title has been fully Steamified with both achievements and trading cards included. Furthermore, it is designed for both single-player and local co-op...meaning no online play...which may or may not be an issue depending upon your own personal preference. For me, I simply view it as an intriguing single-player game to journey inside of.
So alas the burning question remains, is it worth procuring?
While Neon Chrome doesn't do anything exceedingly ground-breaking or revolutionary, what it does do it does superbly well, sticking to tried & true gameplay ideas & mechanics wrapped inside a very pretty package...one where the supraliminal exploration of this unnerving dichotomy between freedom versus tyranny inside of a futuristic cyberpunk setting has never been so much fun. And thus I would wholeheartedly recommend it as a very worthy addition to one's library for fans of this genre at its very reasonable new release price, while confidently rating it at a solid 4/5 stars.

The Tl;Dr is that this game is a Cyberpunk Rogue Legacy with a "linear" map progression. I say linear map progression, because you generally have to go to floor 1, then 2, etc, but the floors are different every time.
For everyone else, it's a top down rogue like shooter. You play as super hacker who is trying to take down an evil corportation. You do this by sitting in a chair, picking a bot/person from a list, and sending them forth into the levels. You get to pick from three different people that are random. The more weapons and abilities you find, the more diverse your picks can become. There are also static upgrades, so you can give your units more health, energy, luck, damage, etc. These are static upgrades, if you get em, they stay. You can also buy a weapon, that you've unlocked, and you'll start with it on your next run, same with abilities.
Another neat thing I noticed was that completing achievements nets you in game money. It's not a lot, but 1200 credits can still be a few levels, depending on how early in the game you are.
This game can feel a little grindy, but that's the just nature of the rogue like.
A small note is that this game felt VERY weird to me initially. The controls are very simple, but there is no dodge, which I thought was weird. After the first hour, I adapted, and the game is awesome.
After you beat the game, it'll kick you to the equivalent of new game plus. You can swap between difficulties at any time, which is a really cool design choice. Over all, still a fantastic game.
I'd totally recommend if you're a fan of rogue like games with progression.
The music is also really awesome.

I am not a huge fan of the graphics and the random generated offices and laboratories can sometimes feel a bit random indeed (some people claim the graphics are great but it is obvious that this is meant to be an ios/Android game first, especially the UI is bad and sometimes confusing)
but the carnage, the explosions, the destructable walls (it`s so satisfying slashing your way through a wall to get into an enemies back) and last but not least the gore make for a very physical and very fun gameplay. especially if you have an explosive round waiting in your barrel ;)
you have a fine arsenal at your disposal and although it`s neither as big or creative as what Enter the Gungeon has to offer I`m having more fun using it (one reason for that is the unlimited ammo, so you can actually have fun with your guns). there are different kinds of weapons, from shotguns, smgs, assault and burst rifles to grenade launcher or experimental weapons like a rail gun.
and then you have varioues special abilities of course like homing missiles, cluster grenades or laser beams.
perks are very fun, well thought out and plentyful, some are a bit overpowered though ("friend of mines" for example does not only disarm all mines for you, it also deactivates floor based auto cannons in the level which is too easy imo).
the controls feel unfamiliar at first, after half an hour you will be able to do some very elegant moves while mowing down large groups of enemies and bosses though. if you played Enter the Gungeon before this then you will probably miss the dodge roll button immensly...
conclusion: extremely satisfying rogue like gameplay with meh graphics and great physics, definitively worth it for the asking price if you like top down shooter!

So who wants to go to a dark and depressing abyss where you don't end as a winner with lots of monies and cookies, but rather a worn-out survivor with varying degrees of psychological damage? If not, then I guess don't play this game. But you would be missing out, because you don't see games like this very often at all.
My closest comparison to this game would be Spec Ops: The Line because both take you into very dark places and when you finish it you are more likely to feel exhausted than jubilant. Unlike Spec Ops however, This War of Mine has no set storyline to follow. None of the countless horrible events you can come across in this game are guaranteed to happen for you, and everything you do in this game is entirely your choice. So in that regard it is a step up from that lovely adventure into a sand-storm ravaged Dubai. Because in this game, when you decide to have your characters do something horrible, it was your choice. Nothing forced you to do that. And you (or rather, your band of survivors) have to live with that.
This game is about as unpleasant as it gets, and yet despite that this game was necessary since it shows the often forgotten side of war: the civilians whose hometown ends up becoming a battlefield. I can't say you will have fun (you probably won't, even if the gameplay is quite good), but I can say that it will be an experience you will think about for quite sometime.

Well, both games have their own experience to give; both games have their own stories, characters and themes to follow, both games I feel have individual strengths over the other which makes both of them stand out. Bioshock 2 is a different journey through the dilapidated streets of Rapture, there are new locations to explore, new secrets to uncover, new weapons to use and new enemies to use them on...
To start out on what I feel are direct improvements over the previous game: The process of hacking machines has been improved tenfold, it's no longer a distracting element that takes the player out of the environment temporarily so they can solve a puzzle, it's a sequence of actions and reactions that tests the players reflexes and rewards them for success. Instead of a frustrating puzzle it's a needle simply moving back and forth waiting for the player to activate it while it's over a green area of the meter, this is a vast improvement over Bioshock 1 in my opinion because it's not distracting in the slightest, and instead of giving the player a massive mess to sort out its a simple imput system thats easy to use and understand.
The options on how to manage Little Sisters is a much more engaging experience, you can choose to harvest or adopt them temporarily. Adopting them gives you the option to use them to harvest Adam from corpses, which can increase your Adam intake by a large sum while still keeping your conscience clean, afterwards you can take them to a vent and again you are given the option to rescue or harvest them, what you do is your choice.
Now to summarize the rest of the game: The story places you in the role of Subject Delta, an early prototype of the infamous Big Daddies: Your Little Sister has been taken from you and you have been killed in the process only to be revived by a Vita-Chamber, with no recollection of how you ended up there your only goal is to reuinite with your Little Sister, Elanor Lamb. To do this you must brave the run-down streets of Rapture which have seen eight years of neglect since the events of the first game. All the while the story reacts to your choices on how to deal with Little Sisters and other NPCs, giving the player one of (from what I understand) several different endings.
Throughout Rapture you will come across some familiar enemies, Splicers, and some new blood-thirsy additions to the stock. Notably the Big Sisters, the Brute Splicers, the Rumbler Big Daddies and the Alpha Series. Each of the new enemies gives a lot more to the experience and are spread out, keeping the game from being unjustly overwhelming. The new weapons are a lot of fun to use and are adaptive to your respective playstyle thanks to the alternative ammunitions available to each one, allowing the player to be either extremely aggressive, you can be exploitive of your enemies weaknesses or being defensive setting up clever traps. The weapons and Plasmids, like Bioshock 1, are all reactive, fun to use and have a good powerful feeling to them. I'm especially fond of the spear gun, that little gem will forever hold a special place in my heart.
Levels are again fun, flawless and well paced, with plenty of opportunity to explore and discover, and in doing so the player is rewarded with extra ammo and health as well as audio diaries delivering exposition to Rapture's recent years or not-so-ancient past. Not to mention the jaw-dropping visuals, haunting soundtrack and out-of-this-world graphics.
Now the question that will always nag at me: Do I like this game or the original Bioshock more? All points and aspects considered I will have to go with the original. I like the story and characters so much more, it delivered a larger impact to me about a man struggling to break free of the chains keeping him enslaved without him even knowing it. Where Bioshock 2 takes on a sort of rescue story, which doesn't lend itself to the kind of tale that can justify the sheer amount of discovery that Rapture offers.
Ultimately Bioshock 2 cannot compete with its predecessor (but what can? That game was almost perfect in every regard), but still its a great game thats well thought-out and is a lot of fun to play through, keeping the elements of the original in place while giving the player some new toys to use.

This game has been out for years, and has been notoriously buggy the whole time it's been on the market.  2k Games has the werewithal to remove GFWL in order to sell this pile of♥♥♥♥♥♥on Steam, but can't be bothered to fix long-standing, game-stopping bugs?  Unbelievable.
It's hard not to recommend this game, because so much of it is just really, really good.  At times, better than the original Bioshock. The problem with Bioshock 2 is that it is crash-prone.  If you manage to not have frequent crashes, then chances are you are either extrememly lucky, or you found one of the so-called fixes that help.  It seems like there is a different fix for every level, because every single time I was heading into, or was playing in, a new area it would crash and I'd have to hunt down a so-called "fix".
Let's see, at various times I've forced it to run in directx9 mode, set it to use directx10, deleted saves from the savegame folder, turned down the graphics to their lowest possible setting, turned off the reverb, edited the ini file, verified the game files, killed the ATI Catalyst Control program, I have no antivirus running, nor any bakground programs other than Steam, I've set it to run in compatibility mode, and I've set it to Run as Administrator.
Even when you do manage that, a second even uglier issue may arise:  dropping to the menu system to save your progress only to find the save button isn't there.  Not only is it not there, but hitting escape to go back to the game asks you if you want to quit to windows.  You can select continue or load game, but it will erase your progress anyway.  This has happened to me so many times and I'm only half way through the game.  And whatever you do, don't save your game on exit - it's known to corrupt your saves.
I was able to use the various "fixes" found around the web to get around one crash or another throughout playing this game, but I've come to a point in the game where nothing I do matters.  It crashes like clockwork, on cue, in the loading transition between Dionysus Park and Fontaine Futuristics.  Ya know what?  I'm done.  I really don't have the time and fortitude to put up with this game any longer.  And I will certainly be sure not purchase any products from 2K Games in the future.

This is a great game.  It's a first-person stealth adventure with a healthy dose of whodunit storyline set in the New England wilderness of the 1600s.  This will be on my Best of 2014 List without question.
These notes reflect day 2 on Steam, so they may get patched over time.
[PROS]
- The black-and-white esthetic is beautiful, but replaceable if you're not into that.
- The storyline is amazing and the characters you meet are written to make you like or hate them -- a lot.
- The stealth combat is great -- creep into shadows and expect to get owned if you go running at two bad guys like an idiot.
- Shadows count toward stealth
- Wind counts toward stealth
- When you're nearby important items, there are audio cues to draw your attention
- Four hits and you're dead
- You are rewarded for exploration
- You can't lose aggro -- enemies will follow you until either you are dead or they are dead
- Very simple inventory system; tons of lore and each clue you find is recorded just in case you want to review it later.
- While sprinting, you never get winded
- In my opinion, good game length
- If the combat is too difficult or time consuming, there's a button for that
- Full rekeybinding with warnings when you unbind a key
- Audio cues are important, but if that's an issue, there's an option to turn them into visual cues
[CONS]
- Limited graphics options (no 1080; MAX = 1280x720)
- There is no warning when you are exploring and walk into an "exit zone" to the next area.  So while exploring, you might accidentally leave the area and then have to come back -- which is a pain.
- FOV slider goes to 110, but it looks very weird visually and really hinders you given how important it is to zoom in to hit targets at range with your bow and arrow.
- Light refraction off of water is junky
- Enemies always walk in a triangle, so you can anticipate where they'll be.
- Enemies occasionally walk on top of a tree
- Enemies make a huge ruccous when they spawn
- There's no letter or other device to tell you why you're here at the start of the game.  You can piece together the story as you go along, but the first fifteen minutes of the game could be a lot more informative
- Game is very linear all things considered
- Each area takes about an hour to fully explore and technically you have to explore them twice (I won't spoil why)

I have long been a fan of Freelancer to the point I have spent years lementing the fact that my system no longer supports it. I have played more games then I can honestly count, here I have found some thing of that long lost love. This game gives yopu a huge freedom of movement and choice, an interesting story where you actually effect some of the outcomes, not to mention addicting combat. If you want a game that is strangely addicting, well made, with a good sound track (honestly the best I have ever heard) It is like Firefly meets Freelancer.
