Been ages since I played this game, and I don't know how well it aged, but for what it's worth it was a really fun JRPG.
The Last Remnant's greatest strength comes from its combat system.
Turn based; tactical; large scale warfare. Although you start with a small party of just 2 characters - as the story unfolds you will gain access to more options. Expanding your team and building your little army.
Combat is based on squads - large teams with formations which you can customize & arrange. You can adjust the tactics, team members and more. Their combat ability and available actions will differ depending on soldier's individual qualities, chemistry between troops, roles and more.
Most commands cannot be issued directly. There's no "attack, magic, item" here. Instead you tell the unit what to do in general terms and they will pull off what they think is right. It adds that element of surprise, of educated guessing and hoping for a specific result. Combat become unpredictable with just enough predictability to allow tactical gameplay and thinking.
The formations and position of your units is critical.
Have a triangle formation with your leader in the front and the weak casters in the back - and frontal attacks won't endanger your weaker troops. Get a hit from behind however and these troops are vulnerable.
Positioning is also key: you can pincer attack, attack from behind, lock them up, intercept attackers or have your own attacks interrupted !  It really is a unique  engaging system. As turns and commands take time to actually execute:
So for instance if  you send a squad to attack a group from the front - but you recklessly ignore another group laying between you and  the enemy on the sidelines - that group can attack you - and they will meet you in the middle and intercept your attack. Dropping an ambush on you and gaining some Morale and advantage. Or for example - attack a unit from all sides to have the upper hand.
The battle also lays heavily on a Morale system - where momentum can shift between you and your foes -depending on your heroes actions- you successes or failures. Lose a lot of soldiers and your morale drops. Fell a great monster and it will sky rocket.
So the combat here feels like a turn based tactics game mixed with classic JRPG action.
The action is also accompanied by simple QTE system that allows dishing out critical hits.
The soundtrack is absolutely awesome.
The world is based on many separate area maps - which you can discover and access through 1 big World Map. You will fast-travel from one area to the next. This includes plains, forests, deserts, swamps, caves - you name it. The world also offers  beautiful and unique looking fantasy-medieval cities - that are very different from one another
The cast of characters are pretty good. Especially Emma- a powerful fearless and loyal warrior. The conqueror- a mysterious and fearsome villain. King David - the leader of the good guys basically and a few others.
This game is seriously underrated, and while it's not super-incredible by any means - it's still enjoyed it more than most JRPGs.

I love this game to bits and it's also my favourite of all time, so I decided to take a look at its reviews and such. After reading tons upon tons of not recommended reviews all I keep seeing is "Oh, the levels are extreamly linear" or "The battle system sucks". So maybe I can put a shroud upon those "issues" and make them seem like not such a bad thing; perhaps deceptisol or fortisol or something.
So firstly, the levels ARE linear mostly up until around near the end of the game but did you consider the storyline up until that point before pointing it out as an "issue"?... I don't think so.
What I'm trying to say is that each main protagonist has a single minded goal and the routes they take to complete them are obviously going to be the most direct ones. Have a think, EACH character has their own seperate goal up until, you know, that pivotable point I mentioned. For people who want to buy this game and play it for the first time try not to read the blacked out text but don't listen to reviews stating that the level designs are an issue, their visuals are stunning and most of the time their linear-ness just blows over your head.
And for the battle system, up until this point in Final Fantasy, combat has always been pressing a button or clicking a key to queue attacks and wait for you characters to execute them. This time Square Enix added the element of real-time strategy gameplay rather than turn based gameplay, so it makes sense that you can only control a single character rather than the entire party. They also added an Auto-Battle feature that kind of hand holds you through battles, however its not made to be abused. Many reviews have told the story of "It makes the game boring because you can just abuse it"... but isn't that the case with any feature in any game. The feature was made so that if you don't have a clue what ability to use, it will give you a somewhat idea of what to use, therefore you can queue up abilities to better target your enemies weaknesses. It's just silly to criticise a game for doing something a little differently that adds a bit more variety into it. I commend Square Enix for trying something new as the same formula over and over becomes tedious.
All in all, they're the small minded reviews about this game that you should stay away from. I'm not saying this port is perfect, no way, but the game itself is wonderful. It's visuals are stunning, the soundtrack is amazing, the story and lore has depth and you'll grow to admire the main protagonists as the game progresses. However a small amount persisting bugs, though not game breaking, can be worked around but are still awaiting a patch *cough cough Square Enix cough*.

Just a quick first impression because I don't feel like most the reviews actually tell you anything important the game. Most of them revolve around the games theme and marketing strategy. That's irrelevant to whether the game is actually good or not. I'm profession so I'm not going to write like one, so here's a list of notables from my my experience. pluses (+) and minuses (-), plus-minus=Good but with issues, minus-plus=bad but not too bad
-+The game runs like♥♥♥♥♥♥for me sometimes. It's playable most of the times, but sometimes it just locks up for a couple seconds or stutters for a second or so, but most of the time it's smooth sailing. I play the game at max settings (just like all the games I play). It's not game breaking but it's happens enough for me to mention it.
+-For the most part I don't have issues with the controls. I certainly don't die because of them and I play the game on extreme. If I die, it's because I didn't play right. Though, there are issues with how fluid the controls are.
For instance:If you crouch, the only way to stand up again is to press the crouch button and sometimes it doesn't respond. I don't know why but that's something I have an issue with. Secondly, you can't just press the sprint button or roll like other games to break out of a crouch. It's not a major issue, but it's annoying sometimes.
The other issue is the execute button is the same as the switch weapons button (on the controller anyway) which will end in you unwittingly switching weapons before you execute, resulting in you fighting the swat team with a pistol. This is extra weird because the dpad is used exclusively for switching weapons so there's no reason for the execute button to be used as a weapon switch button.
+You get to play as Nathan Explosion and he's a BRUTAL as you expect.
+After every execute, Nathan says a BRUTAL one liners such as "Only my weapon understands." "Maybe I kill them too fast."
+The BRUTAL is Nathan's life blood. I.E. shooting/stabbing someone in the face revitalizes you. That's the only way to heal.
+The game look exactly like the trailers and screenshots. I think the visuals are beautiful.
+Looks like sin city with only certain things have color.
-Sometimes this result in♥♥♥♥♥♥being hard to see (sewer level). Fortunately you have a button that highlights objects of importance(e.g. people and weapons)
+The game's levels generally pretty open with (mostly) very basic objectives (kill X amount of people).
-The sewer level is mostly linear
+The game is pretty detailed for a 20 dollar twin shooter.
+-Highly destructible environments. (not so much in the sewer level)
-+Seriously, the sewer level sucks in comparison to the others.
+The game is reasonably difficult. You'll never complain about the game being unfair or the controls being too broken.
+I got into a car and realized I didn't know how to drive. After I figured it out, I was overjoyed when I realized that this game has the worst driving controls I have played with.
+Have fun almost always crashing your car inside of a building
-Cars hate you and will explode if anyone so much as to cough on it. That means don't hide behind them if you want to live.
+Cars also hate everyone else, so after you are done crashing it into the police station (or on top of the second story sign some how). You can rest assured that after it finds out someone ate it's last Smores Poptarts, everyone in the immediate area will die. It will also leave a fire that will murder anyone stupid enough to walk into it.
+The innocent civilians run around aimlessly (and sometimes into you). While the law enforcement are intelligent and will use grenades and even flank you and realistically clear rooms.
+The game in no way pats you on the back for murdering. There is no scoring nor is there any "good job" screens.
Overall it's a fun game. I'll probably edit this in the future. Right now, I gotta go to work. Hope this helped anyone.

So, the thing about why this game is good and what it's bad points are.
Let me start of with the bad points.
- Short game. Could use more missions/modes/whatever.
- Few weapons. It's fun at start, but damn it, give me more things to shoot with.
- Kicking is your melee. How about melee weapons instead? Chainsaw could work.
- Not much to do other than follow the objectives. Could use some more variety in general.
- Some minor glitches and performance issues.
Now, here is what is good:
- Endless violence. Nobody is safe.
- Executions. Always a nice touch to add.
- Immersive environment. It really puts you into the role of someone who really hates everything.
- Decent Graphics. I didn't expect that.
- Physics are nice. Also didn't see that coming.
What I get from this game is what I was promised: You play as a guy who really hates everything. It does not matter how he came to this conclusion. People vary, and the human mind can go nuts for many different reasons. You grab what you can and go out to kill everyone, no matter who they are, or what they do. In the end, you expect to die violently in some horrible way. At least you take as many as you can with you. It's simple stuff, the game tells you what to kill and you go kill it. You can always just roam around and kill other things, find things that the game didn't tell you to kill (yet) and be happy you can release your hatred on a virtual world rather than the real one.
My final conclusion about this game is that it gave the people what it promised it would give them. The price is reasonable and the game can be fun for a short while. Is it worth it? Only if you like mindless violence and/or old-school iso-top shooters.

Im conflicted about my review of this game. It has very good lore, it's built off of the same engine as my favorite games of all time (AKA portal 1 and 2), and it has an element of mystery that I absolutly love. However something that frustrates me more then anything else in the world, is a game, movie, or tv show that has a GREAT story but a rediculously sub-par ending (Anyone remember that TV show "Lost"?). Game mechanics work fine, if your not hacking the game I haven't encountered any bugs. I was immediatly intrigued by the story, and played to solve the mystery. The narrarator to me seem to both make and break the game. To elaborate, this game feels incredibly empty without the narrator who constantly breaks the 4th wall and has good humor, but there are many times where the narrarator just dosen't stop talking and I get disinterested and simply want him to be quite. There are many facets to this story, and I wanted to keep playing to find out how to really beat the game. What really intrigued me was that the invironment changes slightly every time you make progress, so even though the narrarator is annoying half the time I pressed onward because I live for story rich games. That is till I found out you can't actually beat this game, its simply a game where you make a series of "Yes" "No", or "Left" "Right" decisions that lead you to a different ending based on your "Choices". I say choices liberally because your choices really don't effect anything in the game environment as much as you initially are led to believe they do. If you make the same choices twice in a row, guess what 9 times out of 10 you will get the same exact ending with no progress made except with mabey some minor changes. Kind of like those text-based java script games from way back in the day, but with a 3D environment to go with it. The story has no real satisfying ending for story rich players like myself, it left me feeling empty as there where many interesting objects in this game that I wanted to learn more about that apparently meant nothing. If you are a story driven player, like myself, your likely to not enjoy the ending(s) you find as they are nothing but unsatisfing, although mabey a bit funny. Which is why I will not be recommending this game. If you want lore, games like portal, and horizon zero dawn are a better choices for you. But if you get this game cheap and don't care much for story, its worth a couple hours of your time.

I really like this series.  I've played through and beaten every one of them.  I like the story, I like the characters, I like the gameplay.  Unfortunately, I don't like this game.
My biggest complaints about SR3 and SR4 were 'if you want my character to act like Jonny Gat, just let me play as Jonny Gat.'  Well, here you go.  You're Jonny Gat (or Kenzie Kensington, if you prefer), off to save the boss.  The story seems like typical SR stuff, which is to say that it's brimming with absurdity.  All of the typical Saints Row flavor is mostly present, but this game really feels rough.  There are some parts that are just really choppy for no apparent reason, especially considering earlier iterations of this franchise had identical or similar mechanics that just worked better.  Combat pretty much sucks.  Melee finishers have this earlier-mentioned choppiness problem, and gunplay feels unsatisfying.  There's nothing really new here in terms of gameplay either, it's just more Saints Row IV but with a different environment, which coincidentally makes it feel like a janky version of Crackdown, not just in feel, but in style.
I can't reccomend this game at it's full retail price, and I really can't move past a 'well, if you've got nothing else to do' reccomendation on this title even if it's on sale.  If you're a diehard Saints Row fan, there might be something here for you but if you've never played a game in this franchise but are considering this one, skip it, spend a couple extra dollars and give SR3 or SR4 a shot instead, which are both more enjoyable games.  For that matter, 1 is probably better, because it does a better job being a GTA clone than this game does as a Crackdown one.

I'm an older gamer who's been playing video since I was twelve (Pong and Asteroids, anyone?)
I rarely write reviews. Some games are great and I enjoy them immensely. Others disappoint and I end up regretting the time and money I spent on them. But I rarely feel inclined to wade into the fray. For X Rebirth, I've decided to make an exception.
I've been addicted to space games forever. X-Wing vs. Tie Fighter. Homeworld, Sins of a Solar Empire, Eve Online, Galactic Civilizations, Distant Worlds. Evochron. The X Series. I've played them all at one time or another.
X Rebirth is a game I've had my eye long before it was released.  Well, the release didn't go well (understatement) and the plethora of bugs and complaints kept me on the sidelines for almost a year. Well, this holiday season, I decided that  with the release of 3.0 and a sizable discount, I'd bite the bullet.  I always felt the screenshots looked great, but I really wasn't expecting much, especially in light of its notorious history.
Well, color me surprised, because I'm loving this game!  The flight mechanics (and graphics) are awesome and after a couple of dozen hours, I haven't run into a bug yet. It's got a fairly steep learning curve  (with Trading, Building, Crafting and such), but with a game of this complexity, that's to be expected.
What I didn't really expect was for Egosoft to continue suporting this game and turning a steaming pile of digital garbage into one of the most enjoyable gaming experiences I've had all year. So, Egosoft, shame on you for releasing a broken game. But Thank You, sincerely, for sticking with it and turning it into an encredibly enoyable Space Sim.
If you like casually flying around a HUGE open world (universe?) and picking and choosing the role you want to play within it, then I strongly recommend giving this game a chance. Like me, you may just end up loving it.

This War of Mine, an amazing game that came up on Steam not to long ago, but it gained MASSIVE response. This game explores an area that isn't explored in many other games: what is it like for the citizens of a country that is in the middle of a war. And it isn't talking about militia, or heroes that defeated an empire: These are buisnessmen, chefs, football coaches, and just regular people, trying to survive what seems to be a neverending war.
Now gameplay: You take control of 3 survivors at the start of a playthrough, and you find a large building with a good amount of supplies. However, you will find out that what you start out with, will not be enough. At night, you will have to scavenge different areas of the city, all while trying to stay hidden, get as much as possible, and to not die. Shall you mess up, and you will most likely find yourself in combat. In combat, you are usually at a disadvantage, shall you find yourself with no weapon or tool. However, fighting usually isn't worth it anyway, because if you do end up being the killer of another person or group, your survivors will have real effects from it. They will slowly become more and more depressed as you continue to do morally wrong things. Now, once the hell of night washes over, you get to experience the hardships of day.
During the day, you mainly focus on your "home", building other workbenches, feeding your survivors, and otherwise taking care of them, such as through medical aid, or with just a simple bed. Sometimes, you will encounter a stranger at the door, asking for help, asking to live with you (letting you control them, but it is another mouth to feed.), or even possibly asking for trade. When you choose to go back into the night, you will have to station certain people to do certain things, such as having one person getting to sleep, one on guard at your "house", and one scavenging.
Overall, this game is amazing, the graphics are great, gameplay is fantastic, and while it seems like there is no story at first, one will surely develop during your playthrough.
Rating: 9.5/10

After some additional gameplay I've decided to change my review.
This is a randomly generated platformer game where you need to collect white blocks that generate next tile for you to jump on.
You start with randomly picked character, some of them has special abilities:
- white guy - no special abilities
- sportsman - faster movement
- spaceman - so called moon-jumps
- double-jump man - well, ability to do double jump
- Elvis - nothing special
- guy that automatically picks white blocks - probably the most useful
What is somewhat weak is that those characters are choosen randomly - when you die you start off with a different one. This makes this game totally random.
Tiles that you step on slowly disappear, probably to make the player move his character ever forward (well, at least forward meaning collecting blocks). From time to time you can find a space rocket and start a minigame like Space Invaders where you can shoot about 3-4 UFOs and big UFO for additional points. That would be good unless that minigame wasn't so slow - the rocker starts, it floats up for some seconds and then you can shoot some ufos and then, after shooting a boss ufo, you fall down for some seconds. That is really too long!
This is clearly a ladder based game, where the only motivation is to beat the high score.
Pros:
- gameplay is really fast, respawning takes about a second
- characters with special abilities give some fun to the game
- minimalistic graphics fit the type of the game
Cons:
- boring
- no point in playing this game other than beating the high-score - no unlockables, no nothing
- those special characters are picked up randomly thus if you want to have a particular one you need to loose with the character that was chosen randomly until you get what you want
Overall - I don't think that this game is really interesting. Maybe it's not my type of game, maybe it's just boring. You can check it yourself but I would recommend getting it during some Steam Sale.

A game born from an exceptional idea, an enticing premise. Finally, I thought, a 'post-apocalyptic' without the zombie-filler, full of moral dilemmas and drama.
But, sadly, it fails in choosing a fitting game formula. It is enthralling for the first... 2 hours, but at a certain point, sooner or later, the facade fades and the underlying game disappoints.
Living in a warzone would mean a struggle for the most basic needs. These would be food & water (which are consumed quite rapidly), tools (which do not degrade as quickly as most modern games would make us believe), warmth (clothing & fuel) and weapons (which are either basic tools or heavily limited through ammunition). These are the things I would expect to fight for.
But just in the resources and crafting system the ugly mechanics of the game show, it is just like playing a mobile game. (be prepared to click A LOT). Food and Water was a non-issue for me (although constantly producing filters to 'produce' rain water was an annoyance) and tools were an annoyance (what are these rapidly degrading shovels made of?). Instead I found myself constantly carting massive quantities of wood and generic 'components' back into my base in order to upgrade my stove. In a post-apocalyptic world, building an independent, self-sufficient settlement is absolutely unrealistic and undermines the core of the setting. Building furniture and tools would be for a me a horrible waste of time and energy, especially if i have to carry wood and 'components' through the entire city first. To cut it short, the resources and crafting system is bloated, is missing a lot of balancing, and it's focus is chosen poorly.
Characters and moral conflicts are present but unfulfilling. The characters feel lacking and uniform, they generally seem to feel the same to any events in the world. The fixed base which is chosen for you takes a lot of opportunity out of the game, and the limitation of a single scavenger at night feels artifical and arbitrary (and reminded me of the new XCOM). Others raiding your camp should be a major event of a game and a situation of life or death for all your companions. Instead, it's a random text event, and a minor wound is allocated somewhere. Even more depressing.
I have to openly confess that I barely played three hours of this game before writing this review. The game effectively pushed me away. I've been scavenging for multiple days for the same generic items. I looked at my prospects and tried to plan the following days. I realized I had to constantly FARM basic goods for multiple days in order to earn a basic upgrade to my work bench or stove, which achieves barely any difference I turned the game OFF.
The reason for the massive amount of praise this game receives eludes me. The premise is original and brave, but not the gameplay, which undermines the whole idea of it. It shows again that the focus of too many critics is on the presentation of a game and its initial impression.
If I am playing Minesweeper with a new, dark, sinister, cynical coat of paint on it, I am still playing Minesweeper.

After playing this title during the free weekend, I feel content in my decision to skip it at release.  The game is clearly tuned for a play style unlike my own.  When I play 4x games, I focus on rapid expansion above all else.  Beyond Earth, however, absolutely punishes those who expand rapidly in the early game.  The ability to create colonists is buried away in the tech tree (I guess humans don't naturally reproduce in the future), and the health mechanic that replaces last game's happiness index is awful.  EVERYTHING reduces health, but there's nothing that can raise a city's health above its population.  This would be OK if there weren't also a massive amount of global health decay with no way to counter early to mid-game.
Since Civ IV, it has been hard to really recommend a Civilization game prior to expansions - maybe I shouldn't be shocked that Beyond Earth is lacking balance at present.  What I can't excuse, however, is the horrible interface.  The entire game (at least for the planet/race combinations I've tried) is cast in a palette of dark blues and browns which reduces the utility of contrast as a visual cue.  Text uniformly appears as medium-dark glyphs written on black backgrounds (I have an astigmatism and HATE this - listen up, Steam).  Units, resources, and geographic features just kind of blend in to the scenery with no real visual flair.  The map is covered with toxic gas with a very slight green hue, but since my race used the green color to map their borders it was nearly impossible to spot the toxic miasma.  Selecting a trading caravan highlighted the gas in red but I could not find any other filter to prominently display the miasma.  Even just deducing terrain types was a chore, since the tooltip is for some reason anchored to the useless minimap; you must focus on the terrain, then one corner for the tooltip, and finally the opposite corner for your unit's actions.
More than once, I found myself frustrated when a modal dialog popped up with an enemy faction offering diplomatic options.  The only choices are to accept or refuse - there is no way to look at the faction's stats, holdings, allies, etc. prior to making the decision.  This same lack of consideration typifies the Beyond Earth experience as it now stands.  The music is absolutely uninspiring: the same tune that plays during the introductory video periodically plays in the background, but otherwise the soundscape is limited to vague atmospheric tones.  Sadly gone are the faction-specific tunes that both play in the background and change as you zoom into a town.  Even the completion of world wonders and other milestones is rather underinspiring.  There aren't any neat Civ2 style animations or any Leonard Nimoy voice-overs, just a blue-on-blue line drawing with what sounds like a text-to-speech robot voice speaking a few lines.  It's hard to overlook the big issues when even the small things are poorly executed.
Aside from the horrid UI and insipid theme, the biggest single issue with the game as it currently stands are affinity points.  Basically, Beyond Earth introduces three affinities: harmony, purity, and supremacy.  The idea is that your research (using the horribly designed jumble of a tech. tree) will naturally earn rank in various affinities throughout the course of the game.  Affinity rank can be exploited with the creation of affinity-specific units and buildings.  So far, so good.  But, for some foolish reason, almost all of the victory conditions are tied to a specific affinity!  This senseless coupling exposes the affinities as an illusion of choice.  If a player, for example, strives for a "promised land" victory, they will need to heavily focus on purity tech.   This being the case, why not just integrate the whole purity affinity into the default tech tree and eliminate an unnecessary concept?  Looking at the tech tree (piecewise, of course, because you have to zoom so far out to see the big picture that you can't even see individual icons), I have to wonder if this is why it's so unwieldy.
Civ has needed expansions to smooth out the balance and overall game concept for the last few iterations - maybe that will work wonders here, too.  A series that has been very slowly refined over multiple decades has no excuse for a poorly designed interface, however, and that's something that I don't think is likely to improve with time.  6/10

I will admit: I went into this game with low expectations. I was in on the early access, and while I liked the idea it just wasn't shaping up to wha I wanted to me. Color me shocked, but I have to say my expectations were simply surpassed. I still have my misgivings, but this is overall a good game. THIS is how a game should be developed. Start with a rough edge, sharpen, an evolution of characters and ideas, until finally you have a finished product. And on that note alone I would recommend this.
First: The good.
Atmosphere. The game drips with a thick atmosphere set in a pre-colonization american wild. There is no wildlife or humans save for you and one other. You are the only sane man in a cursed world, and this game does an excellent job at establishing that hard-to-nail lonely feeling.
This game is also quite frightening in the fun way that everything is scarier that it should be. Mortal enemies consist of soldiers and natives. The Spanish soldiers are literally some kind of inhuman beast-men, and the indians are more like zombies than humans. Then you have spiritual foes; consisting primarily of spell-casting skeletons and wraiths. Its just that everything you encounter is so strange and unnatural in ways you don't execpt. Armed with only simple weapons and your stealth skills, this game does a good job at making you feel helpless and alone in a diffuclt situation; proving that, once again, taking away the weapons doesn't make a game scary on its own so much as the feeling of helplessness and weakness does. A wide variety of intimidating monsters and plentiful surprises makes the game consistantly intense and frightening; no spoilers included.
Except one: NIne foot tall Infantryman in the first area.
Weapons work well on that note. You have a small arsenal of five or six weapons that can be upgraded in quality to improve performance. Each weapon has strengths and drawbacks. Bows are weaker, but being able to recover ammo is practical. While a pistol or musket packs a punch they are also noisy and very limited. You also have a dagger sidearm for fending off swarming enemies, and a tomahawk that serves as a sort of grenade attack that can get rid of anyone except some of the nastier foes with one good throw.
It is also worth noting this game is very hard at times. You can take about two to three shots before dying if you don't use a health flask, enemies often attack in groups, and many foes possess a rage ability that makes them more resistant to damage when they go into attack. This is primarily a stealth fps where sneak attacks and avoidance are preferred, and open conflicts are dangerous and cost you a lot of valuable ammo. A well placed arrow to the back can kill a soldier in one shot, but if he spots you? Not even a high-quality musket shot to the chest will kill him then. You have to be quick and accurate in this game, and it is very rewarding.
In summary, the gameplay is intense and legitimately scary a lot of times. Its a good challenge, and working with old-world weaponry is good fun and rewarding to get the hang of. The gameplay is definitely there.
The bad:
I'm going to skip over some of the nitpicks like the night being too easy at times or enemy path-finding being a little clumsy, and loading being a bit too long for my tastes and get on with the one big problem I have with this game.
Story and objectives.
The setup is good to be fair. You are some kind of traveler going to America when your ship is gunned down by a Spanish warship and you are stranded in a strangely cursed colony where everyone is mysteriously dead, and ghosts roam freely. You have one companion in all this mess, a woman in red robe, but she doesn't even know her own name. Its up to you to figure out what is going on.
And here is where it falls apart. You never figure out what is going on.
You spend most of the game finding white ghosts, people who committed horrible acts of betrayal (hah) and sin, and are now cursed to undeath, and helping them remember their sins in order to give them peace. But each character is its own little side story that ultimatley shapes up to have nothing to do with the whole curse problem. After completing the fourth investigation and helping the ghosts remember their sins, I still don't know what is going on. You also find pages that seem to log thoughts of the colony, but they are all worthless it seems; with many of them talking about mundane things like the quality of an indian arrow vs an englishman's arrow.
There's also a mechanic where you find certain treasures that you can give to the girl in red that I 'think' is some sort of investigation mechanic where you see how she reacts to certain things in order to find out more about her and help guess who she is later, but even on that I don't know.
The game is just cryptic. I feel like the main 'plot' doesn't go anywhere, and I'm just doing a bunch of fetch quests to collect clues to help people remember things that I don't care about. There is just no point to it, and if there is than its waited too long to make it, as I am sure I am already halfway through the game.
That's another thing though: clue collecting. Its interesting to use a sort of sixth sense to find little treasures and points of interest to collect clues to help the ghosts remember things, but its all linear and prescripted. All your responses are single-lines that force the stories along in an unpleasant way. It lacks intelligence.
To summaraize that: The story just isn't good. Its got a nice setup, but it holds the player by the hand, drags them along at a snail's pace, and presents itself in a broken incoherent mess of sidestories that just make absolutely no sense in the grand scheme of things. And finally, for a game that oozes with 'mysterious', there is just no mystery, since everything you say is pre-determined. You should be able to collect clues, put the stories together yourself, and figure out whether the evidence saves or condemns the soul in question, but instead its all a straight line and often painfully predictable.
Overall:
I remember the developers saying they wanted to make a simple well-polished game rather than one bloated with ugly features, and I can agree with that bit of wisdom to an extent. But I have to say, Betrayer's biggest flaw, and a big flaw at that, is the lack of complexity. Weapon variety feels a little limited, the stories of the ghosts are easy to figure out and don't really involve the player, and overall its just a big fetch-quest that serves as an excuse for the player to go out into the darkened wilds to explore and face monsters.
But that doesn't stop the gameplay one bit, which I would say is top notch when it all comes together in tense stealth action and brutal conflicts. Its a well-made, if overly simple, game that is fun to play and a decent challenge. For an atmospheric game, the lack of a good engaging story is a massive flaw in my eyes, but the one-of-a-kind setting and pre-american FPS gameplay is just enough to redeem its shortcomings.
I recommend this game, if barely. I wish it could have been better, but its fun enough as is and definitely worth the twenty dollars.

I can see why Bioshock 2 doesn’t get the same attention as the first game or Infinite. Don’t get me wrong, it has some great features to it. The game play is way more fluid than the original, which would influence the play of Infinite (having both plasmids and weapons ready instead of choosing one or the other). But this gain comes at a cost. YOU WILL DIE A LOT! You could be the best FPS player, but the game tends to spawn enemies like no tomorrow. You could be ambushed in rooms you just cleared by Spider or Houdini Splicers. If you pop out of a Vita Chamber with low health and low ammo, you could be overwhelmed by respawned enemies which will cause you to die again, again, and again. Many times I’ve raged quit over this. The best solution is to Insect Swarm a room before entering.
You play as a Big Daddy, which give you cool Big Daddy gear and adds a new mechanic of harvesting Adam with a Little Sister. It’s cool at first, but it gets a little tedious after a few levels, especially if you want to rescue all of them (about 3 a level) and get that good ending. After rescuing all the Little Sisters in a level, prepare to fight the Big Sister. If you are not well-equipped and prepared, prepare to die again, again, and again.
Haven’t explored multiplayer much since no one seems to be playing it. I think there are some Steam communities that do, so don’t let that discourage you. It actually looks kind of fun.
Why should you still play this? Returning to Rapture! As a Bioshock fan you’ll regret not playing it. I think of this game more as a companion piece rather than a sequel. You don’t really follow any of the original characters save a cameo from Dr. Tenembaum and Radio Diaries of Ryan and Fontaine. You do get to learn more about Rapture and its expanded history. Set almost a decade after the first game, you also get to see the city decay and the sea beginning to reclaim it. Don’t want to give too much away for those interested, but it’s safe to say the city is the main focus. If story is not your thing and you just want to run and gun, than avoid this title.

Okay, serious review time.
This game brings back nostalgic memories from Bioshock 1, but then amplified by playing as a big daddy.
If you pick this game up while not having played Bioshock 1 you might not be able to grasp how cool it is to play as a big daddy. For this was the first and almost only reason I picked up this game, but I was suprised on how much more this game has to offer then the obvious "you are a big daddy so here are bigger guns to shoot stuff with".
Take the Story for instance, the Bioshock series set this "reference point" for having a good story line. Always with some unexpencted story twist at the end (even though this game doesn't have that as much as infinite or the first one). Without any spoilers I can only say its good, but nothing like infinite.
Gameplay whise I wasn't all to suprised, like I said before its basically the gameplay of Bioshock 1 with bigger guns. But that doesn't mean its bad, infact, the gameplay and movement is super solid and extremely satisfying. You can combine plasmids, guns and genetonics to perfect your "build".
The enemies have a good variety, not just the typical splicer, all the different enemy types make up for changing gameplay. But later on in the game the variety of splicers become boring, late game you are so powerful that you cut through everyone in seconds, even big daddies and sisters. And the only way the game compensates for that is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ out a bazillion enemies at you, so late game becomes more or less a grind and the variety stops.
All and all, its a good game. Super solid gameplay, storywise lacking a bit for a bioshock game. And the variety in builds you can do, make me come back to this game constantly.

Everything about this game is unique and cool and weird, so it's hard for me to start somewhere in particular talking about it. The game itself seems to know this, too--it throws you in there and says, "You have to get these magical, destructive underpants from your jerk brother, and you have a laser and stuff. This is how you use them. Now, go, and have a good time."
The laser and other tools in this game are really fun to use--you can chop up nearly everything with your laser, then drag it around with your rope, then launch it as far as you like with the rocket. Using these tools, you move around, discover hidden areas, and grab cassettes (that unlock new songs by indie bands for the player to listen to, and they are all super good and fit the environment--I'm glad I bought the soundtrack with the game). The player has ample opportunity to choose to screw around and explore the area, too. If you have fun with physics, you'll be all over the gameplay here. Plus, I imagine this would be a fun, challenging game to 100%, and there are leaderboards if you're the kind of person who loves trying to beat levels quicker than everybody else.
I love the visual style of this game--all dialogue is delivered in speech bubbles, and the overall look of the game reminds me of something I'd see in a weird manga or an indie comic or a webcomic. And, just to emphasize this, the music in this game is amazing.
The story is simple and silly, but the stakes actually do manage to feel high by game's end.
Basically, if you think, "I might like this game" while watching the trailer, you definitely will. It's great fun.

Early Access Watcher Public Service Announcement
Game: Economic Conquest
Update Version: Initial Early Access Release
Disclosure: This game copy was bought by the reviewer.
Game Footage:
Economic Conquest is a economic strategy game developed and published by Frismos. This will mark the developer's first venture into the Early Access program as well as their first Steam release. The game bolsters thirty missions with six of them representing the tutorial portion, which does a decent job of easing the player into the core concepts of the game. Aesthetically, the game offers a rural appeal with simple colors while the soundtrack is limited to a couple of looping tracks. Overall a great start to a basic strategy game, but maybe a bit to basic to appease everyone.
The core mechanics center around how well the player can establish a stable income and the ability to protect territory with the use of influence. Income is generated per day depending on the level of the business, the market value of processed goods and the possible bonuses available in the territory the business was built in. The higher the income, the more stable the ability to manage territories can be as the match progresses. This is increasingly important late game when buyouts become important, which cost a flat rate depending on the level of the businesses on the territory and the influence level. As long as the influence of a territory is above 70 the territory cannot be bought, which can be difficult when the player has multiple countries to manage and the AI is continually decreasing a territories' influence by the use of mutiny (-10 per purchase). Regardless of difficulty level (Easy, Medium, Hard), the AI presents a challenge and with the way random events change the earning power of resource, waiting to start a business can be a blessing or a detrimental error.
Market values for the six resource types fluctuate constantly and the changes are random, making it imperative to have a diverse selection of businesses to overcome the risk of having a 152% resource gain plummet to 79%. The use of the territory bonuses (25% increase) help alleviate the strain this could put on late game play, which is why it is always recommended to build lumber mills where trees are abundant and oil fields in oil rich coast lines. Low resource earnings, however, can provide an opportunity for early game construction at cheaper prices. Business starting cost are influenced by the resource price, so buying into something offering lower returns is cheaper than buying into something with high returns. This is a giant gamble, but it can pay off later and be a crucial move to combat the AI, which always starts with the first increased resource and tends to only follow the same pattern regardless of the risks.
Building upgrade prices also fluctuate depending on certain random events as well as the I.R. requirements needed to start a new business or acquire contracts in new countries. Gaining I.R. is easy (business levels and each five levels of influence), but using the lowered requirements grants a income boost through new businesses that can make or break a game. The other changing value comes in the form of influence, which is mandatory to protect countries from buyouts and to raise the max business upgrade level (5 levels per 50 influence). Influence costs increase naturally with how many territories are owned and the current influence level in the territory, but also go up or down depending on the random event factors. Charity is the primary form of influence (100% guaranteed 10 influence), but bribery is also available at a risk to losing $8000 and 1 I.R. Loans can also be taken out to provide instant income and is increased based on the player's total I.R. I have not seen any downsides to not paying it back, except the inability to have it for use later if something happens.
Thankfully, the game runs smoothly with very little load times. It did give me a few problems when I tried launching the game, something I still have to circumvent from time to time. I also ran into an annoying issue with how the menus work. When accessing a menu for a business or to adjust influence ratings, the game zooms into the country in question and requires the user to click outside the menu's window to exit the menu. I have run into several cases of clicking outside the menu, only to instead open the menu for the country neighboring it. This can be averted by using the ESC key, but regardless of the method used, the game remains zoomed in on the country and requires a scroll out. Considering the hectic nature of the AI during some of the later missions, these are seconds that can drastically change the course of a round. As far as glitches go, I only noticed one dealing with the incorrect tally of Influence increases calculating into I.R. I would influence a territory five times (0 to 50) and not receive the I.R. conversion. This happened randomly throughout my time with the game and can be a major issue depending on how the random events effect I.R.
Strategy is a vast genre with plenty of interesting variations in game types. Frismos has made a decent economic focused title and the promise of multiplayer later down the line could bring some much needed life to a game suffering from a predictably routine AI. The game also only has one map with fixed positions for each resource bonus. This isn't to say I didn't have fun with the game. It is an interesting concept that can easily entertain during a short break, but the sum of its' parts might not be enough to warrant the $8 price tag. It is just hard to recommend at this time.

I have tried very hard to like FFXIII, despite having been subjected to earlier opinions both positive and negative.
I just can't recommand this product.
It isn't because of the "walking through a tunnel" syndrome the game definitely suffers from and is so frequently mentioned in other reviews. I knew of it before I bought the game, thought it wouldn't be that bad, it turned out to be worse, but far worse than that it turns out to be not the game's actual problem. Yeah, this game players like you're walking through a tunnel all the time, your movements confined and forced in one single direction except the token sidepath which is guaranteed to give bonus loot. That's not what makes this game bad. One could argue that that is what makes this game story-driven, and near as I can tell the story's actually good.
The problem is that this isn't much of a game, and far more of a movie.
Starting FFXIII, we're subjected to some of the main characters, most of which who portray stereotypical or archetypical figures from what we're used to from pop culture and/or previous Final Fantasy games. I could probably decently compare most of FFXIII's characters to previous FF games and draw clear parallels, which is okay, because that is part of a Final Fantasy game, right down to the airship captain named Cid. As the game progresses we find out, mostly through flashbacks, that all of these people are somehow related to the central story: the nature of the fal'Cie, a group of mystical beings that provide the functions humans need to survive in their artificial bubble-world called Cocoon, and the nature of their enforced servants, l'Cie, humans "gifted" with a brand that provides them both with magical powers and with the curse of turning into a monster if they do not complete their Focus in time, a task set to them by the fal'Cie that doesn't come with a proper set of instructions.
It is around the relationship between fal'Cie and humans, the bubble-world of Cocoon and the nature of the planet below the artificial Cocoon world, called Pulse, that the game revolves. Pitting polar positions against each other with human servants in the middle, the story appears beautifully crafted, as beautifully as the world(s) and enviroment you find yourself in while playing the game.
The real problem is that all of this doesn't really become apparent until you're 15-20 hours in. The time before that is spent by the game telling you what it wants from you: that it wants you to press buttons in the way it wants to and if you do that right, it'll entertain you with its story. It's like a sullen child. You give it cake, and it'll clean its room.
I understand that a good tutorial, especially enmeshed properly in gameplay, is a good feature. Except that a tutorial should not take 15-20 gameplay hours. I will admit that I am not a seasoned Final Fantasy player, and that it could be done a lot faster if I knew what I was doing, but these are not merits by which to judge a game. I am not judging this game compared to other games of its kind, I am judging it on its merits alone, because I expect each game I buy to provide me entertainment value for its own sake. If after 10 hours of gameplay the game still needs to teach me basic functionality, if after 15 hours of gameplay I apparently still get to play with new characters, but more importantly than that STILL don't have the freedom to decide on my own party 'cause the game just HAS to tell the story this way... that's when I get annoyed, and that's primarly 'cause some of these characters play as comfortably as a brick car with square wooden wheels and a sharp metal spike for a seat.
This is where the story fails. These characters could be interesting, if I did not have to play with them. Two specifically, Snow and Sazh, are horrible to play with, especially when they're the "main" character of the group, and lo and behold a bit of googling reveals that they are the ones irrelevant to the "meta" of most useful characters. Similarly one of the best characters to play with, Fang, does not come under your control until 15 hours of playtime. However the game insists on putting me in scenarios where I have different characters with different roles/specializations in control, just so I can experience all possible combinations in a tutorial-esque way until I finally get the point where I probably have full customization.
The result is that I don't feel like I am playing a game, the game is playing me. It is a sullen, insecure movie disguised as a game, that demands that I press some obligatory buttons before it'll continue telling me its story.
It would help if combat was actually engaging or interesting, but it isn't. The biggest challenge of combat, is starting a fight with Preemptive Strikes, which is achieved by manipulating the amazingly stupid AI into turning its back on you so you can run into them undetected. The rest of combat is primarily playing with the Paradigm system, which defines the roles that your AI controlled characters use (while letting you perform token manual abilities with the "main" character), which barely keeps me engaged in the fight. Manipulating paradigms is crucial to succesful combat, especially in the case of the harder bossfights in the game... but it's not difficult, and it's not engaging.
The most difficult part of the game by far is dealing with its frequently occurring error: repetitive command lock. I understand that FFXIII is a console port, I don't mind that. However it's a console port that apparently (after googling the issue) doesn't like that you don't have a controller hooked up to your computer. Frequently and apparently randomly, the game will lock your controls into repeating the same button command over and over, effectively making the game unplayable by making your character behave as if you were pressing the same button over and over. Not even terminating the game function through Windows will fix this, when this error occurs you could open notepad and see it write the same letter over and over until you restart your computer.
In the end I tried hard to like this game for the sake of its story, which I truly believe could be good. The world is beatifully crafted. The characters eventually turn out to be intersting enough. The gameplay is pretty terrible but I could sludge through it if it at least proved to be reliable and consistent, but even if I were to ignore the frequently occuring error that causes me to restart my computer and ruin my progress, playing this game just feels like a chore. It reminds me of the Stanley Parable, where the protagonist's job is to press a button when queued to do so and work will continue.
That is all FFXIII is. Do combat sequence, before you get to continue with otherwise interesting story. It's not a game. It's a movie you have to work for.

I was on the fence about a 2D space combat game, but having played it it's a fun game.
It has some problems, the control system seems to be based around a gamepad so there are a few limitations on the UI that wouldn't otherwise be there. There are also some curious design decisions like being unable to access your cargohold/factions list/tactical menu etc while docked.
There is no RPGesque character development, the only limitation on what ship/equipment you can use seems to be money and to a lesser extent faction.
The combat in the game is fun. There is a large variety of equipment available to outfit your ship in order to compliment your playstyle. For instance you can gear your ship up for long range sniping, close range, and even fitting special deflector shields in order to cause extra damage ramming into other ships. In general the combat seems very well thought out.
On the other hand the trading and mining feel a bit lacklustre. Mining, even with the "perfect" mining setup is haphazard and rarely nets you anywhere near the amount of money combat would in the same amount of time. Trading seems too random in that it's very hard to charge what good will be worth more at any given station. I freely admit though I haven't spent a lot of time trading, so it's very possible that if I invested more time in it I'd understand the system more.
I've read complaints about the save system. It's a standard autosave only game, and the autosave only takes place when you dock. This means that if you pick up 3 missions, complete 2 and then die in the 3rd one you'll lose all that progress. However, that's not necessarily a bad thing as you just weigh up the risk and dock if necessary to save.
The soundtrack in the game is...interesting. I kind of liked it at first, but it becomes very repetitive after a couple of hours. However, using the launcher you can easily add your own music.
In summary this game is definately worth picking up if you enjoy space action games.

X Rebirth offers an incredible sense of depth. The game opens up everything that was confining about X3. Instead of jump gates and loading screens, we have fast moving highways and a large seamless universe. Instead of being mostly trapped in your spaceship, you can now explore the interiors of stations and ships. Instead of only seeing other characters as animated thumbnail images in the corner of your screen, you can now interact with characters face-to-face. Instead of restrictive SETA time compression (which still felt slow), your ship now has a powerful boost drive. Instead of mostly empty space with scattered stations, we now have huge space cities full of life and personality. Every ship now has a purpose, making the economy more dynamic and real. The main plot is engaging and offers good tips and explaination throughout so you aren't left wondering to do.
For me, X Rebirth successfully combines all of the great things about X3 and Freelancer and offers a wonderfuly rich universe to explore.

You could go the easy route and describe This War of Mine as "The Sims, but set in Hell." And you'd be right.
The game can be better described as an 'entropy simulator': There's plenty of things to pick up initially. Just through initial walks through the area you can find a bunch of resources you can use for initial improvements to make for your war hovel. But eventually, that stuff will start to run out, and you will not be able to play it safe anymore. If you're smart, you'll have someone who is good at bartering and items to supply the demands of rich survivors with, and you might be able to get through the war without blood on your hands.
If you're no longer able to play it safe, that is where the real This War of Mine begins.
It is easy to lose control of your circumstances concerning what your group needs. If you have to keep pushing your wounded and your sick, they will get worse. But there's points where you just can't, because you need to keep a tight budget on what little resources you have. Raiders will come by, you will get a small winter, and your group members will get hideously depressed from having to hide from the war in a cold, destroyed house. All of these things will add up, and not having what you need to keep them sane and healthy will eventually destroy your chances of seeing the end of the game.
You'll have to be a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ to get what you need, and the mental tax that your actions will cause will be heavy. Sure, you can poke your scavenging survivor to stab an armed thug in the back, but he will hate himself for it the next day. You can brandish your pistol at the elderly couple hiding out in their nice home to take their supplies. You can carefully sneak through homes and take things that survivors not unlike yourself have been hoarding for a rainy day, putting them in  poverty to get what your group needs. And, of course, you can sneak through shadows and stab people in the back, trying to ignore their frightened pleads as you put the blade in to keep others from noticing all for the sake of some things you could have, in better days, gotten from a supermarket for five dollars.
This game is one of those games where it can make you feel like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ for trying to survive, and the more desperate you have to get to feed your group, the more it works. It's a horrible ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ feeling generator when the game is at it's toughest.

After playing this title during the free weekend, I feel content in my decision to skip it at release.  The game is clearly tuned for a play style unlike my own.  When I play 4x games, I focus on rapid expansion above all else.  Beyond Earth, however, absolutely punishes those who expand rapidly in the early game.  The ability to create colonists is buried away in the tech tree (I guess humans don't naturally reproduce in the future), and the health mechanic that replaces last game's happiness index is awful.  EVERYTHING reduces health, but there's nothing that can raise a city's health above its population.  This would be OK if there weren't also a massive amount of global health decay with no way to counter early to mid-game.
Since Civ IV, it has been hard to really recommend a Civilization game prior to expansions - maybe I shouldn't be shocked that Beyond Earth is lacking balance at present.  What I can't excuse, however, is the horrible interface.  The entire game (at least for the planet/race combinations I've tried) is cast in a palette of dark blues and browns which reduces the utility of contrast as a visual cue.  Text uniformly appears as medium-dark glyphs written on black backgrounds (I have an astigmatism and HATE this - listen up, Steam).  Units, resources, and geographic features just kind of blend in to the scenery with no real visual flair.  The map is covered with toxic gas with a very slight green hue, but since my race used the green color to map their borders it was nearly impossible to spot the toxic miasma.  Selecting a trading caravan highlighted the gas in red but I could not find any other filter to prominently display the miasma.  Even just deducing terrain types was a chore, since the tooltip is for some reason anchored to the useless minimap; you must focus on the terrain, then one corner for the tooltip, and finally the opposite corner for your unit's actions.
More than once, I found myself frustrated when a modal dialog popped up with an enemy faction offering diplomatic options.  The only choices are to accept or refuse - there is no way to look at the faction's stats, holdings, allies, etc. prior to making the decision.  This same lack of consideration typifies the Beyond Earth experience as it now stands.  The music is absolutely uninspiring: the same tune that plays during the introductory video periodically plays in the background, but otherwise the soundscape is limited to vague atmospheric tones.  Sadly gone are the faction-specific tunes that both play in the background and change as you zoom into a town.  Even the completion of world wonders and other milestones is rather underinspiring.  There aren't any neat Civ2 style animations or any Leonard Nimoy voice-overs, just a blue-on-blue line drawing with what sounds like a text-to-speech robot voice speaking a few lines.  It's hard to overlook the big issues when even the small things are poorly executed.
Aside from the horrid UI and insipid theme, the biggest single issue with the game as it currently stands are affinity points.  Basically, Beyond Earth introduces three affinities: harmony, purity, and supremacy.  The idea is that your research (using the horribly designed jumble of a tech. tree) will naturally earn rank in various affinities throughout the course of the game.  Affinity rank can be exploited with the creation of affinity-specific units and buildings.  So far, so good.  But, for some foolish reason, almost all of the victory conditions are tied to a specific affinity!  This senseless coupling exposes the affinities as an illusion of choice.  If a player, for example, strives for a "promised land" victory, they will need to heavily focus on purity tech.   This being the case, why not just integrate the whole purity affinity into the default tech tree and eliminate an unnecessary concept?  Looking at the tech tree (piecewise, of course, because you have to zoom so far out to see the big picture that you can't even see individual icons), I have to wonder if this is why it's so unwieldy.
Civ has needed expansions to smooth out the balance and overall game concept for the last few iterations - maybe that will work wonders here, too.  A series that has been very slowly refined over multiple decades has no excuse for a poorly designed interface, however, and that's something that I don't think is likely to improve with time.  6/10

Presentation
The main story is , we (Johnny Gat and Kinze Kensington) have to rescue the President (the previous main protagnist from Saints Row 1 to 4) from the abduction of Satan who wants to marry her daughter , Jezzebel , to the President . In order to get rescue him , Gat and Kenzie must deliver a fulll destruction and wrath to Hell in order to get Satan's Attention . With the help of Dane Vogel , the previous main antagonist of Saints Row 2 , the character will have numerous quests from him and the other hands of Allies , like Blackbeard , Shakespeare , Vlad , and DeWynter sisters . In the progress of the game , you as a player will gain their trust after completing every quests that they gave it to you . But the main problem from this point is the lack of the main storyline that has no motivation for you to save The President . For the players , the only reasons you get here in Hell is because you want to mess with "the taste of hell" . The other problem is that the characterization of each character are not developed well , even with the two main protagonist , Gat and Kinzie . In this section , this is the first critic
Gameplay
In Gat Out of Hell , Power is the main thing that leads you in every way of this game . You will gain a lots of power in the progress of the game . And most of my favorite is the weapons itself , especially The 7 Deadly Weapons - Sloth . This baby is the number reason why you wanna put some mess in Hell . With powerfull Minigun in the left and right side of this couch , and also with the powerfull 5 missiles everytime you want to shoot some explosive , this one is the Over Powered weapon . And with upgraded power of this weapon (where you can upgrade the weapon until to the unlimited ammo) , you almost can create a massive riot in one area , no kidding . Although The 7 Deadly Weapons - Sloth was the best weapon in this  game , there are still a lots of weapons that still blow your mind , from SMG to the explosive weapon etc . Beside all of that , the game also provides you with 4 magical powers that were given from your allies . Each power will give different impact to the enemy . But my favorite is THE STOMP . This baby is the second reason why you wanna go to the worst of place in the end of the universe . With a lots of upgrading option , this one will put your enemy in a misery . Overall this section was one of the best point for this game
Graphics
Although it's been upgraded since the previous Saints Row's game , but the graphics will not lift up the hype . Maybe some special effects are cool , but not gonna put your jaw drop for a long time . That's all
Features
In this section , it's the same thing like the Gameplay , it's cool , mostly to the upgrade options of weapon , characters , and magical powers . Unfortunately you can't customize your own character . You can't buy some clothes etc . Maybe the reason is that they are in Hell .... so what could they bought in the worst place of eternity . But the upgrading sections in this game is why i love this and the reason why I don't want to finish the main story quest .
In the end , The Good and The Bad of this is
The Good
+Powerfull weapons

The Bad

Had some problems starting out,  but a few restarts set things straight.  Good game until my Capital glitched and I couldn't access it's production queue.  Every other city was fine, but my Capital was stuck producing whatever I had selected before, however I couldn't even track that because it showed it set perpetually at "10 turns" to finish something that wasn't on the queue before.  That's kind of a big deal in a game like Civ.  Also, a more general annoyance; diplomacy still sucks.  Getting any AI to deal or agree to cooperate is impossible without breaking the bank in trade, and Favors were a nice touch, but are ultimately useless if you can't get a Cooperation Agreement with whoever owes the favor.  Dunno how I feel about an IOU as payment for trade in a 4X game... and then there's Affinity.  A very interesting twist, but unfortunately, until you get it levelled up your military will be laughable in early-game numbers.  Wouldn't be so bad if it wasn't as slow and unpredictable as it is.
Ultimately, this is a $50 Early Access Civilization 5 Expansion.  Very pretty, cool unit/building design, definitely good Sci-Fi... but I've had to reboot the game and restart maps too often due to glitching and uncharacteristically aggressive aliens.  I'll buy it and recommend it when the bugs are patched, the price drops, and some variety is introduced to the factions.

This War of Mine, an amazing game that came up on Steam not to long ago, but it gained MASSIVE response. This game explores an area that isn't explored in many other games: what is it like for the citizens of a country that is in the middle of a war. And it isn't talking about militia, or heroes that defeated an empire: These are buisnessmen, chefs, football coaches, and just regular people, trying to survive what seems to be a neverending war.
Now gameplay: You take control of 3 survivors at the start of a playthrough, and you find a large building with a good amount of supplies. However, you will find out that what you start out with, will not be enough. At night, you will have to scavenge different areas of the city, all while trying to stay hidden, get as much as possible, and to not die. Shall you mess up, and you will most likely find yourself in combat. In combat, you are usually at a disadvantage, shall you find yourself with no weapon or tool. However, fighting usually isn't worth it anyway, because if you do end up being the killer of another person or group, your survivors will have real effects from it. They will slowly become more and more depressed as you continue to do morally wrong things. Now, once the hell of night washes over, you get to experience the hardships of day.
During the day, you mainly focus on your "home", building other workbenches, feeding your survivors, and otherwise taking care of them, such as through medical aid, or with just a simple bed. Sometimes, you will encounter a stranger at the door, asking for help, asking to live with you (letting you control them, but it is another mouth to feed.), or even possibly asking for trade. When you choose to go back into the night, you will have to station certain people to do certain things, such as having one person getting to sleep, one on guard at your "house", and one scavenging.
Overall, this game is amazing, the graphics are great, gameplay is fantastic, and while it seems like there is no story at first, one will surely develop during your playthrough.
Rating: 9.5/10

A game born from an exceptional idea, an enticing premise. Finally, I thought, a 'post-apocalyptic' without the zombie-filler, full of moral dilemmas and drama.
But, sadly, it fails in choosing a fitting game formula. It is enthralling for the first... 2 hours, but at a certain point, sooner or later, the facade fades and the underlying game disappoints.
Living in a warzone would mean a struggle for the most basic needs. These would be food & water (which are consumed quite rapidly), tools (which do not degrade as quickly as most modern games would make us believe), warmth (clothing & fuel) and weapons (which are either basic tools or heavily limited through ammunition). These are the things I would expect to fight for.
But just in the resources and crafting system the ugly mechanics of the game show, it is just like playing a mobile game. (be prepared to click A LOT). Food and Water was a non-issue for me (although constantly producing filters to 'produce' rain water was an annoyance) and tools were an annoyance (what are these rapidly degrading shovels made of?). Instead I found myself constantly carting massive quantities of wood and generic 'components' back into my base in order to upgrade my stove. In a post-apocalyptic world, building an independent, self-sufficient settlement is absolutely unrealistic and undermines the core of the setting. Building furniture and tools would be for a me a horrible waste of time and energy, especially if i have to carry wood and 'components' through the entire city first. To cut it short, the resources and crafting system is bloated, is missing a lot of balancing, and it's focus is chosen poorly.
Characters and moral conflicts are present but unfulfilling. The characters feel lacking and uniform, they generally seem to feel the same to any events in the world. The fixed base which is chosen for you takes a lot of opportunity out of the game, and the limitation of a single scavenger at night feels artifical and arbitrary (and reminded me of the new XCOM). Others raiding your camp should be a major event of a game and a situation of life or death for all your companions. Instead, it's a random text event, and a minor wound is allocated somewhere. Even more depressing.
I have to openly confess that I barely played three hours of this game before writing this review. The game effectively pushed me away. I've been scavenging for multiple days for the same generic items. I looked at my prospects and tried to plan the following days. I realized I had to constantly FARM basic goods for multiple days in order to earn a basic upgrade to my work bench or stove, which achieves barely any difference I turned the game OFF.
The reason for the massive amount of praise this game receives eludes me. The premise is original and brave, but not the gameplay, which undermines the whole idea of it. It shows again that the focus of too many critics is on the presentation of a game and its initial impression.
If I am playing Minesweeper with a new, dark, sinister, cynical coat of paint on it, I am still playing Minesweeper.

I purchased this game during Early Access and really enjoyed it at the time. Soo much has been added to the game I won't list it all here. Betrayer is made by some of the original F.E.A.R. devs and that alone got my attention.
It has a moody atmosphere, spooky enemies, classic weaponry, color pallette/contrast sliders and a low amount of handholding.
I reccomend playing in the black and white but it looks like the color options have gotten some adjustments, making them better as well.
The dev's have made a lot of adjustments from the feedback they were given in Early Access, while remaining true to the vision they had for Betrayer.
The way the trees and grass sway with the gusts of wind add a nice touch to the eerieness of the game, though you can use wind that to sneak up to enemies undetected. Also there is a listen ability that you can set to have a visual que, it will help you find the right direction.
So far this is an awesome fps to have in the collection. Betrayer is not a cutscene/QTE game, story is given to you as you talk and find clues around the locations.
I wish there were more music but that is personal preference and it would probably take away from the experience/atmosphere the developer was aiming for.

An underrated, lesser-known Square Enix RPG. The game features involved tactical combat and party-building with rewarding action commands that keep the action fresh and features plenty of content and side-content. A must for any RPG fan.
Overall very recommended!
The Good:
★ Deep, tactical turn and squad-based combat
★ Fairly challenging and throught-provoking
★ Fairly good balance of party power and challenge
★ Rewarding use of action commands keep a turn-based game fresh a lot longer
★ Pretty good degree of customization, including a wide variety of weapons, skills, formations and classes
★ Interesting non-human race characters can join the party
★ Fair autosave system prevents loss of hours of progress
★ Lengthy storyline and generous amounts of side-quests, optional areas and recruitable characters, possible to have 100+ hours worth of gameplay
★ New game +
★ Has aged well graphically, including a comprehensive and aesthetically pleasing UI
★ Grinding generally optional and can be detrimental, built-in turbo option function can speed up the process
★ Excellent bang for buck value
★ Fair amount of option customization, including a turbo button and an undub
★ Rebindable controls, unlockable FPS
★ Good amount of guides and extra resources for those that want or need them
The Neutral:
○ A lot of information isn't made obvious to the player, such as classes, ideal for people who like to experiment
○ Much of the party customization is streamlined so that party members ask for advice and materials instead of being skilled and geared personally, possibly to avoid the hassle of having to do this for dozens of different characters
○ Scaling difficulty
○ Musical score has highs and lows, in my opinion
○ Overall pacing can be rather slow
○ Much of the lore and world-building is hidden behind NPC conversation and sidequests
The Bad:
☆ Relatively old game, some cards might experience minor graphical glitches
☆ Might have to work a few kinks out in the configuration file
☆ Combat is slow and lengthy, use of turbo button can disable the ability to manually input action commands
☆ Difficulty can spike semi-randomly based on character growth and battle rank
☆ Battle rank system not quite explained
☆ Some mechanics can be costly or underpowered/rarely used, such as upgrades and some skill trees respectively
☆ Somewhat clumsy storytelling and face animation
☆ Generally unimpressive main character

I'm aware this might not be extremely relevant compared to the original release of this game. But I had to post this as this game definitely is a LOT better than most people give it credit for. Yes, the story of good vs evil and such might not be extremely innovative, but then again wasn't Final Fantasy always about that and how it affected friendships anyway? On top of that it's actually told in an interesting way with plenty of very high quality cutscenes with characters that have a believable interaction. Speaking of visuals, this game oddly enough is the best looking game from this trilogy. Probably has to do with which game version got ported or something. As for the combat system, this is all based on staggering enemies, choosing the correct attack stances from more offensive and defensive modes. It's a system that actually has a few ways of adding more depth to an otherwise simple system, but honestly people who complain about the system might simply not understand how some enemies really do require you to switch attack stances, stagger the enemy and switch to a more defensive mode healing your party or you will be too late trying to heal your party through potions. The AI of your party is also decent enough to prevent unfair deaths. Ignoring the tutorials in this game is probably a very bad idea. The difficulty curve is decent, as long as the game is played more or less as the combat system requires. So yeah, I actually like the combat system quite a lot, but it's also a bit more traditional turn-based combat versus the more recent FF games. In short, don't expect much manual dodging incoming attacks or anything. The best thing of this game is the world design and art style. As much as the game plays very much like a linear RPG, the amazing world design with sci-fi fantasy style totally makes up for it. Well worth playing. For it's current already low price it's easy to recommend at 'full' price.
