Right, I'm writing this review after only 8,3 hours on record, I just can't bring myself to play any more of this mockery of the card game I love, and let's look at a few of the reasons I dislike this game.
1. This game changes magic fundamentals. Nowhere in magic is it a rule that you can only play 3 uncommons, 2 rares and 1 mythic of a certain type. Either the makers of duels are trying to suggest here that the paper card game is broken or they are suggesting that players are too stupid to make good decks if they're not given certain limitations. Just stop it, I've not gotten to know a single magic player on a personal level who didn't dislike this.
2. Lack of cards to start with. Now first I'd complain about the shallow pool of cards to pick from overall, but I realise getting the game to work with a ton of different cards takes time and effort. What I can not understand however is why the pool of cards you start out with is so shallow you have difficulties creating a decent themed deck. Honestly with the promise of this game being the last game and that they would only build upon this game in the future, they should have the players start out at least with all of the common and uncommon cards in the set. Just give the players some tools to work with here to make the grind any fun.
3. The grind and the deck wizard. I was surprised to see I wasn't getting any quest completion when I won duels, then I googled the issue and discovered you only get quest completion if you use the terrible deck wizard. In most card games  that have a deck wizard you can just ignore it, generally those wizards are worse at making decks than the players anyway. In this case however I found myself incredibly frustrated trying to build a fun deck when the deck wizard was making me choose between a handfull of absolutely terrible cards. I'd go as far as to say even new players do not benefit from this wizard. Any player who has taken the time to learn about manacurve and land count will be able to make a decent deck on his own. Stop trying to handhold the players through frustrating deck wizards.
I could continue to complain about other features such as the UI but those three points are the main reasons I really dislike this game. I can't recommend it to anyone who plays the physical card game, it's only going to be a frustrating experience.

The end result being you're out of ammo and out of money to purchase more.  Your only option at this point is to load a saved game.

I had never played Magic, so this free title has been my chance to learn the game and get to know the story and lore of Magic the Gathering. That said, my review has nothing to do with the any previous games in the series or missing features, but my experience with this game alone.
You have to play story mode first in order unlock the other features in the game. You learn that the Magic universe is made up of multiple plains (kind of like dimensions) and there are 5 different types of Mana (aka Magic). Then you learn that certain gifted people can travel between these plains at will, but only if they've been through a difficult ordeal and their plainswalker "Spark" is ignited. You play through 5 story led duels that teach you the basics (which I really appreciated) and each hand is predetermined to give you the best chance of making it.
After the first Plainswalker's story is over, your hand is held a bit less. You can create a personal deck from the starter set and play against some AI (more on that later), or continue the story. The story immediately becomes difficult. You don't get a predetermined hand, and the AI will not go easy on you. Each of the 5 duels in each arc can take anywhere from 1-5 attempts (or more) depending on the hand you get and the hand your opponent gets.
I honestly felt a little discouraged and helpless because of this. I researched strategies, took my time, and played carefully, but it never mattered, because it was usually based on the luck of the draw. However, it was incredibly satisfying to beat the story, and the the story itself is fantastic. I love the plainswalkers they chose to follow, and after playing 10-20 attempts per story arc, I felt like I understood the struggles they went through. I honestly wish there was more story, because the rest of the game can be just as hard with no story.
The deck builder is pretty fun. You can build your own custom deck using the cards you have, or use the deck wizard to build a deck based around certain strategies. This helped me a lot with learning how cards can go together. You can select cards from a list of 5 suggestions (based on the cards you've selected so far and the deck's focused strategy) but after playing this game for nearly 40 hours now, I keep going through the wizard wondering why a certain card doesnt show up in the suggestions. If that happens to you, it's time to try building a custom deck :) Many of my decks are now custom versions of the ones built in deck wizard and are much better for it!
Here's where things get... aggrivating.
"Hey I'm new to MtG, and I just made my first deck! Lemme play some AI on easy and test it out! Oh look, a plainswalker! Oh look, a titan! Oh look, and 8/8 flying Demon!"
::loses game::
This is a regular occurance, and seems rediculously broken to me. Luck based or not, I don't have access to any of those cards, therefore I
see them played against me on EASY. That would be the equivalent of playing Skyrim on easy and there being a 1:2 chance that a skeever (giant rat) will be replaced with a bear, mammoth, or giant in the tutorial dungeon. There should be a moderate expectation of survival when you play a lower difficulty.
Free game or not, this is a great way to discourage new players (which this game is clearly aimed at) and stop people from spending real money on the game. I've earned over 15 boosters and I'm just starting to be able to defend against these monstrous creatures, but that should lead me to start playing on Medium. To compound the issue, I recently discovered I can win on hard. I have beaten more hard opponents, per game played, than easy ones. That is just stupid.
Thankfully, the game often provides suggestions on what to play via an orange/red arrow over the cards. Often it is the best play, but sometimes it isn't. Regardless of how hard the opponent is, those arrows oftem help a newb like me see something I might not have.
This is where I have encountered the first (and really only) bugs and non-difficulty related issues. You have to try 4-5 times before you can get into a game with another player ("server is busy or full" it says). Also there's no way to talk to another player. When I play with my friend we have to skype because there's no way to talk to him in game. This would be a big problem if you played 2 headed Giant with a randow ally and you couldn't strategize with your teamate.
One of the biggest issues I have in Multiplayer is the timers. I have lost the game numerous times because you have 10-15 seconds to set blockers and there are 20-30 creatures on the field, or started with a horrible hand because I took too long to decide to draw a new one (i.e. the next hand had 6 mana cards then the timer ran out). I realize the timers are there to stop players from walking away from their computer while the opponent waits, but I have lost many multiplayer games simply because I like to think and plan carefully.
Here's the deal. This game is free-to-play, it taught me how to play MtG, and it can be really fun. That's the short of it. I will not be spending any money in this game because it would not improve the experience for me. If some of the issues I've had were fixed, I would spend money to help support the game. However, as is, I feel like I could buy 10 booster packs, play a game on easy and get hit with Liliana Vess and 3 demons and lose anyway. I would rather grind away and get boosters for free (which is totally doable), and just play for fun, by myself or with a friend. If you play like that, you might enjoy this game too :)

Bioshock: the first in a series of very thought provoking and well produced gaming. I entered this fandom from the back from Infinite and would have been delighted to follow from the top just from the base game. But credits to the writers at 2K that managed to loop Infinite's DLC around to Bioshock 1 again to create one of the most beautiful and also symbolic games, that might take a lot of significance in the coming years' events.
Bioshock is a game representing fanatic fundamentalism. In this first installment, it presents the idea of capitalism to its extremes and what it entails: a society entirely bent on out-competiting the rest in almost every area, science, art, business and even child-raising. Consequently, the moral structure of society falls and what we are left with is Rapture. A fantastic city below the sea, and how that essentiallly protects but also contains its citizens. A main feature of the Bioshock series is its invention of the Plasmid, gene reconstruction and/or improvement that allows the player special abilities spanning the elements and even hypnotism and such.
Gameplay is a tad 'retro', in that it still has the clunky elements that we don't see today. Also, the series is set in the 1940s, surrounding the Cold War, atomic industrialisation and the beginnings of women's freedoms, albeit not as much. As such, the music is timeless and classic, soundtrack apt, and the technologies are of the time, yet also, not.
It is annoying when it comes to keybinding and the plasmids you have access to can't be easily rearranged, and it is tedious everytime you gain a new one. The Remastered version is still getting its kinks, i have to say, the stability of it is disappointing given its marketing, however, it has certainly improved, and helpful user guides are available, if you're brave enough, to fix the game files. It is definitely more stable than Bio2 remastered, an abhorrent disappointment worse than Bio1, as you cannot even begin a game.
The player follows a man stranded at sea, and unlike Infinite, you do not have any control over your moral actions. What this game does, is instead take you through the actions and consequences of abscence of morality and how that applies to you, is how you choose to accept it. Harvest the Little Sister's? the source of Adam, the genetic fuel of your powers, or save them? Do you choose to follow in the footsteps of the city before you and inherit it? Or do you perish the old and begin anew, with the girls who did not have the chance?
Overall a decent experience, and if you were not a fan before, and still loved the ride, or open to being one now, Bioshock is a pleasing experience for you

The Stanley Parable is a type of game genre that's become more popular over recent memory known as a walking simulator. As the name would suggest, all you really do is walk around in a first-person point of view while occasionally interacting with the environment, making the gameplay itself very lacking. As such, these games take a large risk since they entirely rely on the story in order to engage the player, and if they find it to be lacking...well, the game as whole will suffer.
But the Stanley Parable's story is not only exceptional, but one of the most innovative and smart narratives I've seen in gaming.
The game is told via voiceovers from The Narrator, who explains that the protagonist Stanley is a man who works in an office building, and is tasked to monitor data coming on a computer screen and press buttons appropriately without question. But suddenly, one day the screen goes blank without warning. Unsure of what to do, Stanley begins to explore the building and finds it devoid of people. What happens next is a game that flips videogames entirely on their head.
The writing is entirely self-aware and knows that it's a game. So it decides to have as much fun with itself as possible, so no matter how absurd the scenarios appear to be or how many dead ends you run into, it all connects perfectly to the engaging and fascinating meta-narrative.
The game not only constantly breaks the fourth wall, but breaks it down entirely. Which is of course guided by the Narrator, who is fully-voiced and by far the best aspect of this game.
He's just filled with so much charm and wit that despite him being against what matters in videogames the most, choice...well, it's more or less a commentary about videogames's structural tropes, poking fun at them and highlighting how little choice players truly do have a majority of the time despite having the illusion of choice.
While he may seem friendly and amiable, his patronizing tone makes you feel like a child who must follow the orders of an adult. And so naturally, you would do what children are famous for: rebel.
Doing so will cause the narrator to lose his temper and become exceptionally more rude and malicious, saying that this's his story and that you will follow it the way he's envisioned it. And since this causes him to do everything in his power to stop you, even directly controlling the game itself, he suddenly becomes an antagonist.
The first choice that you're given is between two doors: the left door, which is the one he tells you to go through, and the right door, which he doesn't tell you to go through. So will you follow the Narrator's directions, and despite not having any choice or input, have the game works in your favor? Or disobey him and try and decide your own choices, but instead have the work against you?
You can even choose to follows his orders for a while, and then suddenly decide to rebel in order to trigger entirely different endings and events, each one more unpredictable than the next. What's crazy is that this game has has a total of SEVENTEEN endings (including two joke endings), so despite it being short, it has a ridiculous amount of replay value if you're curious to see all the possible outcomes.
While I won't spoil them, my personal favorite ending is when the game referenced other PC games.
The graphics are the basic, stock-Valve graphics engine used for games such as Half-Life 2, Team Fortress 2, Left 4 Dead 2 and Garry's Mod, and that's due to this game originally being a mod of Half-Life 2. Yet it's not the graphics themselves that are interesting and impressive, but just seeing the many creative nooks and crannies that reside in the office building.
The only flaw to the game is that the loading times when starting a new game from the main menu are a bit long, which is counterproductive since you need to constantly reset the game in order to try different routes and endings. While you can do this from the pause menu, you also have the ability to make make multiple saves, and the only way to load them is from the main menu.
Despite simplistic gameplay and graphics, and long loading times when starting up the game, The Stanley Parable is a game with an engaging story that explores how many videogame stories confine the player to its rules by having someone that does exactly that, has many different routes and endings depending on the player's actions, well-written dialogue that constantly breaks the fourth wall, and a charming and memorable narrator who is voiced exceptionally well.
While it may look simple on the surface, I recommend it to anyone, even those that dislike walking simulators, since I'd say that the narrative more than makes up for the lack of gameplay.
What's even more interesting is that before the term walking simulator was coined, this time of game genre was called 'interactive fiction.' Walking simulator definitely sounds a lot better.
*9/10*
Note: The true challenge will be trying to get all ten of the Steam achievements. If you do, then you seriously deserve a medal.

From the very first moment you get thrown into the world of Bioshock , you get a sense of wonder and mystery. You start off as a regular guy minding his own business on a plane which eventually crashes into the ocean. From then on you take control of the protagonist and lead him to an abandoned lighthouse which holds the entrance to Rapture , the underwater city. After entering Rapture , you meet a mysterious man who calls himself Atlas who tells you that this city was built by a tyrannt named Andrew Ryan and talks you into helping him kill Ryan. From then on the game becomes a joyride , as you explore the amazing underwater city of Rapture and find out more about the plot as you progress. If you want to get the most out of the plot , I recommend finding and listening to all the audio logs scattered throught the game.
The core elements of the game are the multitude of guns and powers you get as you progress through the story. At the beginning of the game , the protagonist injects himself with a strange serum named "plasmid" which is made using compressed ADAM. Each plasmid does something different , from electric , fire and ice damage to telekynesis and even a swarm of insects. The guns you get are pretty awesome too , but sadly , they are outshined by the powers which are way cooler.
The game puts great emphasis on decision making. Earlier I mentioned a substance called ADAM. If you harvest enough of it , you can get awesome new powers and upgrades , now the real question is how you choose to do it. Through Rapture , creatures known as "Little Sisters" roam freely and collect stuff they come across. Now these Little Sisters are your main source of ADAM and you must harvest it from them. The only problem is , they are protected by genetically enhaced humans who had their body replaced by a big diving suit called "Big Daddy". In order to get the ADAM you have to kill the Big Daddy and then find his respective Little Sister. But there's two ways of collecting ADAM from her , one is to harvest it directly which will kill her in the process and the other is to rescue her which will turn her back into a normal girl but you recieve less ADAM. This will also affect the game's outcome. Atlas tells you to go with the more efficient way aka killing them but if you don't , you will gain trust of a woman called Tennenbaum which will be of great help later on.
Surviving in Rapture isn't easy as you need to constantly collect medical kits and EVE (substance which powers plasmids) in order to get through all this craziness. Hacking is also a major part of the game , even though the game does not require it. If you get skilled at hacking , you're going to have an easier time surviving. The hacking system is as follows "connect the pipes before the stream catches up" just like in the old school game. You can hack almost everything from turrets to security cameras and even drones.
The game's bosses aren't anything spectacular or over the top (excpet for the final boss which I'm not going to spoil) but that just goes to show that people are the real bosses we have to overcome in life.
Overall I say this is a classic and a must play for anyone who loves stories that make you think and for everyone that enjoys a solid first person action game in general. I did not encounter any problems with the remasteres version (I might have just been lucky) but I guarantee you're going to have a good time with whichever version you choose. I give this game a solid 9.5/10

As a fan of previous X games, I pre-ordered X Rebirth and started playing it within minutes of release. Like many others, I was struck both by the sweeping changes to the “X” formula established in the preceding few titles, as well as the horrid, god-awful, soul crushing bugs and technical hang-ups.
I invested approximately 180 hours in the first couple of months, doing my best to study the universe and bludgeon my way through the infuriating campaign, and after doing so (the dev’s released a steady stream of patches through this period, turning the game from utterly broken to sort of kind of maybe just a little playable), and my private verdict to my gamer-y friends and family was “Do Not Recommend, Stay Far Away!” Which hurt a little, because I could see the game’s potential glimmering far down in the deeps.
I think the thing that troubled me most back in those early days was the fact that even if you got past the bugs, which many did by editing game files, the new universe was essentially simplistic and lifeless. Even if all the game’s systems worked flawlessly (and they didn’t, not by a long shot), there was really no point in playing because, in my opinion, the universe and the mega-stations that looked so darned pretty from a distance, were essentially just empty shells, no more interesting or compelling than glittery Christmas ornaments on a well dressed up tree.
Now fast-forward a year & umpteen patches later to the release of v 3.0 and the expansion Teladi Outpost.
What a difference a year makes. After letting the game gather dust since early last January, I finally re-booted and started a new Free Play session and dove back in. Right away, I noticed a plethora of changes, ranging from cosmetic graphics enhancements to radical shifts in the design of the game’s UI and underlying mechanics, most of which a very vocal crowd had screamed to the rafters that the dev’s either couldn’t, or wouldn’t, change a year earlier.
-The menu had been switched from a cumbersome, un-intuitive radial style menu to an easily manipulated sidebar style menu, one that was lightning fast to navigate and cool as all hell to look at. Contained within this menu was a newly redesigned map, complete with two different information modes, and a wealth of new tools for tracking and maintaining my property.
-Now there was a reason to actually go into the stations other than to crawl around inside their air ducts: to find loot that was useful for crafting items that was either worth a ton of money, or even better, could be used in exchange for virtual seminars (training videos that could be applied toward your hired officers, increasing their various stats) or even better yet, hiring permanent Trade Agents on any given station who would constantly update your trade computer with current buy/sell offers from that station, the XR equivalent to X3’s Advanced Satellite Network.
--Haulers/Traders from far off systems now populated the universe, such as the factions LI or PMC from Albion trading with stations in Omicron Lyrea, or Canterran vessels docking at the No Limits Spice Farm in Albion space. This had the overall effect of making the universe seem a lot more meaningful and bringing it to life, for me.
--Faction owned destroyers patrol and react to threats and many haulers travel with either fighter or frigate/destroyer class escorts, and the player is free to assign these kinds of escorts to his/her haulers, too.
--Redesigned mission offers & rewards; now there is always something for the pilot to do, patrolling zones and engaging in frivolous but fun dog fights, protecting stations, sabotaging rival factions’ stations, etc. These missions are plentiful and updated regularly, and function not only as a means to put some credits in the players account during the early game phase, but also to build faction rep for the later stages when the player begins to build their trade fleet/station network.
--There are now ways and means to order your squad around that actually work pretty well. Not exactly fleet management, but getting there.
--The ability to place stations anywhere I liked.
--Small shipyards open for business! More capital ship choices for purchase in general, as well as an overall increase of the types/styles/configuration of ships in the galaxy.
--Redesigned highway travel. On this note, I’d just like to point out that with the release of the Teladi Outpost expansion, Egosoft is now introducing a whole new style of sector to explore (new to XR): in Teladi space, you are given a huge area to explore, filled with hidden lockboxes, interesting new stations and nebulous electrical storms that obscure your view and potentially damage your ship, and you are not given any highways to show you the way around. This seemingly small touch does a lot to increase the sense of mystery and epic adventure that was missing from the initial release, essentially forcing the player to explore again.
--Most bugs have been squashed, leaving no game-breakers that I could find. That is not to say that XR does not have bugs, I’ve found some ranging from irritating to downright aggravating, but in all cases they were minor and easily ignored.
I could go on and on listing the improvements, but I think I’ve made my point clear that the dev’s have been hard at work tightening up their systems and introducing new content. I’ve got roughly 100 hours into v 3.0 and I feel that I’m hardly scratching the surface. The bottom line is that they’ve created a rich, compelling, beautiful space-fantasy for the player to become engaged with and tinker about in, a universe that can easily gobble hundreds of hours of the players time.
The best way to approach X Rebirth is to just enjoy it for itself and not hold it up in comparison to it’s older siblings.
Final verdict 80/100

While I'm not normally fond of side scrollers This War of Mine is a rare exception. Trade with others barely holding on? or will you just take what you want.
This game will have you choosing between letting your people die or gunning down that kid and his elderly parents for a couple of cans of food and maybe, a bottle of meds. All the while praying your base doesn't get raided and those people you are now murdering a small family for, are not killed.
For those that don't like to look at the meaning behind their actions (in a video game) or the story you'd best not get this. Everyone else will see this game for what it is, a hard, soul-crushingly depressing, remorseless look at the horrors of war that'll have you playing just to see your guys though this hell hole until a cease fire is finally announced (picked at random).
Those that are sensitive to emotionally taxing experiences may want to also avoid this game, at times you may be given the choice to help that woman being dragged off by an armed soldier, that main lying in the middle of the path with a sniper edging closer, and closer to you, or if killing that elderly couple is worth saving three lives.
While this game is a side scroller it more then makes up for it in the meaning behind every action you take, and the consequences. If I had to give it a score? 9/10 and it only loses 1 because I had to kill a kid with my rifle to stop my group from starving. :(

By the developer 10TONS LTD, Neon Chrome is a top-down, Cyberpunk, indie, shooter with many thick elements to the game as well as basic elements that’s just plain fun. You start Neon Chrome with a cut scene setting up the plot and your base objective. Overthrow the evil overlord with completely reasonable actions like shooting everything and everyone in sight and breaking through any wall that stands in your way.
Neon Chrome is a lot more complex than it looks. At first it looks like a basic top down shooter with fun enemies to shoot and completely destructible environment but its exactly that along with a fun leveling system, merciless death system, a class system, and situations that’ll smother you with enemies.
The class system in Neon Chrome gives you the ability to play how you want to play, giving you options to play like an assassin sneaking in the shadows, a brute destroying everything in your path, a techie with the help of a robot partner, and many other classes you can think of. Each class giving you a new experience in gameplay and mechanics and even being able to switch it up as time goes with the quick upgrading system you can find around the map to either help boost your defense or build your destructiveness.
As well as the upgrading system within every level there is also a main leveling system to boost your max damage, max health, power meter, luck, and other properties; the only catch is you have to die first to level your character. Might even being the most complex top-down shooter I’ve played, Neon Chrome is also merciless and hard. Not only does it smother you with enemies at your lowest points but once you die you have to start everything over (Except your main leveling system) along with all your solider you’ve upgraded. The only way to get a check point is beating a boss and moving to the next floor even though I’ve never been able to even beat the first boss…
The destructible environments are top notch with just about everything beings destroy-able. A room that has multiple walls and crates can be shot down to a room full of ruble and bodies with the help of some well places explosives, lots and lots of well places explosives. Even with the added bonus of destructible environments, the levels themselves change every time you die! No level is the same the second time around and each one is as challenging, if not more challenging, than the last! Not only is it fun to play, Neon Chrome also comes with an amazing soundtrack that brings the whole game together. Very energetic and gets you pumped seconds before getting slaughter! It’s hard to not notice the music while playing, nothing annoying and frantic.
Overall, Neon Chrome is an amazing game with a shine to it that screams endless fun. I absolutely loved the game and I’m not even a fan of top-down games (Excluding Hotline Miami). Neon Chrome came out of nowhere but I will definitely be playing more of it and it’ll eventually have mod support, level editor, and more! But meanwhile I wait for that I’ll probably be trying to at least beat the first boss.. I give Neon Chrome 9.0/10! You can get Neon Chrome on Steam for $14.99 but it’s 10% off till May 5th And you can also buy the soundtrack for $4.99! Keep up the good work 10TONS LTD!! Cant wait to see what you do next!

Disclosure: I received a free beta key for this game from the developer.
This game is great. I put over 30 hours into it during the beta test and I still can't get enough. In my opinion, 10tons (the guys who created the amazing crimsonland) have made a masterpiece of a true "game" in the purest sense.
Neon Chrome combines the great gunplay from crimsonland with a good dosis of rogue like randomness and a gameplay that starts on the surface but becomes very deep the further you get into it.
I have beaten the game once and I am on my second run through, which is very challenging and as much fun as the first time.
This is due to some key elements, that make the game as great as it is:

Atmosphere: The cyberpunk setting of the game is fitting and provides a good atmospheric basement for the experience. Any time you wasted another cyborg clone you feel like the bad guy in "The prestige" having just killed another version of yourself from the vast amount of alter egos in cybernetic sleep tanks. The theme is very well executed and the game has a vibe of bladerunner and hard reset, which I find extremely appealing. The fact that you have to fight your way to the highest floor of a futuristic megatower adds a feeling of constant challenge and evokes that "just one more run" urge in a big way.

Gunplay: Like crimsonland, the guns are a lot of fun to shoot. Different firearms perform differently and vary in impact and damage. Certain guns require a specific playstyle. It is great fun to sneak around a level as an assassin, becoming invisible in the shadows and sniping away enemies with the railgun. It is also fun to storm through the floors of the tower, making a bloody mess of enemies with a laserburstrifle and melee strikes with your cybernetic arm as the cyberpsycho. There are several character classes to choose from, everyone with a different random loadout, that you might also finetune if you have the cash to do so. This makes for an almost endless variety in playable characters, as you find more enhancements and weapons through the level, your litte alter ego gets more and more powerful and more and more specialized in dealing with the many enemies the overseer throws in your path. If you die, it's over. Permadeath is a bummer, but also the reason for you to cheerish every run on its own as a achievement.

Leveldesign: The levels are randomly generated. They differ in appearance and style from floor to floor. 10tons did a great job of assuring a huge amount of variation in the levels and giving every floor of the tower its own theme. While you will certainly recognize some room patterns every now and then, the levelsign in itself works great and I never had the feeling of repetition during my 30 hours of beta play. Another exciting feature is the fact, that the levels are almost completely destructible. Guns can shoot through many walls and often provide you with a tactical advantage, be it hitting someone in the back by destryoing the wall he is hidden behind or simply blast entire levelsections to pieces with a grenade or by hitting an explosive device.

AI: After I knew what was going on in neon chrome i was expecting the kind of mindless enemy behaviour I knew from similar looking games like alien shooter or Alien Breed. But instead of bad guys running at me in a straight line, I experienced quite a diversitude of KI routines. Some guards might charge at you directly, others will try to get you from another angle. Enemies will run around mines that you have placed on the floor and clump together to overhelm you. Every now and then patrols will appear and searchteams will enter the level to snuff you out. I find the enemies in the game extremely challenging especially in the later levels when heavy armoured guys will join forces with commander cyborgs that are quite hard to overcome and require some planning.

Sometimes I had an almost hotline miami approach on the rooms, on other occasions it feels more like isaac, but it is always challenging and every error will be punished.

Upgrades: The game features an upgrade system similar to hard reset, where you occasionally find upgrade stations that allow you to choose from a selection of body implants to be inserted in your cyborg body. Like the perks in crimsonland, these upgrades and finding the right combination of them, is key to beating the game. In combination with the different loadouts and the chosen characterclass, you will have a great deal of customization. As you progress towards the top of the tower you will unlock more and more upgrades for you to choose from. The feeling of constant progression is one of the many joys of the game...

I could go on and on about how much I enjoy neon chrome, but I will end this little overview with the remark, that this game feels like a REAL "game". I is a little oldschool, but highly polished and with so much depth and replay value, that I almost thought I would never see this kind of game again. Neon chrome reminds me of a time, when a game was simply a game: easy to understand, hard to master and with enough to offer to start it again and again until it had revealed all of its secrets. I still play it every other day and have more fun than with any of the "big budget triple something" titels in recent years.
I applaud 10tons for bringing out a title like this and hope, that it will pay off for them.
I cannot recommend this game enough....
PS: and the soundtrack is also great:)

I would have liked to enjoy this game. I'm a big fan of the Civilization series, and anything scifi is always a plus in my book. However, this game... Starting off, you have extremely limited options as to where to start your first city, which can seriously set you back in the early game. The science tree or graph or whatever is an absolute mess, nearly unreadable, confusing for old fans of Civ and completely overwhelming for any newcomers. All the tiles look the same (I had to hover over most tiles to figure out what they were), the aliens are absolutely everywhere, stopping your explorers and then randomly killing them for no reason... And the miasma, which could have been interesting, is just far too abundant to be anything but a serious annoyance. The actual civilizations themselves, or the colonies as they were, in addition to being very few in number, are also extremely bland and seem to have practically no differences from each other. The leaders have next to no personality, and all their little log excerpts seem to be dime-a-dozen platitudes about the loss of Earth and the squandering of natural materials - or then destruction of the aliens.
It's such a shame, because this could have been the best game in the entire series with a little development. The basic idea was there, and there were so many ways this could have gone. I would give wads of cash for something more akin to Civ meets Mass Effect, where there's an actual variety of species and planet types. The civ leaders could have actual character, and the aliens, too - why were they not sentient? Why could I not play as them? Why are the aliens so meaningless to the game?
And don't even get me started on the problems with the multiplayer. I got kicked out more times than I can count, and I probably stared at loading screens more than I got actual playtime in. Finally, I had to give up without completing the multiplayer game, because my constant dropping was making it stand still for everyone else. Additionally, the game would occasionally freeze for no reason and force me to restart it to be responsive again. I've never had issues like that with any other game. I don't know if the free weekend was crowding the servers or what, but it was basically unplayable.
Such a shame. I guess I'll have to get my Civ fix and my scifi fix separately, then.

This War of Mine is a sometimes bleak, sometimes hopeful take on the survival genre of games: survive a war, as a civilian.  The interface is dead simple and clearly designed with portability to tablets in mind, but it is largely effective.  Your band of survivors often has serious qualms with violence and thievery, and learning how to avoid stealing from other groups of survivors while also avoiding starving to death can be a bit of a handful.

The game has come a long way from its initial release, with the option to actually select your survivor group and thus the scenario you're likely to be playing through.  Different characters have different strengths and weaknesses they bring to the group, and these advantages can make a huge difference.  Playing with a weak group with few or no obvious advantages brings its own challenge.

I play in English and notice occasional quirks in the characters stories, but nothing too jarring to affect my enjoyment of the game.  This one's a winner.

As a Civ IV fan, I might be biased toward Civilization: Beyond Earth before I even started to play the game. I never got going with Civ V, and BE, as a glorified standalone expansion of V, reminds me some of the worse moments of the latter, like the tediousness of 1upt army management and lacking of micro-management (specifically, cities).
Despite the similarity, I do believe Cvi:BE has shown some potentials of becoming a better game. It creates a world that is novel, exotic and filled with curiosity, with things to discover and learn. The first 100 turns were great. (Again, similar to V.) There is a brave new world full of excitements. There are many ways for you to develop your colonies, many tiles and sites for you to explore, many jobs to assign to your limited number of units.
But it's just not enough. Novelty fades quickly, so does the difference between the new planet and the old Earth. And life just becomes redundant and less rewarding.  Little left to explore, to expand, or to know. You are still clicking to give a lot of instructions, but you know you are on "one more turn" autopilot that is the exact gameplay of Civ V. Maybe you'll have a good time if you are new to the franchise. But for Civ veterans, it might not be enough. Why can't we have cities that float on the sea, submerged under water, fly in the sky or dug beneath the surface? And where are space-fighting units? I'm not sure if Firaxis just didn't have the time and budget to implement the more demanding new mechanisms or just simply lacks imagination.
A lot of buildings and techs make very little sense for game-winning. Take the late-stage tech "Human Idealism" for example. It's extremely expensive to research and serves no purpose other than enabling the construction of a wonder that provides 4 culture. Wonders in general are weak and most of them offers little incentive to compete to build them (after researching the respective "wonder tech", of course).
The tech web is a let-down. There are many techs that you will research not because your civilization needs them to grow, but only to advance your affinity level, which is your actual military tech and essential to achieve almost all kinds of victories. On the one hand, it's commendable to create a new approach for technology development; on the other, it is implemented poorly and killed immersion for me. It almost feels as if so many techs are just some names with perks and incremental benefits. I understand it must be difficult for developers to come up with so many future techs and assign meanings to them, but a better approach should be assigning functions to them, instead of a tech that "provide 48 harmony XP points". Also, the web offer exploits towards the luck-based Contact Victory.
Civ:BE, like vanilla Civ V, feels unpolished. And people are already talking about future expansions, in the hope that they will fix things, like they did for Civ V. Another concern why you should think twice before paying too much for this "base game".

Neon Chrome is an excellent top-down roguelite shooter.  The gameplay mechanics, weapon variety, and perks make this game very fun to play.  I highly recommend this game to those that enjoy this type of genre and newcomers as well.
The game can be played with KB+M or controller.  As for gameplay there are 28 stages, each stage consists of going from point A to point B, sometimes there will objects that you have to do in order to advance to the next stage.  Throughout the levels you will find money, weapons, perks, and weapon upgrade stations.
The environment is semi-destructible, you can shoot or smash walls down to create new entry ways.  I should note that this is limited, but the feature is there and works very well.
After you die and you have the option to purchase upgrades that will remain permanent throughout your entire gameplay.  Also the game has save points, if you exit mid-stage, upon starting the game again you start at the beginning of the stage.  If you beat a boss, this will unlock a new starting point so if you die at any stage after the boss, you won't have to start from the very beginning again, you continue right after the boss.
I don't have any major gripes.  I will say that not having the ability to dodge is kind of a bummer, but does not ruin the overall experience.
As for hours to price ratio, you will definitely get your money's worth and much more.  I've played a variety of roguelites/likes and none of them really gives me that strong "just one more run..." feeling like this game does.  This is due to the very awesome gameplay this game offers.  I can die in-game all day long and I wouldn't care because the game is really fun.

Ok, so I generally do not write reviews, because I like what I like and do not expect others to like it. However, this is a game that I would not have initially considered, and it has turned out to be a diamond in the rough.
First, it is simple. It is naval combat...in space. Sure you can run cargo missions, or rescue missions, but in the end you will be fighting some faction, and it is simplistic in its approach. When I say simple, I mean it takes away some of the more complex aspects of gameplay and makes navigating and aiming the most important. Everything else is handled automatically or assumed for you. I like not having to think about complex aspects of a game. I like knowing where to go for a mission, and how much to repair my ship, and knowing that when I buy a new ship everything I previously purchased gets moved to my new ship.
Rebel Galaxy has done a great job in making a game fun to play, whether you are a hard core gamer, or a casual one.
I highly recommend this game.

Summary:
This is not a business stimulation game. It is more like Risk but with businesses instead of armies. It is a GREAT game especially for so early in early access. There are definetely some features that are missing that are wants and needs but there is also already a full single player campaign that is already worth the price of the game. The few negative reviews I've read on this game seem to be reviewing it as a game in the $15-$20 price range instead of in the $5-$10 price range. Once they add requested features, one of which is already promised, it will be a game worth $15-$20 so BUY IT NOW before the price goes up.
Positives:
-A well done tutorial that teaches you all the basics of the game while leaving the deeper strategies for you to learn in the single player campaign.
-A great single player campaign that has a slow enough difficulty ramp to allow you to learn but a fast enough one to keep things interesting and challenging.
-Completely polished. In 11 hours of gameplay I've encountered no roughness or bugs which is highly unusual for early access and should be applauded.
Negatives:
-Needs a multiplayer mode. Promised but not here yet.
-The entire single player mode is scenarios played on the same map. I wouldn't change it but I would add more single player campaigns with different maps.
-It needs a sandbox mode where the player can choose the number of opponets and the win conditions.
-No real Steam features as of yet. No save syncs, no achievements, no cards, no workshop. Save syncs are promised.
Conclusion:
Buy this game if you like Risk type strategy board games and are looking for a diffrent spin on one. Buy this game if you aren't expecting a AAA huge game experience but would still like AAA polish. Buy this game.

Neon Chrome is a cyberpunk top-down shooter from the same company that brought us Crimsonland.
Gunplay: The gunplay is quite similar to Crimsonland, and is very polished. You'll have a huge array of weapons ranging from pistols to miniguns, and laser shotguns to plazma burts rifles. There is no shortage of weapons here, and they are all unique and fit different play styles. Similar to Crimsonland, is the fact that all guns have unlimited ammo. Personally, I love that. This game in punishing enough it's a relief to not have to worry about running out of ammo. The gunplay overral is great.
Graphical quality: The graphics in the game are gorgeous. They really have that neon/cyberpunk feel and it's just beautiful to look at. The animations are butter smooth, and I have never had any framedrops or lag issues, even in heavy combat situations. The game is very well optimized and has a fair amount of graphical options. The graphical quality overral is awesome.
Soundtrack and sound effects: Neon Chrome's phenomenal music is one of the best part about this game, it's breathtaking! The music is epic, very cyberpunky and I really hope the game get's an OST DLC. The sound in this game is quite good too. Every gun sounds different, and all the impact sounds and explosions sounds great too. The audio quality overall is incredible.
Gameplay elements: The gameplay in this game is extremely good. The environment is nearly fully destructible which makes for some very tense boss fights. That first boss was insane, you had nowhere to hide because all the cover would end up getting destroyed. I would have to say this game has some of the most adrenaline-pumping boss battles I've ever encountered. The gameplaye-style has some great rouge-like elements that are quite similar The Binding of Isaac. You get to choose from 3 randomized characters at the beginning, and it's fun to be able to play with different characters that have different unique attributes. The levels are quite spectacular, no level is the same, they are all randomly generated (exept that story levels) and flow really nicely. I've died so many tiems yet it never feels like you play the same level again. This gives that game a lot of replayability and a reason to keep playing. The game also has checkpoints so you don't have to start from the beginning each time. There is also permanent upgrades which you can buy with in-game earnt money that give you a small boost. You will also be collecting a lot of perks, which are similar to that of Crimsonland, and they really add to the randomness as well. The game get's really hard but you never feel that it is unfairly punishing. You will always be getting better, becoming more skilled, getting more upgrades, unlocking more weapons and perks, you're always making progress, so death never feels like much of a penalty. The A.I. in this game is reactive and never bugs out, which is great. The game allows you to be stealthy as well. The gameplay overall is satisfying and very fun.
Story and features: The story of the game is that you're trying to stop an evil "Overseer." I didn't really pay much attention to it, but at least the story is there, unlike Crimsonland. As you can tell from the trailers and pictures, the game takes part on a giant megastructure in some sort of futuristic city. The setting is really nice and the music, gameplay and graphics all come together nicely. One nice feature I would like to note is like Crimsonland, blood and corpses are permanent. This gives this game a great aftermath and really makes a difference. The story overall is interesting and intriguing, nothing too special, but definitely great for a top-down shooter.
Verdict: In conclusion, if you enjoy roguelikes, top-down shooters, a fun and challenging co-op experience, or even like cyberpunk in general, definitely try this game out. I have never played a top-down shooter that was as polished, well made and fun to play as this. The game is so addicting, and luckily there's abosultey no microtransactions which is a plus. I can not think of anything to fault this game for, it's just pure goodness.
TL;DR: Overall, this is probably the very best top-down twin-stick shooter game I have played. Incredible music, balanced and fair game-play, awesome bosses, a dynamic destructible environment that makes fights more intense, gorgeous graphics, and I love the rogue-like elements and replayablity.
I give this game 2 thumbs up.

I've finally completed this game .
And to say the least , I'm pretty satisfied with everything that this JRPG had offered me.
As some of you might have already known , this game is often criticized by its Battle Rank System , In which you gain ranks by fighting enemies , but sooner or later you find yourself in a situation where you are facing a certain monster / certain part of story event bosses , that is just seemingly impossible to beat . However , I believe that this problem had been fixed in the PC version , where you can rest assure to just kill everything that you see whenever you want / can , just like in a normal JRPG game . However just don't overdo it as it still might result in some problems in the early-to-mid game .
For me , there are sometimes where I feel like this game is just way too draggy in some sense that makes me feel bored . For example , your party members rely on you to find the components for upgrading their weapon for them . Although some of the main characters , excluding
, do upgrade by themselves from time to time , majority of the other members do not . Just by finding the components for them alone is time consuming . And also , there are sometimes where the RNG factor matters too much in a battle . As in your character's chances of evading or landing hits , may easily cost you the round against some particularly tough bosses that you have been fighting for the past 20 min .
But what really draws me in is the gameplay and not to mention also , the graphics and the legendary soundtrack .
The Last Remnant consist of around 3-hour plus of cut-scenes and to say the least , they were not annoying to get through with . For a game that is quite dated , this surely doesn't seem like the case . No lag nor crashes were encountered by me during my gameplay and its just an overall pleasant experience .
Storywise , its solid for me . SquareEnix games always have their way in expressing themselves through the story they present and The Last Remnant was a great example of it . The characters were interesting and the dialogues they presented are not awkward either as there are cases where the dialogues in some games that are just unbearable .
However , let me just point out a single major bug for me that kind of throws me off a little .
TLDR : This game certainly had its flaws and tough moments , but if you are into games like Final Fantasy series or any RPG based games , then why not give it a try .
At the very least , it worked out for me .

I am a long time Final Fantasy fan, and I think that others coming from this background may be a bit dissapointed with this game. The visuals are definitely breathtaking, and play on the Final Fantasy style that we've all come to know and love. The story is deep and engaging, though a bit hard to follow.
Where this game really seems to lose people is the god-awful battle system, the extremely linear gameplay, and the lackluster leveling (crystarium) system. The battle system consists of you controlling only who your party leader is, and chaining together attacks, though most people will opt for mashing the "auto battle" button. The game's paradigm system allows you to switch jobs on the fly, which is an essential feature if you'll need to utilize if you want to make it through battles. That's more or less the extent of the battle system. It's boring, and usually ends up with you repeatedly selecting auto-battle.
The levels are extremely linear, much to the point that it becomes a chore to get through them. The only variety you get here is the ocasional short path to the left/right to grab a treasure chest. It basically feels like an RPG on rails.
The leveling system, or the crystarium system, consists of leveling up different classes for each character. You battle, collect crystarium points (CP), then use this CP to move your pointer on each character's crystarium to gain attributes. It's very boring, clunky, and not fun at all.
You can upgrade your weapons using collected materials, but it's not important  to do so (and kind of a waste of materials) until closer to the end of the game.
I can recommend this game to Final Fantasy fans based on the visuals alone, but be prepared to get bored of the linear gameplay fairly quickly.

To help put things in perspective, know that I first had completed Bioshock 1 and Infinite in my gaming lifetime. An odd order, yes. But it did help put things in perspective, both the evolution of the series as well as the reviews associated with it.
In terms of gameplay, Bioshock 2 is a straight upgrade from 1. The looting and exploration is just as enjoyable as it was before, and bullet stock micromanagers will have a moderately satisfying day. The game isn't too hard, even on the highest difficulty. It may be rough to start out, as you don't have the Plasmids and Tonics yet that befit your playstyle. But as time passes on, you will be able to gather your bearings. As long as you somewhat try to use your ammo sparingly or at least wisely, you will have maximum ammo on most of your weapons, and your wallet will be full as well.
A feature I've always liked, as money in this game isn't as much a currency as it is a resource which you can hold only a limited amount of. I've always admired how Bioshock's "Money" dynamic made it stand apart from many other shooters and RPG's and what not.
When keeping visual design in mind, changing from a 'human splicer' in the predecessor to an 'alpha version Big Daddy' brings a visual change that really helps you immerse in the role. All the former weapons are present, but in bulky versions befitting what you are. The revolver is replaced with a Rivet Gun, but still fires just like it, the pump shotgun with a double barrel one and the crossbow with a spear launcher. It's a detail, but an important one.
As a Big Daddy, you are still tasked to defeat other Big Daddy's to lay claim on their LIttle Sister. With the new weaponry and evolved plasmids, this task has become much more interesting. Setting up traps and following your plan like a script will help you get some proper first blood damage in, and then you can finish off the bugger with your weaponry. A task that is still quite intimidating, as the melee Daddies still know how to quickly close in on you, and the ranged ones carry some very hefty firepower. Even as a Big Daddy yourself, you'll need to Tonic up before you can take a prolonged beating. Wits are still very much required.
And these wits will serve you well, as now you can fullfill your role as Big Daddy when finally claiming a big sister. Beyond the options you had in the first game, you can also have the Little Sister harvest ADAM from specific corpses. Each little sister can only harvest twice, and there's always more corpses than can be used. So exploration for more ideal locations does pay off.
Which is where your trap laying skills yet again prove handy. Instead of taking on a mobile Big Daddy, you now need to strategically defend a stationary target while she drains adam. The act of draining seems to always attract a big crowd of Splicers. And it needs no explaining that the Splicer AI is well capable of ambushing you now if you think of cheesing it out.
Not to mention the Big Sisters, who always come for you when all the Little Sisters in the level have been dealt with. They are pretty much twice as strong as a Big Daddy, much more agile and beat your face hard with an array of Plasmid skills. Being unprepared generally leaves you dead and beaten.
But worry not, because you've got a new wide array of new and/or improved Plasmids to help you defend. Whirlwind Trap alone is a poster boy of this, as you can now imbue Level 2 traps with any other Plasmid skill you have, adding a unique feature to the trap. Ranging from Shock and Fire, to Hypnotise traps. The latter is especially handy to place with a Little Sister, in case a Splicer reaches her. Send that f*cker right back to fight his friends, or into another trap.
Pretty much all Plasmids gain unique features with every level. But the Tonics get very interesting as well. Basic ones as Boozehound are now accompanied with reducing Eve usage, and there even is a Tonic in the late game where you can drastically reduce your Eve usage in return for only using your Drill (your new Melee weapon). I have tried the Melee build, using damage reduction and melee damage increase, and I can guarantee you that it's quite viable. Doing a Drill Charge (a skill the storyline will teach you) is very satisfying and lethal, although quite taxing on your Drill Fuel.
Speaking of the Story...It's a mixed feeling. Of course it's not as impressive as the first one was. That said, it would take exceptional work to make that even possible. The story isn't bad, and certainly gives you enough encouragement to go on, it's just not as good...
Which does explain why Infinite tried so hard to focus on it's story counterpart, sadly leaving behind some of the features we had loved the first two for.
If you liked Bioshock 1 and want more of it, this game is absolutely worth it. If you think Infinite couldn't get any better... well, maybe you'll like it less, but it might still be worth it to put some context to some of the Infinite DLC.
All in all I would say it's been a worthy successor, filling that Bioshock hunger I was having.

This game is basically the first Postal but remade with modern graphics: Same isometric perspective, same concept of a disturbed person deciding he's going to kill everyone, same core gameplay of shooting everything and everyone in mini-sandbox levels, and even similar black comedy one-liners whenever the protagonist kills someone. Hell, it even starts identically with the protagonist standing outside his house before you open fire on civilians. From there you run around an open map going to marked locations (killing civilians and cops/SWAT along the way) such as shops/malls/hotels/bars/etc., kill more NPCs then go somewhere for the level to end. Afterwards, you do the same thing in a different level. If you find a car with its doors open you can hijack it and drive around running over people, but they're a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to control and not worth the bother outside the hilarity factor of crashing them through walls - that's another good thing, there's plenty of destructible environments in the game, with walls and furniture falling apart and crumbling completely if explosions happen nearby or you crash objects through them.
The biggest problem with the game is the same one most games of its genre have: the isometric perspective makes combat a pain since you don't know exactly where your shots will land or if they will go over certain objects, the black and white colour filter makes it even more disorienting to move around and doesn't help matters.
Since its announcement, there's been a ton of drama surrounding this game due to its concept and some of the developers being affiliated to neo-Nazi Polish groups. Playing it, you'd be hard-pressed to find any overt racism, misogyny or what have you (though there's a snarky Feminist achievement) since you kill all types of people.
If you're buying this just to get back at people who anger you on the internet I'd suggest you reconsider, you're part of the group that the developers are baiting and counting on to buy this game since it's nothing special. But it's your money, so do whatever.
I bought this expecting a game similar to Postal and that's exactly what I got, but in the end I'm not sure if I'd recommend it to anyone unless, of course, you also liked the original Postal. It's a dumb, trashy game that happens to have pretty graphics. Despite being a few hours long you'll have seen everything the gameplay has to offer in less than half hour. Get it when it's u$15 or less during a sale if you're really curious about it.

The last remnant is an okay game. It has that AAA quality to it but it lacks a certain 'grab' (aside from the amazing soundtrack). Its very into its own world, there is no 4th wall breaking and it takes itself very seriously. The battle system is deceptively complicated, especially in the more difficult fights. Also it does that thing in which leveling up your characters makes the game harder so you have to LOVE grinding to enjoy it. The main character is a fish out of water go-getter that you don't even have to use in combat if you don't want too (you probably should though as he becomes really powerful). You can recruit Unique Party members to your group who show up in the towns you visit and you can talk with them over the course of the story to unlock more info about them and become more 'synergized'.
There are serveral weird bugs in this game concerning your party members. When they ask if they want to become more magic or attack focused or balanced, NEVER TELL THEM TO BE BALANCED. For some reason it messes up their equipment. Unfortunately, you can't equip weapons to your party members as they handle that themselves as they grow in experience. HOWEVER they will ask you to 'borrow' a weapon if you have it in your inventory. (this happens rarely, and will only do it if its a really great weapon)
The game has a main story but the bulk of the time is spent trudging through the 'side content'. There are missions you can do that pop up in the 'Guilds' you visit to recruit party members.Such missions unlock MORE missions and party members.
Speaking of which, the main story is epic in scope and full of mystery. I still don't know exactly what was going on. There are a lot of layers to the 'drama' so to speak.
TRY THE DEMO if you want to get a good example of the battle system which is the bulk of the playtime spent.

After playing and loving BioShock Infinite I had high hopes for this, the game that is widely held to be the best of the series. Bioshock games are of the sort that when you sit down to play, you dont get back up until its over. The story is so gripping that you are totally immersed in the world during the ten or so hours that you are in it. This spirit is destroyed by the intermittent crashes that will inevitably come throughout your playthrough. I had heard of this problem and decided I would hold off on until the remaster came out. The fact that this wasnt fixed is an absolute disgrace.
With about an hour to go my game crashed for maybe the fourth or fifth time in the playthrough and I went back to find that the past hour of play was lost. This was right at the climax of the story and was a total immersion breaker for me. I was furious. So much so that I uninstalled it and watched the ending online. Whilst there are some fantastic moments, (dont get me wrong, they are FANTASTIC moments), this petty issue will stick out more in my memory. If you are new to BioShock, play Infinite or get this on a console. Avoid this lazy PC port like the plague.

The Fifth Circle of Hell is where the wrathful and sullen are punished for their sins. Transported on a boat by Phlegyas, Dante and Virgil see the wrathful fighting each other on the surface of the river Styx and the sullen gurgling beneath the surface of the water. Again, the punishment reflects the type of the sin committed during lifetime. While passing through, the poets are approached by Filippo Argenti, a prominent Florentine politician who confiscated Dante’s property after his expulsion from Florence.
The Seventh Circle of Hell is divided into three rings. The Outer Ring houses murderers and others who were violent to other people and property. Here, Dante sees Alexander the Great (disputed), Dionysius I of Syracuse, Guy de Montfort and many other notable historical and mythological figures such as the Centaurus, sank into a river of boiling blood and fire. In the Middle Ring, the poet sees suicides who have been turned into trees and bushes which are fed upon by harpies. But he also sees here profligates, chased and torn to pieces by dogs. In the Inner Ring are blasphemers and sodomites, residing in a desert of burning sand and burning rain falling from the sky.

I have only played 5 hours of the game as of this review, but I can already say that it's one of my favorite rogue-like games to come out in quite a while.
Neon Chrome has a slightly slower pace to the combat than most twin-stick rogue-likes that I have played, and that gives it a really unique feeling compared to others.
No dodge button means that using cover is important, and since it's destructable, the game can really make you think on your feet at times. The gunplay feels great, and the progression system is rewarding so far.
The different "classes" are different enough to feel unique, but still balanced enough to where I can't pick a favorite, and none stand out as the "best" at everything.
I'm a big fan of the setting and little bit of story that I have encountered so far. The cyber-punk asthetic is pretty cool, and the fact that the game uses polygons and not pixel art is refreshing (I can't believe I have to say that).
The music is FANTASTIC. It fits the theme perfectly.
After five hours straight of playing the game, my only real complaint is that there is no rumble support if using a controller.
I saw that the game was made by the makers of Crimsonland, a game that I was obsessed with over a decade ago. I took a chance and picked it up based only on that, and I am glad I did. This game hits a lot of sweet spots for me.

I want to reccomend this game.  Really I do.
Class based Dino vs Human,  it's exactly what you think it's like. But a few things get in the way.
BIGGEST ISSUE = Primal Carnage Extinction.    Goggle it,  check it out, it's on Steam as an eary access game. What is it?  This game,  it's quite literally this exact game, avaiable  I'm not telling you to go buy it however,  I don't own it.  But it's the same game.   Unless they release it as a free update (they aren't)  then there's literally no sense in buying this game.   That's just one thing though, and isn't fair to this game as it is, so I'll go a little deeper.
The game is actually a little fun. Humans are, what you tink they'd be.  It's a standard FPS sorta thing with your generic classes  DPS, Sniper, average, alpha, utlity, etc.  What more do you want, these guys weren't straying too far outside the box here.   You're not here to play as people.  If you are,  why are you playing this game?
Shooting dinosaurs has been around since Toruk (yes it's older, don't care)  and you can literally play oodles of any other soot dinosaurs games.   Yes, even freaking Orion Prelude.
Dinosaurs are indeed unique.   You do dinosaur things unless you want to play the T-rex,  because those are hard capped and you're never there early enough to do it.  Why?
BIGGEST ISSUE NUMBER TWO = Low Server population.   -  Again, this isn't a fault of the games design, and the aforementioend PC: Extinction probably has a lot to do with this. But simple enough,  even if you enjoy the gameplay,  there really aren't many matches.  Sometimes only 2 active servers depending which time you play.  1AM - 5AM in America? Forget it.   Suppose that's punishing Australians as well.
Once you have gotten a few matches, and mastered flying the Pteranodon,  it really just shows how little there is.  "Get to the Chopper" game mode is sorta fun for a bit, but that's about it. NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Neon Chrome is a frantic cyberpunk twin-stick shooter from the developers who made Crimsonland.
In Neon Chrome, you play an unknown hacker who, through the use of a neural interface immersion chair, is able to hack into countless cryogenically frozen cybernetic bodies and control them in your battle against the Overseer, the megalomaniacal ruler of a futuristic megacity arcology called Neon Chrome.
Each of your available bodies is one of a small number of roles -- assassin, hacker, psycho, etc. -- each with its own special ability. For example, the hacker bodies have drone followers and can hack into strongboxes and other in-game objects, whereas the assassin bodies have cyberwear that lets them hide in the shadows.
After picking a body (an 'asset') and waking it up, control switches directly to that body, and you enter the lift on your way up the 30 levels to the top of the arcology, where you will do deadly battle with the Overseer.
Graphics - When I first loaded up Neon Chrome I thought, "Oh yes... ." The title screen is fantastic!
Then when I entered the game, at first I thought the graphics looked a bit blurry, but I think I just didn't like the film-grain effect. After turning that off in the settings menu, everything looked much sharper, and more to my liking. Either way, though, the graphics are fantastic.
Everything is just spot on. From the subtle purple neon glow of the pause menu boundaries, to the animated screens that litter the various early levels of the game, to the great explosions and small, but detailed, enemies. It all looks good, moves well, and really sucks you into the story.
Other than the aforementioned film grain, there are also settings for bloom, anti-aliasing, and more, as well as the standard resolution settings. I played on my old gaming laptop (Nvidia 485m graphics card) in full HD with everything except for film grain turned on, and it didn't skip a beat.
I just wish I could zoom in closer to the action on occasion, and zoom out for an overhead or map view.
Sound - As with the graphics, the title screen music grabbed me from the start, and didn't let go even once while I was playing. Throughout everything there's an electronic vibe, but it ranges between a hard and heavy sort of industrial feel with thumping beats, almost to elevator musak in some places. It's very well done, enhancing the atmosphere created by the story and graphics.
Sound effects are good, too, with appropriate bleeps and bloops, great gun and explosion sounds, and occasional grunts and groans when your current asset or one of its many human enemies is hurt.
The overseer's voice in the introductory section seemed overdone to me, for about the first 10 seconds, but it grew on me quickly. Occasional voices while you're playing the game (e.g. when you get a new implant) are very well done, and once again add to the great atmosphere.
Gameplay - As with the graphics and sound, I was blown away by the introduction. I started the game and thought, "WTF is going on!?", but within a few seconds it all started to come together and, then I died. Then the overseer's voice threatened to find me -- the real me -- and this was displayed on the screen:
I was grinning from ear to ear!
The basic game plays like any other twin-stick shooter: WASD (or left controller stick) moves you around, while mouse (or right controller stick) aims your weapon. Neon Chrome gives you two weapons to use at any one time, an infinite-ammo primary weapon, and a secondary weapon that you need to refill with energy that you collect, as well as a simple melee attack, for when enemies get too close.
Rogue-like elements have been perfectly blended with the basic gameplay, leading to procedurally generated levels that are different with each asset you control, random loot of varying rarity and power levels, and random enemies (within reason) on normal levels. There are also a number of 'special levels' randomly spread around with each play through.
And then there are all of the cool enhancements available to you. After each run and before your Unknown Hacker chooses another asset to send to its death, you can spend credits collected from previous runs on stat increases (permanent), or temporary purchases of abilities, cyberwear, and weapons, which will be given to your next asset. As the Unknown Hacker's hideout, the 'home room' really enhances the atmosphere, too.
While playing an asset, he or she can gain various upgrades and weapons, too, as well as temporary effects like penetrating shots or a vampiric field around you that sucks the life out of anything that walks into it and transfers health to you.
The game has a local co-op multiplayer mode as well, which I can only imagine must be amazingly cool, but I haven't had a chance to try it. There's no online multiplayer, unfortunately.
Pros:
+ Fantastic graphics throughout. I still catch my breath when I see that title screen
+ Excellent sound
+ Great atmosphere
+ Lots of explosions; most objects can be destroyed
+ Very replayable
+ Full controller support
+ Achievements and trading cards as well
+ I haven't found a spelling or grammatical error yet
Cons:
- No zoom in for close up of the action or zoom out for overview, or map of the current level
Neon Chrome is one of the most polished indie games I've ever played. It drips cyberpunk atmosphere and continues to impress me over and over again. It is a fantastic game.
I told myself I wasn't going to give half marks, but I think with Neon Chrome I have to: it's not quite a 10, but it's definitely better than a 9!
